It is to your EXCELLENCY (great Prince) that this TREASURY of the languages of the UNIVERSE <note>The author uses "Universe" here to mean the known world</note> must first be presented, since you are today one of those Christian Princes who can grant it a most assured safe-conduct to ensure it is well-received for its utility among the most distant nations of the earth, for whom it was primarily prepared: so that through the various characters (with which it is filled) and the understanding of their scripts, one nation may more easily communicate with another regarding human society, and especially the treasury of the Holy Gospel of our Lord JESUS CHRIST in these final centuries and the end of times. But what nation in the world could one choose today that is more capable of practicing the instructions in the <term>Oriental languages</term> <note>In the 17th century, "Oriental" referred to any languages East of Europe, including Hebrew, Arabic, and Syriac</note> contained in this treasury than the Dutch people? Who, under the fortunate leadership of your Excellence, unfurl their triumphant and victorious banners on sea and land through your valor and good fortune, even to the ends of the earth and the most distant regions. It is therefore by right (my Lord) that this first copy is presented to your Excellence, so that from you it may receive its "passport" of your favor—if you judge it useful to the public—to be not only well-received by the Dutch, but also to be by them trans- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "transported" or "transmitted," continuing onto the next page</note>

The author presents his linguistic "Treasury" as a tool for international communication and the global spread of Christianity, facilitated by Dutch maritime power.</summary>

carried into all nations where the various languages contained therein are in use: and where the characters represented here can serve to express their thoughts in writing, and make known the virtues, magnanimity of heart, and valor of your Excellence, to serve the advancement of the glory of the Almighty, and the worship of the Christian religion in those lands: as also to the happy memory of the author of this book, the late Mr. President <note>The title "President" here refers to a high-ranking judicial official in a regional court (Parlement)</note> **DURET**, of Moulins in Bourbonnois <note>Bourbonnois was a historical province in central France</note>, renowned among the scholars of this time, who to serve the public in the assembly of this Treasury (after several other works brought to light by him) employed his labor until the final days of his life. His life, by the will of God, having been cut short in the middle of his course, he was unable to put the finishing touch to polish it further; but such as it is, he left and recommended it to Madamoyſelle **FLORIMONDE BERGER** his wife, the honor and virtue of her family and worthy of all merit, who having consigned it into my hands to have it printed by my people, with the power to present it to that Prince whose protection I believed would be agreeable, to let it see the light of day under his favor, I have taken the boldness to present and dedicate it to your Excellence. This was in the hope I had that, being a benign Prince and a lover as much of letters as of arms, you would receive with a kind eye this work, diversified not only in characters: but in the most signaled and remarkable histories of the Universe, in the corruption of languages <note>Early modern linguists often used "corruption" to describe how languages naturally evolve and diverge over time from an original source</note>, and their change and progress through the valor of the great Princes and Captains of past centuries, and to testify also to you by this little Treasury the goodwill and the Zeal that I have to be known by your Excellence.

->The most humble and very<-
->affectionate servant,<-
->**PYRAMUS DE CANDOLE**.<-

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues from the dedication to Maurice of Nassau. While the previous page focused on the book's intellectual and spiritual goals, this page serves as the legal "Privilege"—a royal decree granting the publisher exclusive rights to print the work, protecting it from 17th-century piracy.</meta>

* uij <note>This is a signature mark used by early modern printers to keep the pages in the correct order during binding.</note>

**Louis**, by the grace of God King of France and Navarre, to our beloved and loyal counselors, the members of our Courts of Parliaments in Paris, Toulouse, Rouen, Bordeaux, Dijon, Aix, Grenoble, and Brittany; to the Bailiffs, Provosts, Seneschals, or their deputies; and to all our other justices and officers whom it may concern, Greetings.

Our well-beloved **Pyramus de Candole**, merchant bookseller, has represented to us that he recently acquired a book titled **The Treasury of Languages** <note>original: "le Thresor des langues"</note>, composed by the late **Claude Duret**, who in his lifetime was our Counselor and President at the Presidial court of Moulins in Bourbonnois <note>A "Presidial" was a mid-level royal court established to ease the burden on the higher Parlements</note>. Because this book is worthy of being brought to light and shared with the public, he wishes to have it printed. However, he fears that after incurring the heavy expenses required for said printing, other booksellers or printers of this our Kingdom might attempt to do the same. This would deprive him of the reward he expects from his work. Therefore, he has very humbly petitioned us to allow him the sole right to sell and distribute said books in this our kingdom, with a prohibition against all other booksellers or printers from selling or printing them without his acknowledgment and consent, and to grant him our necessary letters for this purpose.

For these reasons, being inclined to the prayer and petition of the said **de Candole**, we have permitted and granted, and by these presents do permit and grant, that after having the aforementioned book printed, he may sell and distribute it throughout this our Kingdom, lands, and territories under our obedience, through such merchant booksellers or printers as he sees fit. No other booksellers or printers shall, for **six full and consecutive years** counting from the day the printing is completed, print, sell, or distribute the said books without the express permission of the said **de Candole**, under penalty of confiscation of all copies found, as well as all costs, damages, and interests, and a fine of five hundred *livres* <note>The "livre" was the currency of France until 1795; 500 livres was a substantial sum, roughly equivalent to a year's wages for a skilled artisan</note>.

We therefore command you, and enjoin each of you in your respective jurisdictions, to ensure that the said **de Candole**, or his widow or heirs, fully and peacefully enjoys the benefits of our present permission, privilege, and grant during the said time, without allowing any hindrance or impediment to the contrary. For such is our good pleasure, notwithstanding any prior edicts, ordinances, mandates, or prohibitions to the contrary.

->Given at Paris the ninth day of May, in the year of grace one thousand six hundred and thirteen,<-
->and of our Reign the third.<-

->By the King in his Council<-

Signed
->**DERDIN**.<-

Checked against the original.

<summary>This page contains the official Royal Privilege granted by King Louis XIII to the publisher Pyramus de Candole, granting him a six-year monopoly on printing Claude Duret's "Treasury of Languages." It establishes legal protections against unauthorized copying and outlines the penalties for copyright infringement in 1613.</summary>

JUST AS the Queen of Sheba, driven by an unheard-of desire for learning and by the distinguished fame of King Solomon, arrived at Jerusalem (the city of perfect beauty and the joy of the whole earth) so that she might attentively hear his incredible wisdom, perfectly understand his admirable knowledge, and intimately gain his singular friendship; and since, in her laborious journey, she endured many hardships and moved through a foreign land. She heard, understood, and won over King Solomon, and she proclaimed those to be happy who always stood in his sight. With great grace of speech, she declared that God uniquely loves the people of Israel and wishes to preserve them, because He placed King Solomon there to deliver judgments and to exercise justice.

So I, with an incredible eagerness for reading and by the exceptional renown of your name (most distinguished President), have desired to set out for the city of Moulins (a faithful city and full of judgment), my most sweet homeland and the most pleasant place of my birth, so that I might gather and perceive the most abundant fruit of your wisdom, knowledge, and friendship in due season. Then indeed, I would call those blessed who enjoy your exceptional presence, and with the remarkable humility of the centurion, I would declare that the Lord (who shall judge the world in justice and the peoples in equity) vehemently loves the people of Moulins and wonderfully guards them, since He has called you (most honored man) to the highest and loftiest office of President. Having been called, He has honored you with the gentleness of Moses, celebrated you with the knowledge of Daniel, and illustrated you with the equity of Samuel, appointed to declare the laws (which are the bonds of the city) and to judge with just judgment. What then? I cannot [praise] your wisdom in—

# APPROBATION.
<note>An "Approbation" was an official statement by a theologian or authority confirming that a book's content was not heretical and was fit for publication.</note>

I, Claude Feydeau, doctor of Theology and Canon law, Theological canon and Grand Penitentiary in the Archiepiscopal Church of Bourges, certify that I have seen and read this *Treasury of Languages* composed by the noble Claude Duret, President at the Presidial seat of Moulins in Bourbonnois. I have found nothing contrary to the Catholic religion; therefore, I have judged it worthy of being printed, as being useful and necessary to show and teach the antiquity, dignity, and variety of languages.

->Done at Bourges this 2nd of June, 1607.<-

->CLAUDE FEYDEAU.<-

If the father of Roman eloquence <note>Cicero</note> calls history the witness of the times, the light of truth, the life of memory, the mistress of life, and the messenger of antiquity: it shall further be permissible for me to name this *Treasury of Languages* (composed by the noble Claude Duret, President at the Presidial Court of Moulins in Bourbonnois) with these same beautiful titles of honor and praise.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' decorated with foliate and scroll motifs.</image-desc>AS FAR as I can judge from my smallest talent of knowledge, that sentence of Saint James seems worthy of being inscribed on the glorious Delphic column <note>The "Delphic column" refers to the monuments at the Oracle of Delphi, traditionally inscribed with wise maxims like "Know Thyself."</note>, in which he pronounces that God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. This very truth is clearly manifest in the arrogant builders of the Tower of Babel, whom God, the all-powerful maker of all things, confounded and threw into disorder; on the other hand, the humble builders of the Tower of David <note>A metaphor for the Church or the Apostles, contrasting the "confusion" of Babel with the "distinction" of tongues at Pentecost.</note> were gathered and restored by God, the Lord of all sciences, through a beautiful distinction of languages. He filled the Apostles with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak in various tongues. And what of it? The "vessel of election," Saint Paul (who carried the glorious name of the Lord before the gentiles, kings, and children of Israel), proposes and extols the different kinds of languages among the most ample and noble gifts of God.

Now, in the most flourishing city of Moulins, my sweetest homeland, I honor you (most distinguished President) with respect, I greet you with a holy kiss, and as much as I am able, I extol you to the heavens. For I understand that you are one who has not merely broken off a single twig (as most do) from the entire garden of all the sciences, but has gathered a harvest such as no one else has. Yet you have delighted your mind with that sweetest flower of the Apostle: "not to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise, but to be wise unto sobriety" <note>A reference to Romans 12:3, "Non plus sapere quam oportet sapere, sed sapere ad sobrietatem," a common Renaissance exhortation toward intellectual humility.</note>. You have so established this that you have never turned even a hair’s breadth from the line of moderation. The traces of this wisdom are not only lightly impressed upon your whole life, but are also expressed for the memory of all following ages in the *History of Languages* given by you to posterity. In this work, you describe, explain, and illustrate the various shapes of letters, the ancient customs of nations, the excellent laws of peoples, the fruitful opinions of the Learned, the useful examples of Magistrates, the necessary counsels of governors, and the notable deeds of Princes. Thus it happens that, acting as an envoy of the public will, I beseech you (most distinguished President) that without any...

# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, LORD CLAUDE DURET, OF THE SENATE OF MOULINS <note>original: "Senatus Molilensis." Referring to the sovereign court or local high administration in the city of Moulins, France.</note>

*To a most deserving President, Claude Feydeau, Doctor of Sacred Theology and Canon Law, and Dean in the Collegiate Church of the Blessed Mary, prays for eternal peace in every place from the God of peace.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' with floral and foliate motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

<margin>2 Thessalonians 3</margin>
<margin>Matthew 25</margin>
<margin>James 4</margin>
<margin>Genesis 11</margin>
<margin>Song of Solomon 4</margin>
As far as I am able to judge from my own smallest talent of knowledge, that sentence of Saint James seems worthy of being inscribed upon the Delphic column <note>The "Delphic column" refers to the ancient practice of inscribing wisdom at the Temple of Apollo in Delphi; here it means the quote is of supreme importance.</note>, wherein he declares that "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." On the contrary, the humble builders of the Tower of David <note>A metaphorical reference to the Church or the spiritual assembly of the faithful.</note> were gathered and restored with a beautiful distinction of languages by God, the Lord of sciences, who filled the Apostles with the Holy Spirit, so that they began to speak in various tongues.

*THIS teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth <note>A reference to Saint Paul the Apostle.</note> (who was caught up into Paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for man to utter, and who proved his commission as an Apostle with signs, wonders, and powers), teaches that we are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as of ourselves: but our sufficiency is from God, who works in us both to will and to do according to his good pleasure.* <margin>1 Samuel 2; Luke 1; 1 Corinthians 14</margin> *Now, having attentively listened to and seriously noted this Apostolic doctrine, contemplating human frailty <note>original: "imbecillité," used here in its older sense of physical or moral weakness rather than mental incapacity.</note> and admiring divine power, let us humbly pray to God—who is the Lord of Knowledge—that he might grant us the knowledge of salvation, so that we may say things that are to his honor and glory, to the edification of the listeners, and to your consolation. We can say as much of all the other Prophets who (as the Jews reproached our Lord) are all dead. Under the Law of Grace—the law of perfect liberty, the holy Gospel (which is the power of God for the salvation of all believers)—among the Apostles, the most notable of them, to whom were given the keys of the Eternal kingdom and the power to bind and loose on earth and in heaven, has undergone the sentence of death along with all the others. Among the deacons, Saint Stephen, ordained a deacon by Divine Wisdom (which disposes all things sweetly) and who was full of faith and power, performing great miracles and signs among the people, is dead. Deborah, Rebecca’s nurse, was seized by death and buried below Bethel; Rachel died on the road that leads to Ephrata; Isaac died in Mamre, the city of Arba; Moses died in the land of Moab; Aaron died on Mount Hor; Jehoiada died in the city of David; Eutychus died in Troas; and many others have died in various places, and their death is precious in the presence of the Lord.

# ON THE ORIGINS OF LANGUAGES
### ACCORDING TO THE OPINION OF PHILOSOPHERS

## CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'L' decorated with floral scrollwork and an urn, set within a square frame.</image-desc>
The divine Plato, wishing to represent the original condition of the human race under the cover of a fable, feigns that at the beginning of the world the gods were alone, before there were any mortal animals. But when the fatal destiny of generation arrived, these gods produced them in the bowels of the earth, and formed them from fire and earth mixed with other things added to these two: and wishing to bring them into the light, they commanded Prometheus and Epimetheus <note>In Greek mythology, these two brothers were Titans. Prometheus means "forethought," while Epimetheus means "afterthought."</note> to distribute to each their strengths and properties. Then Epimetheus prayed to Prometheus to let him make this distribution in his presence: and so he moved forward alone to proceed with it, giving to some strength without speed, and to others speed without strength. He armed some, and for those who were without arms <note>Here meaning natural weapons like claws or horns.</note>, he invented other means of help. Those whom he had enclosed in small bodies, he raised into the air with feathers, or commanded them to crawl on the ground; he equipped those grown in great mass with their very mass: and similarly proceeded with the others, distributing to each their virtues and faculties. After he had thus equipped and supplied them: so that they would not destroy one another, he gave them the means to defend themselves from one another, and to remain in the open, clothing some with thick fur, shells, carapaces, scales, feathers, or hard skins against the inclemency of winter or summer, and from these same things prepared for them litters and natural beds, adding to their feet spurs, claws, nails, and callosities to their heads, horns, teeth, and trunks. Then he distributed their food, making some graze on the herbs of the earth, others eat the fruits and roots of trees, and others—more gluttonous—to devour one another, provided that those who would live by prey should be somewhat sterile, and the others, subject to their gluttony, more fertile: so that the species might endure. For divine providence was very wise in this, having made it so that all animals that are fearful and good to eat are greatly fecund, so that by being frequently eaten, they would not fail; whereas harmful and mischievous beasts produce few offspring. Therefore the hare is very fertile, and alone among all the animals of the hunt, overcharges its preg- <note>The text ends mid-word: "sa portée" (its litter). This entire passage is a summary of the myth found in Plato’s "Protagoras".</note>

...ted, because man, beasts, and birds pursue it to the death. Likewise, the doe-hare of the rabbits is found so full of bunnies, that some are still without fur, others are a bit more formed, and others are emerging from the womb; but the lioness, who is the strongest and boldest of all other beasts, in her life (according to the Egyptians) bears but a single time, and only a single cub. 

Now, Epimetheus <note>Prometheus’s brother, whose name means "afterthought" or "late-wise."</note> being hardly wise, he gave everything to the brute beasts, reserving nothing for man, whom he left alone without strength, without virtue, without property, completely naked, without weapons, without clothing, without shoes, without suitable food, and destitute of all things: so much so that he could not resist the other animals, who were then more excellent than he. For the stags ran more lightly, the lions and bears were stronger, the peacock more beautiful, the fox more subtle, the ant more diligent, the snail better housed; each beast found the proper medicine for its illness and injury, of which man was ignorant. From this arose such confusion that little by little men were perishing by various kinds of cruelties, so that their species would have soon been reduced to nothing without the counsel of the prudent Prometheus. 

He, seeing such a great fault, in order to remedy it, stole from Vulcan and Minerva <note>Vulcan (Hephaestus) was the god of fire and smithing; Minerva (Athena) was the goddess of wisdom and strategic war. Together they represent technical skill and intellectual strategy.</note> technical wisdom <term>artificielle sagesse</term> <note>Original: "l'artificielle sagesse." In this period, "artificial" referred to "artifice" or "craft"—the wisdom of making things by art and skill.</note> along with fire, it not being possible to recover or use it without fire; and thus he distributed it to the human race. By means of this, men began, for their common utility, to assemble for fear of the beasts in order to resist them, giving help to one another and seeking here and there safe places for their habitation. They learned to make houses and clothing to avoid the bitterness of the cold and the force of the heat, to set aside fruits for necessity, to prepare weapons for their defense, and to find other conveniences for life—which finally necessity itself, the inventress of all things, made known in detail to the understandings of mortals. 

To these mortals were given for help their hands, speech, and reason: reason to invent, speech to communicate, and hands to accomplish what they would invent by themselves through reason, or learn from others through speech. For no other animal truly speaks, since speaking proceeds from reason; and no other has hands, though some may have something similar to hands. 

Wherefore man first found through reason the most necessary things, such as food, clothing, and weapons, then those which serve for pleasure, ornament, and magnificence. He imposed names on all things, invented letters of many kinds and diverse manners of writing, and established all the mechanical and liberal arts—proceeding so far as to measure the earth and the sea, and by instruments to reduce the vast mass of the heavens (hardly understood by his mind) and place it before his eyes. 

Furthermore, the same Plato affirms that before men lived in congregation and spoke together, or before they had begun to invent and exercise the arts—inasmuch as they alone among all animals participated in divinity, endowed with an immortal soul because of this divine kinship—they first thought that there were gods, and honored and prayed to them. From this, religion, policy, and the judiciary took their beginning; trade by sea and land was introduced, laws established, magistrates created, trades invented, houses built, villages and towns constructed, and then cities, towns, fortresses, and Empires, Kingdoms, and Republics.

Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note>, a Greek author, in the first book of his *Historical Library*, chapter 1, following the opinion of the most ancient pagan and idolatrous philosophers and historians, has left in writing that men at the beginning of the world had the sound of their voices confused and unintelligible, but that little by little, making distinctions, they named each thing by its own name and title. God, the sayings of wise men, philosophy, and generally all the doctrines and sciences transmitted continuously from hand to hand to those who follow. Some have criticized this invention, such as Thamus, King of Egypt, in Plato’s *Phaedrus*, who replied to Theuth <note>Theuth (or Thoth) is the Egyptian god credited with the invention of writing. King Thamus argued that writing would actually weaken human memory by making people dependent on external symbols.</note> (who was boasting of it) that he had not found a remedy for memory, but rather for reminiscence. For this reason, the Pythagoreans and the Gallic Druids <note>Ancient Celtic priests and scholars who famously forbid the writing down of their sacred teachings, preferring oral tradition.</note> wrote nothing; rather, they passed their mysteries to one another without writing, so that by relying on letters, they would not exercise their memory any less. However, experience—the mistress of all things—has clearly shown their error: for by writing nothing, the memory of their doctrine over the long course of years, through human frailty, has been totally lost, with not a single appearance or ancient mark remaining today.

Since letters are therefore very necessary, after they were invented, those who considered them more closely divided them into vowels, mutes, and liquids, calling **Grammar** the art that could serve to know, discern, and assemble them to create syllables, nouns, verbs, and speech. And although Pliny, relying on the authority of Epigenes, believes the use of letters to be eternal, he is nevertheless contradicted in this by countless ancient authors, as I will explain more fully hereafter. See the great and strange curiosities concerning this matter by **J. Trithemius**, Abbot <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German monk and polymath known for his works on cryptography and hidden knowledge.</note>, in his fifth book of *Polygraphy*; and what **Polydore Vergil** writes on this subject in book 1, chapter 3, of *On the Discovery of Things*.

## *On the origins of languages according to the opinion of Hebrew, Greek & Latin theologians.* CHAPTER II.

Le grand & admirable Prophete Hebrieu Moyse <note>The author uses the name Moses (Moyse).</note> in chapter 11 of his history of Genesis, and Josephus, the Hebrew historian, in book 1, chapter 4, of *Jewish Antiquities*, have clearly demonstrated that the confusion of languages—besides the Hebrew language, the first and most ancient in this universe—was first introduced during the construction and building of the Tower of Babel. This is despite what Philo the Jew <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who used allegorical methods to interpret scripture.</note> seems to want to say otherwise in his treatise *On the Confusion of Tongues*, interpreting the words of the aforementioned Moses in an allegorical manner according to his usual fashion. Alexander Polyhistor and Abydenus, very ancient authors, and the Sibyl have said as much as the aforementioned Moses and Josephus, according to the report of Eusebius of Caesarea, a Greek author, in book 9, chapter 4, of his *Evangelical Preparation*.

This being presupposed, we will learn that according to the true and certain calculation of the Hebrews, this confusion of languages (other than Hebrew) occurred three hundred and forty years after the universal Deluge, as it is detailed in the Hebrew book titled *Seder Olam* <note>original: "Seder Olam" — The "Order of the World," a 2nd-century Hebrew language chronology.</note> composed by Rabbi Abraham son of David <note>Likely referring to Abraham ibn Daud, a 12th-century philosopher and historian.</note>, although Berossus, in book 4 of *Of Times*, writes that it was one hundred and thirty-one years after the said flood. Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish rabbi and scholar.</note>, a Hebrew author, and some other Hebrew Rabbis and the common chronologists among them hold that it was one hundred and one years after the said flood; others say it was 150 years after the said flood. **G. Genebrard** <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine scholar and translator of Josephus.</note>, in book 1 of his *Chronography*, provides proof that it was 340.

The Hebrews say that Noah the Patriarch lived for a long time after this confusion of languages occurred through some of his posterity; the Lord God wished to test him in his patient faith. In reward for this, He allowed him to see the effect of His blessings in the family of Shem, where the Hebrew language remained, along with the doctrine and discipline of the true Church. This is detailed at length by B. Pererius <note>Benedict Pererius (1535–1610) was a prominent Jesuit theologian known for his massive commentary on the book of Genesis.</note> in his commentaries on the 11th chapter of Genesis, following Saint Augustine in book 18, chapter 39 of his *City of God*, and Juan Luis Vives in his commentaries on that chapter. 

Regarding what is deduced above concerning the division of languages that occurred during the building of the Tower of Babel, as Moses reports in chapter 11 of Genesis previously cited, it seems that chapter 10 of the same book of Genesis entirely contradicts it, holding that the children of Japheth divided the islands of the nations, each according to his language and family. Noticing this, Philaster <note>A 4th-century bishop and writer who composed a catalogue of various heresies.</note> in his catalogue of heretics, chapter 106, dared to assert that even before the construction of the Tower of Babel, there were several variations and diversities of languages among the first men of the world. And it matters not to the contrary (he says) that Moses wrote in chapter 2 of the same Genesis that the earth had but one language, seeing as that should be interpreted as "preeminent"—as one says—for a language understood by all the men of the entire earth, even if they spoke other languages. 

But this opinion of Philaster has been entirely rejected by the doctors of the Church, notably by Saint Augustine in the book *On the Miracles of Holy Scripture* <note>original: "de mirabil. fcriptur." This work is now attributed to an anonymous 7th-century author often called Pseudo-Augustine.</note>, chapter 9; Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, in book 2, chapter 7 on Genesis; and Alfonso de Castro in book 9 *Against Heresies*, for many reasons founded upon Holy Scripture. All the Rabbis and Hebrew doctors, as well as Greek and Latin theologians, hold it as a most certain thing that at the time of the Babylonian division and of the languages, the one and only Hebrew language remained in the house of Eber to be, as it were, hereditary to those who would be of that family. This is confirmed by Josephus in book 1, chapter 9 of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, and Saint Chrysostom in his 30th Homily on Genesis. 

And to resolve the aforementioned doubt of Philaster—that before the building of the Tower of Babel the children of Noah divided the islands of the nations, each according to his language and family—we learn that this must be understood through **anticipation** <term>Anticipation: also known as prolepsis, a literary device where a future event is described as if it had already happened to provide context for the reader.</term>; thus, the matter was first described as it was to pass thereafter. This was very well deduced by Ticonius <note>A 4th-century African theologian whose "Seven Rules" for interpreting scripture were highly influential on Saint Augustine.</note> in the understanding of passages of Holy Scripture, which contains several clauses by anticipation, which are afterwards arranged in their proper order and sequence. Saint Augustine strongly praises this in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, and in book 16, chapter 34 of his *City of God*; as do Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), whose literal commentaries on the Bible were a standard reference in the late Middle Ages.</note> in his commentaries on the 10th chapter of Genesis cited above, the author of the *Ordinary Gloss* <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, the standard medieval collection of biblical annotations.</note> on this passage, and Felician Capito in his *Catholic Explanations*, part 1, explanation 7. Along with these, one should see what B. Pererius writes of these divisions of the earth according to peoples and nations in his commentaries on the 15th book of Genesis, and the refutation of this opinion of Philaster in book 16, dispute 9. ## Of the City of Babylon.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' within a rectangular woodcut border featuring floral or foliate motifs.</image-desc>

ABRAHAM Ortelius, in his geographical synonyms and treasury, said the following regarding Babylon:

> Babylon, called *Babylon* <note>original: "Βαβυλὼν"; the Greek spelling.</note> by Ptolemy and others, is the primary city of Assyria and Babylonia. Herodotus in Book 1 and Curtius in Book 5 describe it accurately. Likewise Philostratus in Book 1. Pausanias records it was the greatest of all the cities the sun ever looked upon, but that nothing remains of it except its walls. Dio Prusa <note>Dio Chrysostom.</note>, in his sixth oration, makes it four hundred stadia <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance; 400 stadia is roughly 46 miles.</note> in circumference. To this, Orosius adds eighty more in Book 2, chapter 6. To André Thevet it is *Boughedot*; to Giacomo Castaldo, *Baldach*; to João de Barros, *Bagadad*. Guillaume Postel, in his *Oriental History*, has *Bagdat* and *Bandas*. Laonikos Chalkokondyles calls it *Pogdatim* and elsewhere *Pagdacia*, and George Kedrenos <note>referred to here by his title "Curopalates".</note> calls it *Bagdan*. I believe it is thus variously written and pronounced according to the different idioms of nations. There are those who wish the city called *Susa* by the ancients to be so named today, such as Marcantonio Sabellico and, in his historical compendium, Jean Bodin; but they are in great error, since Susa is the metropolis of Susiana, situated on the river Eulaeus <note>The modern Karun River.</note>, and Babylon, by the testimony of all authors, is placed in Assyria on the Euphrates, where this *Baldach* is also seen today. Otto of Freising writes in Book 7 that the part of ancient Babylonia which is still inhabited is called *Baldach*, as he had learned from peoples across the sea. But if we too may be permitted to guess at a matter so distant and obscure, I would dare to assert that what happened to this Babylon is what occurred to *Augusta Rauricorum* <note>An ancient Roman archaeological site in Switzerland.</note> and others: that just as for this *Augusta* (which has vanished today into an insignificant village, commonly called Augst), we accept the famous and nearby place of Basel, so for that Babylon (which it is certain has completely perished), we allow *Baldach* to be thrust upon us as its nearest neighbor and the noble seat of the Caliph of Babylon. Johannes Zonaras is in a similar error where he interprets the ancient Venetian city of Aquileia...

This lasted until the followers of Ali <note>original: "Haliens"; referring to the Shiite branch of Islam.</note> divided, and because of this schism, there were two sovereign heads called Caliphs—one in Egypt and the other in Babylon—inasmuch as the Persians could not suffer a companion, and the Egyptians and Syrians would not obey anyone else. The Persians and their associates depended on the Babylonian Caliph just as the Syrians did on the one in Egypt. Whoever wishes to see more beautiful research on this matter should read Haython the Armenian’s <note>A 13th-century monk and historian who wrote about the Mongol Empire and the East.</note> *Book of the Tartars*, chapter 11, and Marco Polo the Venetian, book 1, chapter 8, of his *Travels in Persia*.

### Concerning Nimrod. CHAPTER IV.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'L' featuring floral and vine patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc>
The children of the Patriarch Noah having multiplied, as the Prophet Moses describes in the census in chapter 10 of Genesis, they began to spread out and take up various habitations, though not very far from one another so soon after the Flood. Among the other sons of Ham is listed Cush, the father of Nimrod, of whom Moses records that he began to be a *Gibbor* <note>original: "Gibbor"; a Hebrew term for a mighty warrior or giant.</note>, powerful on the earth—that is to say, in Hebrew, robust and strong, otherwise a giant—and that he was a mighty hunter before the Lord. The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh in the land or region of Shinar <note>original: "Sennaar"; the biblical name for Mesopotamia.</note>. The Hebrews, interpreting these words, explain them in two ways. The first is that Nimrod was the first after the Flood who gave some suitable form to public government, and by the consent of many families who had observed his wisdom and valor, he was accepted as governor and master to civilize and arrange many families together. For this reason, he was surnamed "Mighty Hunter before the Lord," because he repressed by main force the wicked who, like wild beasts, ravaged the lives...

### CHAP. V.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap A decorated with intricate floral and scrolling leaf motifs.</image-desc> Abraham Ortelius in his *Synonyms and Geographical Treasury* writes:
The Jews, who are also called Hebrews and Israelites, are a people who once inhabited Judea, or Palestine; but now indeed they wander scattered through the whole circle of the earth, possessing a home of their own nowhere. Everywhere and among every race of men they are hated and subject to tribute. 
<note>original: "Iudæi qui & Hebræi & Israelitæ, gens quæ quondam Iudæam, siue Palæstinam habitauit: nunc verò per totum orbem terrarum diuersa vagatur, nusquam proprium locum possidens. Vbique & apud omne genus hominum odiosa, & tributaria."</note> 
Manetho, cited by Josephus, writes that they were called Hycsos <note>original: *ὑκσὼς*</note>, or *Hycsussos* <note>original: *ὑοκσύσσος*</note>, as Eusebius reads in the 10th book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*. This name, according to the sacred language of the Egyptians and the testimony of Josephus, signifies "king-shepherds," or as the same author says, "captives." Artapanus, cited in the 9th book of the same work, writes that they were called *Hermiuth* <note>original: *ἑρμὶυθ*</note>. Sedulius and Fortunatus call them *Manzeres* <note>A term derived from Hebrew referring to those of mixed or prohibited parentage; "bastards."</note> in the Hebrew tongue, as if calling them mongrels. **A.** <note>Likely a reference to a specific scholarly annotation.</note> Pierre Gilles and Nicolas de Nicolay say they are called *GSifont* by the Turks today. Among Europeans, they still retain their ancient name. For the Germans, Spaniards, Italians, and French call them *Joden*, *Judios*, *Giudei*, and *Juifs*. Palestine <note>original: *παλαιστίνη*</note> is, according to Ptolemy, a region of Asia which in Holy Scripture is called *Pelisthim*, *Canaan*, and the *Land of Promise*. It is called *Phylisthim* <note>original: *φυλιστὶνμ*</note> by the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the 3rd-century BCE Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. Saint Jerome, in his work on Hebrew places, says it should be noted that among historians, Judea belongs to Palestine, while Galilee and Samaria belong to Phoenicia; its inhabitants were the *Canaanites*. Today, all Europeans call it the *Holy Land* <note>original: "Terram sanctam"</note> using various names according to the difference of their languages, but all meaning the same thing. *Palestine I* is mentioned in the imperial decrees, in which sits the city of Caesarea mentioned by Strabo. The *Book of Notices* mentions *Palestine II* and *Palestine Salutaris*, as well as *Palestine III*: see *Arabia Petraea*. *Syrian Palestine*, according to Galen, is where the "Judaic stone" <note>A fossilized sea urchin spine, historically used in medicine to treat bladder stones.</note> is found; this seems to refer to Judea. For Eusebius writes in the 10th book of the *Preparation* that in his time it was called by this name. *Palestine of Petra* is a place mentioned by Agatharchides near Arabia Felix. See *Sittacene* and *Interamna*.

Those who wish to see how the Holy Land, otherwise known as the Land of Promise, was anciently partitioned and divided, should read what was most learnedly written after the ancient authors by Friar Brocard in his description of the Holy Land; Gilbert Génébrard in Book 1 of his *Chronography*, pages 84 and 85; and Benito Arias Montano in his apparatus for the Great Antwerp Bibles, in the treatise *Canaan, or of the Twelve Tribes*, and in the treatise *Caleb, or the Partition of the Land of Promise*. I treat this matter at length in the subsequent chapter.

# History of the Origin of the Region of the Hebrews, Israelites, or Jews.

### CHAP. V.

Abraham Ortelius in his *Synonyms and Geographical Treasury*.
The Jews, who are also called Hebrews and Israelites, are a people who once inhabited Judea, or Palestine; but now indeed they wander dispersed throughout the entire circle of the earth, possessing a home of their own nowhere. Everywhere and among every kind of men, they are treated as odious and subject to tribute. Manetho, according to Josephus, writes that they were called *Hyksos* <note>original: ὑκσὼς or ὑσκούσσος</note> as Eusebius reads in book 10 of *Preparation for the Gospel*. This term, in the sacred language of the Egyptians, according to Josephus, signifies "shepherd kings," or as the same author says, "captives." Artapanus, cited by the same author in book 9 of the *Preparation*, writes that they were called *Hermiuth* <note>original: ἑρμισθ'</note>. Sedulius and Fortunatus call them *Manzeres* <note>A corruption of the Hebrew word *mamzer*, referring to someone of illegitimate birth.</note> in the Hebrew tongue, as if they were bastards. Petrus Gyllius and Nicolay say that they are called *Cifut* <note>original: GSifont; a derogatory Turkish term for Jews</note> by the Turks today. Among Europeans, they still retain their ancient name. For the Germans, Spaniards, Italians, and French call them *Juden*, *Judíos*, *Giudei*, and *Juifs*. Palestine <note>original: παλαιστίνν</note>, according to Ptolemy, is a region of Asia which in the sacred scriptures is called *Pelisthim*, *Canaan*, and the Land of Promise. It is called *Phylistim* <note>original: φυλιστίνμ</note> by the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the 3rd-century BCE Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. Saint Jerome, in his *Hebrew Places*, says it should be noted among historians that Judea belongs to Palestine, but Galilee and Samaria belong to Phoenicia, and the *Canaanites* are its inhabitants. Today, it is named the *Holy Land* by all Europeans using various words according to the difference of languages, but all meaning the same thing. "Palestine I" is mentioned in the official records <note>original: *authenticis*</note>, in which is located the city of Caesarea mentioned by Strabo. "Palestine II" and "Palestine Salutaris" <note>A Roman province encompassing the Negev and Sinai.</note> are mentioned in the *Book of Notices* <note>Likely the *Notitia Dignitatum*, a document of the late Roman Empire's chancery.</note>. There is also a "Palestine III": see *Arabia Petraea*. "Palestine Syria" is used by Galen, where he writes that the "Jewish stone" <note>Lapis judaicus; fossilized sea urchin spines used in ancient medicine.</note> is found; this seems to stand for Judea. For Eusebius, in book 10 of the *Preparation*, writes that in his time it was called thus. "Palestine of Petra" is a place near Arabia Felix according to Agatharchides. See *Sittacene* and *Interamna*.

Those who wish to see how the Holy Land, otherwise the Land of Promise, was anciently partitioned and divided, should read what has been very learnedly written (following the ancient authors) by Brother Brocard in his description of the Holy Land, Gilbert Génébrard in book 1 of his *Chronography* (folios 84 and 85), and Benito Arias Montano in his *Apparatus* of the Great Antwerp Bibles, specifically the treatise "Canaan, or the Twelve Nations," and the treatise "Caleb, or the Partition of the Land of Promise." I treat this matter at length in the subsequent chapter.

<meta>This page transitions from the history of the Hebrews into a philosophical and linguistic exploration of the "Logos" (Word/Reason). It discusses the distinction between man and beast through speech and writing, using the Spanish colonization of the Americas and Jewish mystical traditions (Kabbalah) as primary examples of how knowledge is transmitted.</meta>

->Languages of this Universe.<-

The Greeks, not without a great mystery, include under this single word *logos* <note>original: *λόγος*; a term meaning both "speech" and "reason."</note> that by which man principally differs from animals and brute beasts, with whom he shares on one hand the sensory faculties of the soul, and on the other, the natural faculties shared with trees and plants. Now, this speech, assisted by reason, is within us what the first eternal emanation is within the divinity—namely the Word, or Wisdom, "which came out of the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature" <note>original: *quæ ex ore altissimi prodiuit primogenita ante omne creaturā*; from the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 24:5</note>. Furthermore, this word is twofold: one is animated by the living voice, proceeding from the stomach through the tongue in articulate and distinct words; and the other, namely writing, which performs the office of speech as if mute and silent, separated apart from us, for which the hand is the instrument. Both serve to express the inner conceptions of our soul, upon which depends the principal knot and bond of human society. This society could not be preserved without a well-ordered government <term>police; here referring to "polity" or organized civil administration</term>, nor could such government be established except by means of reason. Although reason is the lady and mistress of all things, without the benefit of speech—which casts it from potentiality into action—it could not produce its effects, but would remain as if uselessly buried within itself in the stomachs of persons.

But again, what would either of these do without the help of writing, their common assistant, which cannot be restricted by any boundaries but extends everywhere? Very little indeed, as can be seen among the savages of the West Indies <note>The Americas</note>, who are so barbarous, uncivilized, and beast-like through being deprived of its use. So much so that when the Spaniards conquered them, they held writing in such admiration and respect—seeing that by its means the Spaniards made their thoughts understood to one another from one place to another, regardless of the distance—as if there were a demon or familiar spirit enclosed within these characters. One could hardly keep them from worshipping the packets and dispatches placed in their hands to carry. This served greatly to keep these barbarians in obedience and subjection, and to dissuade them from all enterprises, conspiracies, and revolts. 

Indeed, as Peter Martyr <note>Pierre Martyr d’Anghiera (1457–1526), an important chronicler of the early Spanish explorations.</note> recounts in his *Decades*, if there was a question of discussing something secret among them, they took great care not to approach a tree that grows in their region called the *Copey* <note>The *Clusia rosea*, or "Autograph Tree," known for thick leaves that can be written upon with a stylus.</note>. Because for lack of paper, the Spaniards were accustomed to write to each other on its leaves with a stylus; these leaves are very large and thick, like those of a Water Lily. 

What is said above is represented to us in some way by the Law given by mouth to the prophet Moses, and the Written Law, which is like a soul to the other, holding the place of the body. For the Law given by mouth—as the Hebrew sages say in their most secret theology <note>Kabbalah</note>—has no foundation or authority except for the Written Law; no more than the moon has any light except what it receives from the Sun. Plato calls this the clarity transmitted and infused from the divinity into our souls to lead and raise them to the knowledge of the intelligible world; that of the moon is the instinct and natural discourse of reason, through which, as it is exercised, we acquire the knowledge of celestial and elementary things in the sensible world. But the Kabbalists, for their part, following this verse of Psalm 19: "Day unto day utters speech, and night unto night reveals knowledge" <note>original: *Dies diei eructat verbum & nox nocti indicat scientiam*</note>, call that light "the day," because...

It follows from this that man has nothing more excellent, nor more exquisite emanating from him,
than speech and writing, as they are the two actions that most closely approach
that which elevates him and makes him differ from the brute beasts. And these two
parts are within him like two beautiful, great winged steeds, or Pegasuses <note>The author uses the plural "pagaſes" to metaphorically describe speech and writing as divine, elevating forces.</note>,
harnessed to a triumphal chariot: not to parade him upon the earth, nor to roll
him across the wide expanse of the sea, as Neptune does his own in
the 13th [book] of the *Iliad*: but rather to raise him through the clouds into the air, to the temple
of immortality. For although deeds take precedence over
words and writings—there being no one who would not rather desire
to be Pompey or Lucullus <note>Roman generals known for their military conquests.</note> than Virgil or Livy, or Achilles such as
Homer celebrated him than the Poet himself—nevertheless, all their fine
feats of arms, all their prowess and victories, would soon have remained
extinguished and swallowed by oblivion without speech, which from hand to
hand, through a certain tradition <term>cabale; here used in the sense of an oral transmission or "tradition" that carries history through time</term>, successively transmits the memory
to endure in perpetuity. But even more so without writing, which performs
this duty far better, beyond comparison, than speech: for as
one of our ancient captains used to say: there is no breastplate so strong,
even if it be proof against all things, that the well-sharpened or steel-tipped pen of a good
author cannot lightly pierce it. This is notorious in the case of the orators
Demades and Hortensius <note>Hortensius was a rival of Cicero; Demades a rival of Demosthenes. Both were famed for their live delivery but left few or no writings.</note>, compared with Demosthenes and Cicero; for
the first two, one Greek and the other Latin, though they were most eloquent and fluent
above all others before and after them, having nevertheless left nothing
in writing, have not had such a lasting vogue of renown among
posterity as the other two: whose memory of their excellent works
can never perish, but through so long a succession of centuries has
shone without being obscured, and does so now more than ever, like two bright
stars throughout every corner of the earth. Thus, the glory that is
procreated and acquired by speaking well may indeed be more prompt and
hasty, and more immediately plausible, being seconded by the vitality
of the voice and the grace of action—which have more force than
mute things, as the orator Aeschines demonstrated to those who read
the two orations of the "Crown" delivered by himself and Demosthenes—
but that of writings is, in compensation, of much longer duration, in imitation
of trees and plants, and of the fortunes of men; indeed, of the condition
of all human things, whose nature it is to pass away
sooner or later according to how they come, so that
letters alone can acquire immortality without deeds: but
deeds without letters, no: following what the Italian
poet says properly of writing,

> It draws man from the grave and preserves him in life. <note>original: "Trahe l'huom del ſepulchro, en' vita il ſerba."</note>

So that it is without doubt that there are many people who would
rather be deprived of the use of speech than of the pleasure of reading and
writing, given the consolation and the renown that can be so much better acquired
from these two than from speaking. However, there are various considerations
in favor of both: the Law itself, which Moses received atop
Mount Sinai from the mouth and own hand of the Creator, consisted
of speech and writing—which writing, as the
Kabbalists <term>Cabaliſtes; scholars of Jewish mysticism who look for hidden meanings in the Hebrew text of the Bible</term> claim, has this advantage over speech: that many secrets of the
divinity are represented in writing which cannot be expressed by mouth:

For there is not a single small point or accent in the **Torah**, or Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, that does not carry some great mystery; and it was written (so they say) expressly all in one sequence, without any separation of words or clauses from the beginning to the end, so that the whole appeared to be only a single word. This was done so that the common people—despite having it before their eyes and knowing it by heart—could not understand its secret significance for fear of it being held in contempt. Instead, it was only for those of the council to whom Moses communicated what was necessary for the exercise of their duties, and according to what their capacity could handle. He reserved for himself the remainder of the sacred secrets, particularly those of the Trinity; for fear of leading the Israelites into idolatry (to which they were quite inclined), as they could not comprehend such a high mystery of a plurality of persons in such a perfect union, he never wished to reveal it to them except in veiled words. However, he did share it with *Aaron* and the seventy of the **Sanhedrin** <term>Sanhedrin; the supreme council or assembly of elders in ancient Israel</term>, and they with their successors in like manner, as I will deduce more particularly hereafter. From this proceeded the name **Kabbalah** <term>Cabale; meaning 'tradition received by hearing,' or oral transmission</term>, which means a tradition received by ear without anything being committed to writing. The *Pythagoreans* and the *Druids* later conformed to this practice, according to *Julius Caesar* in the 6th book of his *Commentaries*.

But these Kabbalistic mysteries proceeded from the written law and did not consist so absolutely in a verbal tradition that the scripture did not comprise the better part of it—both in the form of the characters, their points, accents, order, sequence, and placement, as well as in the transposition, commutation, and coupling of letters. These are what the Hebrews call ***Ethbas*** <gloss>Atbash; a substitution cipher</gloss>, ***Timurah*** <gloss>Temurah; the permutation of letters</gloss>, and ***Ziruph*** <gloss>Tzeruf; the combination of letters</gloss>, as well as ***Notariacon*** <gloss>Notarikon; using letters as shorthand or acronyms</gloss>, the equivalences of numbers, and ***Gematria*** <gloss>Gematria; the calculation of the numerical value of words</gloss>, along with other such devices and observations. Among all authors, a certain Spanish Jew named *Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla* <note>original: "Rabbi Ioſeph Cicatilia"</note> of the city of Salamanca composed extensively on this in three large books titled ***Ginnat Egoz*** <note>Hebrew: גנת אגוז; translated as 'Garden of the Nut'</note>: the first treating of words, the second of letters, and the third of points and accents, as I shall clearly demonstrate hereafter.

Furthermore, just as writing is more spiritual than speech—which partakes more of the body because it falls under the sense of hearing (a coarser and more material sense than that of sight, which governs writing)—so too secret notes or ciphers are more spiritual than common writing. Therefore, they relate to the mystical sense of the law, hidden beneath the "bark" or shell of the literal text. On this subject, the same *Rabbi* mentioned above, in the first book of the *Gates of Light* <note>Gikatilla's famous work *Sha'are Orah*</note>, discusses the difference between these two words: ***Amirah*** <note>Hebrew: אמרה; 'speech' or 'word'</note>, coming from the verb *Amar* (to say or speak), and ***Dibburah*** <note>Hebrew: דברה; from 'Dibbur,' to reason or discourse</note>. He posits that the first denotes the law given by mouth to Moses, which is represented by the divine name **Adonai** <note>Hebrew: אדני; meaning 'Lord'</note>; the other, namely the utterance *Dibburah*—as when one finds in the Hebrew Scripture *Medabber* (meaning "He spoke," referring to God)—signifies the written law, denoted by the sacred, holy **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH: יהוה</note>. Moreover, the written law, being more spiritual and mysterious, is explained by the oral law, which is the temple and tabernacle of the written law—just as *Adonai* is for the ineffable four-letter name. And just as there is no other access to reach that sacred name except under the guidance and direction of the name *Adonai*, which draws all its blessings and effects from it, so too there is no other way...

# Languages of this Universe.

...to introduce oneself into the mysteries of the written law, except through that which was given by mouth. From the above, then, we learn that just as the **tetragrammaton** <term>tetragrammaton; the sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew (YHWH)</term> **Yahweh**, or **Jehovah**—according to how it is most commonly pronounced—is much more sublime than **Adonai**, or Lord; and the written law more so than that which was dictated by mouth, which is but a husk or shell of the other; in a similar way, Writing must also be more excellent than speech. **Aristotle** and his disciples say that speech in man is nothing other than a **flowing stream of reasonings** <note>original Greek: ῥεῦμα λόγων (rheuma logon)</note>, whose source is the **mental discourse** <note>original Greek: διάνοια (dianoia)</note>; and the stream that flows from this fountain is speech, which corresponds with God, the source of reason within us. And just as there is no water in the channel or in the pool created by it that does not proceed from the fountain, so too no word comes out that was not first conceived internally in the soul; of which word, spoken sounds are the signs and marks, just as letters are the marks of words.

On this subject, the Philosopher **Ammonius** <note>Ammonius Hermiae, a Greek philosopher and commentator on Aristotle</note> said that letters do nothing but express and state, and things are only stated; but words and intellectual concepts both express and are expressed. Words are expressed only once, though in two ways: first, when reason flows and distills onto the tongue, then when the tongue strikes the air, the sound passes to the intellect and hearing, and from there the things they represent penetrate through the ear to the understanding where they attach and imprint themselves. On the contrary, the intellectual concepts of things are expressed doubly—namely, by speech and by writing—but they express only a single time, whether by the living voice or by Writing, which is silent of itself. This variety demonstrates to us the nature of our words, insofar as they communicate partly with the spirit and partly with the body, so much so that they prepare for us an intermediary access to bring us closer to God. This is the cause of the virtue found in certain words and characters.

Furthermore, there are ciphers of certain languages forged for pleasure as well as for Writing, such as the jargon of beggars and **Bohemians** <note>A historical term often used for the Romani people</note>, and others like them, of which a thick dictionary was once seen printed in Venice, so ample and complete that there is nothing whatever that cannot be said or written in it, far more distinctly than in **Genevan**, **"true-speaking" Breton**, or in **Basque**, nor perhaps even in **Scottish**. There are, moreover, ciphers that act as intermediaries between speech and writing, insofar as they are silent like writing, yet at the same time act just like speech: attached and joined to the person, who expresses them through gestures of the fingers, expressions and winks of the eyes and lips, so that they are of almost infinite varieties, sharpened by the shorthand and abbreviations of **Cicero**.

For each person forges them according to their fantasy, just as they do with alphabets, shared with those who understand them—some in one way, some in another, more or less artificial and ingenious according to the dexterity of their mind, or as they happen to be instructed by others. In fact, all writing—both the common kind and that which consists of secret notes or ciphers—is hardly anything other than **anagrams**, considering the few letters which, by their various transpositions and assemblies, can express so many diverse and dissimilar meanings unto infinity. These are reduced first into syllables, then syllables into words, and these words into enclosed sentences and complete speech. Wherein excel above all...

...others, the Hebrews, who possess numbers that never deviate from their alphabetical characters, and in which there is always some sense of great mystery and importance. This is because they believe their said characters to be divine and formed by the very hand of God himself (**Exodus 32**), and this even before the creation of the world, as stated by **Rabbi Moses the Egyptian** <note>Also known as Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher.</note> in the 65th chapter of the first book of his *Guide* <note>Original: "directeur," referring to *The Guide for the Perplexed* (*Moreh Nevukhim*).</note>, following the **Talmud** in the book of the *Second Passover* <note>Original: "Pesah seni." This refers to the tractate Pesahim in the Talmud.</note>, second chapter. In these characters, there is nothing frivolous or idle, nor anything without some occult significance in their shapes, assemblies, separations, twists, directions, omissions, additions, greatness, smallness, conformity of likeness, titles, accents, crowns, enclosures, openings, sequences, values, and arrangements. 

And because these Hebrews do not have vowels arranged specifically in alphabetical order, the consonants must perform that duty according to their various positions and accompaniments. There is hardly any sequence of letters in the Hebrew language from which some meaning cannot be drawn, in all the ways they can be reversed or turned about. Furthermore, they are all square and without any connections <term>ligatures; the joining of two letters into a single glyph</term>, such as those found in **Syriac** and **Arabic** scripts. They are very elegant and of a pleasant appearance, intended to show that this language, its writing, and its people have never had anything in common with other peoples and nations; rather, they have always remained apart, like a thing separated from the rest of the generation of men. 

Furthermore, regarding this writing, the Law that God gave to Moses on the two aforementioned tables was written all in one continuous flow, without any separation of syllables or words, and pierced through from one side to the other. Thus, as the Rabbis say, everyone read it differently according to their own imagination: to the right, to the left, from the front, and from the back; from top to bottom and from bottom to top. Moses kept the true, hidden understanding for himself, as God had revealed it to him. The secret of this consisted partly in the form of the characters and partly in the true and proper distinction of the words—something not found in this manner in other languages and scripts, as I shall demonstrate visually hereafter. 

This is why the Hebrews have dared to assert that the considerations of all things depend on the 22 letters of their alphabet, which form the true foundation of everything. For before the creation of the world, these letters were first extracted from the ten **Sephirot** <term>Sephirot; the ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself</term> or divine attributions. These were most simple above all simplities, without any addition of matter, and held until their explanation within the **Belimah** <note>A Hebrew term meaning "nothingness" or "without anything," often used in the *Sefer Yetzirah* to describe the mystical state of the Sephirot.</note>, the taciturnity or silence of the Divinity. 

These letters act like the parts of the body, and their points and accents serve in place of spirit and life. For this reason, one should not find it strange if they are held to be the proper handiwork of the Creator, since they are one of the principal instruments used to celebrate and magnify Him in the aforementioned *Belimah*, or silence; for they are mute in themselves and not talkative. Thus, they have much more emphasis than spoken words, as is well witnessed by that beautiful and excellent gesture used by our Lord in **St. John 8** toward the Scribes and Pharisees, whom he confounds and astonishes more by writing to them I know not...

Among these, there are three elements—as we shall discuss more fully hereafter—twelve associated with the 12 signs of the zodiac, and seven associated with the 7 erratic stars or planets in the celestial world, just as the other three are in the elementary world. These letters are pronounced in two ways: either by a loose and relaxed utterance, or by a striking and sharp one. This remains so until the points serving as vowels are attached to them, which gives them a kind of life and movement. Yet even then, the matter is not brought to its entire perfection until it receives the accents. These serve in the place of operative forms, corresponding to the superior movements and influences. In this manner, the Kabbalists maintain that whoever knows how to duly pronounce the Hebrew language—and preserve their quantities and accents as is required—represents thereby the entire celestial harmony, and the supramundane harmony as well. This cannot happen in other languages and scripts, which are destitute of this mystery. 

This is the reason why, even in our own religion, we still keep some Hebrew words <note>Examples include "Amen," "Hallelujah," and "Hosanna."</note> as having greater virtue and efficacy. Through the letters, then, all the parts of composed things are represented, being like the matter of them; through the points, all the strengths of the forms that vivify them; and through the accents, all the proper operations of matter and form joined together in the constitution of a body, corresponding to their celestial principles and their divine ideas. From these three come the production not only of species, but of the individuals themselves. 

The aforementioned Kabbalists have been so speculative as to think that, through the various assemblies of letters, they might attain knowledge of the number of created things. This could well be calculated, but not spoken, nor hardly even understood, except by Him who knows the count of the stars and gives names to them all—the hairs upon our head and all the rest of the person, the grains of sand on the earth, and the drops of rain that fall from the sky below. It is like a second emanation that issues from our understanding and its conceptions; being silent in itself and able to be understood only by sight—a sense which is the physical medium for all people—it is consequently more spiritual and mental than speech, for which it serves as a representative. In this way, writing participates in thought by being silent just as thought is; and it participates in speech because, being somewhat material, it falls under one of the physical senses, though the most delicate and subtle of them all.

By this means, writing takes the place and performs the office of speech, not only face-to-face and in person, but at whatever long distance there may be—which is a property more of the spirit than of the body. For writing is a certain outward expression of the conceptions of our soul, which go to incorporate themselves into sensible notes, marks, and signs, to manifest themselves peacefully to one another. And this conception of thought is like a symbol of God the Father; the marks and notes are symbols of the incarnate Son; and the meaning contained beneath them is a symbol of the Holy Spirit. Thus, just as writing must hold something of the body and the spirit, which are its two extremes, so also the body and the Deity—two extremes—came together in Christ to create a middle disposition and a mediator between God his father and his brothers by adoption.

To this also corresponds the making of the world. Sovereign, eternal, infinite God—incomprehensible above all form and matter, and holding in this context the place of our internal conception—produced outwardly a kind of writing formed of the heavens and the shining bodies placed there, and of the earth with what is produced upon it, and in the water. All these take the place of letters, as I shall clearly demonstrate hereafter, as does the result which redounds to the glory of the Creator and the meaning contained beneath this beautiful universal cipher. For all things were made mediately for the sake of God, and immediately for the sake of man; that is to say, God created this beautiful temple of nature—namely the world or the universe—for the love of man, and man for the love of Him. "I made all things for you," <note>original Latin: *omnia propter te feci*</note> says the <term>false prophet Muhammad</term><note>A common polemical description of the prophet Muhammad in Early Modern European literature.</note> in his Quran, introducing God speaking thus to man: "and yourself for me" <note>original Latin: *teipsum autem propter me*</note>. On this subject, Cicero in the second book of *The Nature of the Gods* says that in the beginning the world was made for the sake of the gods and of men, together with all the things within it. Regarding this, <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term><note>A legendary Hellenistic figure perceived as the author of the Hermetic Corpus, a series of sacred texts on philosophy and magic.</note> posits that God made two things in his image and resemblance: the world, to praise himself and delight in infinite beautiful masterpieces; and man, in whom he would put all his pleasure and contentment, so that for so many graces and benefits he might be revered, honored, and loved by him above all things. This is the agreement he made with the Patriarch Abraham and the other fathers in the name of all creatures, of which he speaks thus in the 33rd chapter of Jeremiah according to the Hebrew truth: "If my covenant were not [with day and night], I would not have appointed the ordinances of heaven and earth" <note>original Latin: *nisi esset pactum meum, statuta cæli & terræ non posuissem*</note>. Speech is an outward projection of the internal conceptions of our soul, according to Aristotle in the book *On Interpretation*, stating that the duty and purpose of speech is to announce the hidden project of thought and to make evident the intention of the one who speaks. These three senses are:
1. The **literal**, which relates to the elementary world, being more material and coarse.
2. The **allegorical**, relating to the celestial world.
3. The **anagogical**, relating to the intelligible <note>The "intelligible" world refers to the realm of pure thought and divine ideas, beyond the physical or stellar realms.</note>.

Its three aforementioned coverings—bones, flesh, and skin—are the three ciphers reiterated one upon the other, where the meaning is as if drowned and buried. This candlestick denoted the seven planets in the celestial world and the seven lower **Sephirot** <note>original: "Zephirots." In Kabbalah, these are the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note> in the intelligible world, from which flow incessantly into the celestial bodies all the faculties and virtues that they influence from there down to here within the elementary world. 

In the fourth chapter of **Zechariah**, these seven lights are interpreted as the many eyes of the Sovereign, which run incessantly throughout the whole earth in its circuit. The **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> would have transcribed this almost word for word, along with the greater part of its mysteries, which it was able to draw (as the Prophets of the old law did) from the same source of the **Archetype**, where all things are always similar; as they move further from it, they become more diversified and altered. 

These beautiful and sublime speculations, crossing the furthest borders of the universe even to the throne of the essence and glory of God, are the proper pursuit of the Kabbalists and are applied to the **Merkavah** <note>original: "Mercaua." This refers to the **MESSIAH** and his two natures, divine and human; and as for us, to the soul and the body, and to thought and speech or writing—to the apparent sense and the mystical sense hidden secretly beneath. For just as some have treated their philosophy through numbers and proportions; others through geometric figures; others through harmony and musical chords; others under the veils of fables, enigmas, allegories, parables, and similar paths—different from one another in their manner of proceeding and according to the subjects they have taken as a foundation specific to themselves, as **Epicurus** used atoms, **Pythagoras** used numbers, **Plato** used ideas, and **Aristotle** used his <term>entelechy</term> <note>Entelechy: In Aristotelian philosophy, the realization of potential; the soul is often described as the "entelechy" of the body.</note>, all finally arriving at the same goal—in a similar way, the **Kabbalists** manage their own philosophy through the occult writing of ciphers. By which means (not without great mystery, any more than all those other ceremonies), the Catholic Church instituted the beginning of **Lent**, which is the time of penance, always at the new moon; and specifically at that of the last month, **Adar**, which corresponds to our month of February. It is as if this denoted that, just as when the moon (through the deprivation of the Sun's light from our perspective) is reduced to the final point of its shadowy darkness, it then begins to be illuminated again little by little by a new reception of its rays; in the same way, those whose souls have become entirely tarnished and obscured by the filth of a dark sensuality through their foul concupiscences and excesses, when they come to repentance for their misdeeds and recognize themselves in this holy time especially ordained for us for this purpose, they receive little by little (if they do not resist) and from day to day a clarity of divine grace and mercy. 

This continues until finally, through very bitter and poignant contritions of the heart, long macerations of the flesh, a displeasure for one's offenses, devotions, prayers, fasts, and alms, they are entirely illuminated by the divine splendor at **Easter**, where the full moon of the month of **Nisan** always occurs—that is to say, March the first, and the renewal of the year with the spring equinox. At that time, the <term>supramundane sea</term> <note>The "sea beyond the world," referring to the divine source of life and blessing in mystical thought.</note> is completely overflowing and filled to the brim with blessings. ## *Concerning the first and oldest language of the world, and why it was called Hebrew, and how the Hebrews were named Israelites and Jews.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' with floral patterns and scrolling foliage.</image-desc>

The same Moses previously cited says at the beginning of chapter 11 of Genesis that some years after the flood, and at the time when the descendants of Ham departed from the eastern regions and came to dwell in the plain of Shinar, all the earth was of one language and the same speech; that is to say, the Patriarch Noah, his sons, and all the families issued from them, though they did not all live together, all spoke the same language. This was Hebrew, which had been taught and given by the Eternal to our first father Adam in the earthly paradise at the beginning of the world to be for him and his successors unique and proper among all others that might exist in the future in this universe. And the Indians are not to be believed, according to the report of a certain Hebrew Cofras <note>likely a reference to a source cited by Genebrard, possibly referring to a Hebrew chronicler or a corrupted name of a scholar</note> who had read their chronicles—for they have been so wicked as to name the father and teacher of Adam, according to the words of Gilbert Génébrard in Book 1 of his *Chronology* <note>original Latin: "chronog." for Chronographia</note>. And it is credible that Noah, his sons, and all their families did not come from the east to the plain of Shinar; rather, the opinion of those who hold that Noah and Shem with their families did not distance themselves so suddenly is more acceptable. They did not immediately join themselves with those builders who wished to show off <note>The original French "piaffer" suggests a sense of proud, stomping defiance like a horse</note> against the power of God. 

And to show clearly that the first language of the world was Hebrew, which was taught and given by God to our first father Adam at the beginning of this world: we understand that Moses says expressly in chapter 2 of Genesis that the Eternal had brought, at the beginning of the said world, all the beasts of the fields and all the birds of the heavens to Adam, so that he might see what he would call them; and that whatever name Adam gave to every living thing, that was its name. Therefore Adam had placed and imposed names upon all four-footed animals, the birds of the heavens, and all the other beasts of the fields. The wisdom with which Adam was excellently adorned before his revolt and sin meant that he gave suitable names to the creatures who were subjected to him by the command of the Eternal. And although since that revolt and sin, the search for and knowledge of these names of the animals of the earth and birds of the heavens is very difficult, it is not entirely impossible. To provide proof of this, we will say that the Hebrew names of the said animals and fish contain their natural history, even though since the revolt and sin of Adam this knowledge has been greatly obscured. For instance, the stork, so praised for its charity toward its father and mother, is called in Hebrew *Chafida* <note>original Hebrew: "Chasidah" (חסידה), meaning "the pious or kind one," derived from the word for loving-kindness</note>, which is to say gracious, charitable, and endowed with piety.
