Schor and Yashar <note>The author likely refers to the eagle here; while *Schor* usually means 'ox' in Hebrew, the description of looking directly at the sun is a classic medieval attribute of the eagle, often associated with the root *Nashar* or *Nesher*.</note>, of which one signifies to look, and the other to be upright, because among all others this bird has a steady gaze and is always raised toward the sun. Furthermore, one sees the vivid description in the 39th chapter of Job, as also of the ostrich and several other birds in various places of the Holy Hebrew Scripture. The horse, named *Sus*, is esteemed to come from the verb *nasas*, if rather this verb is not derived from it, which signifies to raise oneself: for among all four-footed animals this one is brave and proud, as Job elegantly describes it in chapter 39. The Lion has three names, namely *Ariech*, *Labi*, and *Laysch*. The first comes from another which signifies to tear and rend; the second relates to the word *Leb*, which signifies the heart, and *Laab*, that is to say, to be in solitude. The third word ordinarily signifies a great and furious lion, and has an affinity with the verb *Iosch*, which signifies to trample or knead something, because this animal tramples and mauls its prey. Whales and other great fish of the sea are called *Thannin*, a word which signifies snake, serpent, or dragon: because such fish are long, they turn and fold, and for the rest are no less dangerous at sea than serpents and dragons are on land. In Job, the whale described by him in chapter 40 is named *Leviathan*, which some derive from the verb *Lauah*, which signifies to borrow and take a thing for one’s own use, because this fish seems to play in the sea as in a place it has on loan and where it is comfortable. The crocodile, which lives in the water as on land, is named *Hatsab*, a word which seems to have taken its origin from the word *Tsab*, which signifies the covering of a chariot <note>original: "la couverture d'un chariot," referring to the Hebrew word for a litter or covered wagon, likening the crocodile's scales to a protective covering</note>, because of the length and thickness of the hide of this great animal. As for fish, the Hebrews ordinarily speak of them in general, because they are as if in another world, and removed from the sight and conversation of men, and they distinguish them into three ranks: namely ordinary fish, large fish, and very large fish. This they express by the words *Dagt*, *Thannin*, and *Leviathan*.

The Chaldean Paraphrast <note>The author of the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible</note> has very well explained in his Chaldean version the words of Moses alleged above, with which one can see Josephus in chapter 1 of the *Antiquities of the Jews*. This conforms to the author of the ancient *Zohar* <note>original: "Zoar," the foundational work of Jewish Kabbalah</note>, a Hebrew book, saying that Adam imposed the true and proper names on all things of this universe, composing each of these names by letters that denoted the influences of the stars destined for the ministry and service of the thing they represent. This is even verified by Suidas, a Greek author, speaking of Adam, because of which Pythagoras attributed supreme and sovereign wisdom to the one who first imposed names on all things of this universe. This is a subject which the divine Plato in his *Cratylus* strives to prove by several great reasons to have been done by a power and wonder more than human, with which Aulus Gellius agrees in book 10, chapter 4 of his *Attic Nights*.

The Hebrews constantly maintain that this **Heber** <note>Also known as Eber, the great-grandson of Shem.</note> was in no way mixed with the builders of the **Tower of Babel**, but was far from them. As a sign of the audacity of those builders—of whose dispersion he had certain warning—he named the son born to him at that time **Phaleg** <note>Peleg</note>, which means *division*; for this reason, Moses says in **Genesis 10** that in his time the earth was divided. And so as not to leave anything worthy of remark in this place, we shall report that the Hebrew word <term>עבר</term> <note>original: "Ever"</note> **Heber** means *passing* or *at the passage*, or else, as the Syrians would have it, *wheat*. This name was given to the son of **Shelah** in **Genesis 10** and he was thus called Heber; from him the Israelites were named **Hebrews**, as is contained in the **1st [Book] of Chronicles** <note>original: "paralipomenon," the traditional Catholic name for the Books of Chronicles</note>, and as affirmed by **David Rabbi Kimhi** <note>A significant medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator (c. 1160–1235).</note> in his commentaries on chapter 12 of Genesis, and **Francesco Giorgio of Venice** in accord with the 2nd part of book 8, song 3, and the last part of his *Harmony of the World*. Because of him, the Hebrews and Jews call their language the Hebrew tongue, <term>לשון עבר</term> <note>original: "Lashon Ever"</note> *Lazon Heber*, as confirmed by **St. Augustine** in book 16, chapters 3, 11, and 12, and book 18, chapter 39 of *The City of God*, and **Eusebius** in book 1 of his *Gospel Preparation*. The Hebrews themselves call it otherwise <term>לשון הקודש</term> <note>original: "Lashon Ha-Kodesh"</note>, which is to say, the **Holy Tongue**.

It is true that some Hebrews or Jews maintain, following **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Commonly known as Rashi (1040–1105).</note> on chapter 10 of Genesis, that these Hebrews were so named from the Hebrew preposition *Eber*, which signifies in the Latin language *trans ultra* <note>across and beyond</note>, and in French *oultre & pardela* [beyond and further], and that from this the Patriarch **Abraham**, for having been the first to cross the **Euphrates River** to go to the land of Canaan by the command of God, was first called Hebrew—as if one were to say "the crosser." This is confirmed—following Rabbi David Kimhi on chapter 25 of Exodus—by **Sebastian Münster** in his commentaries on the Hebrew Bible (Genesis 11) and in his *Chaldaic Grammar*; **Father Louis of Portugal** in his *Globe of the Canons and Secrets of the Holy Tongue*, chapter 1; **Gilbert Génébrard** in book 1 of his *Chronography*; and **Benito Arias Montano** in chapter 9 of his *Canaan, or the Book of the Twelve Nations*. For this reason, **Paul, Bishop of Burgos** <note>original: "Bruges," but likely referring to Paul of Burgos (Pablo de Santa María), a Jewish convert who became a bishop in Spain.</note> in Spain, a man very learned in Hebrew letters, was of the opinion along with Rabbi Solomon on Genesis 10 that the Hebrews were so named as if one said "travelers in a strange land," because they traveled as strangers in the lands of Canaan and Egypt.

Whatever the case may be regarding the time of the said **Heber**, son of Shelah—which Heber was, according to the saying of **Rabbi Jose**, a wise prophet for having named his son Peleg (meaning *division* because in his lifetime the languages and regions of the world were to be divided by the power of God)—the confusion of the said languages occurred. However, he always kept his first language of the world as his mother tongue, because he did not consent in any way to the construction of the Tower of Babel, as is confirmed by the *Fasciculus Temporum* <note>A popular 15th-century world history book.</note>. Some of the Hebrews have dared to assert that the Hebrew language has always been kept and preserved pure and entire in the house and family of **Shem** after the Deluge, from whence it has since been always communicated down to the **seventy-two Sanhedrin**—that is to say, the ordinary judges, scribes, or judges of Israel—who had the legal power to make and give judgment, as is contained in the **Talmud** and in **Porchetus** <note>Porchetus Salvago, a 14th-century Genoese monk who wrote against Jewish theology.</note>, part 1, chapter 2 of his *Victory Against the Jews*; and from them, consecutively, to the Jews of today.

# Languages of this World #

**Judah** <note>original: *Iehudah*</note>, a word that signifies in Hebrew: "he who acknowledges God," that is to say, he who confides in God, believes in Him, and follows Him, as **Pierre Galatin** <note>Pietro Galatino (c. 1460–1540), a Franciscan friar and scholar of the Kabbalah who wrote "The Secrets of the Catholic Faith."</note> notes quite well in book 5, chapter 11 of *The Secrets of the Catholic Faith*. Pintus** in his commentaries on the first chapter of Daniel, citing **Josephus** in book 1, chapter 6 of his *Antiquities of the Jews*; **Pliny** in book 5, chapter 14; besides which one may see **F. de Belleforest**, volume 2, book 3, chapter 13 of his *Cosmography*; and **Andre Thevet**, book 6, chapter 6 of his *Cosmography*.

And so as not to omit reporting in this chapter everything we judge worthy of notice: we shall say that the Hebrews have written that **Canaan**, son of **Ham** (of whom mention is made in Genesis 10), was the one who gave his name to the country of **Palestine**, which is a province included within Syria. This province was otherwise called **Judea**, and previously bore in the Hebrew scriptures the name of *Philistine*, then *Canaan*, after this son of Noah, Ham, who repopulated it, according to the opinion of **Josephus** (book 1, chapters 6 and 7 of the *Antiquities*) and the author of the *Seder Olam Rabba* <note>A 2nd-century Hebrew language chronology.</note>, whose race was driven out by the Jews who usurped it by force and violence. Now we must know that the twelve lineages of the children of Jacob included in their portion all the land of Palestine, and indeed in some places stepped over into Syria, and far into Arabia, the whole being comprised under the name of Judea, until the kingdom was first divided under **David**, between him and the children of **Saul**. But soon after, it returned and he enjoyed the whole country of Palestine, as also did his son **Solomon**, who left it to **Rehoboam** his son, under whom the great division was made, there being one king in Israel and another in Judea. At that time, Palestine comprised more than Judea, since the King of Israel possessed the lands subject to ten of the Israelite families. **P. Gilles** and other modern travelers assert that the Jews are currently called **Chifont** <note>derived from the Turkish word *Cıfıt*, a historical term for Jews in the Ottoman Empire</note> by the Turks.

As for **Judea**, named in Hebrew יהודה <note>Yehudah</note>, meaning "praise" and "confession," it has to the west and south the country of Idumaea, and to the east and north Samaria and Galilee, provinces embraced within Palestine. This was the region that the Jews named the **Land of Promise**, and Christians the **Holy Land**, because it was promised by the living God to Abraham and his posterity, and because of the holy and admirable actions and miracles of **Jesus Christ** our Lord, the Holy of Holies. In this region, the Hebrew language remained entire and uncorrupted after the Babylonian confusion until the time of Abraham, when it degenerated into **Syriac** <note>Aramaic</note>, one of its dialects, as **Elias Levita** deduces in his preface to the *Methurgheman*, and after him **G. Genebrard** in book 1 of his *Chronography*. Now this region has for a long time, for the sins of Christians, fallen into the tyranny of the Turks and infidels.

The Hebrews hold that the word **Israel** is derived from these three Hebrew words: ראה <note>Ra’ah</note>, which is "to see"; אל <note>El</note>, "God"; and איש <note>Ish</note>, "Man": so that this word *Israel* signifies "man seeing God." **Saint Jerome** interprets it as "Prince with God."

# On the Kabbalah of the Hebrews or Jews, and of their Kabbalists.
## CHAPTER VII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' with floral patterns and a border.</image-desc>

It has seemed very necessary to me to begin this chapter with the definition of the word *Kabbalah* <note>original: Cabale</note>, which according to the Hebrews, is the name of their science, doctrine, or tradition given by hearing—otherwise called the reception from the mouths of holy persons by hereditary succession. Or rather, it is the acroamatic <note>A term for knowledge shared orally with a select group of students; from the Greek "to hear."</note> science (that of the ear), not set down nor redacted in writing. To speak more properly, it is a symbolic reception or tradition of divine revelation, given or left from hand to hand by succession for the salutary contemplation of God and of the separate forms <note>Likely referring to spiritual or angelic beings existing apart from material bodies.</note>. Those who are illuminated by the celestial and divine Spirit in this are called *Cabalisci*, and their disciples and followers *Cabalæi*, and those who follow and imitate them *Cabalistæ*. This Kabbalah is thus named in the Hebrew language קבלה—*Kabbalah*—from the Hebrew verb קבל—*Kibbel*—meaning to receive <note>original: accipere</note> or to learn. This is asserted by Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai <note>A 2nd-century sage traditionally credited with the authorship of the Zohar.</note> in the *Zohar*, the Hebrew author of the book *hacadua, vau, hé, Iod* <note>Likely a reference to the Tetragrammaton or a specific mystical treatise on the Divine Name.</note>, and the Egyptian Rabbi Moses <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the famous Jewish philosopher and physician.</note> in his expositions on the Pentateuch. It is also cited by Rabbi Ha-Kadosh <note>Meaning "The Holy Rabbi," often used for Judah the Prince.</note> in the book titled *Gates of Light* <note>The "Sha'are Orah" by Joseph Gikatilla.</note>, the author of the book *On Faith and Expiation*, Josephus in book 10, chapter 10 of his *Antiquities of the Jews*, and Eusebius in book 3, chapter 8 of his *Preparation for the Gospel*. It is further mentioned by Justin Martyr in his oration against the Gentiles; Elias Levita <note>A famous Jewish grammarian and scholar (1469–1549).</note>, a Jew, in his *Tishbi* on the word *Kibbel*; Francesco Giorgio of Venice <note>original: G. Venitien</note> in his *Introduction to the Harmony of the World*, book 2, chapter 7; Porchetus <note>Porchetus Salvaticus, a 14th-century Carthusian monk.</note> in book 1, chapter 7 of his *Victory Against the Jews*; Paul Fagius in his commentaries on chapter 26 of Genesis and chapter 11 of Numbers in his Chaldean Bible; and Paolo Riccio, an Israelite who became a Christian, in his book *The Balance of the Just*, in his *Isagoge*, and in his books *On Celestial Agriculture*. Also: Pietro Galatino in book 1, chapters 1, 5, and 6 of his *Secrets of the Catholic Faith*; Sante Pagnini in his Hebrew *Treasury* on the word *Cabal*; Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>A famous Italian Renaissance philosopher who integrated Kabbalah into Christian thought.</note> in his *Apology*; Agostino Giustiniani in his preface to the aforementioned Porchetus and in his scholia on the Psalms; Johannes Reuchlin (also known as Capnion) in his three books *On the Kabbalistic Art*, in his *Ocular Mirror*, and in *The Mirific Word*. Further citations include: Antonius Margaritha's book on Jewish ceremonies; the Spaniard Pablo de Heredia in his book *On the Mysteries of the Jewish Faith*; Giles of Viterbo <note>original: Egidius Viterbiensis</note> in his book *On the Holy Letters*; Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa in his treatise *On the Vanity of Sciences*, chapter 47, concerning the Kabbalah of the Jews; Guillaume Postel in the *Book of Origins*, chapter 17, and book 1 of *The Concord of the World*; Lodovico Ricchieri in book 10, chapter 1 of his *Diverse Lessons*; and Gilbert Génébrard in his discourse on the *Historical Kabbalah* by Rabbi Abraham Levita, son of David <note>Abraham ben David of Posquières, known as Raavad.</note>, which Génébrard translated from Hebrew into Latin. This is a reference to 1 Timothy 1:15, where the author plays on the word "acceptance" (acceptione) as a synonym for "Kabbalah."</note>

The majority of Hebrew authors maintain that this Kabbalah—called by Pliny in Book 30, Chapter 1, by the corrupted word *Jochabela*—was given and taught by the living God to the Prophet Moses on Mount Sinai. Since that time, through the succession of ages and years, it was communicated and left only by word of mouth by the ancient fathers to one another until the latter times of Ezra, as we shall discuss more particularly hereafter. This is why the Hebrew people, speaking to Moses, said:
> "Speak you to us and we shall hear; let not God speak to us, [for] you (they say) we shall hear." <note>original Latin: "loquere tu nobis & audiemus, non loquatur nobis Deus, te (inquiunt) te audiemus." This refers to Exodus 20:19.</note>

Onkelos, the <term>Chaldaic paraphrast</term> <note>A translator who rendered the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic (Chaldaic), often adding explanatory details.</note>, expressed this as *Necabel*, because of which it is written thus in the Hebrew book titled *Pirkei Avot* <note>Ethics of the Fathers, a compilation of ethical teachings from the Mishnaic period.</note>:
> "Moses *Kibel*, that is, Moses heard and received the law from Sinai, from which *Kabbalah* is named, signifying an acceptance through hearing." <note>original Latin/Hebrew: "Moses Kibel, id est Moses audiuit, & accepit legem de Sinaï, vnde Kabala dicitur ab auditu acceptio."</note>

An ancient Hebrew author, commenting on this word <term>Mishnah</term> <note>original Hebrew: משנה. The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions.</note>—meaning study, repetition, or *deuterosis* <note>A Greek term meaning "repetition" or "second tradition."</note>—says these words:
> "Why is it called Mishnah? Because it is second to the law: for the law which all Israelites heard on Mount Sinai is the written law. But Moses our teacher heard the *deuterosis* from the mouth of the Divine Power a second time, and it is the law delivered by word of mouth." <note>original Latin: "cur vocatur Mischna? propterea quod est secunda à lege:lex enim quam omnes Israëlite audierunt in monte Sinaï, est lex scripta. Moses autem præceptor noster deuterofin ex ore diuinæ potentiæ vice secūda audiit,&est lex ore tenus tradita."</note>

Therefore, according to the Hebrews, the law that Moses received at the top of Mount Sinai from the very mouth of God and the very hand of the Creator consisted of both speech and writing. This writing, as the Kabbalists allege, has this advantage over the spoken word: many secrets and mysteries of the divinity are represented in writing that could not be expressed by the mouth. For there is not a single point or accent in the <term>Torah</term> <note>The Law of God.</note> or law of God that does not carry some great and marvelous mystery. According to these Kabbalists, this law was expressly written all in one sequence, without any separation or distinction of words or clauses from its beginning to the end, so much so that the whole appeared to be only a single word, if such a thing could be so long. This was done so that the common people—notwithstanding that everyone had it before their eyes and knew it by heart—could not understand its secret significance or interpretation, for fear of it being despised or treated with contempt. Rather, it was understood only by the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The supreme council or court of the ancient Jewish people.</note>, or those of the council, to whom Moses communicated what was necessary for the exercise of their duties, and according to what their capacity could handle. This is confirmed by Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Better known today as Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> in Book 1, Chapter 70 of his *Guide* <note>The Guide for the Perplexed.</note>, following the traditions of the aforementioned Sanhedrin, saying:
> "The words that I have communicated to you to be kept only in your heart, it is not permitted for you to divulge them by writing. And a little later: one shall not reveal the secret mysteries of the law to a stranger, but only to those of the council, and even then only to those who are wise, discreet, and learned."

This same Rabbi in the place cited above also used these words:
> "This has been observed among us at all times: to set nothing down in writing regarding the secrets of the law, in order to avoid the sects and partiality of opinions that could spring from it if everyone wished to interpret them according to their fantasy. Instead, they are communicated only by mouth, to be kept in the heart and in the mind. And even then, not to all persons indifferently, nor to any others but those of our nation who are at the same time wise and..."

### Languages of this Universe

...word-endings and final letters <note>original: "uoth & ſop Theuoth," likely referring to the Hebrew *Otiyot* (letters) and *Sof Teivot* (the mystical study of word-endings)</note>, and infinite other Hebrew observations deduced hereafter, of which a certain Spanish Jew named Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla <note>original: "Cicatilia"</note> of the city of Salamanca composed three large books titled <term>גנת אגוז</term> <term>Ginnat Egoz</term> <note>Garden of Nuts</note>; the first treating of words, the second of letters, and the third of points and accents. It is in imitation of these aforementioned observations that most of the ciphers of past and future centuries have been and will be invented and constructed. And just as writing is more spiritual than speech—which has more "body" because it falls under the sense of hearing, which is coarser and more material than that of sight, in which writing consists—so too are ciphers more spiritual than common writing. Therefore, they relate to the mystical sense of the law hidden beneath the "bark" of the literal letter. 

On this subject, the <term>Holy Rabbi</term> <note>Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi, the traditional compiler of the Mishnah</note> previously cited in the book of the <term>Gates of Light</term> <note>The *Sha'are Orah*, a fundamental Kabbalistic text by Joseph Gikatilla</note> regarding the difference between these two words: <term>אמירה</term> <term>Emirah</term> (an utterance or word coming from the verb <term>אמר</term> <term>Amar</term>, to say or speak) and <term>דברה</term> <term>Daberah</term> (from <term>דבור</term> <term>Dibur</term>, to reason or discourse). He posits that the first denotes the law given by mouth to Moses, which is represented by the divine name <term>אדני</term> <term>Adonai</term> <note>My Lord</note>. The other—namely the articulation, *Daberah*, as when one finds in the scripture <term>מדבר</term> <term>Medaber</term>, "He spoke," referring to God—signifies the written law denoted by the sacred, holy <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <term>יהוה</term> <note>The four-letter name of God, YHWH, considered too sacred to pronounce</note>. 

Furthermore, this written law, being more spiritual and mysterious, is explained by the law given by mouth, which is the temple and the tabernacle of the written law: just as *Adonai* is the tabernacle of the ineffable Four-Letter Name. And as there is no other access to reach this sacred name except under the guidance and direction of the name *Adonai*, which draws all its blessings and effects from it, so too there is no other way to be introduced into the mysteries of the written law than by that which was given by mouth, called the <term>Cabale</term> <note>Kabbalah</note>. 

Josephus, in book 4, chapter 7 of his *Antiquities of the Jews*, held that Joshua was first taught by Moses in this Kabbalah, which he then taught to the seventy members of the <term>Sanhedrin</term>. These men, in turn, communicated it in order to the Prophets, and the Prophets to the Sages—that is, to the scribes and Pharisees—from whom the Rabbis boast they learned it, as is well noted by the Hebrew author of the book titled <term>Pirke Abot</term> <note>Ethics of the Fathers</note>, chapter 1, in these words: 

"Moses received the law from Sinai, and delivered it to Joshua, and Joshua to the elders, and the elders to the Prophets, and the Prophets delivered it to the men of the Great Synagogue." <note>original Latin: "Moſes accepit legem de Synai, & tradidit eam Iehofchuæ, Ioſchuæ verò ſenioribus, Seniores Prophetis, Prophetæ tradiderunt eam viris ſynagogæ magnæ."</note>

Regarding this passage, the commentator said: "By 'law' here, the Hebrews do not understand the written law, but that spiritual or mystical law, that is, the sense or explanation of the law. For the opinion of the Jews holds that Moses received a twofold law from the Lord on Mount Sinai: one which they call <term>Thorach Bictab</term> <note>Torah She-bi-Khtav</note>, that is, the law which is in writing, or delivered in writing; the other which they name <term>Thorah ſcebealpé</term> <note>Torah She-be-al Peh</note>, that is, the law which is in the mouth, or delivered by mouth. And they affirm that this latter law was derived through Moses to posterity by a successive order, such that Joshua was the first of all to receive it from Moses, who then gave it to the elders, they in turn to the former Prophets, and the former Prophets to the latter, among whom the very last were Zechariah, Haggai, and Malachi. These delivered it to the men of the Great Synagogue, who were namely Ezra and his company, who restored the law to its former splendor. From them, the subsequent wise men received it..." <note>original Latin: "Per legem hic Hebræi non ſcriptam legem, ſed ſpiritualem illam... Tenet enim Iudæorū opinio, Moſem duplicem legem à domino in monte Sinai accepiſſe... vnā quam Thorach Bictab... alteram quam Thorah ſcebealpé... Atque hanc poſtremam ſuccedaneo quodam ordine..."</note>

council what was necessary of the divine law for the exercise of their duties, and according to what their capacity was capable of, he reserved for himself the remainder of the secret facts and mysteries, particularly that of the Trinity, for fear of leading the Hebrews into idolatry, to which they were quite inclined, for being unable to understand this so high and admirable mystery of a plurality of persons in such a perfect union: which was the reason that he never wanted to reveal and demonstrate these things to them except in veiled words: although he did make Aaron and those of the more secret council participants in it. This seems to be confirmed by Gregory Nazianzen in the book *On the State of Bishops* and in book 1 of the *Theology*, Eusebius book 7, chapter 28 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, St. Hilary on Psalm 2, page 193, collection 1, Michael of Medina book 7, chapter 14 *On the Right Faith in God*, Melchior Cano book 3, chapter 3 *On Theological Places*, Julius Rugerius chapter 16 on the *Senses of Holy Scripture*, Oleaster chapter 11 of his works, and Stapleton book 12, controversy 7, chapter 13.

From what has been deduced and discussed above has come and proceeded this name of Kabbalah, as if one were to say a tradition received by hearing, without setting anything down in writing. <note>The word Kabbalah literally means "received" or "tradition."</note> In this, the Razenians taught by Janus, the Semnothei by Samothes, the Saronides by Saron, the Druids by Drys, the old Egyptians by Thoth <note>original: "Thoyt"</note> or Mercury, the Bactrians by Zoroaster, the Thracian by Orpheus, the Indian Brahmans by Abraham, and the Pythagoreans by these same Indians, conformed thereafter; they taught their doctrine by mouth and by tradition from one to another only, without setting it down in any way in writing in the form of the Hebrew Kabbalah: but these Hebrew Kabbalistic mysteries proceeded from the written law, and did not consist so absolutely in a tradition that Scripture did not include the better part of them, as much in the form of the characters, their points, accents, order, sequence, and placement, as in the transposition, computation, and fulfillment of the Hebrew letters: which the aforementioned Hebrews call in their Hebrew language: *Themurah* <note>Transposition of letters to find new meanings</note>, *Ziruph* or *Ziruf* <note>The combination or permutation of letters</note>, *Atbash* or *Ethbas* <note>A substitution cipher where the first letter is replaced by the last, etc.</note>, *Gematria* <note>The calculation of the numerical value of words</note>, *Ghilgul* <note>The cycling or transformation of letters/souls</note>, *Notariacon* <note>A system of shorthand or using letters as acronyms</note>, *Rashe Tevot* <note>original: "Raſce Theuoth," meaning the initials of words</note>.

...oth and the end of the letters <note>original: "uoth & sop Theuoth," likely referring to the *Otiyot* (letters) and *Sof Teivot* (word endings), which are techniques in Kabbalistic letter permutation</note>, and infinite other Hebrew observations detailed hereafter, about which, above all others, a certain Spanish Jew named Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla <note>original: "Rabbi Ioseph Cicatilia"</note> of the city of Salamanca composed three large books titled **Ginnat Egoz** <note>גנת אגוז, meaning "Garden of the Nut"</note>, the first treating of words, the second of letters, and the third of points and accents. It is in imitation of these aforementioned observations that most of the ciphers of past and future centuries are and will be invented and constructed. 

And just as writing is more spiritual than speech—which holds more of the body because it falls under the sense of hearing, which is coarser and more material than that of sight, in which writing consists—so too are ciphers more spiritual than common writing. Therefore, these ciphers relate to the mystical sense of the law hidden beneath the "bark" of the letter. 

To this purpose, Rabbi the Holy <note>original: "Rabbi Hacados," usually referring to Rabbi Judah the Prince, though the text here attributes Gikatilla's work to him</note>, previously cited in the book of the *Gates of Light* <note>Sha'are Orah, a seminal Kabbalistic text</note>, on the difference between these two words: **Emirah** <note>אמירה</note>, a diction or word which comes from the verb **Amar** <note>אמר</note>, to say or speak; and **Daberah** <note>דברה</note>, from **Dibur** <note>דבור</note>, to reason or discourse. He posits that the first denotes the law given by mouth to Moses, which is represented by this divine name **Adonai** <note>אדני, "The Lord"</note>, and the other—namely the pronunciation, *Daberah*, as when one finds in the scripture **Medaber** <note>מדבר</note>, "He spoke," meaning God—signifies the written law denoted by the sacred and holy Tetragrammaton **יהוה** <note>The four-letter name of God, often rendered as Yahweh or Jehovah</note>. 

Furthermore, that this written law, being more spiritual and mysterious, is explained by the law given by mouth, which is the temple and the tabernacle of the written law: just as *Adonai* is for the ineffable Four-Lettered Name. And as there is no other access to reach this sacred name except under the conduct and direction of that of *Adonai*—which draws all its blessings and effects from it—so too is there no other way to enter into the mysteries of the written law than by that which was given by mouth, called **Kabbalah**. 

Josephus, in Book 4, Chapter 7 of his *Antiquities of the Jews*, held that Joshua was first taught by Moses in this Kabbalah, which he then taught to the seventy Sanhedrin <note>The supreme council of sages</note>, who since then, from order to order, communicated it to the Prophets, and the Prophets to the sages—that is, to the scribes and Pharisees—from whom the Rabbis boast of having learned it, as is well noted by the Hebrew author of the book titled *Pirkei Avot* <note>Ethics of the Fathers</note>, Chapter 1, in these words: *“Moses received the law from Sinai, and delivered it to Joshua, and Joshua to the elders, the elders to the Prophets, and the Prophets delivered it to the men of the Great Synagogue.”* <note>original: "Moses accepit legem de Synai, & tradidit eam Iehofchuæ, Iofchuæ verò fenioribus, Seniores Prophetis, Prophetæ tradiderunt eam viris fynagogæ magnæ."</note> 

Upon which passage the commentator has said: *“By 'law' here, the Hebrews do not understand the written law, but that spiritual or mystical law—that is, the sense or explanation of the law. For the opinion of the Jews holds that Moses received a twofold law from the Lord on Mount Sinai: one which they call Torah Biktav, that is, the law which is in writing, or delivered in writing; the other which they call Torah She-be-al Peh, that is, the law which is in the mouth, or delivered by mouth. And they affirm that this latter law was derived through Moses to posterity in a certain successive order, such that Joshua received it from Moses first of all, then the elders, then the former Prophets, and the former Prophets to the latter Prophets—among whom the very last were Zechariah, Haggai, and Malachi—and these delivered it to the men of the Great Synagogue, who were namely Ezra with his company, who restored the law to its former splendor; from them the subsequent sages received it, following in succession...”* <note>original: "Per legem hic Hebræi non scriptam legem, sed spiritualem illam, siue mysticam... ab illis acceperunt subsequentes sapientes, succedē-"</note>

Having heard these words, Adam took from them a full and perfect consolation. From that time, according to the aforementioned Rabbis, the Kabbalah of the Hebrews took its principle and origin. After this occurred, Adam, having revealed this vision and revelation to his wife **Eve**, gave eternal thanks to the great Sovereign God by being the first to sacrifice a bullock or bull on an altar he specifically built for this purpose. Afterward, Adam taught this Kabbalah to his son **Abel**—**Cain** having wanted nothing to do with it due to his wickedness and impiety. After the death of Abel, Adam taught it to his son **Seth**, who left it to his son **Enos**. Then Enos passed it to **Enoch**, whom the Kabbalists maintain was Adam's secretary from the first century. Enoch then showed it to the ancient fathers, who communicated it from hand to hand to their descendants, and they to theirs, until it reached the patriarch **Noah**. Noah afterward taught it to his beloved son **Shem**, whose teacher in this Kabbalah (according to the aforementioned Kabbalists) was the Angel **Jophiel**. From Shem, it passed through successive generations until the Patriarch **Abraham**, whose teacher was the Angel **Zadkiel**, according to the same Kabbalists, in the aforementioned Kabbalah that Raziel had first taught to our first father Adam. Abraham afterward showed it to his son **Isaac**, whose teacher in this Kabbalah was the Angel **Raphael**. Then Isaac taught it to **Jacob**, whose teacher was the Angel **Peliel**. From Jacob, the Kabbalah passed from father to son until reaching **Moses**, whose teacher was the Angel **Metatron**. Then Moses instructed **Joshua** (as was mentioned above), from whom it finally reached the seventy of the **Sanhedrin** <term>Sanhedrin: The supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jewish nation</term> and the great council of Sages, and from them...

And among all the good and excellent books we have today in this Kabbalah, the books of Rabbi Joseph ben Abraham Gikatilla of the city of Salamanca, titled *Ginnat Egoz* <note>original: "Ghinat Egoz," meaning The Nut Garden</note>, carry the most weight, as we have already remarked previously.

As for the division of this Kabbalah, some Kabbalists divide it into only two types: one of *Bereshit* <note>original: "Beresith," meaning Creation or "In the beginning"</note> which deals with natural and sensible things, and the other of the *Merkavah* <note>original: "Mercaua," meaning the Chariot</note>, or divine throne, which concerns intellectual things abstracted from gross matter. The first type is true Physics and natural philosophy, declaring this great workmanship of the world and secret things covered under allegories, and refuting the opinions of other philosophers contrary to the Law of God; the other type is named *Merkavah*, or Throne of God, after the vision of Ezekiel, where the Majesty of God accompanied by His Angels is depicted, which is high and difficult, yet ravishes the intellect in admiration and contemplation of the intelligible world that the Hebrews call the "super-celestial waters," and Physics calls the "lower waters." Solomon in the 22nd chapter of his Proverbs seems to divide it into three parts: <term>words of truth</term> <note>original Hebrew: "אמרי אמת" (Imrei emet)</note>, words of truth written <term>according to the way of truth</term> <note>original Hebrew: "עלי דור האמת" (Al derekh ha-emet)</note> which is the Kabbalah—at least as held by the "Egyptian Rabbi" <note>Maimonides</note> and the "Rabbi of Gerona" <note>Nachmanides</note> in their writings. Some others of the aforementioned Kabbalists divide it into five parts according to the report of Rabbi Hammai in his *Book of Speculation*: namely into rectitude, combination, prayer, judgment, and calculation <note>Likely referring to Gematria or other numerical methods</note>. The great Giovanni Pico della Mirandola seems to adhere to this in his 900 questions or conclusions <note>The OCR says 90, but Pico famously published 900 Theses</note>, saying: "Whatever other Kabbalists may say, in the first division I would distinguish the science of Kabbalah into the science of *Sefirot* and *Shemot*—that is, of numbers and names—as into practical and speculative parts, etc." <note>original Latin: "quicquid dicant cæteri Cabaliſtæ, ego prima diuiſione ſcientiam Cabalæ, in ſcientiam Sephirot & Semoth id eſt numerorum & nominum, tanquam in practicam & ſpeculatiuam distinguerem &c."</note>

# History of the Origin of the...

Rabbi Joseph Bar Abraham of Salem <note>Likely referring to Joseph Gikatilla (1248–c. 1305), a major Spanish Kabbalist; "Salemitain" may refer to his association with Salamanca</note>, and a large portion of the other Kabbalists, follow the opinion of Solomon cited above. They believe that their Kabbalah is not only to be contemplated in three ways, but also fully practiced according to the triple condition of all things: number, figure, and weight. They hold that this entirely allegorical Kabbalah occurs when one thing is understood for another—when one sentence stands for another, one word for another, or one letter for another. 

First, one word is taken for another, either by transposition—which is called <term>Metathesis</term> <note>The rearranging of letters within a word</note>—or by an equal numerical value contained within the words. A letter is taken for a word either at the beginning, at the end, or anywhere it is placed, by adding a mark. A letter is taken for another letter through a "revolution" of the Hebrew alphabet <note>A system of substitution ciphers where letters are swapped according to a specific key</note>, so that every proportion is fulfilled—namely Arithmetic, Geometry, and Music—as the author of the <term>Sefer Yetzirah</term> <note>original: "Sepher Iezirah"; The "Book of Formation," one of the oldest and most fundamental Kabbalistic texts</note> discusses at length. 

Other Kabbalists divide this Kabbalah into the calculation of numbers called <term>גמטריא</term> *Gematria* <note>original: "Geometria"; A method of interpreting Hebrew words by calculating their numerical value</note>, similar to a mutual numerical dimension of terrestrial characters. However, this depends on an "Arithmetic" that cannot be grasped by the senses because of its abstract simplicity; consequently, it is not subject to the crude skills of apprentices and novices. This is why this part is called "Geometry" rather than "Arithmetic," though in truth both serve this Kabbalistic use and art, since letters and syllables are sometimes transformed in such a way that the word itself is transformed, or the verb is simply converted and changed. 

Secondly, a letter is often put for a whole word; this is called <term>Notarikon</term> <note>From the Latin "notarius" (scribe); a system of shorthand using initial or final letters to form new words or phrases</note>, named after the marks or abbreviations used by scribes. In this "Notarikon," each letter is adorned above with certain Hebrew accents or points to show that it is a sign for an entire word. 

Thirdly, this practice and art consists of the mutation and changing of letters; this is when one letter is ingeniously substituted for another, which is called "commutation" <note>This is the method of <term>Temurah</term></note>. For this reason, Rabbi Joseph of Salem titled his books on Kabbalah <term>גינת</term> *Ghinat* <note>original: "Ghinat" (Garden); an acronym for Gematria, Notarikon, and Temurah</note>, meaning "Garden," because of the three letters of this word, each of which denotes a part of the Kabbalistic art: *Gimel* signifies Gematria, *Nun* signifies Notarikon, and *Tav* signifies Temurah. In this way, Gematria (that is, Arithmetic) together with Notarikon and Temurah form the principal parts of the entire Kabbalistic craft, according to the author of the aforementioned *Yetzirah*; Rabbi Joseph Carnitol <note>Another reference to Joseph Gikatilla</note> in his books *The Gates of Justice*; Rabbi Jacob Cohen in his book *Exposition of the Holy Names*; Rabbi Akiva; Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra in the *Book of the Mysteries of the Law*; Rabbi Judah, the first among the Hebrew grammarians, in his works; Marinus in his twenty books of *Literal Instruction*; and Samuel Nagid in his twenty-two books on the same subject. 

Now, among the modern Latin authors who have written on the Kabbalah, Pietro Galatino <note>Pietro Colonna Galatino (1460–1540), an Italian theologian and scholar of Hebrew</note> spoke of it as follows in the first chapter of his first book, *Secrets of Catholic Truth*:

> ,, To refute the perfidy of the Jews through their own Talmudic Scriptures <note>original: "Ad Iudæorum perfidiam per Talmudicas eorum Scripturas conuincendam..."</note>,
> ,, it is necessary above all else to know that there are two kinds of dogmas among them,
> ,, upon which their Synagogue has never ceased to rely, both now and in the past,

Finally, the fourth part, which they call the **Hagiographa** <note>original: "Chetuuim," literally "The Writings"</note>, contains eleven books. The first of these is titled **Chronicles** <note>original: "Dibre haiamim," literally "the words of the days"</note>, which we call by the Greek word **Paralipomenon** <note>meaning "things left out," as the book contains details omitted from the books of Kings</note>. The second is **Tehilloth** or **Tehillim**, or by a linguistic contraction **Tillim**, meaning **Hymns**; although *Tillim* also signifies "heaps" or "mounds," the singular of which is **Tel**. This is not irrelevant to our purpose, since the psalms are like gathered heaps of sacred thoughts. We call this book by the Greek name **Psalter**. The third is **Mishlei Shelomo**, that is, the **Proverbs**—or rather, the **Parables**—of Solomon. The fourth is **Iiob**, which we call by the corrupted name **Job**. The fifth is **Ruth**; the sixth is **Kohelet**, meaning a "gathering" or "sermon," which we call **Ecclesiastes**. The seventh is **Eicha**, meaning "How," which is titled by us the book of **Lamentations** or **Threnes**. The eighth is **Shir HaShirim**, that is, the **Song of Songs**. The ninth is **Esther**; the tenth is **Daniel**; and the eleventh and last is **Ezra**, which they count as one book along with Nehemiah. 

The Jews regard only these twenty-four books which we have listed as sacred and divine. For although they possess the book of **Jesus son of Sirach** <note>also known as Ecclesiasticus</note>, **Judith**, **Tobit**, and the **First Book of Maccabees**, they do not count them among the twenty-four. As for the **Third and Fourth books of Ezra**, I myself have not yet seen them in Hebrew; however, some of them say they have been recently found and located in Constantinople. Furthermore, I have never found the **Second Book of Maccabees** or the book of **Philo the Jew** (which is called the **Wisdom of Solomon**) among the Hebrews, but have only seen them in Greek. Moreover, the **Hymn of the Three Children**, and the histories of **Susanna**, **Bel**, and the **Dragon**—which we have within the book of Daniel—they do not have at all. 

Beyond the aforementioned twenty-four books, it is certain that no scripture existed among the Jews until the time of Ezra. Indeed, the commentaries on the Law themselves, both literal and spiritual or mystical, were spread among the Prophets and the wise men by a sort of oral succession from the time of Moses the lawgiver until the Babylonian exile. However, after the Babylonian captivity, when Ezra himself rewrote the Law (which had been burned during the destruction of the city of Jerusalem and the temple), the other wise men began to write down the explanation of that Law. They did this so that if another destruction of the city should happen in which all the wise men might perish, the explanation of the Law would not perish along with them. This was indeed done, so that all those wise men who lived from the Babylonian exile until the first writing of the **Talmudic volume**—who are also called the **Men of the Great Assembly** <note>original: "viri magnae Synagogae"</note> in the **Pirkei Avot** <note>original: "Pirke Auoth," the Chapters of the Fathers</note>—and who are known to have taught the Law, handed down the exposition of that Law to their listeners both by word and by writing. Their authority among the Jews is so great that their writings, from which the **Talmud** was later compiled, hold the primary place after the Prophets. Nor is this without merit, since their doctrine was handed down to them immediately by the Prophets themselves, whose disciples and successors they were.

The teacher of the law himself handed down the exposition of the law to the High Priest Simon, who is called **Jaddua** <note>original: "Iaddus"</note>. This Jaddua, or Simon, then handed the exposition of the law to **Antigonus of Socho** <note>OCR reads "fichæo"; this refers to Antigonus of Soko, a 3rd-century BCE scholar</note>. Antigonus handed it to **Jose, son of Jochanan** <note>original: "Iosepho Iohannis filio"</note>, and **Jose, son of Joezer**. However, it is clearly shown that they are lying, for from the time of **Hyrcanus I** (during whose reign this Joshua flourished) until the time of **Pilate** (under whom Christ suffered), 110 years passed. These men, Nittai and Joshua, in turn handed the exposition of the law to **Judah, son of Tabbai**, and **Simeon, son of Shetah**. These handed it to **Shemaiah** and **Abtalion**. They, in turn, handed it to **Hillel** and **Shammai**, about whom **Josephus** relates many famous things in his book *Antiquities*. 

Hillel flourished—as it is said at the beginning of the book *Shabbat*—100 years before the destruction of the Second Temple; or, as one reads in *Bava Batra* <note>original: "bana bathra," a tractate of the Talmud</note>, it was 80 years before. He had many disciples, all endowed with excellent wit and learning. Because of their discipline, they were all called his "sons," and they were so outstanding that (as is read in the same place) thirty of them were worthy for the <term>Divine Presence</term> <note>original: "divinitas"; likely referring to the *Shekhinah* or Holy Spirit</note> to descend upon them, just as it had upon **Moses** himself. Thirty others were worthy for the Sun to stand still for them, as it did for **Joshua** <note>the biblical successor to Moses</note>. 

The remaining twenty were called "mediocre," the greatest of whom was **Jonathan**, or Jonathas, son of Uzziel. The smallest of them all was **John, son of Zakkai**, whom the Jews call **Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai**. Yet, as the ancient <term>Talmudists</term> <note>scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Jewish law</note> said, he did not fail to know the Scripture, the Talmud, nor everything else down to the fables of foxes and stories of demons. If this man, who is remembered as the "smallest" of all Hillel’s disciples, turned out to be such a great wise man, what must we think of the others?

Hillel and Shammai handed the exposition of the law to this same John, son of Zakkai, and to **Simeon the Just**, who was Hillel's own son. This order of succession, as deduced thus far, is drawn from the "Chapters of the Fathers" called the **Pirkei Avot** <note>original: "Pirke auoth," a collection of ethical teachings from the Mishnaic period</note>. There, at the very end, is placed Simeon the Just, who took Christ in his arms <note>the author identifies the Simeon from the Gospel of Luke with the Simeon of the rabbinic tradition</note>. 

However, **Rabbi Moses the Egyptian** <note>the famous philosopher and jurist Maimonides</note>, following this order of teaching further, says that this same Simeon the Just had as his student **Gamaliel**, surnamed "the Elder," at whose feet **Paul the Apostle** learned the law. This Gamaliel was thus that teacher of the law most highly respected by the entire Jewish people. After him, his son **Rabban Simeon** (who was later killed by the Emperor Hadrian) was his student. Finally, he had his own son as a student, named **Judah**, whom the Jews—because of the excellence of his learning and integrity—surname **Rabbeinu HaKadosh**, which means "Our Holy Master."

For both place their faith in the traditions of their ancestors, even when no rational explanation is given.

„ But they are distinguished by this arrangement of their roles: the happy and blessed Kabbalist transfers and translates all his study, effort, counsel, labor, diligence, and the entire intention of his mind from the sensible world <note>The physical world perceived by the senses.</note> ultimately to the intellectual world <note>The spiritual or divine realm accessible through the mind.</note>. The Talmudist, however, remains within the sensible world and does not transcend the soul of this universal world. Even if he occasionally proceeds freely toward God and the blessed spirits, he does not approach God Himself as immanent and absolute, but rather as the Architect and Cause of things who is occupied with His creations. He assigns the angels to daily ministries and to executing the effects of the divine will, always referring the contemplation of the highest things back to this lower world.

„ Nevertheless, one of these branches often borrows the insights of the other and draws them toward its own desires. Sometimes the Talmudists and Kabbalists <note>original: "Emmuniero," likely a reference to 'Emunah' (faith) or a specific grouping of believers</note> communicate their studies back and forth between themselves, much like the active and contemplative lives. Although they use one and the same context of Holy Scripture, one usually invites the reader toward servile fear <note>Obedience motivated by fear of punishment.</note> and the other toward filial love <note>Obedience motivated by the love of a child for a parent.</note>, each in his own manner with pleasant persuasion.

„ For it will appear that the Talmudist resides with sharp study over the precepts and mandates of the law—explaining, arranging, directing, venerating, and cherishing them—so that we might rightly define the Talmud as nothing other than the explanation of the law according to the intention of its author. Hence the Talmudists are called "expositors" and "Pharisees" <note>Historically, a Jewish sect known for strict adherence to the written and oral law; here used as a term for legal scholars.</note>, who, from the pulpit and chair of Moses, are always intent upon their work, preaching and exhorting the common people, saying with the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note>: *Serve the Lord in fear* <note>original Latin: "seruite Domino in timore"</note>, and with Joshua: *Fear the Lord and serve Him* <note>original Latin: "timete Dominum & seruite ei"</note>.

„ Indeed, they say: "Do this in this way, and omit that in that way," with such-and-such moderation. From this, they have reduced the 613 precepts, encompassed by the single word **Taryag** <note>original Hebrew: תריג; in Hebrew numerology, these letters add up to 613</note>, into two headings: "Do" and "Do not do," which you are accustomed to calling the affirmative and negative commandments—matters very beneficial to know and highly necessary in practice.

„ The Kabbalists, however, although truth bears witness that they are men who piously observe the law, apply themselves more to contemplation; therefore, they are called "men of speculation" among the masters of the law. Leaving the care of the state and private domestic affairs, the rites and customs of war, and judicial and moral matters—along with their history—to the Talmudists, they reserved for themselves only those things that pertain to the quiet and tranquility of the soul and the love of God.

„ For they say: "The intention of the entire law consists of two things: the good disposition of the soul and the good disposition of the body." For the whole law tends primarily toward the perfection of man, and through it, we attain two perfections: one of the mind and the other of the body. Far more worthy and of a higher pre-eminence is that which aids the soul and perpetuates life, although a suitable physical condition and proper composition of the body is prior in time and nature.

„ Therefore, the Kabbalists are to be held in a higher place and worthier rank, following that exposition of the law which, through certain symbols, most powerfully impels the elevation of the mind to the heavens and to divine matters. This the Greeks call **anagogic** <note>original: "anagogicam"; an interpretation that leads the mind from the literal or historical to the spiritual or celestial</note> instruction, which not only...

**Johannes Reuchlin** (also called Capnio), Book 1 of *On the Art of the Kabbalah*: »If in human affairs, and in the lowlier crafts of the workshop, men receive and believe what they hear from those they consider to be endowed with singular learning beyond others, shall we then think that in the science of the highest and most divine matters—which we can scarcely reach by our own strength, not even one or two of us—the tradition and "reception" of holy men should be despised? This reception is called **Kabbalah** in Hebrew. For Kabbalah is the symbolic reception of divine revelation, handed down for the sake of the life-giving contemplation of God and the separate forms <note>i.e., angels or abstract spiritual essences</note>; those who obtain this through heavenly inspiration are rightly called **Kabbalici**; their disciples we shall call by the name **Kabbalaei**, and those who otherwise strive to imitate them are to be named **Kabbalists**.« Following these words, this figure <note>Reuchlin</note> mentions the revelation made to **Adam** by the **Angel Raziel**, which was the principle and origin of this Kabbalah, as we noted previously in this chapter. From then on, Adam, his children, and his successors were instructed in this Kabbalah one after another by particular angels and celestial intelligences, as stated above; he also subsequently mentions the ancient authors of the said Kabbalah. Who, because of their **Talmudic** <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> disputations, are sometimes called **Thanaim** <note>The Tannaim (from the Hebrew word "to repeat" or "to teach") were the rabbinic sages whose views are recorded in the Mishnah.</note>, or *Dictators*; and because of their meditations on the highest things—rising from individual lower things to the most excellent, received from the ancestors and handed down to posterity, upon which they lean with all their zeal—they are called **Mekablim** in Hebrew. In our age, they are called **Kabbalists** or **Kabbalici** by the Latins, following the lead of **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**, before whom their name was unknown to the Roman language. Philosophy, but also <term>Sophia</term> <note>original Latin: "Sophia ipsa"—the Greek word for Wisdom, often personified in mystical literature</note> itself, which is to say, wisdom. Hence they are rightly called "the wise," as the preacher Solomon says, because they proceed toward where life is; and as far as mortal capacity allows while still dwelling in these small bodies, they ascend from time to eternity and from the lowest things to the highest, and so forth.

And toward the end he says:

With the weight of worldly cares removed, and the sophistries of old wives' arguments held in contempt, the blessed Kabbalist, through **Kabbalah** <note>original: "Cabalam," derived from the Hebrew word for "reception" or "tradition"</note>—that is, the path of what is received and believed—breaks through the darkness and leaps into the splendor. By this, he reaches the light, and so from light he migrates into the Light, and through the Light, as much as human nature can grasp, he understands that luminous Word <note>original: "verbum luminare"</note> under the mode of being, but not of non-being, unless this happens through the abstraction of all things that are not the absolutely first principle. And since frequently by this way, through ineffable joy and alacrity of spirit, the very mind of the Kabbalist—leaving behind humble and earthly things within the secret of deep silence—is transferred to super-celestial and invisible things that transcend all human sense; then, even though still a guest in mortal skin, he nevertheless becomes a companion of the **Angels**. He becomes like a resident of a super-celestial dwelling, whose conversation is known to be in the heavens. Then, at times, he walks toward higher places with them as companions of his ways and visits the souls of the **Messiah**. At other times, however, he descends to the lower powers, both the celestial and the other virtues of nature, under Angelic guidance—yet not without his own reason—and he studies to understand their dignities and operations, and to venerate them with singular honor. From this arises the intimate friendship of the Kabbalist with the Angels, through which, sometimes correctly knowing the **Divine Names**, he accomplishes wondrous things which the common folk call miracles.

As an example, **Rabbi Meir** <note>A famous 2nd-century Jewish sage. The story referenced involves him rescuing his sister-in-law from a state-enforced brothel by using a miraculous phrase.</note>, through the Divine Name (even when spoken by a Gentile), preserved his own wife’s sister from the corruption of a brothel where she was held; though she was forced into prostitution, no lecher, no matter how robust, was able to violate or defile her once the word was spoken. These things are recited in the beginning of the *Gates of Light* <note>original: "Porta Lucis," the Latin title for Joseph Gikatilla's influential 13th-century Kabbalistic text, *Sha'are Orah*</note>, and many other things of this kind are recounted with their authors. Indeed, the operation of miracles was so easy in the memory of the fathers of the Kabbalists that they were often ignominiously called "cunning magicians" by the envious and the profane—as if **Michael** <note>The archangel associated with protection and the people of Israel.</note> had not performed those works, but rather, and most especially, **Samael** <note>In Kabbalah, an important archangel who is often the accuser, seducer, or figure of severity/evil.</note>, namely through Egyptian incantations and certain secrets.

Nevertheless, the rod of the Kabbalists always devours the rods of the tricksters <note>A reference to Exodus 7:12, where Aaron's rod swallows the rods of Pharaoh’s magicians</note>, and any divine thing acts more healthfully than any demonic thing. For the artifice of Kabbalah always tends toward the salvation of men, whereas, on the contrary, the poison of magical vanity always tends toward perdition—the latter through the names of darkness and evil spirits, the former through the names of light and blessed Angels.

In the third book, following:

We feel that Kabbalah is nothing other than—to speak in the Pythagorean manner—**symbolic theology**, in which not only letters and names are signs of things, but even the things themselves are signs. By this, we observe that almost all the philosophy of **Pythagoras** <note>The ancient Greek philosopher who believed that numbers were the ultimate reality; Renaissance scholars often argued he studied under Jewish prophets.</note> originated from the Kabbalists, as he likewise transferred the symbolic method of teaching to the Greeks.

From here arises that enumeration of the **fifty gates of intelligence** <note>original: "quinquaginta portarum intelligentiæ"—a Kabbalistic concept representing fifty levels of understanding of the created world</note> about which the studies of the Kabbalists so greatly labor, which were received divinely by Moses, the servant of God; the knowledge of which he also handed down to us, his descendants, concerning the founding of the universe...

"...explaining the nature of these things, and our masters have already said that fifty gates of **intelligence** <term>Intelligence: In this context, 'Binah,' one of the higher divine emanations in Kabbalah associated with understanding and structure.</term> were produced in the world, and all of these were delivered to **Moses** except for one, because it is said: *You have made him a little lower than the gods:* <note>original: "minuisti paulo minus à diis" — a reference to Psalm 8:5.</note> concerning this discourse of the **Kabbalists**, **Ramban** <note>Rabbi Moses ben Nachman, also known as Nachmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar.</note> said in the *Preface to Genesis* that everything of this kind delivered to Moses through the gates of intelligence is contained in the divine law of the Jews, either in the literal sense or the allegorical, through the utterances, or arithmetic calculations <note>Refers to Gematria, where letters have numerical values.</note>, or the geometric shapes of the letters—whether as written or transformed—or the harmonies resulting from the forms of the characters, their junctions, separations, twists, direction, defects, abundance, smallness, greatness, crowning, closure, opening, and order.

And through that same law, by the divine spirit, **King Solomon**—the wisest of all—attained everything he knew. Of him, it is written in the **Book of Kings** that God gave him wisdom and very much prudence, as vast as the sand on the seashore; and the wisdom of Solomon grew beyond the wisdom of all the people of the East and the Egyptians. He was wiser than all men, and he disputed concerning trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon even to the hyssop that grows out of the wall; and he discoursed of beasts, and birds, and creeping things, and fishes. Beyond this, **Gerundensis** <note>Another name for Ramban/Nachmanides, who was from Gerona.</note> confirms our opinion and concludes thus: he knew all these things through the Law, and found them all within it through his expositions, through grammatical subtleties, through its letters, and through its decorative flourishes <note>original: "calamistrationes" — referring to the 'crowns' or 'tagin' on Hebrew letters.</note>.

However, this happened to him after he had attained the full account of the forty-eight <note>The text says "duodequinquaginta," which literally means "two from fifty," or forty-eight.</note> gates of intelligence, which open the knowledge of all creatures. For all things are universally distributed into five conditions: for they are either elements, or things made of elements, or souls, or celestial bodies, or super-celestial incorporeal beings. Perhaps each of these receives ten considerations, the headings of which are as follows: the most general genera, special genera, general species, the most special species, and individual things—which further consist of matter and form, or things proportional to both, and are uniquely limited by differences, properties, and accidents.

These ten modes—of essences as well as intelligences—multiplied by five, open the **fifty gates**, through which we enter into those inner chambers of the creatures designated by the prominent marks in the works of the six days, and diligently grasped and received by the Kabbalists. Now, by this same device, the enigmatic knot proposed by the **Count of Mirandola** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who integrated Kabbalah into Christian thought.</note> among his 900 conclusions will easily be explained in that same rush-basket <note>An idiom meaning to find a knot in a bulrush—looking for difficulty where there is none, or explaining a riddle.</note>: for he spoke thus: *He who shall know what the number ten is in formal arithmetic, and shall recognize the nature of the first spherical number, shall know the secret of the fifty gates of intelligence, and of the Great Jubilee, and of the thousandth generation, and the kingdom of all ages.*

This same personage continues afterward: We conjecture this to be the meditation on the Law which was finally delivered from the mouth of God to Moses after the Law was given in fire, and after the stone tablets were broken and repaired. For first, as the Kabbalists assert, God wrote His law into a globe of fire, by **dark fire upon white fire**: for **Ramban Gerundensis** says that it appears to us through the Kabbalah that the writing was in dark fire upon the back of white fire. Whence that passage in **Deuteronomy 33** stands out: *From His right hand, a fiery law for them.* And then the letters were (as they say) confused and massed together, which the most studious men, looking upon speculatively and diligently..."

<margin>cc</margin>Those who consider these things, led by the Holy Spirit, could easily select, read, and collect from here and there, up and down, hither and thither, and form a sentence into any words they chose, signifying a good meaning among the good, or an evil one among the evil. But **Moses**, having been taught by God, reduced all these things into the order in which they were to be published to the people, so that everyone might know and observe what pertained to the Law. Thus, the Law was divided into books and placed in the Ark, just as he had received it from the Lord. However, the **art** of ordering and varying the letters, and of most sweetly interpreting the sacred scripture for the elevation of the mind—received then from the Divine Majesty as a most divine thing, imperceptible to the unlearned—he did not reveal to the common people. Instead, he delivered it "mouth to mouth" <note>original: "ore ad os" — referring to oral tradition or "unwritten" law.</note> only to the chosen ones, **Joshua** and the **Seventy**, from whom the most select individuals have always received it thereafter. This reception, as you have heard before, is called **Kabbalah** <term>Kabbalah: From the Hebrew word 'Qabbalah,' meaning 'reception' or 'tradition.'</term>. From these things, it appears even to certain very learned Christians that Moses delivered the text of the Law to the common people, but reserved the mysteries, parables, and symbols for himself and the more excellent men. We have received testimony from **Solomon** that this art of Kabbalah was divided into three ways; he says in Proverbs 22: *Have I not written to you three times in counsel and knowledge, that I might make known to you the certainty of the words of truth?* <note>original: "certe scripsi tibi tripliciter..." — refers to Proverbs 22:20-21.</note> For our people are accustomed to speak thus when mention is to be made of Kabbalah, calling it **Words of Truth** <note>original Hebrew: אמרי אמת (Imrei Emet)</note>, that is, the Words of Truth written **according to the way of truth** <note>original Hebrew: על דרך האמת (Al derekh ha-emet)</note>, which is the Kabbalah. This custom was frequent for the **Egyptian** <note>Refers to Moses Maimonides.</note>, the **Gerundese** <note>Refers to Nachmanides, who was from Gerona.</note>, and others. Others, however, exhibited five parts of Kabbalah, as **Rab Hamai** does in his *Book of Speculation*: rectitude, combination, prayer, sentence, and calculation. Your **Mirandulanus** <note>Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who integrated Kabbalah into Christian thought.</note> wrote in his 90 conclusions <note>Though Pico is famous for his "900 Conclusions," the text specifies 90 here.</note> in these words: "Whatever other Kabbalists say, I would distinguish the science of Kabbalah in its first division into the science of **Sephiroth** <term>Sephiroth: The ten emanations or attributes in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</term> and **Semoth** <term>Semoth: Hebrew for 'Names,' referring here to the divine names of God.</term>, that is, of numbers and names, as if into practical and speculative."

But **Rabbi Joseph Abraham Salemitanus** and by far the greatest part of the Kabbalists follow King Solomon in this: they plainly believe that the art can not only be contemplated but also practiced in a threefold manner, according to the triple condition of all things: **number**, **figure**, and **weight**, for they reduce those five parts into these three. Since the whole business is allegorical, and one thing is understood for another, or through another, so that the meaning itself is transformed, we will say openly that either a word is placed for a word, or a letter for a word, or a letter for a letter. First, a word is taken for a word, either through transposition—which is called **metathesis** <term>Metathesis: The rearrangement of letters in a word to form a new word with a hidden meaning.</term>—or through an equal numerical value contained in the words <note>This is the practice of Gematria.</note>. A letter is placed for a word, either at the beginning or at the end, or anywhere else by a mark placed above it. A letter is placed for a letter through alphabetic revolution, all so that every proportion may finally be completed: Arithmetic, Geometric, and Musical. For example, in that verse of Psalm 21: *Lord, in thy strength the King shall rejoice*, we understand this Kabbalistically as referring to the **Messiah**, saying: "Lord **Tetragrammaton**, in thy strength the Messiah King..." (you may understand "comes" or "acts"). For the Messiah is the power of God, and he acts in the power of the Tetragrammaton <term>Tetragrammaton: The four-letter unspoken name of God (YHWH).</term>. I am led to this by the word **shall rejoice** <note>original Hebrew: ישמח (Yismach)</note>, for if its letters are transposed, it becomes **Messiah** <note>original Hebrew: משיח (Mashiach)</note>. In another place, the Lord said to Moses: *Behold, my Angel shall go before thee* (Exodus 23). Who is that Angel according to the Kabbalists? Some say it is **Michael**, for by transposing the letters of "my angel" <note>original Hebrew: מלאכי (Malakhi)</note>, it becomes Michael. Others, taking him according to the method of the Kabbalistic art, affirm that it is **Metatron** <term>Metatron: A high-ranking angel in celestial hierarchy, often described as the celestial scribe or the "lesser YHWH."</term>, because God said, "for my name is..."

> » ...of King Euergetes, after I came into Egypt, and when I had been there a long time, I found books left behind of no small or contemptible learning. From which words it is clearly gathered that, besides the Law and the Prophets, other books were also written among the Hebrews long before the coming of Christ, since Ptolemy Euergetes himself—the first in whose times this **Joshua** <note>Referring to Jesus son of Sirach, author of Ecclesiasticus.</note> reports having found such books in Egypt—died nearly two hundred and nine years before the birth of Christ.

This same author, in the following chapters 3, 4, 5, and 6, discourses at length on the Hebrew authors from whose writings the Jewish **Talmud** was made and compiled, as I shall repeat in the next chapter; and he says the following concerning the Kabbalah:

> » This name "**Kabbalah**" is found neither among the holy fathers, nor among the doctors of the Church, nor among our masters. Because of this, the name itself is rendered highly suspect. This faculty, which the Hebrews call Kabbalah, was in ancient times forbidden to be handed down to anyone except the most learned and those of advanced age. For this reason, not even a small portion was allowed to be committed to writing; hence, besides those things reported to be handed down by **Rabbi Simeon**, son of Jochai, few or no other things written by the ancients are found. For as it is said in the book *Chagigah* <note>original: "Haghiga"</note>, that is, of the "Solemnity," in the chapter *Ein Dorshin* <note>original: "Endorsin"</note>, that is, "They do not preach," no one was allowed to write anything concerning the Kabbalah, but they handed it down only by mouth. From this, they not inaptly called it <term>Kabbalah: קבלה</term>, which is translated in Latin as "reception." However, the doctors of more recent Jews, lest that paternal dogma vanish, published something of this faculty in writing, though sparingly, and obscured by certain veils he wrote concerning Christ. Wherefore more recent Jews, deceived by the similarity of the name, think this was that person. Therefore, almost all those whom we have mentioned as presiding over the Jewish Academies after Ezra, and others almost innumerable from among their students, left behind many things in writing concerning the explanation of the Law. From these, the Talmud was later fashioned. **Rabbi Moses the Egyptian** <note>Referring to Maimonides.</note>, in the beginning of his *Deuteronomy* <note>The *Mishneh Torah*.</note>, relates that up until **Rabbi Judah**, son of Simeon, who lived 120 years after the burning of the second Temple, no one had committed anything to writing regarding the explanation of the Law; but among the wise men succeeding one another, it was revealed only by word of mouth. It is true that Rabbi Moses the Egyptian asserts this, which we must think he did for two main reasons. Firstly, so that to the Messiah...

**Elias Levita**, a Jew by nation, in his *Tishbi* <note>original: "Thesbite" — a famous Hebrew dictionary of the 16th century</note>, in the interpretation of this Hebrew word *Kibbel* <note>to receive</note>, used these words:

It is divided, however, into two parts, namely the speculative and the practical. And I indeed am not worthy to explain its business, for because of my sins I have not learned this wisdom, and the knowledge of these holy ones I have not known, nor do I understand it."

**Lodovico Celio Rodigino** <note>original: "Lodouicus Cœlius Rhodiginus"</note> in book 10, chapter 1 of his *Ancient Lessons* <note>original: "de ſes antiques leçons"</note>:

The Talmudic heresy is observed to take its beginnings not very long ago, as it is found to have been cobbled together by the Hebrews against us a little less than two hundred years after Christ. Those who truly set out to explain the secrets of the Bible by philosophical reasons—the Egyptian **Moses** <note>Moses Maimonides</note> being the chief among them—do not precede the times of **Averroes**, from whose death more or less 330 years have passed. The third remains: the **Kabbalah**, the oldest of all and especially true. For the constant opinion is that it was suggested to Moses by the Best and Greatest God, and shortly after Moses himself laid it open to the most fit men. ...[Moses] had written by command, and imparted it to the people; but the other part he did not share at all, except to communicate it only to seventy wise men in number, by whom it was later handed down to others likewise destined for it, by voice alone. From this the name **Kabbalah** <note>original: "Cabalæ"</note> arose, which in the language of that nation signifies "Reception" <note>original: "Receptionem"</note>, because through successive generations, it was preserved unharmed without any written records at all. In the following age, however, even these mysteries were captured in books, in which almost everything is found to be not inconsistent with our faith: since they are said to have been composed before Christ, by minds free from all prejudice. And because the science of Kabbalah was held among the secrets in ancient times, it became customary among the Hebrews that whatever is less common and more passive is sanctioned by the name of Kabbalah. 

In general, however, they are observed to have honored two sciences with that name: the art of combining, which they call the **alphabetical revolution** <term>alphabetariam reuolutionem: a method of rearranging letters of the Hebrew alphabet to find hidden meanings</term>; and the other, by which the powers of higher things are explained, which is also called **Magic**. But the whole matter was soon disturbed among the Hebrews by the emergence of several individuals, not at all different from sorcerers, who claim the name of Kabbalists for themselves especially, and preach that they primarily hold the secret names of God, and possess powers by which they have authority over demons and are able to perform miracles. Indeed, they even claim that Christ performed such admirable things often by no other method than that which they use. They further assert that this is the true and twin Kabbalah, which is said to have been handed down by God to Moses. 

Indeed, many things seem to support the idea that the highest God revealed mysteries to that great Prophet which were contained in the Law: but especially that prophetic word of **Ezra** <note>original: "Esdræ"</note>, where the Lord, speaking about Moses, says: "I told him many wonders, and showed him the secrets of the times, and the end: I commanded him to make some things public, and to keep others with him in secret." Furthermore, the great **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian</note> explaining that word of the Apostle Paul—"first indeed because the oracles of God were entrusted to them"—says it must be considered why he did not say the letters were entrusted, but the **Oracles** <note>original: "Eloquia"</note> of God. From this it may be perceived that something else besides the law contained in letters was granted to the Jews, which Paul calls the oracles of God: which you would say is nothing else than the Kabbalah itself, that is, the truest interpretations of the law, emanating from the divine mouth. Moreover, the 70 elders to whom the secrets alone were communicated, Origen calls "wonderful counselors," whose place the **Cardinals** are thought to hold in our religion.
