Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who integrated Kabbalah into Christian thought</note>, the Count, asserts in the fifth question of his *Apology* that in these last seventy books is contained that entire more secret exposition of the divine law which is called by the Jews **Kabbalah** <note>original: "קבלה Cabalah"</note>, which is to say "Reception." For Kabbalah is a more secret exposition of the divine law received from the mouth of God by Moses, and received from the mouth of Moses by the fathers through continuous successions—not indeed in writing, but by the living voice. It bears a resemblance to that exposition which we call **anagogical** <term>anagogical: an interpretation that leads the mind beyond literal meaning to spiritual or heavenly realities</term>, which is for that reason more sublime than the others, because it leads us upward from earthly things to the celestial, from things of the senses to things of the intellect, from the temporal to the eternal, from the corporeal to the spiritual, and from the human to the divine. The same Pico reports the origin and occasion of these seventy volumes, according to the opinion of Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>original: "Rabbi Mosis Ægyptij"; this refers to Maimonides</note>, fully in these words:

<margin>cc</margin>

He likewise commanded them not to betray it in writing, but to reveal it to their successors by the living voice, and they in turn were to open it to their posterity, always preserving that same order in perpetuity. Furthermore, because God...*

## Languages of this Universe. 71

...that [this tradition was received] not through letters, but by a certain succession and hereditary right, one person from another. Just as in the Church of Christ, certain unwritten <note>original: "ἄγραφα"</note> traditions are believed to have been transmitted to us as if through the hands <note>original: "quasi per manus"</note> from the Apostles until now. For the Kabbalah <term>Kabbalah: From the Hebrew root 'to receive'; refers to the Jewish mystical tradition originally passed down orally</term> was nothing other than a teaching handed down by the living voice <note>original: "viva voce"</note>, containing the most certain interpretation of the written divine law. It is read that Ezra, on the advice of seventy most learned men, committed this to books so that the secrets of celestial doctrine would not perish if the custom of oral transmission established by the ancestors could not be observed due to wars and captivities. Justin Martyr, in his *Oration Against the Nations*, asserts that the Jews preserved these books so diligently in their synagogues not without the singular providence of God: lest Christians, when presenting them, should be seen as counterfeiters or provide the slanderous with a pretext for tampering <note>original: "προφάσει ῥαδιουργίας"</note>. Hence, they are called the "porters" or "scroll-keepers" <note>original: "baiuli sive scriniarii"</note> of the Christians by the blessed Augustine. (See 4 Kings 2; Josephus book 10, chapter 10; Eusebius book 3, chapter 8).

Elias Levita <note>A prominent 16th-century Hebrew grammarian</note> in his preface to the third *Masoreth Hammashoreth*, following Rabbi Moses <note>Referring to Maimonides, the Great Jewish philosopher</note> in his preface to the *Sepher Mizuoth* <note>The Book of Commandments</note>, and on the Talmud in the *Treatise on Vows*: The Great Synagogue succeeded the Prophets, whose leaders were Ezra, Nehemiah, Mordecai, Zerubbabel, and Joshua. These presided over the council which 120 men—some noble, others commoners—entered into for the purpose of emending the sacred books and establishing their canon according to the prescription of the Kabbalah. There they also decreed that Joshua had been so taught by Moses, the Elders by Joshua, and the Prophets by the Elders. The notary or scribe of the Council (for so he is called in Ezra 7) was Ezra, whom they also record was joined or rather led by Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, Mishael, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. Michael Neander <note>A German scholar and teacher</note>, in his treatise on the Kabbalah of the Jews, seems to confirm the above, as curious readers may see; also Guillaume Postel <note>A French Renaissance polymath and orientalist</note> in Book 1, chapter 3, of *The Concord of the World*. The Hebrews had, besides the sacred scripture, their own interpreters of two kinds. For from Moses himself until Christ there were men of remarkable innocence whom they called by the Greek word Sanhedrin <note>original: "συνέδριον" / "סנהדרין"</note>—you might call them "assessors"—because they would meet in one senate or court when dealing with the highest matters, and would pass judgment on things which took the place of law and judicial decree. These spoke with "two tongues" (as it were), since they relied on the authority of sacred scripture.

For among them and the Prophets there was a certain common revelation of mysteries, which they judged a sin to commit to writing. Therefore, they explained it only by word of mouth to their successors—those called to that duty according to the merits of their lives. For that reason they called it Kabbalah <note>original: "קבלה" / "Gahalah"</note>, because it was received from one to another. It certainly contained the greatest mysteries and was very similar to our own anagogical <term>Anagogical: A method of spiritual interpretation that leads the mind toward heavenly or mystical meanings</term> sense, by which we lead minds from corruptible things to celestial ones. The other "tongue" was the interpretation common to all the learned, representing an allegory which used to be committed to writing and preserved. Thus, the anagogical ones were called Kabbalists; much later, the allegorical ones were called Talmudists. However, when Jesus Christ came in the times of Simeon—whom not only the Gospel but also they [the Jews] call the Just and Holy—then the teacher and lawgiver failed from Israel. And a foreign king gained power. Then also the Holy Spirit departed from them, nor was there any prophecy or tradition of doctrine among the Jews thereafter. Then the wise men and the remnants of the Jews collected what they could from both interpretations into one body, so it would not perish, and first called it in Hebrew...

# History of the Origin of the

### Languages of this Universe. 72

*Mishneh Torah* <term>Mishneh Torah: Hebrew for "repetition of the law"; here referring to the oral tradition that would become the basis for the Mishnah</term>, that is, the secondary law; finally, as other opinions were added as time produced those authors who were found, they wrote the first Talmud from the Mishnah. Having gathered the Jews from everywhere to Jerusalem, they called it the Jerusalem Talmud, approximately 300 years after the passion of Christ. Thereafter, as other [opinions] arose, they composed another Talmud about 70 years later, having gathered the Jews in Babylon, whose doctors they had summoned from the whole world; they use that Talmud now. Many Kabbalistic traditions abound in it, but nevertheless, they are scattered separately in many volumes.

Gilbert Génébrard <note>A 16th-century French Benedictine scholar and Hebraist</note>, in Book 1 of his *Chronography*, speaking of the first age of the world and of the Kabbalah and the unwritten traditions through Adam and his children and descendants living during this age, said: 

> “In this first age, the foundations of the pure and salvific religion transmitted to us—and which will last until the end of the age—were laid and flourished. The faithful were called the ‘sons of God’ (Genesis 6). They were ruled by revelations (Genesis 2, 3, 4, 6, 7) and by the traditions of Adam; for traditions are older than the scriptures. Then they were ruled by the prophecies of Enos and Enoch: for it is not probable that Adam would have begrudged his sons and descendants the traditions necessary for salvation, since this would be unworthy of any parent. This is especially true concerning God, His word, and His Spirit, whom Adam had seen and spoken with (Genesis 2) regarding the creation of the world, of which he had been the most noble part—so much so that, by God's command, he imposed names upon things according to their individual natures (Genesis 2). [He taught] of the divine inspiration of the soul and its production in the image and likeness of God, which he himself had experienced (Genesis 1); of the dignity of man and his dominion over the rest, which he himself had received (Genesis 1). Of the state of innocence from which he had fallen; of the fall and the sin he had committed as the source of all calamities. Of the garden of pleasure, a type of the future immortal life, from which he had been ejected; of the angels, some of whom protected the entrance of the garden with a flaming and turning sword (Genesis 2). [He taught] of the devils, the enemies of the human race, and of their temptations, one of whom had deceived him and his wife through the serpent. Of the seed of the woman, that is, Christ, who had been promised to him as the medicine for sin and misery (Genesis 3). Of the sanctification of the Sabbath because of the benefit of creation; of the sanctity and laws of marriage, about which he himself had prophesied (Genesis 2). Of the sacrifices and worship of God; of God’s precepts and will; of death, of repentance, and of the punishments for sins—all of which he had learned by experience, or had conceived through the Spirit of God or the excellence and perfection of his own mind, talent, and nature. Finally, [he taught] of all the mysteries most necessary for salvation, with which God had fully imbued him, not only as a Prophet but as a man created immediately by Himself. Indeed, for this reason, God seems to have extended his life to the year 930—that is, more than half of the first age—so that he might leave long roots of piety.”

To this, Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a prominent medieval rabbi and grammarian</note> applies the verse from **1 Chronicles 4**: *These are ancient words*, namely referring to the **Kabbalah**, the **Reception**, or the **Masorah** <note>original: "Massorā", the tradition of the transmission and preservation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, that is, the tradition of the ancestors. And Rabbi Abraham <note>Likely Abraham ibn Daud</note> testifies regarding **Psalm 118** <note>Psalm 119 in most modern numbering</note>: specifically concerning those precepts which have testimony from the fathers as eyewitnesses or ear-witnesses, not from the written scripture; these constitute the law received through tradition without being written. The same author, in the second book of the same *Chronography*, reports that **Ezra the prophet**, secretary or scribe, was the first among the Hebrews to collect and put into writing seventy books of this **Kabbalah**. He notes that by Ezra's counsel and ministry, the holy books were first corrected, which gave rise to the *Tikkun Soferim* <note>original: "Tikkun Sopherim", meaning the "Correction of the Scribes"</note>, or the *Tikkun Ezra* (the correction of Ezra), as mentioned in the **Masorah, number 12**. It is as if this Ezra were the prince of Secretaries or Scribes; and to those seventy books cited above, he added the doctrine of the seventy-two Elders, of whose number was the author of the **fourth book of Ezra**, as is contained in **4 Ezra 14** <note>An apocalyptic book often excluded from the modern Protestant Bible but found in some Latin Vulgate editions</note>. This same Génébrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine and scholar whose work this text is discussing</note> provides a long discourse on what these books contained, which he repeats in his treatise on the historical Kabbalah by Rabbi Abraham Levita, son of David <note>Abraham ibn Daud (c. 1110–1180)</note>, which he translated from the Hebrew language into Latin and had printed.

Today, the Jews scattered throughout the Levant, the South, and Europe teach their Hebrew language and their Kabbalah to Christians, provided that they supply large quantities of money. This they did not dare to do several centuries ago because it was forbidden to them by their Rabbis for many reasons and occasions unworthy of being recited here, some of which are touched upon by **Rabbi Moses the Egyptian** <note>Maimonides (1138–1204)</note> in book 1, chapter 70 of his **Guide** <note>The "Guide for the Perplexed", a foundational work of Jewish philosophy</note> previously cited at the beginning of this present chapter. At present, these Jews are divided into three sects: namely, the **Philosophers**, the **Talmudists**, and the **Cabalists**.

The **Philosophers** are those who, having left the worry of worldly things, judgments, and political customs—both public and private—to their companions, give themselves entirely to contemplation and the highest life. They relate the senses of all Holy Scripture to the **Archetype** <note>The original divine pattern or idea</note>, and have interpreted all things of this Universe either through numbers, symbolized reason, or through the anagogical <note>Spiritual or mystical interpretation of the afterlife or divine realm</note> and corresponding sense.

The **Talmudists** are those who declare and explain the law and Holy Scripture insofar as it pertains to this low, sensible world and the active life. These feed only upon the bark <note>The outer shell or literal meaning</note> of the letter of the said law and Holy Scripture, as did **Rabbi Solomon** <note>Rashi (1040–1105)</note>, **David Kimhi**, **Levi Ben Gerson** <note>Gersonides (1288–1344)</note>, **Rebunachi** <note>Possibly a corruption of "Ramban" or another rabbinic title</note>, and **Moses son of Maimon** called the Egyptian, surnamed by some **Rambam**, and several others of whom we make ample mention later in the subsequent chapter, and others following that treat the Hebrew language.

The **Cabalists** are those who have been taught by divine oracle: for **Kabbalah** signifies in Hebrew as much as "Collection" or "Reception by mouth," as was said above; or rather, those who had been taught in the law and Holy Scripture, such as those who followed the first and most ancient Hebrews, the children and grandchildren of Adam

# History of the Origin of the
<header>History of the Origin of the</header>

Hebrews, and there were also some which were entirely and in every way contrary to one another, or which can be placed in debate and controversy. Based upon these, some of the Talmudists <term>Talmudists: scholars and students of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism</term> have held and continue to hold diverse and dissimilar opinions, which can be divided into five species or categories.

The first consists of the mandates and precepts taught from the very mouth of that Prophet Moses, which are somewhat founded upon the order of the literal text, or upon a certain law or mode of arguing; and regarding this species or category of mandates and precepts, there has never been any debate or contention in the synagogue of these Talmudists.

The second consists of all those mandates or decrees which are held to have been given by God to Moses on Mount Sinai, and which, although they are not founded on any precept of the written law or logical argument thereof, are nevertheless carefully kept and observed without any question or inquiry.

The third consists of the mandates or decrees which were not taught or given by the mouth of Moses, but were explained by a certain method and fashion of syllogism <term>syllogism: a form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two assumed premises</term>. For this reason, such a species or category of interpreting the divine law has infinite sorts of diversities of opinions; insofar as these are followed and embraced by the majority of the wisest, they are entirely and everywhere embraced and kept by their descendants and successors.

The fourth consists of the institutions which the Prophets and the wisest among the Hebrews introduced and put forward across several and various centuries and times—not because the divine law prescribed them, but because they serve as a bulwark <note>original: "propugnacle"</note> for that law, for fear that the most fundamental and radical precepts and commandments of that law might easily become nullified or weakened.

The fifth consists of the constitutions and customs of things which seem to belong less to any express mandate of the law, but rather to the assembly of several Prophets or sages, or which are approved by an ancient custom for the common welfare of the Hebrews.

Therefore, all these things consisting of these five species or categories specified above are contained and comprised within the **Mishna** mentioned above, drawn up in the form of a compendium <note>a concise summary or collection</note>. This was, by its author cited above, divided and distributed into six principal parts by him called סדרים *Sedarim* <note>original Hebrew: "Orders"</note>, that is to say, orders, or ordinations, or rather directions. The **Talmud** is, to tell the truth, nothing but a commentary on this Mishna, which is, just like the said Mishna, partitioned and divided according to some of the Hebrews into four parts: in the first of which it treats of holy things, feasts, and ceremonies; in the second, of plants and seeds; in the third, of marriages and women; and in the fourth, of judgments and rights. It is true that Peter Niger <note>Petrus Nigri (1434–1483), a scholar who wrote on Jewish law from a Christian perspective</note> has divided it into six parts, with whom the majority of the Hebrews agree.

[The first] section is called **Seder Zeraim**, that is, the **Order of Seeds** <note>original: סדר זרעים; *Seder zeraim, id est ordo seminum*</note>, which is to say the order of the seeds of things growing from the earth, whether sown or planted together; [it treats] of the rest of the land, of its "uncircumcision" <note>Refers to *Orlah*, the law prohibiting the use of fruit from a tree for its first three years</note>, of the first-fruits and tithes, and other distributions of the fruits of the soil.

The second part is called **Seder Moed**, that is, the **Order of Festivals** <note>original: סדר מועד; *Seder Moed, id est ordo festorum*</note>, which is to say the order of feasts, or otherwise of times, which treats of the seasons of the year, the feast days, and the various conditions for observing these days.

<margin>3</margin>
The third part is **Seder Nashim**, that is, the **Order of Women** <note>original: סדר נשים; *Seder Naschin, id est ordo mulierum*</note>, which is to say the order of women, treating the rights and statutes of marriage, the writ of divorce, and all other things depending upon the marriage between a man and a woman.

<margin>4</margin>
The fourth is **Seder Nezikin**, that is, the **Order of Damages or Injuries** <note>original: סדר נזיקין; *Seder nezikin, id est ordo damnorum seu nocumentorum*</note>, which is to say the order of damages and nuisances, treating all things concerning lawsuits, disputes, business, exchanges, and mutual commerce and trades between men.

<margin>5</margin>
The fifth is **Seder Kodashim**, that is, the **Order of Sanctifications** <note>original: סדר קדשים; *Seder Cadascim, id est ordo sanctificationum*</note>, which is to say the order of Sacraments, sanctifications, or sacred things, which treats and explains the law and observance of sacrifices and offerings.

<margin>6</margin>
The sixth is **Seder Taharot**, that is, the **Order of Purifications** <note>original: סדר טהרות; *Seder Terahoth, id est ordo purificationum*</note>, which is to say the order of the expurgations and purifications of these [items]. Each of these parts is divided into several [sub-sections], which further divides and partitions the whole **Talmud** <term>Talmud: the vast collection of Jewish law and tradition</term> into **Massekhet** <note>original: מסכת; *Maffechot*</note>, which is to say books, and each **Massekhet** (namely a book) into several **Perakim** <note>original: *Perakim*</note>, which are distinctions of things, or chapters; and these chapters into lessons. This is confirmed by **Elias Levita** <note>A renowned 15th-16th century Hebrew grammarian and scholar</note>, a Jew by nation, in his *Tishbi* <note>original: *Thesbyte*, a dictionary of Rabbinic Hebrew</note>, interpreting the Hebrew word **Seder** <note>original: סדר; *Sadar*</note>:

> *Among the Rabbis the name Sadar is often found; hence it is that they call even a Parashah <note>a weekly section of the Torah</note> from the Law "Sadar" or "Sadarah." Likewise, they divide the entire Talmud into six orders, which are Seder Nashim, that is, the order of women; Seder Nezikin, that is, the order of damages; Seder Zeraim, that is, the order of seeds; Seder Taharot, that is, the order of purifications; and Seder Kodashim, that is, the order of sanctifications, etc.*

The greatest part of the Jews have divided their Talmuds in this fashion.

<margin>1</margin>
**THE FIRST PART**, named the Order of Seeds, is divided into eleven books, the first of which is called **Massekhet Berakhot** <note>original: מסכת ברכות; *Maffechoth Berachoth*</note>, which is to say the **Treatise of Blessings**; it is divided into nine chapters, in which is principally treated the blessings of thanks that one must render to God, and divine prayers and praises.

<margin>2</margin>
The second is called **Massekhet Pe’ah** <note>original: מסכת פאה; *Maffecheth Pea*</note>, which is to say the **Treatise of the Angle** or the corner, or the angular part; it is divided into ten chapters, in which is treated the angular part of the harvests and fruits that one must leave for the poor.

<margin>3</margin>
The third is called **Massekhet Demai** <note>original: מסכת דמאי; *Maffecheth Demai*</note>, which is to say the **Treatise of the Doubtful**; it is divided into ten chapters, in which is treated the manner of giving or paying the tithes of doubtful things.

The fourth is called **Massekhet Terumot** <note>original: מסכת תרומות; *Maffecheth terumoth*</note>, which is to say the **Treatise of the Offerings** (literally "the two out of the number one hundred") <note>This refers to the *Terumah Gedolah*, usually given as 1/50th or 2% of the harvest to the Priests</note>; it is divided into eleven chapters, in which...

The second [tractate] is called **Massekhet Ketubot** <note>original: מסכת כתובות; "Tractate of Marriage Contracts"</note>, which is to say the treatise on contracts. It is divided into thirteen chapters, which deal with marriage contracts, dowries, and the obligations that a husband must observe toward his wife, and a wife toward her husband.

2 The third is called **Massekhet Nedarim** <note>original: מסכת נדרים; "Tractate of Vows"</note>, which is to say the treatise on vows. It is divided into eleven chapters, which deal with the vows of women.

3 The fourth is called **Massekhet Nazir** <note>original: מסכת נזיר; "Tractate of the Nazirite"</note>, which is to say the treatise on the Nazirite. It is divided into nine chapters, which deal with the vows of the Nazirites—that is, those separated from the vanities of the world. During the term of their vow, it was not permitted, among other things, to drink wine, nor to taste any liquor or anything produced by the vine, nor to cut their hair, nor to touch any dead body.

4 The fifth is called **Massekhet Sotah** <note>original: מסכת סוטה; "Tractate of the Wayward Wife"</note>, which is to say the treatise on diversion or divorce. It is divided into nine chapters, which deal with the diversion or divorce occurring when a woman leaves her husband to marry another.

5 The sixth is **Massekhet Gittin** <note>original: מסכת גטין; "Tractate of Divorce Deeds"</note>, which is to say the treatise on the scrolls of divorce. It is divided into nine chapters, which deal with the legal documents of repudiation and the divorce of a marriage.

7 The seventh is **Massekhet Kiddushin** <note>original: מסכת קדרושין; "Tractate of Betrothals"</note>, which is to say the treatise on engagements. It is divided into four chapters, which deal with betrothals and matters pertaining to them.

1 **THE FOURTH PART** of the aforementioned Talmuds, named the **Order of Damages** <note>original: *Seder Nezikin*</note>, is likewise divided into seven books.

The first of these is called **Massekhet Nezikin** <note>original: מסכת נזיקין; "Tractate of Damages"</note>, which is to say the treatise on dangers and nuisances. Like its corresponding part, it is divided into three **Bavot** <note>original: בבות; "Gates" or "Positions"</note>.

2 The first of these is called **Bava Kamma** <note>original: בבא קמא; "First Gate"</note>, which is to say the first position. It is divided into ten chapters, which deal with all the dangers and nuisances commonly caused both by men and by brute beasts.

The second is called **Bava Metzia** <note>original: בבא מציעא; "Middle Gate"</note>, which is to say the middle position. It is also divided into ten chapters, which deal with lawsuits, rights, usury <note>The practice of lending money at interest</note>, and rentals.

3 The third is called **Bava Batra** <note>original: בבא בתרא; "Last Gate"</note>, which is to say the final position. It is likewise divided into ten chapters, which deal with sales, communal fields, heirs, and inheritances.

4 The second book is called **Massekhet Sanhedrin** <note>original: מסכת סנהדרין; "Tractate of the Sanhedrin"</note>, which is to say the treatise on the ordinary judges. It is divided into fourteen chapters, which treat extensively of judges, judgments, and other matters pertaining to the law. It also treats of those who have a portion in the world to come, the Messiah, and principally in the **Perek Helek** <note>original: פרק חלק; "Chapter: Portion"</note>, which is to say the chapter beginning with "Helek," which means "portion."

The third is called **Massekhet Shevuot** <note>original: מסכת שבועות; "Tractate of Oaths"</note>, which is to say the treatise on oaths. It is divided into eight chapters, which deal with oaths and especially the safeguarding of property.

The fifth is called **Massekhet Avodah Zarah** <note>original: מסכת עבודה זרה; "Tractate on Foreign Worship"</note>, which is to say the treatise on foreign servitude <note>The author interprets "Avodah Zarah" (idolatry) as "foreign servitude" or "foreign worship."</note>. It is divided into five chapters, in which is treated Idolatry, and the things in which Jews must not communicate with other peoples, concerning both their conversion and their food and drink.

The sixth is called **Massekhet Avot** <note>original: מסכת אבות; "Tractate of the Fathers"</note>, which is to say the treatise of the fathers. It is named by almost everyone **Pirkei Avot** <note>original: פרקי אבות; "Chapters of the Fathers"</note>, which is to say the chapters of the fathers, in which is treated the ancient fathers who flourished among the others either in doctrine or sanctity of life, from **Moses** until **Simeon the Just** <note>Simeon the Just was a High Priest during the time of the Second Temple, famous for saying the world rests on Torah, service, and deeds of kindness.</note>.

The seventh is called **Massekhet Horayot** <note>original: מסכת הוריות; "Tractate of Decisions"</note>, which is to say the treatise of sentences. It is divided into three chapters, in which is treated the sentences determined by the **Sanhedrin** <note>original: Sanhedrin; the supreme legal assembly of ancient Israel</note>, which is to say ordinary judges, and especially the penalties for those who contravene them. Some add to these books a certain one called **Massekhet Makkot** <note>original: מסכת מכות; "Tractate of Lashes"</note>, which is to say the treatise of persecutions <note>more commonly translated as "lashes" or "corporal punishment"</note>, and they place it in the third position, in which is treated the persecutions for which the guilty were to be punished by the sentences of the judges. But those who attribute only the seven books specified above to this part do not distinguish this second book, but of these two books they make only one.

**THE FIFTH PART** of the aforementioned **TALMUDS**, named the **Order of Sanctifications** <note>known in Hebrew as Seder Kodashim (Holy Things)</note>, contains eleven books.

The first of these is called **Massekhet Zevachim** <note>original: מסכת זבחים; "Tractate of Animal Sacrifices"</note>, which is to say the treatise of immolations. It is divided into fourteen chapters, in which is amply treated the immolations of sacrifices and the method and place of sacrificing.

The second is called **Massekhet Chullin** <note>original: מסכת חולין; "Tractate of Profane Things"</note>, which is to say the treatise of killings <note>referring to ritual slaughter for non-sacrificial use</note>. It is divided into twelve chapters, in which is treated the killings and immolations of pure and clean animals.

The third is called **Massekhet Menachot** <note>original: מסכת מנחות; "Tractate of Meal Offerings"</note>, which is to say the treatise of flours. It is divided into thirteen chapters, in which is treated the wheat flours which must be offered at the temple.

The fourth is called **Massekhet Bechorot** <note>original: מסכת בכורות; "Tractate of Firstborns"</note>, which is to say the treatise of the firstborn. It is divided into nine chapters, in which is treated the firstborn of animals, both those which must be offered and others which must be redeemed.

The fifth is called **Massekhet Arachin** <note>original: מסכת ערכין; "Tractate of Valuations"</note>, which is to say the treatise of prices. It is divided into nine chapters, in which is treated the prices of things which had been promised as gifts to God.

The sixth is called **Massekhet Temurah** <note>original: מסכת תמורה; "Tractate of Exchange"</note>, which is to say the treatise of permutation. It is divided into seven chapters, in which is treated the prohibition against making any permutation of sacrifices.

The seventh is called **Massekhet Meilah** <note>original: מסכת מעילה; "Tractate of Sacrilege"</note>, which is to say the treatise of transgression. It is divided into six chapters, in which is treated the transgression of those who had made use of things not permitted for sacrifices.

The ninth is called **Massekhet Tamid** <note>original: מסכת תמיד; "Tractate of the Continual [Sacrifice]."</note>, which is to say the treatise of the continual or continuation—namely of the sacrifice. It is divided into six chapters, in which is treated the continual sacrifice of the two lambs, which was to be performed at the Temple.

10. The tenth is called **Massekhet Middot** <note>original: מסכת מדות; "Tractate of Measures."</note>, which is to say the treatise of dimensions. It is divided into five chapters, in which is treated the dimensions and measures of the Temple.

### THE SIXTH PART of the aforementioned Talmuds, named *Order of Purifications*, is divided into twelve books.

1. The first of these is called **Massekhet Kelim** <note>original: מסכת כלים; "Tractate of Vessels."</note>, which is to say the treatise on vessels. It is divided into thirty chapters, in which is treated the purification of vessels of whatever kind and material they may be, and of fabrics and garments, which could be polluted by some contamination.

2. The second is called **Massekhet Ohalot** <note>original: מסכת אהלות; "Tractate of Tents."</note>, which is to say the treatise on habitations. It is divided into eighteen chapters, in which is treated the purification of houses and other things from the contamination caused by the impurity of a dead body.

3. The third is called **Massekhet Negaim** <note>original: מסכת נגעים; "Tractate of Afflictions."</note>, which is to say the treatise on wounds or persecutions. It is divided into fourteen chapters, in which is treated the purification both of human bodies—concerning the impurity contracted as much because of leprosy and other wounds as also by all other things destined for human use—on account of these afflictions.

4. The fourth, concerning the heifer, is called **Massekhet Parah** <note>original: מסכת פרה; "Tractate of the Cow."</note>, which is to say the treatise on the heifer or small cow. It is divided into twelve chapters, in which is treated the ashes of the heifer or red cow, by the sprinkling of whose blood both men and all other things that were polluted by a dead human body could be purified.

5. The fifth is called **Massekhet Taharot** <note>original: מסכת טהרות; "Tractate of Purities."</note>, which is to say the treatise on purifications. It is divided into ten chapters, in which is treated the purification of impurity that occurred by means other than that of a dead human body.

6. The sixth is called **Massekhet Mikvaot** <note>original: מסכת מקואות; "Tractate of Collections [of water]."</note>, which is to say the treatise on congregations or collections of waters. It is divided into ten chapters, in which is treated the fountains and waters in which men were baptized <note>The author uses the Christian term "baptized" to describe *tevilah*, or ritual immersion in a Mikveh.</note> and submerged, so that they might be purified of all their filth, both corporal and spiritual.

Thus we see, by what has been set out above, that the entire Talmud contains six principal parts, sixty books, and five hundred thirty-two chapters, in which are found here and there, on every subject, an infinity of **Gemaroth** <note>original: גמראן; Gemara, the completion or commentary on the Mishnah.</note>, that is to say, concluded traditions or determined conclusions, containing several secrets and mysteries of the Messiah, which entirely agree with our Christian religion, according to the traditions given in the aforementioned Talmud by the ancient Jews. In fact, one hardly finds in the aforementioned Talmud any **Gemara** <note>original: גמרא</note>, that is to say, tradition or conclusion, finalized and determined, left by the tradition of the aforementioned ancient Jews, which does not contain within itself—clearly, openly, or obscurely and figuratively—some secret or mystery of our aforementioned Christian religion, as is amply verified by Porchetus in his *Victory over the Wicked Jews* <note>original: *Victoria Porchetti adversus impios Hebraeos* (1303), a polemical work by Porchetto Salvago.</note>; P. Some have asked how the tradition of the divine Law, left by the Prophet Moses, could be continued from father to son among the Hebrews, by word of mouth, until the time that the Talmuds of the Jews were composed. # History of the Origin of the

...some who were very persistent <note>original: "pertinax"; meaning stubborn or resolute.</note> and imitators of the divine law and its observation, and this was a little before the time in which the Jews were in great wars and civil divisions. These Pharisees, having abandoned Judea and their country, wandered as travelers and vagabonds among the Gentiles; since they were not at all concerned with the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, they were esteemed as not being guilty of any crime or misdeed. The other Pharisees, whom our aforementioned Lord Jesus Christ argues against and notes for every kind of wickedness and guilt, were those Pharisees who—by the greed for power and by a fury of ire and vengeance—had our same Lord Jesus Christ put to the cruel torture of the cross. The testimony and names of these men have been taken away and erased from the said Talmuds <note>original: "Thalmuds"</note> by the Jews, just as from the book of life. Others, for and by reason of the depth and sublimity of a certain mystery, did not observe or embrace the faith of Jesus Christ and the sacrament of the cross, but they also did not hold it in great execration nor did they condemn it. Others, being in great number, followed the faith of Jesus Christ just as it is contained in the Acts of the Apostles, but they also asserted very constantly that it was necessary to keep the Mosaic law <note>The Law of Moses.</note> as a shadow and image of the eternal law—not for fear of punishment, but rather for the love of exemplary virtue, which they were permitted to do for a time. All of these, teaching the exposition of their divine law by word of mouth one after the other, were the cause of its finally being reduced to writing in the aforementioned Talmuds. Regarding this subject of the Pharisees, G. Galatin <note>Pietro Galatino (c. 1460–1540), a Friar Minor and Christian Hebraist who sought to find Christian truths within Jewish texts.</note> in book 1, chapter 4 of his *Secrets of the Catholic Truth* has said:

> After the Lord's resurrection, the Jews were divided into a threefold genus <note>original: "in triplex, Iudæi fuerunt diuisi genus"; meaning three types or groups.</note>. For some, seeing the sayings of the Prophets fulfilled in him, adhered to him in both faith and deed, as did that old man Galiel <note>likely referring to Gamaliel the Elder, a famous Pharisee mentioned in the New Testament.</note>, whose sayings are of the greatest authority among the Talmudists. And almost infinite others did this—not only from the common or ignorant people, but from the more noble and wise. For as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, a very great part of the priests obeyed the faith. And some of these wrote many wonderful things about Christ, some of whose small works still exist among the Jews, although they strive with all their might to hide them so that they do not come into our hands. Some of them truly believed that the Lord Jesus himself was that Messiah of whom the Prophets had spoken, yet they were unwilling to desert the Mosaic observances. These adhered to Christ only in faith and not in deed: because while they confessed Christ, they nevertheless persevered in Judaism, such as (as I believe) Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> was, and almost innumerable others of whom the book of the Acts of the Apostles mentions in chapters 15 and 21. Where it is said: "Do you see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealots for the law?" Very many of these also wrote some true things about Christ and correctly explained the prophecies in many places. Finally, others of the Jews, wishing to adhere to Christ neither in faith nor in deed, remained in their persistent perfidy...

...some who were very stubborn and zealous for the divine law and its observation, a short time before the period in which the Jews were in great wars and civil divisions. These Pharisees, having abandoned Judea and their country, wandered as travelers and vagabonds among the gentiles; because they were not involved in the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, they were considered not to be guilty of any crime or misdeed. The other Pharisees, whom our aforementioned Lord Jesus Christ reproaches and marks for every kind of wickedness and guilt, were those Pharisees who—driven by a greed for power and a fury of wrath and vengeance—caused our Lord Jesus Christ to be put to the cruel torture of the cross. Their testimony and names, as if from the book of life, have been removed and erased from the said Talmuds by the Jews. Others, for the reason of the depth and sublimity of a certain mystery, did not observe or embrace the faith of Jesus Christ and the sacrament of the cross, but they also did not hold it in great execration nor condemn it. Others, being in great number, followed the faith of Jesus Christ as it is contained in the Acts of the Apostles, but also maintained very constantly that it was necessary to keep the Mosaic law as a shadow and image of the eternal law, not out of fear of punishment, but rather for the love of exemplary virtue—which they were permitted to do for a time. All of these, teaching the exposition of their divine law by word of mouth one after the other, were the reason that it was finally redacted into writing in the aforementioned Talmuds. Regarding this subject of the Pharisees, G. For some, seeing the sayings of the Prophets fulfilled in Him, adhered to Him in both faith and work, as did that elderly Gamaliel, whose sayings are of the greatest authority among the Talmudists. ...they chose to remain stubborn, as if blind. Yet they could not entirely deny the truth (behold how great is the power of truth!). For in explaining the Law and the Prophets, compelled by the truth alone, they were unable to keep it entirely silent in many matters. We must believe that this was not done without divine arrangement, so that we might hold testimonies of the truth itself against its enemies and those who deny it, provided by those very same people. Nor does it harm the truth that they themselves did not believe; rather, it adds more weight to the testimony, because even the unbelieving could not deny it. From their sayings and writings, and those of all others who handed down anything in writing after the Babylonian captivity, the Talmudic code <note>The Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> was compiled and compacted. *Sixtus of Siena* <note>A 16th-century Jewish convert to Catholicism and a pioneering biblical scholar.</note> in book 2 *of his Sacred Library*, notes that *Epiphanius* <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Salamis known for his "Panarion," a treatise against heresies.</note> very frequently cites certain traditions of the Jews without naming an authority. From these authorities, Epiphanius brings forth—against the *Hieracites* <note>Followers of Hieracas, who denied the resurrection of the body.</note>—the genealogy of *Melchizedek* as being from the nation of the Sidonians; and against the *Melchizedekians* <note>A sect that believed Melchizedek was a divine power greater than Christ.</note>, the genealogies of the Prophets *Elijah* and *Daniel*. Likewise, against the *Antidicomarianites* <note>A group that opposed the doctrine of the perpetual virginity of Mary.</note>, he shows from these same traditions that *Joseph*, the spouse of the Virgin *Mary*, had another wife before *Mary*, and by her had fathered four sons, who are named in *Mark* and *John* as *James, Joses, Judas, and Simon*, and two daughters, *Mary* and *Salome*; and that when she died and he was a widower of eighty years, he took the Virgin *Mary* as his wife. Likewise, against the *Collyridians* <note>A sect, largely of women, who worshipped Mary as a goddess.</note>, he records that the parents of the Virgin *Mary* were *Joachim and Anne*. Again, disputing against the *Manichaeans* <note>Followers of a major dualistic religion that competed with early Christianity.</note>, he proves from these same sources that *Lazarus*, when he was raised by *Christ*, was thirty years old, and lived thirty more years after his resurrection. Saint *Jerome* also cites other Hebrew traditions in his book of Hebrew Traditions; because these were not written down, they are called *agrapha* <note>original Greek: ἄγραφα; meaning "unwritten things."</note>.

-># Languages of this Universe <- <note>original: "Langues de cest Vniuers." Though the text is in Latin, the header is in Middle French, likely the title of the larger work.</note>

than he who rejects the gospel: for if the constitutions of the Church are cast aside, it is inevitable that the Gospel itself will be thrown away. This is clearly attested by the divine Basil <note>St. Basil the Great (c. 330–379 AD), an influential theologian and one of the Three Holy Hierarchs of the Eastern Church.</note> in his book *On the Holy Spirit*, specifically in the 27th chapter, with these words: "If we begin to reject unwritten institutes and customs as if they lacked great power, we will secretly and step by step condemn the very established meanings of the Gospel, or rather, we will reduce its preaching to an empty name." <margin>«</margin> Therefore, I consider it an Apostolic duty to remain even in those traditions which are <margin>«</margin> not written; but we have spoken more extensively on these matters elsewhere. <margin>«</margin>

Stratonicus, the Bishop of Cumae, maintains in his collected works that these traditions were the decrees and decisions of the Jewish secret councils. For, as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (37–c. 100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian who is our primary source for the different sects of Second Temple Judaism.</note> and Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD), a bishop known for his "Panarion," a catalog of various heresies and sects.</note> write, there were four ways of living among the Jews: one practiced by the Pharisees, another by the Galileans, a third by the Sadducees, and a fourth by the Essenes.

The doctrines of the Pharisees were as follows:

<margin>1</margin> That all things are governed by Fate—that is, by the presence and immovable decree of God—while yet leaving the free assent of the human will. For the best God moderates the affairs of men with such a balance that, although all things depend on His deliberation, man still possesses the unimpaired faculty for choosing virtue or vice.

<margin>2</margin> That souls are incorruptible and immortal, and their judgments occur under the earth, where rewards or punishments fall to each according to the merit of their virtue or wickedness.

<margin>3</margin> That the souls of the pious return from the underworld to this life into new bodies, and from these they migrate again into other bodies; but the souls of the wicked are condemned to perpetual prisons and tormented with endless punishment. <note>This description of the Pharisees believing in the transmigration of souls (reincarnation) is a common interpretation of Josephus's text by early modern scholars.</note>

<margin>4</margin> That elders are to be venerated, and it is not permitted to talk back to those who give counsel or to speak against them.

The **GALILEANS**, who took their origin from Judas of Galilee, from the town of Gamala, followed the same beliefs as the Pharisees, adding only this one point: that only God is to be held as Lord, and no mortal prince is to be obeyed, but one must endure every hardship and severity for the sake of asserting liberty. Josephus relates that this class of men often incited the people to cast off the kingdom and the rule of masters, and to refuse the payment of taxes (which is a manifest testimony of servitude). There are also those who believe that from this sect were those Jews whom we read of glorying in their liberty, saying to Christ, in whom they had recently believed: *We are the seed of Abraham, and we have never served anyone.* <note>original: "Semen Abrahæ sumus, & nemini seruuimus vnquam." See John 8:33.</note> And for that reason, they adhered to Christ because they hoped he would eventually be the asserter and avenger of Jewish liberty.

<margin>1</margin> **SADDUCEES**: Their opinions were different from these; namely, that there is no fate at all, nor any decree of divine declaration, but all things are so within the power of men that each person is the author of his own happiness or misfortune.

<margin>2</margin> That souls are entirely extinguished along with the body, and no rewards or punishments remain after this life.

<margin>3</margin> That there is no nature of angels, but only names; by which are designated either the movements which God breathes into men, or those demonstrations of His power which He Himself brings forth.

<margin>4</margin> That besides the books of Moses and the divine laws contained in those same volumes, there is no other authority of scripture or of human tradition.

<meta>This page concludes a discussion on Jewish legal traditions and provides a detailed list of the customs of the Essenes, a Jewish sect known for its asceticism. It continues from page 89, which introduced the four main Jewish sects as described by historical sources like Josephus and Epiphanius.</meta>

->### History of the Origin of... <- <note>original: "Histoire de l'Origine des." This is a French header in an otherwise Latin text, likely the title of the chapter or work.</note>

...that tradition must be accepted.

The **ESSENES**, distinguished practitioners of piety and not much different from Christian monks, bound themselves by these laws and sanctions:

1. That all things are governed by fate—that is, by the will of God—and that nothing happens to men except by the decree of fate.
2. That souls are immortal, and after this life, rewards and punishments are paid out according to one's deeds: for the good, there is a region beyond the ocean where neither cold nor heat oppresses, but the breathing West Wind <note>original: "Zephyrus," the personification of the gentle west wind in classical mythology.</note> makes it pleasant; for the wicked, however, there are places of hardship in the underworld, full of lamentations.
3. That every oath must be avoided as if it were perjury, because whatever a perfect man says should have the force of an oath; anyone who is not believed unless he calls God as a witness is condemned as being guilty of falsehood.
4. That after God, the highest reverence must be shown to the lawgiver Moses; if anyone blasphemes him, let him be condemned to death.
5. That primary study must be devoted to the divine scriptures and the writings of the ancient fathers, and from there one must seek the remedies that ease the cares of the soul.
6. That the leader of the communal fellowship must be obeyed in such a way that nothing is permitted to be done without his command.
7. To lead a continent and celibate life, and to abstain entirely from all marriage throughout one’s whole life.
8. That all resources are common property, and there is one single patrimony for all, which is distributed by communal stewards.
9. That they shall neither buy nor sell anything among themselves, but it is free for all to receive whatever is needed from whomever they please.
10. That white garments must be used, and clothing and shoes are not to be changed unless they are either completely torn or worn out by long use.
11. That such care for cleanliness must be maintained even in natural waste, that each person daily digs a pit for himself in the most secret places with a small hatchet <note>original: "dolabella." This small tool was a signature accessory given to Essene initiates for hygiene and work.</note> to relieve his bowels, having first wrapped a garment around himself for the sake of covering the body, and then returning the earth he had dug up to its place, so that no insult is done to the splendor of the divine light.
12. That before the rising of the sun, the author of the light about to be born must be celebrated with public praises; afterwards, however, each person must go to his own crafts and studies.
13. At the fifth hour of the day, they must gather in a communal dining room, dressed in sacred garments—that is, linen coverings; there, they sit in silence and eat from the same bread and pottage. It is not lawful for anyone to taste anything unless a public prayer precedes and follows the meal, which praises God, the giver of food, both before and after the meal.
14. After the meal, having laid aside the sacred garments, each must return to his own work until evening.
15. Those recently approaching the worship of the Essenes are not to be admitted into the fellowship immediately, but, dressed in a white robe and a loincloth and girded with a small hatchet, they are to be tested by their overseers for three full years until they have given proof of their tried virtue.

**Jerome**, in his third commentary on Isaiah, in his tenth question to Algasia, and on the third chapter of the Epistle to Titus, writes that these are certain constitutions of the Jews called *deuteroseis* <note>original Greek: "δευτερώσεις," meaning repetitions or secondary laws</note> by the Greeks. These were first taught among the Hebrews before the coming of Christ by **Shammai** and **Hillel**, whose school was taken up by **Akiba**, the teacher of Aquila the proselyte; after him came Meir, who was succeeded by Johanan, the son of Zakkai, and after him Eliezer, and in order Delphon, and again Joseph, and finally Joshua, up until the final destruction of the Holy City.

**THOMAS Aquinas**, in his commentaries on both epistles to Timothy, asserts more than once that the name "traditions" signifies that vast and immense work of Jewish traditions called the **Talmud** <note>original Hebrew: "תלמוד" (Thalmud), meaning 'instruction' or 'learning'</note> by the Jews; in this work are collected all the decrees of the aforementioned masters—Shammai, Hillel, Akiba, Joseph, and the sons of the Hasmoneans—together with countless other statutes of the Rabbis, their opinions, and explanations of both divine and human laws by which the entire Jewish nation is now governed. This work had its beginning, as the Talmudic commentators themselves write, in the year 150 after the final fall of Jerusalem, by **Judah**, son of Simon <note>Known to history as Judah ha-Nasi</note>, who gathered into a single volume the explanations of the Law and the Prophets and all the writings that the above-mentioned Rabbis and other doctors had written up to that point, both before and after the coming of Christ. They called this volume the **Mishnah** <note>original Hebrew: "משנה" (Misnah), meaning 'repeated study' or 'repetition'</note>, that is, a repeated reading. In the three-hundredth year after that same final devastation of Jerusalem, **Rabbi Johanan**, having taken as colleagues **Rav** and **Samuel**, joined the Mishnah itself and certain other writings into one volume, which they called the **Jerusalem Talmud**, because it was written amid the ruins of the city of Jerusalem. Again, in the year 436 from that same destruction (which was the year of Christ 476), **Rabbi Ashi** and **Rabbi Ammi**, living in the Babylon of Egypt—which is now called **Cairo**—reduced all the previous writings into one and constructed a new body of many volumes called the ***Babylonian Talmud***. When they were prevented by death from finishing it, Rabbi Meir, the son of Rabbi Ashi, put the final hand to the work.

Everything mentioned above proves what we have already deduced at length in the preceding chapter: namely, that the Hebrews used two principal kinds of laws and interpretations. One is named in the Hebrew language ***Torah she-bi-khtav*** <note>original: "Thorah scebiechafnu," meaning the Law which is in writing</note>, the Law that was given and left by Moses in writing. The other is ***Torah she-be-al peh*** <note>original: "Thorah scebealpe," meaning the Law delivered by mouth</note>, the Law given orally by the same Moses. The first is that which is compiled in writing in the Hebrew language within the **Pentateuch**, or the five books of Moses. The other is partly treated within the aforementioned five books of the Pentateuch, within the books of **Kabbalah** mentioned by us above, and in the **Talmuds**. This Talmud contains the glosses and commentaries of the aforementioned compendium or summary of the *Mishnah*, together with all the other laws, ordinances, and new constitutions which have been made and promulgated at various times and places, along with many secrets and mysteries of the holy Hebrew language, and other reveries, fables, wickednesses, and impieties of the Talmudists. As for the latter and recent Talmudists, although several among them have been very eminent in erudition and probity of life, nevertheless their opinion and authority is not followed, except insofar as it conforms to what is written and decided in the aforementioned Talmuds. In short, the aforementioned Rabbi Moses the Egyptian <note>Better known as Maimonides (1138–1204), the most influential Jewish philosopher of the Middle Ages.</note> in the place cited above asserts that the aforementioned Talmuds treat four principal kinds of things.

The first: that they particularly interpret everything that is deduced in the *Mishnah* <note>The first major written collection of the Jewish oral traditions.</note>, and curiously examine everything that is ambiguous and doubtful in the authors of the glosses, and resolve the arguments of other commentators.

The second: that they give judgment and firm, assured resolution to the variety of opinions concerning the order of words and glosses, insofar as they depend on new ordinances and constitutions made for the explanation of the aforementioned *Mishnah*.

The third: that they report and teach the things that subsequent Talmudists, one after another, learned from the foundations of those Talmuds, while also resolving the arguments used by those Talmudists; and what is more, they expose all the things that were enacted and ordained after the aforementioned *Mishnah* was brought to light.

The fourth: that they insert in very appropriate places colloquies and homilies <note>Known as *Aggadah*, these are non-legalistic exegetical texts involving stories and folklore.</note> which, if they were presented just as they are on the outside and were taught and understood in a trivial way, would seem entirely to be like ridiculous and humorous things, even completely removed from the right path of reason. But considering them more closely, according to the type and figure contained within in the form of a riddle, one comes in truth to penetrate sublime things, and the most hidden secrets and oracles of wisdom. These are covered and wrapped in a veil of riddles and allegories, for fear that the doubtful and uncertain, as well as the ignoble common people, might come to defile these sacraments of divine truth, and pollute pure and clean things with the foul and filthy. This is also so that those who are eager for sincere religion, and more excellent in spirit, might devote themselves more vividly to the contemplation of the more hidden and secret things, and raise themselves more ardently even into the interior of heaven, toward the seat of the existence of divine and eternal wisdom. Galatin <note>Pietro Galatino, an Italian friar and scholar of the Kabbalah.</note> in Book 1 of *The Secrets of Catholic Truth*. Michael Neander, in his dedicatory epistle to his *erotemes* <note>original: "erotemes de la langue saincte"; *Erotemata* are introductory textbooks written in a question-and-answer format, in this case concerning the Hebrew language.</note> of the holy language, used these words:

,, But the Talmud—that is, the doctrinal and disciplinary book of the Jews, in which the entire Jewish tradition has been gathered with intense zeal, and which they possess in two versions, the Jerusalem and the Babylonian—is comprised of six orders containing over seventy massive books. This volume is held by them in no less or equal veneration than any other, yet it contains almost mere trifles, fables no better than old wives' tales, and furthermore, blasphemies against the Son of God—whom they call sometimes a bastard, sometimes the hanged one <note>original: "spurium, nunc suspensum"; a derogatory reference to the crucifixion.</note>, and sometimes by other names—as well as against Mary his mother, his disciples the Apostles, and all Christians individually and collectively. Indeed, they blaspheme Christ himself wickedly and impiously against these things, at the devil's dictation, through their writings and fabrications. It contains, moreover, ridiculous superstitions and foolish traditions, and narratives that are clearly lies, sometimes even horrific and cursed. Thus, I do not know whether Pope Clement did a worthwhile thing when he ordered the Talmudic fables to be translated into Latin in the decree *Concerning Teachers* <note>original: "Clement. de magistris"; refers to a canon from the Council of Vienne (1311) intended to promote the study of Hebrew, Arabic, and Chaldean to aid in conversion.</note>, or whether those of our age have correctly spent their time and leisure who, with immense labor but without private or public benefit, have turned most of the Talmudic books and many Rabbinic commentaries into Latin.

> But since not only Rabbi Mayr, but also his ancestors and his successors, had collected through each of the books of the Talmud not only many and execrable insults and blasphemies against Christ our God, but had also written many sanctions and precepts against the very Law of Moses which they profess, and against all the law of nations and all natural law, which they themselves, as humans, are bound to observe, it seemed right to the Supreme Pontiffs and other Christian princes that the reading and use of such wicked doctrine be forbidden to all Jews living under the dominion of Christians, and that all Talmudic books in the whole Christian world be committed to the flames. Which many trustworthy writers testify has often been done, among whom Bernard of Luxembourg, in his *Catalog of Heretics*, book 2, reports that Pope Gregory, the ninth of that name, in the year of our Lord 1230, condemned all Talmudic volumes to the flames, and that Pope Innocent, the fourth of that name, did the same again in the year of our salvation 1244. Again, when these same volumes had been restored by the Jews and, by the help of the art of printing, propagated in almost infinite numbers, Pope Julius the Third, having promulgated a new edict, ordered them to be searched for, and in the year 1553, while the Feast of Tabernacles was being celebrated by the Jews in the month of September, to be burned throughout all the cities of Italy. Pope Paul the Fourth, together with the senate of the Most Holy Roman Inquisition, in the year 1559, again ordered the same to be done, and willed the Talmudic books to be counted among the writings condemned by the Catholic Church. <note>original Latin: "Sed cùm tam Rabbi Mayr... connumerari voluit."</note> Finally, he says the same: I have considered it necessary to place here the catalog of all Talmudic volumes formerly transcribed by me from that most opulent library of the Jews of Cremona, from which in the year of salvation 1559, at the command of the senate of the Most Holy Roman Inquisition, twelve thousand <note>original Latin: "duodecim... millia"</note> Talmudic codices were burned.

The authors of the annotations on these Talmuds call the commentary of Rabbi Solomon <note>Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi (1040–1105)</note> composed on them *Kuntheres* for the following reasons, explained by Elias Levita <note>A Renaissance Hebrew grammarian</note> in his *Thesbyte* <note>The *Tishbi*, a dictionary of Rabbinic Hebrew</note> on the interpretation of this word:
> *Kuntheres*: the authors of Talmudic annotations call the commentary of Rabbi Solomon, which he published on the Talmud, *Kuntheres*. They say it was so named because he first composed that commentary in individual quires <note>original: "quinterniones," small gatherings of paper</note>, from which one book was later made, etc.

The same author says these words regarding the word *Midrash*:
> A book in which the words or deeds of kings and Prophets are written is called *Midrash*, namely because whoever seeks those things will find them there: hence it is called *Midrash* and is pointed with a <term>Mem with a Hirek</term> <note>A Hebrew grammatical notation for the short "i" vowel sound</note>: they call *Midrash* every commentary that is not written according to the simple or literal sense: such as the *Midrash Agadah* <note>Narrative or homiletic teachings</note>, or the *Midrash* of our Rabbis.

# History of the Origin of...

" ...received chiefly from the holy ones, and among other traditions this one of **Abraham** regarding creation, or rather formation, which, although it was not described by Abraham himself exactly as it stands here, the meaning is indeed consistent with eternal truth. But the title shows to which category it belongs: for it is of the third class of authority. In the first class are the sacred scriptures; in the second are the **Talmud** and **Mishnah**; in the third place are the <term>Baraithot</term> <note>original: "Bariethoth"; refers to "external" rabbinic traditions not included in the Mishnah</note>, that is, external writings, both those that relate to the Talmud and those that pertain to other parts of doctrine.

Therefore, the first of all the *Baraithot* is the <term>Sefer Yetzirah</term> <note>original: "sepher Iesirah"; the "Book of Formation," a foundational work of Jewish mysticism or Kabbalah</note>, and for that reason it is a book very rare to find and much rarer to understand. In it, the account of the entire <term>Cosmopoeia</term> <note>The creation or "making" of the world</note> is set forth, but by way of reason, whereas in Moses and the sacred books it is explained by way of authority. Thus, although it has circulated through the mouths of the wise since the very creation of the world and was set forth by Abraham three thousand five hundred years ago, yet until the account of creation had been established by the force of authority through all these three thousand years, there was no one who could truly reveal such a treasure to the world.

Since, therefore, in things to be proved by human reason and in those received in religion, faith and pure belief must necessarily be placed before reason, it was so arranged by divine providence that while this was set forth in Plato, Pythagoras, and Cicero—in what they treated concerning nature and the universe—this book remained hidden among its own people until the sacred things were divinely set forth and received through authority and pure faith. Thus, reason now happens to be our guide, serving as the priest of highest wisdom alongside the account of sacred doctrine. In this, providence seems most admirable: that those things which are in the third class of authority so persuade the primary account of eternal truth that no one in the whole world will fail to subscribe to it under the guidance of reason.

How great the authority of this <term>Baraitha</term> was among the fathers is handed down in many places and authorities, but it is most faithfully received and written by **Rabbi Judah**, author of the book <term>Bitachon</term> <note>original: "Bithchon"; meaning "Trust" or "Confidence"</note>, where he teaches that other prophets—all the more so as they were greater, and especially **Jeremiah**—were so well-versed in that book that revelation was made to him with a command to spend three whole years upon it. He studied it to such an extent that by the power of that science, he saw a 'new man' fashioned before him, as it was in the first divine intention. For that figure of a man fashioned before him bore on its forehead an inscription that both showed God to be man and affirmed that He would die. <note>This refers to a legend where Jeremiah and his son Ben Sira used the Sefer Yetzirah to create a Golem, an artificial human. In many versions, the word "Truth" (Emet) is written on its forehead; if the first letter is erased, it spells "Dead" (Met).</note> 

But the purpose of this was that, when the twenty-two letters of the alphabet had been inscribed in the most excellent dust of the world according to the holy desires of the human heart, men themselves (who are the most excellent dust) might see and feel the 'new man' himself completely transfused into them. To this end, therefore, does this study of the mystery of creation or formation and this book tend: that we may know how God created us, and in what way God, having become human, transfuses Himself into us, making us similar to Himself in mind and body and immortal, so that we may praise Him forever for such a great benefit. 

Rightly, therefore, we shall call this book <term>Baraitha</term> <note>The author here plays on a linguistic distinction between "Bariatha" (creation) and "Barieta" (constitution)</note>, that is, creation, and not *Barieta*, that is, an eternal constitution. For I am of the opinion that although it cites some sacred texts published long after Abraham himself, I do not doubt that it was always in the records of all the fathers, since it explains the manner of formation, whereas Moses expressed only the fact. The book is therefore of **Adam** and the holy succession of fathers; for it is certain that before things existed in themselves, they were arranged in their forms and numbers with God through Ideas—the knowledge of which Ideas is easily the first, and prior to the exposition of **Genesis**, although it...

<margin>cc</margin>Genesis has hitherto been held as the more noble work. For just as a work must exist before the things themselves, so it is established that nature was prior to grace, though grace is the more noble; yet grace would have had no place unless nature had first existed. In the same way, unless there had been <term>Yetzirah</term> <note>original: "Iezira"; the World of Formation in Kabbalistic thought</note>, there never could have been <term>Beriah</term> <note>original: "Beriah"; the World of Creation, which in this context represents a higher level of reality</note>.

<margin>cc</margin>The learned Gilbert Genebrard <note>A 16th-century French scholar and Benedictine archbishop</note>, in the second book of his *Chronography* speaking of Ezra and his writings, has said:

> <margin>cc</margin>He restored the Scriptures, which had been burned by the Babylonians under the captain of the guard Nebuzardan, and he brought them back into this order which the Hebrews for the most part still observe today.
> <margin>cc</margin>Regarding him, Rabanus Maurus <note>A 9th-century Carolingian scholar</note> writes in *On the Instruction of the Clergy*, chapter 54: Inspired by the divine spirit, he repaired all the ancient sacred books when the Jews had entered Jerusalem. He corrected all the volumes of the prophets which had been corrupted by the Gentiles and organized the entire Old Testament into twenty-two books, so that there would be as many books in the Law as there are letters in the alphabet. Otherwise, it was not within the power of Nebuchadnezzar to destroy all copies, especially since the ten tribes were already in the East, outside of his jurisdiction.
> <margin>cc</margin>For some make Ezra the author of the <term>vowel points and accents</term> <note>The "Niqqud" system used to indicate vowels in Hebrew, which is otherwise written only with consonants</note> with which the Hebrew Bibles are marked today. But they are mistaken, since it is clear from the books of the blessed Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> that in his time none existed. They were, however, invented a little after the time of the Emperor Honorius, in the 436th year from the destruction of the Temple, which is the 476th year since the suffering of Christ, in the city of Tiberias in Galilee.
> <margin>cc</margin>The leaders of this work were Aaron ben Asher and Jacob ben Naphtali, who, while they disagreed among themselves regarding the points of certain words, divided the Jews into two factions. For the Easterners, and those who inhabit Babylonia near the river Nearda, follow the reading of the latter, while the Westerners follow the former.
> <margin>cc</margin>Forty-one years earlier, the Babylonian <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note>, or book of doctrine, was begun, collected from the writings of the ancient masters by Rav Hina and Rav Ashi, and was later completed by Rav Meir and his son. It contains the canon law of the Jews, which in the time of Christ had not yet been committed to a full writing but was preserved partly from fragments and partly from oral traditions. It began to be written down by Rabbi <term>Judah the Holy</term> <note>original: "R. Hakkados"; Judah ha-Nasi, the 2nd-century editor of the Mishnah</note> in the times of the Emperor Antoninus, in that shorter form called the <term>Mishnah</term>. And that is regarding the Babylonian Talmud: for the Jerusalem Talmud was written in the year of Christ 300, and the Babylonian about a hundred years later.

<margin>cc</margin>The same author, shortly after treating the ruin of Jerusalem that occurred under the Emperor Vespasian, says:

> <margin>cc</margin>At the time of the destruction, there flourished Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai and his disciple Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, who wrote the book *Pirke* <note>The *Pirke De-Rabbi Eliezer*, a work of midrash</note>, concerning the arrangement and properties of the spheres of the earth and all the wonders in astronomy. > <margin>cc</margin>After the destruction came Rabbi Tarphon and Rabbi Akiba. Following them, after the Emperor Hadrian, were Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Judah, Rabbi Jose, Rabbi Simeon ben Azzai, and Rabbi Hananiah; and under Antoninus, Rabbi Judah the Holy (also called "Rabbi"), Rabbi Nathan, and Rabbi Joshua ben Korha.
> <margin>cc</margin>Soon after came the <term>Tannaim</term>, authors of the Mishnah, or the Talmudic text, and finally the <term>Amoraim</term>, authors of the <term>Gemara</term> <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis of the Mishnah</note>, or the Talmud itself. What the Jews did after the Roman exile, and how they conducted themselves regarding the Talmud, Gemara, <term>Midrashim</term> <note>original: "Derasim"; refers to homiletic interpretations</note>, and Geonim, up until the year 1108 from the said destruction, when Maimonides (Rabbi Moses ben Maimon) was writing—which is the year of Christ 1148—can be found by consulting the preface of his book and the *Kabbalistic History* of Rabbi Abraham ha-Levi. And these things indeed concern the ancient people.

# History of the Origin of the [Jews]

„ The same author <note>Referring to Gilbert Génébrard, mentioned on the previous page</note>, continuing to speak of the Jews who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity, says:
„ Not all returned for their own good. Indeed, a multitude of exiles—as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> writes in *Antiquities*, book 18, chapter 12, and the Talmud relates—founded a city on the bank of the Euphrates. They called it Neardea <note>Nehardea, one of the earliest and most important centers of Babylonian Judaism</note>, a name in the Chaldean language. This happened because the Jews who had been led away to Babylon, oppressed by seventy years of exile and servitude, had gradually unlearned the Hebrew language; the elders had passed away, and the children had absorbed the foreign tongue.
„ They named it Neardea, meaning the 'river of knowledge.' There, they constructed synagogues and academies which flourished for many centuries in every kind of science. From these, a long time later, around the year of Christ 470, they published the Babylonian Talmud, which is full of great knowledge.
„ Following their example, the others whom Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah had led back to Judea established many literary schools in Jerusalem. They eventually published the Jerusalem Talmud, which is four times smaller than the other, through the work of Rabbi Johanan, a hundred years before Rabbi Ashi published the Babylonian version.
„ The core text of this work, called the <term>Mishnah</term> <note>The first major written collection of the Jewish oral traditions</note>, existed thanks to the benefit of Rabbi Akiba under the Emperors named Antoninus, as Rabbi Moses <note>Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher</note> notes in the preface to his commentary. The same author, in the third book of his *Chronography*:
„ In the year of Christ 188, that part of the Talmud called the Mishnah was completed by the Jews; the other part, the <term>Gemara</term> <note>The rabbinical commentary and analysis of the Mishnah</note>, was finished in the year 505.
„ The first of the sages of the Mishnah (the Talmudic core) was Simeon the Just, who is said to have received Christ in his arms <note>A traditional Christian identification of the high priest Simeon with the Simeon from the Gospel of Luke</note>. The last was Rabbi Judah the Holy <note>Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi</note>, who was dear to Antoninus. Elias says in *Thesbites* that he is understood by the name 'Rabbi' in the Talmud. Rabbi Moses [Maimonides] says that with his death, the priesthood ceased. „ Rabbi Solomon Jarchi <note>Commonly known as Rashi, the famous 11th-century commentator</note> says the same regarding Genesis 9. From this point began the teachers called the <term>Amoraim</term> <note>Jewish scholars who 'explained' the oral law between 200 and 500 CE</note>, the first of whom was Rabba and the last was Rabbi Ashi in the year 426, according to Moses [Maimonides]. Hence, our Rabbi 'the Holy' is usually called the writer of the Mishnah, and Rabbi Ashi the author of the Gemara.
„ Afterward, in the year of Salvation 505, the Babylonian Talmud was finished by Mar, the son and disciple of Rabbi Ashi. This was specifically the part they call the Gemara, about 100 years after the Jerusalem Talmud, 317 years after the first part of the Mishnah, and 29 years after the vowel points [were added]. This edition was preceded by the authors of the Midrashim and the Mechilta, and was followed by the <term>Geonim</term> <note>The 'Excellencies' or heads of the post-Talmudic academies</note>, who were the professors and interpreters of the law who illustrated the Talmud, as Maimonides says in his preface.
„ The same author continues: in the year 469, the Jerusalem Talmud was finished by the Jews. Rabbi Johanan presided over the work, arranging that doctrine into almost as many book titles as are contained in the Babylonian version, though the books are much more concise, according to the Hebrew Chronicles.

„ Around the year 909, the Miramolinus <note>A corruption of 'Amir al-Mu'minin,' a title for the Caliph</note> of the Saracens sent naval forces from Cordoba under the leader Auidamaim to harass Christian ships and coastal cities. Of these, Rabbi Shemariah was sold in Egypt to the Alexandrians, and Rabbi Chushiel in Africa to the people of Kairouan—which was then the most powerful of the western Saracen provinces—where he fathered Rabbi Hananel, who upon his death left ten thousand gold pieces in his coffers.
