In the year of salvation 1002, Rabbi Hai Gaon lived in Babylonia; he was the most excellent of the <term>Geonim</term> <note>original: "Gheonim"; the title for the heads of the Babylonian academies</note>, that is, the Talmudic legal experts, and the last of the House of David and the royal blood of Jeconiah. Yet he was not the "Prince of the Exile" <note>The Exilarch, or secular leader of the Jewish community in Babylon</note>, because neither he nor his parents wished to purchase that office with money from the Muhammadan Kings in whose region they lived as exiles. He administered the Jewish school for forty years. According to the same Rabbi Abraham in the *Book of Tradition*, the Muhammadan King fixed Rabbi Sherira, the father of Rabbi Hai Gaon, to a gibbet <note>A gallows; he was executed</note> after confiscating his goods. — In the same place.

At that time, Rabbi Samuel the Priest <note>Samuel ben Hofni Gaon</note>, son of Hophni, was celebrated and wrote many books.

Around the year 1000, there was a famous Academy of the Saracens in Babylon, in which the disciplines—especially Medicine and the astrology of the Chaldeans, Arabs, Persians, Egyptians, and Jews, and others of the Indians—were taught. *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book 3, chapter 34.

Al-Mansur <note>The de facto ruler of the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba</note> was reigning in Spain and Mauritania when Rabbi Enoch was professing the Talmud with great celebrity at Córdoba, cultivating the Hebrew Academy begun by his father in the year of our Lord 995.

Around the year 1020, Rabbi Hezekiah succeeded to the school of Rabbi Hai Gaon in Babylonia, but due to the slander of his own people, he was killed two years later by the Saracen king along with his entire family, with the exception of two sons who fled to Spain to Rabbi Joseph the Levite <term>Ha-Nagid</term> <note>The "Prince" or leader; Joseph ibn Nagrela</note>, until a persecution was stirred up in the kingdom of Granada. Rabbi Joseph himself perished, according to Rabbi Abraham in the *Book of Tradition*, namely in the year of Christ 1064. Thus says Rabbi Joseph the Priest in the *Chronicle of the Kings of France and Turkey*.

With this Rabbi Hezekiah, the Geonim—that is, the Talmudic legal experts—ceased, as did the Babylonian schools which had previously been so famous that Jews from the West itself, from Spain, Africa, Egypt, and Palestine, would send their sons there for the sake of study.

Then in Spain, Rabbi Solomon—whom Ibn Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a prolific scholar and poet</note> (on Genesis 3) calls *Baal Hassirim Hassekulim*, that is, the "Master of Songs of certain and constant measure"—seems to have flourished. For it is said he refuted certain opinions of Rabbi Samuel, son of Hophni, who was then living in Babylon. Thus, around these times, the Poetics of the Hebrews began, which today utilize the <term>Yated</term> <note>original: "Iathed"; meaning a 'peg' or long syllable</note> and the <term>Tenuah</term> <note>original: "Tenuhoth"; meaning 'movement' or short syllable</note>, that is, spondees and syllables with rhythms.

In the year of salvation 1121 <note>This date is likely an error in the source or transcription, as Hai Gaon died in 1038</note>, Rabbi Hai Gaon perished in Babylonia, the last and most skilled of the interpreters of the Talmudic rhapsody, so much so that all students of the law walk in his light from the rising of the sun to its setting. Indeed, with him, the Hebrew schools in the East were almost extinguished—those to which the Jews formerly sent their sons from Egypt, Palestine, Spain, and finally the entire West—and were thereafter transferred into Spain. Rabbi Abraham in the *Book of Tradition*.

The *Targum* <note>The Targum refers to the Aramaic translations or paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible, which were used when many Jews no longer spoke Hebrew fluently.</note> was composed while the kingdoms of the Babylonians, Greeks, Romans, and Persians ruled over Judea. This occurred nearly three hundred years after the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, a fact openly verified by Gorion's son <note>Refers to the author of the *Josippon*, a medieval history of the Jews often attributed to a descendant of Josephus</note> in his Hebrew and Greek history, by Rabbi Nathan in his *Aruch* <note>A famous 11th-century dictionary of the Talmud and Midrash</note>, by Elias Levita in the preface to his Hebrew dictionary and in his Chaldean <note>Chaldean was a common term used by Renaissance scholars to refer to the Aramaic language</note> lexicon, by Sebastian Münster in his small book titled *Perusch Saperufchin*, and by Michael Neander toward the end of his *Grammatical Questions* on the Hebrew language; see what I deduce hereafter in the chapter on the Chaldean language.

## On the various sects of the Hebrews, their Rabbis, and their synagogues. CHAPTER 9.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring floral and scrollwork motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

It seems to me very appropriate to treat in this place, and in the subsequent chapters, the various sects of the Hebrews—their Rabbis, Kabbalists, and Talmudists—before entering into the origin, greatness, perfection, and decline of the Hebrew language. This is especially necessary because we mention the opinions of the said Rabbis, Kabbalists, and Talmudists at every turn in this treatise. To enter into the matter without repeating what we have deduced above, we will presuppose that Josephus, in Book 13, Chapter 18, and Book 18, Chapter 2 of his *Antiquities of the Jews*, and Book 2, Chapter 7 of the *Jewish War*, writes that in his time the Hebrews who were lovers of the wisdom of their country were divided into three sects: namely, the Essenes, the Sadducees, and the Pharisees. All were diverse and dissimilar in their garments and ways of living. He adds that there was also a fourth sect proceeding from a certain Judas the Galilean, which agreed in everything and in every way with the sect of the aforementioned Pharisees. This is confirmed by Philo the Jew in the book he wrote on his nation; Saint Jerome in his book of Hebrew traditions; Hegesippus in Book 1, Chapter 12; Eusebius in Book 8 of his *Preparation*; Caelius in Book 5, Chapter 9 of his *Various Lessons*; Andreas Osiander in Chapter 5 of his *Gospel Harmony*; Sixtus of Siena in Book 2 of his *Holy Library*; Gabriel du Préau in Volume 1 of *The State and Success of the Church*; Gilbert Génébrard in Book 2 of his *Chronography*; and Joseph Scaliger in Book 6 of his *Correction of Time*.

On the contrary, Epiphanius in Volume 1 holds that these Hebrews were divided into Sadducees, Scribes, Pharisees, Hemerobaptists <note>A group whose name means "day-baptizers," known for daily ritual washings</note>, Nazarenes, Ossenes, and Herodians. Tertullian speaks of these in Chapter 45 of his *Prescription Against Heretics*: "I say nothing of the heretics of Judaism—I mean Dositheus the Samaritan, who first dared to reject the prophets as if they had not spoken by the Holy Spirit; I say nothing of the Sadducees, who, rising from the root of this error, dared in this heresy even to deny the resurrection of the flesh" <note>original: "taceo Iudaismi hereticos Dositheũ inquam Samaritanum, qui primus ausus est prophetas quasi non in spiritu sancto locutos repudiare, taceo Saducæos, qui ex huius erroris radice surgẽtes, ausi sunt ad hanc hæresim, etiam resurrectionem carnis negare"</note>. And Justin Martyr adds the Merists, Genists, Hellenists, and Galileans. Suidas mentions those he calls in his Greek language the *Therapeutae* <note>original: "θεραπεύται"</note>, meaning "worshipers" or "healers." The same Epiphanius also makes mention of four sorts of sectaries among the Samaritans: namely, the Essenes, Sebueans, Gorothenians, and Dositheans.

# History of the Origin of 

André Osiander <note>A German Lutheran theologian known for his work on Gospel harmonies</note>, in chapter 15 of his *Gospel Harmony*, speaks of seven types of Pharisees according to the Jewish Talmud. The author of the *Bundle of Times* <note>original: "Faifceau des temps", referring to the *Fasciculus Temporum*, a popular 15th-century world chronicle</note> adds to these the Arboneans and Genistes, as confirmed by François de Belleforest in book 2, chapter 4 of his *Universal History*. Carlo Sigonio, in book 5, chapter 11 of *The Hebrew Republic*, provides a deduction of other sects among the said Hebrews, distinct from those previously mentioned. A certain individual named Otto Heurnius <note>original: "Otthon Henonius", a Dutch physician and philosopher</note>, in his *Antiquities of Barbarian Philosophy*, in the treatise titled *Indicus*, chapters 21 through 25, discusses this quite extensively, even speaking of the Rechabites <note>original: "Recabees", a biblical group known for their asceticism</note> and their successors the Essenes or Hossiens; as does Gilbert Génébrard on pages 197 and 198 of the second book of his *Chronography*.

Regarding the Hebrew Rabbis, we learn that the Hebrews have always named those of the greatest and most eminent knowledge among them *Rabbanim* <note>original: "רבנים"</note>, which is to say masters or personages of great dignity. In fact, he who among the Hebrews possesses great doctrine in the Holy Scripture is always called *Rabbi* <note>original: "רבי"</note>, master; and among the Chaldeans <note>A common term for Aramaic speakers in this period</note> *Rabbon* <note>original: "רבון"</note>, which means the same. These words derive from the root *Rab* <note>original: "רב"</note>, which in Latin signifies "great" or "much" <note>original: "multus"</note>. The force and virtue of this root is explained in several places in the Talmud, in the *Tishbi* <note>original: "Thesbyte"</note> of Elias Levita, and in the discourse of Angelo Canini on the explanation of passages from the New Testament. For the specific explanation of these words mentioned above, we refer to the account of Porchetus <note>Porchetus Salvaticus, a 14th-century monk who wrote against Jewish theology</note> in part 1, chapter 2 of his *Victory Against the Jews*, where he states that Rabbi Nathan said the following in the Talmud:

> The word Rabbi is attributed to the Sages of the land of Israel, upon whom hands 
> were laid in the assemblies and councils of the Hebrews. This is said because of 
> the laying on of hands by the eldest and most senior, who place their hands upon 
> certain individuals and name them "Rabbi," my master. These Hebrews grant 
> this created and initiated Rabbi the power to judge cases that merit 
> punishment—a ceremony which is still practiced today in the promotion of 
> Jewish Rabbis. Furthermore, we find in the same Talmud the terms *Rabban*, 
> *Rabbana*, and *Rabbon*. The word *Rabbon*, which is pure Syriac <note>Aramaic</note>, 
> does not signify merely a simple master or Lord, but one who is called by 
> the Greeks "absolute ruler" <note>original: "$\alpha\upsilon\tau\omicron\k\rho\alpha\tau\omega\rho$" (autokratōr)</note>, and by our legal scholars, "he who 
> possesses pure command" <note>original: "ille qui habet merum imperium", a legal term for supreme jurisdictional power</note>. Even when the Hebrews mention God 
> in the *Mishnah* <note>original: "Mischne"</note>, they use the word *Ribbon* <note>original: "רבון"</note>. This is why Mary 
> Magdalene greeted our Lord Jesus Christ, raised from death to life, by the

...abbreviations of the Hebrews, and *Gilbert Génébrard* <note>A 16th-century French Benedictine scholar and Hebraist</note> at the end of his annotations on the Hebrew book *Seder Olam Zuta* <note>A small 9th-century chronicle of Jewish history</note>, both of whom assert that the word <term>Rab</term> <note>original: "Rab", meaning "great" or "master"</note> was in former times attributed to the sages and doctors of Babylon; the word <term>Rabbi</term> to those of the land of Israel; <term>Rabban</term> or <term>Rabbana</term> to the sages of the house of David; and <term>Mar</term> or <term>Mor</term> to the sages of Babylon who were patriarchs and governors of the exiles. *Elias Levita* <note>A famous Renaissance-era Hebrew grammarian</note> in his book *The Tishbi* writes: "They use Mar for Rabbi or Rab; and Mar is said of everyone who is from Babylonia, while Ribbi is used for anyone from the land of Israel. There are those who are accustomed to pronounce it Mor with the vowel *Holem*; but if that were so, I wonder why it is not written with the letter *Vav*." <note>original Latin: "Mar, dicunt rabbi, rab & Mar dicitur omnis qui est de Babylonia, ribbi, vero quicunque est de terra Israel, & sunt qui pronunciare solent Mor cum Holem quod si ita est, miror ergo qui fiat quod non scribatur cum vau."</note> See the same author in his interpretation of the words *RAB* and *RABAZ*. *Riccoldo da Monte di Croce* <note>original: "F. In the time of our Lord Jesus Christ, the synagogue of Jerusalem flourished, which Alexander the Great favored with several privileges, according to *Josephus* and *Eusebius* in their works. *Epiphanius* <note>Bishop of Salamis</note> in his book on weights and measures makes mention that the Jewish synagogue did not cease to continue after the destruction of Jerusalem. *Saint Jerome*, writing to Pammachius, writes that Pompey, after the Mithridatic War, held the synagogue of Antioch in great reverence, and that he was taught in Antioch by one *Apollinaris of Laodicea* from this synagogue, which is mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 13. Besides this one, there was another of equally great honor and authority in the city of Ephesus, where, in addition to the Rabbis and <term>Archisynagogues</term> <note>Leaders of the synagogue</note>, there were very great and excellent doctors in the interpretation of Holy Scripture, as *Justin Martyr* confirms in his dialogue against the Jew *Trypho*. There was also a synagogue in Caesarea, which the Romans exempted from guardianships and public charges, as can be seen in the law *sed & reprobare* in the Digest *on the excuses of guardians*; and in that place *Origen* taught the Holy Scriptures, according to *Eusebius* in book 6, chapter 10.

The first beginning of the institution of these synagogues among the Jews was during the Babylonian captivity, as written by *Carlo Sigonio* in book 2, chapter 8, of *The Hebrew Republic*, since which beginning they were continued both in Judea and in several other regions for many centuries, according to the account of the same author in book 5, chapter 10 and those following. At present, when the Jews wish to leave their synagogue, their service being completed in all points, in place of our *Benedicamus Domino* <note>Let us bless the Lord</note>, the Minister is accustomed to say this: "May He who makes peace on high, in His high manor, also make peace upon us and upon all the people of Israel." To which the congregation responds, "Amen," and while retreating three steps backward—at the first of which they bow toward the right hand, at the second to the left, and at the third forward—this denotes nothing else...

Regarding the <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>original Hebrew: סנהדרין; the supreme council of ancient Israel</note>, these were, according to the testimony of Rabbi Moses Hadarshan <note>An 11th-century scholar from Narbonne</note> in his commentaries on Genesis, seventy-two elderly and ancient personages, otherwise called ordinary judges, established and ordained by Moses among the Jews in every city under their power and dominion, as seen in the Book of Numbers, chapter 11. These men dispensed justice to those who requested it at the city gates, as stated by Elias Levita in his *Tishbi* and Pietro Galatino <note>An Italian Renaissance theologian and Hebraist</note> in Book 4, chapter 5 of *Secrets of the Catholic Faith*. These Sanhedrin taught and explained to the common people the most arduous and difficult cases and trials to judge, and exercised justice in various ways, as is amply contained in the Hebrew book titled *Sanhedrin*, of which Porchetus <note>Porchetus de Salvaticis, a 14th-century Genoese monk</note> makes ample mention in Part 1, chapter 2 of his *Victory Against the Jews*. They were first ordained and instituted by the Prophet Moses, as can be seen in Exodus chapter 17, Numbers chapter 11, and Deuteronomy chapter 16. In ancient times, they were called in the Hebrew language <term>Sanhedar</term> <note>original: סנהדרי</note>, a word proceeding from the Greek term—for the Greeks call the benches (upon which the judges sit) *synedria* <note>original Greek: συνεδρια</note>. Regarding this, the aforementioned Elias Levita, a Jew by nation, in his *Tishbi*, in the explanation of this word *Sanhedar*, spoke the following words:

> "Sanhedar, seventy; the seventy elders of the Great Consistory which was in Jerusalem were called Sanhedrin. It is also often used in the Hagiographa <note>The 'Holy Writings,' the third section of the Hebrew Bible</note>, as in 'in the assembly of the elders,' the Targum says 'and in the Sanhedrin of the wise.' Likewise, 'Boaz went up to the gate,' the Targum says 'to the gate of the house of judgment,' which was known to be the Sanhedrin; and there are many such instances. Nor is it found in the singular number. It is clearly a Greek word: for the Greeks call the benches (upon which the judges sit) a 'seat of judgment' <note>original Hebrew/Latin: מושב דין / subsellia</note>, to which Psalm 122 alludes: 'For there the seats are set for judgment.' # History of the Origin of [the Hebrew Language]

...Adam made and composed during his life a book in his Hebrew language on all the virtues and properties of the planets. Knowing through a prophetic spirit that the world was to be ravaged by the universal Flood, he placed and situated it within a strong and hard dressed stone, which he sealed in such a way that the waters could not spoil or rot it in any way. He did this so that in the future, those who remained after the said Flood—and their children and successors—might see and read it. The great Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure often identified as a combination of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth; he was considered the author of the *Hermetica*.</note> found this stone in his time and broke it open, taking the book he found enclosed within. He made use of it and was aided by it in many beautiful and good things. This same book was once in the hands and power of Saint Thomas <note>Likely referring to the legendary "Gospel of Thomas" or various apocryphal traditions associated with the Apostle Thomas's travels to the East.</note>, who performed infinite wonders and miracles with it, which is confirmed by Antonio de Torquemada <note>A Spanish writer (c. 1507–1569) whose *Hexameron* is a collection of dialogues on natural history and the supernatural.</note> in the third day of his *Hexameron*. By these aforementioned remarks, we may learn and know that Hebrew letters were in use long before Abraham and Moses, regardless of what Eusebius says in Book 9, Chapter 4 of his *Preparation* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea's *Praeparatio Evangelica*.</note>, citing Eupolemus and Artapanus—even though Philo, a Jew by nation and a man of great authority among his people, attributes the invention of these letters solely to the Patriarch Abraham.

But this must be understood with a modification: namely, that they were first invented by Adam, or at least by his sons or grandsons in the first age of the world before the Flood, and preserved by Noah and his children and successors until the time of the aforementioned Abraham, and then to Moses. This is agreed upon by the Hebrew Kabbalists <term>Cabalists: Practitioners of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism that seeks to find hidden meanings in the Hebrew scriptures.</term>, who assert that these Hebrew letters were the first in this entire universe, and that they are divine and formed by the very hand of the great Eternal God even before the creation of the world. The same Hebrew Kabbalists hold that the writing of God, which is Hebrew, has been for all time in the external connectivity of the machine of the world. Rabbi Gerondense <note>Referring to Nahmanides (1194–1270), also known as the Ramban, who was from Girona.</note> and other Rabbis, of whom I make ample mention in this present chapter and in the subsequent chapters, agree with this.

Certain other authors report that the ancient Hebrews had several different kinds of characters. The first belonged to those who were very old and ancient, used and practiced by Moses and the Prophets, which must not be divulged or demonstrated to mortal men.

The last kind are those given to the Patriarch Abraham at the crossing of the river, when he departed from Chaldea to come into the land of Canaan.

The Hebrew Rabbis, in this regard, write concerning the first chapter of Genesis—"In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth"—that this refers to the matter of both, from which He afterwards formed the Heaven and Earth themselves. To the former, He gave form on the second day when He said, <term>Rakia</term> <note>Hebrew: הרקיע. From a root meaning to beat out or spread thin, like metalwork.</note> or <term>the firmament</term> <note>Greek: τὸ στερέωμα (stereōma); Latin: Firmamentum.</note>, "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it make a distinction between the waters and the waters." This refers to the expanse, or the deployed curtain of all the heavens, of which it is later said in the same chapter of Genesis: "God called the heavens Rakia." This is a word which, according to some of these Rabbis, does not signify "firmament" (as the author of the common version <note>Referring to the Latin Vulgate translation.</note> translated it), but rather the "ball and mass of all the heavens." This seems to be clearly proven by the subsequent words of the aforementioned first chapter of Genesis: "God made two great lights, and the stars, and set them in the Rakia." George the Venetian <note>Francesco Giorgio (1460–1541), a Franciscan friar and Christian Kabbalist known for his work *De Harmonia Mundi*.</note> agrees with this interpretation in Book 3, Chapter 1 of his *Harmony of the World*. Conforming to this, Sebastian Münster <note>A German cartographer and Hebrew scholar (1488–1552).</note> in his commentaries on the Hebrew Bible has said that the word *Rakia* does not signify the firmament, but an "extension," following what is carried in Holy Scripture: "He stretched out the heavens like a skin." In fact, God made from the waters a very extended thing, together with the spheres; these, like the supreme heaven created first by Him, the Hebrew Scripture calls <term>Shamaim</term> <note>Hebrew: שמים.</note> and the Greeks call <term>Ouranon</term> <note>Greek: οὐρανον.</note>. It is true that the Hebrews name the machine of the inferior heavens <term>Sovev</term> <note>Hebrew: סובב, meaning "that which surrounds" or "revolves."</note>. Reuchlin <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a pioneering German humanist and scholar of Greek and Hebrew.</note>, also known as Capnio of Pforzheim, in Book 3 of his *Kabbalah of the Jews*, leaves 78 and 85, says of it what follows: Isaiah:

> "Creating the heavens and stretching them out, establishing the earth and what sprouts from it, giving breath to the people upon it, and spirit to those who walk on it." <note>original: "Creans cœlos & extendens eos, firmans terram & quæ germinant ex ea, dans flatum populo, qui est super eam, & spiritum calcantibus eam, seu ambulantibus in ea."</note> These things are directed by the influences of angels and spheres, and this whole is called the <term>World of the Sephirot</term> <note>original: עולם הספירות (Olam ha-Sefirot), the realm of the ten divine attributes or emanations in Kabbalah.</note>, that is, the age of elements; and in it is man, who is called the <term>Primordial Adam</term> <note>original: אדם קדמון (Adam Kadmon), the first spiritual prototype of humanity.</note>, that is, the "small age" which the Greeks call the <term>microcosm</term>, that is, the lesser world, or more correctly, the small world. For in man himself shine the properties of all creatures, both the highest and the lowest. God made the firmament of heaven—according to Rabbi Eliezer—from the light of His created garment. For God was clothed in ten garments when He created the world, as the Kabbalists say, and from the light of His final garment He took and created the heavens—not indeed the sensible ones, but those invisible and intellectual heavens, that is, spiritual entities of which the Psalmist says: *The heavens declare the glory of God*. There, the word is not written simply as <term>Shamaim</term> <note>original: שמים, referring to the orbicular or physical heavens.</note>, as Rabbi Ama notably observed in the book of secrets regarding Psalm 19, but rather as <term>Ha-Shamaim</term> <note>original: השמים</note> with the article *ha* added, just as in the summary argument of Genesis one reads: "In the beginning God created Ha-Shamaim," that is, those exalted heavens, those famous ones, those admirable ones never seen, nor to be seen by mortal eyes. For the other heavens, which are not written with the article *ha*, are indeed the firmament, but they are still called by the name of heaven; wherefore it is written, "and God called the firmament heavens," and it is called the firmament of the invisible heaven itself, they say, which is called the "heaven of heavens," from which follows: "Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven." Surely that extension, like a skin, as if inscribed with letters by the lights and stars, is called *Rakia* because of its local expansion, which we call "firmament" because of its firmness, and so forth.

The great Origen in his commentaries on the first chapter of Genesis, held that in what is carried in the Hebrew Holy Scripture—namely, "That the luminaries of heaven be for signs"—this tacitly gives us to know that they signify, and are effectual causes insofar as God wills it, and that they are like an open book which contains in writing all things to come: which one can even prove by the Stars, which very often signify what has passed, but that this book cannot easily be read and understood by human eyes and spirit.

In this sequence, <term>Albert the Great</term> <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prolific medieval scholar and philosopher.</note> in chapter 34 of his *Mirror* names the starry sky, with good reason, the **universal book**, which according to the Psalmist is stretched out like a skin of parchment, in which the first mover and first cause has written and placed the second causes, so that they might engender other causes, renewing and continuing nature and prime matter; just as after Pliny (book 1, chapter 3 of his *Universal History*), it is deduced very amply by Johannes Stoeffler, a German, in his commentaries on the *Sphere of Proclus* (chapter on celestial signs), Sixtus Senensis (book 2 of his *Holy Library*), and Guillaume Postel in his treatise on the configuration of celestial signs.

And without stopping too long at these beautiful and curious Kabbalistic researches, we will only report that St. Augustine (book on *True Religion*, chapter 3, and on Psalm 41, question 45), Prosper (against the *Collator*, chapters 14 and 26), and St. Ambrose (Epistle 84 to Demetrius) have called the world and the parts thereof **Pages and popular instructions**, exposed to the sight of everyone, inasmuch as the contemplation of the members and parts of this Universe raises our souls and our spirits to God; thus in chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Hebrews it is stated that the ages <note>original: "siecles", often translated as "worlds" or "eons" in this theological context.</note> are like clear mirrors of the divinity, which otherwise stays in secret and hidden within itself. # Languages of this Universe.

The Hebrews assert that these characters were found on a statue on the banks of the **Jordan River**, upon which were engraved the names of the children of **Israel** when they crossed that same Jordan river, as is recorded in the book of **Joshua**. This is confirmed by **Abraham de Balmis** <note>original: "Abraham de Palmis," an Italian Jewish physician and scholar (c. 1440–1523) known for his work on Hebrew grammar</note>, a Jew by nation, in his grammatical observations as reported by **Theseus Ambrosius** <note>Teseo Ambrogio degli Albonesi (1469–1540), a pioneering linguist of the Renaissance</note> in his appendix on several and diverse languages, saying:

> **Augustinus Pantheus** <note>Giovanni Agostino Panteo, a Venetian priest and author of the alchemical work Voarchadumia contra alchimiam (1530)</note> of Venice, a priest, mentions four Hebrew alphabets in his *Voarchadumia*: the first is the common one, which everyone uses everywhere. The second was granted by Almighty God to **Moses** on Mount **Sinai**. The third was granted to **Abraham** at the crossing of the river. The fourth, which is older than the others, was handed down to **Enoch**; it follows the order and number of our alphabet but includes three additional aspirated letters: *Ch*, *Ph*, and *Th*. **Abraham de Balmis**, a Hebrew doctor, in his grammar printed some time ago by **Daniel Bomberg**, knew only two Hebrew alphabets: the common one and the "crossing of the river" <term>Transitus Fluvii</term>. **Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa**, in his books on *Occult Philosophy*, reported that the **Cabalists** have various ways of forming characters. Besides the two mentioned alphabets, he says there is another "celestial script" among the Hebrews (just as astrologers are accustomed to drawing images of signs from the patterns of stars), where they show the letters of their alphabet placed and figured among the stars. There is another script which they are accustomed to calling ***Malachim*** or ***Melachim***, meaning the writing of "angels" or "kings." Having thus recounted six kinds of Hebrew letters, I thought it worthwhile to add to our appendix other characters of the Hebrews that should by no means be disregarded, excerpted from various authors of high repute. Among the books of **Antonio de Fantis** of Treviso <note>A 16th-century physician and editor of philosophical texts</note>, once an excellent philosopher and astrologer, I remember seeing the works of **Raziel**, the ***Picatrix*** <note>A famous medieval grimoire of astrological magic</note>, **Bailum**, **Hermes**, **Pietro d'Abano**, **Solomon**, and that interpreter **Apollonius**, and many others. From these, as if from a living and blooming meadow, I gathered the flowers of various letters and diverse characters. I read those books diligently—before they passed into the power of **Vulcan** <note>original: "Vulcani potestatem"; a poetic reference to being burned or destroyed</note> by our fathers, into whose hands they came by will—for no other reason than to transcribe the various figures of those letters. Indeed, in the second treatise where **Raziel** <note>Referring to the Sefer Raziel HaMalakh, a practical Kabbalah grimoire</note> speaks of precious stones, he rejects the opinion of those who say the twenty-two letters he discusses were invented by **Gamaliel**. He asserts that the angel **Raphael**, in the book called the *Book of Fire*, gave them written to **Adam** the first-formed, and for this reason, the sons of Adam cannot reject them; the figures and names of these letters are written below.

We have represented above the characters of which we made mention earlier.

Following what is said above, we will therefore remark that there are two other sorts of Hebrew characters; one of which consists of capital letters, extracted from the ancient marbles of the Holy Land, but slightly different from those declared above, which is represented here.

# History of the Origin of

...masters of astrology in the celestial world: where, beyond what can be attained and understood through the movement of the heavens from East to West, as well as the planets in their spheres moving in reverse, there presides what is called <term>Bathcol<gloss>original: "Bathcol", from the Hebrew "Bath Kol", literally "Daughter of a Voice," referring to a divine echo or inspiration</gloss></term>, the universal voice. This is interpreted by the *Zohar* and other most distinguished <term>Kabbalists<gloss>practitioners of Jewish mysticism</gloss></term> as the mediating and moving power of the entire universe: namely, the intellect of the Messiah or the Word—the <note>original: "Mens mentium"</note> "Mind of minds," as they call it—through whom the sovereign Father moves all things. 

The voices of the <term>Sibyls<gloss>ancient female prophets or oracles</gloss></term> were dedicated to the elementary and inferior world, for the conduct and regulation of human affairs. This was the reason the Romans embraced them more willingly, being entirely devoted and inclined to such matters. Thus, there were three principal disciplines among the ancient sages: 

First, that of the Hebrews, which tends only to conform our thoughts, actions, and behaviors to the straight path prescribed by the divine ordinances and precepts. These express how God wishes to be honored and served, and teach that we must maintain ourselves through a mutual and reciprocal charity from neighbor to neighbor, for the preservation of human society. Nothing on earth is more pleasing to the great monarch and ruler of the entire universe than this, according to the testimony of <term>Cicero<gloss>a famous Roman orator and philosopher</gloss></term> himself, despite him being a <note>original: "Ethnique & Payen"</note> Heathen and Pagan. 

The second discipline concerns the effects proceeding from the Heavens and the variety of their diverse influences here below. We are granted foresight of these so that we may prepare for them, accommodate ourselves to them, or oppose them: <note>original: "vir sapiens dominabitur astris"</note> "The wise man shall rule the stars," says the astrologer Ptolemy. This study was more specific to the Chaldeans, and later to the <term>Brahmins<gloss>Indian priests or scholars</gloss></term>, <term>Gymnosophists<gloss>ancient Indian philosophers who lived naked and practiced asceticism</gloss></term>, and other sages of the East who followed the first rays of the Sun daily at its rising from the Ocean, as if it had come to refresh itself from its bed and reinvigorate itself with new strength, just like a stag leaving its resting place. 

The third was of things constituted beneath the Heavens, within the elementary world, where the earth serves as a base and foundation. There, notions and omens cannot be better assigned than through those animals most closely joined by the spirit of life to the material mass of the body—such as the heart, liver, and other <term>internal organs<gloss>original: "precordes"</gloss></term> where this spirit has its principal seat and dwelling. This was for the interpretation of prodigies and similar signs that warn us of some notable disaster or calamity to come. This was the particular domain of the Egyptians and the Etruscans, who were excellent in <term>haruspicy<gloss>the ancient practice of divining the future from the entrails of sacrificed animals</gloss></term>. 

From these three mixed together, the <term>Magi<gloss>the "Wise Men" or ancient Persian priests</gloss></term> composed their own fourth discipline. In this, there appears a kind of "cross" of the world, in which the Hebrews hold the center; the Chaldeans and Indians the far East; the Celts and Etruscans the West; the Egyptians and Ethiopians the South; and the Scythians the North—acting as the four principal hinges of the earth, to which everything else relates.

# History of the Origin of Priests

masters of astrology in the celestial world: in which, beyond what can be grasped and understood by the movement of the heavens from East to West, as well as the Planets in their Spheres in the opposite direction, there presides that which is called the *Bathcol* <note>original: "Bathcol"; from the Hebrew *Bath Kol*, meaning "Daughter of a Voice." In Jewish tradition, this is a divine echo or heavenly voice that reveals God's will to mankind.</note>, the universal voice. The *Zohar* and other most distinguished Kabbalists interpret this as the mediating and moving power of the entire universe: namely, the intellect of the Messiah or the Word, the **Mind of minds** <note>original: "Mens mentium"</note>, as they call it, through whom the sovereign Father moves all things. 

The disciplines of the Sibylls were dedicated to the elementary and inferior world, for the conduct and regulation of human affairs; this was the reason the Romans embraced them more willingly, being entirely inclined and devoted to such matters. Thus, there were three principal disciplines among the ancient sages: 

First, that of the Hebrews, which aims only to conform our thoughts, actions, and behaviors to the straight path prescribed by divine ordinances and precepts, which express how God wishes to be honored and served; and that we must maintain ourselves through a mutual and reciprocal charity from neighbor to neighbor, for the preservation of human society. Nothing on earth is more pleasing to that great monarch and ruler of the entire universe than this, according to the testimony of Cicero himself, despite him being a Gentile and Pagan. 

The second discipline concerns the effects proceeding from the Heavens and the variety of its diverse influences here below; foresight of these is granted to us so that we may anticipate, accommodate ourselves to, or obviate them: **"The wise man will rule the stars,"** <note>original: "vir sapiens dominabitur astris"</note> says the astrologer Ptolemy. This study was more specific to the Chaldeans, then to the Brahmins <note>original: "Brachmanes"</note>, the <term>gymnosophists<gloss>Ancient Indian philosophers who lived in asceticism and were known as "naked wise men."</gloss></term>, and other sages of the East who followed the first rays of the Sun daily at its rising from the Ocean—as if it had come to refresh itself from its bed and reinvigorate itself with new strength, just like a stag leaving its resting place. 

The third discipline concerned things constituted beneath the Heavens, within the elementary world, of which the earth serves as the base and foundation. In this realm, omens and signs cannot be better assigned than in those animals most closely joined by the spirit of life to the material mass of the body, such as the heart, liver, and other <term>internal organs<gloss>original: "precordes"</gloss></term>, where this spirit has its principal seat and dwelling. This was for the interpretation of prodiges and similar signs, which warn us of some notable disaster or calamity to come. This was the particular domain of the Egyptians and the Etruscans, who were excellent in **haruspicy** <note>The ancient practice of divining the future by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals.</note>. From these three disciplines mixed together, the Magi compose their own fourth discipline. 

Thus, in this there appears a certain "crossroads" of the world, of which the Hebrews hold the center; the Chaldeans and Indians the edge of the Levant [East]; the Celts and Etruscans the West; the Egyptians and Ethiopians the South; and the Scythians the North—much like the four principal hinges of the earth, to which all the rest relates.

Some other authors have said that Moses possessed and made use of only two kinds of Characters [scripts]. One was that in which the two tables of the Decalogue [Ten Commandments] were written or engraved by the very hand and finger of God, as we shall deduce in great detail hereafter. These Characters are full of great and profound mysteries in their shapes, all depending on the **Yod** <note>original: "Iod"; the tenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. In Kabbalistic thought, the Yod is the fundamental point from which all other letters are formed, representing a spark of the divine.</note>, as will be said later. ### Languages of this World

...priests and Levites for spiritual matters only—though the <term>Sanhedrin<gloss>the supreme council and tribunal of the ancient Jewish nation</gloss></term> was not excluded from it either—which we should in no way doubt was the same script we have today. This is evidenced by those two Hebrew letters, **ס** (*Samech*) and **ם** (*Mem-final*), which remained miraculously intact within the fragments of the first tablets of the Law that were broken because of the golden calf. <note>According to Jewish tradition in the Talmud (Shabbat 104a), because these two letters are entirely closed shapes, they were held in place by a miracle when the Ten Commandments were engraved all the way through the stone.</note> This script was later released to the general public by **Ezra** upon the return from the Babylonian captivity. The other set of characters, which are said to belong to the **Samaritans**, were used for secular purposes such as justice, governance, trade, and similar worldly affairs; as such, they were the common script used by all the Jewish people. These were the same characters used by the ancient **Chaldeans**, which were later shared with the **Phoenicians**. From these—just as with the Hebrew—came **Syriac** and **Arabic**; from them was born **Greek**, and consequently **Latin**, which consists entirely (or nearly so) of Greek capital letters, as we shall describe later.

**Berosus** and **Saint Jerome** (in his prologue to Galatians, on chapter 9 of the Prophet Ezekiel, and in his preface to the Book of Kings) and the Hebrew author of the *Massekhet Sanhedrin* <note>original: "Mafechet sanhedrin", a volume of the Talmud dealing with judicial procedures</note> write that after the capture of Jerusalem and the restoration of the Temple under **Zerubbabel**, **Ezra** found the Hebrew letters which the Jews and we ourselves still use today. This seems to be confirmed by **Philo the Jew** in the second book of *The Life of Moses*. Some modern scholars agree with this more readily than with everything said above, seeing as the Hebrews and Jews before this Ezra used Samaritan characters, which I treat at length hereafter in a separate chapter on the Samaritan language. Even some of the Rabbis themselves agree with this, holding for a certainty that these Samaritan characters were the first in the world. They allege several reasons for this, among others that these Samaritans always possessed the **Torah**, or **Pentateuch** <note>the first five books of the Bible</note>, in this specific Samaritan script of theirs. Furthermore, the most ancient medals and pieces of gold, silver, and other metals—which have been found since time immemorial in the ruins and countless locations in Jerusalem and Palestine—were inscribed and engraved with Samaritan letters. This is confirmed by **Benito Arias Montano** in the third volume of his *Apparatus* (in the chapter on the Shekel, near the end) and after him by **François Louis** in his *Globe of the Canons and Secrets of the Holy Language and Divine Scripture*, chapter 1. 

This indicates that the Hebrew letters of today are not the same as the earliest and most ancient ones. This is because the Hebrews (or Israelites), during the revolt of the ten tribes when they broke away from the crown of Judah under **Rehoboam** (son of Solomon, with whom only the tribes of **Judah** and **Benjamin** remained), went to establish themselves under **Jeroboam** in the middle of Judea, in the region of Samaria at **Shechem**, the capital city of their entire state. There, they turned to idolatry. Because they kept the ancient Hebrew characters, Ezra—or his son **Jeshua** the High Priest—and the other Jews who had remained in the true religion of the great God, wished to use different letters and a completely diverse script so as to have nothing in common with them. Thus, they invented the current script at that time, while the Samaritans and their descendants and posterity to this day have always kept the ancient characters of their fathers and ancestors.

Several other matters of consideration on this subject are treated in Egidius Cardinalis <note>original: "Egidius Cardinalis," also known as Giles of Viterbo (1469–1532), a cardinal and scholar of the Kabbalah</note> in his *Book on Hebrew Elements*, Paulus Riccius in his medley <note>original: "farrago," meaning a miscellaneous collection</note> taken from the book of the *Talmud* of the Jews, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in his letter addressed to his unknown friend, Pietro Crinito <note>original: "P. Louys Viues Portuguaiz"</note> in book 1 of his *Globe of Canons and Secrets of the Holy Language and Divine Scripture*, chapter 1.

There are also other Hebrew characters, besides those represented in the figures above, which are always without any [vowel] points or accents, practiced and used by the majority of the Hebrew Rabbis in their commentaries and traditions. These are called the "running hand" <note>original: "lettre courante," referring to cursive script</note> because they are written more quickly than the preceding [square script], being less square and more rounded; for this reason, they lack such grace and visual pleasure. This is called the "small" or "minute" writing, or *Masquet* <note>original: "Masquet" or "Maschket"</note>, a word which in the Arabic language signifies "thin" or "extenuated," as was very well noted by Elia Levita <note>original: "Elias Leuita," a famous Renaissance Hebrew grammarian</note> in his *Tishbi* <note>original: "Thesbite"</note> in the interpretation of this word *Maschket*. Here are the forms of these: the first used by the Jews living in Germany <note>Ashkenazi cursive</note>, and the other by the Jews living in Spain <note>Sephardic cursive</note>, as confirmed by Sebastian Münster in his *Chaldaic Grammar*.

what the late Guillaume Postel <note>A 16th-century French polymath and mystic known for his obsession with universal harmony and world languages</note> had written about it in his treatise on the Phoenician letters, one should not be surprised by it, given the inconstant and mutable nature of men, who shift and change their handwriting every day, and even their printing styles. They write and print their books in one way at one time, and in another entirely different way at another time, seeking what is more proper, more beautiful, and more delicate. 

And because the Hebrews have no vowels arranged in alphabetical order, and because the consonants must serve that purpose—adorned and illustrated with points <note>referring to 'niqqud,' the system of dots and dashes used to indicate vowel sounds in Hebrew</note> according to their various positions and combinations—there is hardly a sequence of letters in this Hebrew language from which some meaning cannot be drawn, in all the ways they might be reversed or turned about. Furthermore, these letters are all square and without any ligatures <note>connections between letters</note>, unlike those seen in the very elegant—yet to some, unpleasant-looking—Syriac and Arabic scripts. This is to demonstrate that this Hebrew language has never had anything in common with those of other peoples and nations, but has always remained apart, like something separated from the rest of the generation of men. 

It is most certain that from the beginning of the world until the present, this language has never received any alteration or corruption in its dialect or way of speaking. On this matter, see Saint Jerome <note>The 4th-century priest who translated the Bible into Latin</note> in his prologue to the Prophet Jeremiah, in his last Epistle to Paula of Rome <note>original: "Paule Vrbique"</note>, and in his exposition on the third chapter of Zephaniah; Abraham de Balmes <note>original: "Abraham Balmenſis," an Italian Jewish physician and grammarian</note> in his treatise on Hebrew letters; Ludovico Carreto <note>original: "Carretius Iuif cõuerty," a 16th-century Jewish convert to Christianity</note> in his Hebrew Epistle addressed to his children; Johannes Reuchlin <note>original: "Iean Reuclin Capnion," a key German humanist who pioneered Hebrew studies among Christians</note> in his books on the Kabbalah of the Jews; Sebastian Nossenus <note>original: "Sebastian Nozenus," likely referring to the 16th-century Hebraist</note> in his treatise on the first lesson of Hebrew speech; Agostino Steuco <note>original: "Auguſtin Steuchus"</note> in his annotations on the 37th chapter of Genesis; Pero Mexía <note>original: "P. # History of the Origin of...

...we have been brought back to the Alphabet with much zeal; and Marranus, we have certainly become like children again; this is that Pythagorean rebirth <note>original Latin: "Palingenesia", referring to the concept of the soul's rebirth or the restoration of ancient knowledge</note> of yours, Philolaus. To which Simon said: "Do not reject it," he said, "it is indeed a great matter, and worthy of philosophers—if you believe your Plato—and not at all ridiculous, as it seemed to Socrates in the *Cratylus* <note>A dialogue by Plato regarding the origin of names and whether language is natural or conventional</note>, to know the letters. For we have nothing better," he says, "by which to judge the truth of the first names, 'since imitation [of essence] happens through syllables and letters, it is most correct to distinguish the elements first.' <note>original Greek: "ἐπεὶ ταῖς συλλαβαῖς τε καὶ γράμμασιν ἡ μίμησίς τυγχάνει οὔσας, ὀρθότατον ἐστὶ δι ελέσθαι τὰ στοιχεῖα πρῶτον"</note>"

From this, I think "elements" <term>elementa</term> were named as if they were "hyle-ments" <note>A wordplay suggesting the Latin word for elements comes from the Greek "hyle," meaning matter or substance</note>, that is, material things, from which the smallest things become the largest; as in that saying of Hesiod: "If you add a little to a little, and put it all together, a great pile will finally be made." 

"Go on, Simon," Philolaus said, "for everything you say is true; we were only joking in this conversation with your permission." 

Then Simon said: "I will pass to the numbers of the discipline of Arithmetic, which are designated by Hebrew letters. For there is no other language in the whole world whose letters show any numbers so perfectly. The newcomers among the Greeks, however, tried to imitate the Jews, so that they might similarly express numbers with their alphabet. But it was necessary for them to insert two extra figures for both the sixth and the ninetieth places, which figures are not literally from the order of the Alphabet. For these two signs, ϛ <note>stigma</note> and ϟ <note>koppa</note>, are the inventions of later men led by a desire for imitation, for which matter we cite the Homeric books as witnesses. Indeed, the Romans explain only a few numbers with letters, a matter about which you once read Priscian of Caesarea writing to Symmachus regarding numbers, weights, and measures."

"Let us therefore make four grades of numbers: the first is of digits (units), the second of tens, the third of hundreds, and the fourth of thousands. The first grade is noted by the figures of the Alphabet from Aleph to Teth. There are nine signs referring to the nine numbers individually, as is אב גד הו זחט <note>The Hebrew letters Aleph, Beth, Gimel, Daleth, He, Vav, Zayin, Heth, Teth</note>, that is: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine."

"The second order, of tens, contains these figures of the alphabet: יכ, למ, נס, עפ, צ <note>Yod, Kaph, Lamed, Mem, Nun, Samekh, Ayin, Pe, Tsadi</note>, that is: ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety."

"The third grade, of Hundreds, similarly has nine characters: קר ש ת ד ם ן ס ץ <note>Qoph, Resh, Shin, Tav, and the five final forms of letters used to reach 900</note>, that is: one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, five hundred, six hundred, seven hundred, eight hundred, and nine hundred."

"The fourth grade is of thousands, in which one must return to the figures of the earlier numbers, although they ought to be larger in stature, so that it is called a 'Great Aleph'; as if it were a broad Aleph, and it is pronounced with a *patha* <note>A Hebrew vowel mark</note> like the Italian 'A'. Thus a Great Beth signifies two thousand. From there up to nine thousand; finally, a Great Yod signifies ten thousand. In this order, some are accustomed to mark the figures with points <note>apices</note> to indicate their status. After this, they do not use figures but words, that is: 'a thousand thousands,' 'two thousand thousands,' and the rest."

"The Kabbalists <note>Jewish mystics</note> have greatly embraced this path of the alphabet of numbers; they say that two thousand years preceded the beginning before this world was made. This is because before the word 'Beginning' <term>Reshith</term>, the Scripture places a Great Beth, saying 'In the beginning' <term>Bereshit</term> <note>The first word of Genesis begins with Beth, which has the numerical value of 2; mystics interpreted the size of the letter as signifying 2,000 years of pre-creation existence</note>. Thus our wise men explain that passage in Proverbs 8: 'The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from then.' But whatever exceeds thousands is held in the place of the infinite. For the end of numbers in the sacred texts is thousands; just as when David wished to show the infinity of value in Psalm 119, he said: 'The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver,' that is, without number."

## On the Etymology of Hebrew Letters and Others.

### CHAPTER II.

<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap letter 'L' decorated with scrolling foliage and a small human figure standing amidst the vines.</image-desc>
The Hebrews call a letter in their language אות *Oth*, which is to say, essentially a "sign." In fact, this word אות *Oth* is a sign, as can be seen in Ezekiel chapter four; the plural of this word is אותיות *Hothijoth*, which is to say, "letters." It is defined as a sign of will imposed upon the human voice. In this regard, Saint Augustine, in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, said that the signs of words—which pass suddenly through the air when it is struck or pushed—were established by letters. And with good reason, Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, the 7th-century author of the first great medieval encyclopedia</note> in the third chapter of his *Etymologies* wrote that these are the indices and marks of things, and signs of words. The same Saint Augustine, in the second book of *On Order*, chapter 13, asserts that Grammar was named *Litteratura* <note>Literary or written learning</note> because of the letters which it professes to study; and in this place, that holy personage treated excellently the occasion for the invention of grammar and the distinction of letters, syllables, and verbs. Among the Latins, according to the aforementioned Isidore in the first book, chapter three of the said *Etymologies*, a letter is so called as if providing a path for readers <note>original Latin: "littera dicitur quasi iter legentibus præstans"</note>, or because it is repeated in reading <note>original Latin: "quod in legendo iteretur"</note>. Or else, according to Priscian, a letter is named from "litura" <note>smearing or erasing</note> because they are written and erased <note>original Latin: "littera à lituris, cùm scribuntur, & delentur, dicta"</note>. On this subject, one may see Caelius Rhodiginus in book 24, chapters 5 and 6 of his *Various Lessons*; Goropius Becanus in his *Heremathene*, book three, page 34 and following; and Pierre Grégoire in book 16, chapter 3 of his *Syntax of the Admirable Art*. Letters are also called "elements" <note>original Latin: "elementa"</note>, following the likeness or similarity of the physical elements, for just as elements are the first thing in the composition of any natural thing, and no reduction is possible except down to the elements, so too any language is composed of letters as if from elements <note>original Latin: "nam sicut elemēta sunt primùm quod est in cōpositione cuiusq; rei naturalis, nec fieri potest resolutio, nisi vsq; ad elemēta, ita etiā quodcūq; Idioma ex litteris tāquā ex elemētis cōponitur"</note>. According to Aristotle in book 1 of the *Poetics*, chapter 7, an element is an <margin>cc</margin> indivisible sound—not just any sound, but only that which is by its nature intelligible. <margin>cc</margin>

### On the Etymology of Hebrew and other letters.
#### CHAP. II.

The Hebrews call a letter in their language אות <note>original: "Oth"</note>, which is to say, essentially a sign: in fact, this word **Oth** is a sign, as can be seen in Ezekiel chapter four; the plural of this word is אותיות <note>original: "Hothijoth"</note>, which is to say, letters. It is defined as a sign of will imposed upon the human voice. In this regard, Saint Augustine, in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, said that the signs of words—which pass suddenly through the air when it is struck or pushed—were established by letters. And rightly so, Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, whose "Etymologiae" was the standard encyclopedia of the Middle Ages.</note> wrote in the third chapter of his *Etymologies* that these are the indices and marks of things, and signs of words. The same Saint Augustine, in the second book of *On Order*, chapter 13, asserts that Grammar was named *Litteratura* <note>original: "Litteratura," meaning literacy or the study of letters.</note> because of the letters which it professes to study; and in this passage, this holy personage has treated excellently the occasion for the invention of grammar and the distinction between letters, syllables, and verbs. Among the Latins, according to Isidore above in the first book, third chapter of the said *Etymologies*, a letter is called *littera* as if it were a "path for readers" <note>original Latin: "quasi iter legentibus præstans"</note> or because it is "repeated in reading" <note>original Latin: "quod in legendo iteretur"</note>; or else, according to Priscian, *littera* is named from "smears" <note>original Latin: "à lituris"</note>, because they are written and erased. On this subject, one may see Caelius Rhodiginus in books 24, chapters 5 and 6 of his *Diverse Lessons*, Goropius Becanus in his *Heremathene*, book three, page 34 and following, and Pierre Grégoire in book 16, chapter 3 of his *Syntax of the Admirable Art*. Letters are also called **elements** <note>original: "elementa"</note> after the likeness or similarity of the [physical] elements, for just as elements are the first things in the composition of any natural thing, and no reduction can be made except down to the elements, so also every language <note>term: "Idioma" (Language)</note> is composed of letters as if of elements. Furthermore, an element, according to Aristotle in book 1 of the *Poetics*, chapter 7, is: <margin>cc</margin> An indivisible sound, not indeed every sound, but only that which is by its nature intelligible. <margin>cc</margin>

The Kabbalists <note>original: "Cabalistes"</note> have been so speculative and curious as to weigh the various combinations of these Hebrew letters to reach the knowledge of the number of created things—which might well be calculated, but neither uttered nor almost comprehended, except by Him who knows the count of the stars and gives them all names; the hairs of a man's head, and the grains of all the sand of the sea, and the drops of rain. For from the diversity of the *ziouphs* <note>original: "ziouphs," likely a French transliteration of *zivugim*, meaning mystical couplings or pairings of letters.</note> or pairings and sequences of letters, without any mixture of points, there results a number that is as good as infinite to our eyes: **11,240,025,908,271,968,000,000**. If one wished to add the vowel points, the number could neither be expressed nor conceived by us mortals, even though **Archimedes** in his treatise **The Sand Reckoner** <note>original: "L'Arene"</note> presumed to find a way of counting that goes toward infinity. But that is reserved for God alone and surpasses the apprehension of His creatures. From Him, as from the archetype and first pattern in whom consist the supreme and primary sources, proceed secondarily the streams and channels—as the Kabbalists call them—flowing downward, and the primordial foundations of all things denoted by the four letters of the great ineffable name **Jehovah** <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH.</note> which represent the four elements. From there ultimately results all the diverse multitude of individuals caused by the variety of these first and second influxes and outpourings in all that has been produced, and will be produced until the end of the age. Furthermore, the book of *Bahir* <note>original: "Habbair"; the *Sefer ha-Bahir* or "Book of Brightness"</note>, or the *Elucidarius*, writes that the Hebrew letters can be paired with the human body, the accents with the spirit, and the points serving as vowels with the soul; for they lead the letters, which are silent by themselves, to some significance, just as the soul moves the spirits and the body in which they are immersed. Some of the modernizing Kabbalists say that the simple letters of the Hebrew alphabet denote the common people and the order of artisans and laborers who live from day to day by the work of their arms; the points serving as vowels represent the bourgeoisie who already possess some wealth and means; the words represent the nobility and the principal and most prominent citizens; the clauses represent the Princes and great Lords; and finally, the completed work represents the sovereign magistrate. Writing is a certain outpouring of the conceptions of our soul, which become incorporated into notes, marks, and sensible signs to manifest themselves peacefully to one another. This conception of thought is like a symbol of God the Father, the marks and notes of the incarnate Son, and the meaning contained beneath them of the Holy Spirit—as the aforementioned book confirms. Such writing presupposes reason, the most precious thing in the world, without which writing could not exist at all. All these preceding deductions demonstrate that it is no invented thing or something made for pleasure by the Hebrew Kabbalists to say and assure that the letters of the Hebrew scripture—in whatever way one wishes to fold, return, turn, and take them as situated in the alphabet—consist of number, weight, measure, sacraments, mysteries, and miracles. This is certainly confirmed by **Rabbi Simeon ben Jochai** <note>A 2nd-century tannaitic sage to whom the Zohar is traditionally attributed</note>, **Elkanah** <note>possibly referring to Elkanah ben Jeroham, a figure associated with Kabbalistic traditions</note>, and other Hebrew Rabbis who have strived not only to interpret all Hebrew sentences and words but also to give a reason for the smallest letters and figures of their alphabet, together with the points and accents placed below and above them. They prove this through infinite trials, which can teach and show the passage and opening to the decoration of all other curiosities and research that one might desire in this matter. It is a certain thing that eternal wisdom and truth have assured us that Holy Scripture must be anatomized and searched by us down to a single **Yod** <note>original: "Iod"; the smallest letter of the Hebrew alphabet</note>, which is like a small point, the least of all the Hebrew letters, yet their mother and matrix and the end and beginning of the members. The Jews hold this as indubitable, saying that they have always learned through their Kabbalah that there is no letter or tittle <note>original: "apicule"; referring to the smallest stroke or point in a letter</note> in their law upon which several great and high mountains do not depend—that is to say, several great, high, and arduous mysteries and miracles.

### CHAP. XIII.

The Hebrew Rabbis and Kabbalists <note>The Kabbalists are followers of Kabbalah, a school of thought in Jewish mysticism aimed at explaining the relationship between the eternal God and the mortal universe.</note>, in order to demonstrate that all the arts and sciences of the world are found comprised within the divine law—which is written and composed in the Hebrew language in the Old Testament—have taken it upon themselves to share with posterity the means and the method for attaining the knowledge of this contemplation. They say that the Holy Scripture in general can be understood, examined, and interpreted through four primary ways and manners: namely, *the literal*, *the moral*, *the allegorical*, and *the analogical*.

The first of these, being like the great beaten path and a very wide gate where all sorts of people may enter, and which can only demonstrate an outward appearance, is named by the said Hebrews in their language דֶּרֶךְ הַפְּשָׁט <note>original: "Derec hapefcat"; modern Hebrew: *Derech ha-Peshat*</note>, the level, extended, and smoothed path. The Roman doctors <note>Referring to Christian scholars and theologians of the Western Church.</note> call this the *historical sense*, as if they wished to say that the literal sense places before the eyes only the outside and exterior face, like the bark of trees or the skin that serves as clothing for the body. Within it, as in a painting or a large map, we can observe in the figures and characters arranged there the lives and deeds of those chosen and loved by God, as well as the wicked and the reprobate.

*The moral sense*, being more modest and cutting away much of the great license of the literal, has acquired among the Greeks the name ἠτικός <note>original: "etikos"; meaning "ethical" or pertaining to character</note>, and among the Latins that of *moral*, and among the Hebrews this fine title of מִדְרָשׁ <note>original: "Midraſz"; modern: *Midrash*</note> *search* (although it is a neighbor to allegory, and the term seems somewhat to confound it with it, as I shall say hereafter, and transfers the meaning and property to that which is called in Greek *tropologia* <note>Tropology is the use of figurative language or the moral interpretation of the Bible.</note>, so called because it teaches us the way to interpret the phrases, figures, and properties of words and sentences). It aims and tends toward this single goal: to tame and conquer the rebellions and revolts of the flesh, in order to acquire a simple and natural beauty.

*The allegory*, of which this latter is a species, is a sort of inversion or trope <note>A "trope" is a figurative use of a word or expression.</note> that occurs when we turn a word away from its proper and natural meaning to use it in a sense that is improper and distant from its nature. It differs from a metaphor in that a metaphor is attached to one or two words at most, whereas *the allegory* is a continuous translation, so called because it expresses and designates things other than what the words propose. This is considered diversely, either according to history or according to the world, and is found based on the figure of the Church, or on the symbols of both numbers and Hebrew letters; from this, it follows that it is either *historical*, *worldly*, *figurative*, or *symbolic*, all of which I shall mention hereafter when the need arises. Therefore, *the allegory* belongs to an entire and perfect sequence of speech, and relies entirely on similarities or comparisons—which cannot be between things that are conformable and fitting to one another, but rather those that take their source from the marriage of heaven and earth, and from corporeal, sensible, and perishable things, compared and related to those that are everlasting, invisible, and devoid of any bodily accident. We can also understand under the general name of the mystical and historical allegorical sense—as under its own genre—that which I have previously stated was named by the Hebrew interpreters *Midrash*, which I have before...

compared to <term>Tropology</term> <note>The "moral" interpretation of scripture, explaining how one should act.</note>, which in the judgment of many belongs to and consists entirely of doctrine. And although <term>Elias Levita</term> <note>A renowned 15th-16th century Hebrew grammarian and scholar who worked with Christian Hebraists.</note> understands under the word <term>Midrash</term> <note>original: "Midrasz"; a method of interpreting biblical stories to find deeper legal or moral truths.</note> everything that lies outside the terms and purposes of the literal letter, it is my opinion that we can very well pair it with Scholastic doctrine. This is because it is founded on the authority and tradition of the <term>Rabbis</term> and <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note>, just as our own school adheres and conforms in every way and in every place to the resolutions of the old Church Fathers. Under the scope of this word, the Hebrews include the **moral sense**, which declares the battle between the flesh and the soul: <term>Tropology</term>, which stirs the dispute between the letter and mystical intelligence; and **allegory**, which assembles and allies inferior things with superior ones. Allegory treats, as some assert, the War of the Church Militant against the agents of the devil—though in the opinion of these thinkers, this must be understood insofar as it draws its reasons and arguments from Ecclesiastical history, where the mystery of the Church is contained.

And so as not to cut our discussion too short here, we should understand that **Allegory** wanders and spreads throughout all of nature. Being aided and supported by two or three "strings," it hoists itself up through nature or above the heavens to communicate with the Angels, and then it is called *Theological*. Sometimes, sliding back down from there, it returns toward us and is called *Natural*. At other times, balancing between the two in the supreme region, it depicts various miracles of the middle and the "in-between," and it is called *Celestial*. In this way, it observes and maintains the "compositional method" while ascending, keeps the "analytical and dividing method" while descending, and follows the "definitive and bounding method" when it remains between two waters. 

There are still others who derive **contemplative prayer** from Allegory; the nature of such prayer is to completely hold back from everything of this world and its conversation, in order to strive for the ornament and divinity of the soul, having the gifts of the Holy Spirit as its subject. By this means, it would be distinguished from Tropology, near which they place it, in the same way that we discern the good religious and contemplative person from the secular man of the Church. For this reason, Tropology—as it is close to the **Moral Sense**, which has as its proposed goal the moral virtues (which consist, according to the opinion of the Philosophers, in action)—retains much of its nature. It seems to hold such a place among spiritual expositions as the intellectual virtues hold among those concerning morals and those named *Theological*. 

**Anagogy**, as a reduction or a "reconveyance," must be reported—just as from a Center and point which is everywhere in virtue and power, to a circumference which is nowhere—everything that we can see, touch, taste, smell, hear, understand, and love, stripped of its accidents. It leads to Him who, as the Father of eternal and sensible things, is nevertheless above all feeling, dwelling solitary in His Eternity. Up to this point, **affirmative theology** extends, and here, in abundance, the science of the **tree of the ten names** <note>The Sephirot of the Kabbalah, representing the ten attributes through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note> and divine dimensions is supported. To these, as if under ten universal categories, the reasons for all things are related. Above this, if we desire to fly, we enter into an abyss and are like lost and wandering souls—true scholars and apprentices in **negative theology**. The aforementioned Hebrew Rabbis and <term>Kabbalists</term> <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, the ancient Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation of the Bible.</note> since the earliest times have used, in place of numbers, the specific characters of their common and public Hebrew writing. The Greeks, in imitation of the Hebrews, similarly made their characters serve as numbers. In this regard, so that their *Iota* <note>The ninth letter of the Greek alphabet.</note>, which relates to the Hebrew *Yod* <note>The tenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet.</note>, might likewise be found in the tenth position (where it is otherwise only the ninth), they inserted into their alphabet the character ϛ <note>The Stigma, used as a numeral for 6.</note> in the sixth place, which serves as an abbreviation for *st*. And to mark the thousands, they use the capital letters in the very same order: which sufficiently shows that they borrowed many things from the Hebrews; or else they applied an acute accent to the lowercase letters.

This was first devised, so they say, by the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, whose traditions are nothing other than a true Hebrew Kabbalah. Regarding this, he employs that passage from Wisdom 11:
<margin>,, ,,</margin> *You have ordered all things in number, weight, and measure* <note>original Latin: "Omnia in numero, pondere, & menſura diſpoſuiſti." Even Aristotle and Ptolemy do not contradict this, freely admitting that letters mystically carry within them certain numbers which, in the proper names of persons, kingdoms, empires, cities, and republics, contain something of the secret of their fortunes and destinies. > *And they say names are so composed of letters,*
> *That some possess many numbers, and others few:*
> *Whenever they enter the uncertain dangers of battle,*
> *Where the larger number stands, victory favors,*
> *While the smallest sum reveals the omens of death.*
> *Thus they say Patroclus perished by Hector’s hand:*
> *Thus they say Hector soon fell to Achilles.*
> <note>translated from the original Latin verse in the text.</note>

Specifically, by taking the names of two people who wish to enter a duel or single combat, the one whose name’s letters surpass the other’s (according to the aforementioned calculation) will likewise obtain the victory. In experience, this happened to Hector, who put Patroclus to death and was shortly after killed by Achilles. ...the fire, and the foundation of the great man, through a most excellent alliance: all this proceeding from the anagrams, permutations, and regroupings of the letters of this word *Bereshit* <note>Hebrew: בראשית; the first word of Genesis, traditionally translated as "In the beginning."</note>. From this, Moses takes the occasion to represent the three worlds through the human body—namely the intelligible, the celestial, and the elementary.

By the head, where understanding, knowledge, and reasoning reside, he intended to denote the intelligible world. From the neck to the navel is the second part, where the heart dominates; it is the source of the heat of life and movement, just as the Sun acts in the heavens, which is held to be of fiery substance by reason of its purity and its continual agitation—by which means fire is here taken to represent the Heavens, as even *Anaxagoras* <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher.</note> used to say. The third and inferior part, from the navel downward, where the generative faculty resides, is the elementary world, beneath the sphere of the Moon, where generation and corruption occur.

And just as the feet are like a base and foundation upon which the whole body of man is placed, so also the elementary world—specifically the earth, which is the lowest portion of it—is here called the foundation. For it is put there to represent the entire mass of the low, corruptible elements by the same Moses at the very beginning of creation; and the poet Hesiod calls it the firm foundation of all things; Orpheus calls it the seat of the immortal world.

Then, finally, is added: *Through a most excellent alliance*, because these three worlds correspond harmonically to one another through a most well-tuned concord, which the philosopher Plato calls Love, Homer calls the golden chain, and Holy Scripture calls Jacob's ladder. From Psalm 48:10.</note>.

> For it pleased the Father that in him all fullness should dwell <note>Original Latin: "In ipso complacuit Patri, omnem plenitudinem inhabitare."</note>. 

All things being thus produced and the mass of the human race gathered together, from there was set apart the people whom God wished to choose for himself, called the congregation of Israel, represented by the *Tau* <note>The Hebrew letter Tav (ת).</note>. In this way, everything reported above regarding the sequence of these six letters of *Bresit* means nothing other than this: 
> *In wisdom, which is the Word and the Son of the sovereign* FATHER, *the first matter of all things was produced: then afterwards, from the inexhaustible source of all goods, form was given to them: and consequently everything was filled with the opulent goodness of God for the human race, and especially for his Elect.*

Such secrets and mysteries, and others still, are found almost everywhere in the scriptures, where they are hidden and concealed beneath the shell of the literal context, just as a secret meaning is hidden inside a cipher. But above all words is the most holy name, the Tetragrammaton יהוה <note>The four-letter name of God, often rendered as Yahweh or Jehovah.</note>, which could never be exhausted, no more than the true essence of God, which these four characters carry within them. These are ineffable to our sight and incomprehensible even to the nature of Angels; at this point, divinity withdraws to plunge itself into the vast abyss of its *En-soph* <term>Ein Sof</term> <note>A Kabbalistic term meaning "The Infinite," referring to God's essence before any self-manifestation.</note>, or infinity, which Orpheus and Hesiod call "the night." Allusion to this is also made in Isaiah chapter 16: 
> Make your shadow like the night in the midst of the noonday <note>Original Latin: "Pone quasi noctem vmbram tuam in meridie."</note>. 

In imitation of this, Plato constructed the greater part of his *Cratylus*, in which, among other divine names, Socrates examines that of Απολλων <note>Apollo.</note>, with no less mystery than the Kabbalists <note>Original: "Cabalistes."</note> do with the name of the sovereign God.
