Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and geographer.</note> agrees with this when he says that only those who are breathed upon by the divine spirit know how to predict specific details: because these depend upon universalities, which are in the first exemplar and the original essence behind God. And it is there that the Kabbalists <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism.</note> dwell and move about, deciphering the words of the Prophets who spoke through these enigmas and profound obscurities, so as not to reveal the secret wonders of God to the unworthy; besides the fact that these mysteries can hardly be manifested by human words, there being no terms sufficiently proper and emphatic to express them. Therefore, they have restricted themselves in this to certain types of ciphers—not of writing, but of figurative speech—removed from common usage. This is much like when one transposes or exchanges one letter for another, whereby the context becomes altered in such a way that it is no longer readable except to those who possess the alphabet. As for the *Bath Kol*, or "daughter of the voice" mentioned above <note>original Hebrew: *Bath Kol*. In Jewish tradition, this refers to a heavenly or divine voice that proclaims God's will.</note>: it was yet another kind of vocal cipher, not a silent one, but like one that might be set up for the hearing with the sound of trumpets or similar loud instruments that can be heard from afar, used in place of letters. This is just as signals are made for the sight, with lights by night and smoke by day, by means of which one can make one's thoughts understood to those under siege, or from one place to another. This artifice is quite common and of long standing, for Polybius, the Roman captain, makes mention of it, as reported by Girolamo Cardano in Book 12, Chapter 61, *On the Variety of Things* <note>original Latin title: *De Varietate Rerum* by the 16th-century polymath Cardano.</note>, where he recounts some of these devices, and again in Book 17, *On Subtlety* <note>original Latin title: *De Subtilitate*.</note>. This *Bath Kol* was therefore like a kind of Echo, or the resonance of a voice (as I have amply noted in the preceding chapter), which, coming to enter and strike back within certain cavities suited for this, came out from there with the air it struck, multiplied in several iterations—much like a ball which, for one strike against the ground, will bounce back several times over. In a similar case, these visions are like images which, proceeding from the archetype, come to reverberate in His creatures, neither more nor less than the rays of the Sun; these, scattered through the air, are gathered in a hollow mirror or a vial full of water into a figure resembling the sun, and from there are spread out again by reflection as in the preceding example. And when they pass through some tinted glass, they take on the appearance of the color imprinted there, just as the divinity does with His *Sephiroth* or "ornaments" <note>The *Sephiroth* are the ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note>, through which—while remaining hidden as to His essence—He communicates with His creatures, who could perceive nothing of Him otherwise. ...general of all things, commits their production to his word or *Chochmah* <note>original Hebrew: *Chokhmah*, meaning Wisdom</note>, which is Sapience; this *Ensoph* <note>original: *Ein Sof*, the Infinite or Divine Origin in Kabbalistic thought</note> is that great supra-mundane Ocean, a perpetual source that waters the tree of life—as the Zohar <note>The primary text of Jewish mysticism, the Kabbalah</note> puts it—the reason of all <margin>cc</margin> reasons, the cause of causes, the intellect and life of the body. These same four waterers of the whole earth (Genesis 2) proceed from <margin>cc</margin> paradise or from this sea: the *Tetractys* <note>A triangular figure of ten points, sacred to the Pythagoreans</note> or quaternate of *Pythagoras*. These are the *Tigris* and the *Gihon* (or the *Nile*), which represent air and fire, the two superior elements over which man has no command—for this is, as the aforementioned *Poets* say, the dwelling of the blessed Gods. The other two are the *Euphrates* and the *Pison* (or the *Ganges*), representing earth and water, the inferior elements which are at the disposal of man. In these, the "cross" of the entire universe is perfected. These are further designated by the four animals of *Ezekiel*: the *Tigris* and the air by the *Eagle*; the *Nile* and the fire by the *Lion*; the *Euphrates* and the earth by the *Ox*, intended for plowing; and the *Ganges* and the water by the *Man*, because of his aqueous seed, of which *Virgil* would have tacitly said: <margin>cc</margin> *The stirred waters swell* <note>original Latin: *Agitata tumescunt æquora*</note>. Regarding this idea that the rivers or divine emanations proceed from this great sea or pool of blessings—for *Berachah* <note>original Hebrew: ברכה</note> signifies both "blessing" and "pool"—and return there, *Zoroaster* taught among his other magical traditions that the soul of man had wings; when the feathers fell from them, the soul was precipitated down here into the body, and after they had returned to it, the soul flew back again to heaven. When his disciples asked him how they could, in a short time, make this plumage grow back in order to mount back up there as soon as possible, he answered them: "By continually wetting them with the water of life." But where could they recover this water? From the four rivers with which the earthly Paradise was watered: the one from the eastern part called *Chiddekel* <note>The Tigris</note>, which is as much as to say "light"; from the west, *Dichon* <note>likely a variant of Gihon</note> or "expiation"; the one from the South, *Perath* <note>The Euphrates</note>, which we can interpret as piety, religion, devotion, and zeal—toward which southern region the holy Father *Abraham* always directed his path in Genesis 12, as a place from which all evil spirits are excluded, according to the doctrine of the Hebrew Kabbalists and the Moors; and from the North, *Pison*, meaning equity, reason, and uprightness, favorable to his son *Isaac*, who gathered a hundredfold from a single grain of wheat. Since it is not permitted for us to reach this degree—as, in truth, it has no longer existed since the fulfillment of all prophecies, visions, dreams, and oracles—our only recourse will be to meditate upon them. Therein, that which depends entirely on the three worlds and the knowledge assigned to them is contained, albeit in various types of interpretations: namely, the **literal**, **allegorical**, **analogical**, **anagogical** senses, and infinite other sorts and manners previously deduced by us. Saint Augustine briefly encompasses all the divine dreams and visions of which the aforementioned Hebrew theologians have spoken into five types, including human dreams among them, both being understood by the word **Dream** <note>original Hebrew: חלום, *Hhalom*</note>, which is the same as the Greek **Enypnion** <note>original: ἐνύπνιον</note> and the Latin **Somnium**; and **Vision** <note>original Hebrew: מראה, *Mareh*</note>, which is the same as the Greek, according to Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene, a 4th-century philosopher-bishop who wrote a famous treatise on dreams</note>, **visionary sights** <note>original: τὰ ὄναρ θεάματα, *ta onar theamata*</note>, in Latin **Visiones**. 

The difference between the two is great: the true divine dream is received while sleeping, and the vision occurs while slumbering with an impression upon the imaginative soul, which represents things as if they were seen with the eyes. These are entirely different from human dreams and those of brute beasts, which have nothing but the natural impression in the imagination just as they were seen while awake. Among these divine dreams and visions there are several degrees: The first degree being the revelation in a dream to devote oneself to good; of this, the Hebrew Scripture says that "the Spirit of God rested upon someone," or else that "God is with him." The third degree <note>The text continues a numbered list of prophetic levels</note> is when the purified and cleansed Spirit sees a figure in a dream and at the same time understands what it intends to express, just as it is written in Zechariah. 

The fourth is when one hears words without seeing any figure of any kind. 

The fifth is when one sees, while sleeping, a man who speaks and reveals divine things. 

The sixth, when it seems that one perceives an Angel speaking while sleeping. 

The seventh, when it seems during sleep that God speaks, as is contained in Isaiah chapter 5, and in Ezekiel, Micah, and other Prophets. 

The eighth, when the prophetic vision comes with the word of God; in this degree, the ancient Hebrews place the visions of Abraham, except for the one in the valley of Mamre mentioned in Genesis 18, which they place in the ninth degree. 

The tenth, when one perceives the Angel speaking face to face, as at the sacrifice of Abraham. 

The last, which is the greatest and most excellent of all others, is to see and speak to God face to face, while awake and without any intermediary; this was unique to Moses alone, as I have already said above. Thus, when Isaiah writes in chapter 6 that he saw God, we must understand that as a vision, and not while awake; and when we read in Ezekiel that he was transported to a field between heaven and earth, that happened while he was sleeping. 

In fact, all theologians agree that the holy Prophets did not all have the same gifts of Prophecy: some never had more than one vision of God, or two or three divine dreams, while others possessed these gifts of Prophecy throughout their entire lives, such as <term>Samuel</term>, <term>Elijah</term>, <term>Elisha</term>, and others.

> In ancient times, there were three types of prophets among the Hebrews. The first was of those who, whenever the situation required, obtained oracles, visions, or prophetic dreams, such as Moses, Samuel, and others; whom the ancient age called "Seers," though the common people of the Jews usually call them "Former Prophets." The second type was of those who, while they could never elicit oracles, visions, or prophetic dreams by their own will, yet whenever it seemed good to God to teach, warn, or rebuke the people through them, they prophesied by divine inspiration; and these the Jews call "Latter Prophets," because the greatest part of them were active after Solomon under the idolatrous kings—such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the twelve called the "Minor Prophets"—since that better [first] type had almost ceased around the time of David. The third type consists of those who, although they never obtain oracles, visions, or prophetic dreams from God, yet having been educated by prophets of the higher type as if by teachers, and being taught by the internal anointing of the Holy Spirit, rightly understand the prophetic writings. They are able to recount these to others, give right counsel to those who ask it from the same writings, and perceive those things which necessarily follow by right reasoning from their words. The ancient age called these the "Sons of the Prophets," but Paul, writing to the Corinthians, simply calls them "Prophets." And regarding the former types, whatever was divinely revealed to them for the instruction of posterity concerning the future kingdom of Christ, they left behind for future generations recorded in writing; and it is to be believed that all those things still remain whole and safe. However, the latter type [the Sons of the Prophets], just as they were most occupied in teaching, so they almost always abstained from writing, especially in the Old Testament. <note>original Latin: "Tria, Prophetarum genera olim fuere apud Hebræos..."</note>

The learned Gilbert Génébrard <note>A French Benedictine monk and leading Hebraist of the 16th century</note>, mentioning the gifts of prophecy, visions, and dreams of the Hebrews in the first book of his *Chronography*, used these words worthy of being recited by us in this place:

> In the time of Saul and Samuel, the era of the Prophets began (Peter, Acts 3). Thus, the profession of Prophecy, which was nearly dead after the death of the Elders, began to flourish again as many joined the same college and devoted themselves to this institution under the presidency of Samuel (1 Kings 19). Moreover, it should be known that this prophetic calling was not always extraordinary, since it consisted of men who voluntarily devoted themselves to this profession, so that they might more conveniently devote their time to prayer, contemplation, the interpretation of the scriptures, preaching, and study. From among these, God occasionally raised up some to perform the duty of predicting events before Kings, Peoples, and so forth. Sometimes He also elevated others to this prophetic gift from other walks of life, but then their calling and mission were extraordinary. Such was Amos, whom He raised from the pasturing of cattle to the honor of prophecy. <note>original Latin: "Tempore Saul & Samuelis incepit tempus Prophetarum..."</note>

<meta>This page continues the historical survey of the Hebrew prophetic tradition, moving from the individual nature of divine revelation discussed on the previous page to the institutional succession of prophets and the eventual transition to the Great Synagogue. History of the Origin of [Languages]

Prophets existed since the beginning of the world, but they were rare and outside the usual order. From the time of Samuel, they became more frequent, appearing regularly and in a continuous succession. For this reason, the Hebrews consider him the founder and author of the Prophets, or the schools of the prophets. Apart from these, there existed 48 most celebrated Prophets—partly men and partly women—whose names appear in various places throughout Scripture. From among these, I will list the Prophetesses here. As for the men, the proper place and century for naming them in their order will occur later. The Prophetesses are therefore Sarah, Miriam (the sister of Moses), Deborah, Huldah, Hannah (the mother of Samuel), Abigail, and Esther. Thus it is recorded by the Hebrew [chronicle] in *Seder Olam* <note>original Latin: "Seder cap. 20. & 21."; referring to the *Seder Olam Rabbah*, a 2nd-century CE Hebrew language chronology detailing biblical history</note>, chapters 20 and 21.

See the aforementioned author <note>Likely referring to the chronicler Gilbert Génébrard, whose work "Chronographia" is a major source for this text</note> treating, alongside the succession of Hebrew kings and high priests, the perpetual order and number of the Prophets until the Babylonian captivity, through all the subsequent books of his said *Chronography*. In these books—specifically in the second book—he says: The Great Synagogue <note>The "Great Assembly" (Anshei Knesset HaGedolah), a council of 120 sages who, according to Jewish tradition, led the people at the start of the Second Temple period</note> succeeded the Prophets; its leaders were Ezra, Nehemiah, Mordecai, Zerubbabel, and Joshua. These presided over the council, which consisted of one hundred and twenty men—some noble, others from the common people—who came together for the purpose of correcting the sacred books and establishing their canon according to the prescription of the Kabbalah <note>Here used in its literal sense of "tradition" or "received lore," rather than specifically mystical practice</note>. There they also ordained that Joshua had been so taught by Moses, the Elders by Joshua, the Prophets by the Elders, and the Great Synagogue by the Prophets. The notary or scribe of the council (for so he is called in Ezra 7) was Ezra, whom they say was also assisted by—or rather presided over by—Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, Mishael, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. [See] the preface of Elias [Levita] <note>Elias Levita (1469–1549) was a renowned Hebrew grammarian whose work "Masoreth Ha-Masoreth" explained the history of the Hebrew text</note> to the *Masoreth Ha-Masoreth*; Rabbi Moses <note>Maimonides (1135–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note> in his preface to the *Book of Commandments*; and in the Talmud in the treatise on vows.

In this regard, one should see what we have discussed above in chapter 7 concerning the Kabbalah of the Hebrews.

## On the points, accents, and other notes and marks of the Hebrews.

### C H A P. XXIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' intertwined with floral vines and two small figures at the base.</image-desc>

All Hebrew words and expressions are entirely deprived and destitute of vowels, consisting only of consonants and letters alone, without action or movement, like a body devoid of a soul. Considering this, the Hebrews—in order to make these letters, which are mute and immobile by themselves, live and move—decided to place points below and above them. For this reason, these points were named by them תנועות <term>Tenu'ot</term> <note>translated as "motions" or "movements"</note>, that is to say, movements by which the letters are moved and pronounced, from the verb נוע <term>Nu'a</term>, meaning "to move." These are of two different kinds. Those below the letters are mostly named in the Hebrew language נקודות <term>Nekudot</term> <note>translated as "points"</note>, because of their thinness, smallness, and tininess, from the verb נקד <term>Nakad</term> <note>translated as "to puncture" or "to point"</note>, as in Song of Solomon 1:11; otherwise...

As for the points above the Hebrew letters which are commonly called accents—the Greeks call them *prosodies* <note>original: "προσωδίας"</note> and the Hebrews call them *Ta'am* or *Ta'amim* <note>original: "טעם Taam, טעמים Taamin"</note>, which is to say "tastes"—as reported by *Elias Levita* in his book on Hebrew accents, and in the *Tishbi* <note>original: "Theſbite"</note> regarding the interpretation of this Hebrew word *Ta'am*. Therefore, every Hebrew word is ordinarily constructed of three consonants as a sign of matter, form, and the composite; it consists of points, or movements of its elements, like a mutable soul within a body. As the Cabalists say, the office of the spirit is to govern and moderate the blinded impetuosity of the animal part. And just as life is to composite things, so do the points serve the letters and characters of the Hebrews. Just as all things flow from and receive favor and nourishment from supra-mundane fountains, so too do words and speeches uttered in Hebrew proceed from and retain vigor and efficacy from the understanding, upon which is imprinted the image and beauty of the eternal Word <note>original: "Verbe eternel"; the Logos or divine reason</note>, where these divine properties are unspeakably arranged and situated.

> Meanwhile, however, it must not be overlooked that just as the Hebrews—as we have learned from their grammarians—use the **Rebia** <note>original: "Rebia"; a Hebrew accent mark</note> (a single dot placed above the word, positioned so it does not look like a **Holem** <note>original: "Holem"; a Hebrew vowel point indicating the 'o' sound</note>) for sub-distinctions in speech. For a full distinction, they use the **Zatephraton** <note>original: "Zatephraton"; likely a variant name for a Hebrew accent or pause</note>, which consists of two dots above the word. In the segment known as the **Athnahta** <note>original: "Athnahta"; a major pause accent, often shaped like a crescent</note>, they use a semicircle, much like a rainbow, placed below the word; and the **Pasek**, which is a line or stroke written below the word after a number at the end, to signify a complete and perfect sentence, as is their custom. The Greeks and Latins also have their own types of punctuation marks, invented to demonstrate what has been said, which are to be sought from the Greek and Latin grammarians. The Macedonians and Russians, and the inhabitants of both Mysias <note>Moesia: an ancient region in the Balkans, modern-day Bulgaria and Serbia</note>, as well as the Illyrians and Dalmatians, declare the incomplete and complete senses of sentences through punctuation, as can be seen in their books published by printers <note>original: "Calcographis"; literally 'copper-plate engravers' or early printers</note> long ago in their own letters and language. The Indians also have a custom of writing two dots between individual words of a speech, and indicating the end of a line and the conclusion of a sentence with four dots. The Chaldeans <note>A term often used for Aramaic speakers</note> and Syrians have only two types of punctuation for an incomplete or suspended sentence, where they are accustomed to using only a single dot. At the end and conclusion of a sentence, however, they are accustomed to adding four dots, depicted in black and red colors. The Arabs also have four types of dots: either two dots between words, as we use a comma <note>original: "Cesa" and "commata"</note>—similar to the Hebrew **Sheva** <note>original: "Seua"; a Hebrew vowel mark of two vertical dots</note>—or just a single dot, or three in the shape of a **Segol** <note>original: "Segol"; a Hebrew vowel mark of three dots in a triangle</note>, which they use in three ways: either pointed straight toward the heavens, or with the head reflected toward the North or South poles. They also use a quadrangular form with four dots positioned so that one seems to look toward the sky, another toward the earth, the third toward the South, and the fourth toward the North, which they use for sub-distinctions, distinctions, segments, and sentence endings. In these, it should be noted that every Punic <note>In the 16th century, "Punic" was often used broadly to refer to Semitic or "Oriental" scripts, here likely referring to Arabic or its derivatives</note> word that has **Aliph Ce**, **Quiph** with **Manuben** is the end of a part. For **Manuben** always stands at the end of a part of speech. Likewise, if **Aliph Ce Quiph** follows **Geu**, it is the end of a part; even if a dot is sometimes not added, it is always understood by this general rule. In questions and—if it is permitted to say—answers, the Arabs use various modes, as could be clearly known to us from the Gospel of John, chapter 9, if it were written here in Arabic letters. But since we lack those type-forms, we will try to express it in Latin words with the points added in their proper places: *And Jesus said: For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind. Christians divide the precepts of these two tables differently; for Origen in his 8th homily on Exodus, and Athanasius in his synopsis, hold that in the first table there were only four precepts pertaining to the service of God—namely, first, the adoration of God alone; second, not to have images; third, not to abuse the name of God; and fourth, the sanctification of the Sabbath—and in the second table, the six other precepts necessary for the love of one's neighbor.
Saint Augustine and some ancient Latin Fathers divide the precepts of these tables into groups of three and seven. They hold that at the head of all the precepts, there was a brief proeme <note>proeme: a formal introduction or preface</note> of the whole law, namely this: *I am your God* <note>original Latin: "Ego sum Deus tuus"</note>, which the Hebrews hold to be the first precept. After this proeme, they place these three precepts belonging to the service of God: the first of which is, "You shall have no strange gods"; the second, "You shall not take the name of God in vain"; and the third, regarding the Sabbath. In the second table, they place these seven precepts: the first, to honor one's parents; the second, to avoid homicide; the third, not to commit adultery; the fourth, not to steal; the fifth, not to bear false witness; the sixth, that one must remove all concupiscence—which is a single precept among the Hebrews and contained in the tenth place in the Decalogue—Saint Augustine dividing it into two, namely: the prohibition against the concupiscence of riches (which is the sixth precept), and the prohibition against the concupiscence of the flesh (which is the seventh and final precept). > authors of Eastern law have written concerning these laws as follows: "Moses completed the law with three kinds of precepts: moral, judicial, and religious or ceremonial <note>original Latin: "moralibus, iudicialibus, religiosis siue ceremonialibus"</note>. These are of such weight that the moral ones still bind even in the Gospel, because they are of natural and divine law. The judicial ones are mostly retained, though a few are left behind, corrected, or softened, because they were laws established for a specific people and time. The ceremonial ones are received partly according to the spirit—a hidden understanding and sense—and partly according to the letter. There are two kinds: some are figurative, having a shadow of the future Christ and the Church, such as circumcision, sacrifices, Sabbaths, and unclean foods. Others are purely ritual, pertaining simply to the worship of God. The former were abolished and imposed only until the time of correction. Others are still used so that the solemnity of God's worship might be perpetuated, such as dedicated temples, choirs, vows, lustral water <term>lustral water: water used for ceremonial purification or cleansing</term>, blessings, religious vestments, genuflection, ecclesiastical orders, tithes, firstfruits, processions, visits to sacred buildings and places, the raising of hands, the festivals of Pentecost and Easter (with the use of animal sacrifices removed), singing, images, organs, fasts, etc."

Michael Neander, in his commentaries on the Jewish Talmud, mentions the fourteen books of Rabbi Moses son of Maimon (called "Rambam" <note>The source text says "Ramban," a common early modern confusion between Maimonides (Rambam) and Nahmanides (Ramban)</note> by the Jews), counting the mandates of God that must be necessarily observed according to the Law of Moses as 613 in number. One part consists of affirmations or commands, which number 248—matching the number of members in the human body. The other consists of negations or prohibitions, which number 365—matching the number of days in the solar year. All these are explained in the Talmudic books, along with certain other mandates later handed down by the house of judgment <note>The Sanhedrin, or high court</note> and the Prophets according to various times and causes. The supreme doctor of the Jews after holy Moses—who is himself called "the Egyptian," though he was Spanish as he names and writes himself—Moses (I say), son of Maimon, briefly called Rambam, divided the treatment of all these precepts into 14 books <note>This refers to the *Mishneh Torah*, Maimonides's comprehensive code of Jewish law</note>.

In the first book, he treats in five chapters the articles of faith: what is to be believed concerning God, the doctrine of the law, idolatry, and repentance.

In the second, he treats of loving and worshipping God, and the reading of "*Hear, O Israel*" <note>The *Shema*, the central prayer of Judaism</note>, their sacred garments, the blessings of the priests, and circumcision.

In the third, he treats the precepts of the festivals according to the seasons, such as the Sabbath and Passover; including yeast and unleavened bread, Pentecost, the Tabernacle, as well as shekels, new moons, fasts, and the Dedication <note>Hanukkah</note>.

In the fourth, he treats of marriages and divorces, of the brother's widow <note>levirate marriage</note>, young virgins, suspected wives, dowries, and betrothals.

In the fifth, he treats of forbidden unions, of permitted and forbidden foods, and the slaughter of animals.

In the sixth, he treats of oaths, vows, the Nazirite, excommunication, and communion.

In the seventh, he treats of seeds of doubt (or of two species) <note>laws regarding agricultural mixtures or *kilayim*</note>, and of sacred dona-

...which David composed almost all of them, except for a few, as Aben Ezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish rabbi and biblical commentator</note> assures in his preface to them, reciting various opinions of the Rabbis in this regard. Among others, several assert that all the Psalms found in the body of the Bible were composed by David alone. Rabbi David Kimhi <note>David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a medieval rabbi and grammarian also known as Radak</note> and some other Rabbis hold, following the opinion of the Talmudists in the Talmudic tractate *Bava Batra* <note>original: "Baua Batra"</note> in the *Perek* <note>Hebrew for "chapter"</note> or chapter 1, that David composed his work of Psalms from those composed before him by ten ancient Hebrew personages: namely Adam, Melchizedek, Abraham, Asaph, Heman, Jeduthan, Moses, and the three sons of Korah <note>original: "Coré"</note>—Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph <note>original: "Aser, El Kana, & Abiceseph"</note>. This is contained in the 1st book of Chronicles <note>original: "Paralipomenon"</note>, and in the aforementioned place in the Talmud, in the Hebrew book titled *Midrash Tehillim* <note>original: "Midrasch Thehilim"; a rabbinic commentary on the Psalms</note>, and repeated by St. Jerome in his letters to Sophronius, as reported by Gilbert Génébrard <note>A 16th-century French Benedictine scholar and Hebraist</note> in Book 1 of his *Chronography*.

Some ancient Fathers, such as St. Cyprian, Origen, Anastasius, and others, hold that Solomon composed some of them; the Greeks attribute several to Ezekiel, Jeremiah, Haggai, and Zechariah, as noted by Sixtus of Siena <note>original: "F. This is confirmed by Matthäus Rademacher <note>original: "Matt. Brademachius"</note> in his commentaries on the Psalms, in the chapter on the authors of the Psalms, and by Richard of Saint-Victor <note>original: "Richard Senonois"</note> in his preface to the commentaries on the Psalms, with whom John Crichton <note>original: "Iodocus Chrichtoneus"</note> will be seen in Book 2, chapter 12, on the praises of the three ancient fathers.

Whatever the case may be, these Psalms were not anciently arranged in the same order as they are today, according to the same Hebrews; for it is quite certain that one cannot say truly which was the first or second during the time of the Fathers, according to Hilary in his commentaries on them, conforming to the opinion of the Hebrews. This is confirmed by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in his *Apology*, question 5, regarding Magic and Kabbalah, and by Gilbert Génébrard in his commentary on Psalm 9.

Some ancient authors, such as St. Jerome and St. John Chrysostom, have reported that Ezra <note>original: "Esdras"</note> was the first who edited and reduced them into a single volume after the Babylonian captivity, they having been dispersed and spread here and there according to the diversity of the times of their composition. Athanasius, in his *Synopsis*, maintains the contrary, saying that these Psalms were compiled in writing in a book during the said Babylonian captivity by the friends of King Hezekiah <note>original: "Ezechias"</note>, in the number that we have, drawn and extracted from three thousand Psalms of David which were then found among the Jews. St. Hilary in his prologue to them and Eusebius in his preface hold that these Psalms were anciently divided into five books, which is confirmed by Epiphanius in his book *On Weights and Measures*, Sixtus of Siena in Book 1 of his *Holy Library*, and Johannes Drusius in Book 2, question 57, of his *Hebrew Questions*.

But the seventy-two Greek interpreters <note>The Septuagint scholars</note> were so meticulous as to give order and sequence by number to them, as reported by Pico della Mirandola in his *Apology*, question 5, and Johann Reuchlin <note>original: "I. Reuclin Capnio"</note> in Book 2 of *On the Miraculous Word* <note>original: "de verbo mirifico"</note>. For the Jews, wherever they may be spread and scattered, read and sing them, both in their private prayers in their homes and in public prayers in the synagogues, in the pure Hebrew language, having held them as their own from all time and antiquity under the name of *Sepher Tehillim* <note>original: "Sepher Theillim"; Hebrew for "Book of Praises"</note>.

The Arabs, Turks, and Moors of Arabia, Egypt, and Barbary—indeed, all Muslims <note>original: "Musulmans & Mahometistes"</note> in general—hold them in such great regard and esteem, just as they were commanded by their Prophet Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> in suras <note>original: "azoares"</note> 11, 27, and 64 of his Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note>, maintaining that these Psalms were dictated to David from the very mouth of God, and contain all the acts of the world, both great and small. For this purpose, they are translated from Hebrew into the Arabic language (their grammatical language) and also into their common and vulgar tongues, Turkish and Moorish. They are called in their language *Zebur* <note>The Arabic term *Zabur* refers specifically to the holy book of Psalms revealed to David</note>, a word derived from the Hebrew words *Sepher Tehillim* mentioned above, using this word *Zebur* instead of *Sepher* (which means "book"), as if this Book of Psalms deserved par excellence to be called "The Book."

The Persians, under the rule of the Shah <note>original: "Sophy"; referring to the Safavid dynasty of Persia</note>, also being Muslims, have likewise translated them into their Persian language, which is widely used throughout Asia. The Great Khan <note>original: "Cham"</note>, sovereign emperor of the Tartars, with all the hordes and cantons scattered and sown in several parts of the North and the East—though they be idolaters and pagans—together with the inhabitants of Cathay <note>An old name for Northern China</note>, China, Japan <note>original: "Iappō"</note>, with the adjacent islands and the mainland, likewise have them in their own languages. The Great Negus <note>The title of the Emperor of Ethiopia</note>, called Prester John <note>original: "Prestagiani ou Preste Ian"; a legendary Christian king of the East</note>, king of the Ethiopians and Abyssinians, also has them in his language within his southern Christian Church. Likewise, all the Greeks, Muscovites <note>Russians</note>, Armenians, Georgians <note>original: "Zorzaniens"</note>, Jacobites, Maronites, Copts <note>original: "Cophtites"</note>, and Syrians have them in each of their languages, along with all the Catholics of the Latin Church, with the branches and offshoots of the particularities and subdivisions of one and the other, in the Latin language proper and particular to them. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the history of the liturgical use of the Psalms, transitioning from their general popularity across cultures to the specific origins of how they are sung in the Christian Church.</meta>

...that each day should have certain proper Psalms to be sung while saying the Hours <note>The "Divine Office" or "Liturgy of the Hours," a set of daily prayers marking the times of the day</note>. This Psalter being thus divided and partitioned, the aforementioned Pope commanded that it be read throughout all Christian Churches, and he was the first to decree that the Psalms should be sung alternately and by two choirs in the Church. It is true that there are some who attribute this—according to the account of Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a 14th-century Byzantine church historian</note>, Book 13, Chapter 8—to Saint Ignatius, Bishop of Antioch, who lived in the time of the Apostles. This was because, while slumbering, he had heard angels singing these Psalms in the very same manner they are now sung in the Church, with one choir responding to the other. On the contrary, Theodoret (Book 2 of his *History*, Chapter 24), the *Tripartite History* (Book 5, Chapter 32), and the author of the *Fasciculus Temporum* <note>A popular 15th-century universal history by Werner Rolevinck</note> write that Flavian and Deodatus, or Diodore, were the first to divide the choirs of singers in the Church in Antioch into two parts. Socrates (Book 6, Chapter 8) and Sozomen (Book 8, Chapter 8) <note>Socrates Scholasticus and Sozomen were 5th-century historians of the early Church</note> attribute this to Saint John Chrysostom regarding the Church of Constantinople.

G. Genebrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard, a prominent 16th-century French scholar and Benedictine</note>, in Chapter 17 of his *Apostolic Liturgy*, treating several rare matters concerning this subject, wrote that those are clearly in error who wrote that Pope Celestine, in the time of Saint Augustine, "instituted the 150 Psalms to be sung in order with Antiphons" <note>original: "150. Psalmos cum Antiphonis cantari per ordinem instituisse"</note>. This includes writers such as Platina, Polydore Vergil, and the Centuriators <note>The Magdeburg Centuriators, a group of Lutheran historians</note>, who took it from common authors of the divine offices, claiming that Pope Celestine instituted the singing of the 150 Psalms in order with their antiphons <note>Short sentences sung before or after a Psalm</note>. 

Instead, it should have been said that he instituted, or rather permitted, the leaving aside of full Psalms in the celebration of the divine liturgy due to the lack of devotion and the impatience of the people; and that certain verses should be drawn from them for the entrance of the sacrifice <note>The Introit</note>, for the Graduals, for the Offertories, and for the Communions, leaving there only the "Glory be to the Father" <note>original: "Gloria Patri"</note>. From this, Saint Gregory later, as a supplement and composition for so many omitted verses, substituted the "Lord have mercy" <note>original: "Kirié Eleizon"</note> from the Greek Church, as a summary and epitome of all the Psalms. This is deduced at length by the aforementioned Genebrard following the chapter cited above and others following.

Polydore Vergil (Book 6, Chapter 2 of *On the Discovery of Things*) treats this matter at length and asserts that this fashion of singing the Psalms alternately in the Church was drawn from David. According to Josephus (Book 7 of the *Antiquities*, Chapter 10), David instituted seven ranks of singers, and as they sang first, he followed them and sang after them when the Ark was carried into Jerusalem. Or perhaps, in this, they imitated Asaph, master of the singers, who among the Hebrews was the author of the order of those who sang before the Ark (see 2 Samuel 6 and 1 Chronicles) <note>original: "2. des Roys 6. & 1. du Paralipomen"</note>. See George the Venetian <note>Francesco Zorzi, a Franciscan friar and mystic</note>, Volume 3 of the *Oracles of Prophecies*, Section 1; Theodoret, Books 2 and 5, Chapters 24 and 32 of the *Tripartite History*; Sabellicus, Book 7, Chapter 7; G. Genebrard, Books 1 and 3 of his *Chronography*; René Benoist, Book 1 of his *Stromatology of the Bible*; Sixtus of Siena, Book 1, chapter on the Psalter, and Book 2 under the word "David," and in Book 8, Heresy 5 of his *Holy Library*; André Thevet, Book 18, last chapter of his *Cosmography*; René Choppin, Book 3 of *Sacred Civil Policy*; and Blaise de Vigenère in the introductory epistle to his version of the Psalms.

# That the Angels and celestial intelligences, and the souls of the blessed, sing and shall sing the Psalms of David in the Hebrew language, in Paradise.

## CHAP. XXVII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'L' initiating the chapter, featuring two human figures (likely Adam and Eve) within a floral and architectural frame.</image-desc>

THE Hebrew Prophet Zephaniah <note>The prophet Sophonias in the Latin Vulgate</note> in his prophecy or prediction, chapter 3, promises through divine inspiration that the Eternal <margin>cc</margin> will restore and re-establish at the end of the world the "chosen lip," or <margin>cc</margin> idiom, and chosen speech: so that all may invoke the name of the Lord Jehovah and all serve him with one shoulder. These words the Chaldean Paraphrast <note>Referring to the Targum, the ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible</note> has translated into the Chaldean language <margin>cc</margin> <note>Aramaic</note> in this fashion: *At the end of the world I will distribute through all the Peoples and <margin>cc</margin> Nations a single chosen locution, so that all pray in the name of the Lord and <margin>cc</margin> serve before him with one shoulder.* Upon this passage, the Talmudists <note>Jewish scholars and commentators on the Talmud</note> in their commentaries write that this "Chosen Lip," or Idiom, or Chosen Speech, must be interpreted as the Hebrew language. This is the language which God once elected and chose above all others to communicate and speak with Adam and the Ancient Fathers and Patriarchs, and to give them his divine law. It is also chosen because this language speaks holily, chastely, and honestly of all things, however immodest or foul they may be, as one can see in reading the context of the Hebrew Bible, and as Rabbi Moses <note>Moses Maimonides (1135–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note> confirms in book 3, chapter 9 of his *Guide* <note>original: *Moré*, referring to the *Moreh Nevukhim* or *Guide for the Perplexed*</note>. St. Jerome in his commentaries on this Prophet, St. Augustine in question 108 on Genesis, and Origen on chapter 11 of Numbers and homily 11, have all written that the largest and most sound portion of Hebrew authors have maintained that the Hebrew language, as the mother and matrix of all other languages, was born at the very beginning of the world. Just as it was the first, so shall it be the last of this Universe; for its use has been for all time and shall be in the future in Heaven, while the saints and the blessed—as the Psalmist says—will praise God from age to age. For this reason, Pietro Galatino <note>An Italian Franciscan and scholar of Kabbalah (1460–1540)</note> in several places in the 12th book of his *Secrets of the Catholic Faith*, reciting the Hebrew words of this Zephaniah, has written that the Hebrew Kabbalists and Talmudists held the opinion that after the final Day of Judgment at the end and consummation of the World, the souls of the blessed enjoying eternal beatitude, together with the Angels and celestial intelligences, will sing and perform the Psalms in praise of God in the single and unique Hebrew language. They argue that just as before the division of languages that occurred at Babel, the whole universal earth possessed but one language, likewise in the general resurrection all the men of the world will speak only the same Hebrew language, which was familiar to Adam in the earthly Paradise. So let it be that the Prophet Isaiah in his sixth chapter writes that he heard the Seraphim Angels singing before the Throne of God in the Hebrew language these words: *Kadosh, Kadosh, Kadosh, Yehovah Tzabaoth, Melo khol Ha'aretz Kevodo* <note>original: *Kadofch, Kadofch. ## Of King Solomon and of his writings composed in the Hebrew language.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'L' featuring an ornate frame with a figure inside.</image-desc>

King Solomon was thus named in the Hebrew language *Salomoh* <note>original Hebrew: שלמה</note>, which is to say "sweet and peaceful." He was the son of King David, mentioned above, after whom he attained the Crown of Israel, as seen in the third [book] of Kings and in the *Seder Olam Rabbah* <note>A 2nd-century Hebrew language chronology</note>, chapter 16. According to the report of Josephus in his *Antiquities* and Saint Jerome in his preface to the *Chronicle of Eusebius*, he composed his books in Hebrew hexameter and pentameter verse. The first of these is named in Hebrew *Maslot* <note>original Hebrew: *Mishlei*</note>, in Greek *Parables* <note>original Greek: παροιμίας</note>, in Latin *Proverbs* <note>original Latin: "prouerbia"</note>, and in French *Parables* or *Proverbs*. It contains adages, similes, and common maxims regarding many human events necessary for the conduct of life. The latter part of this book—namely from the twenty-fifth chapter to the end—was collected by Shebna and other scribes of Hezekiah, King of Judah, from other books of Solomon, according to the Jews. The second book is named in the same Hebrew *Goheleth* <note>Kohelet</note>, in Greek *The Preacher* <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησιαστὴ</note>, in Latin *Ecclesiastes* or *The Preacher* <note>original Latin: "Ecceleſiaſtes" or "concionator"</note>, and in French *Ecclesiastes*. The third is *Sirhasirsin* <note>original Hebrew: Shir ha-Shirim</note>, in Greek *Song of Songs* <note>original Greek: ᾆσμα ᾀσμάτων</note>, in Latin *Song of Songs* <note>original Latin: "Canticum Canticorum"</note>, and in French *Song of Songs*, which the Jews forbade reading except by those who had passed the age of thirty. Some authors hold that the maxims of these three books were gathered by Isaiah the Prophet from many books of songs and proverbs which the Holy Scripture notes were composed by Solomon, being preserved by the Holy Spirit as the most useful among the others to be included and inserted into these three books, as noted by Sixtus of Siena <note>S. See also Sabellicus in book 7, chapter 7; the historical library of Josias Simmler and Conrad Gessner; Agathio Guidacerio in his proem to the *Song of Songs*; Benito Arias Montano in his great Bibles printed in five languages by Plantin at Antwerp <note>The Antwerp Polyglot Bible (1568–1572)</note>, in volume 3; and the aforementioned Sixtus Senensis in book 1, the chapter on the three books of Solomon, and the chapters on the *Wisdom of Solomon* and *Ecclesiastes*, and book 2, the chapter on Solomon, making mention of several other Hebrew books composed by this King, which he repeats in books 6 and 8 of the same *Holy Library*. Gilbert Génébrard, in book 1 of his *Chronography*, recounts several beautiful and curious research findings concerning the writings of this great King.

### Of the Prophet Isaiah & of his writings composed in the Hebrew language. C H A P. X X I X.

The Prophet Isaiah was thus called in Hebrew ישעיה <term>Isaiah</term> <note>meaning "The Lord is salvation"</note>, as if one said saved and protected by the Lord; he was the son of Amoz, a citizen of Jerusalem, and flourished during the time of Kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah in the year 3356 from the creation of the world, at the time of the migration of the Jewish tribes, as is contained in the catalog and succession of the Kings of Judah and Jerusalem inserted in the short *Seder Olam* <note>original: "Zeder olam," a 2nd-century Hebrew chronology of biblical history</note>. The Hebrews assert that this Prophet composed his prophecy in verse, or at the very least in a measured Hebrew order, to which Saint Jerome seems to agree in his epistle to Paulinus, in his preface to the *Chronicles of Eusebius of Caesarea*, and in his prologue to the book of this Prophet, saying that he did not merely weave or fabric a simple prophecy, but rather a Gospel. This is because he is infinitely articulate and eloquent in his Hebrew tongue, having nothing rude, harsh, or coarse about him. Thus, into whatever language one might translate him, he cannot be represented and expressed with the same eloquence and naturalness <note>original: "naïfueté," referring here to the innate purity or original character of the prose</note> of words as he possesses in the said Hebrew language. For he has described—using metaphors, allegories, and other tropes and figures—all the mysteries of our Lord Jesus Christ and of his Church so vividly that one cannot think he predicted future things, but rather composed writings of things already done and passed. This is confirmed by Saint Augustine in book 18, chapter 29 of *The City of God* and Sixtus Senensis in book 1 of his *Holy Library*; this is easy to see for those who wish to and are able to read him in his own natural Hebrew language. And it was no wonder if our Lord Jesus Christ, while wandering here below, chose and selected from among all the other books of the Hebrew Prophets his writings to read and explain publicly in the synagogue of the Jews. Manasseh, King of Judah, had him sawn through the middle of his body with a wooden saw, and he was buried under the oak of Rogel in the Tribe of Benjamin in the year of the world 3240 <note>Note: There appears to be a chronological discrepancy in the original text's dates</note>. See the 4th book of Kings, chapters 19 and 20; Saint Jerome in his commentaries; book 18, chapter 24 of *The City of God* by Saint Augustine; Michael Neander in his catalog of Hebrew, Chaldean, Ethiopian, Arabic, Greek, and Latin books; and others making mention of the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin authors who have written commentaries on this Prophet, including Sixtus Senensis in book 1 of his *Holy Library* in the chapter on Isaiah, and Philippe de Mornay in chapter 26 of *The Truth of the Christian Religion*.

As for the language which these Angels and celestial intelligences use—even though they have no body, nor any tongue—many great and learned figures have held various opinions. # Languages of this Universe

Regarding angels and celestial intelligences, their language must be Hebrew, given that it was the first language of this universe, which issued from the very mouth of God to the first man in the earthly Paradise. Furthermore, it has always been preserved in its entire purity, whereas all others have suffered many changes and alterations. Even <term>demons</term> <note>evil spirits or fallen angels</note>, when possessing people, speak this Hebrew tongue more willingly than any other, provided they can be understood. Because of this, the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>practitioners of Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism</note> maintain that the Hebrew letters must also be the first of all, and that they were forged in heaven at the same time as the speech that God taught to Adam. Adam, having been created by Him at a perfect age, was apt and capable of speaking whatever language he was taught. This is confirmed by <term>Francesco Giorgio of Venice</term> <note>a Franciscan friar and Christian Kabbalist</note> in his *Harmony of the World* (Book 8, final song), and by <term>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa</term> <note>a famous 16th-century occultist</note> in Book 3, Chapter 23 of his *Occult Philosophy*. What is more, it is quite certain that in ancient times, the angels and celestial intelligences ordinarily spoke to the ancient Fathers, Patriarchs, and Prophets in the pure Hebrew tongue and no other, as can be seen in countless places in the Bible. This is noted very well by <term>Saint Augustine</term> in his letter to Honoratus, and by <term>Saint Denis</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note> in his book on the *Celestial Hierarchy* (Chapters 4, 7, 11, 12, and 15). This is also because this language is the first, issued from heaven and from God even before the creation of the world; indeed, it is the one in which God engraved with his own finger his Law given to the ancient Hebrew Fathers. They spoke and used no other tongue, and even the well-beloved son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, while in this world, used it (though the <term>Syriac tongue</term> <note>Aramaic</note> was the vulgar and common language of the Jews during the time of our Lord). Many other things worthy of remark and consideration in this matter are deduced in the works of <term>Theodor Bibliander</term> in his commentaries on the common reason of all languages; <term>Johannes Reuchlin</term> (also called Capnio) in Book 3 of *The Art of the Kabbalah*; <term>Johannes Drusus</term> in Book 1, Question 61 of his *Hebrew Questions*; and <term>Pierre Grégoire</term> in Book 12, Chapter 12 of his *Syntax of the Admirable Art* and Volume 4 of his commentaries on the same (Chapters 9 and 11, concerning Angels). Following from the above, we are moved to report in this place what <term>Theseus Ambrosius</term> <note>an Italian linguist and scholar of Oriental languages</note> mentions in his appendix on various letters and languages. In a letter written from Ferrara on August 8, 1537, to the late <term>Guillaume Postel</term> <note>a famous French polymath and mystic</note>, he mentions that he is sending him a conjuration by a certain magician named Louis of Spoleto, featuring characters invented and given by demons.

These discussions are drawn from the calculations of the books of the Old Testament, which are placed in the first order of the sacred canon. Hereafter we will deduce into how many and what partitions these books are divided by the Greeks, Latins, as well as the Hebrews.

The first partition and division of these 22 books of the said Old Testament into three classes—namely, the books of the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms or Poems—is the one which our Lord Jesus Christ is held to have used after his resurrection, when opening the sense of the scriptures to his disciples, he interpreted for them all the things that were written of him in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms (St. Luke chapter 24). It is also used by Josephus in Book 1 *Against Apion* the grammarian.

> The ninth and tenth books are the Deeds of Kings,

> Then David [Psalms]; then three of Solomon:
> Ecclesiastes, the Song, and Proverbs.
> And likewise five of the prophetic spirit.

# History of the Origin of [Hebrew Bibles]

...Hebrew Bibles, divided into chapters and verses, such as we currently have in the Hebrew Bibles printed in Italy, Germany, France, Spain, and other places, is recent and modern. In fact, the Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and other authors who wrote five hundred years ago did not specifically cite any chapter or verse of the Old Testament in their works, except for the Psalms. Regarding the Psalms (as appears in the Acts of the Apostles), from the beginning of the early Church, these authors were accustomed to mention them by the numbers added to them. These numbers, as St. Hilary confirms in his preface to the Psalms, were attached to the Psalms by the seventy-two translators <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>. But as for the divisions of the chapters and numbers that we see today in the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin copies, they were drawn from the Latin copies. Evidence of this is that the ancient doctors and interpreters of Holy Scripture partitioned, divided, and also cited the Holy Scriptures not by chapters and numbers, but by references to particular stories. St. Augustine reports having done this himself from the beginning of Genesis until the expulsion of our first parents from the earthly Paradise, and St. Gregory from the beginning of the Book of Kings <note>modern 1 Samuel</note> until the anointing of King David. Furthermore, these same ancient Hebrew doctors and interpreters of Holy Scripture divided and interpreted that Scripture by "places," or periods, or verses, or small verses, or sentences, which they sometimes called chapters or headings. The ancient Jews observed this as well; their books were partitioned and divided by sentences, points, members, and verses, and distinguished by certain intervals according to the report of St. Jerome in his preface to Chronicles <note>original: *Paralipomenon*</note> and Isaiah. Jerome asserts that for the convenience of the readers of Holy Scripture, he used in his translation the same partitions and divisions of points, members, verses, and intervals that he had found in the Hebrew copies. These were distributed into *Parashiyot* and *Sedarim* <note>original: *Parsijoth* & *Sedarim*</note>, meaning sections and orders: fifty-four in number for the weeks of the embolic year <note>A leap year in the Hebrew calendar containing an extra month</note>, expressed by three large Hebrew letters *Peh* [פ] or *Samekh* [ס]. Additionally, they used *Pisqot* <note>original: *Sitthoh*</note>, or paragraphs, represented by three small *Pehs* or *Samekhs*, and then into verses designated by intervals, or commas, or colons <note>original: "two points"</note>. On the contrary, Elias Levita, a Jew by nation, in his preface to the book *Masoret Ha-Masoret* <note>A famous 16th-century work on the tradition of the biblical text</note>, asserts according to the opinion of the Rabbis that all the Hebrew Holy Scripture was anciently written with or as a single *Pasuk* <note>meaning "verse" or "sentence"</note>—that is to say, a single sentence, to which all the words of that Holy Scripture were entirely joined and assembled without any distinction of verses. But 436 years after the final destruction of the city of Jerusalem, this same Holy Scripture was divided by the Jews of Tiberias into *Pesukim*, that is to say, verses and sentences. The author of the book of Hebrew Questions on the Book of Kings, whom St. Thomas [Aquinas] believes to have been a Jew made Christian, writes that the Jews partitioned and divided the books of Holy Scripture into a certain number of sentences or verses, when he says that among those of his nation, the Book of Proverbs contains 915 verses. Rabbi Kimhi <note>David Kimhi, a medieval biblical commentator and grammarian</note>, in his dictionary of the paths of the Holy Language, asserting that the Bible among the Hebrews was written by verses, writes that in the Law <note>The Torah</note>, or books of the Law, there were 5,845 verses; in the Pro-

...Hebrew Prophets, 9,294 verses; to the Hagiographa <note>The "Holy Writings," the third section of the Hebrew Bible, including books like Psalms, Proverbs, and Job</note>, 8,064. But so that one is not mistaken in this calculation, it must be known that the partition and division of verses is different among the Jews than it is among the Greeks and among us. In fact, the ancient Greeks and Latins distinguished verses by an equal number of words <note>original: "dictions"</note>, writing almost always in each verse six words, partly monosyllables. This is demonstrated by St. Augustine in the *Mirror of Holy Scripture*, in which, often noting the number of verses previously collected by him but omitted from the holy books, he gives as an example of one verse this saying from Psalm 99: "His people, and the sheep of his pasture" <note>original: "Populus eius, & oues pascuæ eius"</note>; and for an example of two verses, this sentence from Psalm 118: "How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment on those who persecute me?" <note>original: "Quot sunt dies serui tui, quando facias tu de persequentibus me iudicium?"</note>. And for an example of three verses, these words from the 148th Psalm: "Let them praise his name in the dance; with the timbrel and harp I will sing praises to him, for the Lord takes pleasure in his people" <note>original: "Laudent nomen eius in choro, in tympano, & psalterio psallam ei, quia benè placitum est domino in populo suo." These verses are actually from Psalm 149</note>. If one wants to count the distinctions in these passages, one will find in the first, six voices or words; in the second, twelve; in the third, eighteen. Following this calculation or count, one must understand the division of Holy Scripture made by the ancients, who were accustomed to showing the size and thickness of the holy books by the number of verses—as St. Jerome does when he writes that Origen had composed nearly twenty thousand verses on the *Song of Songs*, and that St. Gregory had completed all his works in thirty thousand verses. As for the Jews, in distinguishing their verses, they do not take account of the number of words, nor do they follow the divisions of the clauses or punctuation of the speech, but only a certain ancient custom based on the authority of their ancestors and predecessors and the tradition of their Rabbis. They give no other reason for their partition and division than this: namely, that the great Ezra and the masters of their Great Synagogue <note>A council of 120 elders who, according to Jewish tradition, led the people after the return from Babylonian exile</note>, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, thus partitioned and divided their Holy Scripture. From this, it happened that among them the *Pesukim* <note>original Hebrew term for verses</note>, that is to say, verses, are almost all equal, as appears at the beginning of Genesis, where the first *Pasuk* or verse is: "In the beginning God created the Heaven and the Earth" <note>original: "In principio creauit Deus Cælum & Terram"</note>. The second is a little longer: "And the earth was without form and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters" <note>original: "Et terra erat inanis & vacua, & tenebræ erant super faciem abyſſi, & spiritus Domini ferebatur super faciem aquarum"</note>; after which verse the third follows, which is shorter: "And God said, etc." <note>original: "Et dixit Deus &c."</note>.

Thus, the ancients used the partitions and divisions of the Hebrew Holy Scripture as we have reported above. Whoever wishes to see more of this, let them read what I write hereafter in the subsequent chapter on the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> language. But as for an Ammonius of Alexandria, or Eusebius of Caesarea, or Tatian, who particularly divided the four Evangelists into chapters—namely, the Gospel of St. Matthew into 355 chapters, that of St. Mark into 235 chapters, that of St. Luke into 343 chapters, and that of St. John into 232 chapters—they did not do this to introduce a certain partition and division of Holy Scripture, but only to teach the concordances and harmonies of the Evangelists. After those named above, one finds in the ancient authors no numerical division of the aforementioned Holy Scripture except in Hilary, who partitioned and divided the Gospel of St. Matthew, interpreted by him, into thirty-three canons <note>A system of sectioning used for reference and cross-comparison between the Gospels</note>. that some have written that the Gospel of Saint Luke in the commentaries of Saint Ambrose is divided into 64 titles, and in the commentaries of Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 672–735), an English monk and scholar</note> into ninety-nine chapters. This was done, in the judgment of the most learned, not by the aforementioned authors, but by those who copied, transcribed, and printed their works. To be brief, some of the Greek interpreters of Holy Scripture who flourished five hundred years ago began to part and divide all of said Holy Scripture into distinct numbered parts, or annotated with characters of numbers, which they sometimes baptized with the name of "Titles," and other times "Chapters." In this fashion, Euthymius—or according to some, Oecumenius <note>Euthymius Zigabenus and Oecumenius were Byzantine commentators on the New Testament</note>—distinguished and divided the Gospel of Saint Matthew into 68 titles or chapters. The first of these he titled: concerning the Magi <note>original: "de Magis"</note>; the second: concerning the slain children <note>original: "de pueris interfectis"</note>; the third: of the preaching of Saint John; the fourth: of the doctrine of Jesus Christ. Some divide the chapters from the titles, and by this means part and divide all of the said Holy Scripture into titles, and subdivide those titles into chapters, as confirmed by Suidas and Arethas. They say that the Gospel of Saint Matthew was divided into 68 titles and 355 chapters, and the Gospel of Saint Mark into 48 titles and 56 chapters; and that St. Andrew <note>Likely referring to Andrew of Caesarea, an early commentator on the Apocalypse</note> divided the Apocalypse of Saint John <note>The Book of Revelation</note> into 24 parts, and each of those parts into three chapters, the whole making 72 chapters.

The Latins who have lived for more than a thousand years have used a double numbering of chapters: namely, one that is older but much more abundant in numbers, such that the Gospel of Saint Matthew in the oldest and most ancient copies contains 94 chapters; the Gospel of Saint Luke, 107 chapters; the Epistle to the Romans, 50 chapters. The other is later and more modern—the one we currently have today in common Bibles—but it is less copious and abundant in these numbers and comprised of fewer chapters. This system was used and served by Hugh, Priest and Cardinal of Saint Sabina <note>Hugh of Saint-Cher (c. 1200–1263), credited with the first modern chapter divisions of the Bible</note> in the year 1240, Alexander of Hales, Albert the Great, Thomas Aquinas, Bonaventure, and other Scholastic theologians <note>Scholasticism was a method of critical thought which dominated teaching in the medieval universities</note> up to this day. Rabbi David Kimhi <note>A famous medieval Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian, also known as Radak</note> and other modern Jews follow this division, calculation, and citation of chapters in the books of the said Old Testament, as confirmed by Friar Sixtus of Siena in book 3 of his *Holy Library*, method 4, on partitioning; and Gilbert Genebrard <note>A French Benedictine scholar and Hebraist</note> in book 4 of his *Chronology*, page 644. See what Sixtus of Siena writes regarding this in book 4, and others regarding the aforementioned Cardinal Hugh of Saint Sabina, which Gilbert Genebrard repeats in book 4, page 645 of his *Chronology*. He also makes mention on page 714 following, that Bishop Agostino Giustiniani <note>A Genoese bishop and polyglot editor of the Bible</note> distinguished the New Testament by verses, in the ancient Hebrew fashion, and by numerical notes; it being previously divided by paragraphs, noted by the letters A, B, C, etc.

# On the City of Jerusalem. CHAPTER 34.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' within a square frame featuring floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>
Abraham Ortelius <note>A famous 16th-century Flemish cartographer and geographer</note> in his *Geographical Treasury and Synonyms* describes <note>original Latin: "Hierosolyma, Ιεροσόλυμα, urbs totius Orbis terrarum primaria, & Iudeæ Metropolis"</note> Jerusalem as the primary city of the whole world and the Metropolis of Judea. Lysimachus writes that it was first named Hierosyla, and later Hierosolyma, as Josephus witnesses in his work *Against Apion*. This city is called Jerusalem, Salem, and Jebus in the Holy Scriptures. It is called Solyma, or the Solymi, by the Poets. Ptolemy records that it was called <note>original Greek: ἀιλία καπιτωλία</note> Aelia Capitolina in his time, named after the Emperor Aelius Hadrian who restored it, as Dion Cassius adds. It is also called "Capitolia" in the works of Antonius. Empolemon, in book 9, chapter 4 of Eusebius's *Preparation for the Gospel*, names it <note>original Greek: ἀργαριζὶν</note> Argarizin (which signifies "the most high mountain"). Annius of Viterbo <note>A 15th-century friar known for his historical writings</note> writes that it was made a "four-fold city" or tetrapolis, formed from the union of Salem, Jebus, Sion, and Moriah; Johannes Herold agrees with this in his continuation of the *History of the Holy War*, and adds this couplet regarding its synonyms:

> Solyma, Luz, Bethel, Jerusalem, Jebus, Helia,
> The sacred city is called Jerusalem and also Salem.

But he incorrectly writes "Helia" for Aelia. Masius, in his commentary on Joshua, noted that it was previously called <term>Zededk</term> [Justice/Righteousness]. Petrus Laieśtáin says in his work on Palestine that it is still called Capitolia today. Luis del Mármol Carvajal in his *Description of Africa* and Nicolas de Nicolay in his *Oriental Observations* report that it is called <note>A corruption of the Arabic "al-Quds al-Mubarak," meaning The Blessed Holy City</note> *Guzumobarech* by the Turks. Guillaume Postel and Jean Pinet have it as *Godsbarich*. It appears to be the same name, though corrupted. It is also found as *Codsbarioh* in the works of André Thevet, who adds that it is also called *Lecoust* by the Turks, and asserts that both names signify "the holy city." Giosafat Barbaro also uses the name *Goz*. Thomas Minadoi uses *Godz*. Rauwolff reports that it is called *Churz* today by the inhabitants, and was formerly called *Kurzitadon* by the Saracens.

<note>original Greek: πεπύζα</note> Pepuza, a city of Phrygia mentioned by Callistus (from which the Pepuzian heretics take their name), was once a city but is now a deserted place, according to John of Damascus and Epiphanius. They also write that it was situated in the middle of Galatia, Phrygia, and Cappadocia, and was called "Jerusalem" by those heretics, as Harmenopoulos writes.

<note>original Greek: Τύμιον</note> Tymion, a small town in Phrygia according to Eusebius and Callistus, was also called "Jerusalem" by the Montanist heretics, as Haymo adds.

->History of the Origin of Religions<-

religion was first announced and taught both by Him and by His Apostles; and also there has been no city or town in the world that has endured as many evils, nor fallen into such servitude as she has, as one can still see today. As for her treasures and sumptuous buildings, she was without equal among the cities of the world; thus Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist and author of "Natural History"</note> praises her above all the cities of the Levant. Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian</note> in Book 6 of the *Jewish Antiquities* describes the three walls with which she was encircled, which were heavily fortified with towers, bastions, and casemates, besides the excellence of the temple, which was unparalleled. Therefore, this city or town was founded in the middle of Judea, at the crest of Mount Sion, which is commonly held and reputed to be the middle and the center of the earth's surface. The Prophet Ezekiel 5 also says that she was set in the midst of the nations. David similarly says in Psalm 63 <note>The author likely refers to the Vulgate numbering of Psalm 73:12: "For God is my King of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth"</note> that the salvation of men was perfected in the midst of the earth, which Saint Jerome shows amply in his commentaries on that prophet. Furthermore, it is written in Genesis that Melchizedek—who according to the interpretation of Saint Paul <note>Referencing Hebrews 7:2</note> means "Righteous King" or "King of Justice"—having defeated four kings who held Lot prisoner, made a sacrifice to God, and that he baptized this city with the name Salem, which is to say "Peace," for which reason he was called King of Peace. Josephus maintains that this Melchizedek gave her the name Jerusalem, which is to say "Vision of Peace," making a single word from Jebus and Salem, so that this city had a name composed of these two names, merely changing a "B" into an "R" <note>An etymological theory attempting to link the "Jebu-" of the Jebusites with the "Jeru-" of Jerusalem</note>. Hegesippus <note>An early Christian chronicler</note> maintains that she was anciently named Solyme, and that after the King of the Canaanites nicknamed "the Just"—who was the first builder of Solyme—had a temple built there (which in Greek is called *Hieron* <note>original Greek: ἱερον</note>), she was named Hierosolyma. But Eusebius <note>A 4th-century historian and bishop</note> in Book 9, chapter 4 of his *Preparation [for the Gospel]* contradicts this, saying that Solyme began to be called Hierosolyma because of the Temple of Solomon, which was built there so superb and magnificent by King Solomon. Salem, then, was the first name given to this city or town. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Dardanus, held the opinion that she was named Jebus because of the Jebusites who possessed her as their capital city from her first beginning until the time of David; he gives her yet other names, and says that finally she was called Aelia Capitolina because of the Emperor Aelius Hadrian, who had her rebuilt and fortified, according to Zonaras <note>A 12th-century Byzantine historian</note> in Volume 2 of his *Annals*. Others maintain that her name is taken from *here*, which is to say "vision," because of the Angel who appeared to Abraham when he wished to sacrifice his son Isaac. The most common opinion is that just as the Jews called her in their language *Jerusalem*, the Greeks and Latins named her *Hierosolyma*, as witnessed by the aforementioned Josephus and Hegesippus; and one should not accept the word of Nicholas of Lyra <note>A 14th-century influential Bible commentator</note> when he says that Jerusalem was first named *Luca* and *Bethel*; for according to Saint Jerome, Bethel is twelve miles away from Jerusalem, as can even be seen in Josephus. Guillaume Postel, in his discourse on the distinguished regions named by the children of Noah, writes that this city once had the name *Chus* and *Chussembarich*. Several other discourses on this subject are treated by Brother Brochard <note>Burchard of Mount Sion, a 13th-century pilgrim</note> in his description of the places of the Holy Land, and by Wolfgang Weissenburg <note>A 16th-century geographer</note> in his description of the Holy Land. Furthermore, it must be noted that this city or town had several particular names that were attributed to it because of the high mysteries that were completed within it, such as *holy sacred city*, *city of David*, and several other similar names, besides its proper name, as Joannes Baptista Villalpando deduces very fully in his *Apparatus of the City and Temple of Jerusalem*. 

And to come to its history: the Jebusites and Canaanites, who were one and the same nation (for Jebus was the son of Canaan, son of Cain <note>The text reads "Cain," though Biblical genealogy usually lists Canaan as the son of Ham (Cham); this may be a printer's error or a reference to an apocryphal tradition</note>, nephew of Noah, from whom these nations took their name), were the lords of Jerusalem at the time when the children of Israel, delivered from the captivity of Egypt, took possession of Palestine and Judea. And it happened that in the division of the promised land made by the twelve tribes of Israel, Jerusalem fell to the lot of the tribe of Benjamin. However, because those of the tribe of Benjamin—whatever feats of arms they performed—could not entirely clear the lands of the Jebusites, they were constrained to tolerate them living among them for more than three hundred and seventy years, even until the time of David. David, being a prophet-king issued from the tribe of Judah, drove out the Jebusites, taking possession of their fortresses, which he fortified anew, and there he built sumptuous palaces, as can be seen in the *Books of Kings* and in Josephus in his book of *Jewish Antiquities*. 

David, then, having driven out the Jebusites, called Jerusalem the **City of God**, making it the chief and capital city of all Judea. During the reign of this king, this city was highly renowned and in great triumph among all nations because of the great and notable victories that David obtained; after his death, the wise Solomon, his son, succeeded him. And although this king applied himself to living in peace, nevertheless Jerusalem grew ever more in renown, riches, and most sumptuous buildings. For Solomon expanded its walls and had great fortifications built there. Furthermore, he constructed several very sumptuous buildings, and specifically that temple so renowned—because of the craftsmanship of its construction and its riches—that there never was, nor will there ever be in the future, any temple in this world that can equal or be compared to it. For as one can read in the *Second Book of Kings*, and the *Third Book of Chronicles* <note>original: "3. du Paralipom." — Paralipomenon is the traditional name for the Books of Chronicles</note>, and Book 8 of the *Jewish Antiquities* by Josephus, and in the first book, chapter 7, of Carlo Sigonio’s *On the Republic of the Hebrews*, the preparation for this temple was infinite and incomprehensible, so much so that for its fame alone, the Queen of Sheba came to visit King Solomon, and several kings and princes of the earth...
