Shalmaneser <note>original: "Salmanazar," an Assyrian king</note>, therefore, coming to the aid of the King of Judah, defeated the King of Israel; and nevertheless led away with him a great number of Jewish prisoners, to whom he gave the Region of Itene <note>likely referring to the region of Media or the Habor river</note> to inhabit, and this was the first captivity and dispersion of the Jews since they had miraculously departed from Egypt. Indeed, shortly after this, the Assyrian King compelled the Kings of Israel to pay him an annual tribute. At that time, the Prophets Hosea <note>original: "Osee"</note>, Isaiah <note>original: "Esaye"</note>, Amos, Micah <note>original: "Michee"</note>, and Jonah <note>original: "Ionas"</note> were in their ministry.

After the death of the unfortunate Ahaz <note>original: "Achaz"</note>, Hezekiah <note>original: "Ezechias"</note> his son succeeded to the crown. This prince was quite different from his father, for he was prudent, just, religious, and God-fearing. Thus, Jerusalem regained its former standing during his time: for he so reformed the administration and restored the service of God to such perfection that, as Holy Scripture bears witness, the Kingdom of Judah never had such a King; likewise, he shone in great prosperity and obtained great victories. This Prince, not content with uprooting all idolatry—to which he saw the people were strongly inclined—and wishing to fully restore the service of God, summoned the other ten tribes <term>lineages|The text uses "lignees" to refer to the tribes of Israel</term> of Israel to live according to the Law that God had given them by the hand of Moses. Many consenting to this, they came to sacrifice in Jerusalem and to celebrate the Passover according to the ordinance of Moses; and yet, according to what can be seen in the holy writings, the others persevered in their idolatry and mocked his summons, despite whatever warnings the Prophets gave them. 

Because of this, they were frequently chastised by the rods of God, both by Shalmaneser and by Sennacherib, who greatly oppressed them. The former, during the reign of Hezekiah—specifically in the fourth year of the reign of Hoshea <note>original: "Ozias," though historically referring to King Hoshea of Israel</note>, King of Israel—this Assyrian Prince waged such a fierce war against the seven <note>The text says "seven," though traditionally the Northern Kingdom comprised ten tribes</note> lineages of Israel for the space of three years that he forced them to abandon their homeland and go to live as slaves among the Medes. And so it was that the Jews were dispersed here and there among foreign nations, never to return to their homes, so that one cannot say what became of them afterward. This was the ruin and the end of the Kingdom of Israel, which had lasted three hundred and seventy years. 

Shalmaneser, on the contrary, sent Assyrians to Samaria to inhabit it, who, taking possession of all the land formerly inhabited by the Israelites, took the name of Samaritans. Eusebius <note>original: "Eusebe," the early Christian historian</note>, however, considers this name to be essential <note>meaning inherent or original</note>, but his opinion does not seem acceptable to the most learned and scholarly, who hold that they were called Samaritans because of Samaria, the capital city of that region. These Assyrians mixed the law of the Jews with their own idolatry; therefore, they were held in abomination as excommunicated people. 

After the defeat and ruin of the Israelites, the Kingdom of Judah alone remained standing: for the good King Hezekiah, to save his people from the fury of King Shalmaneser and to maintain his people in peace, gave him great sums of gold, buying peace by this means for a long time. The Prophet Isaiah <note>original: "Efaye"</note> went to King Hezekiah <note>original: "Ezechias"</note> to comfort him (for this prophet lived at that time), and in one night the Angel of the Lord destroyed one hundred and eighty thousand men in the Assyrian camp. This carnage forced the others to retreat. Thus, Hezekiah, having escaped this peril along with his people, lived the rest of his days peacefully in his kingdom. After God had clearly demonstrated great miracles out of respect for the said king, he died peacefully, leaving Manasseh his son and successor to the kingdom. 

This prince did not follow the path of his father but instead gave himself entirely to all forms of idolatry, committing several abominable things against the law of God, into which he also led the people. Because God was offended by this, He raised up the Assyrians against him, who punished him so severely that, besides the defeat of his men, he was made a prisoner and led captive to Babylon. However, he repented of his sin, which caused God to deliver him from the hands of the Assyrians, so that he returned to his estates and died there peacefully. 

Amon his son succeeded him, who, being wicked and iniquitous, was miserably killed; in his time lived the Prophets Joel, Nahum, and Habakkuk <note>original: "Abachuc"</note>. After him succeeded Josiah <note>original: "Ioſias"</note> his son, who was a prince who feared God and was very vigilant in the reformation of his people. For he drove all idolatry out of his kingdom—which was nonetheless strongly rooted in the hearts and souls of men—and repaired the temple, performing several other acts worthy of a holy and just king. 

Nevertheless, for all that, the wrath of God could not be appeased against the Jews because of the idolatries committed during the time of kings Amon and Manasseh. However, out of respect for Josiah (who died poorly through his great foolishness), God deferred punishing the Jewish people, as He did afterward. This king died from a wound he received on the day he fought against Necho <note>original: "Necar"</note>, King of Egypt. In fact, this was well-deserved, for Necho asked nothing of him, but rather sought his friendship as much as he could, having no other intention than to employ his forces against the King of Assyria. Nevertheless, Josiah went against him out of a certain lightness of heart <term>lightness of heart|The French "gayeté de cœur" suggests a reckless or impulsive whim or acting without serious provocation</term>, which cost him his life. His death was greatly regretted, even by the Prophet Jeremiah, who composed his lamentations because of it. 

Jehoahaz <note>original: "Ioachaz"</note> his son succeeded him, who was given to all iniquity and wickedness; therefore God did not permit him to reign more than three months, for Necho, who had already defeated his father, deprived him of his kingdom, making the land of Judea a tributary of one hundred talents of gold and one of silver every year. Jehoahaz then being deprived of his estates and led prisoner to Egypt where he died, Jehoiakim <note>original: "Ioachin"</note> his brother was installed in the kingdom, where he behaved very badly, for he was entirely given to idolatry and induced the people to do the same. 

Because of this, God raised up as an enemy for him King Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonofor"</note>, who had already reigned forty-four years in Babylon. This king, having obtained victory against the Jewish people, led away as slaves the greatest of all the land and carried off the vessels of the temple. The cause of this was that Jehoiakim <note>original: "Ioachas" - the text appears to use this name interchangeably with Jehoiakim here</note> gave aid to the King of Egypt against Nebuchadnezzar, against the counsel of Jeremiah. Jehoiakim, having then reigned eleven years and remained a prisoner for three years, died in great poverty. To him succeeded Jehoiachin <note>original: "Ioachin, ou Iechonias"</note>, who followed the path of his father, being wicked like him; also in his time God began to deploy the very rigorous rods <note>A metaphor for divine punishment or scourging</note> He had long ago prepared against Jerusalem and deferred out of respect for Josiah,

King Jehoiachin <note>original: "Ioachin"</note>, being unable to resist him, submitted to his will; his mother, his wife, and the principal members of his household [surrendered], and besides this, he made him a gift of the vessels and treasures that were still in the temple. Because of this, King Jehoiachin and the principal members of his court were led captive to Babylon. 

However, Nebuchadnezzar, taking all the assurances and oaths of loyalty he could from Mattaniah <note>original: "Mathatias"</note>, the uncle of King Jehoiachin, appointed and established him as King of Judea, and named him Zedekiah <note>original: "Sedechias"</note>. This king was one of the most iniquitous and unfortunate Princes that ever lived; for not only was he ungrateful toward God for the great graces He had shown him—turning his back on Him and refusing to listen to what the Prophet Jeremiah <note>original: "Hieremie"</note> predicted—but he also broke his promise to King Nebuchadnezzar, who had installed him in the kingdom, denying him his friendship. 

And if this king was worthless, the Priests were even worse, and the common people even less [worthy], so that all manner of abominations and idolatries reigned in Judea, even to the point of profaning the temple, which was held as sacred. And despite whatever remonstrances the Prophets Jeremiah, Ezekiel <note>original: "Ezechiel"</note>, and others made to this king, obstinacy nevertheless always grew within him. For this reason, God raised up King Nebuchadnezzar, who, to take vengeance upon this Zedekiah, in the 9th year of his reign, came to overrun the land of Judea with a large and powerful army, and held Jerusalem besieged for the time and space of two years, where King Zedekiah had retreated for his safety. 

But the besieged, pressed by famine and plague, and being no longer able to endure the siege, were constrained to put themselves at the mercy of the enemy, who, entering the city, put it to fire and blood. King Zedekiah was captured as he was fleeing, and being brought before King Nebuchadnezzar, he had his children killed before his eyes, and afterward had his two eyes put out, and led him in this manner captive to Babylon. 

After his return, he sent Nabuzaradan <note>original: "Nabuzardam," the captain of the guard</note> to Jerusalem, who was one of his principal captains, with the task of ruining the temple. This was 400 years after the building of the temple by Solomon. He did the same to the fortresses and buildings of Jerusalem, tearing down the city walls and ruining the palaces of the kings of Judah. He also carried away all the metal that was in the temple, and led away the priests and all the principal people, both of Jerusalem and of the whole country, with their wives and children, who remained captive in Babylon for 60 years. 

This Babylonian captivity was the one often spoken of in the Holy Scripture and in the writings of the Jews, which occurred about 600 years before the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. As for the common people, they were left in the country to cultivate the land, under the charge of Gedaliah <note>original: "Godolias"</note>, the appointed governor in Judea; but these people mutinied and killed Gedaliah, because of which the remaining Jews, fearing the fury of Nebuchadnezzar, went to live in Egypt, leaving Jerusalem deserted and depopulated. 

St. Jerome <note>original: "S. Hierome"</note>, in his book of *Hebrew Questions*, writes that after the capture and sack of Jerusalem, a good 50 years passed without man, beast, or bird entering it. In this, one could clearly recognize the great punishment deserved by this people, who had been so cherished and privileged by God. Seventy years having passed, God looked with His eye of pity upon the captivity and misery of His people, which was when the Empire fell into the hand...

...of the Persians, who dispossessed the Assyrians <note>The author likely uses "Assyrians" here to refer to the Babylonian Empire, which the Persians under Cyrus conquered in 539 BCE.</note>, and this occurred in the time of the great and powerful King Cyrus, who, moved by the Spirit of God, permitted fifty thousand Jews to return to their country under the leadership of Zerubbabel <note>original: "Zorobabel"</note>, their captain, and Joshua <note>original: "Iosuë"</note>, the High Priest. Having returned to Judea, they began to rebuild the ruins of their city of Jerusalem, offering sacrifices to God according to the ordinance of their law, as is contained in the first book of Ezra <note>original: "Esdras"</note>, and in the *Jewish Antiquities* of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus was a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian whose works are a primary source for this period.</note>, and other ancient authors. Nevertheless, the Samaritans, who were their neighbors, hindered them as much as they could from rebuilding and fortifying Jerusalem, and from repairing the ruins of the temple; several other nations did the same. And yet, despite whatever hindrance was placed before them, the temple was rebuilt and perfected during the time that Darius, son of Hystaspes, reigned in Babylon. At this, all the Jewish people held a great feast; however, the eldest among them, who had seen the ancient state of the temple <note>The first temple, built by Solomon, was legendary for its gold and splendor.</note>, could not keep themselves from weeping to see it so diminished in riches, sumptuousness of decoration, and divine graces, of which I have made ample mention in the preceding chapters. After that time, Artaxerxes permitted Ezra to bring back with him a great number of Jews, who returned to Judea. There, Ezra established a reformation according to the law, conforming the service of God entirely to the ordinances of Moses. During this same time, the Prophets Haggai <note>original: "Aggee"</note>, Zechariah <note>original: "Zacharie"</note>, and Malachi <note>original: "Malachie"</note> were in their reign. Jerusalem being then somewhat repopulated, King Artaxerxes permitted Nehemiah <note>original: "Neemias"</note> to fortify it and build there, which he did; so that the city of Jerusalem was peopled from day to day, and grew in riches and strength. This was approximately 500 years before the advent of Jesus Christ. In that time, the people were governed by the Priests and captains chosen by the people without any title or preeminence of King. For from the Babylonian captivity that occurred under Zedekiah <note>original: "Sedechias"</note>, which lasted 70 years, until Aristobulus, who first wore the title of High Priest and King, there were 484 years according to the reckoning of Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century Christian historian and exegete.</note>. The rest of the history that follows is taken from the Books of the Maccabees and Josephus, along with Africanus, Eusebius, and Eutropius, and several other highly renowned authors. And to begin, it must be noted that from the restoration of the temple until the time of Alexander the Great—a span of more than 150 years—one finds little worthy of memory done by the Jews, except for the history of Queen Esther, of which the Bible makes mention. It also records that Bagoses <note>original: "Bages"</note>, one of the principal captains of Artaxerxes, King of Persia, to avenge the death of Jeshua <note>original: "Iesu"</note> the priest, whom his brother Johanan <note>original: "Ieã"</note> had put to death, came to besiege Jerusalem with a strong army. He held it so closely that he took it by assault, and having sacked it, he returned, having imposed heavy tributes on the Jewish people to be paid annually to the Kings of Persia. Afterward, there arrived Alexander the Great, King of Macedonia, who, after the victory he obtained against Darius, King of Persia, was held and reputed to be the greatest and most powerful King on earth. Josephus mentions that during the siege of Tyre, a city situated at the foot <note>original: "crouppe"</note> of Mount Lebanon, he sent a request for aid in provisions, arms, and other necessaries for his camp to the High Priest Jaddua <note>original: "Iadus"</note>. Jaddua, as a bold Prince, replied to him that by the league he had with King Darius, he must not provide munitions to the camp of his enemy. Indignant at this, Alexander, after he had taken Tyre,

However, as they were ready to be entirely ruined, God raised up for them Judas Maccabeus, who was one of the foremost captains of the world, who, following the path of Mattathias, his father, governed the Jewish people in such a way that, having defeated several captains of King Antiochus, he restored his homeland to its former liberty. Having removed and cast down all the idols that were in the temple, he reformed the people according to the law of God. This Prince, being the High Priest, was of such great renown that the Romans, who then held the first rank in the world, sought to have his alliance and friendship. ## How Jerusalem, and the Kings thereof, came under the subjection of the Romans, and of the state of the Jews until their total destruction.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' with foliate ornamentation.</image-desc>
AFTER the death of Queen Alexandra <note>Salome Alexandra, the last regnant queen of Judea, who ruled from 76 to 67 BCE.</note> mentioned above, Aristobulus and Hyrcanus, her children, were in great debate and contention for the kingdom. But the Romans, who were very powerful, under the pretext of wishing to involve themselves to bring these two Princes to an agreement, took possession of the kingdom of Judea. For Pompey the Great, being in Asia, was respectively petitioned by these two Princes, each separately, to have his favor; but having had very troublesome words with Aristobulus, who was the more powerful of the two brothers, he came with his army against Jerusalem, which he entered by force and ransacked, profaning the temple and the <term>Holy of Holies <note>original: "Sancta sanctorum," the innermost chamber of the Temple where the Ark of the Covenant was kept.</note></term>, where none entered but the High Priest. This having been done by him, he sent Aristobulus as a prisoner to Rome, leaving the title of High Priest to Hyrcanus, and the government of all Palestine to Antipater, son of Herod the Ascalonite <note>Antipater the Idumean, father of Herod the Great; the text refers to him as "Ascalonite" based on traditions of his family's origin in Ascalon.</note>. And in this manner, the country of Judea came under the hand and subjection of the Romans, and remained tributary to them. As for Hyrcanus and Antipater, they had many setbacks on account of the civil wars of Pompey and Caesar, of Brutus and Cassius, and of Octavian and Marc Antony; even Jerusalem was subject to many mutations and changes by reason of these wars: for Cassius seized it by force and carried away the treasures of the temple, which Pompey had not wished to touch. Herod the Ascalonite conducted himself so valiantly and so wisely in his government that the Romans granted him the Kingdom of Jerusalem, in which he maintained himself in such a way that, even though he had given aid and succor to Marc Antony against Octavian Augustus, he nevertheless did not fail to acquire his favor, so much so that he confirmed his kingdom to him.

Thus Herod was the first foreign King who reigned in Judea, for his father was from Ascalon and his mother had come from Arabia. So it was that at that time the Prophecy was fulfilled which stated:
> *That the scepter would not depart from the house of Judah, until he who was to be sent should come:*
also, the people had never been without Kings or Priests of their own nation until Herod, in whose time the Messiah, our Lord Jesus Christ, was born, according as the Patriarch Jacob had predicted <note>Refers to the prophecy in Genesis 49:10.</note>. During his reign, Jerusalem maintained itself in great prosperity, so that according to ancient authors, it was as rich and as sumptuous in buildings as it had been before. From this, it came to pass that this Prince was surnamed "the Great" because of his virtue. ...that this Herod, having taken as his wife the daughter of Hyrcanus <note>This refers to Mariamne I, a princess of the Hasmonean (Maccabean) line. Not content with this, he exterminated those of the House of Judah who lived in any splendor, burned their titles and genealogies, and appointed the sovereign High Priests according to his own whim, not according to Divine Law. Furthermore, (as Philo the Jew <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher whose writings provide a window into Jewish life under the Roman Empire.</note> says) he massacred the Sanhedrin—that is to say, 72 senators of the House of Judah—so much so that through his cruelties, by the 30th year of his reign, he was accepted by all as an absolute King, with the priesthood and the Senate abolished and thrown into confusion.

After he had reigned 36 years, he died, leaving three sons, among whom the Emperor Octavian <note>The Emperor Augustus.</note> divided the kingdom of Judea. By means of this division, the kingdom of Jerusalem fell to Archelaus, who was nonetheless deprived of it by the Emperor Tiberius, who then sent Pontius Pilate to govern in Judea. To Philip, who was one of the sons of Herod the Great, he gave the region of Trachonitis as an inheritance, and to the younger Herod <note>Herod Antipas, the tetrarch of Galilee.</note>, he gave Galilee. It was he who put Saint John the Baptist to death and who sent our Lord back to Pilate after mocking him; likewise, their sins deserved to receive the punishments of God, which occurred in their time. 

To return then to Jerusalem: the greatest fortune and happiness it ever had was to see the Son of God in the flesh preaching among His people and performing infinite miracles, according to what the holy Prophets had predicted of Him. Nevertheless, these wretched people, failing to recognize the noble visitation of our Lord, crucified Him like a thief or a wrongdoer. Furthermore, Suetonius and Cornelius Tacitus <note>Two of the most famous Roman historians, who documented the Jewish War from a Roman perspective.</note> say that during the reign of the cruel Nero, the Jews were the first who wished to revolt against the Romans. They were pushed to this (according to those mentioned above) by a certain prophecy which they held to be true, which carried the message that in those times, the affairs of the Orient would advance greatly, and that a certain person would emerge from the Jewish nation who was destined to subjugate the whole world. Cornelius Tacitus, cited above, understood this prophecy simply as referring to the Empire of the Emperors Titus and Vespasian, but it was intended only for the spiritual reign of our Lord, which, taking its beginning in Jerusalem, grew and amplified throughout the universal world. 

As the revolt of the Jews was discovered, Vespasian and Titus, his son (who were afterwards Emperors), were sent into Judea with a large army; and this war was very cruel while Vespasian remained there. After his return to Rome, Titus remained in the field as Lieutenant General of the Roman army. Having taken several cities of Judea by force, he finally came to besiege Jerusalem, which was then very heavily populated because an infinite number of Jews had arrived there from all parts of the world to celebrate the Passover and to eat the Paschal lamb. Titus, therefore, held Jerusalem in so close a siege that no one could leave, and even less could anyone enter without being discovered and captured. This siege lasted five months, during which the city was heavily battered and well and stubbornly defended. The rest of the country of Syria was distributed among the other Princes and Lords. After the death of Godfrey, the Kingdom passed to his successors, totaling nine Kings, all of whom bore themselves valiantly during their reigns.

Certain modern authors have written, regarding what is mentioned above, that in the Books of Kings and Ezra one notes three migrations of the ten tribes of Israel, carried out by Tiglath-Pileser and Shalmaneser, kings of the Assyrians, under Pekah son of Remaliah, and Hoshea, kings of Israel. The manner of it was such that the Israelites were transported to distant countries—principally the most prominent among them—and other nations were brought in to take their place. Thus the Israelites were transported beyond Media and took over uninhabited lands to clear; from them came part of the Colchians, who in the time of Herodotus practiced circumcision, as reported by Josephus in Book 1 *Against Apion* of Alexandria. Even among the more northern Hordes of Tartary, there are those who have retained the names of Dan, of Zebulun, of Naphtali <note>Three of the twelve tribes of Israel.</note>; thus one should not marvel if there are so many Jews in the lands of Russia, Sarmatia, Lithuania, and other countries bordering the aforementioned Tartars. The same is no less plausible for the Turks, for this word *Turk* in the Hebrew language signifies "exiled people" <note>original: "gents exilez".</note>, and is used among them in contempt. It is quite likely that Muhammad, so as not to offend these great peoples who were then beginning to awaken, retained circumcision and the purifications and ceremonies of the Law of Moses. ### Of the comparison of the Hebrew language with the Greek.

## C H A P. XXXV.

Those who wish to maturely consider the secrets and mysteries of the Hebrew language, as deduced by us above, and the beauties and excellences of the Greek language, which we shall treat hereafter in the chapter on the Greek tongue, will ingenuously confess that the Hebrew language comprises many things in few words. It is wonderfully meaningful and expressive, explaining clearly and briefly everything one might imagine or think. When it is a question of discovering the most secret and enveloped hiding places of the heart, it leaves nothing behind, possessing a gravity, sweetness, vivacity, and a marvelous efficacy in its words, periods, and discourse. These are more admirable than all the beauty, excellence, and sweetness of the Greek language, which—with its synonyms and words of the same meaning, its bold and curiously sought-out epithets, its sublime and subtle metaphors or translations, its highly significant couplings of words, its various tenses, aorists <note>A verb tense in Greek that typically expresses a past action without indicating its duration or completion.</note>, and infinite other fine elegances—is in no way comparable to the aforementioned Hebrew language. 

The proof of this will be easily recognized through diligent and serious consideration of the words, periods, sentences, and discourse of the Hebrew language compared with Greek and all others, not so much through grammars and dictionaries, but through entire books. I shall content myself for the present to say and maintain with certainty that a single Hebrew book of the Psalms, or of Solomon, Job, or Isaiah, contains in each chapter more elegance, majesty, grandeur, figures, and every sort of light for a discourse than the thick books of the Greeks founded in all human wisdom. I speak not of the substance of things, which nonetheless is so happily expressed in the said Hebrew language that Greek and others, whatever trial or effort they may make, can only represent very coarsely and from a great distance what the other makes visible, as if to the life and in its natural state. Whatever thing it wishes to speak of or treat in writing, it does so as one of our most learned French poets <note>Likely a reference to Guillaume de Salluste Du Bartas (1544–1590), whose epic poems often praised the divine nature of the Hebrew language.</note> has well and eloquently remarked in these verses:

> Now when I enter into discourse [about how] the Hebrew tongue
> Explains most happily with so very few words

### History of the Origin of...

I amuse myself by discussing this further.
The same author in his treatise entitled, *Common and Familiar Idioms of the Hebrew Language.* <note>original: "Communes & familiaires Hebraicæ linguæ Idiotiſmi." This refers to the specific way Hebrew expresses ideas, which often differs from Latin or Greek syntax.</note>

<margin>1</margin> Among those things which are considered especially worthy of notice in individual languages, it is primary and most useful to observe what a word signifies properly, and then to what things it may be transferred through similarity. We call "similarity" any metaphor, analogy, expansion, comparison, or affinity of the things or meanings themselves. For example, "Lord" <note>original: "Dominus"</note> is properly said of one who tames and rules another by his command, or who is in charge of a house; however, it is sometimes extended to signify a husband. Furthermore, the chief and highest person in any art or discipline is called a "Lord." So also "Father," <note>original: "Pater"</note> while it signifies one who has fathered another, also pertains to signifying any high master in an art, a president of a college or society, or the head of a matter or business: for instance, we interpret a "father of those playing the lyre" as the highest in that art, the best and most perfect teacher of others, or finally, the inventor.

<margin>2</margin> Verbs are also used figuratively for a greater elegance of meaning: such as "to fly" for being excellent in some thing or action and being carried along with maximum speed; "to drop" <note>original: "Stillare"</note> for speaking; "to watch" for caring diligently; and "to flourish" for acting with great ornament and decorum.

<margin>3</margin> In place of an epithet or adjective, the possessive case is used: such as "son of perdition" for a "lost son"; "son of death" for one "worthy of death" or "condemned to death by law"; and "woman of virtue" for a "strenuous and strong woman."

<margin>4</margin> Scripture uses formal nouns in place of adjectives for the sake of greater emphasis. For example: "Since the just Lord loved justices" <note>original: "iuſtitias"</note>—that is, "just people"; and "Since you are not a God willing iniquity"—that is, "iniquitous people."

<margin>5</margin> Sometimes, under a general and indefinite verb, another specific noun is understood, either derived from the verb itself or explained by a clear observation of the sentence’s meaning: such as "I asked one [thing] from the Lord, and this I will seek"—I understand "thing" as "petition." And "he announced to him"—I hear "the messenger" <note>original: "nuntius"</note> as the implied subject.

<margin>6</margin> Sometimes the antecedent is used for the consequent, or the prior for the posterior: such as, "as the laborer waits for his work," meaning the "wages of the work" (Job 7). And "in buying I will buy from you for an exchange," that is, "for some thing or price" (2 Samuel 24). And "what exchange shall a man give for his soul?" (Matthew 16).

<margin>7</margin> There is also the use of the figure of apposition <term>Apposition: placing two nouns side by side where the second explains the first</term> both with and without prepositions, especially when the latter part of the apposition is a proper name and explains the former: as in "they made an attack on the man, on Lot" (Genesis 19); "observe in the boy, in Absalom" (2 Samuel 18); and "the flesh with its soul, its blood, you shall not eat" (Genesis 9).

<margin>8</margin> Related to these is Anadiplosis, <term>Anadiplosis: a rhetorical device where the last word of a clause is repeated at the start of the next for rhythmic or emotional emphasis</term> which repeats the same words for the sake of greater emphasis and notice: as in "For behold your enemies, O God; behold your enemies shall perish" (Psalm 92). And "The Lord has reigned, he has put on beauty; the Lord has put on strength" (Psalm 94).

<margin>9</margin> There is also the frequent observation of ellipses, <term>Ellipsis: the omission of words that are understood from context, often used to show high emotion</term> which indicate a vehement anguish of the speaker's mind: as in "But you, O Lord, how long?" (Psalm 6). And "My eye is drawn out, and does not rest, nor is there any pause" (Lamentations 3).

<margin>10</margin> Nouns are taken for adverbs, especially when a preposition is added: as in "they made the children of Israel serve in hardness," that is, "harshly" and "grievously."

### Languages of this Universe.

Exodus 1: "he loved them to the end," <note>original: "in finem dilexit eos"</note> that is, exceedingly or extremely (John 13); and "death is swallowed up in victory," that is, victoriously (Isaiah 26).

An infinitive is often taken for a noun, or for a gerund: such as "to eat" <note>original: "comedere"</note> and "to drink" <note>original: "bibere"</note> in Haggai 2; "to sit a little," "to rest a little," in Proverbs.

<margin>12</margin>
A substantive noun doubled in a different gender <note>Hebrew often pairs masculine and feminine forms of the same root to imply totality.</note> encompasses that entire nature in its universal sense, although different in species and forms: as in, "the Lord will take away the stay and the staff" <note>original: "sustentaculum, & sustentationem"</note> in Isaiah 3; and, "can your servant still hear the voice of singing men and singing women?" in 2 Samuel 19.

<margin>13</margin>
A substantive noun doubled, and pronounced in the plural in the second position, signifies excellence in its kind, and indicates the force of a Latin superlative in the first. For example, "Holy of holies," <note>original: "Sancta sanctorum"</note> that is, the most holy; "Song of Songs," that is, the most excellent Song.

<margin>14</margin>
"Vanity of vanities," that is, vanity itself, or the most vain. Two substantive nouns placed together with nearly the same meaning—of which the latter is in the genitive case—explain themselves in such a way that the first indicates a part of the latter: such as "the land of dust" <note>original: "terra pulueris"</note> in Daniel 12, that is, a portion of dust, or very fine earth, such as dust is.

<margin>15</margin>
A repeated substantive noun signifies distribution: such as "seven [and] seven" <note>original: "septem, septem"</note> in Genesis 7, that is, seven from each species. And "he began to send them out two [by] two" in Mark 6, that is, in pairs. And "in the valley of Siddim were pits, pits of bitumen," that is, pits everywhere.

<margin>16</margin>
Verbs or doubled adjectives increase the weight of the sentence and are pronounced with a more vehement voice: such as "unclean, unclean shall he be judged" in Leviticus 13. "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great" in Revelation 18 <note>The text cites Revelation 22, but this refers to the famous cry in chapter 18.</note>.

<margin>17</margin>
Adjectives constructed with verbs take on the nature of an adverb: such as, "it is not good for man to be alone" in Genesis 2, which means "man will not fare well alone." And "It is a light thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob... I will give you as a light to the nations" in Isaiah 49, which means "you are not merely my servant to do only this, but you shall do that as well." And "you Bethlehem Ephrata, it is a small thing that you are among the thousands of Judah," in Micah 5, meaning "it is not for nothing that you are among the thousands of Judah, for from you shall come the ruler."

<margin>18</margin>
A collective noun <note>A singular word representing a group, like "people" or "church."</note> is constructed through *syllepsis* <note>term: syllepsis (a grammatical figure where a verb agrees with the meaning rather than the strict grammatical form)</note> with a plural verb: as in, "let my people go that they may serve me" in Exodus 8. And "all the congregation saw that Aaron had expired" in Numbers 20.

<margin>19</margin>
A plural noun joined to a singular verb is explained by individual partitioning: such as, "The daughters [each] walks upon the wall," <note>original: "Filiæ incedit"</note> that is, each one after another (Genesis 49). "The flies of death makes the ointment stink," that is, any dead fly (Ecclesiastes 10).

<margin>20</margin>
In Hebrew speech, pronouns are placed in a different case than the substantive noun, even though both refer to the same thing: such as, "that night, let darkness seize it" in Job, that is, let darkness seize that night. And "The Lord, in heaven is his throne," that is, the Lord's throne is in heaven (Psalm 11).

<margin>21</margin>
The nominative of a pronoun, which is later repeated in another case with a verb, carries emphasis and a sort of notation of the person and their office: "I in the way, God led me" in Genesis 24, that is, while I was making the journey, I was led by God. And "have you fasted for me, [even] me?" in Zechariah 7. And "as for you also, by the blood of your covenant, I have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit" in Zechariah 9.

22 The past participle sometimes indicates a finished, past, and completed action: as in, "who sit in the graves, and dwell in the observed places," Isaiah 65; <note>original: "qui sedent in sepulchris, & in obseruatis morantur"</note> that is, in those places which have already ceased to be observed. And "he saw that it was expected," Ezekiel 19; <note>original: "Et vidit quod expectatum esset"</note> that is, that it had ceased to be watched, and that watching had been of no use.

23 Hypallage <note>A figure of speech where the natural relationship between two words is reversed for emphasis.</note> is frequent in the language of the scriptures: as in, "and they sent the city into the fire," Judges 1; <note>original: "ciuitatem miserunt in ignem"</note> that is, they sent fire into the city. And, "behold, I have sent Naaman my servant to you that you may gather him from his leprosy," <note>This refers to the story of Naaman the Syrian in 2 Kings 5.</note> that is, that you may gather his leprosy away from him. It would be worthwhile to consider the conjugations of verbs, for great meaning is added to words from their conjugation: for the force of the meaning is either increased, or diminished, or reciprocated, or even changed. This is most obvious to those who know Hebrew. And so far, I would only desire that all theologians—indeed, all students of the sacred letters—would apply themselves to Hebrew grammar, so that they might each be able to read and conjugate; they would certainly obtain great use from it. This labor will take only about one month; the rest will follow with little effort from reading this instructional material.

25 Verb tenses are not always to be strictly observed, for among the Prophets, future things are reported in the past tense, as if they had been made spectators of future events by God; to them, the answers will be as certain as if the matter had already been done and settled.

26 The Hebrews use the future tense to signify those things which are either perpetual, or according to nature, or according to law, equity, and propriety. And that force of the past among them in the sciences is what the present tense is among the Latins. For in the sciences, verbs are released from the indication of time, and they signify the property and certainty of the thing itself, whether of action or passion. This is done by the Hebrews through the future tense, and much more correctly than by the Latins; for the future contains within itself the logic of the past and the present, which is easily proved in the negation of the future. For he who truly denies from the beginning of things in this way—"Man will not be unjust"—would undoubtedly deny the other tenses most truly: "Man was not unjust," and "Man is not unjust." But truly, he who might deny from the beginning in this way—"Man was not" or "is not unjust"—could not immediately say so truly: "Man will not be unjust." Therefore, the future encompasses the other tenses, whereas it is by no means contained by them. And this logic must be diligently observed for the elegant and certain explanation of many passages; the future tense is of the greatest use not only to those who read the Hebrew Bible, but also to those who read the Latin Bible, for whom the future must often be interpreted as standing for all time: as in, "they have a mouth and they shall not hear; they have nostrils and they shall not smell; they have hands and they shall not feel; they have feet and they shall not walk; they shall not cry out in their throat." <note>This refers to the description of idols in Psalm 115.</note>

27 Furthermore, that well-known precept of those who know Hebrew should be noted: the past verb is usually converted into the future, and conversely the future into the past, when the conjunction "and" is added to either. This does not happen always, but where that conjunction in Hebrew is the *Vau* <note>The Hebrew letter Waw (ו).</note> with the vowel *Pataah* <note>The Hebrew vowel Pathach (ַ ).</note>, which the grammarians call the *Vau* conversive.

28 Verbs which signify exhortation or discouragement are explained completively, such as: "Do not fear, do not be broken by fear," Exodus 13.

29 There are certain verbs which, although they do not signify motion, must nevertheless be explained with motion and application when prepositions are added: as in, "he will receive to you" <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "accipiét ad te".</note>

# Languages of this Universe. 307

...[bring] to you a red heifer, <note>original: "ad te vitulam ruffam"</note> that is, one that will be accepted from you (Numbers 19). And "the people began to play the harlot to the sons of Moab" (Numbers 24), <note>original: "scortari ad filios Moab"</note> which means they went over to the sons of Moab for the purpose of harlotry. And "You have profaned his crown to the earth" (Psalm 89), <note>original: "Prophanasti in terram coronam eius"</note> which means that by profaning it, you have cast it down.

<margin>30</margin>
The <term>Dative case</term> <note>The grammatical case usually indicating the recipient of an action ("to" or "for").</note> is often added to a sentence beyond the standard requirements of the verb to indicate usefulness or benefit. For example: "Go out for yourself from your land, and from your kindred" (Genesis 12), <note>original: "exi tibi de terra tua"</note> meaning: you alone, for your own benefit, shall migrate from there. And "Behold, your King comes to you, a just one" (Zechariah 9).

<margin>31</margin>
The <term>Imperative</term> <note>The mood used for commands or requests.</note> sometimes takes on the force of a demonstrative adverb <note>A word used to point something out, like "Look!" or "Behold!"</note>, such as: "Look, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field" (Genesis 27). Or "Look, your words are good" (1 Samuel 15).

<margin>32</margin>
Not infrequently, the imperative is placed in the position of an adverb when joined to another verb: as in, "Hasten, hear me" (Psalm 102), <note>original: "festina exaudi me"</note> meaning "as quickly as possible," or "hurriedly."

<margin>33</margin>
In the idiom of the Hebrew language, the second person of the present imperative is sometimes used for the third person of the future imperative. For example: "Take from among you an offering to the Lord; let each willing person bring it" (Exodus 35), <note>original: "accipite à vobis... conferat eam"</note> meaning "let him take." Or, "Commit yourself to the Lord, let him deliver him" (Psalm 22), meaning "let him commit himself to the Lord."

<margin>34</margin>
The use of the Imperative for affirmative commands and the Future for negative commands is very frequent. For example: "Honor your father and your mother." And "You shall not steal, you shall not kill, you shall not covet." This is because negative precepts are perpetual and binding at all times, and this is correctly signified by the future tense.

<margin>35</margin>
An <term>Infinitive</term> joined with another verb in the third person can be translated into that same person for a better explanation. For example: "And the fathers kindled the fire, and the women to set the dough" (Jeremiah 7), <note>original: "mulieres ponere pastam"</note> meaning "they set it." And, "Even the hind of the field groaned, and to leave, because there was no grass" (Jeremiah 14), meaning "she left [her young]."

<margin>36</margin>
When the same verb is doubled, with the first part placed in the infinitive or gerund form, it signifies certainty and intensity. For example: "In doing, I will do mercy to you for the sake of Jonathan your brother" (2 Samuel 9), <note>meaning: "I will surely show mercy."</note> "In chastising, God has chastised me, but he did not give me over to death" (Psalm 118). And "In coming, it will come, and it will not delay" (Habakkuk 2).

<margin>37</margin>
This same repeated infinitive in a negative sentence intensifies the negation. For example: "In anointing, I was not anointed" (Daniel 10), <note>original: "vngendo non vnctus sum"</note> meaning "I was not anointed at all." And "In revealing, they shall not reveal this people" (Micah 1).

<margin>38</margin>
Verbs of exhortation, calling together, or warning are often placed before another verb to show zeal or eagerness, and are explained through an adverb. For example: "Come, let us make bricks" (Genesis 11), meaning "Come now, let us prepare bricks." "Come, and let us destroy them from the earth," meaning let us destroy them "quickly, diligently, and swiftly."

<margin>39</margin>
Sometimes, out of two verbs, the first is an antecedent to the second. For example: "And you, rising up, Lord, will have mercy on Zion" (Psalm 102), meaning "You will rise so that you may have mercy."

<margin>40</margin>
The third person of the past—and the future as well—is sometimes explained impersonally when the action refers to a multitude or to perpetuity. For example: "for it shall be called the Lord’s release" (Deuteronomy 15). And "from ages past they have not been heard, nor have they been commanded" (Isaiah 64).

<margin>41</margin>
A change of the person of the verb within the same sentence, even though referring to the same person or thing, is frequent in the sacred books, and especially in the songs [Psalms]. For example: "God have mercy on us, and bless us; may he illuminate his face upon us, and have mercy on us, that we may know his way on earth, and among all nations Your salvation" (Psalm 67). <note>Note how the text shifts from "His way" (3rd person) to "Your salvation" (2nd person).</note>

66. And, because they shall be ashamed of the trees which you have desired, Isaiah 1. <note>original: "Et, quia pudefient, ab arboribus quas concupivistis"</note>
<margin>42</margin> Many verbs of the first or second active conjugation have a <term>neuter-passive</term> <note>A verb that is active in form but passive in meaning.</note> sense, as we are taught by the interpretations of the Holy Spirit. For example: "Abraham believed God, and he imputed it to him as righteousness," Genesis 15. This means (as St. Paul explains) "it was imputed to him for righteousness," Romans 4. And "that you may be righteous in your words," Psalm 51; the Apostle interprets this as "that you may be justified in your words," Romans 3. Also, "victory swallowed up death," Isaiah 25; that is, "death is swallowed up in victory," as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15. Likewise, "nor did he open your ear," instead of "your ear shall be opened," Isaiah 48; and "they shall open your gates," instead of "your gates shall be opened." And "because he gathered from the hire of a harlot," instead of "it was gathered," Micah 5. And "nights of labor have withdrawn me," Job 7; that is, "they were withdrawn."

<margin>43</margin> Verbs that signify the authorship of a fault and are attributed to God—who is by no means the author of fault—must be explained in this way: that God acts not <term>actively</term>, but <term>privatively</term> <note>A theological distinction: God does not "cause" the evil, but rather "withdraws" his grace, leaving the person to their own devices.</note> in that matter. From this privation and the withdrawal of God, men cast themselves into deep darkness by their own impulse and with horrendous danger, since they have been prone to evil from their youth. In this way, these passages are to be explained: "I will harden Pharaoh's heart," Exodus 7; and, "Why do you make us wander from your ways?" <note>The source text says "vitiis tuis" (your vices/faults), but contextually refers to wandering from God's ways/paths.</note> Isaiah 63; and, "The God of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelieving," 2 Corinthians 4.

For a fuller understanding of the matter above, see what the same Benoist Arias Montanus has written amply and profusely in his treatise titled *Idioms of the Hebrew Language* <note>original: "Hebraicæ linguæ idiotismi"</note>.

THEODORE Bibliander, in his *Commentary on the common system of all languages and letters*, speaks thus of the Hebrew language:
> The speech of the Hebrews varied according to times and places, even when divine eloquence was celebrated among that nation. Just as in the time of Samuel, a "Seer" <note>original: "Hofed," likely a transcription error for "Hozeh"</note> was the name for one who was later called by the more frequent name *Nabi*, which is "Prophet." And an *Ephraimite* pronounces the Hebrew word meaning an "ear of grain" <note>The "Shibboleth" incident from Judges 12.</note> one way, and a *Gileadite* another, as we read in the history of Judges, chapter 12. Furthermore, there was clearly a different style of writing and speaking in the age of Job and Moses, and likewise of the prophets Isaiah and his peers, as well as of Daniel and Ezra.

And without entering into a long and profuse deduction of this matter (which we have treated amply in the preceding chapters), we will say only that the Hebrew language has lost much of its former grandeur, beauty, and perfection through the frequent exiles, calamities, and changes that happened to the Hebrews and Jews under various Kings, Princes, and Potentates. 66. And, because they shall be ashamed of the trees which you have desired, Isaiah 1. <note>original: "Et, quia pudefient, ab arboribus quas concupiuistis, Isai. 1." This refers to Isaiah 1:29, where the prophet rebukes the people for their idolatry in sacred groves.</note>

<margin>42</margin> Many verbs of the first or second conjugation in the active voice have a "middle-passive" <note>A grammatical term where the subject is both the performer and the recipient of the action</note> meaning, and we are taught this through the interpretations of the Holy Spirit. For example: *Abraham believed God, and he imputed righteousness to him* in Genesis 15. This is (as Saint Paul explains) *it was imputed to him as righteousness* in Romans 4. And *that you might become righteous in your words* in Psalm 51, which the Apostle interprets as *that you might be justified in your words* in Romans 3. And *victory absorbed death* in Isaiah 25, which is to say, *death is swallowed up in victory*, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15. And *neither shall he open your ear* for *your ear shall be opened* in Isaiah 48. And *they shall open your gates* for *your gates shall be opened*. And *because he gathered from the hire of a harlot* for *it was gathered* in Micah 5 <note>Though the text cites Micah 5, this refers to Micah 1:7</note>. And *nights of labor have withdrawn from me* in Job 7, meaning *they were withdrawn*.

43. Verbs that suggest the authority of sin and are attributed to God—who is in no way the author of sin—must be explained in this way: God does not act "actively," but rather "privatively" <note>A theological concept where God "acts" by withdrawing his grace or protection, allowing a result to happen rather than causing it directly</note>. From this privation and withdrawal by God, men cast themselves into profound darkness by their own impulse with horrendous danger, since they have been prone to evil from their youth. In this way we should explain these phrases: *I will harden Pharaoh's heart* in Exodus 7; and *why do you make us err from your ways?* <note>original: "vitiis tuis" (from your vices/faults); likely a variant or error for "viis tuis" (from your ways) as found in Isaiah 63:17</note> in Isaiah 63; and *But the God of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelieving* in 2 Corinthians 4.

See for a more ample understanding of the matter above, what Benedictus Arias Montanus <note>A renowned 16th-century Spanish orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible</note> has written amply and profusely in his treatise titled *Idioms of the Hebrew Language* <note>original: *Hebraicæ linguæ idiotismi*</note>.

The speech of the Hebrews varied across times and places, even when the divine eloquence was celebrated among that nation. Palestine (παλαιστίνη), according to Ptolemy <note>an ancient Greek geographer</note>, is a region of Asia which in the Holy Scriptures is called *Pelisthim*, *Canaan*, and the Land of Promise (Φυλισιειμ <note>Greek for Philistines</note> according to the 70 interpreters <note>the Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>). Saint Jerome, in his work *On Hebrew Places*, says it should be noted among historians that *Judea* belongs to Palestine, while *Galilee* and *Samaria* actually belong to Phoenicia. The *Canaanites* are its inhabitants. Today, all Europeans call it the *Holy Land*, using various words according to the difference of their languages, but all signifying the same thing. *Palestinai* is mentioned in the authentic records, in which the city of Caesarea is located; Strabo mentions *Palestine* and *Salutaris* in his book of the *Notitia*. There is also *Palestine the Third*: see *Arabia Petraea*. Galen refers to *Palestinian Syria* when he writes that the "Jewish stone" <note>likely *lapis judaicus*, a fossilized sea urchin spine used in ancient medicine</note> is found there.

It seems to stand for Judea, for Eusebius <note>an early Christian historian</note> writes in the 10th book of the *Preparation for the Gospel* that in his time it was called thus.

*Palestinian Petra*: Agatharchides places this near Arabia Felix <note>the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula</note>. See *Sittacene* and *Interamna*.

*Sittacene* (σιττακηνή) is, according to Ptolemy, a small region of Assyria near Susiana. As Pliny holds, this was called *Arbelitis* and *Palestine*, and also *Apolloniatis* according to Strabo. However, according to Ptolemy, Apolloniatis, Arbelitis, and Sittacene are distinct. Giacomo Gastaldi <note>a famous 16th-century Italian cartographer</note> now calls it Rabia.

Chaldea <note>Greek: $\chi\alpha\lambda\delta\alpha\tilde{\iota}\alpha$</note> is a region of Babylonia in Asia. Pierre Belon writes that it is called Azamia in these times. By Stephanus it is called the Chalybdic Region <note>Greek: $\chi\alpha\lambda\upsilon\beta\delta\iota\kappa\eta$</note>, and its inhabitants the Cephenes <note>Greek: $\kappa\eta\phi\tilde{\eta}\nu\epsilon\varsigma$</note>, according to the testimony of Josephus.

They were previously named the Arphaxadaei <note>Greek: $\text{A}\rho\phi\alpha\xi\alpha\delta\alpha\tilde{\iota}\text{o}\iota$</note>. According to Strabo, the Chaldeans are also a people in Asia Minor, above Trebizond, who he testifies were called Chalybes in antiquity, and by Homer, the Halizones. But Eustathius writes better on this, calling these people Chaldos and the region Chaldia (which he places in Armenia). A certain ancient author, whose name does not come to mind, writes that the Chaldeans were called Casdeos after Chesed, the son of Nahor, brother of Abraham. Leunclavius teaches that Chaldea is today called Kurdistan, and the Chaldeans are called Kurds by the Turks; he also writes that the region is called *Keldan* by the Arabs. (See Abraham Ortelius in his *Synonyms* and *Geographical Theater*).

...that they divided their science in general into five species which the Greeks called **interchanges of years and months** <note>original Greek: ἐναλλαγὰς ἐτωστῶν καὶ μηνῶν</note>, **changes of the air** <note>original Greek: μεταβολὰς τοῦ ἀέρος; refers to weather patterns</note>, **elections** <note>original Greek: ἐπιλογὰς; the astrological practice of selecting auspicious times for specific events</note>, **nativities** <note>original Greek: γενεθλιολογικὼ; the casting of birth charts</note>, and **interrogations** <note>original Greek: ἐρωτήσεις; seeking answers to specific questions through the stars</note>. These people passed the bounds and limits of Physics, Philosophy, and Astrology through a long and tedious deduction, or rather a confusion of **astrological outcomes** <term>apoteleisms: the effects or results produced by the stars</term> and various dissimilar canons—indeed, strange and **indifferent matters** <term>adiaphora: things that are neither commanded nor forbidden, or here, matters of no consequence</term>. These brought more confusion and entanglement to these observations than teaching or edification to their science. This science has been, since ancient times, an abomination among the Hebrews, viewed as something coming from the sinful and fallen angels. This is confirmed by Moses in **Genesis chapter 41**, Daniel the Prophet in **chapter 2**, and **Tertullian** in his *Apology against the Gentiles*, chapter 35; **Lactantius Firmianus**, book 2, chapter 17 of his *Divine Institutes*; **Julius Firmicus**, book 1 of the *Book of Profane Errors*; **Tatian** in his *Orations against the Greeks*; **St. Augustine**, book 8, chapter 16 of his *City of God*; and the Greek Emperors in book 9, title 18, **"On sorcerers and astrologers"** <note>original Latin: de maleficis & Mathematicis; in the Roman legal code, "Mathematicians" was a technical term for illegal fortune-tellers and astrologers</note> in the Code of Justinian.

The faithful Hebrew historian **Josephus**, in book 1, chapters 7 and 8 of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, has left in writing that the Patriarch **Abraham**, having lived for some time in the land of Chaldea (located above Babylon), departed from there with his kin. Changing location, he came to live in the land of Canaan, which is today called Judea. When famine struck that land, he went down into Egypt, where he demonstrated that the arguments and propositions used by the Egyptians in their religion were full of vanity and contained no truth in them. Because of this, he was greatly esteemed by them, and he kindly shared with them the science of **Arithmetic, Geometry, and Astrology**, which he had learned from his Hebrew ancestors; for before Abraham came to Egypt, the Egyptians had no knowledge of these sciences. Therefore, the Egyptians received them from the Chaldeans, who first practiced them. 

Those who have turned the pages of the oldest Hebrew histories know well that **Zoroaster**—who is none other than **Ham**, son of Noah, or **Mizraim** his son, thus surnamed Zoroaster—was the first [to practice this]. In the Hebrew language, the name is derived from **Zarah** (זָרָה) and **Ascha** (אֵשָׁא), which signifies "**Strange Fire**" <note>This etymology links the name to Ham's perceived spiritual corruption or his magical practices</note>, as much for his impurity as for his magical fire. As Prince or King of the Bactrians, he was the first who, having learned the science of Astronomy from the Patriarch Noah, began to abuse it, mixing in the conjurations of false spirits. He later instructed the Chaldeans in these superstitions and magics which they practiced afterward, as **Pliny** seems to note in book 30, chapter 1 of his *Natural History*. **Berosus**, in the fifth book of his *Antiquities*, holds that **Ninus**, the fifth King of the Assyrians and Babylonians, was the first who advanced these Chaldeans and established for them a college and university in Babylon. However, **Diodorus Siculus**, a very ancient Greek author, in his third book refers this to **Belus**, King of the Assyrians, who was older than Ninus. This Belus was the first (as he says) who began the order of the **Chaldean Priests**. In ancient times, these held the same rank and dignity among the Babylonians as the Priests did in Egypt, inasmuch as they were destined for the service of the Gods, spent their whole lives philosophizing, and were highly learned.

in astronomy, and the science of the course of the stars; this Chaldean race passed this science from father to son, without others being admitted except those who were of their own blood and race destined for it. These individuals were instructed in this field from their infancy, without being constrained or necessitated to do any other thing throughout their lives. They maintained, among other propositions—which they said ought not to be reduced to writing—that men were entirely subject to the movements of the planets, and principally to Saturn and the Sun. These, along with the others, they named ambassadors of the gods, as they predicted through their courses everything that was to happen in this lower world, as Strabo amply discusses in Book 6 of his *Geography*. He says there were various sects or kinds of these Chaldeans: some being called Orchenes, others Borsipenes, others Cephenes, and others named by different and dissimilar names according to the diversity of the sects among them, inasmuch as their opinions were not similar within their own science. 

The Hebrews hold it as quite certain that Arphaxad, son of Shem (who is spoken of in Genesis 10), signifying in the Hebrew language "healing" or "releasing the prey," was the first from whom these Chaldeans took their names and titles. They are named in the Hebrew language **Chasdin**, from the singular **Chasdi**, derived from the word **Chascat**. In more ancient times, they inhabited the area beyond the Ararat mountains, formerly named Arphaxadeans according to the report of Josephus in Book 1, chapters 6 and 14 of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, and afterwards **Chasdin**, from the last Hebrew letters of the word **Arphaxad**. 

Some authors take them to be the Susians, as Benito Arias Montano very curiously remarks in his treatise entitled *Phaleg*, chapter 9. He writes that anciently these Chaldeans were those who inhabited the area near Babylon in Mesopotamia, in a certain region named Chaldea, which is called today by the corrupted name **Arachaldar**, which signifies "sand of the Arabs" or "Arabian deserts." This is because that region is close to and neighboring Desert Arabia, but separated from it only by a mountain bearing this same name, from which the entire province was called Chaldea. However, at other times it bore the name of a King commanding there called Alchemenie, who is thought to have been the first to teach the observation and foolish science of **horoscopes** <term>horoscopes: from the Greek 'hora' (hour) and 'skopos' (observer); the practice of predicting a person's fortune or misfortune by considering the planet ruling at their birth</term>. 

This science later reached Egypt, as Josephus confesses, making the Chaldeans the inventors of it according to the ancient historians. On this subject, one should see St. Augustine, Book 16, chapter 10 of *The City of God*; Hayton the Armenian, chapter 11 of his *Histories*; François de Belleforest, volume 2, book 3, chapter 36 of his *Cosmography*; and Abraham Ortelius, maps 4 and 50 of his *Great Theater of the Universe*.

<term>Chasceddim</term>, which is the name for Chaldeans—under which term are comprised, both generally and specially, all the sects of the wise men of Babylon—properly and particularly signifies in the book of Daniel (according to Saint Jerome) a type of men whom the common Latin speakers call in the Latin tongue <term>Mathematicos</term> and <term>Genethliacos</term> <note>Mathematicians and "Genethliacs," specifically those who cast horoscopes based on a person's birth</note>. > The Chaldeans, being first and foremost practiced in stellar science, attributed all things to the movements of the stars, by which they believed the powers of the world were dispensed, which consist of numbers and their proportions. They worshipped these visible things, not perceiving the invisible and intelligible, examining only their order. Thus, from the circuits of the Sun, the Moon, the wandering stars <note>planets</note>, and the fixed stars, and from the seasons of the year divided into four, and the consensus between celestial and terrestrial things, they thought the world itself was God—by this profane opinion making the creature similar to the Creator.

This is how Philo speaks of these Chaldeans, whom Saint Jerome, in his epistle to the Hebrews, says affirmed that the matter of this visible world was eternal and not produced by anyone. <term>Asaphim</term> signifies those who were called "Philosophers" by an old Latin interpreter, <term>μαγοί</term> <note>Magoi</note> by the seventy Greek interpreters <note>the Septuagint</note>, and "Magi" by the aforementioned Saint Jerome. These were Philosophers concerning all things divine and human; the author of these Magi was, according to the opinion of Origen, Balaam the son of Beor, whom Balak the King of the Moabites called to him to curse the Hebrew people with his magics and incantations.

Here is what the aforementioned Origen writes in his 13th homily on Numbers: <note>Origen (c. 185–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar and theologian.</note> *“If the prophecies of Balaam were inserted into the sacred volumes by Moses, how much more were they recorded by those who lived at that time in Mesopotamia, among whom Balaam was held in high esteem, and of whose art they are known to have been disciples? It is said, then, that the race and institution of the Magi flourished in the Eastern regions from him: who, having among themselves all the things that Balaam had prophesied, also had this written: that a Star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall rise out of Israel. The Magi had these writings among themselves; and therefore, when Jesus was born, they recognized the star and understood the prophecy to have been fulfilled—more so than the people of Israel themselves, who despised hearing the words of the holy Prophets. They, therefore, from these things alone which Balaam had left in writing, recognizing that the time was at hand, came, and seeking him, immediately adored him.”* <note>original Latin: "Si à Mose Prophetiæ Balaam sacris infertæ sunt voluminibus... venerunt, & requirentes eum statim adorauerunt."</note> The author of the "Incomplete Work on Saint Matthew," chapter 2, says: <note>The *Opus Imperfectum in Matthaeum* is an ancient commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, formerly attributed to St. John Chrysostom.</note> *“I have read in some place that these Magi received the knowledge of this appearing star from the books of Balaam the diviner, whose divination is placed in the Old Testament: a Star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall rise out of Israel, and shall rule over all Nations.”* <note>original Latin: "Legi apud aliquem, Magos istos ex libris Balaam diuinatoris... & dominabitur omnium Gentium."</note>

Diogenes Laertius, in Book 1 of the *Lives of the Philosophers*, writes that Zoroaster was the Prince of these Magi, who, like priests, were entirely devoted to the service of the gods. They were accustomed to being the only ones to offer and present their prayers, vows, and sacrifices, as if they were the only ones heard and understood by the gods. They dressed entirely in white and had no bed other than the hard earth. For their food, they ate only herbs, cheese, and bread. They used a reed in place of a staff, at the end of which they placed their cheese to eat it. They held as doctrine and religion that there was one single, first, and Eternal God—which Zoroaster had also taught during his life according to the report of Eusebius in Book 1 of his *Evangelical Preparation*. They also posited other secondary gods or Spirits <note>original: "Genies"</note>, the substance of which they held to be either fiery, watery, or earthy. They rebuked or disapproved of images and statues of the gods, and rejected the opinions of those who thought of them as male and female. They judged that souls, after the dissolution of their bodies, were immortal, and they said that all things that happen here below endure through their prayers and supplications. They believed that men must rise again, and that the bodies of the wicked and iniquitous deceased must be burned by the fire of damnation. They discussed and discoursed upon infinitely beautiful things regarding justice and the other virtues, and they had no use for gold or silver among themselves. Philo the Jew, previously cited, in his book on *Special Laws*, speaks of this wisdom in these words: *“Truly that Magic, that is, speculative science, through which the works of nature are seen more clearly, as something honorable and to be sought, is pursued not only by commoners but also by the greatest Kings of Kings, especially the Persian ones, who are so curious about these arts that it is not permitted to rule unless one has lived familiarly with the Magi.”* <note>original Latin: "Veram quidem illam Magiam, hoc est, speculatiuam scientiam... nisi cum Magis versato familiariter."</note> Saint Jerome, on this subject, says: *“Magi are those who philosophize on individual things; however, common custom accepts ‘Magi’ as sorcerers, who are regarded differently among their own people because they are the Philosophers of the Chaldeans: and for the knowledge of this art, the Kings and Princes of that same nation do everything; whence they also were the first to understand the birth at the nativity of the Lord Savior, and coming to Bethlehem, they adored him.”* <note>original Latin: "Magi sunt, qui de singulis philosophantur... veniētes in Bethlehē adorauerunt."</note>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of various classes of Chaldæan practitioners, moving from the Magi mentioned on the previous page to Enchanters, Sorcerers, and Soothsayers. It establishes a lineage of "corrupted magic" beginning with Zoroaster and discusses the theological distinctions between these practices and the wisdom of biblical figures like Daniel.</meta>

### Languages of this Universe.

**Enchanters** <note>original Greek: ἐπαοιδοὶ</note>, which is to say in Latin *Incantatores*, or as **St. Jerome** prefers, *Harioli* <note>soothsayers</note>, who were entirely dedicated to the enchantments of **Demons**. According to the authority of **Pliny**, **Justin**, and **St. Augustine**, they claimed to take their origin from **Zoroaster**, King of the **Bactrians** <note>an ancient Iranian people</note>, a magician and the first corrupter of true Magic. He was the only one among mortals who burst into laughter on the very day he was born into this world; his brain was said to throb so intensely that it completely repelled a hand placed upon it—a certain omen of his future madness, through which he declined into the follies of incantations. Having learned these things from his predecessors, he was, by a just judgment of God, defeated in battle and driven from his kingdom by **Ninus**, King of the **Assyrians**. The most ancient historians who have spoken of him have written that this **Zoroaster**—whether he was **Ham** himself, the son of **Noah**, or his grandson (the son of Ham)—was the first who, having learned the science of the Stars from **Noah**, began to abuse it, converting it into evil omens and mixing in the conjurations of spirits. He instructed those **Chaldæans** in the superstitious observations that they practiced thereafter. Those who followed him established two principles (according to the aforementioned **Laertius**): one good and the other evil. The good was the God of Heaven, from whom all blessings proceeded, and the evil consisted of the inferior gods, from whom all evils proceed. This is a belief that the **Manichæans** <note>followers of a dualistic religious movement</note> seem to have held among the **Christians**. Among the doctrines they believed, they maintained that the air was full of demons which appeared to them very subtly in the manner of certain vapors. They placed great weight and esteem on their divinations and predictions through the discourses they summoned. They also believed it was no sin to have carnal relations with one’s mother or daughter, which is most wicked and impious.

**Mecasphim** <note>a Hebrew term for sorcerers</note>: those who are called *Pharmakoi* <note>Φαρμακοὶ</note> by the seventy Greek interpreters <note>the Septuagint</note>, in Latin *venefici* <note>poisoners or sorcerers</note>, and by **St. Jerome** *malefici* <note>evildoers/wizards</note>. These men, by using the blood and intestines of sacrificial victims which they viewed and contemplated, divined future things; they also did this by observing dead bodies.

**Gazarims** <note>dividers or soothsayers</note>: those whom the same seventy Greek interpreters named in their Greek tongue *Gazarenoi* <note>Γαζαρηνοὶ</note> and **St. Jerome** in the Latin tongue *Haruspices* <note>diviners who read entrails</note>. Having contemplated the intestines of victims, they would divine. Some ancient authors understand this word *Gazarim* to mean augurs—that is to say, those who boasted of predicting the future by the flight, song, or feeding of birds.

Therefore, under King **Nebuchadnezzar** mentioned above, the parts, types, and divisions of the wisdom of the **Chaldæans** were such as we have described here. Although **Daniel** was fully instructed in these by Chaldæan teachers (as seen in chapter 4 of **Daniel**), just as **Moses** in more ancient times was taught in all the wisdom of the **Egyptians**, nevertheless, according to **Justin Martyr** in his book of *Questions Objected by the Gentiles*, Daniel never wished to use them nor approve of them, abhorring them entirely as contrary to divine Laws; for this reason, he was exposed to the **Lions**.

Whoever wishes to see what Greek and Latin authors have written of these **Chaldæans**, let them read **Eustathius** on Book 1 of **Homer's** *Iliad*; **Suidas** on the word *Chaldæans*; **Strabo**, Books 4 and 15 of his *Geography*; **Marcus Varro**, Book 1 of *On Agriculture*; **Seneca**, Book 2 of his *Natural Questions*; **Cicero**, Books 1 and 2 of his *On Divination*; **Eusebius**, Book 6 of his *Preparation for the Gospel*; **St. Augustine**, Book 4, chapter 23, and Book 12, chapter 10 of *The City of God*; and **Petrus Crinitus**, Book 9, chapter 1 of *On Honest Discipline*.

**DIODORUS Siculus**, a Greek author, in his histories—following **Herodotus** in his *Euterpe*—recounts the history of the debate and contention previously reported by us in chapter 1 of this discourse regarding the antiquity of the first language of this Universe, which occurred between the **Egyptians** and the **Phrygians**. He maintained that the **Chaldæans** were the first to invent the characters of letters, even though the **Egyptians** boast and brag of having done this first. On this subject, the divine **Plato** wrote that these Egyptians do not trace their source and origin to Egypt, but to **Asia** and to those very Chaldæans. **Pliny** writes these words in book 7, chapter 56:
> » I have always been of the opinion that letters were **Assyrian**, though some believe they were discovered among the **Egyptians** by **Mercury**, and others among the **Syrians**. <note>original Latin: "Litteras semper arbitror Assyrias fuisse, sed alij apud Ægyptios à Mercurio, alij apud Syros repertas volunt"</note>
This led **Aulus Gellius** in his *Attic Nights* to hold that among the Egyptians, the aforementioned **Mercury** was the first who invented these letters, and among the Syrians, the same. This demonstrates visibly that the **Hebrews** and **Chaldæans** were the ones who first invented and used letter characters in this universe, which are named **Hebraic**; for the **Chaldæans** are none other than the **Assyrians**. Indeed, it is a certain thing that before **Heber** <note>Eber, the biblical ancestor of the Hebrews</note>, from whom the name of the Hebrews and the Hebrew language first proceeded (as I have fully touched upon previously), both of these two peoples were one and the same kind of people, from whom was first chosen the great Patriarch **Abraham**, so celebrated in the writings of ancient authors.
