### Languages of this Universe

"The Phoenician people themselves," <note>original Latin: *Ipsa gens Phoenicum*</note> (this author including under this term all the Syrians of whom he speaks in this place) "attained great glory for the invention of letters and of the stars, as well as for naval and military arts." Therefore, according to both sacred and secular authors, the first and most ancient characters of letters, and the first and most ancient language of the world, were those of the **Hebrews** or **Chaldæans**. **Moses** himself recognized the nation of these **Chaldæans** as more ancient and antique than that of the said **Hebrews**, as seems to be confirmed by **Josephus** in his books of *Jewish Antiquities* and *Against Apion the Grammarian*; **Eusebius of Caesarea** in several places in his *Evangelical Preparation*; and **Guillaume Postel** <note>A famous 16th-century French linguist and mystic</note> in his treatise on origins, or on the antiquity of **Hebraism**, or the affinity of languages. But so as not to confuse our discourse, we shall take this matter from its first source and origin, and assert that the **Hebrew** language was named from all antiquity the **holy language**, because it was the one in which, at the beginning of the world, God the Creator conferred with his own mouth with **Adam**, and taught him to name all things in this universe by their true and right appellation; for *whatever Adam called every living creature in this Universe, that was its name, Genesis chapter 2.* This language, therefore, as if descended from Heaven to earth, maintained itself in its purity and clarity until the confusion of **Babel**, where that **Hebrew** language was altered and corrupted into seventy-two languages, all diverse and dissimilar, as many as there were already dominions, potentates, and principalities established in the world, as I have previously deduced in the preceding chapters. Since this confusion of **Babel**, it did not fail to remain always in its entirety with the holy Patriarchs and faithful men, such as **Abraham** and his successors until the Prophet **Moses**, to whom God gave his Law by living voice on **Mount Horeb** with **Hebrew** characters, language, and writing—both being such as they still are today, as affirmed by **Rabbi Simeon** son of **Eleazar** in the **Talmud**. From there it continued in the synagogue or Church of God, until the captivity of **Babylon** in the land of **Chaldæa**, where, during the seventy years that the **Hebrews** remained there, it came to be altered into that **Chaldæan** language, which these same **Hebrews** used ever after as their common tongue. The aforementioned **Hebrew** language was then practiced and known only by Priests, Doctors, and Scholars of the divine Law, and by lettered people. It is a very certain thing that during this **Babylonian** captivity these **Hebrews** retained three things: namely, their **Hebrew** language, the clothing of their country, and their names, according to the words of **Elias** <note>Elias Levita, a renowned Hebrew grammarian of the Renaissance</note> in his preface to the *Meturgeman* <note>A dictionary of Aramaic/Chaldean words used in the Targum</note> according to the **Talmud**. Even today, the **Jews**, in whatever country or region they reside, have no notice or knowledge of that **Hebrew** language unless they learn it in schools, just as we do the same with the **Greek** and **Latin** languages; rather, they speak and use the common language of the places where they are settled. > 15th chapter of the Acts of the Apostles: For Moses has had from ancient times those who preach him in every city, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath day.

> Thus says the Lord God, creator of the Heaven and the Earth; and for the Parashah of Noah, "according to the days of Noah," the words of the 54th chapter of the same Prophet Isaiah; and so with the others.

This is believed to have been practiced with the books of Daniel and Ezra which are in our hands.

### Paul Fagius in his Preface to the Chaldean Paraphrase,

> First is antiquity itself, which certainly adds no small majesty to things. For it is established from both Hebrew and Latin writings that our Chaldean Paraphrast, whom they call Onkelos, to whom the translation of the Pentateuch is ascribed, was the son of the sister of the Emperor Titus, and composed his Paraphrase not long after the devastation of the second temple. However, the other Paraphrast, whom they call Jonathan son of Uziel, to whom they attribute the Prophets, wrote his works before the devastation of the temple: although there are those who would have it that both translated the whole Bible into the Chaldean language. The second cause is that almost all places in the Hebrew Bible which seem to have some obscurity and difficulty are beautifully explained in the Chaldean Paraphrase, all obscurity having been removed, especially where there are prophecies about the kingdom of Christ. For wherever in the Hebrew truth Christ is dealt with under a veiled name, there in the Chaldean truth the expressed name of the Messiah is always placed: as is easily evident to anyone inspecting and comparing the passages in both versions. The third cause is the authority which it has even among the Jews themselves, who have no less faith in the Chaldean than in the Hebrew truth: so much so that they can be more easily convinced of their errors from nowhere else than from the Chaldean Paraphrases: as Nicolaus of Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349) was an influential Franciscan teacher and one of the most respected Bible commentators of the Middle Ages.</note>, who had knowledge of both languages, testifies. For he, in his commentaries on Isaiah chapter 8, writes thus: "the Hebrew translation among the Jews is called the Targum; it is of such authority among them that no one has dared to contradict it. It is also, in obscure passages, a declaration of the Hebrew truth." These are his words. Fourthly, the Chaldean Bible should be made not a little commendable to us because this language, which is the same as Syriac, was the vernacular language in the time of Christ and the Apostles, which both he and the Apostles used: as can be seen from many places in the New Testament. Indeed, even today, the writings of the four Evangelists exist in this language: of which thing I produce as a most faithful witness that most distinguished and learned man, Dr. Albert Widmanstadt <note>Albert Widmanstadt (1506–1557) was a diplomat and orientalist who published the first printed edition of the New Testament in Syriac in 1555.</note>, counselor to the Most Illustrious Prince Duke of Bavaria, who holds this treasure hidden away; and through most loving letters which he sent to me, he gave me hope that one day this Treasure would come to light. That this may happen soon, I desire with all my heart, night and day: not doubting that great light will also be added to the writings of the Evangelists from this.

See what F. Lucas <note>Franciscus Lucas Brugensis (1548–1619), a Flemish biblical scholar and critic.</note> writes about this matter in his *Treatise on the Chaldean Paraphrase of Scripture*, placed at the end of the Greek and Latin New Testament newly printed at Antwerp by C. Plantin <note>Christophe Plantin was one of the most famous printers of the 16th century, known for his "Polyglot Bible."</note>.

All the above is even better verified in the Babylonian Targum, the <term>משנה</term> *Mishnah* or *Mischne*, that is to say the *Talmudic Context*, since its first composition and edition, otherwise called the *Repetition of the Law* by Epiphanius in his Greek tongue <term>Δευτέρωσιν</term> <note>original: "Deuterōsin"; a Greek term meaning "repetition," used by early Church Fathers to refer to the Mishnah.</note>, saying these words: <term>The repetitions of the elders are four traditions: one bearing the name of Moses, the second that of the one called Rabbi Akiba, the third of Adda (or Judah), and the fourth of the sons of the Hasmoneans.</term> <note>original Greek: "Δευτερώσεις τῶν πρεσβυτέρων παραδόσεις τέσσαres μία εις ὄνομα, Μυσέως φερομένη, δευτέρα δὲ ἡ τοῦ καλουμένου Ραββὶ Ακιβά, τρίτη Αδδά, ἢ τοῦ Ἰούδα τετάρτη τῶν υἱῶν τοῦ Ασαμωναίου."</note> Concerning which we will remark that Saint Jerome and other Greek and Latin ecclesiastical doctors name it by this same name: Which has moved a great personage of this time to write in his works that which follows.

What is the *Deuterosis* in the Emperor's law, its interpreter corrected. From where the Pharisees are called *Deuterae*, and certain other things. What is meant in the Emperor's *New Constitutions* (Novel 146) concerning the Hebrews by the phrase <term>that which is called among them the "repetition" [Deuterosis]?</term> <note>original Greek: "τὴν παρ' αὐτοῖς λογομένην δευτέρωσιν"; this refers to a law by Emperor Justinian regulating how Jews could read their scriptures and whether they could use the Mishnah.</note>

The "old translation" <note>likely referring to the Septuagint</note> is what they call the second edition. But what a poor explanation that is! The "second edition" and the **Deuterosis** <note>from the Greek word for 'repetition,' referring to the Mishnah</note> are as different as the earth is from the heavens. The second edition is nothing other than the version of the Bible prepared by **Aquila** <note>a 2nd-century convert to Judaism who produced a literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, which in Greek is called the *deutera ekdosis* <note>original: "δευτέρα ἔκδοσις"</note>. However, the **Deuterosis** is a part of the **Talmud**. When I name the Talmud, I mean the civil law of the Hebrews, which consists of two parts: the **Mishnah** and the **Gemara**. The Mishnah is called *deuterosis* <note>original: "δευτέρωσις"</note> in Greek. The Emperor <note>referring to Justinian I in his Novella 146</note> prohibited it entirely, as it contains many obscenities and mostly old wives' tales and fables, as **Jerome** testifies in his *Letter to Algasia*, Question 10, writing thus: "I cannot recount how many traditions the Pharisees have—which they today call *deuteroseis* <note>original: "δευτερώσεις"</note>—nor how many old wives' fables they are; for the size of the book does not allow it, and many are so foul that I blush to speak of them. Yet I will say one thing to the shame of that enemy nation: they have leaders in their synagogues, the supposedly wisest men, delegated to a loathsome task—namely, if they cannot discern by sight whether blood is from a virgin or a menstruating woman, they taste it."

Note here that the Pharisaic traditions are called *deuteroseis*; the **Deuterosis**, however, is the tradition of those things gathered as a body or a formal treatise <note>original: "σύνταγμα"</note>.

<margin>cc</margin>
Nor will it be out of place to bring up a specific term for this matter, which **Jerome** mentions in the same place: whenever they explain their traditions to their disciples on certain days, they are accustomed to say *hoi sophoi deuterousin* <note>original: "οἱ σόφοι δευτερώσιν"</note>, which is to say, "the wise teach the traditions." *Hoi sophoi deuterousin* is the same as the Hebrew *Shanu Hahachamim* <note>original: "Sanu Hahachamim"</note>; in the Syrian (Aramaic) language, they more frequently say *Theno Rabbanan* <note>original: "Theno Rabbanan"</note>, meaning "our teachers repeat the traditions." Jerome notes this in his *Commentary on Isaiah*, chapter 10.

The first of these was Simeon the Just, and the last was Rabbi HaKadosh <note>Judah the Prince, known as "the Holy Rabbi"</note>, a doctor saintly for his holiness of life, according to Moses Maimonides in his *Tractate Avot* <note>original: "Massecheth Auoth" - Ethics of the Fathers</note>, or his prologue to the *Order of Seeds* <note>original: "Zeder Zeram" - Seder Zeraim, the first division of the Mishnah</note> part of the Talmud. 

The scholars of the Talmud were named <term>Amoraim</term> <note>original: "האמוראים" - the "Speakers" or "Interpreters" who followed the Tannaim</note>, or in Greek *speakers of maxims* <note>original: "γνωμολόγοι"</note>; they were so called from the proclamations <note>original: "כריז"</note> which they pronounced, which are called *Amirot* <note>original: "אמירות"</note>, or in Latin, *decrees* <note>original: "Scita"</note>. These are the ones called Amoraim <note>original: "אמוראים"</note>, *speakers of maxims*, or *givers of decrees* <note>original: "Χρησμοθέις"</note>. They were succeeded by the Tannaim <note>original: "תנאים"</note>, the "Magnificent ones," even though in the Holy Bible the word *Tan* <note>original: "תנ"</note> is always a substantive noun, as Elias Levita says in *The Tishbite* <note>original: "Thesbyte" - a famous dictionary of Hebrew and Aramaic</note>.

The Babylonian Talmud is sufficient, being purer and less corrupted than the aforementioned Jerusalem Talmud; the Hebrews and Jews have always used these Talmuds since, having had them printed in pure Hebrew characters as they are seen today. However, these are forbidden to Christians for several reasons and considerations noted by Sixtus Senensis in book 1 of his *Holy Library*, in the chapter on traditions, and by the authors we alleged in the aforementioned chapter 9 of this present work. In this regard, the good King of this realm of France, Saint Louis, in his ordinance made in the year of salvation 1254, enacted the following:

> Let the Jews cease from usury, blasphemies, sorceries, and magical signs; and both the Talmud as well as other books in which blasphemies are found shall be burned, and the Jews who will not observe this shall be compelled to do so, and transgressors shall be punished according to the law. <note>original Latin: "Iudæi ceffent ab vfuris, blafphemiis, fortilegiis, & characteribus, & tam Thalmud, quàm alij libri, in quibus inueniuntur blafphemiæ comburantur, & Iudæi qui hoc feruare noluerint compellantur, & tranfgreffores legitimè puniantur." This refers to the condemnation of the Talmud following the Disputation of Paris.</note>

There are several other works and books among the Jews of today composed in that <term>Chaldaic</term> <note>Aramaic, often referred to as Chaldean in early modern texts</note> language, the characters of which are nonetheless pure Hebrew, but the paraphrases are more vulgar and familiar in their style than those of the Prophets mentioned before, and they do not reflect such great antiquity. Because the Holy Scripture was not anciently read to the common Hebrew people in the Hebrew language, but rather in its place the Paraphrases—which were for the most part explanatory—the authors of these Paraphrases strove to accommodate the intelligence and reach of the simple populace, who spoke a language less polished and eloquent than the Hebrew language. It is roughly similar—if a proper and pertinent comparison can be made—to the relationship between the Italian or rather the Spanish language and Latin.

This was the first alteration of the Hebrew language and the ancient Chaldaic; since then, many others occurred, both in the language and the writing, which are still used today by several nations spread here and there through Asia and Arabia. These people live under the rule of the Grand Turk <note>The Ottoman Sultan</note>, having retained the name of Chaldeans, and under the Sophy King of Persia <note>The Safavid Shah</note>, who tolerates them in his lands. Though they are Christians, they are all tainted by the heresy of one Nestorius, formerly Bishop of Constantinople, whose error was condemned in the third Synod of Ephesus. They place in our Lord two persons—one divine and the other human—and do not admit the Virgin Mary to be the Mother of God, but only the mother of Jesus Christ insofar as he was a man. Furthermore, they deny the presence of His body in the <term>Eucharist</term> <note>the sacrament of Holy Communion</note> except when it is being used, they consecrate leavened bread just as the Greeks do, and they provide communion in both kinds <note>offering both the bread and the wine to the laity</note> even to small children. The bulk of their residence, however, is in Tartary, across a vast expanse of land greater than all of France and Italy combined.

# History of the Origin of
<meta>catchword: Pro-</meta>

Mesopotamia. Optatus of Africa <note>original Latin: "optatus Afer"; a 4th-century bishop from Numidia known for his writings against Donatism.</note> mentions three Syrias. See *Syros*, *Sim*, *Assyria*, and *Euphrantis*. Mesopotamia <note>original Greek: "μεσοποταμία"</note> is a region of Asia according to Ptolemy and others, which an old interpreter of Dionysius <note>likely Dionysius Periegetes, a 2nd-century geographer</note>—whether Priscillian or another—called *Medamna* in Latin. Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century author of a geographical dictionary</note> also calls it *Adiabene* <note>original Greek: "ἀδιαβηνὴ"</note>. In the Holy Scriptures it is called *Aram* or *Charan*, as witnessed by the Seventy Interpreters <note>the Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>. Aurogallus <note>Mattheus Aurogallus (1490–1543), a German scholar who assisted Martin Luther in translating the Bible</note> noted that it is also called *Lowland Syria* in the Scriptures. Moletius <note>Giuseppe Moletti (1531–1588), an Italian mathematician and cartographer</note> names it *Azamia* and *Halapia* with a more recent vocabulary. To Mercator <note>Gerardus Mercator (1512–1594), the renowned cartographer</note> it is called *Diarbech*. To Postel <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), a French linguist and polymath</note> it is *Meredin*; it is *Black Turkey* and *Caraoliuo* to Leunclavius <note>Johannes Leunclavius (1541–1594), a German historian and expert on Ottoman history</note>; or are these other names in other languages? In Belon <note>Pierre Belon (1517–1564), a French naturalist and traveler</note> it is read that Mesopotamia, together with Assyria, is today comprised under the single name *Azamia* by the Turks. A certain part of Mesopotamia, namely that which belongs to Amida <note>modern-day Diyarbakir, Turkey</note>, is called *Armenia* by some, as witnessed by Procopius <note>a prominent 6th-century Byzantine historian</note> in Book 1 of his *Persian Wars*. There is also a prefecture of Mesopotamia which, according to Pliny <note>Book 5, chapter 24</note>, takes its origin from the Syrians; it appears from Book 6 of Tacitus's *Annals* that the same was inhabited by Macedonians. For Anthemusia and Nicephorium, which he [Tacitus] ascribes to the Macedonians, he [Pliny] attributes to this prefecture. See *Plaga* and *Osrhoena*, also *Messa*, for it was called thus as well.

Assyria <note>original Greek: "Ἀσσυρία"</note>, a region of Asia which was later called *Adiabene* according to Pliny. Also according to Theodoret in his history of the saints. The barbarians, changing the "s" to "T", call it *Attyria*, according to Dio <note>Cassius Dio, a Roman historian</note>. Niger <note>Dominicus Marius Niger, a 15th-century Venetian geographer</note> writes that it is called *Adrinza* by the natives; by Girava <note>Jerónimo Girava, a Spanish cosmographer</note>, *Acimia*; by Pinet <note>Antoine du Pinet (1510–1584), a French translator and writer</note>, *Mosul*; by Castaldo <note>Giacomo Gastaldi, an Italian cartographer</note>, *Arzerum*; by Mercator, it is called *Sarh*. Suidas <note>The Suda, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> writes that the Assyrians are Persians. Assyrians who were later called Syrians, so says Trogus <note>Pompeius Trogus, a 1st-century BC Roman historian</note>, Book 1. Xenophon makes the Assyrians neighbors to the Hyrcanians in Book 4 of the *Cyropaedia*.

The region of Euphrantis is the same as Syria according to Stephanus—named thus for the nearby Euphrates river—and is the same as Comagena.

### Concerning Syrians.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial "L" depicting floral vines and scrollwork flourishes, beginning the first paragraph of the French text.</image-desc>

The Hebrew authors write that the word Aram, which is the proper name of one of the children of Shem (Genesis 10), signifies in the Hebrew language—just as in English <note>original French: "autant qu'en François"; the author is comparing the meaning to his own native tongue</note>—height, elevation, or sublimity, and that the Eastern Syrians were in olden times called by this name, Arameans, as Josephus confirms in Book 1, chapter 6 of his *Antiquities*. In fact, the Province of Syria, neighboring Babylon, is named *Aram* in the Hebrew language because Aram was the author and father of the Arameans, whom the Greeks call Arimeans. Arimeans, or Syrians, according to the report of Strabo in Book 16 of his *Geography*; and from this, the region or Province of Syria is distinguished by several and diverse names in Holy Scripture, as reported particularly by Aurogallus in his sacred works, Santes Pagnino <note>a leading philologist and Hebraist (1470–1541)</note> in several places in his great *Hebrew Treasure*, Bonaventure Cornelius Bertram <note>a French Hebraist (1531–1594)</note> in his comparison of the Hebrew and Aramaic languages, and Benito Arias Montano in his *Phaleg*, chapter 9. Moreover, this same Syria was anciently one of the largest provinces of Asia, as is amply confirmed by Strabo in the aforementioned Book 16 of his *Geography*. ### History of the Origin of the [Languages]
->352<-

<margin>,,</margin> Having traversed the whole territory up to the borders of Damascus, it ends at the land of Arabia Petraea itself; in which that entire region is called **Aram** by the Hebrews in the Holy Scriptures. However, the various locations of that region are distinguished by various added titles.

<margin>,,</margin> **Mesopotamia**, therefore, being the largest and most ancient of all of them, is sometimes simply called **Aram** *preeminently* <note>original Greek: κατ’ ἐξοχήν</note>, and the inhabitants of that region are called **Arameans**. Sometimes it is called by a more proper and peculiar name, **Paddan Aram** <term>פדן ארם</term>, which is to say, the "Yoke of Syria," as if you were to say "Syria yoked," meaning it is placed under the yoke of two rivers <note>referring to the Tigris and Euphrates rivers which "yoke" the land of Mesopotamia</note>. Hence, it is also sometimes called **Aram of the Two Rivers** <term>ארם נהרים</term> <note>Aram Naharaim</note>, or "between the rivers"; and sometimes it is signified by the added word **Paddan** alone.

<margin>,,</margin> The first region, which is at the Eleutherus river, is called **Aram Zobah** <term>ארם צובה</term>; it is perhaps **Sophene** <note>An ancient province of the Armenian Kingdom and the Roman Empire</note>. In this tract, there seems to be **Lower Hamath**, which is called by the name **Hamath Zobah** in the second book of Chronicles, chapter 8. It was here that **David** seems to have defeated **Hadadezer** in the first book of Chronicles, chapter 19, and thus reached the limits of the land promised by God, which are commonly placed at the **Entrance of Hamath** <term>חמת לבוא</term>; that is, wherever you shall have entered **Hamath**. Some believe the lower parts of that region to be **Ituraea**. Near that same region, it is certain there was **Aram Beth-Rehob** <term>ארם בית רחוב</term>, located not far from that place on the Euphrates which is called **Rehoboth** in Genesis 36:37.

<margin>,,</margin> The fourth **Aram**, which is called **Aram Maacah** <term>ארם מעכה</term>, was not so far from those spaces, as appears from the second book of Samuel <note>referenced as "Schem" for Shmuel</note>, chapters 8 and 10.

<margin>,,</margin> The fifth **Aram** is called **Aram of Damascus** <term>ארם דמשק</term>, which is enclosed by the Damascene territory, that is, between Lebanon and Arabia; or as others advise (who wish for the Anti-Lebanon and Lebanon mountains to end in Arabia), it is situated between Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon: this is **Coele-Syria** <note>literally "Hollow Syria"</note> or "hollow Syria," as if bounded by the valleys of those two mountains. And these five regions are expressly called by the name **Aram** in the Holy Scriptures.

<margin>,,</margin> Furthermore, there is a certain sixth **Syria** which, although not so expressly called **Aram** by the sacred writers, there is nevertheless no doubt that the name **Aram**, by which secular <note>original: "profani"</note> writers honor it, flowed from the former to the latter. Thus **Strabo** <note>A famous Greek geographer and historian</note> testifies that the inhabitants of **Commagene Syria** or **Antioch** were called **Arimi** by ancient writers—that is, **Arameans**—saying: "The Armenians, Syrians, and Arabs are very closely joined, whether you look at their language, their way of life, or the features of their bodies." And a little later: "For they call those whom we call Syrians, Arameans." Scripture certainly makes honorable and magnificent mention of this Antiochian Syria. It calls such a territory the **Land of Hamath** <term>חמת</term>. Among other things, it attributes to it a distinguished kingdom conquered by the Assyrian Monarch; indeed, it even mentions the metropolitan city, which they call **Hamath the Great** or the Greater <term>חמת רבה</term>. Some also add that this same city is called **Riblah** elsewhere. Therefore, this part of Syria is also worthy of the name **Aram**, not only by those names which we designated above, but especially for this sake: that in later times, this region brought those six superior regions under its yoke and ennobled them with its privileges, and even its language. Before we demonstrate this, it seems necessary to define from where [the name] was derived...

# Languages of this World #

Provinces, given that this region extending from the river Tigris to Egypt is included under the general name of Syria; and that which lies between the great rivers Tegil or Tigris and the Euphrates is called by the Hebrews *Aram Naharim* <note>original Hebrew: "Aram Naharim," literally "Aram of the Two Rivers"</note>, or Syria of the two rivers—this is Mesopotamia. There is another part of this Syria called Coele <note>original: "Cele"; from the Greek "koile," meaning hollow, referring to the valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountain ranges</note> or Basle, which begins at the stream called Valaine, which flows beneath the castle of Valat and empties into the Mediterranean Sea one league from the said castle. After this is the Syria of the Phoenicians, which extends toward the North from the said Valaine stream to Mount Carmel. Beyond this, there is also the Syria of Palestine, divided into three regions, and then the Syria named for Damascus, as described more particularly by Brother Burchard the Monk <note>Burchard of Mount Sion, a 13th-century German Dominican whose "Description of the Holy Land" was a standard geographical reference for centuries</note> in his description of the places of the Holy Land. Some Rabbis or Hebrew doctors write that the aforementioned Aram was the father and author of the Armenians, and some figures maintain that the Syrians gave their name to Armenia because the Arameans came to live in Assur—which signifies Assyria, Media, and Armenia—at which place they stayed on the side of the Euphrates, where the great city of Derbent is now built, currently almost in ruins. See what is written of this region by Pliny, Book 5, Chapter 12 of his *Natural History*; Pomponius Mela, Book 1, Chapter 11; Hayton the Armenian <note>Hethum of Korykos, a medieval Armenian historian and monk</note>, Chapter 14 of his histories; André Thevet, Book 6, Chapters 6, 13, and 14 of his *Cosmography*; Guillaume Postel in his treatise on the famous regions named after the descendants of Noah; François de Belleforest, Volume 2, Book 3, Chapters 10 and 11 of his *Cosmography*; and Abraham Ortelius, Tables 3 and 5 of his *Theater of the World*. Regarding this, a great and learned modern personage of this time, skilled in the most ancient and antique languages, has written the following on this matter:

---

> <margin>cc</margin> The name of Syria is sometimes used by Geographers and other authors, both Greek and Latin,
> <margin>cc</margin> to designate a very large stretch of the Eastern region, which seems to be that which
> <margin>cc</margin> starts from the desert of Shur <note>original: "Sur deserto"; located between Egypt and Assyria at the borders of the Ismaelite territory</note>,
> <margin>cc</margin> passing through Palestine toward the West, and entering the Mediterranean Sea to the North and the
> <margin>cc</margin> island of Cyprus (which was once torn away from the upper continent), then crossing the sea again

> <margin>cc</margin> the Black Sea <note>original Latin: "Pontum Euxinum"</note>. From there, moving East across the Euphrates
> <margin>cc</margin> and Tigris, it permeates all of Assyria and ends at Persia and the Persian Gulf itself.
> <margin>cc</margin> To the south, it borders Arabia. Sometimes, however, the name refers to one specific
> <margin>cc</margin> region included within that larger tract. The origin of the name is reported in various ways.
> <margin>cc</margin> Some believe Syria was named after the island of Syros in the Mediterranean Sea;
> <margin>cc</margin> others from a certain Syrus, son of Apollo; others from Mount Hermon <note>original Latin: "Chermon"</note>,
> <margin>cc</margin> which is called *Sirion* <note>original Latin: "Schirion"</note> by the Phoenicians, who were certainly the most prominent and ancient Syrians.
> <margin>cc</margin> To me, however, the name of Syria seems to be derived from the same place

...taught it first to Theseus Ambrosius <note>Teseo Ambrogio (1469–1540), an Italian humanist and priest who wrote the first comprehensive Western study of Near Eastern languages, the *Introductio in Chaldaicam linguam*.</note> cited above, who afterwards shared it with posterity, as is asserted by the aforementioned Agathius—Guidacerus the Calabrian <note>Agathio Guidacerio (1477–1540), a scholar from Calabria who taught Hebrew in Rome and Paris.</note>—in his Commentaries on the *Song of Songs*, and the same Theseus Ambrosius in his introduction to the Chaldean, Syriac, and Aramaic languages. Ambrosius reports that by the express command of the Pope, he instructed a certain Syrian by birth named Elias, son of Abraham, in the Latin language. This Elias was a disciple of Peter, the Patriarch of the Maronites <note>The Maronites are an Eastern Catholic church in full communion with Rome, centered in Mount Lebanon.</note> in Antioch, of the holy Mount Lebanon and the region of Syria—commonly called *Surie*—so that Ambrosius might better and more easily learn the Syriac language from him. And in order to give full satisfaction to those readers curious about languages, we will report word-for-word the proper words of a certain great and learned figure of this time regarding the most ancient and antique languages:

> The language of the Arameans is not only called Aramaic <note>original: ארמית (*Aramit*)</note>, but is also called the "tongue of the Chaldeans" <note>original: לשון כשדים (*Leshon Kasdim*)</note>. One might reasonably doubt whether the use of the Aramaic tongue began among the Mesopotamians or the Chaldeans, but if a conjecture may be drawn from what precedes—and from the fact that the first mention and traces of the Aramaic language appear in the history of Laban the Mesopotamian (or Aramean <note>original: ארמי (*Arami*)</note>)—it seems to have reached the Chaldeans and Assyrians toward the East from Mesopotamia through the descendants of Nachor <note>The brother of Abraham; Laban was his grandson.</note>. Whether it was first carried westward by these same descendants of Nachor to other regions of Aram beyond the Euphrates is not equally clear for all of them. Certainly, in later times, with the expansion of the Chaldean empire, their language also pervaded not only all those regions of the Aramaic tract, but also Judea itself, Palestine, and Phoenicia. Thus, the Aramaic language seems in some way to have antiquated and almost obliterated Hebrew—not just once, but repeatedly and through its various dialects. Indeed, the Aramaic language and its dialects made wonderful progress. For, having spread from Mesopotamia to the Chaldeans, it was so cultivated in Babylon among the Babylonian nobles and philosophers that it achieved the highest degree of purity there. Rightly, therefore, we make the Babylonian dialect the first and most important of the Aramaic language; in this dialect, Daniel and likewise Ezra, being well-taught, wrote several pages of their own writings. We shall call the second dialect Chaldean or Syriac, which the earlier paraphrasers of the Bible used, such as Onkelos on the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible. Onkelos is the famous 2nd-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic.</note> and Jonathan on both the Former and Latter Prophets. We establish the third dialect as that of Jerusalem, in which the later paraphrases of the Law and the Book of Esther were written. This is called the Jerusalem dialect because the common people of the Israelites, returning from the Babylonian exile, mixed many Ammonite, Moabite, Persian, and Greek words into the Chaldean language. We make the fourth dialect of the Aramaic language a sort of middle ground between the second Chaldean and this third Jerusalem dialect; in this were written the paraphrases or *Targumim* <note>Aramaic translations or interpretations of the Hebrew Bible used in synagogues when Hebrew was no longer the common tongue.</note> on the so-called "Five Volumes" <note>The *Five Megillot*: Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, and Esther.</note>, the Psalms, Proverbs, and Job. From this difference between the above Aramaic dialects, a two-fold Targum is established by the Hebrew doctors: the Babylonian and the Jerusalem. They call both by these names, not because the former was written in the Babylonian language, but rather...

» ...the Jerusalem dialect, except that the former consists of a purer style, and the latter of a less pure one. 
» We add a fifth dialect of the Arameans, namely the **Talmudic**, which is clearly mixed, not only from the aforementioned dialects, but also from Hebrew and its unique idioms, and from Latin, Greek, Arabic, and other foreign words somewhat more boldly adopted. In this dialect, a twofold difference of Talmudic style has also been established: one **Talmud** is called the **Babylonian**, because it was composed in a purer style, while the other is the **Jerusalem** one, which is less pure—for the same reason and by the same analogy as the **Babylonian** and **Jerusalem Targums** <note>Targums are ancient Aramaic translations or paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. We establish the sixth and last dialect of the Aramaic language as **Syriac Antiochene**, also called **Comagenean**, or even **Maronite**. We place it in the sixth and final position, not because we wish to suggest it arose after all the others, but because it has consistently retained its use last of all and has succeeded all the others, making all those ancient ones <margin>100</margin> » obsolete. For that is the one whose use was found not only in that **Church of Antioch**, but also in the rest of the rural territory of that region, and eventually in the entire **Patriarchate** that was at one time assigned to that Church. Hence it happens that its use still endures in the **Palmyrene** region <note>The region around Palmyra in modern-day Syria.</note>; which region, if you look at its wilderness, extends across the **Euphrates** toward **Arabia Felix** and the city of **Petra**. From there, **geographers** also ascribe to it the city of **Maronia**; the **Bishops**, **Monks**, **Hermits**, and citizens of that place were long held to be schismatics, but eventually gave their name to the **Roman Church** <note>i.e., they entered into full communion with the Pope.</note>. Due to the fame of that place and Church, this **Maronite** language is called by some—finally, the people of Mesopotamia commonly use no other language, at least when performing their sacred rites, than this **Syriac**. 

» Furthermore, at this point a question arises: whether this is the very language that **Christ** and his people and contemporaries <note>original Greek: συγχρονοι (synchronoi)</note> used in **Judea**. It is clear from many things—which would be too long to recount—that Syriac had not yet been visited upon the **Jews** in **Christ’s** time. We will bring forward this one point: in the paraphrase of the New Testament in **John 19:13** <note>The source cites John 10, but the context of the "Stone Pavement" is John 19:13.</note>, for *Gabbatha* <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: גבתא</note>—the *Stone Pavement* <note>original Greek: λιθόστρωτος (lithostrotos)</note>—used by other Arameans, there is *Tsipicha* <note>original: ציפיחא</note>, meaning an enclosure <note>original Latin: Septum</note>. From this it seems entirely likely that the **Jews** then used the second Aramaic dialect, in which **Jonathan** <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, the reputed author of the Targum Jonathan.</note>—who lived about forty years before **Christ**—explained the Old Testament to the **Jews** of his time. Indeed, the paraphrase of the New Testament argues for such great antiquity of this language that I would dare to ascribe it to that **Church of Antioch** when it was first being born, and to those **Christians** who were first called by that name there. And this ensures that I believe a knowledge of this Aramaic dialect is more necessary for us **Christians** than any of the preceding ones. For besides various uses that it shares in common with all of them, it provides certain peculiar and proper ones necessary for the **Christian Theologian**. Truly, no one doubts there are very many places in the text of the Bible that have exercised the wits of many, either because of the various meanings of words or even the ambiguities of sentences. The **Syriac** dialect can explain all these things so purely that you would require nothing else for its interpretation. 

A little after, this same author says: "We make the **Hebrew** language the first of all, and the mother, or source, and origin from which all others were derived." As that is more clearly evident in those languages that were used in the vicinity of **Judea**, the beginning of its derivation also seems to be sought from there. We now understand that the **Aramaic** regions were closer to **Judea**. Indeed, from this proximity, the **Hebrew** language was sometimes varied in such a way that the dialects of the Aramaic language succeeded into the genuine place of the **Hebrew** language.

# History of the Origin of Nations

<note>original header: "Histoire de l'Origine des"</note>

The testimony of such a great man brings more light to the understanding of this Index, and more weight to convince everyone of the agreement of the Eastern Church with the Western. Therefore, I subjoin his own words:

> "I thought," he says, "that I would be doing something worthwhile at present if I separated the titles of the chapters interspersed within the text of these books and described them according to the annual feast days—which the Syrians observe according to a very ancient institution derived from the teaching of the Apostles. Having placed the English <note>original: "Latinos," as the author was translating Syriac into Latin for his readers</note> translations in the opposite column, I would attach them to the end of this work. My goal is that those who look with disfavor upon the rites of the Latin <note>Western</note> Church might easily understand from this that among the Syrians (who were the very first of all Christians), these same rites and customs have existed until this present age—or certainly ones not far removed from those over which people have recently broken away from the common consent of the Church. And, so that these matters may become clearer, I wish to briefly pursue a few points with you which came to mind as I was hurrying toward the end of this work through these Indices of days and events. The rest are explained at length in the book titled *The Treasury* <note>original: "Ærarium"</note>, which is based on the authority of Ephrem, James, Balaius, Coquius, and other Syrians excellent in both holiness of life and doctrine.

> The Syrians set the beginning of the **Ritual Year** around the Calends <note>the first</note> of November, so that eight Sundays precede the Nativity of Christ the Lord. On the first, they celebrate the **Dedication of the Temple**; on the second, the *Encaenia* <note>term: Encaenia; a Greek word meaning "renewal" or "dedication," often referring to the rededication of a church</note>; on the third, the **Annunciation to Zechariah** the Priest regarding the birth of his son, John the Baptist; on the fourth, the **Annunciation to the Virgin Mary** regarding the Son of God who would enter this life through her; on the fifth, the **Journey of the Virgin Mother to Elizabeth**, a celebration which Pope Urban VI introduced into the Latin Church from the Apostolic See during that great schism which was finally extinguished by the authority of the Council of Constance; on the sixth, the **Nativity of John the Baptist**; on the seventh, the **Oracle given to Joseph** regarding his wife, who was pregnant beyond expectation and whom he was not to abandon; the eighth Sunday they call the **Pre-Nativity**.

> Following this is the 25th of December, the **Nativity of Jesus Christ**; the next day is the **Virgin in Childbirth**; on the third day is the celebration of the **Holy Innocents**; then the Sunday nearest the Nativity; and afterward (unless it falls on that same day), the feast of the **Circumcision of Christ**. Next, on the sixth light <note>day</note>, follows **Epiphany**, which is called the 'Feast of Lights' <note>original: "luminum feriæ"</note> by the Syrians and is celebrated with the frequent use of lamps. On that night, water is consecrated with a solemn prayer, which is then kept in the sacristies throughout the year. They celebrate the **Beheading of John the Baptist** on the following day, and from Epiphany they count several Sundays, which are followed by the three-day *Rogations* <note>days of prayer and fasting</note> which they call the **Ninevite Fast** <note>A fast observed by Eastern churches commemorating the repentance of the city of Nineveh in the Book of Jonah</note>. After this comes the day of **Christ’s Presentation in the Temple**, and in their proper order, two **Funeral Sundays**: the first dedicated to priests, the second to other deceased Christians, during which they are accustomed to visit their tombs with established ceremonies.

> Then follow six Sundays characterized by the name of **Fasting** <note>Lent</note>, of which the 40th day is notable for the special devotion of the Syrians—marking the completion of the full forty-day fast, just as the 20th day marks the half—and falls on the Friday following the first Sunday. This is followed by the **Sabbath of Lazarus** raised from the dead, and soon the Sunday of **Hosannas**, which we call **Palm Sunday**. The continuous week following, dedicated to the Passion and Rest of Christ, takes its name from those events. In this week, Thursday is called the **Day of Secrets** because of the mysteries of the Holy Communion <note>original: "Synaxeos," from the Greek for "gathering" or "liturgy"</note>; on this day, the Holy Chrism <note>sacred oil</note> is consecrated by the Bishops for the priesthood instituted on that day, and the ceremony of the **Washing of the Feet** is performed. The Sabbath of that week is called the **Sabbath of the Annunciation** for this reason: because on that day Christ, acting among the fathers in the underworld...

...announced to the nations that through his ultimate sacrifice, their salvation had already been secured. The day of the **Lord’s Resurrection** <note>Easter Sunday</note> is called the "Great Day" by the Syrians, and the eighth day from it, the ninth day, and the days passing in the week between them, are called the **Week of the Candidates** <note>original: "Candidatorum"</note>. This is for no other reason than that the Latin Church calls the Sabbath and this very Lord’s Day "Sunday in White" <note>original: "in Albis," referring to the white robes worn by the newly baptized</note>. 

For in former times, those bound by the sacrament of the Christian "military service" <note>a common metaphor for baptismal commitment</note> were washed in the sacred font only during these days and only by bishops. They testified to their profession by wearing white, hooded linen tunics. On this Lord’s Day, they would present themselves to the bishop, lay aside their white garments, and—if they had been baptized at Rome by the Sovereign Pontiffs—they were accustomed to receive sacred amulets as symbols of their Baptism. These were wax seals <note>term: **Agnus Dei**; small wax discs impressed with the figure of a lamb, often blessed by the Pope</note> expressed in the figure of the **Standard-bearing Lamb** and dipped in water consecrated with a mixture of Chrism. 

Indeed, it was so accepted that the ministers of Baptism and those being baptized should be "candidates" (white-clad) that the Bishops—to whom alone the office of baptizing was then deferred—never went out in public without a white linen tunic, lest they be found wanting in their duty should a sudden necessity arise. For this reason, the use of such a tunic has been retained to this day by the Supreme Pontiffs and others (unless the lesser Bishops were called to that rank of dignity from a monastic life). In succeeding centuries, this was also permitted as a mark of dignity for the "Cap-wearing Notaries" <note>original: "Pileatis Notariis"</note> who were once appointed to write the histories of the martyrs in the city of Rome. Furthermore, the mosaic images of those sacred wax figures, which they call *Agnus Dei*, still exist in the apse of the Vatican Basilica above the pontifical altar, preserved from the structure of Constantine's work. Marcellus II <note>Pope in 1555; he was a noted scholar and reformer</note>, a most holy man, once showed these to me while he was still a private citizen, as proof of a ceremony used before the reign of **Constantine the Great**.

But enough regarding the week of the Candidates. From this ninth Lord’s Day, on the fourth day—Friday, if I am not mistaken—are the **Golden Holy Days** <note>original: "auri feriæ"</note>. On these days, the memory of the Apostle Peter healing the lame man at the **Beautiful Gate** is revisited with solemn rest and worship. They were designated by the name "Gold" because of Peter’s response, in which he denied having gold or silver for himself <note>A reference to Acts 3:6: "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee."</note>. **Ascension Day** completes the fortieth day from the Resurrection, and the **Lord’s Day of Pentecost** completes its own, which is the fiftieth. 

On this day, the Syrians pray while resting on their knees, with the upper part of the body held erect. They call this rite "the positioning of the knees," a posture they use only on that day; for on the other days of the year, they show the form of adorers or suppliants either by a forward motion of the body or by kissing the earth, from which they rise without delay. In this, they differ from the Muslims, who are accustomed to use that *Engonasi* <note>original: "Engonasi," from the Greek for "kneeling"</note> posture. They also religiously venerate the Holy Cross, and several Sundays have been named after its feast day. 

They call that unbloody sacrifice the **Qurbana** <note>original Syriac: ܩܘܼܪܒܵܢܵܐ; meaning "Offering" or "Eucharist"</note>, and the rites performed before it the **Qudasha** <note>original Syriac: ܩܘܼܕܵܫܵܐ</note>, which is to say, the "approach" or "hallowing." Therefore, those who attempt to remove the mention of gifts, offerings, and sacrifices from Catholic rites seem to promise too much security to their own opinions. They are persuaded that whatever the Pontiffs of the Latin Church and the Councils of the Fathers decreed in any age has now been revoked by their own judgment. Yet, regarding the stability of these rites, not only the greatest part of Europe but also the **Asiatic and African Churches** not only hold a prior judgment, but judge most severely in this: that they maintain prayers distributed at fixed hours (evening, night, morning, and others); they retain the memory of the deceased in their sacred rites; they maintain Priests and Bishops, as well as temples and altars; and finally, on the night of **Epiphany**, they consecrate water to be distributed to the people in their homes for the whole year. They observe the laws of established fasts with remarkable abstinence, and they preserve the monastic...

### History of the Origin of the [Jews]
->Iui<-

...to the aid of the King of the Egyptians, the one whom we mentioned had been a priest in the temple of Vulcan <note>The Roman name for the Egyptian god Ptah; his temple in Memphis was a major religious center</note>. And then there was an interregnum—which is to say that the Land of Egypt was without a sovereign Prince for the space of two years. Because a people accustomed to royal government could not grow used to an aristocratic government, it was necessary to return to Kings, after twelve governors had commanded with equal power for the space of 15 years. 

But Psammetichus <note>Psamtik I</note>, one of the twelve, having made—against the advice and will of the others—an alliance with the Carians and Ionians in Asia, strengthened himself by their means and subjugated those Egyptians who wished to prevent his usurpation of their crown, as Herodotus recounts in Book 2. Having reigned 54 years, upon his death he left Necho <note>original: "Necos" or "Necao"</note> as his successor, who made war against the Jews and slew in battle Josiah, the good and faithful King of Judah <note>original: "Iudée"</note>, as is detailed in 2 Kings 23 <note>original: "4. des Roys 23"; in older Bibles, 1 & 2 Samuel and 1 & 2 Kings were counted as 1-4 Kings</note> and 2 Chronicles 35 <note>original: "2. du Paralipomen."</note>. Herodotus, referring to the Hebrews, says that the Egyptian defeated the Syrians. 

This Necho, having held the Lordship for 17 years, left it by death to Psammis, who held it for only six years; he was succeeded by Apries, whom Jeremiah calls Hophra <note>original: "Haphram"</note>, who made war against the Cyreneans, who defeated him and put him to flight. This man, having reigned 35 years, left the government to Amasis, the second of that name, during the time when the Jews were led captive to Babylon (Jeremiah, chapter 44). He was succeeded by Amasis <note>The text repeats the name, likely referring to the transition from Apries to Amasis II</note> who reigned 44 years; having revolted against his prince (whom Herodotus calls Apries), he took his crown and held the kingdom in peace, fortune, and rest, being loved and honored by the people. Having reigned 44 years, he was succeeded by his son Psammetichus <note>Psamtik III</note>, whom Cambyses, King of Persia and son of Cyrus, stripped of his Kingdom, making himself Lord of Egypt according to Herodotus, Book 3. 

This occurred when Tarquin the Proud reigned in Rome. The Land of Egypt remained for 110 years under the power of the Persians; but during the reign in Persia of Darius, surnamed "the Bastard" <note>Darius II Nothus</note>, the Egyptians revolted and made a man of royal blood named Amyrtaeus <note>original: "Amarthée"</note> their King. Having held the country for six years, he died and had as a successor Nepherites, who also reigned six years; he was succeeded by Achoris for 12 years, and after him Psammuthes and Nepherites II for one year. They were succeeded by Nectanebo I for the space of 18 years, and after him Teos <note>original: "Theon"</note> for only two years. He was succeeded by Nectanebo II, against whom Darius Artaxerxes—surnamed Ochus, King of Persia—made war, usurping Egypt. Plutarch speaks of this Nectanebo in the *Life of Agesilaus*. Having reigned 18 years in Egypt, he fled with his treasures into Ethiopia. Thus, the Persians once again made themselves masters of Egypt and enjoyed it for 23 years, until Alexander, King of Macedon, deprived them of the Empire of Asia. 

After his death, the Ptolemies made themselves Kings of Egypt. The first of these was Ptolemy, son of Lagus <note>Ptolemy I Soter</note>, one of the captains in the retinue of Alexander; he had wars against Perdiccas and Antigonus, and was defeated at sea by Demetrius, but finally conquered the island of Cyprus. Having reigned 40 years, he left as his successor his son Ptolemy, surnamed Philadelphus—which is to say "brother-lover"—who was a great friend to the Jews and sent offerings to the holy temple in Jerusalem. This Prince greatly cherished men of learning and established that magnificent Library of Alexandria. ...by him also was built the lighthouse tower of Alexandria <note>The Pharos of Alexandria, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, built under Ptolemy I and II</note>. This good prince, having reigned peacefully for 38 years—two with his father and 36 alone—died and left the Kingdom to his son Ptolemy, called Euergetes <note>Ptolemy III, whose epithet means "the Benefactor"</note>. He did not imitate his father at all; instead, by allying himself with the Kings of Syria, he persecuted the Jews and profaned the holy temple in Jerusalem. According to the accounts of Eusebius in his *Chronicle* <note>original: "liur. des temps"</note> and Epiphanius in his *Treatise on Weights and Measures* <note>original: "liure des mesures & poids"</note>, sixty thousand Jews died during this war. Having made the Jews tributary, when Onias the High Priest wished to deny him the tribute, this King prepared to ruin this people whom he hated to death. However, he was appeased by a captain named Joseph, so that he pardoned the fault of the Hebrews. He reigned 17 years and had as his successor Ptolemy Epiphanes <note>Ptolemy V, meaning "the Illustrious"</note>, who reigned 24 years. After him, the sixth King of this race was Ptolemy, surnamed Philometor <note>Ptolemy VI, meaning "Mother-loving"</note>, to whom Aristobulus the Jew dedicated his *Commentaries on the Books of Moses*. Against this king came Antiochus, the Syrian King; but having gained nothing there, Antiochus returned to Jerusalem where he pillaged the temple. This caused Onias, son of the High Priest Onias, to come to Egypt, where he obtained permission from Philometor to build a temple in Egypt <note>This refers to the Temple of Onias at Leontopolis</note>. 

This Ptolemy having reigned 35 years, he was succeeded by Ptolemy Euergetes, the second of that surname, whom they called Physcon <note>original: "Phiscon"; a Greek nickname meaning "pot-bellied" or "bloated"</note> because of his deformity. Having reigned 29 years, he had as his successor Ptolemy Lathyrus <note>Ptolemy IX; "Lathyrus" refers to a chickpea, possibly due to a skin mark</note>, whom others call Soter—that is to say, "Savior." He was afflicted by his cousin Alexander and his own mother, so that they chased him from the Kingdom which he had held for 17 years. But Ptolemy Alexander, having reigned one year, was chased out by his own mother, who held the Lordship for nearly ten years. This caused the Egyptians, who were annoyed by the insolence of this woman, to recall the aforementioned Ptolemy Lathyrus and restore him to his Kingdom. He held it for another eight years in peace, during which time Ptolemy, King of the Cyrenians, died and made the Romans heirs to his Kingdom. This was like an omen of the subjugation of the land of Egypt, as can be seen in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. 

When this Lathyrus died, he was succeeded by Ptolemy called Auletes <note>Ptolemy XII; "the Flute-player"</note>, who was the father of Cleopatra. She became the concubine of the Roman Mark Antony. From the flight of this Auletes—who was chased away by the Alexandrians and came to Rome for protection—came the ruin of many and the cause of great misfortunes; he was restored to his throne by Gabinius. It was also then that this foolish Cleopatra was made queen with her brother, who chased her away. She had recourse to the Romans, such that Caesar restored her to her lands, charmed by the beauty and grace of this lascivious lady, who sold her modesty there to the Roman for the price of her brother’s blood. Her brother, following the fury of Caesar and his sister, thought to save himself by sea, but his boat perished in the waves and the miserable prince was swallowed by the deep. It was then that the city of Alexandria was pillaged by the Romans, and that great library which Philadelphus had established at such great expense was burned, and the face of this beautiful city was deformed by the very woman who should have protected it rather than causing its ruin. In short, this flighty princess was the one who, having won the heart of that great Roman prince Mark Antony, made him conspire against his own people...

In the year 1592, during the Pontificate of Clement VIII, Pope of Rome, the Patriarch of Alexandria in Egypt, along with all the peoples and nations subject to him, performed and pledged obedience to the Holy Apostolic See.

In the year 1595, his legates returned from Rome to their country. ### *Of the Wisdom of the Egyptians.*

The ancient Hebrews placed great value and esteem in their writings on the wisdom of the Egyptians, which they called in their Hebrew language *Chochemath Mizrim* <note>original: חכמת מצריום; "Wisdom of the Egyptians"</note>; the Greeks in their Greek language called it *Sophian Aigyption* <note>original: Σοφίαν Αἰγυπτίων</note>; and the Latins in their Latin language called it *Sapientia Aegyptiorum*. Saint Stephen, the first martyr, in the seventh chapter of the Acts of the Apostles, attributed this to the Prophet Moses as a great praise, saying: "Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in deeds and in words." In former times, this wisdom was divided into four parts according to the sayings of Diodorus Siculus, Diogenes Laertius, Iamblichus, Philo the Jew, and Eusebius of Caesarea: namely, into natural, divine, and moral mathematics. As for Mathematics, being distinct and separated into Geometry, Astronomy, Arithmetic, and Music, these ancient Egyptians practiced it; for they practiced Geometry almost by necessity, since the limits and boundaries of their fields and possessions were confused by the flooding of the river Nile,

### Languages of this Universe

When the Nile <note>Referring to the previous page's mention of the river's floods</note> has retreated into its usual channel, it was necessary for each owner of those fields and possessions to enter into the enjoyment of them. This could not be easily done except by the science of measuring and surveying, which they called **Geometry**, as if one were to say "the measuring of the land." As for **Astronomy**, these Egyptians devoted themselves to it because of the convenience of their country, in which the nights are very clear and serene, and the sky very open, without being in any way obscured by clouds, mists, or fogs that could prevent them from seeing and considering the rising, setting, and courses of the stars and planets. To these two parts, they added **Arithmetic**, that is to say, the science of numbers, as it serves those other parts; without its ministry, those parts would seem to be entirely lacking and imperfect. They devoted themselves to **Music** as much as was necessary for them to sing the praises of the gods, kings, and heroes.

The second part of this **Egyptian Wisdom**, which treats the principles, causes, elements, and works of natural things, called **Physics**, does not distance itself much from <term>Peripatetic Philosophy</term> <note>The school of philosophy founded by Aristotle, characterized by walking while discussing</note>, in that it establishes matter as the principle of all things, and that from it the four elements proceed—from which all things and all animals come. It also holds that the sky is round, like a sphere and a ball, and that all the stars have a fiery heat. Through the tempered mixtures and blends of this heat, all things are born upon the earth. It teaches that the planets have their own souls, and that rains are made and caused by the changes in the air.

The third part of this aforementioned wisdom, containing divine things called **Theology**, has and contains other precepts—namely, that the world had a beginning and is mortal by its own nature. It teaches that humans, at the beginning of all things in this universe, were first produced in Egypt, partly because of the temperature of the sky and partly because of the Nile, which renders Egypt very fertile in all goods by its overflowing. It also holds that the human soul is perpetual, passing by <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>The transmigration of the soul; the belief that a soul moves into a new body after death</note> from body to body; that God is the sole and unique Father and Prince of the other gods; and that the Sun and the Moon are gods, one called **Osiris** and the other **Isis**. It was held that one must make images and statues of the various gods in the temples in various forms and figures because the true images and forms of these gods were unknown. 

A great many of these gods had first been mortal men, who then, for their virtues, merits, and the excellent benefits they bestowed among mortals, acquired divinity and were divinely honored by the living. The Egyptians were accustomed to carrying representations of animals against their enemies on the tops of their helmets and shields in war, by the command of their kings and leaders. After the victory obtained by them against their said enemies, they placed these animals in the rank and number of the gods, as if they had been the sole cause of their victory. 

Regarding their theologians, they had a certain form of mystic and secret writing, by which they hid the most excellent mysteries of their theology and divine service, which they did not want to be divulged to the common people. This is something that **Saint Clement** <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 CE), a Christian theologian who wrote about Egyptian culture</note> in the fifth book of his *Stromata* has very well noted, saying that all this writing was distinguished into three different sorts—namely, into **epistolary** <note>original: "ἐπιστολογραφικὴν" (*epistolographikēn*)</note>, that is, epistolary, suitable...

# History of the Origin of the

to writing common letters, into **hierogrammatic** <note>original: *ἱερογραμματικὴν*</note>, that is, priestly, which is used by those who write of sacred things, and into **hieroglyphic** <note>original: *ἱερογλυφικὴν*</note>, that is, sacred writing, which is engraved. Of this there are two species: one is **cyriologic** <note>original: *κυριολογικὴ*</note>, that is, "properly speaking," which is written through the letters themselves and alphabetic elements in mystical and figurative words; the other is true **symbolic** <note>original: *συμβολικὴ*</note>, that is, signifying through signs. This symbolic type is threefold: namely imitative, tropical (or metaphorical), and enigmatic. The imitative is that which designates things through characters very similar to the things themselves. The tropical or metaphorical is that which transfers various forms and figures of different things—especially animals—to signify the dignities, fortunes, morals, virtues, vices, affections, and actions of either gods or men. The enigmatic is that which results from the joining and mutual mixing of these images. This is why the poet Lucretius said:

> <note>original: *Nondum flumineae Memphis contexere biblos / Nouerat, & saxis tantùm volucreſque feraque, / Sculptaque ſeruabant magicas animalia linguas.*</note>
> *Memphis had not yet learned to weave the papyrus of the river, and only birds and wild beasts, and carved animals, preserved magical languages on stones.*

Pherecydes of Syros <note>A Greek thinker from the 6th century BC</note> asserts in his histories that the Scythians <note>Ancient nomadic people of Central Eurasia</note> formerly used this sort of symbolic writing. He says that Idanthuras, King of the Scythians, sent a symbol to Darius, King of the Persians—who had declared war on him if he and his people did not submit to his obedience—as a substitute for written letters. This symbol consisted of a rat, a frog, a bird, a dart, and a plowshare. The Scythian King intended to give the Persian to understand—not as Orontopagas, a tribune of the Persian guards, suggested, that Idanthuras meant he and his people were submitting to the Persian Empire (conjecturing that by the rat they gave their dwellings, by the frog their waters, by the bird their air, by the dart their arms, and by the plowshare their fields and possessions)—but rather, as Xiphodres said to the contrary: that the Scythians meant that if the Persians did not promptly fly away like birds, and hide inside the earth like rats, or enter into the waters like frogs, they could not avoid their darts and arms; and finally, being killed and slain, they would fatten the Scythian fields and possessions with their bodies and carcasses. In any event, if they were captured and reduced under the Scythian yoke and servitude, they would labor in those same fields and possessions.

The fourth and final part of the aforementioned **Egyptian Wisdom** pertained to morals and the political way of life. Diogenes Laertius attributes their laws and precepts to **Mercury**, whom the Greeks call **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth</note>, meaning "thrice-great," because he was a very great Philosopher, a very great Priest, and a very great King. Under his name we have two dialogues, titled the *Pymander* <note>Poimandres</note> and *Asclepius*, in which he predicted and announced several things to come regarding God, the Trinity, the coming of Jesus Christ, and the Final Judgment; thus, he should be esteemed not only as a Philosopher, but rather as a Prophet of future things. Iamblichus, in his *Book of the Mysteries of the Egyptians*, holds that this Mercury was not only the author and Prince of Philosophy, but also of all the wisdom of the Egyptians. He reports the opinion of Seleucus and Metrodorus, very ancient writers, who hold that this Mercury wrote and composed during his life thirty-six thousand five hundred and twenty-five books on the universal wisdom of the Egy-

## CHAP. XLI.

From what we have deduced above, we shall learn that in ancient times the Egyptians—before the use of letters, or letter characters—were accustomed to declare and make their concepts understood through the representation or portraiture of certain forms: figures of animals, trees, plants, herbs, and by some of their specific limbs or parts. In this practice, they were so skilled and practiced that they had already learned to recognize what all things in this Universe signified through the great and frequent experience they had gained. This doctrine was learned successively from father to son, like the **Kabbalah of the Jews**. This form of writing was called by them **Hieroglyphic**, as we noted above, proceeding from the invention of **Mercury Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with inventing writing and magic</note>, Emperor and ruler of the Egyptians. Furthermore, the Egyptians were a very ancient people, highly renowned in all kinds of arts and sciences, and so powerful that it is recorded that in the past there were as many as twenty thousand inhabited cities, whereas today one barely finds five or six, along with ten or twelve small villages. Moreover, they were so warlike that they extended their conquests and gave the law to the greater part of the earth. This fact means one should not doubt that they also had a language of their own and a script—not only the signs and marks called <term>Hieroglyphics</term> <note>Literally "sacred carvings," used for religious and royal inscriptions</note>, which served them as a secret cipher reserved for Kings and Priests, but also common letters from which a text can be formed, expressing in detail, letter by letter, all sorts of thoughts, just like Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. This is sufficiently implied by the following passage from Apuleius:

The ancient Egyptians had books marked with unknown letters; some used the figures of animals to suggest the condensed words of spoken language, while others used knotted marks, twisted like wheels and clustered like tendrils, to protect the text from the curiosity of the uninitiated.
<note>original: "Veteres Ægyptij libros habuere ignorabilibus literis prænotatos, partim figuris animalium concepti sermonis compendiosa verba suggerētes, partim nodosis, & in modum rotæ tortuosis, capreolatimq; condensis apicibus à curiositate personarum lectione munita." From Apuleius, *The Golden Ass*, Book 11.</note>

Tacitus, in the eleventh book of his *Annals*, says on this subject that the Egyptians were the first who represented their thoughts and concepts through figures of animals. Ancient monuments of these can still be seen engraved in marble. They maintained that they were the inventors of writing characters. In the second book, he says: "From there, Germanicus <note>A popular Roman general and nephew of Emperor Tiberius</note> went to visit the ruins of ancient **Thebes**, where magnificent remains still stood. On massive blocks of stone, Egyptian letters were carved which recorded the vast power they held in past ages." Upon being commanded, one of their oldest Priests interpreted what they meant in their language; he recounted that formerly in this city there were typically seven hundred thousand fighting men, with whom King **Ramses** had conquered Libya, Ethiopia, the Medes, and the Persians. He further conquered the province of Bactria and Scythia, along with all the lands possessed by the Syrians, Armenians, and Cappadocians—their near neighbors—extending his Empire along the coast from the Sea of Bithynia to that of Lycia. One could also read of the tributes imposed on these nations: the weight of gold and silver they were to provide each year, the number of weapons and horses, ivory, spices, and perfumes to offer in the temples, and the quantity of grain and other provisions, utensils, and munitions that each country would contribute. All of this was no less magnificent than the tributes the Parthians now levy on their subjects by force, or the dominion the Romans hold over the peoples they have conquered.

However, Ammianus Marcellinus, in the 17th book of his histories, after explaining how infinite signs and marks called **Hieroglyphics**—representing birds and strange beasts, even, he says, from another world—were engraved on every face of the Egyptian obelisks, adds these words, which seem somewhat to contradict the above: "The ancient Egyptians did not write as they do now, where a limited and easy number of letters expresses everything the human mind can conceive; rather, each character served for a separate word, and sometimes formed a complete sense from several words." By which he seems to infer that...

header: History of the Origin of [Languages]

The ancient Egyptians did not use distinct letters and writing as we do, but only certain signs that represented an entire concept, according to two examples he provides: the **Vulture**, which signified nature, because among this kind of bird no males are found, but only females, who at a certain season of the year are impregnated by the Wind; and the **bee** denoted the King, combining the two conditions he ought to possess: one of kindness and sweetness, conforming to honey, and the other of severity and vigor, represented by the sting. T. Bibliander <note>Theodore Bibliander, a 16th-century Swiss linguist and scholar</note> in his commentary on the common reasoning of all languages and letters says:

<note>original Latin: "Porrò quod Volaterranus negat Hieroglyphica nulli adhuc comperta..."</note> "Furthermore, whereas Volaterranus <note>Raffaele Maffei, a humanist scholar</note> denies that Hieroglyphics have been understood by anyone to this day, in my judgment this conflicts with published books in which authors who should not be dismissed record what the sacred letters of the Egyptians were like and what their use was. Moreover, Diodorus in Book 4 of *On Fabulous Deeds* <note>Referring to Diodorus Siculus's *Bibliotheca Historica*</note> testifies that the Egyptians received the forms of their letters from the Ethiopians—namely those used by the common people. Since that language was utterly destroyed in Egypt, first by the Greeks, then by the Romans, and later by the Saracens and Arabs, and since few words remain in written monuments, it is not easy to judge or pronounce anything as certain regarding the language of the Egyptians. Nevertheless, from those things which have come to our knowledge—from the origin of the People of **Mitzraim** <note>The Hebrew name for Egypt, referring to the son of Ham</note>, which was common with the Ethiopians and the followers of Nimrod in Babylon, and from the proximity of the Idumeans and Israelites, and from the trade of those peoples—it can be gathered that it was no less related to the **Hebrew dialect** than are the Ethiopian, Chaldean, or Phoenician languages. Even if it were as remote as Latin or Scythian, it could still be compared in individual parts with Hebrew, and therefore fit the same standard of art and science."

Of these **Hieroglyphics**, one sees more than enough remains, still found on great and small obelisks, bases, sphinxes, and other marbles brought from Egypt to Rome, of which **Pliny** makes ample mention in the 36th book, chapter 9 of his *Natural History*. Likewise, **Ammianus Marcellinus**, in the place cited before, inserts the explanation of the largest one (under the name of the said **Rameses**) in Greek letters and language. Regarding common speech or language and writing, we have nothing certain. Consequently, these two Alphabets attributed to these Egyptians have left the most curious students of antiquity uncertain and suspicious; especially since the first seems to hold some flavor of that **Capreolatin** <note>A term used to describe the unique, flowery, and "provincial" Latin style of the North African author Apuleius</note> of **Apuleius**, and the names of the letters conform to it, such as you see hereafter, twenty-four in number, just as many as there are in the Greek Alphabet. Nevertheless, **Plutarch**, in his treatise on **Osiris**, lists 25, according to the square multiplication of five <note>5 x 5 = 25; Plutarch linked this to the Egyptian calendar and the life cycle of the Apis bull</note>. Here are the two Egyptian Alphabets represented in figures by **Theseus Ambrosius** <note>Teseo Ambrogio, an Italian scholar of Oriental languages</note> in his appendix on the Chaldean, Syriac, and Armenian languages.
