# History of the Origin of the

After the death of the said Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>, the Arabs preeminently named this Law or doctrine left to them the *Al-Koran* <note>The Quran.</note>. Greek authors have translated this into their own language as "The Writing" <note>original: "τὴν γραφήν"</note>, and in Latin as "Scripture" <note>original: "Scripturâ"</note>, just as the Hebrews name the Holy Scripture *Kara* <note>original: "קרא"; meaning to read or recite</note>. From this root comes the word *Koran*, to which the Arabic article *Al* was added to compose the word *Al-Koran*, which signifies "a lesson" or "reading," according to Johannes Drusius <note>A Flemish Protestant specialized in Hebrew (1550–1616).</note> in the second book of his *Hebrew Questions*, and the author of the *Harmonic Etymology*. A certain Arab who composed a book in his language that is highly esteemed by the Turks, titled *The Doctrine of Muhammad*, along with Juan Andrés <note>A former Muslim scholar (Alfaqui) from Valencia who converted to Christianity in 1487.</note>—once a Moor and jurist, then made a Christian and priest—interpret the word *Al-Furqan* <note>original: "Al-phurcan"; meaning 'The Criterion' between right and wrong.</note>, which is another title for Muhammad's doctrine, as meaning "verses, chapters, sections, or distinct figures and sentences separated as if by articles from one another." This is because Muhammad did not receive his revelations all at once—unlike Moses receiving the Law, David his Psalms, or Jesus Christ his Gospel—but rather at many different times and seasons. John Mandeville <note>A famous (though largely fictionalized) 14th-century travel writer.</note>, a knight flourishing in the year of our salvation 1322, wrote the following about the *Al-Koran* in his travels composed in the Romance language:

> "The book of the law of the Saracens <note>original: "Serrasins"</note> which Muhammad gave them, they call it the *Al-Koran* <note>original: "Alcora"</note>; others call it the *Al-Sira* <note>original: "Alcera"</note>, and others *Al-Khera Mesaliaf*, and in another language they call it *Barbin Anavia*." <note>These terms are corruptions of Arabic words for the Quran, Sura, and Mushaf (the physical codex).</note>

Guillaume Postel <note>A 16th-century French linguist and polymath.</note>, in his *Republic of the Turks*, writes that this book is named Al-Koran because it must be read often, and *Al-Furqan* because it is divided into various parts called *Suras* <note>original: "Azoares"</note> or Prophecies. Pierre Belon <note>A French naturalist and traveler (1517–1564).</note>, in book 3, chapter 3 of his *Observations*, holds that the word *Al-Koran* signifies a collection of chapters or a gathering of Psalms.

This *Al-Furqan* or *Al-Koran* is so revered and adored by the Muslims <note>original: "Musulmãs"</note>, Muhammadans, Arabs, Turks, and Moors of today that in all the modern caravans <note>original: "Carouaanes"</note>—that is, companies of people who travel the countryside in troops for fear of Arab thieves—which go to Mecca and Medina, there is usually a camel of very high price, most superbly equipped and harnessed. This camel carries the book, enriched with gold and precious stones, inside a valuable case upon a Cairene carpet <note>original: "tapis chairin"</note>. Before this book, they bow and prostrate themselves, just as the Jews do before the book of the Law <note>The Torah scrolls.</note> which is carried in the month of September on a certain feast day <note>The festival of Simchat Torah.</note> around their synagogue. Upon the return from their journey, they publicly sacrifice this camel, and a great crowd of people each takes a morsel of its meat, which they keep as if it were a most holy and devout reliquary. This is confirmed by Giovanni Antonio Menavino <note>A Genoese who was captured by pirates and served in the court of the Ottoman Sultan.</note> in book 2, chapter 16 of his *History of Turkey*. Modern histories, as confirmed by John Bale <note>original: "Balee"</note> in the second century, chapter 80, of his *English Writers*, and Enea Silvio Piccolomini <note>Pope Pius II.</note> in chapter 42 of his *Europe*, report that the first person to translate all the books of this Quran from the Arabic language into Latin was Robert of Ketton <note>original: "Robert Kenetense"</note>, a Briton of Anglo-Saxon descent and Archdeacon of Pamplona in Spain, around the year of salvation 1143. Having learned the Arabic language in Asia from the Saracens, according to John Bale, he performed this task at the persuasion and prayer of Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, who was mentioned above, at the time that...

Muslims <note>original: "Mahometistes"</note>, they would perform prayers and orisons in the month of Ramadan, in March, and in each month they would read the entire Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note>. In this regard, I remember having read in the *History of the Saracens, and the origin, manners, religion, deeds, order, policy, and discipline of the Christians*, chapter 20, these words worthy of being reported in this place:

> Among other particular divisions concerning the ceremonies of the Turkish law, and the rites, institutions, and worship held among them, there are four solemn opinions regarding the path to salvation, each distinct from the others. Each group within that sect holds firmly to its own view and follows it, so much so that not only does one group disagree with another, but they even persecute one another by force of arms and by fortifying camps. This often disturbs the entire kingdom, and unless the king intervenes, they can by no means be pacified. The first group <note>original: "generatio"</note> consists of the Priests who are held in great reverence among them, acting as rulers of the people, executors and dispensers of the law, doctors, and judges. They preside over spiritual benefits, churches, and gymnasiums <note>schools or places of study</note>. Their opinion is that no one can be saved except through the law of Muhammad <note>original: "Machumeti"</note>. They teach and persuade everyone of this, and although they cannot prove it by any reason, authority, or example, they nevertheless attempt to resist any who contradict them in every way they can. These have many followers among the people, especially among the princes and the great lords. The second group is of those called the *Deomischler* <note>Likely referring to dervishes or a specific religious order; the term may be a corruption of a Turkish word for "God-seekers"</note>. They are religious men held in much veneration, regarded as the survivors and successors of the saints, the keepers of the whole kingdom, and the friends of God and Muhammad, of whom more was said in chapter 13. Their opinion is that the law itself is of no use, but that it is the grace of God by which every man must be saved. This grace, which they call *Rachmatallach* <note>original: "Rachmatallach", from the Arabic 'Rahmatullah', meaning 'Mercy of God'</note>, is sufficient for salvation without personal merit or the law. They do not base their opinion on any reason or authority, but try to prove it through wonders and signs, as was shown above in chapters 14 and 15. These also have many supporters, especially among those who are more spiritual, devout, and humble in their way of life. The third group is of those called the *Czofilar* <note>original: "Czofilar", referring to the Sufis</note>, who are meditative or devoted to spiritual exercises. They are held in high regard as the successors of the Prophets and the Fathers who founded this sect, and they claim to have more authority than the others. They have no foundation for their opinion other than saying it was handed down to them from antiquity. Their opinion is that every person must be saved through personal merit, and that this suffices for salvation without the need for grace or the law; they call this *Pere Ketallach* <note>original: "Pere Ketallach", likely 'Barakatullah', meaning 'Blessing of God'</note>. They are very diligent in their private prayers and spiritual exercises, such as vigils and meditations. Indeed, they never cease from continuous prayer, which they call *Chillaraitmach* <note>original: "Chillaraitmach", likely from 'Chilla', a 40-day period of spiritual seclusion</note>. At night they gather and, sitting in a circle, they begin to say "There is no god but God" <note>original: "Layla illalac", a transliteration of the Shahada: 'La ilaha illa Allah'</note>, repeating it while moving their heads for a period of time. After this, they say "To Him" <note>original: "Lahu"</note>, repeating it in the same way, and finally they say "He, He" <note>original: "Hu, hu", referring to God</note>, repeating it until they fall down and sleep as if they were dead. These also have many supporters of their opinion, especially among those who boast of the antiquity or nobility of their lineage, who are called *Effiler* and *Embieler* <note>Likely referring to the 'Evlad-i Enbiya', or descendants of the prophets</note>. **T**hese are considered authentic because their lineage does not accept the mixture of other nations, nor has it departed from the original founders of that sect.

Thus these three groups <note>original: "generationes"; referring to the schools of thought mentioned on the previous page</note> with their opinions are known to all the people, and they carry out many disputes among themselves both in private and in public. These people are held in contempt by the Turks and are regarded as schismatics; if they are found out, they are burned. Therefore, they hold their opinion not openly, but in secret. I found one man of this group while I was in Chios, who entered the church of the Christians, marked himself with the sign of the Cross, and sprinkled himself with holy water. He said openly: "Your Law is as good as ours," which no Turk of any other opinion would do to save his life.

Richer, in the second book of the *History of the Turks*, and F. de Belleforest, in the second volume, second book, chapter nine of his *Universal Cosmography*, have written as much. John Leo <note>Jean Léon, also known as Leo Africanus (c. 1494–1554), a famous Berber Andalusi diplomat and author</note>, an Arabic author, in the third book of his *Description of Africa*, asserts that a certain Arabic author named Elacfani <note>likely Al-Isfahani</note> mentioned in his writings sixty-two sects that proceeded from the Law of their Prophet Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>, which were ultimately reduced to two sects, namely the Ash'ari <note>original: "Leshari"</note> and the Imami <note>original: "Imanie"</note>. This same person, in the subsequent eighth book of his same description, in the chapter on the customs, clothing, and manner of living of the inhabitants of Cairo, says what follows:

Having acquired a great reputation through their marvelous doctrine and the esteem in which their writings were held, they were the leaders and first authors of these four religions, so much so that all Muhammadans follow the opinion of one or the other. Even those who possess literary skill do not believe their law to be true or simply good, but the intensity of their pleasures settles the judgment of their reason—as the wise man says—just as many learned men among Christians do not keep the law of the Gospel, even if they believe it to be true and good. A Christian, indeed, would never become a Muslim at the moment of death, but rather during his life; a Muslim, however, becomes a Christian at the moment of death rather than in life. Therefore, both choose to die as a Christian rather than as a Muslim, unless they are prevented by force in some way.

This suggests that Christ, after the apostasy and horrific deformation of the Church, will—near the end of the world—once again occupy the islands and the continents of the world. This will be accomplished by the truly Christian sword, which is the Word of God, so that John, Paul, Peter, the Apostles, and the Prophets (whose writings remain) may again prophesy to the Gentiles, peoples, tongues, and many kings."

### On the Priests and Ministers of the Arabs and Turks.

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial letter 'E' featuring floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

AMONG the Arabs and Turks, the Priests and ministers of their religion—or Muslim <note>original: "mahometane"</note> superstition—are as follows: namely *Thalismas* <term>likely a corruption of "Danishmend," a student of law or a teacher</term>, *Paracadis*, *Cadis* <term>Qadi: a judge in a Muslim community</term>, Priests, and Judges, *Menistssmarls* <note>Likely an OCR error for "Muderis" (professors) or "Moulays"</note>, and *Imans* <term>Imam: one who leads prayers in a mosque</term>, who are well-privileged and exempt from all taxes.
At the beginning of the establishment of the Law of Muhammad <note>original: "loy Mahometique"</note>, the Caliphs in this religion were both Kings and Pontiffs <note>The author uses "Pontiff" to explain the Caliph's spiritual authority in terms familiar to a Catholic audience</note>: one in Baghdad <note>original: "Bagadeth"</note>, the other in Cairo. Since then, the Sultans have taken Royal authority and have introduced the *muftis* <note>original: "muphtis"</note>, who are regarded as sovereign patriarchs in place of the Caliphs as administrators of religion. They judge sovereignly in matters of the Law, by which are ordained not only prayers and divine ceremonies, but also political and military affairs. They have the power to retract the ordinances of the Sultans and the sentences of their *divans* <term>Divan: a high council of state in the Ottoman Empire</term> or councils, which do not conform to, or seem to contradict, the Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note>. Every Muslim prince keeps one near him or in his principal city with large pensions. The Grand Khan <note>original: "grand Cam"</note> of the Trans-Volga Tartars <note>original: "Tartares Zauolheens"</note> keeps his at Samarkand; the Safavid Shah <note>original: "Sophy"</note> at Tabriz <note>original: "Tauris"</note>; and there are others throughout Africa at Fez, Kairouan <note>original: "Caroan"</note>, Tlemcen <note>original: "Telmessen"</note>, and elsewhere. The Grand Turk <note>The Ottoman Sultan</note> shows his Mufti more honor and reverence than any other man in his Empire. It is true that today there are still two Caliphs among the Muslims: one residing in the city of Baghdad in Assyria—the ancient seat of the Chaldean Caliphate—and the other in Cairo. These Caliphs, now bearing this name as a title only, grant possession to the Sultans without involving themselves in any way in state affairs. In doing this, they receive three thousand *seraphs* <term>Serafi: a gold coin used in the Middle East</term> because of their pretended right, in order to retain some form of the original religion, the sovereignty of which is no longer governed by them, but rather by the Muftis, as has been said, who act as Patriarchs overseeing divine matters and judging sovereignly in matters of religion and conscience.

As for the name of *Xeriph*, *Zeriph*, or *Sheriff* <note>original: "Zeriphe"</note>—a name of great and eminent dignity among the aforementioned Muslims after the Caliphs—it is, in relation to the Caliph, much like what the *Sincelli* <term>Syncellus: a high-ranking cleric in the Greek Church who lived with the Patriarch</term> were formerly to the Greek Patriarchs. For after the death of the Patriarch, the *Syncellus* succeeded him and was put in his place. Those who descended in a direct line from Muhammad or from Ali, his son-in-law, are held in great honor among the Turks and are called *Seithi* <term>Sayyid: a title of respect for descendants of Muhammad</term> by them and by the Tartars, and *Sheriffs* by the Arabs. The Ottoman Emperors, to make their own names even more august and venerable, wish to be called Sheriffs.

As for the Priests, Monks, and Hermits of the Turks, one should see what is written by Cuspinianus <note>Johannes Cuspinianus, a 15th-century diplomat and historian</note> in his works; Sansovino <note>Francesco Sansovino, author of "History of the Turks" (1560)</note> in Book 3, chapter 24 of his history of the Turks; André Thevet in Book 1, chapter 7, and Book 11, chapter 7 of his *Universal Cosmography*; Theodor Zwinger <note>Theodor Zwinger the Elder, a Swiss scholar</note> in his *Great Theater*; and Pierre Belon <note>A French traveler and naturalist</note> in Book 3, chapter 22.

## On the Philosopher Averroes or Avenroys & his works composed in the Arabic language.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'A' featuring floral and foliate patterns inside a square border.</image-desc>

SOME authors write that Averroes or Avenroys, an Arab
by nation, was so named in the Arabic language because

versed in the knowledge of the Hebrew language know well

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'A' featuring floral and foliate patterns inside a square border.</image-desc>
ABohaly or Abu Ali ibn Sina was surnamed Abinsene, or Avicenna, for being descended from an Arab named Sina—as if one were to say "son" or "grandson" of Sina, as Jacopo da Forlì writes in his commentaries on the first part of Avicenna’s writings. He had for a father an Arab by nation named Ali, according to Elias Levita in his *Tishbi*. He was a physician of Seville <note>original: "Hispale"; the author likely confuses the Persian-born Avicenna with a Spanish-Arabic scholar, or refers to the heavy influence of his texts in Spanish medical schools</note> and wrote during his life a great multitude of books in his Arabic language, as Gerard of Sabbioneta <note>original: "Gerard Sabiō"; a 13th-century translator of Arabic medical texts</note>, a native of Cremona in Italy, and other figures maintain in their translations and explanatory commentaries, as well noted by Conrad Gessner and Josias Simmler in their historical libraries. Commentaries; and what is more, he perfectly [learned] the books of Euclid’s *Geometry* without any teacher, as Nicholas Massa writes in the *Life of Avicenna*, following the Arab Zorzane <note>likely Abu 'Ubayd al-Juzjani, Avicenna's famous pupil and biographer</note>. Rabbi Abraham in his Kabbalah asserts that he began to flourish from the year of salvation 1140, during the time of the reign of Ali ibn Yusuf <note>original: "Albo Haly Aben Teffin"</note>, third Commander of the Faithful <note>original: "Miralmumin"</note> of the Almoravid race, or King reigning over the Moors of Africa and Spain, as noted by Gilbert Génébrard in Book 4 of his *Chronography*. Nicholas Massa and Andrea Alpago, under the authority of the Arab Zorzane, have assured us that this figure died at the age of 58 from a severe illness that overcame him because he had been too licentious <note>original: "paillard"; a reference to the historical tradition that Avicenna's health was undermined by overwork and physical excesses</note> in his youth, and that he flourished along with Rhazes <note>Al-Razi</note>, Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar</note>, and other great Arab figures of the time of Mansur, Marin, and Joseph, Moorish Kings of Africa commanding over Morocco, Fez, Tlemcen, and Spain, who were excellent in their religion, or rather Mahometan superstition. Some historians hold that he was a Bactrian by nation, a native of Bukhara <note>original: "Baccora"</note> or Basra, a city of the Uzbek Province, or the region of the Chagatais in Tartary, and not an Arab; but rather that he was in the pay and service of the Moorish kings of Africa who had come there, and who afterwards passed into Spain, as recorded by Giovanni Battista Ramusio in his preface to the travels of Marco Polo the Venetian in Tartary, and following him Garcia de Orta in Book 1, Chapter 3 of his *Epitome of the History of Spices*. In that work, the Arabic language is called *Araby*, that is to say, Arabic, in which one finds the works of Galen and other philosophers composed in this tongue; the language of the Mauritanians being called *Maghrebi* <note>original: "Magaraby"</note>, as if one were to say the language of those who inhabit the West, for *Gharb* <note>original: "Garbi"</note> signifies West in the Arabic language, and the word *Ma* signifies "of them." 

This Avicenna was the most universal among all the Arabs, and the most eminent in Philosophy, Mathematics, Poetry, and Arabic Theology above all others. Writing several works on medicine in his Arabic language, he treated very well—in the judgment of the most learned in this art—the signs and causes of diseases and infirmities, applying to them several remedies neither understood nor practiced by the Greeks, Latins, and others. This can easily be learned by reading his writings contained in four large volumes translated from the Arabic language into Latin by one Gerard of Cremona <note>original: "Gerard Sabion, ou Sablonede"</note>, an Italian native of Cremona, and illustrated with commentaries by Gentile da Foligno <note>original: "Gentil Fulginate"</note> and others who are well known and studied by those who make a profession of medicine, to the great relief of the sick and indisposed. Nicholas Massa, cited above in the life of this personage, reports that one Andrea Alpago, a physician by profession, was the first who translated the works of this physician from Arabic into Latin, having gone specifically to Syria to learn the Arabic language. See Conrad Gessner and Josias Simmler in their historical libraries; André Thevet, Book 16, Chapter 21 of his *Cosmography*, and Volume 2, Chapter 134 of his *Prosopographical History*; François de Belleforest, Volume 2, Book 4, Chapter 1 of his *Universal Cosmography*; and Louis Le Roy, Book 8 of *On the Vicissitude of Things*.

### Of the satirical poet Eldebag, and of his poems composed in the Arabic language.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' depicting a figure or landscape within a square frame.</image-desc> Eldebag <note>likely the 13th-century Andalusian poet Al-Dabbaj, known for his wit</note>, an Arab satirical poet by nation and a native of the city of Malaga in Granada, was well renowned and known in this Province of the Moors. During his life, he was very eloquent and fluent in his Arabic language, and admirable in his ability to disparage others, having been one of the truest satirists ever to exist among the Arabs. In fact, one day he was passing through a very well-walled city situated on the borders of Numidia <note>a historical region in North Africa</note> in a land abundant in walnut trees. Through this city flows a large river, and it is located two hundred miles from the Mediterranean Sea to the south; it is named Tebesse <note>the modern city of Tébessa, Algeria</note>. Its inhabitants were very mechanical <note>meaning of low social status or lacking in refined culture</note>, miserly, and brutal; so far from honoring or welcoming strangers were they, that they did not wish to see them in any capacity. Having been treated rudely by these inhabitants, the poet composed these very stinging and biting verses. Their substance was translated from the Arabic language into Italian (or Tuscan) by John Leo the Arab <note>better known as Leo Africanus, the famous 16th-century traveler and geographer</note> in Book 5 of his *Description of Africa*, as follows:

> *Except for walnuts, there is nothing in Tebessa* <note>original: "Fuor, che le noci, altro non è in Tebessa"</note>
> *That can be considered prized or worthy.*
> *I erred. There are also the walls, and the clear waters*
> *Of the nearby river: but of virtue it is empty.*
> *Shall I say it? It is hell, and so many Pigs*
> *Are the inhabitants of its houses.*

These verses, as translated into the French language by Jean Temporal <note>the 16th-century translator who brought Leo Africanus's work to the French public</note>, mean the following:

> *Tebessa has nothing of any value* <note>original: "Tebesse n'a rien qui soit de valeur"</note>
> *Save for walnuts; I am mistaken, it has the fortune*
> *Of possessing a river whose crystalline waters*
> *And the wide circuit of its notable walls*
> *Give it luster; yet as for virtue,*
> *The people are so stripped of it*
> *That Nature, knowing this place yields*
> *To every vice, produces walnuts in abundance*
> *As if knowing that along with the sweet waters,*
> *Brutal spirits feed themselves like swine.*

The writings of this poet are not easily found today in Asia or Turkey, despite the diligent research I have conducted to recover them. See the aforementioned John Leo, Book 5 of his *Description of Africa*, in the chapter regarding Tebessa.

## On the poet Ibn al-Farid, and his poems composed
## in the Arabic language.

Ibn al-Farid <note>Umar ibn al-Farid (1181–1234), considered one of the greatest Sufi poets in Arabic history</note>, a native of the city of Fez in Africa <note>The author likely confuses his origin; Ibn al-Farid was actually born in Cairo, Egypt</note>, an Arab by nation and a Muhammadan <note>an archaic term for Muslim</note> by religion, was from his childhood a great and admirable Arabic poet. He applied himself to writing a certain doctrine that he followed in very graceful, exquisite, and flowing Arabic verses and poems, but all filled with metaphors and allegories, so much so that he seems to deal with nothing but love. This prompted a certain person, also Arab by nation named Elfragani <note>Sa'id al-Din al-Farghani, a prominent 13th-century Sufi commentator</note>, to comment on his poems, from which he derived the rule and the stages through which one must pass, numbering fifty-two, to reach the knowledge of the Angelic nature, as he says. This knowledge, once acquired, is so strong and powerful that man can no longer err or sin, even if he tried to, as the Muhammadans believe and assert. This poet adorned and enriched his Arabic writings with such great and perfect eloquence that the followers of his doctrine recite and sing no other poems or songs in their private and public festivals and dances than his Arabic verses and poems; for no one has been found for over four hundred years who has written as articulately and elegantly as he. Those who have followed and do follow his doctrine maintain that the celestial spheres, the firmament, the elements, the planets, and all the stars are Gods, and that one cannot err in any faith or law whatsoever, because all men intend to worship That which deserves to be worshiped, and if they thought they were doing wrong, they would not want to do it for anything in the world. Leo Africanus <note>Joannes Leo Africanus (c. 1494–1554), a renowned traveler and geographer</note> by nation, in Book 1 of his *Description of Africa*, in the chapter on the way of life and customs of the Arabs living in Africa, writes that these Arabs hold poetry in high regard and greatly admire it. Devoting themselves to it, they compose poems most often enriched with perfect elegance, even though their language may be corrupted; and even a poet who is only slightly renowned among them is very welcome before their Lords, who, for the pleasure they receive from their verses, reward them generously. He assures you that it would be impossible to express the great grace they have in their poems. The same author in Book 5 of the same history, in the chapter on poets in the African vernacular, wrote what follows:

Moreover, to show some paragon of their knowledge, practicing the art of poetry, they are accustomed every year on the nativity of Muhammad <note>original: Mahomet</note>, a festival highly recommended among them, to employ the best of their wit to compose songs in his praise. And meeting every morning in the square of the chief of the Consuls, they mount his seat, where they recite one after the other what they have made in the presence of an infinite number of people; and the one who is voted to have written best and most pleasantly recited his verses is published for that year as the **Prince of Poets**. 

But in the time of the illustrious **Marinid Kings** <note>original: Roys de Marin; the Zenata Berber dynasty that ruled Morocco from the 13th to the 15th century</note>, the one who reigned used to invite to a feast all those who had the reputation of being learned and of good brain in the city. Making a solemn festival for all the poets who, by the sweetness, gravity, or eloquence of their verses, deserved the honors of this title, he ordered that each of them should recite a song in praise of Muhammad in the presence of His Majesty and the assembly. For this purpose, a scaffold was erected where the poets recited what they had composed; and according to the judgment of those who were experts, the King made a gift to the best speaker of one hundred ducats, a horse, and a slave, along with the clothes the King wore that day. He also had fifty ducats distributed to each of the others, so that no one among them left without receiving a gift worthy of his merit.

And certainly, there are many who firmly believe that man, by the sole merit of his good works through fasts and abstinences, can acquire an **angelic nature**, saying that by this means one purifies the heart and the spirit so much that he cannot sin, even if he set himself to do so. But before reaching this perfection and celestial beatitude (they say), one must climb fifty degrees of discipline. And even if one happens to fall into sin before he has reached the fiftieth, God no longer imputes to him the faults committed against his divinity. 

By which means, and for the reasons alleged above, this kind of people perform great and strange fasts at the beginning, which makes them emboldened afterward to give themselves all the good times, and take all the pleasures and delights that their lascivious will could represent to them. They also have a strict rule which was left to them written in four volumes by a man of great knowledge and very eloquent, named *Suhrawardi* <note>original: Effehraurdy; refers to the Persian philosopher Shihab al-Din Yahya ibn Habash Suhrawardi, 1154–1191</note> of Suhraward <note>original: Schrauard</note>, a city in Khorasan <note>original: Corasan; a historical region in modern-day Iran, Afghanistan, and Turkmenistan</note>.

### On the region of the Saracens.

### CHAPTER XLVII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring foliage and scrolling vines.</image-desc>

Abraham Ortelius in his *Synonyms* and *Geographical Treasury* speaks of this region of the Saracens.
*Saracena* <note>original: Σαρακηνη</note>, a region of Arabia Petraea according to Ptolemy.
*Saraceni* <note>Saracens</note> are in Arabia Felix, according to Ptolemy and Pliny. *Saraceni* are mentioned in the Panegyric to Aurelian, addressed to Maximian, and that of Pacatus, addressed to Theodosius. These were formerly called *Agareni* <note>Hagarites, descendants of Hagar</note> and *Ismaelites* <note>Ismaelitæ</note> according to the witness of Sozomen. Likewise they are called Arabs and *Scenitae* <note>tent-dwellers</note> by the author Ammianus; Ptolemy places both in Arabia Felix. By the Hebrews, they are called *Chasluhim*, as Arias Montanus writes. Concerning the Saracens, consult the Emperor Leo, chapter 18, number 119. The Council of Chalcedon mentions more than once the "cities of the Saracens" in the province of Palestine. I consider this the same as the tract of Arabia Petraea in Ptolemy. Theodoret calls these *Ismaelite Nomads* in his *Cure of Greek Afflictions*, book 9.
See *Troglodytes* <note>literally "cave-dwellers"</note>.
Pliny and Ptolemy place the region of the *Troglodytes* <note>original: Τρωγλοδυτων</note> in Africa; see the description of them in Heliodorus, book 8, and Agatharchides, book 5, also Strabo, book 16. Today it is called Sirsia by Castaldo. To me, it seems to be called Arabia by more recent writers. Eustathius is the authority that these Troglodytes were also formerly called *Erembi* <note>original: ερεμβοι</note> and Saracens. They are also called *Molgij* <note>original: μονιοι</note> by Diodorus Siculus, book 1, but the reading varies: for it is read as *Bolgi* <note>original: βολγοι</note> and *Bolpi* <note>original: βολποι</note> in the Greek Codex printed by Henri Estienne. I see them also named *Ichthyophagoi* <note>original: ιχθυοφαγοι; "fish-eaters"</note> by Isaac Tzetzes. In the Holy Scriptures they are the *Chanamim*, as Arias Montanus has it, in...

# History of the Origin of the

Pintianus reports that in his work, "Trogodytas" <note>original: "Trogodytas"; a variation of Troglodytes, meaning "cave-dwellers"</note> is always written with a single "l" in Strabo: let the faith lie with him. Juba, in Pliny, writes that the tribes of Troglodytes are called *Therothoas* from hunting <note>original: "à venatu"</note>. Strabo places Troglodytes above the Caucasian mountains, as does Eustathius near the Triballi in Europe; I believe these are the same as those mentioned by Pliny and Ptolemy in Lower Moesia. At the Atlantic sea in Africa, Hanno and Pliny also place Troglodytes. The same Juba tells of an island of Troglodytes where he says the "fountain of Isis’s hair" <note>original: "Iſidos plocamon fonticem"; likely a reference to a specific spring or botanical feature mentioned in classical geography</note> flows out; see Barbary, Catadaei, and Suchae.

---

->About the Saracens.<-

Ptolemy, Book 6, Chapter 11, Table 6 of Asia, speaks thus of the *Saracens*. The entire stretch of country neighboring the mountains of the *Aracene* region situated in *Arabia Felix* <note>original: "Arabie heureuſe"; Latin for 'Happy Arabia,' referring to the fertile southern part of the Arabian Peninsula</note> toward the North is inhabited by *Scenites* <note>original: "Scenites"; meaning "tent-dwellers," from the Greek 'skene'</note>; above them are the *Oadites*, and further toward the south are the *Saracens* and *Thamydetes*. *Pliny*, Book 6, Chapter 28, says these words: the Ancients have joined the *Thymaneans* to the *Nabataeans*, who are now the *Tavenes*, *Suellenians*, and *Saracens*.

*Sozomen*, Book 6, Chapter 38 of his Ecclesiastical History, writes what follows: This nation took its origin from *Ishmael*, son of *Abraham*, as it is also renamed after him. And for this reason, the ancients called them *Ishmaelites*. But so that they might wash themselves of this stain of bastardy and remove the infamous title of being slaves and commoners, and put behind them the obscurity of the blood of *Hagar*, mother of *Ishmael* (for she was a bondwoman and slave by condition), they usurped the name of *Saracens*, as if they had been procreated from the legitimate bed of *Abraham* and *Sarah* his wife. From this claim of lineage, they are also circumcised, following the manner and ceremony of the *Hebrews*, and like the *Jews* they abstain from the flesh of pork, and keep several other observations proper to the *Jewish* nation. If they do not follow all the same rules and laws of living as the Hebrews, it must be attributed both to the long stretch of time they have been separated from their kin, and to the occasion of proximity, having always lived among idolaters. And lest I seem to misuse a single region for all the rest, I have good and sufficient authors from whom we draw and gather that all *Arabs* in general have been named *Saracens*; for as for *Hagarenes*, we have already declared it before, whether from *Hagar* the concubine, or from the city of *Agra* founded by the aforementioned woman.

*Procopius*, Book 2 of the Persian War, speaking of the King of Arabia bearing the name *Arete*, like the other kings his predecessors, uses these words: A short time later, *Arete* and *Al-Mundhir* <note>original: "Almandar"; likely Al-Mundhir III ibn al-Nu'man, a Lakhmid king</note>, captain of the *Saracens*, resolved to make war on each other, without one taking help from the *Romans* and the other from the *Persians*. These two were Kings of Arabia, and yet they are called chiefs of the *Saracens*. With this agrees *Ammianus Marcellinus*, Books 22 and 23, when he describes the land of *Egypt*, saying that on the side facing the East are *Elephantine* and *Meroë*, cities of *Ethiopia*, and the *Catadupes*, and the Red Sea extends as far as the *Scenite Arabs* whom they now call *Saracens*. In short, wherever this author makes mention of the *Arabs* in his writings, he names them no other way.

This is why **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) whose work was the primary text on pharmacology for 1,500 years.</note> calls myrrh "Saracenic," not because it grows among the **Scenites** <note>original: "Scenites"; from the Greek 'skene,' meaning "tent-dwellers"</note>—who are properly the Saracens—but in **Happy Arabia** <note>original: "Arabie heureuſe"; Latin: *Arabia Felix*, referring to the fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula.</note>. These people have been known since ancient times and have shown themselves to be enemies of the Romans, just as they have hardly ever maintained a firm friendship with anyone. It is true that when **Pompey the Great** was waging war in Asia, these Saracen Arabs took up arms under him and were in his pay. But over time they emancipated themselves and, unable to forget their nature, returned to raiding. This was the reason that **Aelius Gallus**, of whom **Strabo** speaks in Book 16, crossed into Arabia and tamed a good part of it. Under **Trajan**, another enterprise was undertaken by that Emperor against these Saracens; but having done their duty, they began once more to run and ravage the borders of the Empire. When **Odenat** and his wife **Zenobia** held the East as their portion, and after this Lady was conquered by **Aurelian** in the year of our salvation 270 (according to **Vopiscus** <note>Flavius Vopiscus, one of the purported authors of the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note>), the Saracens kept quiet until the time of **Constantine the Great**. Having been as if unknown for a long time, they then made themselves recognized by their raids and thefts, so that people began to hold them in great hatred. When the war against the Persians was opened by the children of the aforementioned Constantine, the most expedient thing found for the peace of the Empire was to win over the Saracens—though there was never much reason to trust them because of their inconstancy and disloyalty. This is amply testified by the aforementioned **Ammianus Marcellinus** in Book 14, saying that the Saracens were never good friends to the Romans. Running about in all directions, they ravaged in a moment everything they could encounter, resembling a predatory **kite** <note>A type of hawk known for its scavenging and sudden strikes.</note> which lives only on plundered prey; seeing its meat from afar, it carries it off and snatches it in a sudden flight, and if given food, they do not stop to enjoy it on the spot.

In short, this person <note>referring to Ammianus Marcellinus</note> speaks and discourses on these Saracens and their raids and thefts at length in his 23rd, 24th, and 25th books, always taking these Saracens to mean all Arabs. It must be understood that this people has always been inconstant in its faith and belief, and has never been able to remain in the perfection of one law; above all, they never knew how to settle on the one that was most holy. For it is to be believed that their father **Ishmael** had been instructed by **Abraham** in the fear of one God, and that he had given instruction in this to those who originated from him. But suddenly they forgot the great God and ran after idols <note>original: "simulachres"</note>, retaining no other part of the **Religion of Abraham** than the external ceremony of circumcision. And when they became Christians and were baptized, this Christian reformation was against their hearts, as it was entirely contrary to their ways of doing things. ### History of the Origin of the [Saracens]

...to the damnable law of the false prophet **Muhammad**. **Sozomen** <note>original: "Sosomene"; Salamanes Hermias Sozomenus (c. 400 – 450 AD), a historian of the early Christian Church.</note>, in Book 6, Chapter 38 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, discusses at great length how, under the reign of **Mavia**, their Queen, they received and embraced **Christianity**. This occurred under the Empire of **Valens** <note>The author mentions Valens following Jovian; Valens reigned 364–378 AD.</note>, who succeeded **Jovian** around the year of our salvation 382, which was long before **Muhammad** came into the world to infect it with his doctrine. Some time later, **Zocome**, Prince and governor of a province of the **Saracens**, also became a Christian along with his subjects. They remained in the Christian faith until the **Persians**, ruining the holy places and massacring these Christian Saracens, caused them to forget their faith and doctrine; they then allowed themselves to be led like beasts to the law of the aforementioned **Muhammad**, which is full of license and concupiscence. Furthermore, as soon as these people were emancipated from the Christian faith, they immediately rushed, under the Empire of **Anastasius**, upon the lands of **Phoenicia** and **Palestine** around the year of salvation 504, according to the report of **Paul the Deacon** <note>An 8th-century historian; the work cited is likely the *Historia Romana*.</note> in Book 15 of the *Deeds of the Romans*. The leader, author, and conductor of this incursion was one **Vadicarim**, who succeeded his brother **Agar** in the government of the Saracens. He appeared like a lightning bolt or a whirlwind, passing through so suddenly and wasting everything with a cruel and terrifying fury.

These Saracens were tributaries to **Justinian** the Emperor, as shown by the aforementioned **Paul the Deacon** in the following 16th book of the *Deeds of the Romans*, making mention of **Arethas** <note>Al-Harith ibn Jabalah, a King of the Ghassanid Arabs and a prominent Roman ally.</note>, Patrician and Prince of these Saracens, who came to the court of the aforementioned **Justinian** to bring the tribute and to pray the Emperor to grant him the grace that his children might hold his Kingdom after him. This King **Arethas** was very loyal to the Romans and greatly aided **Justin the Younger** against the King of **Persia**. But in the time of **Heraclius**, everything having changed among these Saracens—some being idolaters to please the Persians, others following Jewish customs, and a small number following the Christian religion—they overran the lands of the **Roman Empire** and threw themselves upon the country of **Syria**. This was when **Chosroes**, King of **Persia**, took the city of **Jerusalem** and caused infinite evils and ravages to the poor Christians in the year of salvation 515 <note>The author’s date here is likely a chronological error; the Persian conquest of Jerusalem under Chosroes II occurred in 614 AD.</note>, according to the *Annals of Constantinople*, Book 18.

In the time of this Emperor **Heraclius**, **Muhammad** <note>original: "Muchamet ou Mahometh"</note> commanded these Saracens, as I have noted in this work. This seducer having reigned nine years, he had as his successor **Ebubezer** <note>Abu Bakr (r. 632–634 AD), the first Caliph.</note>. Because he received a pension from **Heraclius** to guard the borders of the Empire against the Persians, it happened that the official who was in charge of paying them—when these Saracens asked him for what was owed to them—replied proudly: "What? The Emperor can barely pay his soldiers, and must these dogs ask him for pensions?" These words cost the Christians dearly, for **Ebubezer**, informed of the insult done to his entire nation, took up arms and entered **Palestine**, killing the Roman garrisons. He took the city of **Gaza** and all the surrounding country. At this time, these Saracens also defeated the Persians and killed their King **Hormisdas**, bringing an end to that Monarchy. This **Ebubezer** having reigned three years (or two and a half according to the *Annals of Constantinople*, Book 18), he died and left as his successor and Admiral, or Sultan, or Soldan, after him **Haumar** <note>Umar ibn al-Khattab (r. 634–644 AD), the second Caliph.</note>, one of the most valiant and fortunate men of his time. This Arab Prince had war with Justinian, and defeated the Christians, having bribed the general of their army with money, and sent **Muhammad** <note>Muhammad ibn Marwan, a general and brother of the Caliph</note> against the **Roman** [Byzantine] lands, where he did innumerable evils to the Imperialists. 

And in the year 699, the third raid of the **Saracens** into **Africa** was made; having stopped there, they were chased out by the Emperor **Leontios** sending **John** [the Patrician] there. This nonetheless served as a lure for them to return and to plant a **Colony** there, as they did, just as it is written in book 20 of the *Annals of Constantinople*. Armenia having been taken from the Arabs, Muhammad reconquered it, but **Azar** and **Azid** were not so fortunate: for having descended into **Cilicia**, they were defeated there by one **Heraclius**, brother of the Emperor **Apsimar** <note>Tiberios III Apsimar</note>. 

Meanwhile, Abd al-Malik dies, and after him reigns **Al-Walid** <note>original: "Vlid"; Al-Walid I</note>, son of Abd al-Malik <note>original: "Abdalar"; likely a transcription error for Abd al-Malik</note>, a man who was above all others an enemy of the Christian name: as he made himself well felt when he usurped the Church of the Christians in **Damascus** and made it into a **Mosque** <note>The Great Mosque of Damascus, built on the site of the Cathedral of St. John the Baptist</note>. He also forbade that any books be written in **Greek**, because (say the *Annals of Constantinople*) in their Arabic language—which he wanted them to use—one could not write of Unity, duality, nor the **Trinity**, nor the number eight and a half <note>This reflects a Byzantine polemic claiming Arabic was linguistically incapable of expressing Christian theology</note>; by this means the Tyrant wanted to abolish the memory of the Holy Trinity among the Christians. 

In the year 709, **Maslama** <note>original: "Mafalma"; Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik</note> took the city of **Tyana** <note>original: "Tranie"</note>, which he razed from top to bottom and led the people into the deserts; and **Mukhtar** <note>Likely another commander of the same name</note> took several cities in Cilicia, and **Abbas** took the city of **Antioch of Pisidia**. This Suleiman was not a Prince of great effect: for everything was carried out by the two captains Umar and Maslama, the one taking **Cilicia**, the other **Asia Minor** and the city of **Pergamum**, and both of them besieging the City of Constantinople where the Emperor **Leo the Isaurian** <note>Leo III, known for his defense of the city and his iconoclasm</note> reigned, just as it is written in the 21st book of the *Annals of Constantinople*; and from which siege the plague, hunger, and storms drove them away: for from an infinite number of vessels that they had before them, hardly ten escaped being submerged by the violence of the winds, hail, and tempests.

Those who became Mahometans, he exempted from all subsidies <note>Taxes, likely referring to the jizya</note>, but those who remained firm were tormented without cease until death, so much so that many were massacred under this adversary of the Christians: and he made a Law by which it was not permitted for a Christian to testify against a Mahometan, for if he did, his testimony was without effect or any value whatsoever, which is observed among the **Turks** to this day. 

This Umar reigned only two years, and having died, he was succeeded by **Yazid** <note>original: "Gizid"; Yazid II</note>, the second of that name, who, as soon as he was received into his principality, had business against another Yazid <note>Yazid ibn al-Muhallab, who led a rebellion in Iraq/Persia</note> who tried to make himself lord and Tyrant of **Persia**, where he was a native; but he sent Maslama against this usurper, who killed him and returned the Persians to their duty. Toward this Yazid addressed a **Jew**, who made him believe that if he cast down the images in the Churches of the Christians, he would be a peaceful King of his own for the space of forty years: believing this, this foolish Arab set himself to persecute the images, in which he pleased the Emperor <note>Referring to the Byzantine Emperor Leo III's iconoclastic policies</note>, but he was deceived in his hope, for he lived as King for only four years. 

To Yazid succeeded **Hisham** <note>original: "Euclid"; likely a transcription error for Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik</note> his son, who amused himself by building palaces and places of pleasure throughout the cities of his obedience, and by erecting Aqueducts for the ornament and use of the citizens. He still made war against the Romans, and under him two of his Admirals went to besiege the city of **Nicaea** <note>original: "Nicie"</note> in **Bithynia**: but however great an effort they made, and though the number of theirs was infinite, they nonetheless returned without gaining anything. The aforementioned Muhammad or Abdullah having reigned five years, died while his brother **Abdullah** <note>Al-Mansur, the second Abbasid Caliph</note> was at **Mecca**—a place of abomination to this people <note>A common polemical phrase used by Christian writers of this era to describe Islamic holy sites</note>—who did not fail to prepare himself to enter into lordship. But Abu Muslim was tricked by that Abdullah <note>Al-Mansur</note>, who, having him come under his word and with an oath in the great name of the false Prophet **Muhammad**, as soon as he held him, had him hacked to pieces.

Thus Abdullah, the second of that name and 19th Commander <term>Admiral<note>Amir</note></term>, was the sole monarch over the **Saracens**, with only Salih remaining to command over the land of Egypt. It was this Salih who first among the Saracens forbade Christians from building churches, from displaying the cross, and from debating in any way about religion, or from teaching or discussing their Christian religion before the Arabs. This Salih went to wage war against the Christians in the Roman lands of **Asia** <note>Byzantine Asia Minor</note> subject to the Emperor, but hearing that **Constantine V "Copronymus"** <note>original: "Constantin Copronyme"</note> was coming against him toward the land of **Cappadocia**, he returned without having accomplished anything.

Abdullah <note>Al-Mansur</note>, meanwhile, who was the great Sultan or **Caliph**, showed himself hardly any kinder to the Christians, upon whom he doubled the tributes, taxes, and other charges, forcing the monks, the hermits, and the clergy to pay taxes like the laity—something which none of his predecessors had dared to do. And what is worse, he seized the relics and jewels of the churches and had them sold to the **Jews**, who bought them readily, assured that the Christians would not be long in ransoming them.

This gave a marvelous contentment to Harun, who thereby boasted of having subjected the Roman Empire, having made a tributary of the man who bore the title of its sovereign.

But Nicephorus having fortified some places ruined by the Arab, Harun cast them down again, and breaking the peace, came to **Cyprus**, where he ruined the churches and drove out the islanders; he did infinite evils to the Christians throughout Asia. Meanwhile, this sovereign Prince of the Arabs died in **Khorasan** <note>original: "Corasan"</note> in the Kingdom of Persia.

This caused both ruin among themselves and great persecution of the Christians subject to their rule. **Al-Ma'mun** <note>reigned 813–833 AD</note>, a man devoted to the sciences and especially to Mathematics, was incited to this pursuit because the Saracen Kings in Africa and Spain loved letters and kept persons of excellent doctrine in their courts and entourages. Under this prince Ma'mun, the Eastern Saracens overran the **Cyclades Islands** and **Asia Minor**. They built a fort near the city of **Tarsus** <note>original: "Tharſe"</note> so that from there, using fire, they could signal one another all along the sea coast, just as the Turks still practice today; they also led many thousands of men into servitude. This occurred around the year of grace 870 <note>The author's chronology is slightly shifted; Al-Ma'mun died in 833, but the conflicts continued through the 9th century</note>. 

Ma'mun was succeeded by another **Amir** <note>term: Amir; translated here as "Amer", a title for a commander or prince</note> surnamed **Esmān**, who joined with the Arabs of Africa and with the **Manichaeans** <note>The author likely refers to the Paulicians, a Christian sect that allied with the Muslims against the Byzantines</note> who were in the East. However, Amir Esmān was slain near the island of **Negropont** <note>The modern island of Euboea, Greece</note> and lost the greater part of his army there. Beyond these, I find no other **Admiral** <note>term: Admiral; a corruption of "Amir-al", used by Western writers to mean a high sovereign or naval commander</note> who was sovereign over this entire nation, although the **Hagarenes** <note>term: Hagarenes; a common medieval term for Muslims, implying descent from Hagar</note> caused great trouble for the Greeks in the conquest of Asia and to retain the whole of **Syria**, which the Emperors had already attempted to retake, and which they would have captured had it not been for the arrival of the Turks. 

For while **Romanus Lecapenus** <note>Byzantine Emperor Romanos I, reigned 920–944</note> held the Greek-Roman Empire around the year of salvation 910, it is found in the histories of the Saracens that one **Apochapse** <note>Likely Abu Hafs ibn Amr</note>, son of the Great Admiral of the Saracens, was Sultan of **Melitene** in Mesopotamia. He waged war against Romanus and later made peace; upon his death, he was succeeded by **Aposalathe**. Although these were not sovereign Kings, whenever something was stirred up in the East, they were immediately respected and chosen as chiefs and generals of all the Hagarene forces. 

**Amir** the third of that name succeeded Aposalathe and presided over the city of Tarsus around the year 946. However, he was not successful in his enterprises against the Christians, as **Bardas Phocas**, General of the imperial army, defeated him in battle and took from him a good number of cities in **Cilicia** and Syria. The city of **Jerusalem**, nevertheless, remained always in the power of the Hagarenes. This Prince immediately made war on the Christians and rushed upon the lands of *Galicia* in the year 757, but he was defeated by King *Froila*. Meanwhile, in Africa, the two houses of *Umayya* <note>original: "Aben Humeya"</note> and *Abbas* <note>original: "Aben Alabeci"</note> fought for the Crown. In the end, *Marwan* of the blood of *Umayya* was defeated and killed. *Abdallah* of the race of *Abbas*, descended from *Fatima* <note>The text conflates the Abbasids with the Alids; the Abbasids actually descended from the Prophet’s uncle, Abbas</note>, the eldest daughter of *Muhammad*, came to the crown. Thus the Lordships of *Arabia* and *Africa* remained in the race of these *Abbasids* until the *Almoravids* drove them out. Meanwhile, another race began in *Spain*, which came from the *Umayyads*...

...of which the head was a man named *Abd al-Rahman I* <note>original: "Abderahamen, Aben Humeya"; the first Umayyad Emir of Córdoba</note>, who came to *Spain* with the intention of making himself King there and standing against the race of the *Abbasids* <note>original: "Alabeci"; the rival dynasty that overthrew the Umayyads in the East</note>. For this reason, he had no sooner arrived in *Spain* than he made war against *Yusuf* <note>original: "Ioseph"; Yusuf ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Fihri, the last governor of Al-Andalus</note>; he did not cease until he had put him to death and made himself King of *Spain*. Thus the *Muslim* <note>original: "Mahometan"</note> Empire was divided: one King ruling over the Arabs, another over the Africans, and the third in *Spain*. *Abd al-Rahman*, then the first King of *Cordoba* and the tenth in number among the *Muslim* usurpers of *Spain*, resolved to keep his court at *Cordoba*. But because *Toledo* was regarded as the capital of the Spanish kingdom, he desired that his son *Sulayman* <note>original: "Culema Abé Humeya"</note> should be its governor. He then set out to make war against the Christian King of *Spain*, against whom he gained nothing but blows, and worse still befell him: for as soon as he styled himself *Commander of the Faithful* <note>original: "Miramomelin" or "Miramolin"; a corruption of the Arabic title Amir al-Mu'minin</note> of *Spain*, the Moors in *Valencia* refused to obey him, saying they were subjects of the *Abbasid* blood. However, this *Abd al-Rahman* went to besiege *Valencia* and took it. Despite this, divisions continued in *Spain*, as *Abd Allah* <note>original: "Hibduabala"</note> made himself King of *Zaragoza*, though he was soon deposed by his own captains, *Abu Thawr* <note>original: "Abautar"</note> and *Denisfez*. This caused him to travel to *France* to see *Charlemagne* <note>original: "Charles le grad"</note>, who restored him to his kingdom in the year 778, on the condition that the Christians would live in liberty of conscience and have free exercise of their religion in his lands.

*Abd al-Rahman* having died in the year 780, he was succeeded by his son *Hisham I* <note>original: "Hisẽ"</note>, who, although he was the younger son, usurped the state. This caused another division in the Kingdom, as the majority of the neighbors offered their obedience to *Sulayman*, who established the royal seat at *Toledo* and called himself *Commander of the Faithful*. It was from this beginning that the Kingdom of *Toledo* took its start, just as the rest of the kingdoms in *Spain* had their foundations in the divisions of the Moors. The two brothers went to war and fought near *Vilches*, where King *Hisham* was victorious. From there, he went to besiege *Toledo*, which surrendered by treaty without a blow being struck. *Sulayman*, despairing of recovering his heritage, went to Africa to seek reinforcements and recover his losses. *Hisham* then made war to reclaim *Languedoc*, which had been conquered by some of his predecessors; but after achieving some happy exploits, he was ultimately beaten down by the aid of the Emperor *Charlemagne*. This Moorish King was so diminished that most of his cities paid tribute to the aforementioned Emperor, and *Hisham* died of vexation because of it in the year 794.

This valiant King was succeeded by his eldest son *Al-Hakam I* <note>original: "Hali Hatá" or "Alhacã"</note>, who was the first to order a guard of renegade Christians at his gate; he kept five thousand of them regularly near his person, much as the Great Turk today does with the *Janissaries* <note>The elite infantry units that formed the Ottoman Sultan's household troops</note>. While he amused himself with his grandeur, his cousin *Sulayman* plotted with the citizens of *Toledo* and, crossing from Africa to *Spain* with forces, made himself lord of *Valencia* and regained *Toledo*. But his joy was short-lived, for *Al-Hakam* went to meet him and they came to blows; *Sulayman* lost both the battle and his life. His brother *Abd Allah*, whom he had brought from Africa, was captured and treated well by *Al-Hakam*. The King was unable to recover the city of *Toledo* for nine years, but at last he took it by a clever surprise, feigning a desire for peace and fair treatment, only to put to death five or six thousand of the principal citizens <note>This refers to the "Day of the Trench," a famous massacre of the Toledan elite</note>. In that season, the Christians, aided by the French, made great conquests in *Catalonia*. King *Al-Hakam* died in the year 819 and had as his heir and successor his son named *Abd al-Rahman II*.

Nevertheless, there was later a general for the same King *Hisham* who overran the lands of **León** and **Galicia**, performing great feats of arms and making himself terrifying to all those Christians, whose private hatreds were the cause of these disasters. As a result, the greater part of **Catalonia** was once again brought under the rule of the **Muslims**. 

Among them also, divisions arose following the example of the Christians. There was a Moor named *Sulayman* <note>original: "Culemà"; Sulayman al-Musta'in</note> who took the kingdom from *Hisham*, whom he put in prison, and made himself **Commander of the Faithful** <note>original: "miramomelin"; from the Arabic title *Amir al-Mu'minin*</note> of **Córdoba**, having come there from **Barbary** <note>North Africa</note>, from where he drew support. This Toledan King allied himself with the Christians to gain an advantage against the forces of the King of **Córdoba**. Meanwhile, *Sulayman*, driven from his kingdom and favored by the Christians, made war on King *Muhammad*, whom he defeated, and restored himself to his seat. This caused him to release *Hisham*, whom we mentioned above had been driven from his kingdom by *Sulayman*, because he was the legitimate King of the royal succession and family, and he was also received by his subjects. He took several cities in **Andalusia** which had been usurped by tyrants and rebels during the civil wars, and he made war on the **Africans** <note>Berber factions</note> who defended the side of *Sulayman*, his adversary. This Qasim, upon his death, was succeeded in the year 1017 <note>original: "107"; the author frequently drops the first digit of the millennium</note> by Yahya <note>original: "Hiayá"</note>, son of the aforementioned Muhammad. However, he was not King for long, having attained the throne by means of the **Berbers** <note>original: "Berberuzes"</note>. Consequently, the **Spanish** called upon Habus <note>original: "Buz"</note>, Lord of **Granada**, and through his intrigues, Yahya was killed in the city of **Málaga**. The crown then fell to *Abd al-Rahman IV* <note>original: "Abderrahamē"</note>, who reigned only one month and seventeen days. He was succeeded by *Muhammad IV*, whose riches and greed were the cause of his ruin; for his own people, desiring his treasures, had him poisoned after he had reigned only one year and four months.

He had as his successor *Hisham III* <note>original: "Hilem"</note>. At that time, **Spain** was entirely filled with **Petty Kings** <note>term: Roytelets; a diminutive of "Kings" used to describe the leaders of the fragmented Taifa states</note>, there being almost no provincial capital city that did not have a King commanding it. This diminished the glory of the Kingdom of **Córdoba**, whose Kings had previously been the Great Sovereigns of all the **Moors** of **Spain**.

This King also did not last long; not because his subjects hated him, but because he had a lieutenant of low birth who treated the people cruelly. For this reason, they punished the King for the fault of his officer: they drove him out, deposed him from the crown, and gave him as a successor *Al-Mundhir II* <note>original: "Almundir"</note>. He came to present himself to the people of **Córdoba** to be their King, claiming to be of the blood of their false Prophet <note>The author uses this term to refer to Muhammad from a contemporary Christian perspective</note>. He was received and heard, but those who loved him advised him to withdraw his claim to the crown, seeing the perils suffered therein. They argued that with the city in arms and the moods and affections of the citizens so divided, it was better for him to abandon his enterprise than to expose his life to danger.

But this foolish Prince, instead of following their advice and thanking them, replied: "Make me King today, and hold me as such; and tomorrow kill me, if the desire takes you." This was so poorly received by the assembly that, conceiving the opinion that he would be a bad King if he were confirmed in the state, they were far from granting him the term he requested to reign. On the spot, they hacked him to pieces. At that very instant, they commanded *Hisham*—whom they had deposed without killing—to withdraw and leave the palace and the city. This he did with his children and family, going to one of his fortresses. But they, seeing that in the long run this King might do them some wrong or displeasure, went to force the place. They took the King and his children and poisoned them in **Córdoba**.

Now, even though the misfortune was so great for those who reigned in **Córdoba**, there was always some fool found who, out of a desire to rule, made a prodigal sacrifice of his life. Among these was a powerful **Moor**, a native of **Algeciras** <note>original: "Algaſur"</note> named Jawhar <note>original: "Iohar"</note>, who managed to make himself King in the year 1012 <note>original: "112"</note> of our salvation. He held the Lordship for two years, which was a long time considering how little time his predecessors had reigned. During this time, **Don Sancho**, King of **Navarre** and Count of **Castile**, helping himself to and using these **Moorish** divisions, overran everything—burning, killing, and pillaging right up to the gates of **Córdoba**—without finding a single **Muslim** to offer resistance. He returned to his house laden with booty, having acquired a very great reputation. This Jawhar, having reigned for two years as said, died; and he was succeeded by his son, named Muhammad the fifth <note>The text ends mid-word with "cin-"</note>...

Through the failure of this Kingdom, that of **Toledo** gained strength, which we must now discuss, since reason dictates that having removed the Moors from Africa, we see them retiring there again. The downfall of the house of the Kings of **Córdoba** was the cause for the Christian Kings of **Spain** to extend their borders and recover many lands from the **Muslims** <note>original: "Mahometans"</note>, especially on the side of **Portugal**, **Galicia**, and **Catalonia**. Against him, the aforementioned King **Ferdinand I** waged such violent war that, taking the towns of Talamanca, Uceda, Guadalajara, Alcalá, Madrid, and others, he so stunned the Moor that he rendered himself his vassal and did him homage for what he possessed in **Toledo**.

This Ali Maymon was succeeded by a son named Hisham ibn Umayya <note>original: "Hisẽ Abẽ Humeya"</note>, under whom very learned men flourished in **Toledo**, along with many Christians living in liberty of conscience, who were named **Mozarabs** <note>term: Mozarabs; from the Arabic 'musta'rib', meaning 'Arabized', these were Iberian Christians who lived under Muslim rule and adopted Arabic language and culture while remaining Christian</note>, as I have fully detailed before. During the final years of Ferdinand, this Toledan King and several other **Petty Kings** <note>term: Roytelets; minor rulers of fragmented states</note> who held power in the Kingdoms of **Aragon** and **Valencia** were constrained to return to their former obedience. While these things were occurring in **Spain**, there was great division in **Africa** among the Kings and Princes; for just as those of the blood of Umayya <note>original: "Humeya"</note> held **Spain**, those of the line of Ibn Alawite <note>original: "Abẽ Alaueci"</note> were Lords of **Africa**. However, a very rich and powerful family of Moors arose in Africa, bearing the name of the **Almoravids**, who drove from the African Kingdom those of the Alawite race and the blood of the false Prophet. The leader of these Almoravids was named **Yusuf ibn Tashfin** <note>original: "Iofeph Abẽ Tesfin"</note>, after whom a river in Barbary is named in the country and Kingdom of Tlemcen. The Spanish and African Moors who did not love the lineages of Umayya and Alawite placed themselves under the power of this Almoravid.

When the King of **Toledo**, Ali Maymon, died, he had for his successor Hisham, his only son; this occurred in the year of Grace 1074. Those of **Córdoba** made war against him, but he, succored by his friend the King of **Castile**, punished them so well that they no longer had the boldness to raid his lands to harm him. Now, not to leave out the rest of these **Muslims**, there were at that time Kings in **Seville** named Al-Mu'tamid ibn Abbad <note>original: "Almũcamuz aben Amet"</note>; Al-Muzaffar <note>original: "Amũdafar"</note> in **Granada**; and Abu Bakr <note>original: "Abubacar"</note> in **Valencia**. However, as **Yahya** continued in his wicked ways, **Alfonso** was again entreated to drive him out; this he did, and regained the city of **Toledo** for the Christians in the year 1083. <note>Historians generally date the fall of Toledo to 1085.</note> **Yahya**, aided by the same King **Alfonso**, moved his kingdom and seat of lordship to **Valencia**. At this time, **Al-Mu'tamid** <note>original: "Almuncamus"</note>, King of **Seville**, being the most powerful of all the **Moors**, gave his daughter—the most beautiful princess of her time—to **Alfonso**, King of **Castile**. She was named **Zaida** <note>original: "Caida"</note>, but her name was changed at her baptism, and she was called **Mary**. To please his father-in-law and to subject all the **Muslims** <note>original: "Mahometans"</note> of **Spain** to him, this **Alfonso** sent word to **Yusuf ibn Tashfin** <note>original: "Ioseph Aben Tesfin"</note>, King of **Africa**, to obtain forces from the **Almoravids** <note>term: Almoravids; a Berber imperial dynasty from Morocco that established an empire in the 11th century.</note> in order to subject the Kings of **Zaragoza** and **Dénia**. **Al-Mu'tamid**, performing a similar duty, sent to the great Governor of **Marrakesh** named **Ali Aben Axà**, praying him to bring as many forces as possible. This the **Moor** did, but he was not long without finding a convenient quarrel against the King of **Seville**, so that when they came to blows, **Al-Mu'tamid** was slain. This caused all the **Moors** of **Spain** to turn to this **Moroccan**, **Aben Axà**, who, revolting against **Yusuf** his Prince, made himself Lord and Tyrant over all the **Muslims** in **Spain**. He renewed the ancient title of the Kings of **Córdoba**, calling himself **Miramomelin** <note>term: Miramomelin; a corruption of the Arabic 'Amir al-Mu'minin', meaning Commander of the Faithful.</note>, and refused to pay tribute to the Christians. As he raided the lands of **Toledo**, King **Alfonso** came to meet him with his forces, but the King was defeated by the **Moor**, who easily recovered the places conquered by the **Castilian**.

Despite being twice defeated, **Alfonso** did not lose heart; rather, as he came to besiege **Aben Axà** at **Córdoba**, the great King of **Africa** named **Yusuf Tashfin** passed into **Spain** with great forces. He captured **Aben Axà**, had him beheaded, and won **Córdoba**, **Seville**, and all of **Andalusia**. Thus, a union of the **Muslims** of **Africa** and **Spain** was made under a single King and **Miramomelin**. Once this was accomplished by **Yusuf**, he returned to **Africa** and took up residence in the city of **Marrakesh** in the year 1089. This **Yusuf** died in the year of grace 1100, having reigned twelve years over **Spain**, and was succeeded by his son **Ali ibn Tashfin** <note>original: "Haly Aben Tesfin"</note>, **Miramomelin** of **Africa** and **Spain**. He, assembling a furious army of his **Almoravids**, crossed into **Spain** and went against the good King **Alfonso** of **Castile**. The King, being old, sent his son to the war, where the son was killed and the Christians defeated. Nevertheless, the **Moors** did not advance further, fearing the good fortune of the good King **Alfonso**, who, dying without a male heir, left as his heir his nephew <note>Historically, his son-in-law</note> **Alfonso**, King of **Navarre** and **Aragon**. This man raided the lands of the **Almoravids**, whose King, **Ali ibn Tashfin**, died in the year 1130. His heir was **Tashfin ibn Ali** <note>original: "Albo Haly Aben Tesfin"</note>, his son, during whose reign there lived in **Córdoba** the great physician we call **Avicenna** <note>original: "Albo Hali Auinceni"; Note: The author mistakenly places Avicenna (who lived in Persia) in 12th-century Spain.</note>, who flourished in the year 1140. Also in honor and fame during this same season were **Averroes** <note>original: "Aben Roys"</note>, as I describe hereafter, along with **Avenzoar** <note>original: "Aben Zoar"</note>; all were distinguished men, well-versed in the knowledge of natural causes. From these personages of great learning arose the occasion for the troubles that later broke out between the **Moors**, and between the houses of the **Almoravids** and the **Almohads** <note>term: Almohads; a Moroccan Berber Muslim movement that eventually overthrew the Almoravid dynasty.</note>. ## Monarchy of the Moors

This young man was of lowly station, the son of a potter of the earth, though he possessed a bold spirit and an enterprising nature that reflected the ambition brooding in his soul. He was named **Abdelmon** <note>original: "Abdelmon"; referring to Abd al-Mu'min (r. 1130–1163), the first Caliph of the Almohad Empire</note>, and he placed such great faith in the words of the philosopher **Thumert** <note>original: "Thumert"; referring to Ibn Tumart, the spiritual founder of the Almohad movement</note> that, addressing himself to a **Muslim** <note>original: "mahometan"</note> cleric highly learned in the **Quran** <note>original: "l’Alcoran"</note>, he declared to him the prediction of **Thumert**. He begged this cleric to grant him aid and support, promising that if the affair succeeded according to what the stars promised, he would make him the greatest among the **Muslims**. **Almohadi** <note>The author uses "Almohadi" as a proper name here, though it derives from 'Al-Mahdi,' the title claimed by Ibn Tumart</note>—for so this cleric was called—having resolved to help him, could find no finer or more rapid path to sow novelties in their religion than to begin interpreting the **Quran** against the sense of all other doctors. He tailored everything to the humors of the **Africans**; they, astonished by this doctrine, gave him their ear and accepted it, holding this man in high regard for his sanctity. 

Seeing that his design was proceeding according to his desire, he went further, proposing that **Abdelmon** was a person chosen by God, who through him wished to plant His holy **Furqanic** <note>original: "Alphurcaniste"; from 'Al-Furqan,' a title for the Quran meaning 'The Criterion'</note> law throughout the world. Because of this, **Abdelmon** was honored and respected as a being sent by God. It was then that **Almahadi** began to reveal himself and preach against the race of the **Almoravids** <note>term: Almoravids; a Berber imperial dynasty that preceded the Almohads</note>, calling them tyrants and usurpers, as they were the ones who had chased away the family of **Al-Abbas** <note>original: "Alabeci"; likely referring to the Abbasid lineage</note> and the blood of their Prophet **Muhammad**. Moving further, he attacked the person of the **Caliph of Baghdad** <note>original: "Baldac"</note>, the sovereign pontiff of their law, and spoke against the rest of the **Alphaquis** <term>Alphaquis; from the Arabic 'faqih,' meaning a jurist or expert in Islamic law</term> and ministers of their sect. In short, by claiming that **Abdelmon** was of the blood of **Muhammad**, he won over the majority of the nobility, in which he was strongly favored by **Ibn Thumert** with his predictions and astronomical charts. 

With such forces, this son of a potter made himself great and fought often against the sovereign King of **Africa** and the **Moors** of **Spain** <note>original: "Hespaigne"</note>. Thus the **African** state was divided into **Almoravids** and **Almohads** <note>original: "Almehades"</note>. It was necessary to recite this history in this place to clear up several doubts commonly found in the histories of **Africa** and **Spain**. The matter went so far that King **Abu Ali ibn Tashfin** <note>original: "Albo Aly Aben Tesfin"; referring to the Almoravid ruler Ali ibn Yusuf</note> being slain in battle, this noble potter **Abdelmon** was made King and **Miramolin** <term>Miramolin; a European corruption of 'Amir al-Mu'minin,' or Commander of the Faithful</term> of **Africa**. 

The heretical **Almohads** held the lordship and government of all, since the King was of their sect and had been advanced by them; this occurred in the year 1147. During these divisions, **Alfonso I**, the first King of **Portugal**, captured several places that the **Moors** held in **Lusitania** <note>The Roman name for the region comprising Portugal and parts of western Spain</note>, as did the Count of **Barcelona**, knowing well that it was good to fish in troubled waters. But **Abdelmon**, not content with **Africa** obeying him, also prepared to cross into **Europe** to subject the **Moors** of **Spain** who obeyed the **Almoravids**. However, it was **Almohadi** who made this journey, while **Thumert** stayed with the King, who by the diligence of this preacher was made monarch of the **Moors** of **Africa** and **Spain**. There, these **Almohads** began to use strange tyrannies and cruelties, as much against the **Christians** as against the **Muslims** who were not of their opinion. This was done by **Abdelmon**, who, forgetting his origins, used unbearable insolence toward the **Christians**, over whom he made great conquests. After these were put into effect, he returned victorious to **Africa**, where being settled, he established his seat...

And his obsequies were performed by the King with as much honor as if he had been the **Muslim** <note>original: "Mahometans"</note> Monarch himself; and his tomb has been honored and visited just as if it were the sepulcher of a holy man, everyone holding him for a Prophet, and the devil performing great illusions there. **Abdelmon** <note>Abd al-Mu'min</note>, the first **Almohad** King, upon his passing, had for his successor his son **Aben Jacob** <note>Abu Yaqub Yusuf, r. 1163–1184</note>, who, like his father, held the **Muslim** Kingdoms of **Africa** and **Spain**. He was succeeded by **Yusuf** his brother, surnamed **Mamezuth** or **Mazemuth** <note>referring to Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur</note>, who brought great damage to **Spain**, but was constrained to return to **Africa** because of the divisions and factions that were already beginning to rise there.
