->Of the Persian language.<-

## CHAPTER XLVIII.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'P' featuring floral and leaf motifs.</image-desc>
Plutarch in the *Life of Themistocles* and Valerius Maximus, book 8, chapter 7, make a great case and high esteem of the fact that this person, a Greek by nation named Themistocles, being a fugitive in the Kingdom of Persia, learned to speak the Persian language within one year. Agathias and Suidas wish to make us believe that in the memoirs of the ancients it is recorded that Chosroes <note>Khosrow I, the famous Sasanian "Immortal-Souled" king</note>, King of Persia, had the works of the philosophers Plato and Aristotle translated from the Greek language into his Persian language; this clearly demonstrates that this Persian language was, in the time of this great Greek Captain and the aforementioned King of Persia Chosroes, very different and dissimilar from the Greek language. Those who have diligently read the most ancient authors know very well that the Persians in former times during their monarchy—or Empire so great and flourishing, founded by the strength and valor of Cyrus the Great, and continued thereafter for many long years in all perfection, excellence, and prosperity until the last of their monarchs or Emperors named Darius, defeated by Alexander the Great, King of Macedonia—used the Chaldean or Assyrian language <note>The author is likely referring to Aramaic, which served as the administrative "lingua franca" of the Achaemenid Empire</note>, which was like their natural, maternal, and ordinary tongue in their speech and writing, common and familiar. Nevertheless, they made use—according to Herodotus in book 3 of his *Histories* and Esther chapters 1, 2, 3, and 8 in the Bible—in their State affairs, sometimes alongside their aforementioned language, of the Greek language, and sometimes other foreign languages toward their subjects and tributaries, according as they understood and spoke the aforementioned languages, as can be seen through several fine passages cited in the first book of <term>The Government of the Persian Kingdom <note>original Latin: *Regio Persarum principatu*, a 1591 work by Barnabé Brisson</note></term>. Furthermore, we find in ancient histories that Alexander the Great, having found the tomb of Cyrus, King of Persia, uncovered and ransacked, put to death the one who had done it. And having read the inscription which was in Persian letters and language, he wished for it to be also written in Greek letters and language below it, the substance of the inscription being such:

> *O man, whoever you are, and from wherever you come—for I am certain that you will come: I am Cyrus, he who won the Empire for the Persians; I pray you, do not begrudge me this small bit of earth that covers my poor body.*

Nicolas Chalcondyle <note>Laonikos Chalkokondyles, a 15th-century Byzantine historian</note> in book 3 of his history of the Turks: The Persians are called Arzaniens, inasmuch as all those who speak Arzanien are...

# Languages of this World.

Persians and [Turks] use the same language. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely continuing a thought from the previous page regarding the linguistic overlap in the region.</note> Bartholomaeus Georgievicz <note>A 16th-century Croatian writer who was captured by the Ottomans and wrote extensively about their culture</note>, who was for a long time a slave in Turkey, asserts in his travels that the Persian language of today is the same as the Scythian or Tartar <note>Historical terms used broadly for the peoples and languages of Central and Northern Asia</note> tongue. He says that the Persians and the Turks use Arabic letters and characters; the Persian language is the easiest of all the other languages of this world, and whoever knows and speaks it can make use of it throughout all the regions of Persia and Turkey, whether negotiating or conducting business with Persians, Turks, Greeks, Armenians, and Christians of whatever condition they may be, residing in these provinces and regions. The Turks use this language, but in an altered and corrupted form, which is clearly known through the usage of all the other languages. The courtiers of the Sophy <note>The Safavid Shah of Persia</note>, or King of Persia, most often speak the Slavonic or Slavic language in the court of their prince, even on the borders and marches of Slavonia. This same Georgievicz noted and taught some grammatical observations in this Persian language.

The great Cardinal of Cusa <note>Nicholas of Cusa, a 15th-century philosopher and mathematician</note>, in Book 1 of *The Sifting of the Alcoran*, Chapter 4, says: <note>original: "Lingua Persica, arabica lingua patens est."</note> *The Persian language is made evident through the Arabic language.* 

Theodore Bibliander <note>A Swiss Protestant linguist and scholar</note>, in his *Commentaries on the Common Reason of Languages and Letters*, speaks of it as follows: "I have found through my observations that the Persian language—or rather the Scythian or Tartar tongue, common to the Turks and also to the Tartars—has not only in its declension, composition, and conjugation of words, nouns, and verbs, but also in its structure and existence, firmly retained an analogy, much like the Greek or Latin languages. It even has its own peculiar and proper force or elegance, like the aforementioned Greek and Latin languages. And it is quite credible that the language which existed in former times among the Persians and the more ancient Medes (descendants of Shem the Patriarch) was very close to the Hebrew and Syriac languages. This is visibly demonstrated by the origins of both races and nations, and by the following words: *Gaza, Mandy, Chondy, Ginza, Maddo, Chad*, and infinite other words which are pure Hebrew and Syriac."

And let no one have any doubt in believing that the languages of the most ancient Persians and Medes were the same as, or similar and like, the Hebrew language, if he will carefully consider and relate the edicts and ordinances of the Kings of Persia, inserted at length in the Hebrew books of the Prophet Daniel, with the Hebrew words of that same Prophet. But the Persians who are in Persia today are descended from the Parthians, who came and proceeded from Scythia, as modern historians assert. The Persian language of today has great currency and vogue throughout the greater part of Asia, and has as much credit and reputation as the Latin language has throughout the West. This language has proceeded from the mixture and commingling of the Hebrew, Chaldean, Syriac, Saracen, Arabic, Turkish, Moorish, Tartar, and other languages used throughout all Asia. This is confirmed by Marco Polo the Venetian <note>The famous explorer</note> in Book 1, Chapter 13 of his travels in Tartary; Joseph Scaliger <note>A leading scholar of the Renaissance</note> in his book *On the Emendation of Time* in the chapter on the calendar of the Abyssinians; and Giovanni Antonio Menavino <note>An Italian who served in the Ottoman court</note> in Book 2, Chapters 10 and 19 of his travels, who writes that in the Turkish schools, in the third year, they teach the young children who study there from books written in this Persian language; which

Thevet <note>André Thevet, a 16th-century French Franciscan friar and cosmographer</note>, in Book 12, Chapter 3 of his *Universal Cosmography*, reports that the inhabitants of Great Java <note>The island of Java in modern-day Indonesia; Persian was a language of trade and Islamic scholarship across the Indian Ocean</note> use this Persian language, though in a somewhat corrupted form.

The histories of the Saracens <note>A term commonly used in the Renaissance to refer to Arab Muslims</note> record that as they expanded their Arabic language through Asia by force of arms, along with their religion and lordship, they caused the ancient Persian language and its letters to be lost. By order of their Caliphs, they had all the books written in that language burned, believing that as long as the Persians—who previously competed with the Greeks in arms and literature—possessed these books containing the natural sciences, the laws of the country, and ancient ceremonies, they could not be good Mohammedans <note>Followers of Islam</note>.

# On the Monarchy and Kings of the Persians.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'C' featuring stylized foliage and vine patterns within a square border.</image-desc>Those who have read Greek and Latin histories know well enough who the Monarchs and Kings of Persia were, of whom (following the ancient authors) F. de Belleforest <note>François de Belleforest, a prolific 16th-century French writer and historian</note> made ample mention in Volume 2, Book 3, Chapters 8, 9, and 10 of his *Universal Cosmography*, as did J. ...as written by Paolo Giovio <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552) was an Italian physician and historian known for his biographical works and histories of his own time.</note> in Book 5 of *Illustrious Men*, and Book 13 of his *Histories*; and by Henry Pernas in what he wrote concerning him to Cardinal Saulus. Some authors maintain that one should say **Xeque** <note>Sheikh</note>, not **Xa**; which is not true. For even though this word **Xeque** is a title of dignity, meaning an "elder" in the Arabic language, nevertheless one must say **Xa**, and not **Xeque**. This King is otherwise called **Saic** <note>Sheikh</note>, because this Ismael Sophy had with him, at the time of his conquests, soldiers so maddened by the opinion of his greatness that they esteemed him almost as a God; so much so that when at war they marched into combat without any weapons, saying they were going to die for their lord. And while fighting they cried, **Alla Siach Ismael, Alla Siach Ismael** <note>original: "Alla Siach Ismael" — meaning "God and Sheikh Ismael."</note>, that is to say, *God and Ismael*. In this name, the letters have been shifted and changed, placing the "A" before the "I," namely **Saich** instead of **Siach**. It is said that this Sophy was very displeased by this manner of acting, though he did not dare to say so for fear of offending those who held him in such great reverence.

Some Orientals have given another name to this Prince, namely **Seich Ayder** <note>Sheikh Haydar, who was actually Ismail's father, though the name was often applied to the lineage.</note>, which is to say, "good religious man"; the Turks call him **Patissahomos** <note>Padishah</note>, "Great King"; the Persians, his subjects, call him **Pharsic**, "Red Head" <note>original: "teste rouge" — a translation of the Turkish term *Kizilbash*, referring to the twelve-tasseled red hats worn by the Safavid loyalists.</note>, otherwise **Sahi**, **Soldan**, or **Sultan Zmail**, or **Suphy**, or **Sophy**. This last is a corrupted word that signifies nothing other than a sect, religion, or heresy, which the same Turks call **Sophy**, or **Sophylar** <note>Sufis</note>, and not—as Paolo Giovio wishes to make us believe in Book 13 of his *Histories*—"Interpreter of God" or "Wise Man."

I have read in certain modern travelers that some Asian peoples name him **Agemi**, **Chorasmi**, **Copsophery**, and **Tachas**, or **Tammas** <note>likely Shah Tahmasp I, Ismail's successor</note> or **Kezelbass**, because of his head-covering which is red, as well as **Muzauagea** and **Pharsic**, as I have already remarked above. Once this Ismael Sophy had made himself master or Lord of Persia and other surrounding provinces and regions, he desired that the part of Persia named Susiana by the ancients be called by his name **Xaic Ismael**. In this region is built the city of Baldac <note>Baghdad</note>, quite near to ancient Babylon; for while one is in Assyria and the other in Persia, they border each other. It once formed a separate Kingdom called Susa, built by King Darius, who succeeded Cambyses the first of that name, as is detailed in the ancient Greek histories according to André Thevet in Book 9, Chapter 12 of his *Universal Cosmography*.

### History of the Origins of the [Safavids]

...all those of the said race or lineage were called *Sophys* <note>The Safavids, from the Safaviyya Sufi order.</note>, who must live in poverty and in great abstinence from wine and all other meats <note>In this context, "meats" refers to food in general.</note>, and occupy themselves in continual vigils and prayers, though many of them hardly keep to this at present. Furthermore, the proper and true name of the said *Ismael* was, according to some, *Syach* <note>Shah</note>, in Latin *Sychinus*. The ancestors and father of the aforementioned *Sophy* were first Lords of a small region of Asia named *Arduel* <note>Ardabil, in modern-day Iranian Azerbaijan.</note>, because of which all the *Sophys* have been nicknamed *Arduelins*. They are also called *Nazery* by some, because their custom was to wear a cap or turban divided into twelve bands, for *Nazer* <note>The author likely means "Twelve" (Ithna 'Ashar), referring to the Twelve Imams of Shia Islam, though his linguistic attribution to Arabic is imprecise.</note> in the Arabic language signifies twelve. This cap or turban, because it is entirely red, is called *Kufelbass* <note>Qizilbash, meaning "Red-head" in Turkic languages, referring to the twelve-gored red cap worn by Safavid loyalists.</note>. Thus, the sect of the *Sophyans* has had various names and appellations for various causes and reasons, such that the King of Persia is sometimes named *Sophy*, *Syac*, *Ismael*, *Arduel*, *Kufelbass*, *Nazery*, and otherwise, according to the report of the author of the book *The Flowers of the Histories of the Orient* <note>original: "Fleurs de l'histoire d'Orient," a work by Hayton of Corycus (Hethum), a medieval Armenian historian.</note>, chapter 1.

Some modern travelers have assured me that the Persians are, in some places of the Orient, called *Alijs* and *Moalijs* <note>Followers of Ali ibn Abi Talib; the "Mawali" or "Mu'ali."</note>, because they hold to the sect of the aforementioned Prophet *Haly* <note>Ali, the cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad.</note>, as confirmed by *Oforius* <note>Jerónimo Osório (1506–1580), a Portuguese historian.</note> in book 10, chapter 3 of his histories, and by *García da Orta* in book 1, chapters 18 and 25 of his *History of Aromatics and Spices*.

Modern travelers and navigators assure us in their voyages and navigations that the King of *Decan* <note>The Deccan Plateau in India.</note> named *Nizamalucus* <note>Nizam-ul-Mulk, the title of the rulers of the Ahmednagar Sultanate.</note>, residing in the city of *Danager* <note>Ahmednagar.</note>, was not long ago the only one among all the other Kings of the East Indies who made profession of the religion and sect of the *Sophy*.

To give an ample and perfect satisfaction to readers regarding the true and assured knowledge of the origin and race of the said *Ismael Sophy* mentioned above, we will say that *Secaydar* <note>Sheikh Haydar (1459–1488), the father of Shah Ismail I.</note>, otherwise called *Saich* or *Siech Ismael*, was his father. In his life, he stirred up a new sect or heresy regarding the interpretation of the *Alcoran* <note>The Quran.</note>. For, being neither a King nor the son of a King—except that he was descended from the family and race of *Haly*, an ally of *Mahomet* <note>Muhammad</note>—and being a poor companion, yet desiring to aggrandize himself, he joined with some young *Moorish* boys whom he incited to the reformation of their sect. He made them go naked without care for shame, covering, or any wealth whatsoever, being dressed in the skins of goats and bears, decorated and masked, and appearing different from others in *Syria*, *Galatia*, and *Phrygia*. Thus they began to travel and make pilgrimages, living on nothing but the alms of good people, by whom they are still today prized and revered. This is because they go everywhere crying out and invoking the name not of *Mahomet*, like other *Turkish* and *Mahometan* beggars, but of *Haly*, whom they honor above all others. With this ruse and trickery, this fellow gathered a great mass of valiant young men. By means of these men, and under the pretext of his religion, he seized several lands and fortresses, plundering everything where he passed, yet without taking any of the loot for himself, which he distributed to his companions. He even refused the title of King, calling himself the "equitable distributor of goods," because he took from those who had much in order to provide for and enrich the poor. Thus, when he found a rich man who did no good with his wealth, he took it from him to distribute to the poor who lived as good people. Yet he did not strip the owners of everything, but rather left them as much as he saw their [needs] to be...

This Prince is not at present such a minor companion <note>Meaning he is a figure of great importance and power.</note>, for his Empire or Kingdom is great in the Orient, and he holds several large and rich Kingdoms, such as Persia, Media, Greater Armenia, a part of Mesopotamia, the Parthians, Hyrcanians, Turkestan, Desert Caramania, and the kingdom of Tarsus which is Fertile Caramania, and the land of Gujarat, which is in India, formerly called Gedrosia. Thevet in book 5, chapter 7 of his *Cosmography*. The greatest and most reliable part of modern travelers hold that this Emperor or Sophy King is richer, more powerful, and a greater landholder than the Grand Lord in Turkey, as is amply detailed by A. Without any other form of trial, they were condemned to death: some burned, others impaled. Even their wives, children, and families did not escape, but met the same fate. This is confirmed by André Thevet in book five, chapter seven of his *Universal Cosmography*, where he also mentions in the subsequent tenth book, chapter 13, a certain Persian Heretic named Azeleon, who invented during his life a certain Heresy entirely contrary to the Quran of Muhammad, the interpretation of Ali, and the Sophyen sect.

### Languages of this Universe.

Christians of the Levant, such as the Greeks, Georgians, Maronites, and Armenians, use and wear turbans striped with various colors; the Nubians or Ethiopians and Abyssinians, also Christians, wear azure or dark blue <note>original: *pers*, a blue-gray or indigo color</note> turbans; and the Jews all wear yellow ones. For to wear them entirely white belongs only to the Mohammedans, Turks, and Muslims, as confirmed by Pierre Belon in book 3, chapter 14 of his *Observations of Many Singularities in the Levant*. Furthermore, he says in the following chapter 25 that those Turks who claim to be of the lineage of their Prophet Muhammad wear the green turban, which can also be done by those who have been to Mecca twice. André Thevet, in book 6, chapter 5 of his *Cosmography*, mentions these turbans and says they are called *Yeshil bashi* in the Arabic language, and that they are part of the ancient headwear of the Scythians, from whom the Turks are descended. ## Concerning the Magi of Persia.

### CHAPTER XLIX.

<image-desc>Decorative ornamental initial 'L' featuring intertwining vine and floral motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>
Magic was in ancient times held in great esteem and recommendation among the Persians, because it contained within itself the three greatest and most commendable sciences of this Universe: namely, Religion, Medicine, and Astrology. Pliny recognizes three types of this magic: namely, the Persian, the Jewish, and the Greek. He says that Zoroaster, King of the Bactrians—otherwise known as Zarade—who flourished six thousand years before Plato, was the author of the Persian type, having learned it from one Agonaces, who lived 500 years before the Trojan War and who had composed infinite millions of verses on it during his life. Of this rank or number were Apuscorus and Zaratus the Medes, Marmaridus the Babylonian, Hippocus the Arabian, and Zarmogenidas the Assyrian, of whom we have no writings. Moses, Jannes, and Jotape, who were Jews living several thousand years after the aforementioned Zoroaster, were the authors of Jewish Magic according to the words of the same Pliny. Regarding this, in 2 Timothy 3, mention is made of Jannes and Mamrees <note>traditionally Jannes and Jambres</note>, magicians of King Pharaoh who resisted Moses; this is repeated in the Hebrew book *Gemara* <note>a component of the Talmud</note> in the chapter *Kol Korbanot Ha-Tzibur* <note>original Hebrew: "All the Public Offerings"</note> and by Rabbi Nathan.

...in the *Baal Arukh* <note>original: "Baal Haruc," referring to the *Arukh*, a famous 11th-century Talmudic lexicon by Nathan ben Jehiel</note>. Ancient Greek Magic was announced by the Greek poet Homer through the fables of Circe, Proteus, and the Sirens. The more recent form, called "Cyprian," was first brought to Greece by Hostanes the Persian, who accompanied King Xerxes on his expedition into the said Greece. Since that time, Democritus, Plato, Pythagoras, Empedocles, and countless other ancient Greek philosophers abandoned their own countries to go to Persia and India to learn this Magic. A second Hostanes, the second of that name in the following of Alexander the Great, greatly illustrated this magic and communicated it throughout the world. The Romans used it for a long time, as did our ancient Gauls by means of their Druids, so called <gloss>from the oaks</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῶν δρυῶν (*apo ton dryon*), reflecting the belief that the word "Druid" derives from the Greek word for oak</note>, forests, and oak trees which they inhabited, according to the testimony of Pliny, Book 16, Chapter 44. The ancient Britons were so great and excellent in this art that they seemed to have taught it to the Persians rather than having learned it from them, as the aforementioned Pliny asserts in Book 30, Chapter 1. The Hebrews speak of it quite differently, holding that Mizraim, son of Ham <note>the Biblical son of Noah; "Mizraim" is also the Hebrew name for Egypt</note>, was the inventor of this Magic, from whom the priests of the Egyptians, Babylonians, and Persians learned it, as confirmed by Saint Clement, a disciple of the Apostles, in Book 4 of his *Recognitions*. The author of the *Ecclesiastical History*, interpreting Chapter 39 of Genesis on this subject, said:

> Ninus conquered Ham, who was still living and reigning in Bactria or in Thrace, as others will have it, and he was called Zoroaster, the inventor of the magic art, who wrote both this and the seven liberal arts on fourteen columns: seven of bronze and seven of brick against the double destruction of the world that was feared—one by water, the other by fire. Ninus, however, burned his books; from this, also, Idols arose. <note>original Latin: "Ninus vicit Cham qui adhuc viuebat..."</note>

This Zoroaster mentioned above, the inventor of this Magic, wrote a hundred thousand verses about it in his time, which one Hermippus illustrated with commentaries, according to Pliny, Book 30, Chapter 1, cited above; Justin, Book 1; Raphael Volaterranus, Book 20, Chapter 4; Orosius, Book 1, Chapter 4; and Otto of Freising, Book 1, Chapter 6.

Some wish for him to be the same as the Mizraim, son of Ham, mentioned above; others say he was another, and that he flourished more than eighty years before the Trojan War, in the time of Abraham. Suidas <note>referring to the *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek historical encyclopedia</note> writes that he had composed four books on the nature of precious stones and five on predictions through the inspection of the stars. This man, according to Clement in his *Itinerary*, wishing to be reputed as a God and being greatly devoted to the science of the stars, drew sparks of fire from them by magic to lead the common people to honor and adore him. But in the end, continuing his feats, he was burned by the demon whom he invoked too importunately for this purpose—though his disciples maintained that he had been, as one beloved by God, carried up to heaven in a chariot of fire and flames. Because of this, after his death, he was surnamed <term>Zoroaster</term>, <gloss>as if a living star</gloss> <note>original Latin gloss: *quasi viuens astrum*</note>. He lived in the time of Ninus, with whom he waged war; during his life, he predicted to the Assyrians that as long as they kept his ashes, their monarchy would not be ruined or overthrown. Some years ago, one Jean Opsopæus <note>Johannes Opsopæus, a German scholar and physician who edited the "Sibylline Oracles"</note> had a certain Greek book printed in Paris in the year 1599...

In addition to these, I will bring forward this testimony from Abbot Serenus, found in Cassian’s *Conferences*, book 8, chapter 21:

<note>The following is a translation of the Latin passage from John Cassian, an early Christian monk and theologian.</note>

The knowledge of all celestial and sublime things, which Adam had received from God, he passed on to his son Seth. Seth's descendants kept this knowledge untainted, and as long as they remained separate from the sacrilegious lineage of Cain, they practiced this doctrine for the worship of God and for the benefit of common life. However, when they became mixed with that impious generation, they diverted what they had piously learned toward profane and harmful things through the prompting of the Devil; from this, they boldly established the curious arts of sorcery, illusions, and magical superstitions. But as for how this curious and wicked doctrine did not perish in the Great Flood, the cause was Ham <note>original: "Cham"</note>—as ancient traditions report—who was infected by these superstitions and sacrilegious arts. Because he did not dare to bring these arts into the Ark, into which he was to enter with his most righteous father Noah and his holy brothers, he engraved them on plates of various metals which would not be destroyed by the corruption of the waters, and on very hard stones which would not feel the force of fire. After the Flood was over, seeking them out with the same curiosity with which he had hidden them, he transmitted this nursery of sacrilege and perpetual wickedness to his descendants. In this way, therefore, that common opinion—in which it is believed that Angels handed down either sorcery or various arts to men—is fulfilled in truth.

Lactantius, in the second book of his *Divine Institutions*, and Saint Cyprian, in his book *On the Vanity of Idols*, attribute the invention of this Magic to the devil and to evil spirits. Pliny, cited above in Book 30, Chapter 2, recognizes several kinds or species of it, taught in former times by Hostanes, a Prince and doctor of this art. Iamblichus in his *Book of the Egyptian Mysteries*, Proclus in his book *On Sacrifice and Magic*, and Porphyry in his book *On Sacrifices*, identify two types: namely <term>Theurgy</term> <note>literally "god-working"; considered a "high" or "white" magic intended to invoke divine presence</note>, which is the good and laudable Magic; the other is <term>Goetia</term> <note>sorcery or "low" magic</note>, and <term>Necromancy</term> <note>divination through communication with the dead</note>, which is wicked and damnable. Suidas divides it into Goetia and <term>Pharmacy</term> <note>original: "Pharmacie"; here meaning the use of drugs or poisons for magical effects</note>. Hugh of Saint Victor, in Book 6, Chapter 5 of his *Didascalicon* <note>original: "erudition didascalique"</note>, wrote these words which are worthy of being recited in full in this present chapter:

<note>The following is a translation of the Latin passage from the medieval scholar Hugh of Saint Victor.</note>

Zoroaster, King of the Bactrians, is believed to be the first discoverer of Magic; some assert that he is Ham the son of Noah, but with a changed name. Later, Ninus, the King of the Assyrians, killed him after defeating him in war, and caused his books, which were full of the arts of sorcery, to be burned by fire. Aristotle, however, writes of this same man that his books on the magic art, dictated by him, reached as many as two million verses, which were handed down to the memory of posterity. This art was later expanded by Democritus, at the time when Hippocrates was held in high regard in the art of medicine. Magic is not accepted within Philosophy, but is an external thing of false profession; she is the mistress of all iniquity and malice, lying about the truth, and truly wounding souls...

# Languages of this Universe

...it seduces from divine religion, persuades the worship of demons, instills the corruption of morals, and impels the minds of its followers to every crime and wickedness. This subject, taken generally, embraces five kinds of <term>maleficium</term> <note>evil-doing or sorcery</note>: **Mantice** (which signifies divination and vain mathematics), **Sortilegia** (divination by lots), **Maleficia** (sorceries), and **Præstigiæ** (illusions). **Mantice**, however, contains five species within itself.

The first is **Necromancy**, which is interpreted as divination among the dead <note>original: "νεκρὸς" (nekros) in Greek is "dead" in Latin, and "νεκρὸν" (nekron) is called a "corpse"</note>; from this comes the divination performed through the sacrifice of human blood, for which demons thirst and in which they delight when it is poured out. The second is **Geomancy**, that is, divination by earth. The third is **Hydromancy**, that is, divination by water. The fourth is **Aeromancy**, that is, divination by air. The fifth is divination by fire, which is called **Pyromancy**. For Varro <note>a prolific Roman scholar, 116–27 BC</note> said there were four elements in which divination consisted: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire. Therefore, the first, Necromancy, seems to pertain to the underworld; the second to the Earth; the third to Water; the fourth to Air; and the fifth to Fire.

**Mathematics** <note>here referring to the "forbidden" calculation of fates</note> is divided into three species: **Haruspicina**, **Augury**, and the doctrine of **Horoscopes**, which they call **Horospica**. They are called <term>Haruspices</term> as if they were *Horuspices*—that is, observers of the hours <note>original: "horarum inspectores"</note> who watch the times for doing things—or *Haruspices* as if they were inspectors of the *hara* <note>a pen or enclosure for sacrificial animals</note>, who consider the future in the entrails and fibers of sacrifices. 

**Augury** or **Auspicium** sometimes pertains to the eye, and is called *auspicium* (as if it were *auispicium*) because it is observed in the movement and flight of birds <note>original: "auium"</note>. Sometimes it pertains to the ears, and is then called *augurium* (as if it were the "chatter of the ears" <note>original: "garritus aurium"</note>) because it is perceived by the ear. 

**Horoscopy**, which is also called **Constellation**, is when the deeds of men are sought in the stars, just as the <term>Genethliaci</term> <note>from the Greek word for "birthday," those who cast nativities</note> do, who observe births; these were formerly called **Magi** specifically, about whom we read in the Gospel.

**Sortilegi** <note>fortune-tellers</note> are those who seek divinations by lots. **Malefici** <note>sorcerers</note> are those who, through demonic incantations, bindings <note>original: "ligaturas," referring to magical knots or amulets</note>, or other execrable types of remedies, perform wicked things with the cooperation and instinct of demons. **Præstigiæ** <note>illusions</note> occur when, through phantastic delusions regarding the change of things, human senses are mocked by demonic art. 

There are, therefore, eleven types in total. Under **Mantice**, five: Necromancy, Geomancy, Hydromancy, Aeromancy, and Pyromancy. Under **Mathematics**, three: Haruspicina, Augury, and Horoscopy. Finally, three others: **Sortilegium**, **Maleficium**, and **Præstigiæ**. It is said that Mercury first invented illusions; the Phrygians invented Augury; Tages, the first Etruscan, handed down Haruspicina and Divination by lots. Hydromancy first came from the Persians.

One is infamous and ill-omened due to commerce with unclean spirits. The other, if you explore it more thoughtfully, is almost nothing other than the pinnacle of natural philosophy." The Greeks do not greatly call that former one Magic, but **Goetia** <note>low magic or witchcraft</note>, marked by incantations and songs composed by the art of wicked curiosity; they even dare to call it by the more honorable name of **Theurgy** <note>high magic or "divine work"</note>. ...as they are commonly called. For they say that among these is properly found <term>Goetia</term> <note>original: "Goetiam"; a term for black magic or sorcery involving the invocation of spirits</note>, about which books are composed of what the legal expert Ulpian <note>a famous Roman jurist, c. 170–223 AD</note> calls "prohibited reading," and he decreed they should be immediately destroyed, etc.

**Julius Caesar Scaliger** <note>a celebrated Italian scholar and physician, 1484–1558</note> in his *Exoteric Exercises* against **Girolamo Cardan’s** <note>an Italian polymath known for mathematics and astrology</note> *On Subtlety*, section 327:

**Magic is threefold**: The first is the lowest, and truly our own, foul and filthy, involving little chants, corpses, and the ropes used for those who were hanged; anyone who dares to handle such things deserves punishment. The second draws powers from the stars into mirrors, seals, rings, and tablets. The third is **divine**. A mass of imposters has made the name hateful among the common people. But the word "Magus" among the Persians means nothing other than a "wise man"; however, because of the treachery and perfidy of Smerdis <note>a pretender to the Persian throne who was a Magus; his usurping of the throne led to a massacre of the Magi</note>, the name of the Magi was made hateful for a long time. The Magi, who set out from very distant regions to worship Him, recognized through this Magic that the Lord Jesus was the promised King. We have described these things from the books of the Syrians: they say that the powers, paths, and ends of Magic and the "transmutatory art" <note>alchemy</note> are very similar. The work and goal of the **Chemists** <note>alchemists</note> is body into body; the work and goal of Magic is spirit into body. The Magi call their influences "violences" because they exercise their powers beyond those that appear to happen by the order of nature; the Chemists call their work "fortitude" <note>or "strength"</note>: for this is the meaning of that much-celebrated **Elixir**, in whose faith they pledge all of nature.

The greater part of modern authors divide this Magic into **natural** and **non-natural**, the latter of which uses and employs the invocation of demons and evil spirits, as Benito Pereira <note>a Spanish Jesuit theologian, 1535–1610</note> amply explains in his *Treatise on Magic*. A certain modern author, in his 7th book, chapter 8, of the *Syntax of the Admirable Art*, has written the following words:

The name of **Magic** in the Persian language expresses only wisdom and the peak of philosophical perfection: for the Magi among the Persians are the same as the Philosophers among the Greeks, the **Brahmins** and **Gymnosophists** <note>literally "naked philosophers," a group of ancient Indian philosophers</note> among the Indians, the **Druids**, **Bards**, and **Semnothei** <note>ancient Celtic priests or theologians</note> among the Gauls, the **Galertæ** among the Sicilians, the Priests among the Egyptians, the **Etruscan Haruspices** <note>diviners who read entrails</note> among the Italians, the Wise Men among the Latins, the Prophets among the Cabalists, and the **Chaldeans** among the Babylonians and Assyrians. 

But as almost all things that began with very healthy origins have degenerated too far, and some disciples have wandered from the pure and spotless institutions of the Magi and Wise Men—and sometimes being curious beyond measure, or through some affected superstition of knowing, crossing the boundaries of true wisdom—they have fallen into those vain observations of forbidden Magic. And thus the celebrated name of Magic was defiled into hatred: a title previously signifying honor and excellence was turned into disgrace, as **Pliny** teaches in book 30, chapter 1. It is clear, therefore, that Magic is loathed because of its abuse; but insofar as it is contained within its own rules, it is the knowledge of excellent divine and human things, or natural things. One kind is upright—namely, **natural and divine**—the other is improper—namely, **demonic**, born from the abuse of natural things. 

**Natural magic** is that which depends on the natures of things (not known to all, but to the more learned and skilled), operating through either the whole substance of a compound or a certain mixture of others to produce wonderful effects: it is the culmination of physical philosophy and appears like a miracle to the common people. Therefore, this [natural magic] receives its effects from nature and the power of the heavens, stars, elements, animals, metals, [plants...] <note>The text ends mid-word with the catchword "tarum," likely completing "plantarum" or plants on the following page.</note>

Whether it be divinatory, which predicts the future and effects depending on natural causes; or operational, which exhibits wonders to those ignorant of the causes and powers of things. Divine Wisdom or magic, which consists in the virtue, name, and power of God, and not in natural things—such as when the Prophets predict things to come, or when Christians perform miracles in that way, either by faith or prayer. From this comes the true *Kabbalah* <note>original: "Cabala"</note>, which, though defiled by the superstition of the Rabbis, was composed of the names of Almighty God, either expressed in the sacred pages, extracted by some art, or received by hand from holy men. 

Wicked and demonic, vain and superstitious magic is that which is called *Theurgy* <note>sacramental magic intended to invoke spirits or gods</note> and *Goetia* <note>sorcery or "low" magic</note>; and it is either simple, consisting of the invocation and operation of demons; or composite, namely with some added pretense of a certain natural virtue, or with the color of true religion interposed, so that the unwary may be deceived under its pretext—and for the most part, that composite magic deceives with a semblance of right. 

Therefore, composite magic most vainly uses invocations of demons, or silent pacts with them, which is a great abomination to a Christian man; and to hide its frauds, it adds something from the four elements: either from the earth, whence *Geomancy*; or water, whence *Hydromancy*; or *Air*, whence *Aeromancy*; or fire, whence *Pyromancy*. It misuses men, once ordering them to be sacrificed so that entrails might be inspected. It also misuses men as instruments of its impiety, the demon bringing forth oracles through them via the mouth, the chest, the navel, or the genitals, as *Plutarch* writes in *The Obsolescence of Oracles*, *Iamblichus* in *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*, *Origen* in book 7 *Against Celsus*, *Eustathius* on the 2nd book of the *Iliad*, St. *Chrysostom* in homily 9 on the *Epistle to the Corinthians*, and *Caelius Rhodiginus* in book 4, chapter 10. 

Magic also scrutinizes the lines in the hand, from which was born *Chiromancy* <note>palm reading</note>, or the sections and proportions of the face—which, if they do not exceed the bodily temperaments, are not entirely disapproved—this they call *Physiognomy*. It also misuses animals, when it tries to persuade of the knowledge of the future from the chattering of birds: this they called *Augury*, as *Cicero* says in book 2 of *On Divination*. Or when it divines through the inspection of the same, whence *Haruspicy*. <term>Bird-divination</term> <note>original: "οιωνοσκοπία" (oionoskopia)</note> was the invention of Tiresias, according to *Pliny* book 7, chapter 56. Or when it orders the feeding, singing, or flight of birds to be observed, as if there were divinity or knowledge of the future in them, when in fact the birds know neither themselves nor their own futures. I would say the same of other animals that are observed. 

It likewise accommodates plants to its infamy, as *Pliny* says in book 24, chapter 17; stones and metals too, whence <term>basin-divination</term> <note>original: "λεκανομαντια" (lekanomanteia)</note>, which is done with basins full of water after invoking a demon: *Strabo* in book 15 testifies to this Magic among the Persians. There is also <term>mirror-divination</term> <note>original: "κατοπτρομαντία" (katoptromanteia)</note> which is done through mirrors, and <term>axe-divination</term> <note>original: "αξινομαντία" (axinomanteia)</note>, which is done by axes and other iron instruments, whether they are tied to a sieve—from which comes <term>sieve-divination</term> <note>original: "κοσκινομαντία" (koskinomanteia)</note>—or whether a nail is tied to the Psalms, or if someone misuses metals in another way. 

Horrendous also is that which thinks to disturb and call forth the spirits of the dead and the deceased, called <term>necromancy</term> <note>original: "νεκρομαντία" (nekromanteia)</note>, which involves conversations with demons; for which use the superstitious and most vain man transfers characters, fumigations, and ecclesiastical prayers, and the most wicked abuse of the sacraments occurs. And in short, there is nothing holy that the Magician does not usurp and pollute; and therefore, in Magic, there is frequent abuse—I will not say use—of demons, sorceries, eye-salves <note>ointments used to see spirits</note>, ointments, potions, love charms, bindings, suspensions, rings, images, characters...

...plates, papers, specific numbers, the sounds of sacrifices, purifications, solitudes, lots, bindings, fascinations, thoughts or imaginations, mental ecstasy, incantations, wonders, exorcisms, consecrations, devotions, fasts, dreams, prayers, ceremonies, and celestial conjunctions.

**Otto Heurnius** <note>a Dutch physician and philosopher, 1577–1648</note>, a very modern author, in the 28th chapter of his *Indian* work, treatise 6, regarding *Asiatic Magic* and its author **Zoroaster** or **Zarades** the Persian, speaks of it in these words: 

> Magic is threefold. The first is the lowest and our own: truly foul and filthy, involving charms, corpses, and the ropes of the hanged; if anyone should dare to touch these, they would even deserve death. The middle type draws power from the stars into mirrors, seals, rings, and tablets. The third is divine, through which the works of nature are seen more clearly; because it is honorable and desirable, it was cultivated not only by the common people but even by the greatest Kings of Kings, especially those of Persia, who were so curious about it that they did not dare aspire to the governance of the kingdom unless they were steeped in its core. 

However, the supreme dictator of Physicians, **Hippocrates**, shows by this ray of reason that those other two species of Magic are by no means arts. Every craftsman masters his instrument, but the Magician does not master his instrument, since it is more powerful than himself—namely, the devil, a spirit of the greatest power. Therefore, the Magician is not a craftsman, nor is Magic an art. For what the common people believe—that one imbued with Magic can harm another with words—is a trifle. For who taught him those words? Was it another man, and who taught him? It was not celestial intelligence, for who would dare make such an intelligence the author of a curse <note>original: "fascini"</note>? Therefore, it was an evil demon. He did this not to make the man more powerful, but to deceive him through his own belief, and to have him as a companion in both impiety and eternal exile. Thus the demon himself acts, while that foolish and senseless man thinks he acts by his own words. In the same way, the fibers of livers and hearts were once turned, placed beneath, mutilated, or removed by that same demon, who had persuaded those wretched people through his oracles that such sacrifices should be performed. **Zoroaster**, or **Zarades** the Persian, was the first to outstandingly cultivate this filthy imposture. For he, according to **Berosus the Babylonian** and **Athercles** in their commentaries on the affairs of the **Assyrians** and **Medes**, was gifted by nature with excellent talent, but driven by a detestable spirit, he changed the divine and human rites of the ancient Persians.

For the ancient Persians worshiped **Belus** (or **Jupiter**), **Sandes** (or **Hercules**), and **Anaitis** (or **Veneris** <note>the goddess Anahita, equated here with Venus</note>). Their descendants, however, in their divine worship, almost agreed with the **Manichaeans**. For they established two principles: one indeed good, producing all the best things from itself, which they called **Hormisdates** <note>Ahura Mazda</note>, or **Oromazen**, or **Oromagdam**; they asserted that his body was most like light, and his soul most like truth. The other principle was evil, the fountain and spring of all adversities, which they named **Arimamen** <note>Ahriman</note>. They also celebrated a great festival which they called the "removal of evils," in which they killed many snakes and whatever other animals live in deserted places, offering them to the **Magi** <note>the priestly caste of ancient Persia</note> as a proof of their impiety. For by that reasoning, they believed they had performed a good and pleasing work for **Hormisdates**, but an unpleasing one for **Arimamen**. They especially worshiped water, so much so that they would not wash their faces with it, nor touch it for any reason except for drinking or washing. They considered fire to be worthy of the highest honor and most holy. For this reason, the Magi kept it perpetually in certain sacred and hidden shrines, and looking into it, they performed secret rites and gave answers concerning future events. A shameful ritual of burial was also [introduced] by this...

...emanated from Zoroaster. For he, among other impious and horrifying doctrines, taught that it was lawful and consistent with the laws of nature for a brother to be joined with a sister, a father with a daughter, a grandfather with a granddaughter, and—what is most wicked (O laws, O nature!)—a son with his mother. The two great lights of Roman poetry, Catullus and Lucan, sang clearly of these rites, exposing them. Catullus wrote:

> For a Magus <note>a priest or practitioner of Persian magic</note> must be born from a mother and a son,
> If the impious religion of the Persians is true. 
> <note>original: "Nam Magus ex matre & gnato nascatur oportet, Si vera est Persarum impia religio."</note>

<margin>Lucan, Book 2</margin>
> ...Sisters have joyfully entered 
> The bedchambers of brothers, and the sacred pledges of mothers. 
> The unhappy tale of Oedipus’s Thebes condemns 
> Among nations a crime committed unknowingly;
> Yet as often as a Lord of the Parthians, an Arsacid <note>a member of the ruling dynasty of the Parthian Empire</note>, 
> Is born from such mixed blood, it is lawful for him to fulfill the role of a parent: 
> What should I believe to be a sin?
> <note>original: "Iuvere sorores In fratrum thalamos... Quid rear esse nefas?" Lucan here contrasts the Greek tragedy of Oedipus, who sinned in ignorance, with the Persians, who allegedly practiced incest by law.</note>

Hence, the Great Mother herself, Earth, the nourisher of all, fled from such foul and horrifying monsters, and (stirred by the holy God to vengeance) could by no means endure to receive their corpses into her peaceful womb. To cover this disgrace with a veil of piety, Zoroaster taught a most "holy" rite of burial: that the dead should not be enclosed in the bowels of the earth, nor consumed by fire, but cast out into the fields to be dissolved by the air—by whose benefit life is sustained for many ages—or to be torn apart and consumed by birds, which you often nourished with your own body while you lived.

From this, all Persians would immediately carry out the body of the deceased, and having transported it outside the town, they would expose it alone and naked to be devoured by dogs and obscene birds. In this manner, once the flesh was consumed, the bare bones lay scattered and rotting across the fields. Furthermore, if the birds did not immediately fly to a corpse, or if dogs did not run to tear it apart on the spot, they believed that the man's character had been impure, his soul unjust, worthy of the abyss, and dedicated to an evil demon. 

Then, with the greatest sorrow, his friends would mourn him as one utterly dead, having no part in any better fate. But he who was most quickly devoured they proclaimed most happy; they regarded his soul with great admiration as being most excellent, most like to God, and destined to fly to the blessed seats. 

Among the common and more obscure crowds, if anyone in the army was overtaken by an acute disease, they were led out while still breathing and sound of mind. A piece of bread, a jar of water, and a staff were placed beside them, so that as long as they could use food, they would not lack it; and with the staff, they might ward off and drive away attacking wild beasts and scavengers while they still possessed some strength. 

But if they had not yet died, yet the force of the disease had overcome them so that they could no longer move their hands, then the miserable half-dead souls, just beginning to breathe their last, were most cruelly devoured, deprived of all sweet hope of enjoying the vital air. Many, however, having recovered, would return home as if in a scene from a play or a tragedy—returned from the dark gates of the underworld, thin, pale, and terrifying to those they met. If anyone returned in such a state, everyone would turn away from him and flee as if from one marked, still dwelling among those beneath the earth. Nor were they permitted to resume their former way of life until the sacrifice for their expected death had been expiated by the Magi, and life [was restored...]

### History of the Origin of the [Magi]

...as if granted once again. A remarkable event also occurred to certain Philosophers returning from Persia to Rome (during the reign of Chosroes <note>Likely Khosrow I, a powerful Sassanid king</note>, the most powerful King of the Persians), which revealed the reason for this foul burial rite. For when they were resting in what was once Persian territory, they caught sight of the corpse of a dead man, neglected and cast aside without burial. Pitying the injustice of that barbaric law, and judging it by no means right to ignore nature being thus wronged, they covered the corpse as best they could through their servants and buried it, heaping up the earth. 

However, on the following night, while everyone was sleeping, one of them—I truly do not know which one, for I do not know his name—seemed to see an old man. This man was entirely unknown to him but appeared grave and venerable, displaying his devotion to Philosophy both by the style of his clothing and by his long, flowing beard. This figure cried out to him, as if exhorting and commanding:

> Do not leave the unburied and naked corpse in the mounds 
> To be torn by dogs, and to be food for the birds. 
> For Mother Earth, the nurturer of all, does not receive him 
> Who dared to defile his mother by a wicked deed.
> <note>original: "Ne tumulis inhumatum ac nudum linque cadauer / Dilacerare canes, escaque volucribus esse. / Mater enim Tellus cunctorum non suscipit illum / Qui matrem est ausus facto vitiare nefando."</note>

The philosopher, immediately awakened by fear, reported his dream to the others; at first, they were uncertain what the dream might portend. But when they rose at dawn and continued their intended journey, passing through that same field (as the layout of the land required) where they had provided the hasty burial, they found the corpse naked once again, lying on top of the mound, as if the earth, indignant and acting of its own accord, had vomited it back up in disgust. Struck by the wonder of this spectacle, they continued their journey, performing no further final rites for the body. Weighing the dream, they finally reached the conclusion that the Persians suffer this punishment and vengeance because of their shameful unions with their own mothers. 

The successors of this Zoroaster embraced these general doctrines: that the Gods are not to be represented by any image, and that those who assign the distinction of sex to them sin most grievously. For this reason, Xerxes burned all the temples of Greece, deeming it a localized crime for the Gods to be represented by images or confined within the narrow limits of walls. They asserted that the air teems with demons <note>or spirits</note>, which work their way into our eyes like miasmas <note>spiritual pollutions or contagions</note>. They wore white clothing; their bed was the ground; their food consisted of vegetables, bread, and cheese, which they would place in their mouths after fixing it to the tip of a reed staff. 

They were possessed by a supreme devotion to divinations and excelled in them greatly. Hence, when the Parthian throne was vacant and the queen was pregnant (though she was still in the first months of conception), they were consulted by the nobles of the empire to declare whether the Queen was carrying a male or a female. First, so that their responses might be more certain, they brought in a mare near to giving birth and pronounced the sex of her offspring; then they affirmed that the Queen was carrying male progeny. The Princes of the empire, placing faith in this word, placed the *cidaris* <note>a Persian royal headdress or tiara</note> upon the Queen's womb, declared the embryo to be King, and distinguished him with a name. And so Sapor <note>Shapur II, the "Embryo King"</note> was born a few months later already possessing the Kingdom, in which he grew up and grew old, his life being extended to seventy years. 

Furthermore, those Magi who were in the company of the Parthian ambassadors to Sulla <note>the Roman general and dictator</note> responded (from the marks on his body) that his life and memory would be celebrated, as Velleius Paterculus says in Book 3. These same men, when Artaxerxes had been removed from human affairs and his son Ochus took up the reins of the Kingdom, the Eunu-

### On the Region of the Tartars.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated drop cap 'A' featuring architectural elements and floral motifs.</image-desc>

ABRAHAM Ortelius in his *Geographical Synonyms and Treasury* [writes]: The Scythians are called *Sagae* by the Persians, as Mela has it, or *Acae* as Pliny, Solinus, and Eustathius write. Scythia Saga appears in the *Origins* of Cato, which are in circulation. The same Pliny relates that they were called Aramaeans in ancient times, and first <term>Nomaeans</term><note>original: "νομαῖοι", referring to nomadic herdsmen</note>, as Stephanus adds. Josephus relates they were called <term>Magogites</term> after Magog <note>A biblical figure often associated with northern tribes</note>. Tzetzes in his eleventh *Chiliad* reports that the Abasgians, Alans, Sacae, Dacians, Rhos <note>original: "ῥῶς"</note>, Sauromatians, and all the Peoples of the Northern regions are called by the common name Scythians. The same author, in *Chiliad* 8, number 224, divides the Scythian nations into three: the Maeotians, Caucasians, and Oxians. Read the history of the Scythians in Nicephorus Gregoras, who says they were called Cimmerians by Homer, Cimbri and Teutons by Plutarch, and others call them differently—such as the <term>Melanchlaeni</term><note>Literally "Black-cloaks"</note>, Massagetae, Sarmatians, etc.—according to the vicissitudes of time and their migrations.

[He] says they are named after those things done by them. John Curopalates <note>John Skylitzes, a high-ranking Byzantine official and historian</note>, Zonaras, and Michael Glycas call them Patzinacs <note>original: πατζινακοὶ; referring to the Pechenegs, a nomadic Turkic people</note>, who also number the most noble Usica nation among them. Liutprand of Cremona <note>A 10th-century bishop and diplomat</note> calls them Pizenacs, and Regino calls them Pezinats—perhaps due to a clerical error, which writers easily commit with names they do not understand. There is a similar inconsistency regarding this word in Greek manuscripts. Suidas <note>The author of a massive 10th-century Greek encyclopedic lexicon</note> is also an authority stating that in his time they bore the name Patzinacitæ; and Chalcocondylas indicates those Sachateans were called Ghrutingi and Dagi, who are European Scythians.

The Albans are from the race of Scythians called the "wagon-dwellers" <note>original: Hamaxobij</note>, says Evagrius Scholasticus. Nicephorus Callistus also mentions them. Today, however, as Herberstein <note>Siegmund von Herberstein, a diplomat famous for his descriptions of Russia</note> testifies, they are called Tartars by foreigners, but they call themselves Berfermans or Befermans <note>Likely a corruption of 'Mussulmans' or Muslims</note>. Marius Niger claims they call themselves "Diss" in their own language; according to André Thevet, they are called *Ator Albacara* by the Arabs. These are the Scythian nations according to Herodotus: the Auchatæ, Arpoxæ, Catiari, Traspies, and Paralatæ; he adds that the name for all of them is the Scoloti <note>original: σκολοτίς</note>. Many others are listed by Pliny, such as the Alani, Amordi, Apeilæi, Aotsi, Antariani, Arimaspi (who were previously the Cacidiri), Ariacæ, Aroteres, Assæi, Camæ, Camacæ, Cotieri, Daci, Dahæ, Edones, Effedones, Euchalæ, Hiti, Getae, Hamaxobij, Massagetæ, Napai, Oetei, Pesici, Roxolani, Rhymnigi, Sacæ, Sarmatians, and Satarchi. Trebellius Pollio, in his *Life of Emperor Claudius*, also includes these peoples of Scythia: the Peucini, Trutungi, Ostrogoths, Virtingui, and Sigipedes. In the lexicon of Stephanus of Byzantium, we read these: the Apstilas (who are peoples of Colchis in Arrian’s *Circumnavigation of the Black Sea*), Budini, Daias, Dasas, Heluri, Evergetas, Edi, Iamas, Iamos, Bechir, Iseri, Lazi (also in Colchis according to Arrian), Matycetæ, Mæotians, Myrgetæ, Parthyæi, Sannigas (also of Colchis, near Sevastopol, according to Arrian), and Tyrmemenii. Mela places some of them as Nomads.

Likewise, Suidas says they are called "wagon-carriers" <note>original: Hamaxophoretos</note>. Pliny complains of the inconsistency of authors in describing them because, as he adds, the tribes are innumerable—so much so that their name (as he says elsewhere) passes everywhere into the Sarmatians and Germans. Strabo writes in Book 1 that all known regions toward the North were formerly called by one name, either Scythians or, as by Homer, Nomads. Likewise in Book 2, he relates that the ancient Greek writers assigned the name Scythian and Celto-Scythian to all Northern peoples; Ptolemy asserts this view in his *Tetrabiblos*. Those older than them divided them such that those who lived above the Black Sea <note>original: Euxinum</note>, the Danube <note>original: Istrum</note>, and the Adriatic were all called Hyperboreans, Sauromataæ, and Arimaspi, while those across the Hyrcanian Sea <note>The Caspian Sea</note> were called Sacæ and Massagetæ. Philostratus bounds Scythia by the Danube, Don <note>original: Tanaidi</note>, and Thermodon rivers. Trogus Pompeius bounds it by the Black Sea and the Riphean Mountains...

Read about the customs of the Scythians in Theophrastus' *On Airs and Waters* <note>Though usually attributed to Hippocrates, the author cites the philosopher Theophrastus</note>. The region which the Scythians now inhabit is said to have once belonged to the Cimmerians, says Herodotus in his book *Thalia* <note>The third book of Herodotus' Histories</note>. Regarding the European Scythians, I believe he speaks of them; Julius Pollux, in his eighth book on the Athenian courts, noted that the Scythian archers were called *toxotai* <note>original: τοξόται; meaning bowmen</note>. We too, up to this point, and the people of the Scandinavian peninsula—in which the Celto-Scythians dwell—interpret "Scythia" as "to shoot" <note>The author is likely connecting the name Scythian to the Germanic root 'shütze' or 'shoot'</note>. See also Little Scythia, Pontic Scythia, Thracian Scythia, and the Scythogermans; see under "Molsia."

Scythia, according to Ptolemy <note>A 2nd-century Alexandrian geographer</note>, is twofold; both parts are in Asia, distinguished by Mount Imaus <note>Likely the Himalayas or the Pamir Mountains</note>. Therefore, they are named "Within" and "Beyond" the Imaus. Villanovanus <note>The scholar Michael Servetus</note> writes in his edition of Ptolemy that the Kingdom of Cathay <note>An old name for China</note> contains these Scythian lands. That which is within the Imaus seems to me to occupy a great part of Tartary. That which is located beyond the Imaus is called *Mongal* by the Barbarians, and is said to be called "Ancient Tartary" by more recent writers, as reported by Mar. Niger. Arias Montanus, in his Biblical Appendix, believes that Scythia within the Imaus is the *Diklah* <note>A name from the Table of Nations in Genesis</note> of the Hebrews.

There is another Scythia besides these in Europe (which Ptolemy calls Sarmatia) according to Herodotus, Pomponius Mela, and other ancient historians. If I am not mistaken, this is the one Jordanes <note>A 6th-century Byzantine historian of Gothic descent</note> refers to, which he writes the Goths call *Ouim* in their own language; Conrad of Lichtenau reads this as *Ocimnin* based on this author. Strabo calls "Little Scythia" that region which lies between the Borysthenes <note>The Dnieper River</note> and the Tauric Chersonese <note>The Crimean Peninsula</note>. Scythia is also a certain metropolis of Phrygia according to Usuard <note>A 9th-century monk and martyrologist</note> on the third day before the Ides of November. See "Indoscythia."

Ptolemy holds Indoscythia to be a region of India extending along the Indus river; Arrian, in his *Periplus*, named the same region by the simple name of Scythia. "Southern Scythians" <note>original: Νοτιοι Σκύθαι (Notioi Skythai)</note> are mentioned by Dionysius the African <note>Dionysius Periegetes, a 2nd-century geographer</note>.

Because of this, he was called the father of those living in tents and pavilions, as confirmed by Gilbert Génébrard in the first book of his *Chronography*. Asiatic Sarmatia, currently called Sargatia or perhaps Cumania (though Cumania is properly a part of the Colchian country), has for its borders to the North the unknown land, not yet fully penetrated by anyone, being beyond the Riphean mountains <note>A legendary mountain range in ancient geography, thought to be the source of the north wind</note> or the "belt of the world" according to the ancients. To the west lies the Frozen Ocean and the other Sarmatia—that is, the European one—as far as the river Don <note>original: "Tane"; the ancient Tanais</note>, and until it flows into the Black Sea (or Great Sea) at the Maeotian marshes <note>The Sea of Azov</note>. This is how it was described by Ptolemy in book 5, chapter 9, table 2 of Asia. By adding to this description what Pliny (book 6, chapter 17), Pomponius Mela (book 3), and Herodotus (book 4) wrote of the northern lands unknown in Asia during their times, we learn from the accounts of Giosafat Barbaro in the book of his voyage to the Don, Ambrogio Contarini (chapter 7) of his voyage to Persia, Hetoum the Armenian in his books on the Tartars, Maciej de Miechów (book 1) on Asiatic Sarmatia, Sigismund von Herberstein in his *Commentaries on Muscovy*, Olaus Magnus and Johannes, Bishops of Uppsala in Gothia, in their Northern histories, Paolo Giovio (book 14) of his *Histories*, and André Thevet (book 12, chapter 9) of the *Universal Cosmography*, that these lands are today populated and inhabited by various kinds of people and nations.

The most northerly and remote people in Sarmatia do not labor or sow their lands, having no bread, wine, nor ale <note>original: "cervoise"; a traditional hopped or unhopped beer</note>, but live miserably. Keeping to the woods and caves of the earth, they sustain themselves on fish and the flesh of wild beasts, of which they have an abundance, quenching their thirst with beautiful pure water and being clothed in the skins of wild animals. And it is quite certain (though Pomponius Mela in book 3 and Solinus in chapter 26 write of these regions, which they say are very temperate and filled with a pleasant sweetness of air in the deep North) that it is a pure fable to say these regions are temperate. Indeed, it is certain that there is no misery compared to that of those who inhabit them, because they have no bread, wine, nor anything else that a man might desire for his life, and they are constantly assailed by the rigors of winter and the harshness of extreme cold. At the winter solstice they have perpetual night, and at the summer solstice continual day; even then, the heat is very faint <note>original: "tresente"; meaning weak or barely felt</note> and without force, because the Sun at that time casts its rays upon them only obliquely and sideways. Nor does one see—as some ancient and modern authors have believed—men in these countries having only one eye, nor those who were said to have two heads, nor are there found...

their own language, as is confirmed by Marco Polo the Venetian in book 3, chapters 43

Asiatic Sarmatia. All these peoples for the most part inhabit
various woods and forests that are most somber, deep, thick, and obscure; their
houses being only lodges covered with leaves and branches, living without law
or government, wandering and straying through the woods and thickets, wearing no
clothing of wool, but covering themselves only with skins rudely and

and non-precious, except when it is a matter of paying tribute to the
Sovereign to whom they lend obedience; see on this André Thevet,
book 9, chapter 2 and book 19, chapter 9 of his *Universal Cosmography*, and François de Belleforest,

This general Sarmatia contains the Poles, Ruthenians or Russians, Lithuanians, Masovians, Prussians, Pomeranians, Livonians, Muscovites, Goths, Alans, Wallachians, and several hordes of those Tartars. And in this Sarmatia are included the Sarmatians found beyond the Borysthenes <note>The modern Dnieper River</note>, who are currently counted among the Tartars and were formerly named Sauromates and Syrmates by the Greeks. These Sarmatians are entirely different from those who inhabit Poland (who descended from the ancient Slavs); they live only by robbery and theft, being ready for mischief, to which they accustom themselves from their infancy. Furthermore, they are a people who endure hunger and content themselves with little while in pursuit of their prey and readying themselves for some robbery, being altogether similar in manners to the Tartars. 

This general Sarmatia is separated from Germany by the Vistula River, which empties through three mouths into the Northern Sea on the side of Gothia <note>Southern Sweden/Baltic regions</note> and near Pomerania. From this, one can understand how great and spacious its extent is, going from this Frozen Ocean until the Borysthenes (or Dnieper) and the Don mark the separation of Europe from Asia. Belonging to the contribution of this province are the Masovians, subjects to the crown of Poland; likewise, the lords of Masovia are permitted the right to enter the Election, if it is necessary to elect a King of Poland. 

Leaving behind the fabulous tales recited by Herodotus in Book 4 of a son of Hercules and Echidna named Scythe, who gave his name to the country of Scythia—which was actually named for a Scythian, the son of Shem and Araxa, who went to camp there—or perhaps so called after the mountain Araxe, named *Scythit bache* according to the report of André Thevet in Book 19, Chapter 8 of his *Universal Cosmography*. 

We shall say that Lithuania is included in this European Sarmatia; it is entirely marshy and very difficult to access in the summer because, the waters being thawed, everything is covered by them. However, travel occurs there in winter for the trade conducted on the ice, and it is often seen and visited by those of the North. It is named after the Lithuan River, having been anciently inhabited by the Neres and Bodris. This Sarmatia contains several particular provinces known by the Ancients under the names of the Agathyrses, Picts, Gelons, Careotes, Salies, Aorsians, Pargithes, Nascians, Vibions, Hidres, Saturnies, and Alaniens. One of the limits of this Sarmatia is the Bog or Borysthenes River and the Tanais, for the country between the latter and the Danube was anciently the land of the Getae, where the poet Ovid was exiled by the Emperor Augustus. In describing the **Tartars**, it is necessary by the same means to describe several and various nations that are greatly separated and distant from one another. The same Annals cited above report that the name "Tartars" was imposed upon them because of their sect alone, even though they were greatly removed from other peoples and nations. At present, these Tartars are parted and divided into **Hordes**—which is to say, in the Tartar language, assemblies or multitudes—among which the first and principal is that of **Zauolheuse**, then that of **Precop**, then that of **Nahaience**, and others. In these, the Tartars of today are **Mahometans** <note>original: "Mahometistes"; followers of Islam</note>, taking no pleasure—but rather displeasure and dishonor—in being called **Turks**, preferring instead to be called **Besermanis** <note>original: "Besermanis"; likely a corruption of the Persian/Turkic word "Musulman" for Muslim</note>. **Sir John Mandeville**, a Knight living in the year of salvation 1322, writes in his travels that some 160 years before his time, all of Tartary was in subjection and servitude to other neighboring nations, and that it was entirely beastly, knowing nothing other than how to tend to livestock. Here are his words in the Romance language <note>original: "langue Romanesque"; the text here is a variant of Old Catalan or Occitan used in certain manuscripts of Mandeville's travels</note>:

> It has not been 160 years since all of Tartary was in subjection and servitude to the other nations that are around them, for they were all beastly people and knew nothing to do except guard beasts and lead the shepherds. <note>original: "No ha pas clx anys, que tota Tartaria era en subiugacio è seruitut de les altres Nacions, que estât en torn, car Ells eren tots bestials Gents e no sabien fer si no gardar besties, e manar als pastors"</note> Then he continues: But among them there were seven principal nations who were sovereigns over all those, of which the first nation or lineage are called **Tartars**; these were the most noble and the most powerful; the second lineage are called the **Turks**; the third **Armenians**; the fourth **Balaar**; the fifth **Semoch**; the sixth **Meyer**; the seventh **Coboch**.

That is to say, among them they had seven principal nations who were sovereigns over all, of which the first nation or lineage are called **Tartarins**, and these are the most noble and most powerful; the second lineage are called **Turks**, the third **Armenians**, the fourth **Balaar**, the fifth **Semoch**, the sixth **Menyer**, the seventh **Coboh**. This same author, in the chapter on the city of **Surgoyne** and the palace and house of the **Great Cham** <note>The Great Khan</note>, tells and recites several rare things about the Tartars which I will not repeat to avoid prolixity. Some other authors write that anciently Tartary was inhabited by four peoples, namely the **Iecha-mongal**, which is to say "Great Mongols"; the second, **Sumongal**, which signifies "Aquatic," who also because of being neighbors to the river **Tartar** were called **Tartars**; **Merchat** was the third people; and **Metrit** the fourth. Others count seven primary nations of this people whom they commonly called **Mogles**. The first and principal was that of **Tartar**, named after the river, and from which the rest take their name; the second **Taugor**, and the other **Cunar**; the one neighboring it is **Ialait**; the fifth **Sonith**; the sixth **Monghi**, or **Mongal**; and the last **Tebeth** <note>Tibet</note>, which is toward the deserts of **Dauuil**, where it is said that evil spirits appear visibly and cause travelers to lose their way by showing them the road through paths where they can find neither track nor any trail whatsoever, according to the report of **Hayton the Armenian** in his *Book of the Tartars*, chapter sixteen. Nevertheless, after he passed away, the Tartars began to live as vagabonds without a King, each considering himself a lord, until Chingis Cham <note>Genghis Khan</note>—otherwise called Changi, Chinchis, Cinguic, Canguiste, Cingiste, or Tzinciſcanes and Sitziſcanes—from whom all the Emperors of Tartary are descended to this day, was elected by them around the year of salvation 1162. With a feigned and disguised religion, he made himself admired by these people. Having made war against the aforementioned Uncam, who had so tormented the Tartars, he defeated him and made himself King of the East. His successors have since increased the Empire, usurping all of Scythia, now generally called Tartary, as Marco Polo the Venetian seems to confirm in the first book, chapters 51, 52, and 53 of his travels in Tartary, and André Thevet in book 9, chapter 2 of his *Cosmography*, and the subsequent book 12, chapter 17. European histories agree that in the year of salvation 1211, there was seen in Europe in the month of May, for the space of sixteen entire days, a great Comet turning over the Maeotian Marshes <note>The Sea of Azov</note>, over the Tanais <note>The Don River; written here as "Taue"</note>, and over Russia, extending its tail toward the West. This seemed to be a presage of the misfortune that occupied the surrounding provinces by the arrival and raid of the Tartars, whose name was previously unknown, and even less so their strength. Now, this troop of brigands had slain the King who commanded them, named David or Uncam, or Prester John, who had his principality in Asia along the mountains which, starting from the Caucasus, split the Indies in two, as Marco Polo the Venetian writes in book 1, chapter 44 of his travels in Tartary. Not feeling themselves secure, they rushed upon the provinces along the Greater Sea <note>The Black Sea</note> and between the Tanais and the Volga, and even into Europe toward the Neper <note>Dnieper River</note>, now called the Borysthenes. Indeed, overstepping it, they came as far as the Danube and overran the kingdoms of Hungary and Poland. In this, they imitate the **Scythians** from whom they are descended, and even those of the East who are of their own nation and language, keeping to the fields under tents and pavilions, or upon wagons according to the ancient custom of their ancestors; for they have no houses, towns, cities, nor castles or fortresses in which to dwell, staying for some months in one place, then in another. There are some among them who, tilling the earth with a hoe, sow it with millet to make a sort of paste like porridge called **Bairam**; <note>While *Bairam* usually refers to Islamic festivals, the author here uses it for a specific foodstuff, perhaps confusing the term or referring to a festive dish.</note> otherwise they have neither wheat, nor any other grain or legume. Sometimes mixing in boiled and soaked millet, they eat the flesh of small white livestock, still bloody and half-raw; indeed, if a horse dies of disease, they do not fail to feast upon it. They drink water, milk, and an ale made with millet; they call water **Su** or **Suha**, and their ale **Buza**, <note>Boza, a traditional fermented grain drink</note> which the Russians name **Bracha**. No artisans are seen among them, and they use no money, since their trade is done by barter and exchange; it is true that some of their **Hordes** <term>Horde: from the Turkic *ordu*, meaning a nomadic administrative circle, court, or military encampment</term> or Lordships are more communicative than others. <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' featuring floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

THE Histories of the Tartars contain that in the year 1212, having crossed the sea under the leadership of their first Khan or Emperor named Genghis Khan <note>original: "Cingis Chá," "Changius," or "Chāngis"</note> to conquer toward the West kingdoms, lordships, and lands, and to subject them to the dominion of this, their Khan or Emperor, they were deprived of him by his death. Before he died, he had them receive as their Khan and Emperor his eldest son, the wisest and most prudent of the twelve children he had, named Ogedei <note>original: "Hocota"</note>. Having deliberated to march further forward, Ogedei reached the Caspian Gates <note>The narrow pass of Derbent between the Caucasus Mountains and the Caspian Sea</note> placed in that location and continually guarded and closed to prevent passage into Asia by the infinite peoples living beyond them, as if in another world. After this, the Emperor dispatched three armies and placed them in the hands of three of his sons, commanding Jochi <note>original: "Iacchis"</note>, the eldest, to go toward the West, Batu <note>original: "Batho"</note> toward the North, and Chagatai <note>original: "Tagladais"</note> toward the South. He himself, abundant in men, marched with a great and powerful army into the East, conquering all the countries as far as Cathay <note>China</note>, where he established the very powerful and rich Empire that still endures there today, possessed by his descendants. He also entered the Kingdom of Persia, during which journey these Tartars learned the letters of which they were previously ignorant of the use. Hayton the Armenian, <note>Hethum of Korykos, a medieval chronicler</note> in the first chapter of his *Book of the Tartars*, writes that the Cathayans, subjects of the Great Khan of Tartary, have and use very beautiful letters, which are somewhat similar in beauty to Latin letters. they also have the speech and language of the Tartars as a related tongue. <note>original: "Linguagium Tartarorum cognatum habent."</note> The speech of the Tartar and the Turk does not differ except moderately, just as one might say, for example, as the Italian and the Spaniard, or the Pole and the Bohemian; that is to say, that the Turks have emerged and proceeded from the Tartars. The very same customs, ways of living, and common language they have between them clearly demonstrate in fact that both of these peoples and nations use one and the same dress, and the same way of riding a horse with short stirrups <note>original: "à la genette," a style of riding with short stirrups and high saddles, common in Moorish and Spanish cavalry</note>, and of making war with bows and arrows.
