...heresies emanated from that part of Germany, which were condemned; and even in these most recent days, the **Lutheran sect** has arisen, which has stained Christendom in many ways.

The **Fifth Nation** is that of the **Greeks**, who have the Patriarch of Constantinople, archbishops, bishops, abbots, and others of that kind in spiritual matters. In temporal matters, they have an Emperor, and they also have Dukes, Counts, <note>original: "Hisbotum"</note>, etc. However, they are now few in number because the **Agarenes** <term>Agarenes: A medieval term for Arabs or Saracens, believed to be descendants of Hagar</term> and the **Turks** <note>original: "Tuchi"</note> have occupied and hold the greater part of Greece. These people do not obey the Roman Church, although they were at times subject to the Roman Pontiff himself. Nevertheless, they have frequently attempted to tear "the Lord's seamless tunic" <note>original: "inconfutilem Domini tunicam"; a biblical metaphor for the unity of the Church</note>. Hence, twelve divisions of the Greeks are usually counted, which are set down by **Johann Eck** <note>original: "Ioannem Echium"; a prominent 16th-century Catholic theologian and opponent of Martin Luther</note> in his treatise *On the Primacy of Peter*, Book 3, Chapter 16. Now, however, they hold many errors and have been condemned by the Church because they say that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son <term>Filioque: The theological dispute over whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from both the Father and the Son</term>, and because they believe there is no Purgatory.

The **Sixth Nation** is that of **India**, in which is **Prester John** <note>original: "Presbyter Iohannes"; a legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in European chronicles</note>, who rules over that people as a Patriarch. One hundred and twenty-seven archbishoprics are subject to him, each of which is said to have twenty bishops. These people baptize those to be reborn in the Roman fashion at the baptismal font, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. They perform the sacrament of the Eucharist with the same rite, with this exception only: they chant the *Our Father* before the elevation of the sacrament. After the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Apostles Peter and Paul, and Saint John the Baptist, they especially accept and venerate them with honor; they also worship others, and especially **Matthew**, their primary teacher, with the greatest devotion. Furthermore, they follow the blessed Paul the First Hermit, Anthony the Abbot, Macarius, and two other hermits with the highest devotion. 

Indeed, they say their Emperor is most Christian, whom seventy-four kings and almost infinite princes obey—except for twelve rulers who observe **Mahometan** <note>Islamic</note> laws, yet who nonetheless obey the Emperor's commands in all other matters. Truly, in the time of **Clement V**, specifically in the year of our salvation 1306, this Emperor sent thirty legates to the King of the Spains and offered him aid against the infidels, just as a certain Genoese priest, the provost of Saint Mark, declares and wrote in his treatise on the customs of this race, titled *Mappa Mundi* <note>Map of the World</note>. These legates, approaching the aforementioned Pope Clement V at Avignon with reverence, were instructed in many things; with many gifts and Apostolic letters, they came to visit the thresholds of the Apostles Peter and Paul. Having seen these, they returned to their own lands with joy. Truly, while waiting at Genoa for many days for the time to sail, they were asked many things about their tribes, customs, and regions, and they left behind written accounts which the same author has disclosed. **Filippo Bergomensis** <note>original: "Philippus Bergomas"; an Augustinian chronicler from Bergamo</note> says these things in his *Supplement to the Chronicles*, Book 8.

Whenever the said Prester John rides, he always has a wooden cross carried before him; but when he goes to war, he then has two crosses carried: one of gold and the other of precious stones. In that land, the body of **Saint Thomas the Apostle** is held in the greatest veneration. In my opinion, I believe these people should be extolled in our Christian faith, second only to the Latins—namely the French, Italians, Spaniards, and Germans—and should be preferred above all other Christian nations, since they do not differ much from our Christian faith, except that they do not approve of the Roman Pope as the Supreme Pontiff of the whole Church and do not approve of his primacy. They were, however, at other times under the Roman Pontiff, as Johann Eck himself fully declares in his said treatise *On the Primacy of Peter*, Book...

All the Easterners and the **Agri** <note>original: "Agri"; likely referring to the Georgians (Georgiani), often grouped with Eastern Christians in such catalogs</note> were subject to the Roman Pontiff. The **Seventh Nation** of Christianity is that of the **Jacobites**, named after **Jacob**, a heretical disciple of the Patriarch of Alexandria. <note>The Jacobites refer to the Syrian Orthodox Church, named after Jacob Baradaeus</note> These people occupy a great part of Asia in the Eastern regions, as well as the land of **Mambre** <note>likely referring to Mamre, near Hebron</note>, which is near Egypt, and the land of Ethiopia extending toward Judea—more than forty kingdoms in total. These people practice both circumcision and baptism; with a branding iron, they imprint the sign of the cross on their foreheads, and on other parts of the body, such as the chest or the arms. They confess their sins to God alone and not to priests. <margin>Indonesians and Agarenes</margin> <note>original: "Indorum, & Agarenorum"; "Agarenes" was a common medieval term for Muslims</note> They claim that there is only a divine nature in Christ. <note>This refers to Miaphysitism or Monophysitism, the belief that Christ has one single nature</note> Some of them speak the **Chaldaic** <term>Chaldaic: Historically used to refer to Syriac or Aramaic, the liturgical languages of Eastern Christianity</term> language, others speak **Arabic**, and others still use different languages according to the diversity of their nations. 

The **Eighth Nation** of Christianity consists of those called **Nestorians**, named after the heretic **Nestorius**, who was from Constantinople. These people posit two persons in Christ: one divine and the other human. They deny that the Blessed **Mary** is the Mother of God, asserting instead that she is the mother of the man **Jesus**. Likewise, they deny that there is one Christ in the Word and in the flesh, but rather two separate ones: one the son of God, the other the son of man. As **Juan de Torquemada** <note>original: "Ioan. de Turrecremata"; a 15th-century Spanish cardinal and theologian</note> writes extensively about them in his work on certain heretics under the entry for "Nestorians," question 24, article 3. They use the **Chaldaic** language in their scriptures and consecrate the body of Christ with leavened bread. They inhabit Tartary and Greater India, and they are many in number; their land is as vast as Germany and Italy combined. These heretics were condemned at the **Council of Ephesus** <note>held in 431 AD</note> and were separated from the Roman Church, remaining in their stubbornness. The refutations of their errors are written at great length by the same Juan de Torquemada. **Filippo Bergomensis** <note>an Augustinian chronicler, 1434–1520</note> in the ninth book of his *Supplement to the Chronicles* says they hold yet another error preached by the arch-heretic **Nestor**: namely, that living virtuously is of no use for life <note>referring to eternal life</note>, as is found in the aforementioned chapter on certain heretics, because he claimed that predestination determined salvation or dominion, which is entirely false. Here one could apply the subject of predestination, which belongs to theologians, but I will only refer you to **Bernardino de Bustis** <note>a 15th-century Franciscan author</note> in sermon 37, part 2, letters N and O, in the first part of his *Rosary*, where he refutes this error, and more extensively in the 23rd sermon of the second part, where he deals fully with the matter of predestination.

The **Ninth Nation** is that of those called **Maronites**, named after a certain heretic **Maro**, who posit only one intellect and one will in Christ. <note>This refers to Monothelitism, a 7th-century theological doctrine</note> These people inhabit **Libya**, in the Province of **Phoenicia** <note>The text likely confuses the Libanus (Lebanon) mountains with Libya</note>, in great numbers; they are trained and experienced in battle, specifically using bows and arrows. Following the custom of the Latins, they use bells, and their Bishops use rings, mitres, and pastoral staffs. In their divine scriptures, they use the **Chaldaic** script, but in common speech, they use **Arabic**. These people were at one time under the obedience of the Roman Church; indeed, their Patriarch was present at the **General Lateran Council** celebrated in Rome under **Innocent III** <note>The Fourth Lateran Council, 1215</note>, but afterward they withdrew. They were first condemned at the **Council of Constantinople**, later returned to the obedience of the Roman Church, and then returned again to their false opinion, in which they persevere. 

The **Tenth Nation** is that of those called **Armenians**, who live in the Kingdom of Armenia near **Antioch**. They have their own idiom and a language common to all; they sing the Holy Scriptures and the office of the Church and recite them in the vernacular language so that they may be understood by all, both laymen and women. They have their own primate whom they call the **Catholicos**, whom they obey with great devotion and reverence as if he were the Pope. They fast during Lent, during which they do not eat fish or drink wine; however, on Fridays, they do eat meat. In the times of Emperor **Constantine**, they received the faith along with the Scots or Iberians...

...received Christ because they were neighbors to the aforementioned **Iberians** or **Scots** in the Western region. <note>The text reflects a common medieval confusion between "Iberia" in the Caucasus (modern Georgia) and "Hibernia" (Ireland), whose people were often called "Scoti" at the time.</note> And these **Armenians** are established in Asia between the **Taurus** and **Caucasus** mountains. For the Iberians, Armenians, and **Colchians** <note>People from Colchis, an ancient region on the Black Sea coast</note> are joined together under one province or region. The cause of this conversion was **Tiridates** <note>Tiridates III the Great, who reigned c. 298–330 AD</note>, who was then the king of this nation; through a wonderful sign shown by divine power around his house, he received the baptism of Christ. Together with all those subject to his dominion, he submitted his neck to God on one day and by one command. From this, it happened that the Christian doctrine reached neighboring nations and was spread among the multitude; through their trade, the **Persians** also received some of the first rudiments of the faith.

The **Eleventh Nation** of Christians is that of those called **Georgians**, named after the blessed **George**, whom they have as a Patron in battles. They live in Eastern parts and are a people of great beauty, strength, and refinement. They are greatly feared by the **Medes**, **Persians**, and **Assyrians**, in whose borderlands they dwell. They use the Greek language and practice the sacraments according to the Greek rite. The clergy have round tonsures <note>Shaved circles on the head signifying religious devotion</note> on their heads, while the laypeople have square ones. When they come to the **Holy Sepulchre** <note>The tomb of Jesus in Jerusalem</note>, they do not pay tribute to the **Saracens** <note>A medieval term for Muslims</note>, and they enter Jerusalem with their banners raised high because the Saracens fear them. Their women use weapons just like the men; they wear tall hats on their heads a cubit <note>An ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches</note> in height, and when they write to the **Sultan**, whatever they ask for is granted immediately.

**Philippus Bergomensis** <note>Jacobus Philippus Foresti of Bergamo (1434–1520), an Augustinian monk and chronicler</note> in the 9th book of his *Supplement to the Chronicles* says that the Scots or Hibernians are today called the Georgian people, and they worship Christ to this very day, although they are far from the **Apostolic See** <note>The Vatican/Rome</note>, the teacher of truth. He claims they do not preserve the full truth of the Gospel because they are surrounded by barbarian nations. These people (as he says) are established in the northern part, and in the year of Christ 338, during the time of the **Emperor Constantine**, they miraculously received the covenant of the Word of God and the faith of Christ. 

A certain humble Christian woman, held there as a captive, provided the cause for such a great good. <note>This refers to Saint Nino, the "Enlightener of Georgia."</note> As she led a modest and holy life in that region and spent her days and nights in prayer, she became an object of wonder to those nations. When they asked why she afflicted herself so much, she responded that she was thus worshipping her God, who is Christ. The barbarians, wondering at nothing more than this (as we know of such novelties), began to hold the little woman in honor. 

It was the custom of that nation that when a small child was sick, he would be carried around through the neighboring houses by the mothers, seeking remedies. It happened that a certain mother, after she had carried her boy around for some time and found no healing, went to the captive woman as if drunk with grief and sought her help. The woman replied that she knew no human remedies, but that the Lord whom she worshipped, **Jesus Christ**, could grant the healing that had been despaired of by men. Placing the small child upon her hair-cloth garment and pouring out a prayer to God the Christ, she immediately returned him healthy to his mother. 

Soon the rumor of the deed filled the whole city and even reached the **Queen**, who, being afflicted with pain, saw to it that the captive was brought to her. When the woman refused to enter the royal house, she poured out a prayer to God for the Queen, and the Queen was immediately restored to health. Because of this, she was urged to believe in Christ and to adore Him who had provided her healing. Moved by these benefits and words, the Queen asked her husband to become a Christian; though he promised to do so, and despite being frequently urged by his wife, he did not see to his baptism—not so much because he was an enemy of the faith, but because he was doubtful. It happened, however...

...[the King] at one time went into the deepest woods to hunt. When he had arrived there, a storm suddenly arose, and such darkness covered everything that he could not see any of his men, nor could he be seen by them. Not knowing what was best to do, he remembered the promise he had made to his wife, and then he prayed to Christ, asking that if He were the true God, He would deliver him from the present dangers. Without delay, the brightest day was restored to the world. The King, led back to the city, explained to the queen what had happened as a miracle. The captive woman was called, and her counsel was heard. She immediately told him that idols must be rejected and Christ worshipped; she urged him to pray to Him and to build a basilica. Having called the people together, the King preached the Gospel and, though not yet initiated into the sacred mysteries <note>Original: "sacris initiatus," meaning he was not yet baptized or fully instructed in the rites</note>, he became the Apostle of his own nation. The men believed through the King, and the women through the Queen. A temple of great workmanship was built; and when the circuit of the walls was raised with great effort, the columns were placed. But while the first and second were erected, the third could not be raised by any machines or any strength. When they had labored until nightfall and everyone had left, the captive woman alone remained at the Church, persevering in prayer. On the following day, as the people returned at first light, the column was found hanging in the air above its base at a distance of one foot. At the sight of this miracle, all magnified God and recognized the captive woman's true faith. While all were marveling, it was gradually lowered onto its base without anyone touching it. Soon, the remaining columns were erected with great success. Once the Church was finished and the faith of the people confirmed, at the suggestion of the captive woman, an embassy of the entire nation was sent to Emperor Constantine in Greece <note>Referring to the Eastern Roman Empire/Byzantium</note>, the events were explained, and priests were requested to complete the task begun among them. The Emperor granted these requests with a most joyful countenance; thus says **Philip of Bergamo** <note>Jacobus Philippus Foresti (1434–1520), an Augustinian monk and historian</note> in the place cited above.

The **Twelfth Nation** of Christians is that of those called **Syrians** <note>original: "Suriani"</note>, named after the city of **Sur** <note>The ancient city of Tyre</note>, which is prominent in **Syria** or **Assyria**. In their common speech, they use the **Saracen language** <note>Arabic</note>; but in the divine scriptures and the office of the Mass, they use the **Greek language**. They have Bishops and observe the customs of the Greeks, obeying them in all things. They prepare the sacrament of the **Eucharist** with leavened bread, and they hold the opinions of the Greeks against the **Latins** <note>A reference to the theological differences between the Eastern and Western Churches</note>. These are followed by certain Christians who are called **Samaritans** in the Holy Land; they were converted in the early time of the Apostles, but they are not well-grounded in the faith.

The **Thirteenth Nation** is that of those who are called **Mozarabs**. Long ago, there were many of them in parts of **Africa** and **Spain**, but now there are few. They are called **Mozarabs** because they maintained the "modes" or customs of Christians while living among the **Arabs** in many respects. These people use the **Latin language** in their divine offices and obey the **Roman Church** and the Latin prelates. They prepare the bread without leaven <term>azimo: unleavened bread used for the Host</term> just like the Latins, but they differ from them in many ways, because in their divine offices they have very long "hours" <note>liturgical cycles of prayer</note>. Since the natural day is divided into 24 hours of day and night, they have so many offices—namely hours, psalms, and hymns—and they also have certain and exceedingly long prayers, which they do not say in the manner of the Latins. For what the Latins say at the beginning, they say at the end or in the middle. Some of them divide the Sacrament of the Eucharist into seven parts, others into ten. It is a very devout nation; they do not join in marriage except with persons of their own people or nation. Among them, a woman who has lost her first husband never joins another, but remains in perpetual chastity. All these aforementioned sects or nations use three languages, namely **Hebrew** (or **Arabic**), **Greek**, and **Latin**; for as it is recorded in Luke 23 and John 19, the title or inscription on the Cross of Jesus Christ was written in Greek, Hebrew, and Latin. It remains to be seen...

...determines which of them is more excellent. And it seems that Greek is more useful than Latin, which the text in the *Authentica* <term>Authentica: A collection of the "Novels" or new laws of Emperor Justinian</term> concerning the non-alienation or exchange of Church property <note>original: "de non alienādis aut permutandis rebus Ecclesiasticis"</note> in the section beginning "We therefore" <note>original: "§. nos igitur"</note> at the end of the second collection seems to sufficiently prove. There, the text says: "We have written the law not in our paternal voice <note>original: "paterna voce"</note>—that is, in Latin—but in this common and Greek tongue, so that it might be known to all," because of its ease of interpretation, as the Gloss <term>Gloss: A standard marginal commentary on legal or biblical texts</term> says regarding the word "voice." Therefore, the Greek language seems more common than Latin, because not only do the Greeks know it, but also the Latins, who must have an education in the Greek language for the sake of the interpretations and translations of many laws and constitutions which were made in the Greek language, as appears in many laws of the *Digests* <term>Digests: A massive compilation of juristic writings from the Roman Empire</term>. The Greeks, however, care little or nothing for the Latin language. Furthermore, as one reads in divine matters, when the Hebrew language was to be translated into Latin, it was first translated into Greek, so that a translation from it might be made more easily.

Take note that the text, the gloss, and the doctors in the first *Clementine* decree <term>Clementine: Part of the Corpus Juris Canonici, the body of Catholic Church law</term> concerning masters make mention of three languages, namely Hebrew, Arabic, and Chaldean <note>original: "Chaldæa," referring here to Aramaic</note>, which are (as the Cardinal says there) useful to know for the benefit of the faith. As to why he omitted Greek, the gloss says there on the word "Hebrew" that the word "Greek" was struck out in the original; or perhaps it was because of the wording in the text above where it says, "which the infidels use," etc., so that nothing would be superfluous—or it was struck out because the Greeks were then faithful under the obedience of the Church (as seen in the chapter "Although" <note>original: "c. licet"</note> regarding baptism, and what is noted in chapter 1 of "On the Supreme Trinity" in the sixth book). However, today they are schismatics <note>Referring to the East-West Schism between the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches</note> and do not recognize the head of the Roman Church. And as the gloss says in the same place, perhaps the study of their own language would be more expedient than that of others.

The Jews, moreover, have the Hebrew script, but they do not have a special language in the common vernacular. For we hold that their common language has vanished. The Arabic script belongs to the Saracens; the Chaldean to the Chaldeans, about which it is written in the chapter "We Read" <note>original: "c. legimus"</note>... but it is said that this script is not held today, as the said gloss says. And the Cardinal recounts there that there are 72 languages, as the text in the chapter "Seventy" <note>original: "c. septuaginta"</note> in the 16th Distinction seems to prove. But the principal ones are three: namely Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, which divide the whole world. It is also said that once there was one language for all nations, namely Hebrew, and it is probably believed that in the celestial homeland there will be only one language. For in many languages there is variety, and where there is variety and diversity, there is discord. For the diversity of languages, as Augustine says in the 19th book, chapter 7 of *The City of God* <note>original: "de civit. Dei"</note>, alienates man from man; for if two people meet each other and are forced by some necessity not to pass by but to stay together, and neither knows the language of the other, dumb animals even of different species associate with one another more easily than these men do.

But as to which language is more honorable and excellent, Greek seems more useful, as was said above, and therefore more to be praised in its effect; and the text seems to prove this in the said section "We therefore" with the gloss mentioned above. But it seems that this reasoning is not conclusive, since it is certain that very few Latins are knowledgeable in the Greek language, whereas almost all Greeks are skilled in Latin. And if the Greek language could be understood by all and were more common than Latin, there would have been no need to use the circuitous route of translating from Hebrew into Greek and then from Greek into Latin; rather, a Greek translation would have sufficed. Hence, regarding the utility of the Greek language, so that it might be more excellent, the text in the chapter "As of the Ancients" <note>original: "c. vt veterum"</note> seems better; there is a text of Augustine...

...in the 9th distinction <term>Distinction: A division within the *Decretum Gratiani*, a foundational collection of Canon Law</term> of Augustine, who says: just as the reliability of the ancient books <note>The Old Testament</note> must be examined against the Hebrew volumes, so the truth of the new books <note>The New Testament</note> requires the standard of the Greek tongue. This is understood to apply to the Old and New Testaments, and the text also says as much in the final chapter of the 20th distinction. Regarding those causes where no authority for loosening or binding <note>A legal and theological term for granting dispensations or imposing penalties</note> appears in the books of the Old and New Testaments, or the four Gospels, or all the writings of the Apostles, one should recur to the divine Greek writings. 

However, the "Great Gloss" <term>Great Gloss: The standard 13th-century commentary on Canon Law by Accursius or Johannes Teutonicus</term> on the said chapter "As the ancients" <note>original: "ut veterum"</note> says that Jerome, in his second prologue to the Bible, holds the opposite view, saying that the Latin copies are more corrected than the Greek and Hebrew ones. But Augustine, in that same chapter, is looking back to the primitive church, when the Greek and Hebrew copies were not yet corrupted. As time went on and the Christian population grew greatly, many heresies sprouted among the Greeks. Out of envy for the Christians, the Jews and Greeks corrupted their own copies; thus it happened that their copies are more corrupted than those of the Latins. Jerome refers to this later time, or he is referring to Latin copies translated by faithful interpreters. Augustine, on the other hand, is referring to Latin copies translated not by the faithful, but by falsifiers. 

Or, as the said Gloss says, in this matter Jerome is to be believed more than Augustine. For among these three—Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory—Augustine is more to be believed in disputations; Jerome in histories and translations; and Gregory is preferred in moral matters. This is because not all men are skilled in all things, but certain men are skilled in certain things, as the text says in the first law, the section "For all authors" <note>original: "§. omnibus auctoribus"</note> in the Code's title on the drafting of the old law <term>C. de veteri iur. enucleand.: A section of the Code of Justinian regarding the compilation of the Digest</term>. "Nor can we all do all things," as the said Gloss says, which Panormitanus <note>A famous 15th-century canon lawyer</note> cites and follows, and after him Felinus in the chapter "Lest you enter" <note>original: "C. ne initaris"</note> at the end of the section on constitutions. There, Felinus says that this gloss was approved by Ludovicus Romanus in the 15th "exception" <note>original: "fallent."</note> regarding the law on a man's dissolution of marriage, and in several other sections of the Digest.

But the Archdeacon <note>Guido de Baysio, a prominent canonist</note> in the final chapter of the 20th distinction, and after him Prepositus and Geminianus, say that when a written text is found to be contradictory or doubtful, one must recur to the Greek language. This is understood according to the times mentioned in the chapters "As the ancients" and the final chapter, when the integrity of the Catholic faith still resided among the Greeks. But since today they are "headless" <term>acephali: Literally "without a head," referring here to the Greeks being in schism from the Pope in Rome</term> and their copies are corrupted and full of errors, one should not recur to their volumes. It is not likely that those who do not sincerely hold the unity of the Catholic faith would have preserved the integrity of their volumes; rather, they corrupted them out of hatred for the Latins (who are the unshaken observers of the unity of the faith). For adversaries and enemies lie easily, as the text says in the first law, the section "Furthermore" <note>original: "§. præterea"</note> and in several concordances in the Gloss of the Digest <note>original: "π." - the Greek letter pi was often used to represent the Pandects or Digest</note> on the question of Albericus de Rosate. 

Albericus de Rosate, in the first Constitution of the Digest, in the section "That," and in his dictionary under the word "Language" <note>original: "lingua"</note>, says that among all languages, three are most excellent: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. Of these, Greek is said to be clearer and more resonant. Its variety is discerned in five parts: the first is called "Mixed" or "Common"; the second, "Athenian," which the Greek authors used; the third, that which the Egyptians and Syrians have; the fourth, "Ionic"; and the fifth, "Aeolic." Alternatively, one is called Attic, another Boeotian, the third Aeolic, the fourth Doric, and the fifth...

Indeed, the Latin languages are said to be fourfold: namely, the **Ancient** (*prisca*), which was refined and held by the most ancient Italians under Janus and Saturn; the **Latin** (*Latina*), which the Italians use and have used since the time of Latinus and other Kings of Tuscany, from which the Law of the Twelve Tables was written; the **Roman** (*Romana*), which the Roman people used after the kings were driven out; and the **Mixed** (*mixta*), which took hold of the city after the empire was more widely extended, arriving along with new customs and people, corrupting the integrity of the word through solecisms <term>Solecism: A grammatical mistake or intentional breaking of grammatical rules</term> and barbarisms.

All Easterners clash their words in the throat, such as the Hebrews and Syrians; Mediterranean peoples produce their speech in the palate, such as the Greeks and Asians; Westerners, however, break their words against the teeth, such as the Italians and Spaniards. I add that the Northerners and Germans produce words in the chest; we French, however, use the throat, palate, and chest. Hence it is commonly said: **the Italians bleat like goats, the Germans howl, the French sing, and the English shout for joy.** <note>original: "Itali caprisant, Alemani vlulant, Galli cantant, & Angli iubilant."</note> And so says Albericus in the first location cited, who says he found this in authentic writings regarding Genesis, and in the inventory of the entire world, in the section on the building of the Tower, in which there was a diversity of tongues. Isidore also says the same in his book *Etymologies*, where he says that the speech of the Greeks is more elegant than the others, as I said above in the third part. 

Guillelmus Durandi, in his *Rationale of the Divine Offices* <note>A standard 13th-century liturgical manual</note>, chapter 11 on Good Friday, says that the Hebrew language, because of the Law, is the mother of all languages. The Greek language is the teacher, and the Latin language is the interpreter because of the dominion of the Roman Empire and the Papacy. And for this reason, it is said that the Hebrew language was the mother of all languages; for before the pride of the Tower of Babylon divided them, there was one language for all nations, as is held in Genesis 11, where it is said: *And the earth was of one tongue and of the same speech.* And again the Lord says: *Behold, the people is one, and they all have one tongue,* and because of that sin, seventy entirely diverse languages were brought upon them, as discussed below in the 69th distinction, which deals with several famous towers. 

Whence Remigius says regarding that passage in 1 Corinthians 14, "whether tongues shall cease": just as before the Tower of Babel there was one Hebrew language, so certain doctors <note>Church scholars</note> believe that after the final judgment, that same language will remain as the one; and therefore, as I said above, there is variety among many languages, and where there is variety, there is discord. But in the kingdom of the saints, there will be no discord; therefore, there will be no variety of languages. Likewise, Bernard says: "many know many things, but there will be one language for all: unwearied shouting for joy, one affection, eternal love; and the omnipotence, wisdom, peace, justice, and intelligence of all will be communal." In that peace, there will be no diversity of languages. 

Nevertheless, it is a gift to use diverse languages, whence the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 14: *I thank my God that I speak with the tongues of you all*; and the Apostles spoke in various languages in Acts 2. Regarding the praise of this Hebrew language, see more fully in the *Margarita Philosophica* <term>Margarita Philosophica: "The Philosophical Pearl," a popular 16th-century encyclopedia by Gregor Reisch</term> in the section on Hebrew instruction, where he praises it for its antiquity or priority—since it was prior to all others—and for its purity, sanctity, abundance of meanings, and utility, by all of which it excels the others, as is most elegantly proved there. It is held as indubitable that the Latin language flowed from Greek springs, and this is certain among almost everyone; whether this is entirely true, I discussed above in this part in the 17th consideration, where France is praised for the tradition of letters.

Friar Brochard <note>Burchard of Mount Sion, a German Dominican friar who traveled to the Levant in the late 13th century</note>, a monk living in the year of salvation 1283, writes in his description of the places of the Holy Land that in his time the following peoples and nations were found in Jerusalem and the Holy Land.

There are in the Promised Land men from every nation under heaven, and every race lives according to its own way of life, and, to speak the truth, to our great shame, none are found in it worse or more corrupt in morals than the Christians. I believe the reason for this is as follows: When someone in Spain, France, Germany, Italy, or other Christian nations has been caught as an evildoer—such as a murderer, robber, thief, incestuous person, adulterer, fornicator, or traitor—and fears that he will be given the punishment he deserves by a judge, he flees and crosses over to the Holy Land, as if to abolish the evil he has committed. And when he arrives there, he has changed his location, but not his soul; and what was written happened to him: **Can the Ethiopian change his skin?** <note>original: "Nunquid Æthyops potest mutare pellem suam?" — A quote from Jeremiah 13:23</note> There are not a few such people today in the Holy Land who rob pilgrims and their own countrymen who turn to them in good faith, suspecting no evil from them. Those detestable fathers leave behind even more detestable sons, who trample the holy places with polluted feet, and by their wretched life cause the holy things of God to fall into great contempt.

Besides the Christians, there are also various other peoples in the Promised Land, especially the Saracens <term>Saracens: A common medieval term for Muslims</term>, who preach Muhammad and observe his law. They also acknowledge Christ as a great Prophet, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, but they deny that he suffered and died; rather, they say that when it pleased Him, he ascended into heaven. And He sits at the right hand of the Father, as the Son. But they say Muhammad sits at the left hand of God, and is a messenger of God sent only to them. These Muhammadan men are most addicted to impurity, and they take as many wives as they can feed, besides being defiled by the vice of Gomorrah <note>A biblical reference to sodomy</note>. They are, however, hospitable and quite humane, which I have experienced myself more than once. For a small service shown to them, they return a generous reward.

There are furthermore in this land Syrians, who are indeed Christians, but they keep no faith with the Latins <note>The "Latins" refers to the Roman Catholic Church and Western Europeans</note>. They live miserably and very poorly; being devoted to greed, they bestow alms on no one. The wealthiest among them lives no more delicately than the poorest. They live among the Saracens and are mostly employed in their service. In their dress, they differ almost not at all from the Saracens, except that they have a distinction from them by a woolen belt.

The Greeks are similarly Christians, but they are schismatics <term>Schismatics: Those who have separated from the authority of the Church</term> and estranged from the obedience of the Roman Church. They are also entangled in many other errors—God grant that many follies have not also crept in among the Latins. Among the Greeks, almost all Prelates are Monks and people of great abstinence; they are held in great reverence and honor by the common people.

The **Iabeans** <note>original: "Iabeani," likely referring to the Georgians, historically known as Iberians</note>, **Chaldeans**, **Maronites**, **Ethiopians**, **Egyptians**, and many other nations, all of whom indeed confess Christ and have their own Patriarchs. Some are heretics and have taken their name from their heretical leader, such as the **Nestorians**, **Jacobites**, and similar groups. Yet there are many among these sects who are quite simple, knowing nothing of heresies; they are devoted to Christ, macerating <note>meaning to weaken or thin through discipline</note> their flesh with fasts and dressed in the simplest clothes, so that they even far surpass the religious orders of the Roman Church.

The **Nubians** and **Iabeans** say that they or their ancestors received the faith from Saint Matthew, were baptized by him, and received from him the method of baptism which they strive to keep inviolable today, relying on this authority: *He himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.* <note>original: "Ipse vos baptizabit in spiritu sancto & igne" — A reference to Matthew 3:11</note> For when they are baptized, they brand a cross onto the face or another part of the body with a hot iron, and these are considered the most devout among the Easterners.

There is also the race of the **Midianites**, who are now called **Bedouins** and **Turoniani**, who have filled a large part of the Holy Land. These people give their labor only to the nurturing of flocks and camels, in which they abound beyond measure. They have no fixed dwelling, but wherever they find good pastures, they stay there with their tents for as long as it takes until the grass is grazed away, and they are forced to seek another place for their herds. They are most warlike men and have filled all of Syria; they have particularly occupied the banks of the Jordan from Lebanon all the way to the desert of Pharan. The mountains beyond the Jordan supply the best fodder for sheep, goats, and other beasts of burden. They have rams and wethers so thick and fat that a single tail is sufficient for three or four men to eat. <note>The author is likely describing the fat-tailed sheep common in the Middle East.</note>

The **Nestorians** live around Beirut and Byblos in the plains of Lebanon across from Iturea.

The **Maronites**, however, have occupied the region which is around the "Spring of Gardens" <note>likely the area around the Kadisha Valley</note> descending from Lebanon toward Tripoli, and they are said to have forty thousand warriors.

Furthermore, around the fortress of **Arqa** <note>original: "Arachas"</note> beyond Tripoli live the Saracens who are called **Vani**. Associated with these are the Saracens whom they call **Asinini** <note>original: "Asininos," a Latin corruption of "Hashshashin," known in English as the Assassins</note>, living in the mountains as far as the fortress of **Tortosa** <note>original: "Antaradum"</note>, possessing many castles and towns and occupying the most fertile land. These are said to have drawn their origin from Persia; and they have increased so much in number that they claim to be able to produce forty thousand armed men. A few years ago, they wished to subject themselves to Roman obedience <note>i.e., convert to Catholicism</note>, but being hindered by the **Templars**, they recoiled from their purpose. No Sultan has yet been able to bring these "Asinini" into order, but they establish laws and rights for themselves, using them as they please; they are a source of dread to all neighboring nations because of their ferocity.

And since I have touched upon the Eastern nations here, it seemed useful to make a fuller mention of them; for today there are many who, while they know nothing, wish to know everything, asserting that no Christians are found in these vast regions all the way to India, but that the treacherous **Muhammad** <note>original: "Mahumetum"</note> has defiled all places. This is not true; rather, Christ has His worshippers everywhere in the world, except in Arabia and Egypt, where Christians are found rarely, but almost all have given their name to Muhammad.

Indeed, it is true that all these overseas Christians—namely the **Armenians**, **Cappadocians**, **Greeks**, **Chaldeans**, **Medes**, **Parthians**, **Indians**, **Nubians**, **Iabeans** <note>Likely referring to the Iberians, an ancient name for Georgians</note>, **Asians**, **Georgians**, and the rest of the Eastern peoples—are not men accustomed to war. Rather, when they are attacked in war by the **Saracens**, **Turks**, or **Tartars** <note>The Mongols</note>, they become tributaries to them and allow every form of lordship, enduring the tax collectors, provided they can maintain peace and harmony as far as it lies within them. And from this, it happens that those regions which the Christians inhabit are thought to belong to the Saracens and to be subject to their treachery, when in fact almost everyone there is Christian. I experienced this myself in **Cilicia** and **Lesser Armenia**, which obey the prince of the Tartars; yet those who inhabit those regions are pure Christians, frequenting churches, hearing masses, kneeling, and praying devoutly. They also show great honor to religious persons, which I experienced firsthand when I stayed there for some time. Furthermore, those whom we judge to be damned heretics, such as the **Nestorians**, **Jacobites**, **Maronites**, **Georgians**, and the like, I found for the most part to be good and simple men, living sincerely toward God and men. They practice great abstinence, and during **Lent** <note>original: "quadragesima"</note> they eat neither fish nor oil. They listen attentively to the word of God, as I saw on the eve of **Palm Sunday** <note>original: "Ramispalmarum"</note>, seeing what great crowds flocked to the sermon. Moreover, they have their own Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, and other prelates, except for the Nestorians, who in place of a Pope have a prelate whom they call the **Iacelichum** <note>A Latinization of "Catholicos" or "Jathaliq," the title for the head of the Church of the East</note>, whom a great part of the East obeys.

The **Armenians** and **Georgians** truly have prelates whom they call **Catholicos**, who have under them Archbishops, Bishops, and other prelates. These men lead the people with the finest conduct, teaching them equally by word and example. Although they inhabit very well-fortified castles and possess great wealth, they nonetheless dress in cheap and dirty clothes with very wide sleeves. Their outer garment is a thick, red sheepskin, and beneath it they wear a grey and worn-out tunic. Their uppermost garment is a black scapular, cheap and rough, almost like a hairshirt. I was also present once during their sacred rites on the **Day of the Annunciation**, and I noticed that they use almost the same ceremonies and prayers that we do in the Mass, except that they use their own language and not the **Roman** <note>Latin</note> tongue. Note also that the Catholicos himself and all other prelates are monks, and no one except monks is admitted to these ecclesiastical offices. Secular clerics and priests, however, have almost no authority and do nothing other than celebrate the divine offices. At all the [canonical] hours they give the signal with a **wooden board** <note>original: "tabula lignea," referring to the semantron, a percussion instrument used instead of bells</note>, for they do not have bells; and then they rise at night for Matins prayers, waking one another so that all may gather. Nor do they go back to sleep after those short prayers are finished, but they sit in the church teaching the people until dawn. All the priests are married, and no one is permitted to carry out the office of a priest unless he has a lawful wife. They celebrate Mass only on **Saturday** and the **Lord's Day** <note>Sunday</note>; on the remaining days of the week, they devote themselves to their embraces <note>referring to conjugal life with their wives</note>. If a wife dies, the priest shall remain continent, nor can he marry another wife. And if he commits fornication or adultery, he loses his office and his church without any hope of recovery. A certain ancient Spanish author has written the following concerning this matter.

Suppose that the greatest and truest part of Christendom is in Europe and under our mother, the Holy Roman Church; nevertheless, one does not fail to find Christians in all parts of the world, or in the greater part of it. For besides those with whom we commonly associate and of whom we have particular knowledge here, there is—on the side of Germany, Hungary, and Poland within our Europe—a no small Christendom consisting of those from **Russia**, **Prussia**, **Lithuania**, **Muscovy**, **Prasodie** <note>Possibly referring to Podolia or a region in the Baltic</note>, and a great part of **Tartary**, and other Provinces which follow the Greek Church, though not in everything, because in several matters they hold different opinions and are separate from it. Besides these, there are the Kingdoms of **Scotland**, **Norway**, **Sweden**, **Gothia**, and **Westrogothia**, and a great part of the Northern Coast, as we shall describe another time more particularly. 

And leaving Europe, because it is so well known, if we pass into **Libya** or **Africa** (which is the second part of the earth), we shall find that besides the lands the Portuguese have won and converted to our Christian Religion on the southern coast, there are no fewer Christians in the interior than in our Europe. These are all subjects to a Lord or Emperor named **Prester John** <note>A legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in European chronicles; here associated with the Emperor of Ethiopia</note>, otherwise called **Belulgian** <note>A European rendering of a title for the Ethiopian ruler</note>, a name common to all the Kings of that country. [Portu]guese, that this same Saint Thomas died in a province of that India called Coromandel, in the Kingdom of Bisnagar <note>original: "Bisnagar"; the Vijayanagara Empire of southern India</note>, in a city that used to be among the chief cities of that kingdom, called Melie <note>original: "Melie"; modern-day Mylapore, now part of Chennai</note>. This city is now in ruins, and only some old buildings remain, so noble and magnificent that they clearly show the city was once very large and densely populated. Among others, there is a church which the heathens held in great veneration and honor, saying that the body of this holy Apostle was within it, along with another body of a King whom this personage had converted to the faith of Jesus Christ. The Portuguese dug there to find the tomb and found three bodies: one of the King, another of the Apostle, and another of one of his disciples. They recognized the Apostle’s body by certain signs: namely, that there was a spear with him in the tomb, with which, according to local rumor, he had been killed. 

In any case, relics and remnants of this Christianity are found in these Indies, as John Mandeville recounts in his travels <note>original: "Iean de Mandeuille"; Sir John Mandeville, author of a famous and often fantastical 14th-century travelogue</note>, where he says that several peoples of this Christianity live there under the lordship of the Great Khan <note>original: "grand Cham"</note>. When the Khan enters their cities, the priests come out in procession to receive him; he shows honor and reverence to the cross, and they bless five apples that they present to him in a dish. He takes one and eats it, and if he did not do so, they would consider it a great misfortune. Louis Patrice the Roman <note>original: "Louys Patrice Romain"; Ludovico di Varthema, an Italian traveler whose 'Itinerario' was published in 1510</note> recounts that while in Taprobane <note>original: "Taprabane"; a name historically used for Sri Lanka or sometimes Sumatra</note>, he found certain merchants whom he recognized as Christians of that country. They made him great offers to go with them to instruct them in the faith according to the Roman Church, but he did not dare make such a long journey. 

From what has been deduced above, we can see that Prester John <note>original: "Preste Iean"; a legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in European chronicles</note> is not the one in Ethiopia, but the one who was for a time in the East Indies; the name was imposed upon the one in Ethiopia only because the people wished it so. This error caused John the Teuton <note>original: "Iean Teutonique"; likely referring to Joannes Boemus, author of 'The Manners, Laws, and Customs of All Nations' (1520)</note>, in the book he wrote on the customs and manners of peoples, to be similarly confused and mistaken in this matter by following common opinion. He claimed that the Emperor in Ethiopia, in Africa, is Prester John, whereas the other resided and ruled at the edge of Asia where, as I have said, the Great Khan (or Tartar) holds his lordship—who, as is well known, is the greatest, richest, and most powerful lord and King in the world. 

There is also a province of Christians in Asia called Georgia, because it was converted, as they say, by Saint George; however, I believe rather that it is the proper name of the province itself. These Georgians are also called Iberians <note>original: "Iberiens"; referring to Caucasian Iberia</note>, and they always have their ambassadors at the court of the Safavid <note>original: "Sophy"; the Safavid Shah of Persia</note>. Their country is cold and mountainous. ### Concerning the Greek Christians.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial L featuring intricate foliate and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
The Greek Christians of today are more extensive in their reach than the Christians of the Latin and Roman Church. These Greeks, being separated and divided from those of the Roman Church, have chosen another way of life quite different from the Latin one. Just as the Latins recognize a single and unique head of their Church, who has his seat in Rome and whom all nations taking his side obey, similarly the sovereign heads of the Eastern Church are named <term>Patriarchs</term> <note>High-ranking bishops in Eastern Christian churches.</note>, whose seats are variously assigned. There are many peoples and nations who do not use the Greek language but nevertheless remain subject and obedient to the aforementioned Patriarchs.

The first and most excellent Christians among them are the <term>Caloyers</term> <note>From the Greek *kalogeros*, meaning "good old man."</note>, which in Greek means "good old men." These are religious monks who never marry—whereas Greek priests are permitted to be married—and who live in great austerity, abstaining from eating meat their entire lives and eating only fish at certain times. At present, there are at least six thousand of them living in various places on Mount Athos in twenty-four large, ancient monasteries, well-fortified with high walls and scattered here and there both along the seashores and on the mainland, as well as in the city of Jerusalem. This is confirmed by John Mandeville in his travels (in the chapter on the law of the Greeks); Pierre Belon in book 7 of his *Singularities of the Levant* (chapters 36 through 41 and following); and A. Thevet in book 18, chapters 13 and 14 of his *Universal Cosmography*.

The Lord of Villamont <note>Jacques de Villamont, a 16th-century traveler.</note>, in book 2 of his travels, chapter 21, provides a discourse on the ceremonies, customs, and errors of the Greeks and their religion.

Those who follow the errors of the Greek Church include the Circassians and Wallachians...

### Concerning the Patriarchs of the Greeks.

There are four Patriarchs among the Greeks of the Eastern Church: the first and principal is that of Constantinople, the second that of Jerusalem, the third that of Cairo <note>Refers to the Patriarch of Alexandria, who resided in Cairo during this period.</note>, and the fourth that of Antioch. These four Patriarchs hold great power over the Greeks, even though they are not very wealthy; for the annual income each has to live on amounts only to two hundred ecus <note>A French gold coin; the author suggests they live in relative apostolic poverty compared to Western prelates.</note>. Each of them has certain countries under his regime and ecclesiastical government. The one in Constantinople has the lands of Candia <note>The Venetian name for Crete.</note>, Chios, and all the Greeks of the Empire of Constantinople as far as Philippopolis <note>Modern-day Plovdiv, Bulgaria.</note>, and all the territory of Athens and Anatolia <note>original: "Natolie"; the Asian portion of modern Turkey.</note>. The one in Jerusalem has the entire country of Cyprus and Judea, along with the greater part of Galilee. The one in Cairo has the land of Egypt, Alexandria, Africa, and other neighboring lands. The one in Antioch has the land of Syria, Greater and Lesser Armenia, as far as Persia. These aforementioned Patriarchs are chosen and elevated to this office of leadership as men of great age and bearing long white beards; furthermore, they possess such honorable gravity and such sweetness of countenance that they move men to honor them. 

You will perhaps ask me why the said Patriarch and the common people hate us Christians of the Latin Church so much and refuse to follow our law? We shall answer you that they claim to be the first converted to the faith, and they are totally convinced that we others have added to the Gospel. These people err in several points: first, they perform the Last Supper and take communion in the form of leavened bread, and they give the bread separately. Likewise, at Easter, both great and small receive communion under both kinds <note>Receiving both the bread and the wine, a practice that differed from the Roman Catholic custom of the time where laypeople often received only the bread.</note>; this is something that Pope Julius <note>Likely referring to Pope Julius I (4th century), though the historical reference to his "writing to the Bishops of Egypt" on this specific matter reflects 16th-century polemics.</note>, writing to the Bishops of Egypt, rebukes along with several other ceremonies observed by them in various parts. They take no account of the sacraments of the Catholic Church and pay them no reverence; thus, if some priest celebrates the Mass on their altars in the Latin fashion, once the Mass is said, they wash the said altars as if they were polluted and unclean, and as if we Latins were excommunicated. Furthermore, they say, like the Arian heretics <note>Followers of Arius who denied the full divinity of Christ; here used as a general term of abuse for those disagreeing with Roman dogma.</note>, that the good we do for the deceased—such as fasts, alms, prayers, and other intercessions—is in no way profitable to them. And they are also of the opinion, and even affirm, that there is no Purgatory, which a well-born Christian will never grant; for that there is a Purgatory is an opinion...

Ancient histories, according to the testimony of Saint Gregory Nazianzen in his *Oration against the Arians*, and Saint Gregory the Great in his 17th *Homily on the Gospel*, carry the record that the Indians—although they have Saint Thomas as their Apostle, and he is currently the patron of the Christians who are in the East—nevertheless, the Apostolic history gives us proof (in the words of Abdias the Babylonian <note>Pseudo-Abdias, the purported author of a collection of apocryphal accounts of the lives of the Apostles.</note>, book 8 of the *Apostolic History*) that Saint Bartholomew also carried the Gospel to the Indies. Furthermore, after the Apostles, there were also other personages who carried the word of God to the Indians when they had strayed from the true doctrine learned from the Apostles. Thus, in the time of the Emperor Commodus, there was a holy man named Pantaenus <note>A 2nd-century Christian philosopher and head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria.</note>, who had withdrawn from the Stoic sect to Christianity. Being the principal regent of the school of Alexandria in Egypt, he was ordained to announce the word of God to the Eastern regions, which is testified by Saint Jerome in his *Book of Illustrious Men*, and Eusebius in book 5, chapter 10 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. They assure us that in these Indies, this holy man found the Gospel of Saint Matthew (which had been received there before he arrived) in the hands of some who made profession of Christianity in those countries. It appears that this Gospel was announced to those Indians by the aforementioned Saint Bartholomew, who left it written in Hebrew letters and language, and it was preserved until the aforementioned time when Pantaenus was in India. [Upon] the foundation of the Apostles, the devil sowed errors and impieties there to such an extent that those Indians lost (as has also been seen in our own time) all knowledge of the truth. # History of the Origin of

One morning, while he was preaching, a large piece of wood was seen appearing at sea, which came to rest against the shore. The King wanted to have it and commanded that by the strength of men and **elephants** it be brought to land, but it was impossible to move it. The King, annoyed by this, came himself in person, thinking that his presence would further encourage the people, but they gained nothing. Seeing this, the holy Apostle, and seeing that the King was distressed at not being able to have this wood, said to him: "Sire, will you do me this favor—if I make this wood come out onto the land—that you give me as much land as I shall need to build a temple in honor of my Lord, the true God who made heaven and earth, by whose command I have set out?" The King, looking at this poor man, said to him: "And how could you provide for this, since all my forces have not been sufficient?" "With the help of the great God whom I announce, I make myself strong enough to pull it ashore, for He is stronger than you and all men." The King had the land he requested measured and delivered to him; and Saint Thomas, approaching the floating wood, tied it with a cord and belt, and pulled it easily toward the place designated for the building of the Church. At this the King was greatly astonished, but nevertheless, he did not wish to become a Christian. The Apostle used this wood for the building of the Church, which was sufficient for everything that was necessary there, not without the wonder of everyone. And once the Church was finished, the King gave it a certain income from the **pepper** <note>original: "poiure"; a major export of the Malabar coast</note> which is produced in the country of **Coulan** <note>Modern-day Quilon or Kollam in Kerala.</note>, which the Christians of Saint Thomas enjoy even to this day, in remembrance of such a miracle.

In the end, this King persecuted the Apostle, who, following the command of God, withdrew elsewhere and went to the Region of **Choromandel** <note>The Coromandel Coast on the southeastern side of India.</note>, and to the city of **Malabar** or **Maliapur** <note>Mylapore, now a neighborhood in Chennai, traditionally cited as the site of St. Thomas's death.</note>, where he was killed and martyred, and where until the present day his tomb is shown. This author continues, saying that these Christians of Saint Thomas, having no knowledge—or very little—of the holy Gospel, sent to **Armenia** to be instructed in the faith and to receive baptism, and that the Armenian Patriarch sent some Bishops and Priests there, who instructed them as best they knew how. Since then, they have continued to send people there; but a double misfortune occurred, for the Armenians, being **schismatics** <note>The author, likely a Roman Catholic, views the Armenian Apostolic Church as schismatic for its theological differences.</note> and erring in several matters of our faith, watered these people with their false doctrine. Furthermore, by making trade and business of the holy sacraments (as is their custom), they would only baptize those who provided them with payment; and thus they returned burdened with great riches, and sending others in their place, they went to sow more for the harvest of their own profit than for the salvation of the Indians. This is what the aforementioned Armenians still do today, according to the testimony of **Emanuel Acosta** <note>Manuel da Costa (1541–1604), a Portuguese Jesuit who wrote on the history of missions in the East.</note>, a Jesuit, in his *Commentaries on the Indies*.

Therefore, according to the aforementioned **Barbosse** <note>Duarte Barbosa (c. 1480–1521), a Portuguese writer and officer who provided detailed accounts of India.</note>, it was in the city of Malabar or Maliapur that this Saint Thomas was martyred. After those of Coulan had (as we said) persecuted him, he retired to the said Malabar or Maliapur, where, beginning to preach, he made a singular profit, drawing many to the knowledge of the Gospel. And afterwards, persecuted by the **Gentiles** <note>original: "Gentils"; a term used by early European writers to refer to non-Christian/non-Muslim locals, usually Hindus.</note>, he was killed in this manner: seeing himself thus afflicted, this holy person would sometimes go walking through the woods and solitary places to pray; but as he was in these solitudes one day, it happened that an idolater went hunting, and not seeing him, or not being able to discern him, because

[He] asserts that the body of this Saint Thomas is no longer in the Indies, inasmuch as his disciples, stealing it away, carried it to the city of Edessa in Mesopotamia. Empty monuments <term>cenotaphs</term> were erected in several places, either in recognition of some good that had been received from them in those lands, or because some relics of their lineage remained, or because they had stayed there a long time and shown themselves to be human and kind toward their hosts. One may respond the same way, even if one did not know that these monuments or sepulchers were not entirely empty of the relics of this Holy Personage; rather, since the translation of these relics is celebrated,

Now, that the relics of St. Thomas have been dispersed in several places, St. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Early Church Father</note> testifies in a Homily that he gave in praise of the said Apostle, which Father Fronton du Duc, a Jesuit and great researcher of the antiquities of the Church—and especially of the works of St. Chrysostom which had gone astray—brought to light, along with sixteen other Panegyrics made in praise of various Saints. To cut it short, the Indian and Oriental Christians are thus: Their temples are built like ours, except that there are no images or figures in them, only the cross which is placed everywhere, very large and high, to which all Indian Christians show honor and reverence. Those who wish to be appointed to the dignity of Bishop must go as far as their Catholicos <note>a title for the head of certain Eastern Churches</note> who is in Armenia <note>Likely a reference to the Church of the East, which early modern writers often confused with the Armenian Church</note>, who attributes to himself the power to consecrate Bishops, contrary to the authority of the Holy Apostolic See; claiming—though falsely—to be the substitute for Saint Peter and holding the place of the Patriarch of Antioch, wearing a crown in the shape of a cross. These Indian Christians do not baptize their children until forty days after their birth, unless they see an extreme necessity due to the threat of death. They confess as we do and receive the holy sacrament, which they consecrate, if possible, with unleavened bread, just as Catholics do here. Having no wine, because their country produces none, they use raisins from Corinth <note>currants</note> which they soak in water and extract a substance from, which they use in place of wine. They do not use holy unction <note>Extreme Unction or Last Rites</note> for the sick, but in its place, they pray over the patient and give him a blessing. They use holy water as we do and pray for the deceased. They have the four Evangelists with their Gospels, observe Lent and Advent with fasting and prayer, and perform and keep many other fine and great Christian ceremonies concerning the service of God and His Church. They use both testaments, Old and New, according to the interpretation of their doctors, both ancient and modern, as is detailed more specifically by Marco Polo the Venetian, book three, chapters twenty-eight and twenty-nine of his travels; Joseph the Indian, book two, chapters 132, 133, and 134 of his voyages; Alvise Cadamosto, book two of his voyages, chapters fifty-six, 57, and fifty-eight; Ludovico di Varthema, book 6, chapter...

1. & 14. of his *Navigations*, Duarte Barbosa <note>A Portuguese writer and officer in India (c. 1480–1521)</note> in his book on the Indies, in the chapter on the Kingdom of Quilon <note>original: "Coulan," a major port city in Kerala, India</note>; Osorio <note>Jerónimo Osório (1506–1580), a prominent Portuguese historian</note> in books 3 and 4 of his history of Portugal; André Thevet in the place cited above from his *Cosmography*; Emmanuel Acosta in his *Commentaries of the Brothers of the Society of Jesus*; and the aforementioned Father du Jarric throughout both his books on the history of the East Indies. Modern accounts assure us that these Indian Christians live with great sobriety and continence, and are provided with Bishops by the Patriarchs of Babylon. This is also noted by Emmanuel Teixeira in his *Epistles*.

Modern travelers assure us that the East Indians recognize that the first Christians among them were the inhabitants of the Island of Socotra <note>original: "Zocotere," an island off the coast of Yemen</note>, where the aforementioned Saint Thomas first preached and announced the Christian Religion. They have had, and still have, temples and altars like ours, which are decorated with nothing other than crosses and have no images. During the days of fasting, which they observe very strictly, they abstain from eating anything. They marry only one wife and observe the same feasts, and on the same days, as we Europeans—even those of the saints. They pay the full tithes of grains and fruits to their priests. However, they are so ignorant, even though they make a profession of Christianity, that they do not understand a single word of the Christian religion, according to Osorio in book 5 of his history of Portugal and Father Maffei in book 3 of his *History of the Indies*. In short, whoever wished to report here everything that has been deduced about these East Indian Christians would never be finished. He who wishes to see more should read André Thevet, book 11, chapter 18 of his *Cosmography*; Escalante, chapter 16 of his *Relations*; I. Acosta in his *Commentaries of the Brothers of the Society of Jesus*; Father Maffei, books 2 and 8 of his *History of the Indies*; Melchior Carneiro, a Jesuit, in his *Epistles*; the notices and epistles of the Jesuit Fathers, and among others, those of Father Nunes from the years 1554, 1555, and 1558; of Father Quadrus in the same year; and of Father Eroez from the year 1556; the letters of the Jesuit Fathers Pinnerus and Xavier <note>original: "Sciauerins"</note> dated August 20 from Lahore, the court of the Great Mughal <note>original: "mogor"</note> Emperor in the year 1595; and the above-cited Father du Jarric in his books on the history of the East Indies.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'V' featuring intricate floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>Vincent <note>Vincent of Beauvais, a 13th-century Dominican friar and encyclopedist</note> in books 29 and 30 and Nauclerus <note>Johannes Nauclerus, a 15th-century German historian</note> in Generation 42, volume 2, write that Pope Innocent IV, in the year of salvation 1245, sent as an embassy one Ascelin, a monk of the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note>, with three others to the Tatars <note>Mongols</note> and their King Baitho, or Batu, to persuade them to embrace Christianity. However, they achieved nothing there, and this journey lasted three years and seven months. It is indeed true that they reported having seen many Christians in Tartary, commanded by a Prince named Cuine <note>Güyük Khan, the third Great Khan of the Mongol Empire</note>, who supported priests and clerics who celebrated and administered sacred and divine matters, singing and chanting psalms in the Greek manner at certain hours prescribed for this purpose.

Around the year of Salvation 1245, the third Khan <note>original: "Cham"</note> or Emperor of the aforementioned Tatars, at the prayer and supplication of the King of the Armenians, was converted to the faith of Jesus Christ and was baptized, according to the report of Hayton the Armenian <note>a monk and historian also known as Hethum of Korykos</note> in his histories of the Tatars. This Khan afterward undertook the defense of the Christians against the Saracens, having sent forces commanded by his brother Hulagu <note>original: "Hielõ"</note>, who subjugated Persia and a large part of Syria and Mesopotamia. In the year of Salvation 1258, the same man defeated and captured Al-Musta'sim <note>original: "Mustacene"</note>, the Caliph of Babylon <note>referring to Baghdad</note>, who greatly afflicted and tormented the Christians, imposing several punishments upon them under these insulting words from the Gospel: "He says to this mountain, and it is moved" <note>original: "Dicit monti huic & trasfertur," a reference to Matthew 17:20 regarding the power of faith</note>. Having locked him in a tower with all his treasures, he made him die of hunger amidst them. From the time of the Caliph until the Sophy <note>the Safavid dynasty of Persia</note>, the people of Persia had no sovereign doctor of their law. For this reason, in the year of Salvation 1500, this people easily accepted as sovereign doctor of their said law the "Sophy," who traced his origin and doctrine to Ali, the son-in-law of Muhammad, which is confirmed by Jacobus Nauarchus <note>Giacomo di Navarcho</note> in his *Asiatic Epistles*. The Christians at this time being in contention with the Egyptians over the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the aforementioned Hulagu and Abaqa <note>original: "Absaga," the second Ilkhanate ruler</note>, in the same manner that Tamerlane did a hundred years later, descended from Tartary into Syria, declaring themselves neither friends nor enemies. Following pagan superstition, they professed neither Christianity nor Muhammadanism. Although they were summoned by gifts and presents from Baldwin <note>likely Baldwin II, the last Latin Emperor of Constantinople</note> to embrace Christianity, they nevertheless preferred to follow Muhammadanism, according to Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio</note> in book 2 of *Illustrious Men*, in the chapter on Tamerlane. Saint Louis, King of France, arriving on the island of Cyprus with his army to go to the conquest of the Holy Land in the year 1249, received Tatar ambassadors sent to him by a Prince Erchaltan <note>likely Eljigidei, a Mongol commander in Persia</note> with letters, by which he learned that three years previously the Tatars had made profession of the faith of Jesus Christ and had been baptized, as Robert Gaguin writes in book 7. The copy of the letters mentioned above is included in Vincent, book 13, chapter 91. The aforementioned Saint Louis also sent ambassadors to the aforementioned Erchaltan with letters from him, by which this King prayed this prince and the Great Khan to remain firm in the said faith of Jesus Christ. He sent him a tent or pavilion of purple made in the form of a chapel, in which, with singular art, all the deeds and miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ and others concerning the Christian religion were depicted, as is confirmed by the aforementioned Gaguin in book 7 and Vincent in book 3, chapters 92 and 94.

# History of the Origin of the

Some Tatars came to the Council of Lyon <note>The First Council of Lyon in 1245</note> to meet with Pope Innocent IV; upon returning to their country, they made a profession of Christianity and were baptized, as recorded by Blondus <note>Flavio Biondo, a Renaissance historian</note> and Martin <note>Martin of Opava</note> in his *Chronicle*. It is true that some scholars attribute this to the time of Pope Gregory X, according to Book 5, Chapter 1, of the *Continued Sacred History*.

We read in the travels of Marco Polo, living in the Year of Salvation 1275, that Niccolò Polo and Maffeo Polo, Venetians, were sent along with Khogotalus <note>a Mongol official</note>, a great Tatar Lord, on behalf of Kublai <note>original: "Cabyla"</note>, the 6th Khan or Emperor of the Tatars, to Pope Clement. They were to entreat him to send priests or doctors to teach him and his people the faith of Jesus Christ.

In the year 1290, Möngke Khan <note>original: "Mangu Cam"</note>, the 5th Emperor of the Tatars, was miraculously converted to Christianity by his wife, the daughter of Hayton, King of Armenia. He was baptized along with his brother Hulagu <note>original: "Allan" or "Hielon"</note> and his entire family. Afterward, Hulagu descended into Palestine with a great army, carrying a crucifix upon his banners and standards against the Mamluks <note>original: "Cathes Melechmées," likely referring to the forces of the Mamluk Sultan al-Malik</note> in order to recover Jerusalem, according to William of Nangis. Shortly thereafter, these Tatars returned to their ancient impiety; since that time, they have been "Mahometists" <note>Muslims</note>, or rather "Sagomorbases" because of Sagomorbar, their prophet whom they adore just as the Saracens and Turks do Muhammad. This Sagomorbar taught them many things concerning God, policy, and good morals, including an edict that the Great Khans of the Tatars, successors of Genghis Khan <note>original: "Cingis Cham"</note>, must swear at the beginning of their reign: not to afflict the Christians and not to constrain them to pay a greater or more excessive tribute than their other subjects. The aforementioned Hulagu, having defeated the Saracens in this same Year of Salvation 1290, became the peaceful ruler of the Kingdom of Syria and Jerusalem; but three years later, the Sultan of Babylon <note>the Sultan of Cairo/Egypt</note> reconquered it from him, as contained in the continuation of Nangis and in the 9th *Ennead*, Book 7, of Sabellicus.

In the year 1302, Ghazan Khan <note>original: "Cambagade"</note>, the Tatar King of Persia, having renounced the Christian faith, embraced Islam <note>original: "Mahometisme"</note> and made his subjects followers of the Quran. From that time on, the Christian religion was banished from among the Tatars. The Turks, having defeated the aforementioned Tatars under the leadership and power of Ottoman <note>Osman I</note>, their first Great Lord, and the Parthians having defeated the successors of the same Ghazan Khan, occupied Persia in the year 1350 under the leadership of Jani Beg <note>original: "Gepsa"</note>, their Sultan. The rest of these Tatars divided into Hordes across Europe and Asia, each of which established a Prince for itself. For some stayed in the Tauric Chersonese <note>the Crimean Peninsula</note>, now called Gazaria, and those are called the Perekop Tatars <note>original: "Precopites"</note>, whose Prince gave his daughter in marriage to Selim, father of the late Suleiman. Others are called "Mogaues" <note>Moghuls</note>, who do not obey a single Prince but govern themselves in the form of a republic; from these proceeded the Horde of the "Hagutaues" or "Zauolhenses," whose metropolitan city is Samarkand <note>original: "Sinarcand"</note>, which was the birthplace of the great Tamerlane.

Friar Antoine Geffroy, Knight of Saint John of Jerusalem, in his treatise on the origin of the Turks, speaks differently of all the above, deducing in detail the lives and conquests of the Great Khans of Tartary.

<margin>Marco Polo the Venetian, Book 1, Chapters 47, 49, 62, and 63 of his travels.</margin>
