# Languages of this World

<note>The author continues citing Marco Polo's accounts here.</note> In Tartary, he confirms that in his time, there were many Nestorians <note>A branch of Eastern Christianity that spread along the Silk Road</note> found in several different provinces and cities under the rule of the Great Khan of Tartary in Asia. He speaks of them even more extensively in Book 2, subsequent Chapter 61, and in Book 3, following Chapter 50, where he mentions certain other Tatar Christians whom he calls **Nestorian Ruthenians** <note>original: "Ruchenes Nestoriens"; likely referring to Christians of Russian or Eastern Slavic origin under Mongol rule</note>.

**Ludovico di Varthema**, a Roman Patrician, writes in Book 6, Chapter 14 of his *Navigations* that there are in Tartary several Christians subject to the Great Khan of the Tatars. These people are baptized (as we Christians are), believe in the twelve Apostles and the four Evangelists, and write as the Armenians do. They celebrate the Nativity, as well as the death and passion of Jesus Christ; they observe Lent and certain feasts of the saints. This author says he spoke and conferred with these Christians who had arrived in the East Indies, and they assured him that in their Tartary there were several Christian Kings near the borders of the Turkish Empire, named by some ***Rumes*** <note>original: "Rumes"; a term derived from "Rome," used in the East to refer to Byzantines or those associated with the Roman legacy</note>.

The histories of the Tatars, according to **Hayton the Armenian** <note>Hethum of Gorigos, an Armenian monk and historian</note> in Book 1 of his *History of the Tatars*, record that **Möngke Khan** <note>original: "Mangu Cham"</note>, the Great Emperor of the Tatars, was the one who so respected the Christian name. Solicited by Hayton, King of Armenia, in the year 1253, he willed that full liberty be given to Christians throughout all his lands, and that no one should be so bold as to hinder them in their exercise of religion. He received baptism, though his successors cared little for it. He made a law for the Christians, stating that in all the lands the Tatars had conquered, and those they would conquer hereafter, they would swear to leave the Christian Churches intact; both the clergy and the laity were to live in total liberty, exempt from servitude and without paying any tribute whatsoever, except for the taxes imposed by the Kings on the native inhabitants of Tartary. This Law has brought such great benefit to the Christians—it is a marvel!

The **Lord of Joinville** <note>Jean de Joinville, chronicler of the Crusades</note>, in Chapter 19 of the *Life of Saint Louis*, recounts this history differently, as reported by **Nicolas Vignier** in part 3 of his *Historical Library*, citing the book by **John of Plano Carpini** <note>original: "Iean Capin"</note> of the Order of the **Cordeliers** <note>Franciscans</note>, who was sent by Pope Innocent to this Khan; the work is titled *On the Origin, Manners, Ceremonies, Religion, and Manner of War of the Tatars*.

In former times, the **Abyssinians** <note>Ethiopians</note> were those who once held the Indies under the Empire of their **Prester John** <note>original: "Prestelans"; the mythical Christian priest-king of the East</note>. **Genghis Khan** <note>original: "Cingis Cham"</note>, along with his successors, completely drove them out of those lands. By this means, the religion of the Indians was lost—which was the superstition of the heathens, worshipping a plurality of gods—whereas the Tatar worshipped a single God and honored a certain Prophet of his nation named **Shakyamuni** <note>original: "Sagomonbar"; a corruption of Shakyamuni Buddha, whom the author misidentifies as a Tatar prophet</note>. However, the Christian race was not removed, except for those who were native Ethiopians. This is why the Nestorians, Georgians, and Armenians still worship Jesus Christ there and celebrate the mysteries of our religion. These Christians know nothing of the Councils celebrated in the Greek and Latin Churches; nevertheless, they hold to most of the ceremonies of the early Church, which was planted in those quarters by certain Apostles or their disciples. The Tatar Kings and Princes support more than ten million Christians still today in those countries; they live according to the simplicity of the doctrine...

# History of the Origin of the [World]

...Apostolic doctrine. When one confers with these people, they maintain that ever since the Easterners began to be divided on the matter of religion—with one believing one thing and another something else—there soon appeared a **Mahumet** <note>Muhammad</note> among the Arabs, a **Sagomonbar** <note>Perhaps a reference to a Mongol or Turkic leader, possibly related to Shamanism or a specific local ruler</note> among the Tartars, a **Xaqua** <note>Shaka or Shakyamuni, the Buddha</note> among the East Indians, a **Xaholan** among the Bengalis, an **Haly** <note>Ali ibn Abi Talib</note> among the Persians, a **Cheriph** <note>A Sharif, or descendant of Muhammad</note> among the Africans, and an **Azeleon** among the Asians; **Comassan** and **Alxamath** among the Cephalians, and **Kalmorath** among the Abyssinians <note>Ethiopians</note>. These men, under the pretext of preaching a "pure" doctrine and speaking of a single God, won over the entire Levant <note>The East</note> and gained the advantage over the factionalized Christians. 

It is held that one of the ancestors of the Great Khan of these Tartars, when asked why he did not become a Christian—being so fully informed of the excellence of our religion—replied: "How do you expect me to do so, being surrounded as I am by subjects of diverse religions? If I became a Christian, and my ministers did not perform miracles and wonders as great as those done by the priests and enchanters who serve our idols, I would be spinning the rope that would bring about the end of my life." In short, this Tartar acted as a Christian when with Christians, and a follower of Moses or a Jew when with Jews, and became an idolater with his own people; for he celebrated Christmas and Easter with the Christians, as well as other feasts common to them, yet behaved as a Mahometan <note>original: "Mahometistes"</note> with the others.

<margin>See André Thevet, Book 12, Chapter 19 of his *Universal Cosmography*.</margin> 
**Haython the Armenian** <note>Hethum of Gorigos, an Armenian monk and historian</note>, in Book 1, Chapter 2 of his *History of the Tartars*, describing the Kingdom of **Tarsis** <note>often identified with the Uighur Kingdom of Qocho</note> toward Tartary, says that in this kingdom one finds a people called the **Iogour** <note>Uighurs</note>. He claims they have worshipped idols since ancient times, except for ten generations or lineages of the three Kings <note>The Magi</note> who came, led by the celestial star, to worship our Lord Jesus Christ in the city of Bethlehem. He notes that in his time, there were still several great and noble personages of this race among the Tartars who held firmly to the faith of Jesus Christ. This same author, in the subsequent Chapter 4, maintains that in his time a portion of the inhabitants of the Kingdom of **Corasmie** <note>Khwarazm, in Central Asia</note> near the land of Turkestan were Christians living according to the customs and religion of the Greeks, and that they were called ***Soldini***.

**Sigismund Liber** <note>Sigismund von Herberstein, author of *Notes on Muscovite Affairs*</note>, in his history of the affairs of Muscovy, describing the Tartars and their lands and regions at length, says that moving from the East toward the South near the **Maeotian Marshes** <note>The Sea of Azov</note> and the **Pontus** <note>The Black Sea</note>, toward the river Cupa <note>The Kuban River</note> which flows into the aforementioned marshes, are the **Aphgases** <note>Abkhazians</note>. Beyond them are great mountains reaching to the river Merule which flows into the said Pontus; these are inhabited by the **Circassians** or **Cikz**. They obey neither the Turk nor the Tartars, as their mountains are inaccessible; instead, they are Christians living according to their own laws and the Greek religion. They use the **Slavonic language** <note>original: "Eſclauonne"</note> in their common speech and in the celebration of their divine service, as the Ruthenians <note>Russians/Ukrainians</note> affirm.

Today, in the Kingdom of **Mangi** <note>Southern China</note>, currently subject to the Great Khan of Tartary, there is a city named **Cinghianfu** <note>Zhenjiang</note>, inhabited by people who worship idols. Within it, there are two Christian churches, though they belong to the **Nestorians**. These were founded in the year 1274 by a man named **Mar-Sargis** <note>original: "Marsachis"</note>, whom the Great Khan of Tartary had appointed there as governor.

## Concerning the Jacobite Christians.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>
John Mandeville <note>Author of a famous 14th-century travel memoir, though his identity and the veracity of his travels are debated</note>, an English Knight living in the year of salvation 1322, speaks at length of these Jacobites <note>A term historically used for the Syriac Orthodox Church, named after Jacob Baradaeus</note> and their religion in his travels—composed in the Romance language—in the chapter regarding the Law of the Jacobins (that is to say, the Jacobites aforementioned). Hethum of Armenia <note>An Armenian monk and chronicler, also known as Hayton of Corycus</note>, in chapter 54 of his *History of the Tartars*, makes mention of certain Christians named **Rapti** <note>Likely referring to the Copts of Egypt</note>, who lived in his time according to the manner, fashion, and religion of the Jacobites, and who boasted of being the oldest inhabitants of the land of Egypt. Regarding this, one should look at Leo Africanus <note>Joannes Leo Africanus, a Berber Andalusi diplomat and author of "Description of Africa"</note> in Book 8 of his *History of Africa* when speaking of Asioth <note>Asyut, Egypt</note>. The same Leo Africanus, in the aforementioned Book 8 in the chapter on Alexandria within his *History of Africa*, says these words regarding the Jacobites: "There are in Alexandria, among its inhabitants, Christians called Jacobites, who have their church where the body of Saint Mark the Evangelist used to be, which the Venetians stole away, transporting it to their city of Venice." All these Jacobites are involved in trade or practice the arts, paying a certain tribute to the Lord of Great Cairo; in Elchian <note>Possibly Helwan or a city on the Nile</note>, a city situated on the Nile, there are also some of these Jacobites. The author of the *Summary of Kingdoms, Cities, and Eastern Peoples* writes that near Suez dwell certain Christian Arabs, some of whom are circumcised in the manner and fashion of the Jews, and others not; the circumcised ones being named Jacobites, and the others **Malaquiti** <note>Melkites, or "Royalists," who followed the Byzantine rite</note>, who observe two Lents, one at Christmas and the other at Easter as we do. Most of these are hermits and persons of holy life; the others trade in Tor, Jeddah, and Mecca, and are held and reputed by all to be men of good character and conscience. Jacques de Vitry <note>A French historian and bishop of Acre</note>, in his *History of Jerusalem*, chapter 37, writes that in the year of salvation 1171, there was a great number of these Jacobites, who were not only scattered throughout Syria, but also through India and Ethiopia. They still retained circumcision along with baptism, just like the Saracens <note>A term used by medieval Europeans for Muslims</note>; they did not confess their sins to anyone but God alone, and they branded a mark of fire upon the foreheads of their children. André Thevet <note>A 16th-century French Franciscan friar and cosmographer</note>, in Book 11, Chapter 18 of his *Universal Cosmography*, says these words of these Jacobites:

"The Christians who live scattered here and there through the Indies, and who are at the tomb of Saint Thomas, are for the most part Jacobites, a people who differ in belief and ceremonies from all other Levantine <note>Eastern</note> Christians, and who were thus deceived by the most malicious heretic who ever lived on earth; and it should be noted here that before he had embraced Christianity, he had been a Jew, the son of a father named Azzas and a mother called Arama."

# History of the Origin of

of the Island of Karpathos, situated between Rhodes and Thasos <note>original: "Tassos"; likely referring to Kasos, an island near Karpathos</note>, and it happened that he was taken as a slave at the age of 17 and sold to a Greek priest, who had him baptized and gave him the name James <note>French: "Iaques"; referring to Jacob Baradaeus, from whom the "Jacobites" take their name</note>. This priest educated him so well in languages that he earned the position of sovereign Legate to the Patriarch of Alexandria in Egypt; after the Patriarch's death, he himself attained the dignity of the Patriarchate. He lived for eight years in a fairly Catholic manner, but when those years expired, he became a heretic and infected the people of the Orient with his devilish opinion more than Arius <note>A 4th-century priest whose teachings (Arianism) were declared heretical at the Council of Nicaea</note> ever did. It was he who first introduced and admitted this sect of Judaizing <note>Adopting Jewish customs and laws while professing Christianity</note>, approving of circumcision, which many of them still observe today. Secondly, these people never confess their sins to a priest. Their Bishops, priests, and other ministers are married. All Christians have always detested these people, so named after the author of such heresy, and have also regarded them as schismatics; nevertheless, they do not enter into contention or controversy with them through arms or popular sedition, for trade with them is as free and open as it is to others who consider themselves more Catholic. I do not wish to forget to bring to your memory that while crossing the country of Asia Minor, three leagues from the city of Seleucia in a ruined place that the local shepherds call Mellothi, I was shown the tomb of the aforementioned Heresiarch. Having been banished from Egypt and exiled to the Island of Crabusc <note>Likely Karabağ or a similar island off the coast of Lycia</note>—distant from the mainland of Pamphylia by about five leagues—he found the means, with the help of some pirates, to escape to Asia, where he again caused much trouble. Having lived in this madness until the age of 74, he was slain in an ambush by an Armenian lord. 

Those of this persuasion have a beautiful chapel in Jerusalem within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, in which I have often seen them celebrate Mass and other services according to their tradition and custom. I have seen four others: one in Egypt, and the three others in the cities of Jeddah <note>original: "Zidem"</note>, El Tor, and Bubutor, which border the Red Sea. They have a peculiar language which is hardly understood by anyone but themselves, and they have thirty-two letters in their alphabet, which are quite strange.

## Concerning the Nestorian Christians.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' with scrolling vine and floral patterns.</image-desc>
Marco Polo the Venetian <note>The famous 13th-century explorer of the Silk Road</note>, in book 1 of his travels in Tartary, writes that in his time, in several and various provinces and cities under the rule of the Great Khan of Tartary in Asia, there were Christians who were named Nestorians <note>Followers of Nestorianism, a branch of Eastern Christianity that emphasized the disunion of Christ's human and divine natures</note>. Niccolò de' Conti, a Venetian, in his travels to the Indies, and the author of the summary of the Kingdoms, cities, and peoples of the Orient, hold that in their time there were many Nestorian Christians spread throughout all of Asia, just as the Jews are in Europe. Giovanni da Empoli, an agent for the King of Portugal in his voyages to the East Indies, recounts that these Nestorian Christians are otherwise named Nazarenes <note>original: "Nazzareens"</note>. Ludovico di Varthema <note>original: "Louys Vuartoman"</note>, in book 3, chapter 2 of his voyages to India, says that these Nestorian Christians are surnamed by four other names, namely: of Saint John, of Saint James, of Saint Matthew, and of Saint Thomas.

André Theuet, in book 10, chapter 14 of his *Universal Cosmography*, maintains that on the Island of Cizre <note>original: "Gisire" or "Giserte"; located on the Tigris, though the text says Euphrates</note> situated in the Euphrates River in Asia, there are many Armenian, Jacobite, and Nestorian Christians, and that the Great Patriarch of the aforementioned Nestorians makes his residence there. Some Levantine peoples call him *Sind* and others *Sulaca* <note>Likely referring to Shimun VIII Yohannan Sulaqa, who sought union with Rome in the 1550s</note>: whom they hold as their head and sovereign Bishop, and he is in such reputation among them as the Pope is among Catholics. He maintains three Bishops in the principal cities of the Persian country: namely one at the noble city which was first founded by Darius, son of Hystaspes, 521 years before our Lord, named Erbil <note>original: "Darbelle"</note>, and the others at Salmas <note>original: "Salmaste"</note> and Azerbaijan <note>original: "Ador Beigani"</note>, situated eight leagues away, where in former times was built, toward the East, the great city of Nineveh mentioned in Holy Scripture, now named by those of the country *Ninimich*, or otherwise *Nisroch*. I know well that some have previously broken their heads <note>A phrase meaning to struggle greatly or overthink a problem</note> to know where this city of Nineveh had been—a Hebrew word which signifies nothing other than "beauty"—and wished to say that it was on the shore of the Mediterranean Sea at a...

André Theuet, mentioned above, in book six, chapter twelve of his *Universal Cosmography*, writes that the Maronites are Monks, who were formerly heretics, otherwise called **Monothelites**, and bear the name of a certain Maron, who said that in Jesus Christ there was only one will, and consequently one operation <note>Monothelitism was a 7th-century theological doctrine that taught Christ had two natures but only one will; it was intended as a compromise to unite different Christian factions but was ultimately declared heretical</note>: into whose error fell the Emperor Heraclius during the time that the soldiers of Muhammad were performing wonders <note>original: "faisoient merueilles" — here meaning remarkable or startling military feats</note> in Syria, and plundering all the country from Damascus as far as Aleppo. This Maron was not the inventor of the sect, but rather it was a fellow native of Antioch named Machaire <note>Macarius I of Antioch</note>, who was condemned along with him by the Sixth Council of Constantinople, as some Greek Bishops of the country have recited to me, and have also written in their histories. Others say, which is more likely, that this council was celebrated in Rome around the year of our Lord 647 under Pope Martin I, where by two hundred Bishops the error of several Patriarchs of Constantinople was condemned, who had troubled the faith received in the Church, and above all they condemned these Maronites and their accomplices. Since it was thus that the Emperor was infected with this heresy, and the Pope resisted him using the censures due for such a purpose, and not for his own private profit, Constans <note>Constans II, 630–668 AD</note>, grandson of Heraclius, had him seized and put in prison, where he died in great misery in the year 652, the seventh year of his Pontificate; but a short time after, he himself making war on the Catholic Bishops was defeated by the Saracens, and fled like one who did not wish to enjoy the prayers of those who were men of good, but rather the false Prophets who abused and ruined him with their heresies. 

Finally, these Maronites, having been separated from the true faith of the Church for the space of nearly five hundred years, recognized themselves, and detesting their error by the grace of God, embraced union and returned to the same faith, opinion, and belief as us, submitting themselves to the legitimate Pastors of the Church of God. For proof of this, and of the obedience they bore to it, their Patriarch came to the General Council celebrated in Rome in the year 1215 under Pope Innocent III <note>The Fourth Lateran Council</note>, where he abjured for his people the ancient errors, and protested to live under the obedience of the Roman See. However, being at present strayed, as they are, and living more in the mountains than elsewhere, as I have seen while conversing with them—except for those who go as pilgrims to Jerusalem—they know no one to recognize but their Pastors and ministers: these celebrate the divine office in Hebrew <note>The author likely confuses Syriac, the liturgical language of the Maronites, with Hebrew, a common error for European travelers of this era</note>, although in their language they speak Arabic for the most part, and follow the way of doing things of the Roman Church in very few ceremonies; they live for the most part at present on Mount Lebanon and the surrounding lands. The same Theuet speaks again of these Maronites in book 11, chapter 18 of his same *Universal Cosmography*. From all time they used bells in their churches, and their Bishops wore mitres, rings, and crosiers like ours, contrary to the custom of the Eastern Church, as they still do now that they are restored to our Church, using all our ceremonies, and so forth <note>original: "reliqua"</note>.

### Concerning the Armenian Christians.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring intricate floral scrollwork and foliage within a square frame.</image-desc>

PIERRE Belon in book 3, chapter 13 of his *Observations of the Levant* writes that the Armenians, at the very beginning of the Turkish conquest, were the first attacked when those Turks came out of Scythia: for the Armenians, who were then Christians and finding themselves the weaker, lost their Kingdom. But notwithstanding this, they have always remained constant in the Christian faith: as it appears that even today they hold the name throughout all of Turkey: for naming an Armenian in that country is understood to mean a Christian. If an Armenian becomes a Turk <note>meaning if they convert to Islam</note>, he loses his name. They are found living in cities and villages as far as beyond Armenia, and in Azamia <note>Likely referring to Al-Jazira or the region of Mesopotamia</note>, and in Adiabene, given that the King of Persia allows them to live in his country. They are also peaceable and humane people, and are commonly poor farmers, good gardeners, and those who tend the vines well. The priests of these Armenians are married like those of the Greeks, and celebrate the Mass in a chalice like the Latins, and are dressed in the same ornaments of copes and chasubles, and do not consecrate using large loaves of bread like the Greeks, but in a small host like the Latins; all the attendees respond to the priests by singing in Ar-

For the Turks and Saracens do not dare to molest them in any way, fearing that once they return home, they might wish to do the same to their neighbors who are Muslims <note>original: "Muſulmans"</note> and of the Saracen law. The women of these Georgians for the most part resemble Amazons in their ability to shoot the bow and go to war, and their faces and ways of acting show clearly enough that they have a virile and robust courage. The men grow their hair and beards long and use caps on their heads of various colors. They also speak the Arabic, Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note>, and Persian languages, and their priests in their Liturgy and divine service use the Greek language. ## Of the Colchian Christians.

The Colchian people, descended from the Egyptians, were in ancient times circumcised, just like the aforementioned Egyptians according to the report of Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC</note> in book 2, chapter 1 of his *Antiquities*; as I have noted here before. These people currently inhabit Asia in the ancient region of Colchis, which is now divided and split into two provinces: the first bearing the name of Lazica or Laxia, which extends as far as Trebizond <note>A major city on the Black Sea, now Trabzon, Turkey</note> and is more inland; the other being named Mingrelia, which is almost entirely coastal.

Procopius <note>A prominent Byzantine historian of the 6th century</note>, in book 1 of the *Persian Wars*, maintains that these Colchians were Christians long before his age. But Matthew of Miechów <note>A Polish Renaissance scholar and historian</note>, in book 1 of his *Sarmatia*, chapter 7, writes that the history of Moravia records that the Mingrelians were converted to the faith of Jesus Christ by Cyril and Methodius, who were sent there by the Emperor of the Greeks, Michael III, in the year of our Lord 861. Consequently, to this very day, these people follow the faith and religion of the Greeks, having formerly been called Gazares <note>likely referring to the Khazars</note> and currently by the Greeks, Abgazares and Abgazeles <note>referring to the Abkhazian people</note>. 

One must carefully consider these authorities, given that from the Empire of Justinian, in which the said Procopius lived, until this Emperor Michael cited by the aforementioned Miechów, there is a span of about 321 years. This leads some to believe that the Persians, in reclaiming this country, returned it to Paganism, and it persisted in this impiety while the disciples of Muhammad poisoned the Persian Empire with their Quran, until the aforementioned holy persons went there to sow the Christian faith. Since that time, as is probable, these Mingrelians have strayed from the union of the Apostolic Church of Rome. 

Ambrogio Contarini <note>A Venetian diplomat and traveler</note>, in chapter 2 of his *Travel to Persia*, maintains that these Mingrelians did not know how to hold more than three days' journey of land; and even that was entirely mountainous and full of thickets, where the men are brutish, wearing their heads shaved. They are Christians but steeped in various heresies; they celebrate the divine service in the Greek manner and are under the domination of the Turk, who is Lord of the Empire of Trebizond, to which they were previously subjects since the crown of Constantinople was fragmented and divided into two different empires. In the present day, they are constrained and forced to most often sell their own children, for lack of being able to have money to pay the taxes and impositions they owe to the Grand Lord <note>The Ottoman Sultan</note>.

See André Thevet, book 8, chapter 12 of his *Universal Cosmography*, and François de Belleforest, volume 2, book 3, chapter 5 of his *Universal Cosmography*.

## Of the Surian or Syrian Christians.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' with floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
We have previously, in the chapter on the Syrians and the Syriac language, treated extensively of these Surian or Syrian Christians. Among these was one of the "Surians," so named after a city called Sur <note>The ancient city of Tyre</note> where they lived. These people followed the same ceremonies and doctrine as the Greeks <note>The Eastern Orthodox Church</note>, attributing no superiority to the Roman Pontiff, and taking no account of the ceremonies used by Latin Christians <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note> in the celebration of the Sacraments, nor the ordinances regarding the fasts of the Roman Church. On this matter, one may see what I have written toward the end of the chapter on the Saracens and the Saracenic language, and in the chapter on the various types of Christians who are spread and scattered throughout the whole compass of the earth.

For as for those who would make them Assyrians, I reject their claim due to the distance between the one and the other, etc.

freely, and even granted to some cities great privileges, so as not to depopulate the Lands under the burden of heavy tributes, which was what they desired most. The city of Toledo, among others, had the favor of obtaining seven Temples for the exercise of the Christian Religion, namely: Saint Justus, Saint Luke, Saint Torquatus, Saint Mark, Saint Eulalia, Saint Sebastian, and Saint Mary. Furthermore, it was granted that Justice would be administered by Judges of the aforementioned Christian Religion and Christian nation, and according to the laws of the Gothic Kings <note>Referring to the Visigothic Code or *Fuero Juzgo*, the legal system of the Germanic kings who ruled Spain before the Umayyad conquest</note>, along with other privileges. By this means, the aforementioned Arabs, Saracens, Moors, and Africans retained an infinite number of Christian families, who lived and multiplied under them; otherwise, the Spains would have remained deserted, for the aforementioned Arabs, Saracens, Moors, and Africans would not have known how to populate them. 

Those who, being Christians, remained among the said Arabs, Saracens, Moors, and Africans, were called Mus’Arabes <note>Mozarabs, from the Arabic *musta'rib*, meaning "Arabized"; Christians who adopted Arabic language and culture while maintaining their faith</note>, because of the name of the governor of Africa, Musa <note>Musa bin Nusayr, the Umayyad governor and general who led the conquest of the Iberian Peninsula in 711 AD</note>, who wished to make himself famous through this dominion. These Mus'arabes, otherwise called Mozarabs, celebrated their divine offices according to the manner used in the time of the Gothic Kings, and following the institution of an Isidore, Bishop of Seville <note>Saint Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar and theologian</note>, or of Leander, as it was customary in all the said Spains to serve God at that time. And this continued until the service called Gregorian or Roman was introduced there at the time which will be mentioned hereafter. And this Mus’arabe office is still maintained to this day as a mark of antiquity in the chapel of the Company of the Body of God <note>The Corpus Christi Chapel</note> in the great Cathedral of Toledo, and other places in that city.

From the year of Salvation 714 until the year of salvation 950, these Mozarab Christians were in quite great tranquility and rest, not being forced or harassed in their Religion in any way whatsoever; and justice was administered to them, subject to the tributes and pensions imposed upon them. But when Haly Hatan <note>Likely referring to Al-Hakam II or Al-Hakam I, though the description of forced conversion fits later Almohad rulers more closely than the early Umayyads</note> came to the Kingship, he was such a zealot for his Mohammedan religion, and took such a great hatred for that of the Christians, that he had an edict published by which all Christian inhabitants in the lands and cities subject to him were commanded to abandon the Christian Religion, and by being circumcised, to take that of Mohammed, upon pain of death.

But notwithstanding this wretched edict, the Mozarab Christians did not cease to celebrate this office among themselves, both in Toledo and in Castile and León, until the time of King Don Alfonso the Sixth in the year of Salvation 1121 <note>Historical records usually date the official change to the Roman Rite in 1080 at the Council of Burgos</note>. That King, desiring in every way to show himself an affectionate son of the Holy See of Rome, wished for it to be changed; and in its place, the office called Gregorian—because of its author, namely Gregory the Seventh—was received. For this reason, he sent for the Pope’s Bull, which commanded that the said Roman office be celebrated from then on in all the Churches of the Spains, just as was done in France; and for this reason, it is called by some Spaniards the "Gallican office" <note>Though it was the Roman Rite, it was introduced to Spain via French monks and influence, hence the name</note>. To ordain this, a legate was sent to Spain some years earlier by the said Pope Gregory VII, predecessor of Urban II: one Richard, Abbot of Saint Victor of Marseille, who took great pains for the introduction of the new Gregorian or Roman office and the abolition of the said Musarabic office.

or Mozarabic: For this reason, and to put into effect what was ordained in this matter, upon the return from Rome of Dom Bernard, Archbishop of Toledo <note>Bernard de Sedirac, the first Archbishop of Toledo after the Reconquista</note>, a general council was held and assembled in Spain in the city of Toledo. There, the Clergy, Knights, and people of Toledo, Castile, León, Asturias, Galicia, and Portugal were present, or their deputies in great numbers. With Dom Bernard presiding and the King being present, great debates, seditions, and disputes were brought forward, as the Spaniards did not want to abandon their ancient ways to receive a new office <note>The "new office" refers to the Roman Rite, which the Papacy sought to standardize across Europe, replacing local liturgies like the Mozarabic Rite</note>. Consequently, since the arguments and reasons of one side or the other were not sufficient, they came to the furious and beastly manner of trial by duel, which was quite in use at that time. Two Knights were put on the field of battle: one for the King and others who desired the change of the office, and the other for the Knights and people who refused it and wished to retain the Musarabic or Mozarab rite. Juan Ruiz armed himself for the latter, and defeated him who fought for the Roman office, whose name is unknown. 

Nevertheless, such was the persistent insistence of the King, the Queen, the Archbishop of Toledo Dom Bernard, and others of that party, that the matter was submitted to another kind of judgment and experience, namely by fire. For this, having brought two books—one containing the office and usage of Rome, the other the ancient and Musarabic or Mozarab rite—they threw both into a very hot fire. From this fire, the Roman book immediately leapt out, so they say, and the other remained there without being in any way damaged or spoiled. Because of this, it was conjectured that both were agreeable to God; therefore, it was ordained that they would retain the ancient manner of office in the six parishes of the city of Toledo, and that in the great Cathedral Church and others thereof, the Gregorian or Roman office would be introduced and put into use, as well as throughout the rest of the Kingdom of Dom Alfonso. This was decided and agreed more by force, and to please the King and obey the Pope (who confirmed and approved it), than by good will. 

Nevertheless, in several Monasteries of Spain, the Musarabic or Mozarab office remained for a long time afterward; and in the same great Church of Toledo, even to this day, a Mass is sung in Musarabic or Mozarab every day in a chapel called *Corpus Domini* <note>Latin: The Body of the Lord</note>. The six parishes of this city in which this office was preserved had always been held by the Musarab or Mozarab Christians during the time when the Moors ruled there, and these parishes are Saint Luke, Saint Justus, Saint Torquatus, Saint Mark, Saint Eulalia, and Saint Sebastian. Now, whether the Musarabic or Mozarab office anciently used was the same as that held in this time, or if it has been reformed and corrected, is not a thing that can be doubted; for it is certain that in religion all things have been adapted to the times and inclinations and affections of those who have lived from age to age, especially concerning Ecclesiastical order and discipline. ### Of several other Christians.

Pierre Belon <note>A 16th-century French naturalist and traveler</note>, in book 2, chapter 85, of his observations of several

Christian nations most often send men, more or fewer

Lord Jesus Christ. From this, it follows that one counts twelve languages of

before all the others and includes all those obedient to the Roman Church. 
The second is the Greek nation, which is called *Romæos* <note>original: "Romæos", meaning Romans, as the Byzantines continued to call themselves</note> in their language; 
their obedience is not to the command of the Pope, but they 
have their own Patriarchs. The third nation is the Armenian, which 
approaches closer to our ceremonies than the Greek. The other nations follow 
consequently, such as the Jacobites <note>Members of the Syriac Orthodox Church</note>, who are from the region converted to 
the faith by Saint James the Greater. Others are Georgians, who are a 
nation that governs itself by its own laws, and who neighbor the Persians, having 
their borders at East India; they have been subjugated by no one, 
for they are absolute masters of themselves. Others are named 
Christians of the Girdle <note>A term often applied to Copts or Melkites, referring to the 'zunnar' belt they were sometimes required to wear</note>, who have taken the surname of Copts, who were 
brought to the faith by Saint Thomas <note>While the text credits St. Thomas, Coptic tradition primarily identifies Saint Mark as their founder</note>. Others are Indians, who are sent there 
from the land where Prester John <note>A legendary Christian monarch of the East, often associated in this period with the Emperor of Ethiopia</note> rules; they are very black, called *Abyssinians*. 
And because they are baptized in fire, they bear three burns: one 
between the two eyes above the nose, the other two are near the tem- 
ples; they are not as black as the Ethiopians. Others are Nestorians, 
others are called Maronites, who are the same as the Arabs <note>Meaning they share the same language</note>. 
Each of these nations has a chapel of its own, because they all 
differ on some points; they are maintained by the money sent to them 
by the princes of their provinces. The Greeks hold the Choir and have the 
guardianship of the site of Calvary, and the Latins have the guardianship of the Sepulchre.

The cause and argument for the conversion of these peoples was that Taicosama was made a *Came* <note>Original: "Came." The people recognized this through the vivid reasoning preached to them. A vision of a cross also occurred, which moved these peoples to desire baptism and renounce the *Cames* and *Fotoques* <note>Original: "Fotoques." Refers to *Hotoke*, a term used for Buddhas or enlightened beings.</note>, who are their gods and their saints. Things have progressed so far in the Christian Religion that there are presently seven or eight Christian Churches: namely at Bungo <note>Original: "Bungy."</note>, a city situated toward the North at some 33 and a half degrees from the equator; the second at Kuchinotsu <note>Original: "Cutamé."</note>; the third at Hirado <note>Original: "Firande."</note>, which is a neighboring island subject to Japan and very rich, where the number of Christians exceeds two thousand; the fourth at Hakata <note>Original: "Facata."</note>; the fifth in the great city of Kagoshima <note>Original: "Cangoxima."</note>, which is the southernmost of the island, located at some 21 degrees and some hundred leagues from Bungo; the sixth is at Yamaguchi <note>Original: "Almangut."</note>, and this Church and that of Kagoshima were the first ever established on this island, around the year of our Lord 1548. The seventh is that of Kyoto <note>Original: "Meaco."</note>, the capital city of all Japan, where the preachers had the most difficulty because of the university and monasteries of the idolaters who resisted them; nevertheless, the King supporting our own, they preached there freely and converted a great number of people to holy baptism. The last is that of Sakai <note>Original: "Sacaian."</note>, a city situated near Kyoto, but which lives under its own laws without being subject to any King whatsoever. In all these Churches, one sees the newly converted Japanese so ardent in the Christian faith that it is impossible for any fear of death or torments to turn them away. See Father Torres, Jesuit, in his letters from Japan; Father Xavier in his letters from said Japan; Father Frois in his letters; and Father du Jarric of Toulouse in his books on the *History of the East Indies*.

## *On the Origin or Invention of letters, or Characters of languages.*

### CHAP. LVI.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'M' featuring a figure with a fish-like tail amidst foliate scrolls.</image-desc> MARCUS Tullius Cicero, in the first book of his *Tusculan Disputations*, has inferred from the invention of letters the divinity of the soul and spirit of man. He argues that human nature is too excellent to be considered born and proceeded from a merely physical existence alone, saying:
> What is that power, then, which investigates the hidden? What is called invention and thought—does it seem to you to be composed of this earthly, mortal, and decaying nature? Or he who first (which seemed to Pythagoras to be of the highest wisdom) gave names to all things; or he who gathered scattered men and called them to a society of life; or he who limited the sounds of the voice, which seemed infinite, to a few marks of letters? Which gift, delivered from God to mortals, all wise men endowed with judgment and virtue have followed with admiration and the highest gratitude of mind. <note>original: "Quid illa vis, quæ tandem est, quæ inuestigat occulta? ... admiratione & summa gratitudine animi prosecuti sūt."</note>

Caelius Rhodiginus <note>An Italian humanist and scholar (1450–1525) known for his "Antiquae Lectiones."</note> in book 4 of his *Ancient Readings* says:
> For what is that majesty of writing which provides us with knowledge of such great things, prolongs antiquity, and lets nothing perish? And while time consumes all things, writing forces them to yield to our hands. What is more magnificent than this? What is equally to be wondered at? That this has been given to man, over which not even the greedy rapacity of death has any right. What of the volumes of so many and such great laws woven together—what eminence of a more civilized life do they finally offer? What of the faith of sayings and agreements contained in public records against the depravity of minds? I would dare say that without hands <note>Refers here to the act of writing or manual recording</note> we would not only be unarmed, but even more unhappy than the beasts. How could that divine light have the use of reason if deprived of every resource? Hence it seems to me those have done rightly who pronounced that the hands are the servants of reason and wisdom. <note>original: "Quid enim illa scribendi Maiestas ... rationis ac sapientiæ ministras esse manus pronunciarunt."</note>

On the contrary, the saying of that cursed Emperor Licinius <note>A Roman Emperor (308–324 AD) and rival of Constantine; Christian historians often portrayed him as an illiterate hater of learning.</note>, enemy of the Christians, was judged altogether Barbarian and brutal when he held that these letters were the poison and common plague of men. For this reason Pythagoras, Plato, Cicero, and others have judged well and sanely of them, when they maintained that they were entirely derived and proceeded from the celestial and divine nature. “...this learning will make the Egyptians wiser and improve their memory, for a remedy <note>original Greek: "φάρμακον" (pharmakon), which can mean both a medicine/remedy and a poison.</note> for wisdom and memory has been discovered.” “O King, this doctrine will make the Egyptians more wise, more prudent, and more excellent in their memory: for the medicine or remedy for wisdom and memory has been found through it.” <note>original Greek: "τὸ μάθημα Αἰγυπτίους σοφωτέρους καὶ μνημονικωτέρους παρέξει..." This is a quote from Plato’s dialogue *Phaedrus*, where the god Thoth presents writing to King Thamus.</note> The same Plato in his *Philebus* demonstrates this Teuth <note>The Egyptian god Thoth, whom the Greeks identified with Hermes.</note> to have been the first inventor of these letters, and describes how he invented and organized his observations into the art of Grammar. One Philo Byblos <note>A scholar of the 1st–2nd century CE who claimed to translate the works of the ancient Phoenician Sanchuniathon.</note>, the Greek interpreter of Sanchuniathon of Beirut—who, in the time of Semiramis <note>A legendary Assyrian queen.</note>, described the deeds of the Phoenicians in the Syriac language, according to the report of Eusebius <note>The Bishop of Caesarea and a key historian of the early Church.</note>—says what follows: “Sanchuniathon was a most learned and curious person; for, demonstrating that he was not ignorant of all things which from their beginning were worthy of memory, he nevertheless did not fail to attempt to amplify and increase the things that Teuth had invented; for he was not ignorant that this Teuth was the first among mortals to find the letters, and by this means dedicated and consecrated to eternity those things that are memorable and worthy of remark.” The Egyptians called this Teuth *Thoyth*; the Alexandrians, *Thoth*; and the Greeks, *Mercury*. Diodorus Siculus <note>A 1st-century BCE Greek historian.</note> in book 1 speaks thus of the origin of human affairs: “From the beginning of this world, the sounds of the mouth being confused, it is held that little by little men formed and separated their voices, and that they imposed names on all things. And because they were in diverse places in this Universe, they did not use the same and similar words, but diverse and dissimilar ones, as also with the characters of letters.” This same author in book 2 teaches through the deeds of the ancients that the Egyptians attributed to themselves the invention of these letters. Saint Augustine in Question 69 on Exodus, regarding who the “introducers of letters” <note>original Greek: "γραμματῶν εἰσαγωγέῖς"</note> were—the Greeks having interpreted the word *Schotrim* <note>original Hebrew: שֹׁטְרִים, usually referring to officials or overseers.</note>, that is to say, officers, specifically: “Doctors who introduce letters,” <note>original Latin: "Doctores qui introducant litteras"</note>—used these following words:

> » Here it is clearly indicated that before the Law was given, the Hebrews had letters, ,,
> » though when they began to exist I do not know if it can be discovered; for to some ,,
> » it seems they began with the first humans and were brought down to Noah, and ,,
> » from there to the parents of Abraham, and from there to the people of Israel, but how this ,,
> » can be proven, I do not know. <note>original Latin: "Hic sanè fignificatur, quod ante legem datam habuerunt Hebræi litteras..."</note>

Suidas <note>The author of the *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note> on this subject under the word *Adam*, considering the perfection and great wisdom of the first man before he was seduced by Satan, speaks thus according to the judgment of the Church and its ancient theologians:

> » Adam, the first man, made by the hand of God and formed in the image and ,,
> » likeness of the Maker and Founder, who also obtained the honor ,,
> » of inhabiting Paradise. He is most rightly called the first wise man, ,,
> » and the primary figure and image drawn by God himself, since indeed ,,
> » he was abundantly adorned with all gifts, and carried about all the senses, both of mind ,,
> » and body, pure and intact. <note>original Latin: "Adam primus homo Dei manu effectus..."</note>

And a little later, speaking of the very great praises of the first Father of men:

> » He, therefore, was the one who distinguished individual things, ,,
> » and applied to all of them norms, and measures, and boundaries that are in no way ,,
> » to be rebuked. To him belong the arts and letters; to him the rational sciences, ,,
> » and those not bound by the laws of reason; to him belong prophecies, sacred rites, purifications, ,,
> » laws both written and unwritten; to him, finally, belong all— <note>original Latin: "Is igitur extitit qui difcreuit fingula..."</note>

Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> in Book 1 of his *Antiquities* maintains that Seth, the son of <margin>"</margin> Adam, and his children were the first to record in writing the science of astronomy, which they had learned from their first father Adam. This has moved the Arabs to attribute Theology and all the other sciences to this Seth, son of the said Adam; this is very true and very certain, according to what we have extensively discussed in the preceding chapters 2, 3, 5, and 9 of this present work. Theodore Bibliander <note>A 16th-century Swiss scholar and linguist.</note> in his commentary on the common nature of all languages and letters, in the chapter on the origin of letters [writes]:

<margin>" " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " "</margin>
It is consistent with reason that Adam—having fallen into sin through the deception of Satan and soon after being restored by divine grace—depicted his thoughts and the memory of past deeds through letters. This befits the excellence and dignity of the first man. For whom else should we consider to be that "God" or "divine man," as Plato says, who first invented letters? Or to whom rather should we attribute that "divine mind," as it seemed to Cicero and Pythagoras, who reduced so many distinct vocal sounds to fixed laws, and who marked the elements of human speech with suitable signs, than to Adam himself? For according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, he gave the most appropriate names to all things, which God also approved. Indeed, since the power of reason is most vast, and it manifests itself and comes before the senses through both words and works, no work of human reason appears more excellent to me than that which, by the marks and signs of letters, depicts the speech by which reason expresses itself. It even depicts reason itself, depositing it in books as if in a fortress to be preserved, and transfers itself into other minds whose bodies are separated by the greatest distances of both space and time. Thus the mind finds an organ suited to its nature, by which it may grasp divine and human things, things with bodies and things without bodies—and to say it once—whatever a human can comprehend with the mind, it may grasp with this instrument and present to others for perception and judgment. Furthermore, he [Bibliander] sufficiently refutes the opinions of those who attribute the receipt of letters to pagan authors, or to Moses, or to Abraham; or the single writing of the Prophet Enoch, who flourished about 800 years before the flood. It is also pleasing here to transcribe some ancient verses about the inventors of letters, which Petrus Crinitus <note>An Italian humanist scholar (1475–1507).</note> testifies to have found in a perpetual codex of the *Bibliotheca Septimana* in Book 17 of *On Honest Discipline*, chapter 1:

> ->*Moses was the first to scribe the Hebrew letters,*<-
> ->*With a wise mind, the Phoenicians established the Attic [Greek] ones.*<-
> ->*Abraham discovered the Syriac and also the Chaldaic,*<-
> ->*The ones we Latins constantly write, Nicostrata published.*<-
> ->*With no less skill, he brought forth the Egyptian ones,*<-
> ->*Ulfilas <note>original: "Gulfila," the 4th-century bishop who translated the Bible into the Gothic language.</note> produced the Gothic letters, which we see as the last.*<-

Pliny and Solinus <note>Roman authors who wrote on natural history and geography.</note> say that the Pelasgians <note>The indigenous inhabitants of the Aegean Sea region before the Greeks.</note> were the first who brought letters to the lands of the Latins. Some maintain that Nicostrata <note>A figure in Roman myth, also known as Carmenta, credited with creating the Latin alphabet by adapting Greek letters.</note>, mother of the Arcadian Evander, was the one who first gave letters to the Latins. Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>A Greek historian of the Augustan age.</note> in Book 1 recounts that the Arcadians under Evander, who came to Italy after the Pelasgians, brought letters there. Livy <note>Titus Livius, the primary historian of early Rome.</note> in the first book of his *Decades* calls this Evander the author of them, writing in this manner: "Evander, having then fled from the Peloponnese, came to these places where he ruled more by authority and majesty..."

Abraham Ortelius in his *Synonyms and Geographical Treasury* <note>Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598) was a famous Flemish cartographer who created the first modern atlas.</note> wrote: **Greece** <note>original: "Græcia"</note>, the most noble region of Europe, and the source and mother of all learning. By its inhabitants it was called **Hellas** <note>original: "ἑλλὰς"</note>. We have observed that its inhabitants were more frequently called by these names among the most ancient writers: **Achaeans** <note>original: "Achai, ἄχαιοί"</note>, **Achivi**, **Argives** <note>original: "Argiui ἀργεῖοι"</note>, **Danaans** <note>original: "Danai, δαναοὶ"</note>, **Dolopians** <note>original: "Dolopodes, δόλοπες"</note>, **Dorians** <note>original: "Dores, δωριεῖς"</note>, **Dryopes** <note>original: "δρύοπες"</note>, **Greeks** <note>original: "Graij, Graiugena"</note>, **Hellenes** <note>original: "ἑλληνες"</note>, **Ionians** <note>original: "Iones, ἴωνες"</note>, **Myrmidons** <note>original: "μυρμιδόνες"</note>, and **Pelasgians** <note>original: "πελασγοὶ"</note>. But Nicolaus Gerbelius <note>A 16th-century German scholar known for his descriptions of Greece.</note> also noted the same before us. Those who inhabit it today, I understand, name it **Romechi** <note>Likely a variation of "Romioi," the name used by Greek-speaking subjects of the Byzantine and later Ottoman Empires.</note>, and the Turks call it **Horomeli**. To Leunclavius <note>Johannes Leunclavius, a historian who specialized in Ottoman Turkish history.</note>, it is **Rumelia**. It is called **Phobel** by the "70 Translators" <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in Isaiah 61, and **Javan** among the same (where Saint Jerome reads "Greece") in Ezekiel 27 and Zechariah 9.

True Greece is **Achaia**: thus Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger</note> says in his 8th letter to Maximus. This is the same as **Hellas** according to Polyhistor. Regarding this, see Petrus Faber’s *Agonisticon*, book 3, chapter 15. In Xenophon’s *Cyropedia*, book 1, there are also **Asiatic Greeks**. Either I am mistaken, or they are on the coast of the Aegean Sea in Asia Minor, where there are many Greek colonies, or in the region of **Galatia** where the **Gallo-Greeks** <note>A group of Celtic people who migrated to and settled in central Anatolia.</note> dwell; whom Plutarch in his *Apophthegmata* calls the **Asian Greeks**. Greece is also a village from which the region takes its name, if Suidas <note>The Suda, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia and lexicon.</note> is to be believed; see "Achaia."

**Greater Greece** <note>original: "Græcia maior"</note>, or **Great Greece** <note>original: "Græcia magna"</note>, is a region of Italy according to Ptolemy. Between the Bruttii and the Salentini, Pliny calls it **Grecian Italy** in book 36, chapter 5, and the "coast of Greece" in book 3, chapter 5. To distinguish it, Livy in book 7 names the other "Further Greece," which is the true Greece, that is, **Hellas**.

**Achaia** <note>original: "ἄχαια"</note> is a region of Greece which Ptolemy also names **Hellas**. Pliny Caecilius calls it "pure Greece" in his 8th book of letters to his friend Romanus; today it seems to be called **Livadia**. There is another Achaia in the Peloponnese, which is specifically named by the same Ptolemy as "Achaia Propria" <note>Proper Achaia</note>; it is called **Ionia**, **Ias**, and **Olenus** by Diodorus. It is called **Aegialos** by Pausanias and Pliny. Herodotus writes in his *Polymnia* that the inhabitants were called **Aegialean Pelasgians**, that is, "people of the coast." Giacomo Gastaldi <note>An influential 16th-century Italian cartographer.</note> relates that it is now called **High Romania**. Apuleius calls the entire Peloponnese "Achaia"; concerning this, see "Lacedaemon." It is also the name of a city in the Peloponnese according to Thucydides, book 1. The region of Achaia, the village of Achaia, and the Achaean people are found in **Asiatic Sarmatia** <note>An ancient region covering parts of modern-day Southern Russia and Ukraine.</note> near the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea.</note>, according to Ptolemy, Strabo, Pomponius, Dionysius, Appian, and Arrian’s *Periplus*.

Some write **Achæa** <note>original: "ἄχαια"</note> as three syllables; Achaia is also a city on the island of Rhodes, witnessed by Diodorus and Athenaeus, book 8. It belongs to Parthiene according to Appian in his *Syriac Wars*. It is also in Macedonia and Crete, unless Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner, a Swiss polymath.</note> is mistaken regarding the "Achaean deer." Achaia is also a spring in Messenia near the city of Dorium, according to Pausanias. Aelian mentions an **Achaean Gulf** in *On Animals*, book 1, chapter 12.

Nicolaus Gerbelius, in his *Commentaries on the Description of Greece by Sophianos*, in the chapter on the names of Greece, wrote the following:

Before the Trojan War—which is remembered among historians as being among the most ancient events—I find that the Greeks performed nothing worthy of memory under a common name, either at home or abroad. This lasted until Alexander, son of Priam, also called **Paris**, under the most unfortunate omens, snatched away **Helen**, the wife of Menelaus, as we also said above. For then, at the city of Aulis in Boeotia, a conspiracy of the Greek leaders...

# History of the Origin of the [Greeks]
<meta>The header is partially cut off but likely reads "History of the Origin of the Greeks" based on the subject matter.</meta>

...and by the common consent of all Greece, war was brought upon Priam <note>The King of Troy during the Trojan War.</note>. For this reason, Thucydides <note>A famous Athenian historian (c. 460–400 BC).</note> records that before the time of Hellen—whom this same author calls the son of Deucalion, while the commentator on Pindar calls him the son of Prometheus and Clymene, and others the son of Ion—the Greeks were not called by a single name. Instead, he relates that individual peoples, especially the **Pelasgians** <note>The indigenous people who lived in Greece before the arrival of the Hellenes.</note>, imposed their own individual names upon themselves. However, once Hellen and his sons gained power in Phthiotis <note>A region in southeastern Thessaly.</note>, they allied themselves with neighboring cities for the sake of trade. From this social interaction, having become accustomed to one language, they also adopted a single name: specifically, they were called **Hellenes** after Hellen. Nevertheless, this name did not immediately spread to the entire nation, but only to the Phthiotians who served under Achilles in the Trojan expedition. 

Thus, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist.</note> asserts quite learnedly (as is his custom) that Greece often changed its name, and was most often named after its kings. Because a King **Graecus** was born there, it was called **Greece**. Because **Hellen** (as we have said) had presided over the kingdom there, the Greeks were named **Hellenes**. Homer named these same people—and not just in one place—**Myrmidons**, **Hellenes**, and **Achaeans**. However, the Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator or annotator of classical texts.</note> of Homer affirms that only Thessaly was called "True Greece" by Homer. We shall very briefly explain the names that are more common and well-known among authors, which are generally these: **Achaeans**, **Argives**, **Danaans**, **Pelopes**, **Hellenes**, **Ionians**, **Myrmidons**, and **Pelasgians**.

### ACHAEANS.

Xuthus, the son of Aeolus, having taken Creusa the daughter of Erechtheus in marriage, fathered two sons by her: **Ion** and **Achaeus**. One of these, namely Ion, took possession of Athens and called the region of Attica "**Ionia**" after himself, and the Athenians "**Ionians**." Achaeus, after he had stained himself with the slaughter of his own people, fled into Thessaly; having become the Lord of that region, he called the Thessalians "**Achaeans**" after himself. Therefore, Homer often uses the term <term>metonymy</term> <note>original: "μετωνυμίαν"; a figure of speech where a thing or concept is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it.</note> to call Greece "**Achaia**" and the Greeks "**Achaeans**," as in the third book of the *Iliad*:
> To Argos [famed] for horses and Achaia [famed] for beautiful women. <note>original: "Ἄργος ἐς ἱππόβοτον καὶ ἀχαΐδα καλλιγύναικα."</note>
And in the eleventh book of the *Iliad*:
> But come, let us see if we might somehow arm the sons of the Achaeans. <note>original: "Ἀλλ' ἄγετ' αἴκέν πως θωρήξαμεν υἷας ἀχαιῶν."</note>
The remaining matters pertaining to the Achaeans in Thessaly we shall reserve for our later discussion.

### ARGIVES.

The **Argives** were named after **Argus**, the son of Apis and Niobe, as the Scholiast of Homer preferred. There are those who think the Argives and the region of **Argia** received their name from the fame of the city itself. We will discuss this matter more copiously a little later in the section on Regions. But if you inspect the picture <note>Likely referring to a map or engraving included in the original volume.</note> diligently—as I have frequently advised you to do—you will see the city of **Argos**, and you will also see the region of Argia, beautifully and carefully rendered in capital letters. Didymus, in the eighteenth book of the *Odyssey* (if the title is correct), records that all of Greece is called **Argos** because that city is situated in the middle of Greece. Strabo, however, reports in his eighth book (citing Euripides) that **Danaus** lived in the citadel of the Argives. Since he far surpassed previous kings in the greatness of his deeds, he decreed throughout all of Greece that those previously called **Pelasgians** should be named **Danaans** after him, so that this would thereafter be used as their common name. Virgil used both names in these two verses:

### THE DANAANS.

We have already mentioned that the **Danaans** <note>One of the names used by Homer for the Greeks, specifically those from Argos.</note> received their name from **Danaus**. However, a commentator on Homer has explained this matter more clearly. He says that **Belus** (the son of Neptune and Libya, after whom the region of Libya was named, and brother of Agenor), while ruling in Egypt, married Anthinoé, the daughter of the Nile. From her, he fathered twins: **Aegyptus** and **Danaus**. Belus placed Danaus in charge of Libya and Aegyptus in charge of Arabia. Aegyptus conquered the Melampodes people, and the region subsequently took the name "Egypt" from him. Aegyptus had fifty sons by various wives, and Danaus had the same number of daughters. 

When the brothers Danaus and Aegyptus fell into conflict over the kingdom (as often happens), Danaus was warned by an oracle that he would be killed by one of his grandsons. Consequently, he ordered his daughters to kill his brother's sons <note>Danaus had his daughters marry the sons of Aegyptus and kill them on their wedding night to prevent the prophecy.</note>, though one or two were spared. After this crime was committed, Danaus was advised by the goddess **Minerva** to build the first ship. He called it a *pentekontoros* <note>meaning "fifty-oared ship" (πεντηκόντορον)</note> after the number of his daughters, which, as we said, was fifty. Fleeing from Libya in this ship with his daughters, he arrived at Rhodes. There, after erecting a statue of **Lindian Minerva**, he named the destination Argos. **Gelanor** <note>The text reads "Helenor," but classical myth identifies this king as Gelanor.</note>, who was then ruling there, surrendered the administration of the kingdom to Danaus, who then renamed the people of Argos "Danaans" after himself.

### THE DOLOPES.

The **Dolopes** lived in Thessaly; from them, the region of Thessaly itself and the city of Clymene were called **Dolopis**, as recorded by *Apollonius of Rhodes*. This land was once held by **Peleus** <note>The father of the hero Achilles.</note>, who granted the region of Dolopia to **Phoenix** when he arrived as a kinsman. Peleus also entrusted his young son, **Achilles**, to Phoenix to be educated. Homer mentions the Dolopes in this verse from the 9th book of the *Iliad*:

> I dwelt on the far borders of Phthia, ruling over the Dolopes.
<note>original: "Ναῖον δ' ἐσχατιὴν Φθίης, δολόπεσσιν ἀνάσσων." - Homer, *Iliad* 9.484</note>

In this passage, Phoenix narrates this entire history over several verses. Since the **Myrmidones** (whom we will discuss later) fought under Achilles and the Dolopes under Phoenix, Virgil joined them in these verses from the 2nd book of the *Aeneid*:

---

> *...What Myrmidon or Dolopian,*
> *or soldier of harsh Ulysses, could refrain*
> *from tears in telling such things?*
<note>original: "Quis talia fando / Myrmidonum, Dolopumue, aut duri miles Vlyssi / Temperet à lachrymis?" - Virgil, *Aeneid* 2.6–8</note>

**Didymus** <note>A Greek scholar and grammarian in Alexandria.</note> writes in his commentary on the 11th book of the *Odyssey* that Scyros was a city of Dolopia. Furthermore, a commentator on **Pindar** has left a record that the Dolopes were excellent slingers.

### THE HELLENES.

We have previously recounted from **Thucydides** the occasion upon which the Greeks were named **Hellenes**. However, **Eustathius** <note>A 12th-century scholar and Archbishop of Thessalonica known for his commentaries on Homer.</note>, in his notes on the 11th book of the *Iliad*, records that **Hellas** was a city of Thessaly that obtained its name from a king, after whom the name was eventually applied to all Greeks. Homer uses the names **Phthia** and **Hellas** interchangeably...

## IONIANS.

We said above regarding the Achaeans that **Ion**, the son of **Xuthus**, occupied Athens and called the whole of Attica "Ionia" and the people of Attica "Ionians"—a fact we explained carefully in our description of the geography of Greece. A commentator on Homer <note>The "Scholiast"</note> in his thirteenth book names him **Xanthus**, whom he had called **Xuthus** in the first book. Therefore, the passage must be corrected according to **Eustathius** <note>A 12th-century Byzantine scholar and Archbishop of Thessalonica known for his extensive commentaries on Homer.</note>, who writes that **Hellen** was the son of **Deucalion**; from Hellen came Xuthus, and from Xuthus came Ion and Achaeus. It is from these figures, as we have said, that the Greeks are named Hellenes, Ionians, and Achaeans.

## MYRMIDONS.

The **Myrmidons** are Greeks who, as we touched upon regarding the Dolopes, served under **Achilles** as Phthiotians. Homer usually joins them with the rest of the Greeks, as appeared from his verses which we cited. Regarding the origin of the Myrmidons, the following story is told among the ancients. Between Attica and the Peloponnese, situated in the mouth of the Saronic Gulf, is the island of **Aegina**, facing Attica and Athens. While **Aeacus** reigned there, **Juno** <note>The queen of the gods, often depicted as vengeful against the children of Jupiter's lovers; Aeacus was the son of Jupiter and the nymph Aegina.</note> corrupted the whole island with a plague. As the destruction spread further and further, the island was stripped of its people. Aeacus, unable to endure this solitude and the lack of citizens, prayed to his father **Jupiter** to restore the ruined population in any way possible. Jupiter gave to his son a huge swarm of ants, which he had spotted on a nearby oak tree, transformed into humans. From these, they were named Myrmidons, since <term>myrmex</term> <note>original: μύρμηξ</note> is the Greek word for an ant. However, **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian from the 1st century AD.</note> records in his eighth book that the inhabitants of Aegina were not born from ants, but received this name because they lived in caves and excavated hollows after the fashion of ants. Eustathius, in the eleventh book of the *Iliad*, thinks they were named after a man called Myrmidon, son of Perôe. In that passage, he mentions both the mythological story and Strabo’s opinion.

## PELASGIANS.

**Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer.</note>, in his *Description of Arcadia*, has recorded that **Pelasgus** was the first to be placed in command of the empire in Arcadia, because he excelled the rest in the beauty and strength of his body, as well as the excellence of his mind. For Pelasgus was the first to devise little huts so that men might be safe from the cold and heat; next, he invented tunics made from the hides of animals, which were still being used in Euboea and Phocis in Pausanias's time. Because of these extraordinary virtues of the man, the region itself was called **Pelasgia** and the people **Pelasgians**. Eustathius writes that Pelasgus was the son of **Eumonidis** and **Larissa**, and that his brothers were **Phthius** and **Achaeus**; from Pelasgus came Pelasgia and Pelasgic Argos, etc.

### Languages of this Universe.

...beginning, was unknown in the time of the Patriarch **Abraham**, and of the first monarch of Assyria; and yet **Eusebius**, in the *Chronicle* <note>original: "liur. des temps" refers to the *Chronicon* of Eusebius, a 4th-century work on universal history.</note> puts forward, under the reign of **Ninus**, son of **Belus**, a certain **Europs**, who commanded the **Sicyonians**, who was the son of **Aegialeus**, and at that time the Sicyonians held command over all of Greece. And if the history of **Troy** has any truth to it—as **Herodotus**, **Thucydides**, and several other ancient authors believe—one finds no historian whatsoever who, before this Trojan war, makes much account of the Greeks, or who recounts that this nation made itself known in general under this title of "Greeks"; rather, each nation tried to advance itself, to carry its own name, and to hold the power of sovereignty over its other neighbors. For although the poet **Homer** makes **Agamemnon** the Colonel <note>The author uses "Colonel" in the 16th-century sense of a supreme commander or leader of a large force.</note> and chief of the Greeks, it is nonetheless true that each city, country, and Prince held their own place and raised their own equipment for a common cause and defense, and to avenge the injury done to the King of Sparta, **Menelaus**. This is amply verified by **Thucydides** in the preface of the first book of his Greek histories, reporting that before the Trojan war, **Hellas** <note>The Greek name for Greece.</note> had done nothing, and that the whole country was not yet honored with this name; seeing as before **Hellen**, son of **Deucalion**, this name was unknown, and each people had its own, and the Greeks themselves were named **Pelasgians**. So it was that those who were the true Greeks carried the name of **Hellenes**, and the others had their particular appellations, without being placed or counted among the "Barbarians" for that reason. As for this word "Greece" given to the whole region, it came—as **Pliny** says in book 4, chapter 7—from the King of the country named **Graecus**, just as from **Hellen**, the country was called **Hellas**. But I do not know from where **Pliny** fished this out, as it happens that **Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century AD traveler and geographer famous for his "Description of Greece."</note>, a very diligent researcher of the antiquities of all Greece, does not speak of this King at all, and **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient world.</note> testifies that the Greek country took the name of Greece from a village carrying this title. Wherever the name took its origin, it has nonetheless gained such an extent that, whatever misfortune followed this nation and whatever alterations it felt, its name has remained with it. 

Now, these **Hellenes** were called by the aforementioned poet **Homer** as **Achaeans** and **Myrmidons**, although some have since held that **Thessaly** alone bore the name of Greece. However it may be, here are the most known names used formerly among the Greeks to recognize one another in their divisions, leagues, and factions, namely: **Achaeans**, **Dorians**, **Argives**, **Danaans**, **Dolopes**, **Hellenes**, **Ionians**, **Myrmidons**, and **Pelasgians**. 

The **Achaeans** had this origin: **Xuthus**, son of **Aeolus**, took **Creusa**, daughter of **Erectheus**, in marriage, by whom he had two children, **Ion** and **Achaeus**. The eldest, **Ion**, was Lord of Athens and the Attic country; but **Achaeus**, stained by the blood of his subjects, was constrained to flee to **Thessaly**, and making himself master of the country, he called the inhabitants by his name. From this, it later happened that since **Corinth** was in **Achaia** and was the richest city in Greece, the rest of the Greeks were called **Achaeans**, and Greece bore the name of **Achaia**—although, as **Pausanias** says in book 7, only the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans.</note> and **Argives** among all the Peloponnesians bore the name of Achaia by special right. 

The **Dorians** were so named by **Dorus**, son of **Hellen**, who, having emerged...

# History of the Origin of the [Nations]

the Egnites <note>Likely referring to the Aeginetans, the people of the island of Aegina.</note> rushed thereafter into the Peloponnese. But it is likely that the **Argives** were named after the capital city of the country, called **Argos**, even though some hold that they bear this title from **Argus**, son of **Apis** and **Niobe** <note>The text reads "Apri-Niobé," likely a printer's error for Apis and Niobe, legendary figures in the founding of Argos.</note>. However, **Pausanias**, in his second book, gives them another source, saying that the **Argive** region took the name of **Argus**, grandson of **Phoroneus**, by one of his daughters, and he provides a long discourse on this history, which can be seen in his *Corinthiaca* <note>Pausanias was a 2nd-century Greek traveler; his "Corinthiaca" is the section of his *Description of Greece* covering Corinth and Argos.</note>. Now, since the **Argive** princes once held the empire of almost all of Greece, it also happened—either because the city of **Argos** was in the middle of Greece, or because of the power of its princes—that the whole country bore the name of **Argia**, and the inhabitants were called **Argives**. 

After this, **Danaus**, King of **Argos**, having more power than the kings his predecessors, desired that his subjects—who previously called themselves **Pelasgians** <note>The original text uses "Pelagiotes," referring to the Pelasgians, the ancient indigenous people who inhabited the Aegean region before the coming of the Greeks.</note>—should bear the title of **Danaans**, in remembrance of him and for a perpetual memory of his glory and greatness. An edict to this effect was published throughout all Greece, so much so that both the Greeks and the Romans <note>original: "Latins"</note> have adopted this name of **Danaans** when wishing to mention the Greeks in general. 

Now this **Danaus** had come out of **Libya**; he was the son of **Belus** and **Antinoe**, and had a brother named **Aegyptus**, from whom the land of **Egypt** takes its name. A dissension having arisen between the brothers concerning the sovereignty, **Danaus**, having caused the children of his brother to be killed <note>According to myth, Danaus fled with his fifty daughters (the Danaïdes) to escape his brother's fifty sons.</note>, fled to Greece. At **Argos**, **Gelanor** <note>The OCR reads "Helenor," but the historical king of Argos who abdicated to Danaus was Gelanor.</note>, who commanded there, gave **Danaus** a share in his lordship; he, as has been said, wished his subjects to bear his name. This is why the poet **Virgil**, in almost all his verses where he mentions the Greeks, gives them no other name than **Danaans**, whether he is referring to the antiquity of the name or whether he wishes to blame them for the treacheries of this prince. 

The **Dolopes** were in **Thessaly**, from whom both the Thessalian land was named **Dolopia**, and the city **Clymene** was named **Dolopis**. Over this land **Peleus** once reigned, who left the region to **Phoenix**, his relative, who had come to visit him, putting his son **Achilles** into his hands to be instructed. Thus, at the Trojan War, the **Dolopes** were under the charge of **Phoenix**, and the **Myrmidons** under the leadership of **Achilles**, according to the account of **Homer** in the second book of the *Iliad*. 

As for the **Myrmidons**, according to **Strabo** in his eighth book, they are **Phthiotians** and **Aeginetans**, who were so called not because they sprang from ants coming in swarms from a tree and changing into men, as the Greek fables would have it, but rather because they lived in caves and subterranean places, just as ants do—which the Greeks call in their language *ant* <note>original: "μύρμηξ" (myrmex)</note>. Others hold that they were so named by a lord and ancient hero called **Myrmidon**, which is quite plausible since other nations have also partly taken the name of those who first commanded them. Regarding this, one may see what **Eustathius** <note>A 12th-century Byzantine scholar and archbishop who wrote extensive commentaries on Homer.</note> writes on the second book of **Homer**'s *Iliad*. 

Above, we have cited ancient authors mentioning the **Hellenes** and why they were so called; but having since researched other reasons for this name, we have found that there was in **Thessaly** a city named **Hellas**, having taken this name from a king who commanded there, and from it the entire Greek country was afterwards named. Others hold that the Greeks received this title from a certain giant named **Hellech**, who descended from the race of **Japheth**, son of **Noah**, and who was present at the [Tower of Babel...]

Indeed, even the **Gauls** and **Italy** had **Greek** colonies in their lands; as for **Spain**, it is a certain thing that various flights of **Greeks** once populated it, as can be gathered from the ancient *Annalists of Spain*.
