> And indeed that ancient division was between the **Attic** and the **Asian** styles, since the former were considered concise and pure, while the latter were held to be inflated and hollow. In the former, nothing was superfluous, while in the latter, judgment and moderation were mostly lacking. Some, including **Santra** <note>A Roman grammarian and playwright.</note>, believe this happened because, as the Greek language gradually flowed into the neighboring cities of **Asia**, those not yet sufficiently skilled in speaking desired eloquence. Therefore, they began to express in a roundabout way things that could have been stated directly, and they continued in that practice. To me, however, it seems that the nature of both the speakers and the listeners created the difference in speech: for the **Attics**, being refined and discerning, would tolerate nothing hollow or redundant. The **Asian** people, on the other hand, being otherwise more tumid and boastful, were inflated by a vainer glory in speaking. Soon, those who divided these styles added a third, the **Rhodian** genus, which they wish to be a middle ground, mixed from both. For they are neither as concise as the **Attics** nor as abundant as the **Asians**, so that they seem to possess something of the Nation and something of their founder. For **Aeschines** <note>An Athenian orator and rival of Demosthenes.</note>, who had chosen this place for his exile, brought the studies of **Athens** there; and just as seeds degenerate depending on the sky and soil, they mixed that **Attic** flavor with a foreign one. What I think of such an ancient and controversial matter, I have explained in the *Commentary on the Best Kind of Hebrew Grammarians*, so it seems superfluous to repeat it here. Furthermore, the Greek language was not only once distributed into five types—the common dialect, Attic, Aeolic, Doric, and Ionic—for Herodotus counts four dialects among those who use the Ionic tongue. The Rhodians, Cypriots, Cretans, and Chalcidians also had something peculiar to themselves. Nevertheless, all dialects can and should be measured against a single rule and standard. I feel the same regarding all the idioms of the nations to which the Greek speech was once extended. For it was not celebrated in Hellas <note>Greece</note> alone, but also in Epirus, the Peloponnese, Illyria, Macedonia, Thrace, Asia Minor, and in Syria (in which there were most eloquent men in the Greek language, such as Philo, Josephus, and many others). Greek letters flourished especially in Cilicia, in the town of Tarsus, the homeland of Saint Paul; likewise in Alexandria in Egypt.

But it is a very difficult thing to know if the first and most ancient Greeks used the same and similar letter characters, numbering 24, which we use today in Greek books written by hand and printed in various places—be it in France, Italy, Spain, Germany, or other regions of this universe—given that the Greek characters we have at present are quite diverse and unlike the old and ancient Greek characters, of three different styles, which are found engraved and raised in relief here and there on old medals <note>In the 16th century, "medailles" usually referred to ancient coins discovered in archaeological contexts.</note>.

Gilbert Génébrard <note>A 16th-century French scholar and Benedictine</note> on folio 86 of his *Chronology*, following Justin Martyr in his *Address to the Greeks* and other ancient authors, writes that the name Cadmus is derived from <term>מקרם</term> <note>original Hebrew: *mi-kedem*, meaning "from the East" or "the Oriental"</note>. He came from the East to the West, before the expedition of Jason and the Argonauts, sailing from Phoenicia to Boeotia to subdue Europe. He gave the Greeks sixteen letters—that is, the visual form, the outlines, and the names of the letters. For the Greeks had hardly tasted these disciplines until a thousand years later. The Greeks themselves acknowledge that these elements were not their own invention, as found in Varro’s first book *On Analogy*. When the Greek philosopher Crates raised a grammatical question in Greece as to why "Alpha" was not declined as <term>αλφατος</term> <note>original Greek: *alphatos*</note>—following the pattern of <term>Γραμμα</term>, <term>ματος</term> <note>original Greek: *gramma, grammatos*, the standard way to decline the word for "letter"</note>—other Greeks replied that these are not our words, but "barbarous" <note>meaning foreign or non-Greek</note>. Thus, by the Greeks' own confession, it is clear these letters were not their own. The Phoenicians, having received knowledge of letters from the Hebrews due to their proximity, gave the order and number of the letters to the Greek children through the mutual trade between the two nations, according to the Greek author Eupolemus.

Guillaume Postel, in the introductory letter of his treatise on Phoenician letters, wrote that Herodotus ensured that the letter characters used by the Ionians were the same and similar to those used in all ancient times by the Phoenicians, whom the inhabitants of those regions today call Punic. Some authors hold that the characters and language of these Phoenicians were used among them since the beginning of the world, specifically because Phoenicia, Holy Syria, and Judea were part of the Kingdom that used the original Hebrew language. This has moved some to remark that the first sacred place in the world, the sepulcher of Adam, was in the province of Phoenicia; for this reason, it was chosen by divine power for the use of that language. Because of this, the first aspect of the heavens is assigned to this province, so that celestial things relate in every way to divine things, illustrating this region where the use of the divine language was founded and restored—from which proceeded the fountain of sacred things and the property of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Pliny (Book 7, Chapter 56), Plutarch (Book 9 of *Table Talk*, Question 3), and Cornelius Tacitus (Book 11) report on this matter that Cadmus brought sixteen letters from Phoenicia to the Greeks. To these, Cecrops the Athenian and Linus the Theban later made additions; and during the Trojan War, Palamedes added four: <term>ΘΞΦΧ</term> <note>Theta, Xi, Phi, and Chi</note>, and just as many after him were added by Simonides Melicus: <term>ΖΗΨΩ</term> <note>Zeta, Eta, Psi, and Omega</note>. This is confirmed by Guillaume Postel in his treatise on Phoenician letters, asserting that several centuries before Cadmus, the Gauls had the use of letters, and that Sarron, King of the Celts, was the first who opened schools in Gaul to teach these letters. Josephus, in his book against Apion the Grammarian, wishes to claim that the Greeks used no letters before the time of the poet Homer. But without wandering too far, we shall assert that just as the Prophet Moses had—as I have remarked previously—two kinds of characters: one for sacred things, namely Hebrew, which is what we have, and the other for profane things, such as justice, policy, commerce, and similar worldly affairs, and therefore common and used by all the Jewish people (which is held to be the Samaritan script, that which the ancient Chaldeans used, and which was later communicated to the Phoenicians); so, just as from Hebrew came Syriac and Arabic, from Phoenician was born Greek, and consequently Latin, which consists entirely, or nearly so, of capital [letters]...

the Greeks, as can be seen, and as Pliny testifies in Book 7, <note>original: "liure chap. 58." The author likely refers to Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*, Book 7.</note> chapter 58, where he mentions an ancient bronze tablet brought from Delphi to Rome having this inscription here:

->Nausicrates the Athenian dedicated me.<-
<note>original Greek: "ΝΑΥΣΙΚΡΑΤΗΣ Ο ΜΕΝ, ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΕΜΕ ΤΕΘΕΚΕΝ." This is a standard ancient votive formula.</note>

By which he strives to prove that the ancient Greek letters were almost the same as the Roman or Latin ones; and in the preceding chapter 56, he posits those letters to have been Assyrian, or according to others, Syriac. But these are without doubt the Samaritan letters, which—with the exception of *Aleph* and *Yod*, <note>The author highlights these two letters as "mysterious," likely due to their symbolic weight in Kabbalistic or mystical linguistic traditions of the Renaissance.</note> two mysterious characters—are so similar to the Greek and Latin if one considers and takes them in reverse, <note>The author is observing that because Hebrew/Samaritan is read right-to-left and Greek/Latin left-to-right, the letter forms often appear as mirror images of one another.</note> that they are almost the same thing. This is further confirmed by Eusebius by the very naming of the Greek [letters], where, in imitation of Chaldean <note>term: Chaldean — a common early modern term for the Aramaic or Hebrew language and its script.</note>, an "A" has been added to most for their ending, with some transpositions in others, such as *Alpha* instead of *Aleph*, *Betha* for *Beth*, *Gamma* for *Gamel* or *Gimel*, and *Delta* for *Daleth*, etc.

Therefore, it is without doubt that these Greek letters proceeded from the Samaritan ones previously represented by us in a figure in the chapter on the Samaritan language, if one considers and takes them in reverse, the one and the other being almost the same thing. And the reason for this inversion was, according to some authors, that Noah—or Janus <note>In the Renaissance, the Roman god Janus was often identified with the biblical Noah, as both were seen as "fathers of nations" who lived through a transition between two worlds.</note>—and his children, having departed from the East to go to the West, because the movement of the West (that is to say, of the planets) is carried from the left to the right, the "prime mover" being contrary to it, they endeavored—in conformity with the Western movement of the heavens—to invert the use of the letters they had brought from Phoenicia. This seems to be recognized by Suidas, a Greek author describing the life of Abraham, and by Eusebius by the very naming of the Greek letters, in which, in imitation of Chaldean, an "A" was added to most for their ending, with some transpositions in others, such as *Alpha* instead of *Aleph*, *Betha* for *Beth*, *Gamma* for *Gimel*, *Delta* for *Daleth*, and so on for the others. And from what is deduced above, one may see Raphael Volaterranus <note>Raphael Volaterranus (1451–1522) was a famous humanist scholar whose *Commentaries* served as an early encyclopedia.</note> in book 33 of his commentaries; Polydore Vergil in book 1, chapter 6 of *On the Invention of Things*; Alessandro Sardi in book 1, chapter 1 of *On the Invention of Things*; and Guillaume Postel in his treatise on Phoenician letters or ancient characters of the Greek and Latin language.

Furthermore, the Greeks at their arrival were very unrefined, coarse, and barbarian, as recited by Thucydides, Plato, and Aristotle. The first of these were the Athenians, who civilized and polished themselves and their language, which they brought to perfection in the time of Plato, Aristotle, Isocrates, Demosthenes, Aeschines, and other learned Greek personages. Cicero mentions them in his *Brutus*, the Greeks having been so copious and abundant in words that they came to produce, through their inventions and traditions, four languages: the Attic, Doric, Aeolic, and Ionic. From each of these, the Greek poets, coming to choose and select various words and figures as it best suited their fancy, gave birth to another called "Common," <note>term: Common — referring to the "Koine" Greek, the standardized dialect of the post-Classical world.</note> and afterwards, under a single name, they called all five the Greek language.

What is more, the old and ancient Hebrew Testament, translated into the Greek language by the seventy Greek Interpreters <note>term: Septuagint — the influential Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally said to be the work of seventy (or seventy-two) scholars.</note>, and the New Testament first written and composed in Greek by the Evangelists, have made this language known in infinite places of this Universe. T. Bibliander <note>Theodore Bibliander (1509–1564), a Swiss reformer and linguistic scholar who sought commonalities between all human languages.</note>, in his *Commentary on the common reason of all languages and letters*, made such a judgment of this Greek language and of Latin:

> If anyone joins Greek to the Latin tongue, he will receive from both many seeds of the remaining arts. So that, moving from those languages, he will come to no art as a complete novice or newcomer. For he will draw his speech from those authors in whom there will be not just words—indeed there cannot be. For it is necessary that many things from other disciplines be scattered within. And by the same effort, he will come to know both the Greek and Latin languages. Add, that Greek is very learned and rich. And just as the Latin language can instruct and assist others with its abundance, so Greek increases and adorns both Latin itself and others: it is as necessary for the perfection of Latinity as Latin is for Italian or Spanish. No one has been absolutely skilled in Latin speech unless also imbued with Greek: for from Greek speech flowed Latin, and from Latin, Italian, Spanish, and French, to which nations the Latin tongue was once vernacular. Thus we find by experience that the Latin tongue becomes more fertile and fluent from the Greek, and from Latin the rest of Europe [derives its languages]: but especially those three that I just named: which it would be most beneficial to accustom to Latin speech, both so they might properly understand it and through it all the arts, and so they might render their native speech purer and more opulent, derived from it like more abundant water from a fountain. What of the fact that many things are committed to memory in Greek letters in history, the nature of things, private and public customs, medicine, and piety, which are drawn both more easily and more purely from the sources themselves.

>> ...not only in various dialects, but in each one of them. The Attic <note>The dialect of ancient Athens, prized for its clarity and used by authors like Plato.</note> and those dialects closest to Attic are the most necessary of all, because they are the most eloquent and most cultivated. Indeed, whatever the Greeks have produced that is worth reading and knowing has been recorded in these dialects. Other dialects are used by the authors of poems, who are not of such great importance to understand—especially since there is such a great difference between prose and verse, not only in the dialects but in the naming of things and the "color" of the speech, that it does not even seem to be the same language. Not without reason did Antonius—the character in Cicero’s writings <note>Referring to Marcus Antonius, a character in Cicero’s dialogue *De Oratore*.</note>—say that he did not dare touch the poets, as if they spoke a foreign tongue; although even among the poets, the best and those most worth reading are Attic: Euripides, Sophocles, Aristophanes, and what remains of Menander.

The same Theodore Bibliander <note>A Swiss Orientalist and linguist (1505–1564) who wrote *De ratione communi omnium linguarum*, one of the first works of comparative linguistics.</note>, in his commentary on the *Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*, has rightly asserted that the characters of the letters of the said Greek language, like those of other languages, emanated and proceeded from the characters of the letters of the Hebrew language, saying:

>> We previously judged that there were only sixteen Greek letters at the beginning, according to Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (Pliny the Elder), who recorded early histories of the alphabet.</note>, and that Palamedes <note>A mythical Greek hero said to have invented several letters of the alphabet during the Trojan War.</note> added four, and Simonides <note>Simonides of Ceos, a lyric poet credited with completing the Greek alphabet.</note> four more. Plutarch also testifies to the same. The order of the letters differs somewhat from the order of the Hebrew letters; for instance, Theta is placed earlier and Tau in a later position. For the order is reversed between the Hebrew letters, because the Hebrew *Thau* <note>original: "Thau"</note> would more correctly correspond to the Greek <term>Theta</term> <note>The eighth letter of the Greek alphabet (θ), representing a "th" sound.</note>, and the Greek <term>Tau</term> <note>The nineteenth letter (τ).</note> to the Hebrew *Teth* <note>original: "Theth"</note>. However, proverbs testify that the ancients also maintained that order where Alpha held the first place and Omega the last, such as the expression "the Alpha of the cloak-wearers" <note>original: "penulatorum Alpha"; a reference to a poem by Martial, meaning the "first" or "best" of a class of people.</note>. And in the Revelation of the Lord Christ it is said: *I am Alpha and Omega, the Beginning and the End*. Plutarch also explains with reasons why Alpha is the first of the letters. The Greeks also designated numbers by letters, which requires a firm and stable position for the letters—just as the twenty-four books of Homer, that most ancient Poet, are arranged by letters, and in the same way Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician whose work dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> arranged his interpretation of the ancient sayings of Hippocrates and others. Pliny and other good authors who mention ancient letters indicate that the shapes of the Greek letters have changed, and ancient inscriptions testify to the same thing. For example, Terentius Scaurus <note>A Roman grammarian from the 2nd century AD.</note> relates regarding the letters C and K, saying: "I would argue that C is more superfluous than K, since K, as among the Greeks, sufficiently expresses the power of the letter C; but some were deceived by the shape by which this letter was noted, not only among us, but also among the ancient Greeks." This is evidenced by the "Treaty of Greece" engraved on a bronze camel in Caesar’s gardens at the Temple of Powerful Fortune. The ancients wrote the <term>aspiration</term> <note>The "h" sound or breathing at the start of a word.</note> in the verse after the Latin manner; for example, the Boeotians <note>Inhabitants of Boeotia in central Greece.</note> wrote *Muha* <note>original: "Muha"</note> instead of *Musa*. Later writers divided this into two marks: the mark for the "smooth" breathing and for the "rough" or thick breathing, as Priscian <note>A famous Latin grammarian (fl. 500 AD).</note> also teaches in his first book. Scaurus also asserts that *h* is a letter and was written in the verse by the Greeks, and that the Attics used it to denote *hecaton* <note>original: "hecaton", meaning "one hundred".</note>, that is, One Hundred. We see this same mark today among the Greeks; in the "improper" diphthongs, they did not place a point under the vowels alpha, eta, or omega <note>α, η, ω</note>, but placed it to the right side: αι, ηι, ωι <note>Referring to the evolution of the iota subscript.</note>. Nor did the ancient Greeks have so many diphthongs. They also did not mark the prosodies—long, short, acute, grave, and circumflex—with signs as is done now. Indeed, the most ancient...

<page-num>671</page-num>
# Languages of this World.

That as long as the Persians—who previously competed with the Greeks in both arms and in letters—possessed these books containing the arts and natural sciences, the laws of the land, and ancient ceremonies, they could not be good Mohammedans <note>original: "Mahometistes." The author suggests that cultural memory through literature prevents total religious conversion.</note>. This is just as, in earlier times, Christian Prelates attempted to abolish the books of the Gentiles and Pagans, and totally erase the memory of their false and perverse religion, so that they might more freely become Christians and join the bosom of the Catholic Apostolic Church. Then, as these Saracens <note>A common historical term for Muslim peoples during the medieval and early modern periods.</note> moved into Egypt, they exterminated that Greek language from Alexandria along with its academic disciplines; and from Africa, they removed the Latin language, just as the Romans before them had exterminated the African language <note>Likely referring to the Punic language of Carthage.</note> along with its script. It is a most certain thing that as peoples and nations move from country to country, they shift and change their customs, languages, religions, kingdoms, and lordships. The victors snatch away everything beautiful they find in the lands of the vanquished, erasing their titles or destroying out of envy what they cannot carry away, in order to abolish the honor and virtue of the defeated so that only their own glory may be celebrated. Thus do the Turks behave today in their rule over the Christians; and in the same way, in ancient times, did the Goths, Alans, Huns, Vandals, Suebi, Heruli, Lombards, and other peoples. These conquerors, seizing various countries and regions at different times, disdained the local languages; neither understanding them nor knowing how to read them, they altered and corrupted them, creating new ones by the commingling and mixing of their own tongues with those they found. Meanwhile, the poor people remaining after such migrations learned the language of their cruel and inhuman usurpers in order to communicate with them and make themselves more agreeable subjects.

Furthermore, these Barbarians, relating everything to war and thereby despising the sciences and academic disciplines, burned the libraries and the books that had been preserved, in which the learned and scholarly had entrusted their names and memory. Consequently, the loss of languages was followed by the loss of the sciences and disciplines written within them. From this has come great ignorance in this world, which has lasted for a long time. From this process has also emerged—namely from Grammatical Greek—the vulgar Greek of today; and from Latin came Italian, Spanish, and French (in which are found, at least in Spanish, many Arabic words because the Arabs and Saracens held the Spanish territories for so long). From Grammatical Arabic came the vulgar and Moorish tongue used from Syria to the Strait of Morocco, which is as close to its source as Italian is to Latin. From German and French came English; from Arabic, Moorish; and from Tartar came Turkish (the speakers of which understand each other as do those of Italian and Spanish). And thus, from those languages which are in use today, others are being formed, and will be formed in the future.

Even though in the same country and language there appear differences in speaking and pronunciation within a short distance, it is nonetheless true that there are everywhere certain places more elegant and eloquent than others: such as were the Athenians in Greece, the Romans in Italy, and as are today the Tuscans [in Italy], the Castilians in Spain, the Saxons in Germany, the Persians in Asia, and the noble courtiers and learned scholars in France.

**Synonyms,** <note>original Greek: Συνωνυμία, *Synōnymia*</note> Synonyms are the sharing of names and verbs, as interpreted by Aristotle in Book 3, Chapter 2 of his *Rhetoric* dedicated to Theodectes, and by Romulus Aquila in his works. They say that the Greeks used these figures in their Greek tongue when they saw and recognized—in order to speak more eloquently and clearly in their language, the most beautiful and excellent in the world—that the dignity and excellence of a description could not be distinctly and properly signified and expressed by a single word or verb. Instead, they were accustomed to using several nouns and verbs to express it and make it understood more easily. Hermogenian calls these figures <note>original Greek: ποικιλίας τῆς ὀνομάτων, *poikilias tēs onomatōn*</note>, "varieties" or "diversities of names." Greek grammarians call nouns and verbs that differ in letters and vowels but have the same energy and meaning <note>original Greek: Συνώνυμα, *Synōnyma*</note>, which the Latins call <term>Univoca<note>Latin: "Univocal," meaning words with a single, clear meaning.</note></term>. Of these, Aeschylus made the most use among the Greek poets, as Aristophanes remarked. I can boldly say there is no language in the world so full and abundant in synonyms as Greek, as Julius Pollux, the Greek author, demonstrates to all who crave the Greek language in his book of *Onomastics* <note>A dictionary or vocabulary organized by topics rather than alphabetically.</note>, or dictionary of Greek synonyms; and Joachim Camerarius in his *Commentary on the Ornament of Synonyms*. I will not waste time taking the trouble to cite any Greek passages in this regard. Beyond these synonyms, we find in the Greek language <note>original Greek: ὁμώνυμα, *homōnyma*</note> "homonyms," which the Latins call <term>aequivoca<note>Latin: "Equivocal," words that sound the same but have different meanings.</note></term>, as well as <note>original Greek: πολυώνυμα, *polyōnyma*</note> "polyonyms," <note>original Greek: ἑτερώνυμα, *heterōnyma*</note> "heteronyms," <note>original Greek: ὁμογενέα, *homogenea*</note> "homogenes," <note>original Greek: ἑρετωγενέα, *eretogenea* — likely a typo for *heterogenea*</note> "heterogenes," <note>original Greek: ὁμοιδέα, *homoidea*</note> "homoideas," <note>original Greek: ἑτεροιδέα, *heteroidea*</note> "heteroideas," and others explained by Greek grammarians and philosophers in many places, and after them by Fabius Quintilian in his works. See J. Pollux, Book 8 of the *Onomasticon*; Martin Ruland the German in his book of Greek synonyms; Henri Estienne in his great *Greek Treasury* under the word <note>original Greek: συνώνυμος, *synōnymos*</note>; P. Grégoire, Book 2, Chapter 5 of the *Syntax of the Miraculous Art*.
Furthermore, synonyms are called in Hebrew <note>original Hebrew: *Nirdafim*</note>, meaning "sequential" <note>original Latin: *sequentia*</note>. Fray Luis <note>Likely referring to the Spanish mystic and author Luis de Granada.</note> in his *Globe*, Book 2, Chapter 2; regarding this, we shall say that we have a certain Hebrew author who composed a book titled *Ohel Moed* <note>Hebrew: "The Tent of Meeting," a famous 15th-century work on Hebrew synonyms by Solomon ben Abraham Urbino.</note>, concerning Hebrew synonyms.

**Epithets,** <note>original Greek: ἐπίθετα, *epitheta*</note> Epithets, according to the opinion of Aristotle in the third book of the *Rhetoric* to Theodectes, Chapters 2 and 3, and Hermogenian, are adjectives placed next to substantive nouns, as if one were saying <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐπιτίθεσθαι τῷ ὑπαρκτικῷ, *to epitithesthai tō hyparktikō*</note>, "those placed upon or added to the substantives" for the ornament and embellishment of speech. Macrobius, Book 1, Chapter 2 of the *Saturnalia*: <note>original Latin: *Adiectivum quod Graeci ἐπίθετον vocant*, "The adjective which the Greeks call an epithet."</note> Quintilian, Book Eight, Chapter Six: <note>original Latin: *ornat enim ἐπίτεθον quod rectè dicimus appositum, à nonnullis sequens dicitur, eo Poetæ & frequentius & liberius vtuntur, namque illis satis est conuenire...*, "for the epithet adorns, which we rightly call the 'apposed,' and which some call the 'following'; poets use it more frequently and freely, for it is enough for them that it fits..."</note>

[...to] come to the word to which it is attached: <note>The text begins mid-sentence, concluding a thought from the previous page regarding grammatical agreement.</note> **Gaza** <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a Greek humanist and translator who helped bring Greek learning to Italy.</note> for the word **Epithets**, uses the term **Adjectives**: therefore, Epithets are rhetorical figures, or adjective ornaments, which are placed and positioned before substantive nouns with a marvelous grace and beauty for three reasons and considerations: First, to discern and recognize the name of a thing found in two places, or which has two meanings; second, to demonstrate the property or characteristic of the thing; and finally, for its ornament and embellishment. Epithets differ from <term>antonomasias<note>original Greek: $\alpha\nu\tau\omega\nu\omicron\mu\alpha\sigma\iota\alpha\iota$. A figure of speech where a descriptive phrase replaces a proper name, such as calling a king "His Majesty."</note></term> in that Epithets are always placed and arranged in conjunction with a substantive noun, as I have already said. Antonomasias are placed and arranged on their own to stand for a proper and particular name, as **Fabius Quintilian** <note>A famous Roman rhetorician from the 1st century AD.</note> explains more extensively in several places in his works. If there is any language in the world abundant in Epithets, it is Greek, as those who set themselves to reading Greek authors can judge—principally **Homer** and **Pindar**. These authors hardly ever use substantives in their works without instantly accompanying them with admirable and excellent adjectives, which we may otherwise call Epithets. I will not recite passages from them at present, because I have not decided in this place to cite all the elegances and delicacies of the Greeks, which can be seen by reading their books. See **Varinus Phavorinus** <note>An Italian scholar and bishop (d. 1537) who compiled a famous Greek dictionary.</note> in his Greek dictionary and commentary on the entire Greek language, and **Henri Estienne** <note>Also known as Stephanus, a famous 16th-century printer and scholar.</note> in his great treasury of the Greek language under the words <note>original Greek: $ἐπιτίθημι$ (epitithēmi) meaning "to place upon" and $ἐπίθετος$ (epithetos) meaning "added" or "attributed."</note>.

**Metaphors** <note>original Greek: $Μεταφοραί$</note>, *metaphoræ*, metaphors, or "translations" <note>In this context, "translation" carries its original Latin sense of *translatio*, meaning to carry or transfer a meaning from one word to another.</note>, as **Aristotle** explains extensively in Books 3, chapters 2, 3, 10, and 11 of his *Rhetoric* dedicated to **Theodectes** and in his *Poetics*, are figures or tropes by which we mention one thing through a similarity, not by its own proper word or name, but by a different one. We can otherwise say these metaphors occur when nouns or verbs are transported and transferred from their proper place to another, where their own specific term is lacking, and where the transposed word is more eloquent and natural than the proper one itself.

**Cicero** in Book 4 of *Rhetoric addressed to Herennius*: <note>original Latin: "Translatio est cùm verbum in quandam rem transfertur ex alia re, quod propter similitudinem rectè videtur posse transferri, &c."</note> "A metaphor occurs when a word is transferred to one thing from another thing, because the similarity makes the transfer seem appropriate," etc. This form or figure of speech is of great force and efficacy, and is heavily practiced in many forms and manners in Greek poetry and oratory, as the aforementioned Cicero explains extensively in the place cited above, and in the third book of his work *On the Orator*.

**Verrius Flaccus** <note>A Roman grammarian of the 1st century BC.</note> says: <note>original Latin: "metaphorā esse quam Græci vocant, nos translationē, id est domo mutuatum verbum quo vtimur"</note> "that which the Greeks call a metaphor, we call a translation—that is, a word borrowed from its 'home' for our use." These metaphors ravish and silently carry away the readers or listeners to where they desire, and stir them with strange movements with great delight and pleasure. As Cicero remarks in his *The Complete Orator*: <note>original Latin: "Ex omni genere frequentissimæ trāslationes erūt, quod ea propter similitudinē transferunt animos & referunt ac mouent huc & illuc, qui motus cogitationis celeriter agitatus per se ipse delectat, & reliqua ex collocatione verborum quæ sumuntur quasi lumina magnum afferunt orationi ornamentum."</note> "Of every kind, metaphors will be the most frequent, because they transport minds through similarity and bring them back, moving them here and there; this movement of thought, being quickly agitated, is itself delightful. Furthermore, those words chosen for their arrangement act like lights, bringing great ornament to the speech." This same author in his treatise *On the Orator* has written many beautiful things about these figures, which bring a great enrichment to language.

...in speech, because they primarily supplement what is lacking in it. <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion on rhetorical figures.</note> **Quintilian**, after stating in Chapter 6 of his 3rd book that **Hermagoras** <note>A Greek rhetorician of the 2nd century BC.</note> was the first to teach metaphors and translations, says what follows in the sixth chapter of his eighth book: "Let us begin with that which is both the most frequent and by far the most beautiful; I mean the 'transfer' of meaning, which in Greek is called a **metaphor**." <note>original Latin: *Incipiamus ab eo quod cum frequentissimus est, tum longè pulcherrimus, translationem dico que metaphora Græcè dicitur*</note> In short, we find no forms or properties of speech more sublime, brave, or admirable—according to **Cicero** in the third book of *The Orator* cited above—than metaphors. These are called by the Greeks **carefully devised things** <note>original Greek: ἐπενενοημένα (*epenenoyména*)</note>, figures of speech that are difficult to handle and express. **Demosthenes** is greatly filled with them (having been criticized for this by **Aeschines**), as are **Plato**, **Thucydides**, **Homer**, **Pindar**, and other Greek authors. These writers have left almost no similarity or metaphor for anything in the world worthy of note that they have not used to embellish and illustrate their writings, as one can see more particularly by reading them. This is true even though we find the **Hebrew** authors using them in their works ordinarily along with allegories, parables, and various obscure enigmas, using **epitasis** <note>The intensification of a story or argument.</note>, emphasis, hyperboles, amplifications, and other types of figures and ornaments. This is seen by reading the Hebrew and **Chaldean** <note>A term often used historically to refer to Aramaic.</note> writings, and is amply verified by several Hebrew examples taken from the Hebraic scriptures by **Benito Arias Montano** <note>A 16th-century Spanish orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note> in his treatise on the division of things, "from which secret speech is established and symbols are sought." <note>original Latin: *ex quibus Arcanus instituitur sermo ac symbola petuntur*</note> The Latin authors do the same, but not as often as the Greeks.

Cicero and **Fabius** <note>Referring to Marcus Fabius Quintilianus.</note> in the places cited above, **Budé** in his commentaries on the Greek language, and **Henri Estienne** in his treatise on the conformity of the French and Greek languages [all discuss this]. Bringing this curious research to an end, I will only note that metaphors engender and produce other figures that the Greeks call **Catachresis** <note>original Greek: καταχρησις; the use of a word in a way that departs from its strict etymological meaning, often to name something that has no name of its own.</note>, "Abuses," allegories, similitudes, and others mentioned by **Marcus Tullius Cicero** in his *Orator*; by Fabius Quintilian in Book 6, Chapter 6, cited above, and in several other places in his works; by **Varinus Phavorinus** <note>A Renaissance scholar and lexicographer.</note> cited above; and by Henri Estienne in his *Great Treasury of the Greek Language* under the words **to consume** <note>original Greek: καταφάγομαι (*kataphagomai*)</note> and **metaphor**.

### On the Compounding of Greek Words.

The Hebrews firmly hold that just as God consists in a single Trinity and Unity, and that He gave the Hebrew language—which is His language—to **Adam** at the beginning of the world, in the same way, one finds in it no nouns or verbs that have more than three Hebrew letters. If any are found that have more, they are, according to them, foreign or doubled words.

The Hebrews call "root" what the Greeks call "theme" and the Latins "primitive" [stem], from which—through the addition of **servile letters** <note>original Latin: *litterarum feruilium*; these are specific letters in Hebrew used for grammatical functions like prefixes or suffixes rather than being part of the root.</note>—flow the persons, numbers, genders, nouns, and other such distinctions; and it is established that every theme consists of three radical letters. And this is not without a great mystery. For as a word is one... <note>original Latin: *Hebræi vocant radicem quod Græci thema & Latini primitiuum à quo per adiectionem litterarum feruilium fluunt deinde personæ numeri genera, nomina & alia id genre discrimina, & constat omne thema tribus radicalibus litteris. Idque non sine magno mysterio. nam vt vna est dictio...*</note>

This being presupposed, we shall say that there is no one making a profession of the knowledge of ancient languages who does not confess that there is no language in the world more suited for assembling, joining, and coupling words with one another than **Greek**. circumflex, aspirate, tenuis <note>The 'aspirate' refers to the rough breathing mark (spiritus asper), while 'tenuis' likely refers to the smooth breathing (spiritus lenis), indicating whether a vowel is preceded by an "h" sound</note>, apostrophe, hyphen, and hypodiastole <note>A comma-like mark used in ancient Greek to distinguish between words that might otherwise be confused</note>, variously shaped as those who are well-versed in this language know very well. The force and beauty of these are particularly declared by **Demetrius Chalcocondyles** <note>original: "Demetrius condile"; a Greek scholar who taught in Italy during the Renaissance</note>, a Greek author, in his Grammar; by **Theodore Gaza** in his books of the institution of Grammar; by **Clenard** in his Greek Grammar; by **René Guillon** in his *Handbook of Greek Accents*, in his annotations on the Grammar of Clenard, and his *Introductions to the Greek Language*; as well as by **Guillaume Budé** in his *Commentaries on the Greek Language*.

However, the Hebrew language also has its own accents, numbering 34, variously named and formed as I have said above and will say more amply hereafter. These languages—Greek and Hebrew—surpass Latin in this regard, as in others. Latin has attempted in some places to claim accents for itself, but with poor grace, as can be seen in **Quintilian**, book 1 of his *Oratorical Institutions*; **Diomedes**, book 2; and **Isidore of Seville** in his *Etymologies*.

It is a miraculous thing to see the beauty and enrichment provided by accents in the Greek language, which would have no grace or excellence if it were stripped and destitute of them; even though its perfection also depends on the masculine, feminine, and neuter articles which are placed before each noun. These are also placed before the infinitives of verbs with much more grace than in Hebrew. Hebrew uses four letters, **MLBH** <note>original Hebrew: "מלבּה" (Mem, Lamed, Beth, He); these are prefixes used to modify the meaning of verbs or nouns</note>, very elegantly and with an admirable brevity, placed at the front or head of their infinitives to express what other languages do through their gerunds and subjunctives, as **Michael Neander** teaches in the fourth part of his *Inquiries into the Hebrew Language*.

This aforementioned Hebrew language, in place of those Greek articles, uses the letters **H, A, M, T, L, H** <note>original: "ה,א,מ,ת,ל,ח"</note> before its indeclinable masculine, feminine, and common nouns, enriched and illustrated by points underneath. Both of these languages surpass Latin in this, which recognizes none of them, even though it seems that the words *hic, haec, hoc* <note>Latin demonstrative pronouns meaning "this" (masculine, feminine, neuter)</note> have such power and virtue. 

Indeed, we know the Greek language is adorned in most of its nouns by "inclined" figures, enclitics <note>Words that "lean" on the preceding word for their accent</note>, "fictitious" forms, synaeresis <note>The contraction of two vowels into one</note>, and crasis <note>The merging of two vowels into a long vowel or diphthong</note>. It also possesses ligatures, assemblies, and abbreviations of letters in its writing that are very pleasing and refined. It has something rare and marvelous among all other languages: its five Dialects or properties of speaking: **Attic**, **Doric**, **Aeolic**, **Ionic**, and **Common** <note>Also known as Koine</note>. 

The **Attic** dialect was named (according to the Grammarian) after **Attis**, daughter of **Cranaus**; the **Aeolic** from **Aeolus**, son of Hellen; the **Doric** from **Dorus**, son of Hellen; and the **Ionic** from **Ion**, son of Xuthus. The **Common** dialect participates in all four. The properties of these dialects are amply described by **John the Grammarian Philoponus**, **John Tryphon** the Grammarian, **Corinthus** the Grammarian, and **Plutarch** in the treatise on dialects found in Homer. 

In these dialects, the "passions" <note>A grammatical term for the modifications or transformations a word undergoes</note> found in their diction are divided into quantity and quality. The species of quantity are divided into *Endeia* <note>Deficiency or omission of a letter/sound</note> and **Pleonasm** <note>Using more words than necessary</note>. Those of quality are **Metathesis** <note>The transposition of letters or sounds</note> and **Metalepsis** <note>A complex figure involving the substitution of one word for another</note>. In total, there are five true passions: Pleonasm, Endeia, Metathesis, Metalepsis, and *Tinese* <note>Likely referring to Tmesis, the separation of parts of a compound word</note>. **Pleonasm** is a superabundance or superfluity of time and elements...

...**Endeia** <note>original: "Endeie"; from the Greek ἔνδεια, meaning "deficiency" or "want"</note> is a deficiency or reduction of a beat or an element. **Metathesis** is a transposition or mutation of an element from its proper place to another, which is otherwise called *enallaxis* <note>original: "εναλλαξις"; meaning exchange or substitution</note> and *hyperthesis* <note>original: "ὑπέρθεσις"; meaning transposition</note>, signifying Immutation or substitution. **Metalepsis** is a transumption or mutation of an element. **Tmesis** is a section or resolution of a compound word into two terms. 

The types of **Endeia** are nine in number: **Aphaeresis**, **Arse** <note>likely referring to a form of subtraction at the start of a word</note>, **Systole**, **Syncope**, **Synalephe**, **Ellipsis**, **Parellipsis**, **Ecthlipsis**, and **Apocope**. 

*   **Arse** is a removal or rejection at the beginning of a doubled syllable. 
*   **Systole** is a corruption occurring when long syllables are made short, and short ones long. 
*   **Syncope** is a cutting back or a rejection of a syllable in the middle of a word. 
*   **Synalephe** is a contraction or a union of two syllables into one vowel by the rendering of a tone in seven different ways. 
*   **Ellipsis** is a deficiency or rejection of a vowel in the middle that does not form a syllable. 
*   **Parellipsis** is the omission of doubled consonants. 
*   **Ecthlipsis** is an elision or rejection of a consonant between two syllables. 
*   **Apocope** is a cutting back of a syllable at the end of a word.

The types of **Pleonasm** <note>The use of more words or word-parts than are necessary for clear expression, used here for linguistic "addition"</note> are also nine in number: **Prosthesis**, **Anadiplosis**, **Ectasis**, **Epectasis**, **Diaeresis**, **Parenthesis**, **Diaplasmus**, **Paremptosis**, and **Proschematismus**. 

**Prosthesis** is the opposite of **Aphaeresis**; **Anadiplosis** is the opposite of **Arse**; **Systole** is the opposite of **Ectasis**; **Syncope** is the opposite of **Epectasis**; **Synalephe** is the opposite of **Diaeresis**; **Parenthesis** is the opposite of **Ellipsis**; **Diaplasmus** is the opposite of **Parellipsis**; **Paremptosis** is the opposite of **Ecthlipsis**; and **Proschematismus** is the opposite of **Apocope**.

*   **Prosthesis** is an addition or joining of an element at the beginning of a syllable. 
*   **Anadiplosis** is a doubling or different pronunciation of the first and second syllables by the same consonants. 
*   **Ectasis** is the lengthening of short syllables into long ones, and the shortening of long into short. 
*   **Epectasis** is a superabundance of a syllable in the middle of its accent. 
*   **Diaeresis** is a division, resolution, or disjunction of a syllable into two. 
*   **Parenthesis** is an interposition or addition of a vowel that does not itself form a syllable. 
*   **Diaplasmus** is a duplication or addition of a consonant in the middle of a word that does not form a syllable. 
*   **Paremptosis** is an equal division or addition of consonants in the middle that do not complete the syllable. 
*   **Proschematismus** is an addition of a syllable at the end.

There are also infinite other beautiful particularities and singularities of ornaments in this language, which are demonstrated more specifically following the Greek authors previously mentioned by: 
*   **F. Quintilian** in his works. 
*   **Constantin Lascaris** in his *Questions* <note>original: "Droietemates", referring to the *Erotēmata*, the first basic Greek grammar printed in the West</note>. 
*   **Brother Urbanus** in his *Institutions of Greek Grammar*. 
*   **Manuel Moschopoulos** <note>original: "Manuel maſchopolus"</note> in his books on Attic voices. 
*   **Linacre** <note>Thomas Linacre, an English humanist scholar</note> in his book on Greek Grammar. 
*   **George Fabricius** in his *Partitions of Grammar*. 
*   **Raphael Volaterranus** in book 34 of his *Commentaries*. 
*   **Julius Caesar Scaliger** in his books on *Poetics*. 
*   **Valentinus Erythraeus** in his *Grammatical Figures*. 
*   And infinite others treating this matter, including **Urbanus Bellunensis** in his *Greek Institutions* and **P. Gregoire** in book 16 of his *Syntax of the Admirable Art*. 

Regarding the majority of these particularities and singularities of ornaments, the Hebrews are not instructed in them at all, as **Benito Arias Montano** <note>original: "Benedictus Areas Montanus"</note> teaches in his *Common and Familiar Idioms of the Hebrew Language*. From what is said above, it results that we know that **Plato** in his *Cratylus* strives (but in vain) to derive the property of Greek names through the imitation of the Hebrews, which **Ficino** <note>Marsilio Ficino, the Italian Renaissance philosopher</note> also does in his Com-

## On the poet Homer and his writings composed in the Greek language.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap letter P at the start of the first paragraph of the section.</image-desc>

Several ancient authors hold that the Greek poet Homer is the first and most ancient writer who has ever existed among the Greeks; a claim which Aristotle in his *Poetics*, Aelian in his *Various History*, Pausanias in his *Description of Boeotia* <note>original: "Beotiques"</note>, Josephus in book 1 *Against Apion*, Eusebius in book 10, chapter 3 of his *Preparation*, Justin Martyr in his book *Against the Greeks*, Theodoret in book 2 of *Greek Affections*, and Athenagoras the Christian Philosopher in his works, all deny. They maintain that before this poet, there flourished in Greece Orpheus, Linus, Musaeus, Demodocus, Phemius, the Sibyls, Epimenides the Cretan, Aristeas of Proconnesus, Asbolus the Centaur, Isatis, Drimon, Horus of Samos, Protenidas the Athenian, Philammon, Thamyris, Olene, Amphion, Olympus, Orsebantius of Troezen, Syagrus, Dares the Phrygian, and others who had composed and published works in the Greek language before him. These works dealt with divine, celestial, natural, moral, political, and military matters, as well as Music and the secret doctrine of numbers. Tatian and Suidas, Greek authors, seem to agree with this, writing that Homer drew the entire subject of his poems from the Greek works of one Eveclus and Corinnus; the latter was a heroic poet of Ilium and a disciple of Palamedes, who first wrote an *Iliad* during the Trojan War, which greatly served this same Homer. Indeed, it is a well-assured thing according to the report of Solinus that this Poet inserted into his poems several verses from those of Daphne, priestess of Delphi—as confirmed by Diodorus Siculus in book 5, chapter 7—and from those of the Sibyls, as has been well and curiously noted by Gilbert Génébrard <note>A 16th-century French scholar and Hebraist</note> in his writings on the book by Perionius <note>Joachim Périon, a translator of Aristotle</note> regarding the lives of Saintly women, and in books 1 and 2 of his *Chronography*. Saint Clement and Justin Martyr go much further when they assert in their works that this poet made use of the Hebrew writings of the Prophet Moses, which he had seen in Egypt, where he had traveled for that purpose. This poet was first named Melesigenes <note>Meaning "born of the Meles River"</note>, and afterwards *Homer* <note>original: "όμηρος" (Homeros)</note> for two reasons (according to Suidas): the first because in the war between the people of Smyrna and Colophon he was given as a hostage <note>The Greek word "homeros" means "hostage"</note> between them, or because when the Smyrnaeans were deliberating on a matter, he spoke divinely and gave them good counsel to wage war. Others say it was because he was blind, but the best reason is that he was so named "Homer" because he was never conquered or overcome by cupidity <note>desire</note>, which proceeds principally from the eyes. His parentage is uncertain, though many strive to write of it, including Aristotle in the third book of the *Art of Poetry*, and Plutarch in the

## Concerning the poet Homer and his writings composed in the Greek language.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or a personification of a virtue, surrounded by floral and architectural scrollwork.</image-desc>

Several ancient authors hold that the Greek poet Homer is the first and most ancient writer to have existed in all antiquity among the Greeks. This is denied by Aristotle in his *Poetics*, Aelian in his *Various History*, Pausanias in his *Description of Boeotia*, Josephus in book 1 *Against Apion*, Eusebius in book 10, chapter 3 of his *Preparation [for the Gospel]*, Justin Martyr in his book *Against the Greeks*, Theodoret in book 2 *On the Healing of Greek Affections*, and Athenagoras, the Christian Philosopher, in his works. These maintain that before this poet, there flourished in Greece Orpheus, Linus, Musaeus, Demodocus, Phemius, the Sibyls, Epimenides of Crete, Aristeas of Proconnesus, Asbolus the Centaur, Isatis, Drimon, Horus the Samian, Protenidas the Athenian, Philammon, Thamyris, Olen, Amphion, Olympus, Orbeantius of Troezen, Syagrus, Dares the Phrygian, and others. These figures had composed and brought to light works in the Greek language before him, dealing with things divine, celestial, natural, moral, political, and military, together with music and the secret doctrine of numbers. Tatian and Suidas, Greek authors, seem to agree with this, writing that Homer drew the entire subject of his poetry from the Greek works of one Eveclus and one Corinnus. The latter was an Iliene heroic poet and a disciple of Palamedes, who first wrote an *Iliad* during the Trojan War, which greatly served this same Homer. Indeed, it is a certainty according to the report of Solinus that this poet inserted into his poems several verses from those of Daphne, the priestess of Delphi—as confirmed by Diodorus Siculus in book 5, chapter 7—and from those of the Sibyls, as has been well and curiously noted by G. This poet was first named Melesigenes, and later <term>Homeros</term> <note>original: "ὅμηρος"</note> for two reasons (according to the report of Suidas): one because, in the war between the Smyrneans and the Colophonians, he was given as a hostage <note>The Greek word "homeros" means "hostage"</note> between them; or because when the Smyrneans were deliberating on a matter, he spoke divinely and gave them good counsel for making war. Others say it was because he was blind <note>A common folk etymology of "Homeros" related to "not seeing"</note>, but the best reason is that he was so called Homer because he was never vanquished or overcome by greed, which proceeds principally from the eyes. This uncertainty moved the grammarian Didymus <note>Didymus Chalcenterus (c. 63 BC – 10 AD), a scholar in Alexandria known for his prolific output, allegedly writing thousands of books.</note> to compose 4,000 books on the contradictions among Greek authors regarding this question, as Seneca writes in Book 13 of his *Epistles*, Letter 89, reciting several peculiarities of this poet. The time in which he flourished is also uncertain: for some write that he lived in the year of the created world 3150; others 3560; some years after the destruction of Troy; and according to Herodotus, 168 years after the said destruction; according to Crates, 80 years after; according to Archilochus, 500 years after. The poems or poetries [of Homer] are the *Iliad*, the *Odyssey*, the *Hymns*, and the *Battle of the Frogs* <note>The *Batrachomyomachia*, a comic parody of the Iliad involving mice and frogs, once attributed to Homer.</note>. The *Iliad* was not composed by him all in one piece, but at several different times, leaving sometimes a book here and sometimes another there; and being thus scattered, they were redacted and put in order, along with the books of the *Odyssey*—according to Cicero in Book 3 of his *On the Orator*—by Pisistratus, Tyrant of Athens, or by Hipparchus his son, as reported by Pausanias in his *Description of Achaia*, and by Aelian in Book 13 of his *Various History*. Some other authors attribute this to Aristotle, who, by the command of the aforementioned Pisistratus, corrected the rhapsody <note>A "rhapsody" here refers to the epic performance or the songs of the poet.</note> of that poet and was the first to divide it into 24 parts—as many as there are letters in the Greek alphabet. After all these, a certain Zenodotus of Ephesus, a grammarian and poet, disciple of Philitas and tutor to the children of King Ptolemy I, corrected them and put them back in their order <gloss>and</gloss> Suidas, cited above. These poems or poetries are filled with many Greek words and expressions from every Greek dialect, as Plutarch notes in his treatise on the dialects found in Homer. We read in this same author in the *Life of Lycurgus*, in Heraclides in his *Treatise on Republics*, and Aelian in the 13th book of his *Various History*, that the first who brought these poems or poetries from Ionia to the Peloponnese, which were in the hands of the successors of Creophylus <note>original: "Cleophile"; referring to Creophylus of Samos, a legendary early epic poet said to be a contemporary or son-in-law of Homer.</note>, was Lycurgus. Solon had collected them all and placed them in a public location, with an ordinance that each of them should be read and recited in order at every festival of the city, as Julius Caesar Scaliger <note>A 16th-century Italian scholar who spent much of his life in France; a key figure in Renaissance literary criticism.</note> assures in the first book, chapter 4 of his *Poetics*, and Caelius in the seventh book, chapter 29 of his *Readings*. ## On the Philosopher Plato and his writings composed in the Greek language.

Julius Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman senator and astrologer.</note>, having taken the pain to calculate and draw up the horoscope of the Philosopher Plato, wrote that he found by his calculation that this personage was born by Nature to be extremely eloquent, and endowed with a celestial spirit and understanding to comprehend all the secrets of the Supreme Majesty. To this point, the Greeks have asserted that while he was in his cradle, a swarm of bees was found to have placed its honey in his mouth; this presaged the future eloquence of this great personage, just as Aelian relates in Book 10 of his *Various History*, Pliny in Book 11, Chapter 17, and Valerius Maximus in Book 1. It is also said that Socrates saw in a dream a small swan in his lap, which began to clothe itself in feathers with which, soaring into the air, it came to sing very sweetly and melodiously; and that the next day, Plato having been brought to him to be instructed, he said that this was the fulfillment of his preceding dream. Plato was first called Aristocles, and because of his broad shoulders, broad forehead, and large body, or for the amplitude of his speech, he was named <term>Plato</term> <note>original: "Πλάτων"; derived from the Greek "platýs," meaning broad or wide.</note>, as Suidas and Laertius write. He was called the "Attic Honey-Bee," because of which Cicero, following the Greeks, said in his *Brutus*: "Who is more abundant in speaking than Plato?" <note>original: "Quis uberior in dicendo Platone?"</note> and that "If Jupiter were to speak Greek, he would speak as the philosophers say Plato did" <note>original: "Iouem sic, vt aiunt Philosophi Graecè loquatur, loqui."</note>. The same Cicero in his *Tusculan Disputations* calls him the "God of Philosophy." Some call him the imitator of Moses, or the "Attic Moses," as he drew many beautiful things from this Hebrew Prophet; as, following Numenius the Pythagorean <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who famously asked, "What is Plato but Moses speaking Attic Greek?"</note>, Josephus remarks in his argument against Apollonius Molon, Suidas in his dictionary, Justin Martyr in his *Exhortation*, Eusebius in his *Preparation*, Theodoret in his book *On Greek Affections*, Ficino in his *Commentaries on Plato*, and Juan Luis Vives in his commentaries on Book 8, Chapter 11 of Saint Augustine's *City of God*. This Philosopher lived and flourished in the year 3770 from the creation of the world, some time after the Peloponnesian War, and lived eighty-one years, dying around the 108th Olympiad. He was so highly prized by the Greeks that Aristocles of Messene composed ten books comparing him and Homer, according to the report of Suidas; Cicero for this reason called him the "Homer of Philosophers," and Quintilian described him as filled with divine and Homeric eloquence. His Greek style, according to Aristotle, holds the middle ground between prose (or free speech) and verse or poetry, with such sweetness and eloquence that one can imagine nothing more divine and miraculous. ## On the Philosopher Plato and his writings composed in the Greek language.

Julius Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus was a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer.</note> having taken the trouble to calculate and draw up the horoscope of the philosopher Plato, wrote that he found by calculation that this personage was born by nature to be most eloquent, and endowed with a celestial spirit and understanding to comprehend all the secrets of the supreme divinity. To this purpose, the Greeks have asserted that while he was in his cradle, a swarm of bees was found to have placed its honey in his mouth; this presaged the future eloquence of this great personage, as recounted by Aelian in Book 10 of his *Various History*, Pliny in Book 30, Chapter 17, and Valerius Maximus in Book 1. It is even said that Socrates saw in a dream a small swan in his lap which began to clothe itself in feathers; with these wings, it soared into the air and began to sing most sweetly and melodiously, and that the next day, when Plato was brought to him to be instructed, he said that this was the fulfillment of his previous dream. 

This Plato was first called Aristocles, but because of his broad shoulders, broad forehead, and large body, or for the amplitude of his speech, he was named <term>πλατων</term> <note>Original Greek: "Platon," derived from *platos*, meaning "breadth" or "width."</note>, as Suidas and Laertius write. He was called the "Attic honey-bee," because of which Cicero said, following the Greeks, in his *Brutus*: "Who is more abundant in speaking than Plato? Philosophers say that if Jupiter spoke Greek, he would speak thus" <note>Original Latin: "Quis uberior in dicendo Platone? Iouem sic, vt aiunt Philosophi Græcè loquatur, loqui."</note>. The same author, in his *Tusculan Disputations*, calls him the God of Philosophy. 

Some call him the imitator of Moses, or the "Attic Moses," as he drew many beautiful things from this Hebrew Prophet; following Numenius the Pythagorean, this is noted by Josephus in his book written against Apion <note>The text mentions "Apollonie Molon," referring to the rhetorician Apollonius Molon whom Josephus refutes.</note>, Suidas in his dictionary, Justin Martyr in his *Exhortation*, Eusebius in his *Preparation for the Gospel*, Theodoret in his book on *Greek Affections*, Ficino in his *Commentaries on Plato*, and Juan Luis Vives in his commentaries on Book 8, Chapter 11 of Saint Augustine’s *City of God*. 

This philosopher lived and flourished in the year 3770 from the creation of the world, some time after the Peloponnesian War, and lived eighty-one years, dying around the 108th Olympiad. He was so highly prized by the Greeks that Aristocles of Messene composed ten books comparing him and Homer, according to Suidas. For this reason, Cicero called him the "Homer of Philosophers," and Quintilian described him as filled with a divine and Homeric eloquence. His Greek style, according to Aristotle, holds the middle ground between prose <note>Original: "oraison solue," literally "loosened speech," a term for prose as opposed to the "bound" structures of verse.</note> and verse, possessing such sweetness and eloquence that nothing more divine or miraculous can be imagined. This moved the Father of Latin Eloquence <note>A common title for Cicero.</note> to say that he would rather err with Plato than feel correctly with all the other philosophers. And it is no wonder if a Cleombrotus, and another listener of Hegesias, having heard certain of his discourses concerning the immortality of the soul, killed themselves to en-

This is why a certain Antimachus, a poet from Colophon <note>Antimachus of Colophon (c. 400 BC) was an epic poet; the anecdote illustrates that the quality of one's audience matters more than the quantity.</note> (as Cicero mentions in his *Brutus*), while reciting one of his discourses in the presence of several people who, after hearing only a few words, all walked out except for Plato, did not stop his reading. His Greek writings, which are almost all arranged and divided into dialogues in which his master Socrates is always introduced as the speaker, treat many diverse subjects. The great Giovanni Pico della Mirandola proposed during his life to harmonize and reconcile the writings of this man with those of Aristotle, as Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a philosopher whose "Consolation of Philosophy" was immensely popular in the Middle Ages.</note> had previously undertaken. # On the historian Herodotus and his writings composed in the Greek language.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'H' at the beginning of the text. The letter is set against a background of dense foliage and scrolled architectural motifs, with a stylized human face or decorative ornament at the center of the crossbar.</image-desc>

Herodotus, a Greek historian born to illustrious parents in the city of Halicarnassus <note>Halicarnassus was an ancient Greek city at the site of modern-day Bodrum, Turkey.</note>—currently called Meffy <note>A Renaissance-era name for the region near Bodrum.</note>, located at 57 degrees 50 minutes longitude and 36 degrees 10 minutes latitude in the region of Caria in Asia Minor—flourished around the year 3699 from the creation of the world. Cicero, in the third book of *The Orator* and the first of *The Laws*, calls him the **Prince and Father of History** <note>original: "Principem & Patrem historiæ"</note> because he is among the most eloquent and one of the oldest historians of the Greeks. Strabo, in his final book, is of the opinion that Herodotus wrote a false and legendary history rather than a true and certain one, having partially drawn and extracted it from the Greek histories of Xanthus of Lydia, who was older than him. This history is contained in nine books named after the nine Muses <note>The nine goddesses of the arts and sciences; each of Herodotus’s books is traditionally named after one, such as Clio or Euterpe.</note>. He began composing this history in the Greek <term>Ionic dialect</term> <note>A dialect of ancient Greek used by writers in Asia Minor and the Aegean islands.</note> while living on the island of Samos, where he had been exiled by Lygdamis, the tyrant of Halicarnassus. In addition to this history, he wrote a compendium or brief discourse in the Greek language on the life of Homer. These works have been translated from Greek into Latin by several different authors, as taught by Conrad Gessner and Josias Simler in their historical bibliographies. Lucian, a Greek author, in his dialogue titled *Herodotus, or Aetion*, took care to recount how Herodotus became known to all the Greeks in a short time. Quintilian, in book 9, chapter 14 of his *Institutes*, following Aristotle's discourse in his *Poetics*, wrote these words in praise of this figure's Greek histories:

> In Herodotus, since everything (as I feel) flows gently, the dialect itself possesses such sweetness that it seems to embrace even hidden rhythms. <note>original: "In Herodoto cum omnia vt sentio leniter fluant, tum ipsa dialectos habet eam iucunditatem, vt latentes etiam numeros complexa videatur."</note>

And in book 10, chapter 1:

> Many have written history excellently: Thucydides is dense, brief, and always pressing onward; Herodotus is sweet, clear, and expansive. The former is better at depicting intense emotions, the latter at relaxed ones; the former excels in speeches, the latter in conversation; the former in force, the latter in pleasure. <note>original: "Historiam multi scripsere præclarè, densus & breuis & semper instans sibi Thucidides: dulcis & candidus & effusus Herodotus, Ille concitatis hic remissis affectibus melior; ille concionibus, hic sermonibus, ille vi, hic voluptate."</note>

This person died after going into exile in Thurii, one of the Athenian colonies, and was buried there. Some maintain that it was in the city of Pella or Ieuize in Macedonia. See Cicero in his *Orator*; Strabo, book 14; Plutarch on the *Malice of Herodotus*; Suidas in his works; Athenaeus, book 12, chapter 14 of his *Deipnosophists*; Aulus Gellius, book 15, chapter 23; Guillaume Budé in his *Commentaries on the Greek Language* citing Hermogenes; J. Pontanus in one of his letters on this author; Henri Estienne in his *Apology for Herodotus*; Victorius, book 28, chapter 1 of his *Variae*; Gilbert Génébrard, book 2 of his *Chronographia*; Jean Bodin, chapter four of his *Method for the Easy Comprehension of History*; François de Belleforest, volume two, chapter seven of his *Universal Cosmography*; and the Author Du Verdier, book 2 of his *Prosopography*.

## On the Orator Demosthenes and his writings composed in the Greek language.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'C' featuring floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

Those who wish to be fully informed of which parents, country, and city of Greece this great Greek orator Demosthenes was born, should read Plutarch in the *Life of Demosthenes*, and in his treatise on the *Lives of the Ten Orators*, and Suidas in his works. This figure, a native of Athens, utilized and made use of in his life the Greek orations of a certain Zoilus, or Zethus of Amphipolis, and of a Polycrates and Alcidamas, disciples of Gorgias and Isocrates; with these orations, he progressed so much in the oratorical art that he acquired in his time such a reputation as an eloquent man in the Greek language that never before or since has anyone been able to match him. He was a disciple of Plato, whom he heard for some time, and was a friend of Aristotle. He was so accomplished in Greek eloquence that he has been considered the rule and the law of speaking well and orating well in that language; he has such force in his words, and has arranged and ordered them so well that one could neither add nor remove anything from them. For in the legal cases he handled and the orations written by him, one could find no subtlety or finesse that is not included there, nor anything higher, more grave, eloquent, or better adorned and set down in writing than what is encountered at every turn, just as Cicero maintains in his *Brutus*. There is no treatise for governing a Republic that cannot be found within them; these works do not aim solely at utility, but rather at honor and honesty, so much so that Plato and Aristotle are found to have philosophized no better in their schools than he did in the public assemblies of Athens around the year of the created world 3780 <note>This "Anno Mundi" date is a Renaissance calculation; Demosthenes actually lived from roughly 384 to 322 BCE.</note>, as we can easily see in his beautiful deductions and Greek orations printed in several places, containing one large entire volume, the remains of his other writings. This is why a certain person, greatly admiring the orations proceeding from the admirable torrent of eloquence from the mind of this figure, one day asked Cicero—the most articulate and eloquent man of his century—which of Demosthenes' orations seemed the best to him; he replied that the longest and the greatest was the one most to be prized. Saint Jerome said this short word about him in Latin: **Demosthenes is said to have spent more on oil than on wine, and to have outdone all craftsmen with his nightly vigils** <note>original: "Plus olei quàm vini expendisse dicitur Demosthenes, & omnes opifices nocturnis semper vigiliis præuenisse." This refers to the oil consumed in lamps during late-night study, suggesting he preferred hard work over the indulgence of wine.</note>. Cicero, cited above, although a great and perfect Latin orator, holds him in such high regard and esteem that he judged him to have had and possessed in himself all the arts of speaking well and excellently—which all those who attentively wish to contemplate his writings in the Greek language will confess. See what is written of this orator by Lucian in his praise of Demosthenes; Libanius the <term>Sophist</term> <note>A teacher of rhetoric and philosophy in the Greek tradition.</note> in the *Life of Demosthenes*; Ulpian the Rhetorician in his prefaces on the *Orations of Demosthenes*; Caecilius Siculus in his comparison of Demosthenes and Cicero; Pausanias in his *Description of Corinth*; Quintilian in book 10, chapter 1; Cicero in his discourses titled *Brutus* and *On the Orator*; Aulus Gellius in book 3, chapter 13, and book 17, the final chapter; Plutarch in his comparison of Cicero with Demosthenes; and Guillaume Budé in his *Commentaries on the Greek Language*. ## On the Greek Philosophers:

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'P' at the start of the section, enclosed in a square frame with intricate floral and foliate patterns.</image-desc>*Polydore Vergil* in book 1, chapter 16 of *On the Origin of Philosophy*, regarding its two principles and who it was that invented Morals and Dialectic, and introduced disputations and dialogues, writes what follows concerning the Greek Philosophers.
   Philosophy—which *Cicero* in book 1 of *On Duties* and in the 5th of the *Tusculan Disputations* calls the "Love of wisdom" <note>Latin: "Philosophia" / "Amor sapientiae".</note> and the desire for it, and that which seeks virtue and drives away vice—was brought to Greece (as he says) by the Greeks who learned it from Barbarian and foreign nations. It is held that among the Persians, the first were the *Magi*, which signifies "Sages," who flourished in that province. The *Chaldeans* were esteemed among the *Assyrians* and the region of ancient *Babylon*. The *Indians* had their *Brahmans* and *Gymnosophists* <note>Ancient Greek term for "naked philosophers" of India.</note>, the prince and head of whose sect was a certain *Buddha* <note>Original: "Budde".</note>, as *Saint Jerome* testifies against Jovinian. The Britons and Gauls had the *Druids*. The *Phoenicians* had *Ochus*; the *Thracians* had *Zamolxis* and *Orpheus*; the *Libyans* had *Atlas*. All of these, as *Laërtius* says, were the wisest and most excellent among their neighbors and were esteemed as such. The *Egyptians* are of the opinion that *Vulcan* was the son of the Nile and that he declared the principles of Philosophy. *Diogenes Laërtius* affirms that it had its beginning in Greece, because the Greeks hold that *Musaeus* and *Linus* were the first sages raised among them and on Greek soil.
   But *Eusebius*, with better cause, says in the 2nd book of his *Preparation for the Gospel* that Philosophy, as well as the rest of the arts and sciences, took its source from the Hebrew nation. And from this, he concludes that the Greek Philosophers received their knowledge from the Jews, seeing as they lived more than a thousand years after Moses, as *Porphyry* testifies. Furthermore, among the Greeks, the name "Philosopher" was not yet found; rather, *Pythagoras* was the first who named Philosophy—that is to say, the love of wisdom—and called himself a Philosopher—that is to say, a lover of wisdom. He also said that it was to God alone that one should attribute the name and the effect of wisdom, according to *Lactantius* in book 3, chapter 2 of the *Divine Institutes*. For previously, it was called *Sophia*, which is now named Philosophy; and *Sophoi*—that is to say, Sages—were those who are now said to be Philosophers. Now, this Philosophy had two beginnings based on the places where it was celebrated: the first called *Ionic*, after *Anaximander*, because *Thales of Miletus* was of the country of *Ionia*, and it was he who instructed Anaximander. The other principle was nicknamed *Italic*, having its source from *Pythagoras*, who spent a long time in the study of Philosophy in that part of Italy which was later named Great Greece <note>Latin: "Magna Graecia".</note>, and which today is a part of Calabria. *Eusebius*, in the 10th book of his *Preparation*, adds to this a third genre of Philosophers which he calls *Cleantic*, <note>Referring to the school of Cleanthes, a Stoic philosopher.</note> of which sect...

It traces the linguistic shift from "Sages" to "Philosophers" initiated by Pythagoras.</summary>

Furthermore, they divide philosophy into three parts: one of which—according to Cicero in *The Orator*—focuses on the search for the secrets and obscurities of nature; the other on the subtlety of arguments and discourse; and the third treats of life and morals. The Greeks call the first Physics, the second Dialectic, and the third Ethics. As Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian who argued that Greek philosophy was plagiarized from the Bible.</note> also says, Plato borrowed this division from the Hebrews, just as he did with the rest of the precepts and teachings of this philosophy in particular. The principal subject of Physics is to argue about the world and what is contained within it, which Archelaus was the first of all to bring from Ionia to Athens in the Attic country. Ethics pursues what pertains to the forming of morals and the instruction of human life; it was Socrates who was the first to teach this in Athens. Thus Cicero, in the 5th book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, speaks of the said Socrates: "Socrates, recalling philosophy from Heaven before any other, made it enter and settle in the cities, introduced it into homes, and constrained men to inquire about life and morals, and about what is good or bad for the luck and happiness of the soul." But Dialectic <note>Original: "Dialectiq;" — a term roughly equivalent to logic and the art of reasoning.</note> is that which provides reasoning and discourse upon Physics and Ethics; it was invented by Zeno, surnamed the Eleatic. I have proposed this division although I know that others divide it into five parts, namely: Physics, Metaphysics, Ethics, Mathematics, and Logic. But we are overstepping our bounds and limits, for I had not intended to provide a definition for every single thing or to examine everything until a certain reason is given; our design is only to treat the origin of each thing. Therefore, let us resume our first topic. Plato, as [Diogenes] Laërtius teaches us, was the first to introduce arguments through dialogues, or rather excelled more in them and illustrated the invention more than any other. For Aristotle, in book 1 of *On Poets*, holds that Alaxamenes, a native of the island of Scyros or of Teos, was the first inventor of them. Diogenes Laërtius, a Greek author, described very particularly the lives of several of these Greek philosophers in his works, *The Lives of the Philosophers*.

Josephus in his books *Against Apion* the Grammarian. Philo the Jew in his book *On Wisdom*. Theodor Bibliander in his commentary *On All Languages and Letters*, chapter on Wisdom and Philosophy.
