...the Ionians spoke differently, the Dorians differed from them, and the Aeolians had something distinct from both, just as the Attics surpassed the others in sweetness and eloquence; and the common tongue <note>The "Koine" or common Greek that became the standard throughout the Mediterranean.</note> had certain qualities that did not relate to the others. These languages have been recognized as having been in use among authors, as those most learned and well-versed in languages can easily judge and know; on this subject, Velleius Paterculus <note>A Roman historian (c. 19 BC – c. AD 31).</note> says in Book 2, speaking of the city of Athens:

> A single city flourished in eloquence for more years than the whole of Greece did in its works, so much so that you might think the bodies of that race were separated into other cities, but their genius was enclosed within the walls of the Athenians alone. <note>original: "Vna vrbs pluribus annis eloquentia, quàm vniuersa Græcia operibus floruit adeò vt corpora gentis illius separata sint in alias ciuitates, ingenia verò solis Atheniensium muris clausa existimes."</note>

But one must not think there was ever a man so devoted to his own particular tongue that he did not mix some words and dialects of other languages into his works. And the more learned a man was, the more he sowed various words, chosen from the most learned of each nation, into his writings. Plutarch, in a book on the life of Homer, shows this at length when he makes a full discourse on the verses of this excellent Greek Poet, whom he praises for the variety of Dialects and Greek language recognized in his poetry; so much so that the Ionians, Dorians, Aeolians, and Attics can see therein how excellent this personage was, who like a honeybee had gathered the flowers of all their languages together. T. Bibliander <note>Theodore Bibliander (1509–1564), a Swiss Orientalist and linguist.</note> in his commentary on the common relationship of all languages and letters, says:

> The Greek speech was not only divided into five types in the past: the common Dialect, the Attic, Aeolic, Doric, and Ionic. For Herodotus enumerates four different manners of the Ionic tongue. Those of Rhodes, Cyprus, Crete, and Chalcis also had something unique, yet all those Dialects can and should be measured by a single rule and standard. I feel the same regarding all the idioms of the Nations to which the Greek speech was once spread; for it was celebrated not only in Hellas, but also in Epirus, the Peloponnese, Illyria, Macedonia, Thrace, in Asia Minor, and in Syria—in which there were most eloquent men in the Greek tongue, such as Philo, Josephus, and many others. Greek letters flourished especially in Cilicia in the town of Tarsus, the homeland of Saint Paul. Likewise in Alexandria in Egypt. And again in Europe, the Greek speech was common not only in that part of Italy called Great Greece <note>Magna Graecia, the coastal areas of Southern Italy colonized by Greeks.</note>, but also in Gaul. For in Marseille, Greek studies and letters flourished greatly. And the priests of the Gauls were called by the Greek name "Druids," as if you were to say "Oak-men," <note>original: "Quercuarios"; from the Greek word "drys" (oak). The author is connecting the Celtic Druids to Greek etymology.</note> using the Greek tongue especially in divine matters. We have received this as handed down by good authors. The commentaries of Caesar also testify that the Helvetians <note>The ancient inhabitants of what is now Switzerland.</note> once used Greek letters. And it is very likely that the speech of those who hold part of the Island of Britain—which is called Wales and Cornwall—whose speech agrees closely with Greek (as I have learned from learned and trustworthy men), crossed over from Gaul. Just as in our own age we have noticed that the language of the Anglo-Saxons is much altered by the French tongue. Furthermore, Postel <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), a French linguist and mystic.</note> indicates how widely the Greek speech extends today in these words:
>
> If the Greeks were to deny that they received their letters through the work of a certain Chaldean, it could be proven by the names of the letters; and later: they are still in use today in the sacred and common idioms of the Greeks living under the Empire of the Turks in the Peloponnese...

...Greece, Macedonia, Thrace, and the Islands of the Mediterranean Sea, especially <margin>„</margin> those belonging to the Aegean Sea, where it is called in the native tongue *Rhomei* <note>Romaic, a term for the vernacular Greek used during the Byzantine and early modern periods.</note>. Many <margin>„</margin> colonies of these people were moved throughout Anatolia, especially in <margin>„</margin> maritime places and toward Lesser Armenia, which for this reason the Turks call <margin>„</margin> *Rhom* <note>The Sultanate of Rum or the region of Rum, names derived from the "Roman" (Byzantine) presence there</note>, that is, Greece. The same Postel <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), a famous French linguist and polymath.</note> says the common Greek language <margin>„</margin> is very closely related to its grammar <note>Likely referring to the relationship between the spoken vernacular and the classical written rules.</note>. This is what I have found by inquiring of those who have lived among the Greeks.

Now, if this Greek language was once held in such high regard, this can teach us: that all the most excellent men of whatever foreign nation under Heaven have striven to have knowledge of it. To this point, Herodotus in Book 2 writes that Psammetichus, King of the Egyptians, brought Greeks to Egypt to teach the children of his subjects the Greek letters and language. Among the Scythians (according to Herodotus in the fourth book), Anacharsis <note>The original text writes "Anaxarchis," a variant of Anacharsis, a famous Scythian philosopher who traveled to Athens.</note>, a great philosopher and prince of a great house, brought the Greek tongue to the Scythians, along with the learning and calculations—or rather superstitions—of Greece. The latter proved detrimental to him, for by practicing Greek ceremonies, he was killed by the King of the Scythians, his nephew, because he was introducing a new Religion into his kingdom. Our ancient Druids, according to the report of Julius Caesar in his commentaries, along with the Gallic priests and philosophers, used the Greek language in their sacrifices and in their most necessary and important affairs. Furthermore, according to Strabo in his fourth book, and Marcellinus in his fifth book, as written by Caelius Rhodiginus <note>Ludovico Ricchieri (1469–1525), an Italian scholar known for his "Ancient Lessons."</note> in the sixteenth book, eighteenth chapter, the people of Marseille in olden times were such lovers of this language that they had their contracts drawn up in it; from which it happened that the Gallic language has since retained several phrases entirely filled with Greek words and sayings.

The Carthaginians also loved and cherished it, as descendants of the Phoenicians and allies of the Greeks against the Romans, as Livy assures us in the third decade, book 9.

Philostratus, a Greek Sophist, in the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, writes that this great personage, having gone to visit the gymnosophists <note>Literally "naked wise men," referring to ancient Indian philosophers and ascetics.</note> or *Sagenudz* <note>A transliteration of a term for Indian sages.</note> of the Indies, spoke to King Phraotes <note>The text writes "Phroté".</note>, whom he found so well-versed in Greek letters and sciences that he was amazed that a man considered a Barbarian <note>A term used by Greeks and Romans for anyone outside their cultural sphere.</note> could have such perfect knowledge of them. He was even more astonished when he heard the philosopher Iarchas <note>The text writes "Iaebas," referring to the leader of the Brahmans in the Apollonius legend.</note> discourse in the Greek tongue as properly as those who were native to the land of Greece, and even more learned in that language. Roman histories assure us that Augustus Caesar devoted himself greatly to the study of Greek letters and language, and that he remained for a long time in Greece to gain a complete and perfect knowledge of it, which he achieved to such an extent that he composed good and beautiful verses in this Greek language, and took a very great pleasure in speaking Greek when conversing privately with his friends, according to what Suetonius Tranquillus recounts in the life of this Emperor Augustus. The learned Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), an influential Catholic historian.</note>, in the first volume of his *Ecclesiastical Annals*, confirms this very well and provides certain proof that the Greek language was in common use and spoken in Rome during the time of this Emperor.

# History of the Origin of...

[page 692]
### Languages of this Universe.

And who is there who does not well know that the Romans in general sent their children to study in Athens because of the desire they had for them to learn the Greek language? *Titus*, son of the Emperor *Vespasian*, was well-versed in Greek and Latin letters; the Emperor *Alexander Severus*, being at rest after having heard the requests and done justice to his subjects, had no more agreeable occupation than the reading of Greek books; and it is said that if something were read to him, he preferred that it be in Greek rather than in his mother tongue, according to *Lampridius* <note>Aelius Lampridius, one of the purported authors of the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note> in his biography. The Emperor *Hadrian* was devoted to it more than was reasonable; *Antoninus* and *Aurelian*, as they were very learned, also had perfect knowledge of Greek letters. And what is most marvelous is that which *Dionysius of Halicarnassus* relates: that *Romulus*, Father of the Romans and first King of the proud city of Rome, wrote his own deeds and the victories obtained against his adversaries in Greek. In this, one should note the desire that all have had to understand and embrace this language, the most polished and eloquent of all others. Furthermore, the first and most ancient Romans drew their laws to civilize their Republic from the wisdom of the Greeks; thus, *Spurius Postumius*, *Aulus Manlius*, and *Publius Sulpicius* were sent to Athens to retrieve the laws of that City, as well as the ways of life, rights, and customs observed by the rest of the cities of Greece. <note>This refers to the legendary embassy of 454 BCE, which preceded the creation of the Twelve Tables of Roman law.</note> There were also various Lawgivers, such as the very ancient King *Cecrops*, *Draco*, and *Solon* (one of the Seven Sages, whose laws were sought out by the Romans) in Athens; *Lycurgus* in Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>; *Nicodorus* in Mantinea; *Zaleucus* in Locris; and *Minos*, who gave laws and policies to the Candiots <note>Cretans</note>. But what purpose does it serve for me to say that so many great personages in times past studied the Greek language, since the Evangelists and Apostles themselves—though Hebrews and Jews by nation, using their Hebrew or Syriac tongue as their native and common speech—wrote for the most part the sacred books containing Christian doctrine and religion in the Greek language? They did so as much for the sweetness of this tongue as for the fact that almost throughout the entire world there were men instructed in it, who by this means could very easily embrace and follow the Christian religion. And still, these two great Hebrew figures, *Josephus* and *Philo*, Jews by nation and learned in their Hebrew tongue above all others, nevertheless did not hesitate to write their books in Greek rather than in Hebrew for the perfection of this language, which was highly esteemed and cherished by men of all nations. This is asserted by *St. Jerome* in the preface to the second book of his *Commentary on Galatians*. *G. Génébrard* <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine and renowned Hebraist.</note> on this subject in book 1, chapter 5, leaf 25 of his *Liturgy*, reported these words:

This is confirmed by G. Postel <note>Guillaume Postel, a French linguist and polymath.</note> in his book on the *Alphabet of the Twelve Languages*, and by recent travelers to the Levant. In short, the Greeks of today, to whomever they are subjects, are so debased <note>original: "abeştis" — rendered dull or animal-like.</note> and hold letters in such little regard that there is not a single university in all the country of Greece; and what is worse, they do not care if their children are instructed to know anything—indeed, among the Greek priests you will hardly find any who know anything more than how to read. They all speak a corrupted Greek, entirely different from the ancient language. It is true that (as mentioned before) some speak more properly and eloquently than others: those who live in the Venetian cities like Candia <note>Modern-day Crete.</note>, Corfu, Zante, or Cephalonia speak Greek and Italian, but the peasants speak only the Greek language; and those who are in the Turkish cities speak Slavic and the Turkish language. Nonetheless, there are those who mock those who do not speak as properly as they do; even the inhabitants of Constantinople consider that those from the islands could never approach their eloquence and fine speech. As for the customs of these Greeks, the noblemen and citizens differ from others in their dress: those who are very rich dress in the fashion of the princes under whose Empire they live, and excessively imitate their magnificence, whereas the simple commoner still has some unknown trace of his ancient way of doing things in his attire.

### On the decline of the Greek language.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' featuring a floral scrollwork background.</image-desc>

Although languages move and change incessantly like all things in this Universe, and though in the same country and language there appears in a short space of time a great difference in speaking and pronouncing, it remains true that there have always been some more elegant and eloquent than others; such as were the Athenians in Greece, and the Romans in Italy. This settles the question that has been debated among some learned men: namely, whether the ancient Greeks and Romans had two different languages <note>i.e., a "literary" language and a "common" language.</note>, and if Plato, Aristotle, Demosthenes, and other Greek authors, or Cicero, Caesar, Sallust, Virgil, and other Latins, wrote in their mother tongues. But even though their words were Greek or Latin, they retained the phrasing of their own country. So much so that, speaking Greek or Latin, they were always recognized as foreigners, just as we see today the English, Scots, Germans, Flemish, Italians, and Spanish speaking French; unless they learned it when very young. Now these languages, like all human things, have a beginning, progress, perfection, corruption, and end: they are first rough, then they are polished with the civility of manners and knowledge; and after having lasted some time in purity and eloquence, they are altered and corrupted, and finally perish, with no trace whatsoever of their essence remaining over the course of time. The strange and cruel ravages of the Arabs, Saracens, and Turks, both in Asia and Europe, chased "good letters" <note>A Renaissance term for the humanities and classical literature.</note>, sciences, and disciplines out of Greece. From there, they retreated into Italy and France under the guidance of several excellent individuals. Through their work, labor, and study, the sciences and doctrines—enlightened by means of the Greek language—returned to the forefront and began, so to speak, to live again, having been buried and entombed in a profound ignorance since the first destruction the Goths had wrought in Italy.

The first who demonstrated and promoted the knowledge of the said Greek language in Italy was a certain person named **Emanuel Chrysoloras**, father-in-law of **Francesco Filelfo** <note>Chrysoloras was a pioneering teacher of Greek in the West; Filelfo was a renowned Italian humanist who married Chrysoloras's niece.</note>. This Emanuel, having executed his charge as best he could, stayed in Italy and taught publicly in Venice, then in Florence, in Rome, and finally in Pavia. One may still read today a Greek grammar composed by him, printed by **Wechel** <note>The Wechel family were famous humanist printers in Paris and Frankfurt.</note>. He died in Germany at the time of the Council of Constance.

After this person came **Bessarion**, a native of Trebizond and Bishop of Nicaea, a Greek by nation, made and created Cardinal in Rome in the year of salvation 1438 or 1440 (according to **Nicholas Chalcondyles** in book 6 of the *History of the Turks*) by Pope **Eugene IV**. Under the empire of the said **John Palaeologus**, and later of **Constantine**, he retired to Rome after the city of Constantinople was taken by **Mehmed II**, Emperor of the Turks. # History of the Origin of...

...indeed a beautiful Greek library of thirteen hundred volumes of Greek books written by hand.

Some modern authors maintain that before the aforementioned Chrysoloras <note>Manuel Chrysoloras (c. 1355–1415), a pioneer in the introduction of Greek literature to Western Europe.</note>, Constantine Lascaris of Byzantium was the first of all the Greeks to teach Greek letters in Italy and to compose a Greek Grammar there, according to A. Thevet <note>André Thevet (1516–1590), a French Franciscan explorer and writer.</note> in book 18, chapter 2 of his *Universal Cosmography*. We have this Grammar today, printed in several places. His brother John was also the first to compose the Rudiments in that language, according to the same A. Thevet in book 19, chapter 7 of his said *Universal Cosmography*. He also discusses this at length in book 1, chapter 19, and in books 45 and 46 of his *Illustrious Men*.

The successor to the aforementioned Chrysoloras was George Trapezuntius, or George of Trebizond, who kept the name of his ancient country instead of his own; he was born in Candia <note>The Venetian name for the island of Crete.</note>, and his ancestors came from Pontus, a renowned region in Greece. After these came Theodore Gaza, a gentleman of Thessaloniki, expelled from his country by the tyranny of the Great Turk, Murad <note>Sultan Murad II, who captured Thessaloniki in 1430.</note>. The aforementioned George of Trebizond and Theodore Gaza were rivals; however, Theodore Gaza surpassed George of Trebizond in quickness of spirit, dexterity of judgment, and knowledge of both the Greek and Latin languages. He translated from Greek into Latin Aristotle's *History of Animals* and Theophrastus's *History of Plants* <note>Original: *Plantes de phrafte*. Theophrastus was a successor to Aristotle and is often called the "father of botany."</note>. In doing so, he first smoothed the roughness of Latin words, joining them properly, and then assembled or coupled them together following the example of the composition of the Greek language. He preserved the force and virtue of the Greek words through new Latin terms with such dexterity and through such a bold and successful translation that he greatly enriched the Latin language.

He composed grammatical instructions in his own language which are still seen today, as well as several other books on Rhetoric and other subjects.

John Argyropoulos, a native of Constantinople and friend and companion of Theodore Gaza, was the tutor of Piero de' Medici (son of Cosimo) and Lorenzo his nephew <note>Likely referring to Lorenzo the Magnificent, who was actually Piero's son; the term "nephew" was sometimes used more broadly for descendants in this period.</note>. He explained the Greek authors in the city of Florence and later in Rome. Johann "Capnion" Reuchlin <note>Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a key German humanist. "Capnion" is a Greek nickname derived from the German *Rauch*, meaning smoke.</note> heard him teach. Reuchlin was in the city of Rome, and when speaking sometimes of the first conversations he had with Argyropoulos, he recounted the following: having entered the hall where this great man was lecturing, serving as an ambassador for several men, he found there a great number of listeners—Cardinals and old men as well as youths, all of noble and good houses. Having paid his respects to Argyropoulos, he deplored the banishment of the Greeks and said that he desired to be one of his students. Argyropoulos asked him from what country he came and if he understood the Greek language. To this, Reuchlin replied that Germany was his country and that he had learned something of the Greek language. This led Argyropoulos to ask him to read a part of a speech by Thucydides <note>An ancient Greek historian known for his *History of the Peloponnesian War*.</note> and to try to explain and interpret it in the Latin tongue. Reuchlin took the book and began to read in a loud voice, adding the Latin exposition or interpretation with a very sweet and easy pronunciation, explaining...

# History of the Origin of the

...known that the great wisdom and providence of God ensured that the Greek language was planted throughout the vast extent of the great Roman Empire shortly before the time of Julius Caesar <note>original: "Iules Cæsar"</note> the Emperor, for no other reason or occasion than that the Evangelists and Apostles, who were to write, preach, and announce His Gospel in this language, might be more easily understood by the peoples and nations destined to receive them. For this same reason, we must believe that the same wisdom and providence of God permitted the Turks to occupy Greece in the time of our fathers, so that by means of the Greeks exiled and banished from that land, who took refuge and retired to Italy, France, and Germany, the Italians, French, and Germans might recognize the most beautiful and excellent discourses and secrets of this Gospel, originally written and composed in that Greek language. They taught and learned it in the form and manner that has been more particularly detailed above in this chapter.

Palmerius <note>Matteo Palmieri (1406–1475), an Italian humanist and historian.</note> and Polydore Vergil <note>Polydore Vergil (c. 1470–1555), an Italian scholar who wrote a famous history of England.</note> in Book 4 of the *History of England*, following Wernerus <note>Werner Rolevinck (1425–1502), author of the popular history "Fasciculus Temporum" or "The Bundle of Time."</note> in the *Bundle of Time*, hold that Charlemagne was the first to transfer the Academy to Paris. This Academy had, long before, moved from the city of Athens to that of Rome, and this transfer was achieved through the ministry of four disciples of the monk Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 672–735), the famous Anglo-Saxon scholar.</note>, named Rabanus, Albinus <note>Albinus is the scholarly name for Alcuin of York, the primary intellectual advisor to Charlemagne.</note>, Claudius, and Johannes Scotus <note>Johannes Scotus Eriugena (c. 815–c. 877), an Irish theologian and philosopher.</note>. This is confirmed by Erphordiensis in chapter 69 and Cardinal F. Zabarella in the *Clementines* <note>Francesco Zabarella (1360–1417), an influential canon lawyer.</note> on *De Magistris*, question 5. Gilbert Genebrard <note>G. Genebrad (1535–1597), a French Benedictine exegete and historian.</note> speaks of it amply in Book 3 of his *Chronography*, folio 519.

Our History of France records that the late King Francis I, at the persuasion of Guillaume Budé and Jean du Bellay <note>Jean du Bellay (1492–1560), a French cardinal and diplomat.</note>, was the first to institute at the University of Paris the public professors of the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages. For the Hebrew language, he appointed François Vatable; for Greek, Pierre Danés of Paris. To these he added two others: Agathius Guidacerius, a doctor of the Hebrew language, and Jacques Tusan, a doctor of the Greek language. Then, upon the promotion of Pierre Castellanus <note>Pierre Castillan (1493–1552), the King’s "Anagnoste" or reader, who became a high-ranking churchman.</note>, his Reader, he likewise instituted public professors in the Latin language, according to the confirmation of Carion in Book 3 and of Du Tillet in his *Chronicle*.

->On the comparison of the Greek language with the Hebrew language.<-

Those who know and recognize the beauties, perfections, and excellences of the ancient languages, and who wish to look closely at what we have detailed and discussed above regarding these learned tongues, cannot and shall not be ignorant of the fact that the Hebrew language is the least elegant, least copious, and least filled with words, names, phrases, and verbs of any language there is. Nor was anyone ever absolutely skilled in the Latin tongue unless he was steeped in Greek. For from the Greek language flowed the Latin, and from the Latin flowed the Italian, Spanish, and French, for which nations the Latin language was once the native tongue. And we find by experience that the Latin language becomes more fruitful and eloquent because of the Greek, and the other languages of Europe from the Latin, but especially those three I have just listed: which it would be most advantageous to accustom to Latin speech, both so that the language itself and all the arts might be rightly understood through it, and so that they might render their own native speech purer and more opulent, derived from it like more abundant water from a fountain. What of the fact that many things are committed to memory in Greek letters in history, the nature of things, private and public customs, medicine, and piety, which are both more easily and more purely drawn from the original sources themselves? <note>original: "Lingua Græca est erudita admodum & locuplex..."</note>

## CHAPTER LXI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>We shall advise curious readers at the beginning of this chapter that to well and perfectly understand what the Traditions of the Christians are, they must first read all that we have previously said in the preceding seventh chapter concerning the Kabbalah of the Hebrews <note>The author links Christian tradition to the Jewish "Kabbalah," which literally means "reception" or "that which is received" through oral transmission.</note>. Once this is done, we shall say that Saint John, at the end of his Gospel, made solemn mention of Traditions when he said: "There are many other things that Jesus did; if they were written one by one, I do not think the whole world could contain the books that would have to be written" <note>original: "Il y a aſſez d’autres choſes que Ieſus a faictes..."—referencing John 21:25.</note>. Regarding this, the great Origen <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar and theologian from Alexandria.</note>, in a certain part of his writings, writes that Jesus Christ, the master of life, revealed many things to his disciples which they did not wish to write down, lest they become common to the masses. This is greatly confirmed by Saint Dionysius the Areopagite <note>Dionysius was a theologian whose writings were highly influential in the Middle Ages; he was believed to be the Dionysius converted by St. Paul in Athens.</note>, who says that the more secret mysteries were transferred from the authors of the holy religion <unclear>from mind to mind through the medium of the word</unclear> <note>original Greek: "ἐκ νόυ εἰς νόυν διὰ μέσου λόγου"</note>, from soul to soul without writing, through the intervening spoken word. And it is in exactly this way, when by God’s command that true interpretation of the law was revealed and divinely handed down to Moses, it was called the Kabbalah; because among the Hebrews it means the same as "Reception" among us, specifically because they received that doctrine not through written records, but through the regular succession of revelations from one to another, as if by hereditary right. This is confirmed by the most learned Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>A famous Italian Renaissance philosopher (1463–1494) known for his "Oration on the Dignity of Man."</note> in his oration on the dignity of man. A certain modern author in his works says these words:
> The law of the New Testament is also both written and unwritten. The written part contains the four Gospels of Saints Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; it also contains the history of the Apostles, their Epistles, and the interpretation of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>. The unwritten part is contained in the Apostolic Traditions.

Now, the Traditions of the beginning were understood as all that was passed down from mouth to mouth, from hand to hand, from one to another—such as that which, in the infancy of the Church, *Adam* received from the very voice of his Creator. From him it was transmitted to his successors, notably through *Enoch, Methuselah, and Noah*, until *Abraham*; and from *Abraham* through *Jacob and Amram* to *Moses*. Moses was the first who (as I have already remarked) reduced to writing the precepts and ordinances of the divine will, and that which God requires of man here below—all within the context of a history, continued in succession from the creation of the World until the hour of his death, when the *Israelites* entered the land promised to them. 

And thus the divine law was maintained from *Adam* until *Moses* by a verbal tradition from one to another—at the very least the principal points and articles. For it is not to be presumed that God would have wished to leave the human race for so long, especially the gentle and people of good will, without knowledge of Himself. One sees clearly enough through the thread of holy history that the ancient *Patriarchs* recognized and adored none but the one and true God, even though it is said in *Genesis 4* that *Enos* began to invoke the name of the Lord—that is to say, more solemnly than it had yet been done. 

And in chapter 26, God says in express terms to *Isaac* that He will give him such and such blessings, together with his posterity, because *Abraham* had received His word and added to it an indubitable faith, kept His precepts, and observed His covenants, laws, statutes, and ceremonies without infringing upon them. For circumcision, which is the entrance to the Judaic law, had been practiced by *Abraham* long before *Moses*. And that which is ordered in the eighteenth chapter, to instruct his children and family in the ways of the Lord to perform judgment and Justice—is this not repeated in several places in the law of *Moses*? As in *Deuteronomy eleven*: "walk in the ways of the Lord and cling to him"; and in the twenty-fourth: "have Justice in recommendation before your God." # Of the Armenians:

## CHAPTER LXIII.

Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian (c. 64 BC–24 AD).</note>, in the 11th book of his *Geography*, left a written record stating that Armenia formerly took its name from a man from Thessaly <note>A region in Greece.</note> named Armenus, a native of a city in Thessaly called Armenia, which was situated between Pherae and Larissa. This Armenus followed Jason <note>The mythological leader of the Argonauts.</note> on his voyage. After returning from Greece, Jason traveled back to the Levant and conquered the provinces of Mingrelia, Georgia, and Albania <note>Here referring to Caucasian Albania, an ancient kingdom in the Caucasus, not the modern European nation.</note>, which he populated and instructed in the superstitions of the Greeks. After Jason passed away, this Armenus gathered the Greek troops together and brought about the settlement of this province. From this, it happened that in ancient times the Armenians dressed, armed themselves, and spurred their horses in the manner of the Thessalians, which Justin <note>A Latin historian who lived under the Roman Empire.</note> seems to confirm in the 42nd book of his histories. Some authors maintain that Armenia was named after the Arameans or Syrians, whom we have discussed extensively before; these people first came to settle there according to Guillaume Postel <note>A French polymath and orientalist (1510–1581).</note> in his discourse on the notable regions that took their names from the children of Noah, and André Thevet in the 8th book, chapter 13, of his *Cosmography*. Others say it was named after these Hebrew words ארמנייה *Aram Miniah* <note>original: "ארמנייה." Literally "Armenia," though the author interprets it as a compound of "Aram" and "Minni."</note>, and by contraction, "Armenia," meaning the "height of God." At present, this province is still named Armenia, or *Aremnoe*, without having lost its ancient name. It is true that the learned Abraham Ortelius <note>A famous Flemish cartographer and geographer (1527–1598).</note>, in his *Geographical Synonyms*, wrote the following words about it:

> Greater Armenia—called *Armenia* [Αρμενια] by Ptolemy and others, and by Strabo with an aspiration—is a region of Asia. In later centuries, it was nicknamed "the Second," as is clear from the *Book of Notices* <note>The *Notitia Dignitatum*, a document of the late Roman Empire's administrative organization.</note>. Arias Montanus <note>A Spanish orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note> testifies in his *Biblical Appendix* that it is called "Aram" in Hebrew. It is called *Turcomannia* by Mercator and Girava. Thevet writes that the Mesopotamians and Persians call it *Thoura Aremnoe*, that is, "the mountains of Armenia," and the Nestorians call it *Zelbiodibes*, that is, "mountains inhabited by wolves." I would believe that it retains its ancient name because of the Christians living there. Lesser Armenia is nicknamed "the First" in the *Book of Notices*. It is also called *Leucosyria* [White Syria] by Procopius in the first book of the *Persian War*. In the Holy Scriptures, it is called *Ararat*. Likewise, it is called *Uz* according to Arias Montanus. Today, if Girava speaks the truth, it is called *Anaduole*; if Castaldo, it is called *Pegian*. Eustathius writes that Armenia was divided into four parts by King Justinian: the first called *Heptapolis* [Seven-cities], the second *Pentapolis* [Five-cities], the third *Hexapolis* [Six-cities], and the fourth *Tzopharis* and בת ביתן, *Balbitena* <note>original: "בת ביתן." Likely referring to "Beth Bitan" or the House of the Pavilion.</note>.

This province is situated in Asia and its boundaries were set by Ptolemy in book 5, chapter 13, in the third table of Asia: to the North lies a part of Mingrelia, Iberia, and Albania along the River Cur, otherwise called the Cyrus; to the West, it looks toward Cap[padocia]...

To the South, it borders Mesopotamia along the aforementioned Mount Taurus, called Kurdistan <note>Original: "Cortheſtan."</note> where it joins the Euphrates and the Tigris; it also faces Assyria near Mount Niphates. To the East, its limit is partly the Caspian Sea, from the place where the river Cur—otherwise called the Cyre <note>The Kura River</note>, formerly bearing the name Corax and Mede—enters it, down to the mouth of the Araxes <note>The Aras River</note> near the foothills of the Caspian mountain. This same mountain also borders it as far as Mount Niphates. Although Appian <note>An ancient Roman historian</note> writes that it is the Araxes river which divides this province from the land of the Medes, the truth is that it is not the Araxes, but rather the Caspian mountain that creates this separation. Hayton the Armenian <note>Hethum of Korykos, a medieval historian and monk</note>, in his *Book of the Tartars*, chapter 9, partitioned and divided this province into four kingdoms, although almost always a single King held command there. Josaphat Barbaro <note>A Venetian diplomat and traveler</note>, in the fourth chapter of his book on his travels in Persia, writes that the Turks first occupied it in the year 1230, taking it from the brothers Rubin and Leon, which is confirmed by André Thevet <note>A 16th-century French explorer and writer</note> in book 8, chapter 15 of his *Cosmography*. Today, these same Turks command most of it, and the Sophy <note>The Safavid Shah of Persia</note> rules over the other part which extends toward Diarbakir <note>Original: "Diarbeth."</note>. However, the Muhammadan religion has not gained such credit and reputation there that one does not find many Armenian Christians and Catholics within it. These Armenians do not use the exact same ceremonies in their churches as we Christians do in our Roman Church, but they hold almost, or very nearly, the same foundation of belief as ours. This can be seen in the travels of Duarte Barbosa <note>A Portuguese writer and officer in Portuguese India</note> to the Indies, the travels of Brother Nicolle le Hué, a Doctor of Theology and Carmelite monk, and those of an anonymous merchant in Persia; likewise in the treatise on the twelve different languages and alphabets by the late Guillaume Postel <note>A French linguist and polymath</note>, in book 8, chapters 13, 14, and 15 of André Thevet's *Cosmography*, and in volume 2, book 3, chapters 7, 8, and 9 of the *Universal Cosmography* by François de Belleforest. The Catholicos <note>The head of the Armenian Church</note> or Primate of these Armenians—called *Roa* by them and by the Turks, and *Ethasept* by the Persians—sent his profession of faith in the name of all the churches subject to him to the Holy General Council of Trent <note>A major ecumenical council of the Catholic Church held between 1545 and 1563</note>. He submitted himself to the Rule and censure of the Catholic and Apostolic Church of Rome, abjuring and condemning all sects, errors, opinions, and beliefs that have been, are, and shall be condemned by this Apostolic Church. The written decree of this act has been seen by several honorable persons still living today, held in the hands of a certain Chaldean Deacon who came from Rome to this Kingdom to see and note the manner and order that our ecclesiastics observed in the celebration of divine service. These Armenians are unique among all the subjects and tributaries of the Turks in that they are not made and rendered slaves or serfs by them. This is because, as they say, an Armenian once prophesied that the glory and renown of Muhammad would spread throughout the universe; in memory of this, no one of this nation is placed into servitude by the Muhammadans, as asserted by Laonikos Chalkokondyles <note>A Byzantine Greek historian</note> in book 3 of his *History of the Turks*. However, Guillaume Postel, in his treatise on the twelve different languages and alphabets, speaks of it differently, saying that these Armenians are held in great honor and reverence toward

## CHAPTER LXII.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'T' decorated with scrolling acanthus leaves and floral motifs in a square frame.</image-desc>

Theodore Bibliander <note>A 16th-century Swiss linguist and theologian</note> in his *Commentary on the Common Reasoning of All Languages and Letters*, speaking of the language and letters of the Armenians, says the following, following Hayton the Armenian <note>Also known as Hethum of Korykos, a medieval monk and historian</note>, who flourished in the year of Salvation 1300.

"The Armenians have Armenian letters and others which are called Haloen <note>Likely referring to the Caucasian Albanian script, also known as 'Aghwan'</note>. And because their Patriarch, whom they call Catholicos <note>Original: "Catholique"</note>, has a thousand bishops joined with him, all called Christians; and in order to clearly demonstrate in how many places and provinces the use of the Armenian language extends, I will cite in this place the very words of Hayton the Armenian in his histories, saying that in the land of Armenia there are four kingdoms, possessed at all times by one single and unique King." This Hayton, in chapter 9, speaking of these Armenians, says: They have Armenian letters, and others also which are called Haloen <note>Original Latin: "Litteras habent Armenicas, & alias etiam quæ dicuntur Haloen."</note>. The longitude of this land begins from the kingdom of Persia and extends toward the West as far as the kingdom of Turkey; its latitude begins from the city of Mirale, called the Iron Gate <note>The 'Porte de Fer' usually refers to the pass at Derbent or the Darial Pass</note> at the foot of Mount Caucasus <note>Original: "Cocas"</note>, and reaches as far as the Kingdom of Media. And that the ancient language of the Armenians agrees greatly with the Chaldean and Syriac languages is verified both by the origin of these Armenians, who are descended from Aram, son of Shem <note>Referring to the Table of Nations in Genesis</note>, and by the proper names of men, places, and other arguments.

Guillaume Postel <note>A famous 16th-century French polyglot and humanist</note>, a very learned person in this language, speaks thus of this tongue, which was in use among those Armenians in the time of the aforementioned Hayton, and which is still used among them today: "Among all the languages of this World, Armenian is the most difficult to pronounce, since it has several things in common with the languages of the Orientals, several others with that of the Greeks, and several others still with that of the Gauls <note>Postel was known for attempting to find links between all world languages and French/Celtic origins</note>." This language, concerning religion, is not only in use among those Armenians in both Greater and Lesser Armenia, as is commonly believed, but also throughout all the Muslim <note>Original: "Mahometanes"</note> provinces and regions, such as in all of Asia Minor, Syria, Tartary, Persia, and the regions situated around the Pontic or Black Sea, and principally...

ally themselves with the Jews and Muslims than with them; as much for the infamy
they once received from them—having rejected them from their communion as
heretics—as because they agree in most of their
traditions and ceremonies with the Roman Church. But they still retain
some hint of their ancient Nestorianism <note>A doctrine concerning the nature of Christ, often used here as a general label for Eastern Christian practices distinct from the Greek Orthodox</note>. Armenia, for the rest, as
has been said above, has been for a very long time divided into two: Greater
and Lesser. The former is now called Turcomania, of which the Sophy <note>The Safavid Shah of Persia</note>
possesses the greater part: for even the city of Tabriz <note>original: "Tauris"</note>, now the capital

Paphlagonia, and the Great Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>; now almost entirely reduced under
the obedience of the Turk. Some wish to confound it with Cilicia, which

moved by the fact that the city of Seleucia, now Silephica <note>Silifke</note>, which undoubtedly
used to be anciently in Cilicia, is today included within
Lesser Armenia, which, according to Josaphat Barbaro in his *Travels to Persia*
Chapter 4, took that name around the year 1230, when two Princes named Ruben and
Leo—brothers of the Armenian Princess—gave it its name, having recovered it
from the hands of the Turks, who had seized it. For when they came out of
Tartary <note>Central Asia</note>, these Armenians were the first attacked and defeated by them, so
that they lost their Kingdom; nonetheless, they have always continued
since then in the Christian faith, in which they have so constantly maintained
themselves that even naming an "Armenian" throughout all the lands of the Turk
suddenly implies a Christian; but when they convert to Islam <note>original: "se Mahometisent"</note>, they
lose this name of Armenian. As for their belief and religion today,
notwithstanding that they differ in certain things from the Latin Church, they
are much further removed from the Greek: for to further divide themselves from them,
and from the Syrians who are their partisans and rivals, they eat
meat on certain Fridays and drink wine there, along with other intoxicating
beverages for those who use them. Formerly, while they were still governed
under a private Royalty, their *Melich*—that is to say, King—was
sovereign in spiritual matters as well as in temporal ones; but
now they have a Primate whom they call the Catholicos <note>The head of the Armenian Apostolic Church</note>. Their

### History of the Origin of the [Armenians]

...only the Greeks; and they wear a large and wide crown [tonsure] at the top of the head, with the rest of their hair allowed to spread all around and grow as long as it can, and the beard likewise, in the manner of the Nazirites <note>original: "Nazareens"; a reference to the biblical Nazirites who took vows not to cut their hair</note>. For they never trim anything except the aforementioned tonsure, which the laypeople also wear in the same spot, but braided in the form of a cross. This has been the custom since the year 744 when, finding themselves greatly harassed by war with the Syrians, they were advised in a revelation to adopt this style of dress, immediately after which they defeated their enemies. Their priests are very venerable and as reformed as any others; and although their divine service closer resembles Latin ceremonies than Greek ones—even regarding the style of their chalices and patens <note>original: "platines"; the plates used to hold the bread during the Eucharist</note>—they nonetheless celebrate in their vernacular [native language], and the congregation responds in kind. When the Gospel is sung, they all stand and kiss each other on the cheek as a sign of reconciliation, peace, and brotherly love, just as the ancient Christians did when they gave the Kiss of Peace <note>original: "Osculum Pacis"</note>. Their Eucharist is unleavened <note>original: "azime"</note> like ours, that is to say, made of dough without yeast, in the form of a round host. Once it is consecrated, they place it on the paten, and thus lift and show it to the people, and subsequently the Chalice, which is made of either crystal or wood; they do not add any water to the wine.

They have young children confirmed by a simple priest. They do not receive the orders of Deacon or Subdeacon, but only the priesthood itself. They do not feast on the Nativity of our Lord [Christmas] as we do, but instead fast austerely on that day; in return, they solemnize with great devotion the day of Epiphany, which they take for His spiritual birth, believing that on this same day He was baptized by Saint John in the Jordan River. They perform their prayers and orisons almost in the fashion of the Turks or Arabs, crouching low on their heels, and they kiss the earth three times (where the Turks do so only twice, and the Greeks pray standing upright). Of all the saints, they hold in greatest reverence the Apostle Saint James the Greater, whom they consider their protector and patron; they possess a very beautiful church dedicated to him in Jerusalem, built near the place where he was beheaded, and others still where they assemble in large numbers, as confirmed by the Lord of Villamont in book 2, chapter 23 of his *Travels* <note>Jacques de Villamont (1557–1622), a French traveler who documented the Middle East</note>.

As for Lent, they observe it at the same time as we do, but with far greater austerity beyond comparison; for they drink no wine during it, and eat nothing whatsoever that has had life—not even butter or oil, nor any other flavorful liquid. Instead, they live only on herbs and thin vegetable soups seasoned with a little salt, dried olives (not preserved in oil), and similar things of little taste or appetite. Finally, they have their own separate cemeteries, just like all other sects and religions. Their common and everyday speech is Turkish, and their writing is Arabic, because they converse and trade among those peoples; but in their divine service and in their private discussions and business, they use their own particular language and characters <note>The Armenian alphabet</note>. Of these, there are two types, one older than the other, as Josaphat Barbaro <note>A 15th-century Venetian diplomat</note> aptly notes in his *Travels to Persia*, chapter 17, saying:

"The castle of Curchò <note>Korykos, a former Armenian stronghold in Cilicia</note>, on the frontispiece of the great gate, has certain inscrip—"

# Languages of this Universe.

Modern reports coming from the Levant and Italy state that the Primate, otherwise called the Great Catholicos <term>Catholicos: The head of the Armenian Apostolic Church</term> of these Armenians, is accustomed every seven years to send a monk to Rome to render the obedience they have promised and sworn to His Holiness. It is true that if, within the seven years mentioned above, this Primate or Great Catholicos should happen to die, and another is created in his place, this new Primate or Great Catholicos must offer a new oath of obedience for his investiture. In the year 1592, during the time of Pope Clement VIII, the Patriarch of Armenia and the Maronites of Mount Lebanon came to Rome to offer their obedience to the Holy Apostolic See, according to the author of the appendix to the *Chronology* of Gilbert Génébrard <note>Génébrard (1535–1597) was a prominent French Benedictine exegete and orientalist</note>.

Whoever wishes to learn this Armenian language should carefully read the introduction by Theseus Ambrosius <note>Teseo Ambrogio degli Albonesi, an early 16th-century Italian polyglot</note> on the Chaldean, Syriac, and Armenian languages, chapter 13, *On the letters and introduction of the Armenians* <note>original: "de Armeniorum litteris, & introductione"</note>.

### The Lord's Prayer in the Armenian language.

> *Chair mer vr hierchins des srboi ez iſi anoncho ekeſſe archaiotaicho, eZiffius chan Kcho vrbis Kierkins ie & chri zachas mer hanaba gſordtour mez ais aur ie touz mer zaabartis mer vrbis ie mech toſſumo baribanas merus ie mi tamir Zame zprtZo tai ail phirkai Zamer i zare. Amen.*

This prayer was taken from the writings of modern travelers and cosmographers, who seem not to have had a true and complete knowledge of this Armenian language, inasmuch as in that language, one should pronounce the said prayer as I have it before me in Armenian characters and tongue:

> *Hair mer or iercins des ſurb, eglizzi anuncho ecesZZe archaiuthai cho, eglizzin camch cho orpas iercins eu iercri. ZhaZt mer hanapazord tur meZ aiſaur eu thogl meZ zpaartis, mer orpas eu inech thoglumch meroZi partpanazt eu mi tanir zmeZi phorxuthai ail pharceai zmeZi zara zi cho e archaiuthai eu Zauruthai eu pharch iauiteans. Amen.*

> <note>original Latin: "Pater noster qui es in cœlis..."</note> Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, thy will be done, as in heaven so on earth. Give us this day our supersubstantial bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors, and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory forever. Amen.

# History of the Origin of [Languages]

**Pliny.** Ranzanus writes in his *History of Hungary* <note>original: "Hungaria"; Petrus Ranzanus (1428–1492) was a Sicilian bishop and historian</note> that all of Dalmatia, along with the neighboring regions of Illyris and Liburnia, is commonly called **Slavonia** <note>original: "Sclauonia"</note> by all these nations with a single name. And whatever fields are passed through on the journey toward Italy are called **Croatia**: they pronounce it as *Krabatemani*. Regarding the Dalmatian sea, Tacitus refers to it in the third book of his *Annals* as **Illyricum**; Pliny calls it **Illyris** <note>original: ἰλλυρίς</note>; Ptolemy calls it **Illyria**; and Stephanus calls it **Illyricus**. A coin of Trajan mentions the "Illyricians" on an ancient stone. Among geographers, it is a region of Europe extending far and wide; however, Pliny restricts it between the Arsia and Titius rivers <note>The Arsia is the modern Raša in Istria, and the Titius is the Krka in Dalmatia</note>. He says that what was once Pliny’s Illyricum is today called *Slavonia* in Italian and *Windenland* <note>original: "Vuidenland"</note> in German. Lazius <note>Wolfgang Lazius (1514–1565), a humanist scholar</note> is mistaken in saying it was called "Quirinal Illyricum" based on an ancient inscription which states that a triumph was celebrated for the Illyrians on the "Quirinal festivals" <note>original: "festis Quirinalibus"</note>. It is common in the books of the Triumphal Records to add the day of the triumph. Concerning Illyricum, read Appian, Sextus Rufus, Jordanes, the *Register of Dignitaries* <note>original: "lib. Notitiarum"</note>, and Lazius, book 1, chapter 1, where you will find many regions included under this name; see also **Pannonia**.

**Albania**, a region of Asia <note>This refers to "Caucasian Albania," an ancient kingdom in the eastern Caucasus, not modern Albania in the Balkans</note> according to Ptolemy. It is called **Zuiria** <note>original: ἀλϐανία</note> by Girolamo Ruscelli and Alphonso Adriano, and **Chipiche** by Castaldo. Dominicus Niger writes that it is called **Zitracha** by the inhabitants, and by some **Garzena**.

**Colchis** <note>original: κολχίς</note>, a region of Asia whose inhabitants are called the **Lazi** <note>original: λάζοι</note> by Procopius, Gregoras, Suidas, and Isaac Tzetzes. Lycophron calls Colchis **Lygystica** <note>original: λίγυστικην</note>. Stephanus calls it *Libystine* with a "B" in this passage of Lycophron. The same Stephanus considers the Libystine peoples to be adjacent to Colchis. Herodotus also places the **Ligyans** in this tract, and among them the city of **Ligystice**, according to Stephanus. Ma...ger <unclear>illegible</unclear> writes that Colchis was previously called **Arimana**, citing Appian as a witness. He also says it is divided by younger writers into two provinces: namely into **Mingrelia**, which touches the sea, and **Gurcia** <note>Georgia</note>, which is inhabited further inland. These, I believe, are the Lazi of Herodotus, or the **Manrali**, who are placed in Colchis by Ptolemy. Moletius reports that Colchis, Albania, and Iberia are today called by the single name **Comania**. Ogier de Busbecq <note>A 16th-century Flemish diplomat</note> writes in his letters that the people are today called **Mingrellians** by the Italians. In the same place, he says the Albanians and Iberians are called **Georgians**. He describes this Colchis very skillfully. Furthermore, the Sixth Synod of Constantinople <note>The Third Council of Constantinople, 680–681 AD</note> teaches that a few centuries ago this was called **Lazica**; in which it is written: *Theodorus, the Great Bishop of Phasis in Lazica.* No one is ignorant that Phasis is in Colchis. Colchis is also a city of Greater Armenia according to Ptolemy. See **Mengrelia**.

**Macedonia**, a famous region of Greece: it was previously called **Emathia** <note>original: ἠμαθία</note> according to Pliny and Trogus. Livy writes that it was first called **Paeonia**, and then **Aemonia**. Likewise, it was called **Edonia** and **Pieria** by Solinus. Trogus writes in his seventh book that it was also called **Boeotia**. Stephanus and Hesychius write that a part of it was once called **Macetia** <note>original: μακετία</note>, and Eustathius, in his commentary on Dionysius, reports that the whole region took its name from there. The inhabitants were called **Macetae**, whom Trogus calls **Pelasgians**. In later centuries, a part of this was **Macedonia Salutaris** in the *Register of Dignitaries*, which was partly in Macedonia and partly in Dacia. Likewise **Praevalis**, or **Praevalitana**, according to Sextus Rufus. There is also **Maritime Macedonia** in Dio, which he says was inhabited by the Paeonians near Mount Rhodope. This region of Macedonia is called "The First" by Is... <unclear>illegible</unclear>, for he divides Macedonia into four regions. Part...

# Languages of this Universe

### Macedonia
**Free Macedonia** <note>original: "Macedoniæ Libera"</note> is the name used by Caesar in the third book of the *Civil War*. Livy likewise writes that the Romans wished the Macedonians and Illyrians to be free. In later times, there is mention only of **Macedonia I and II**, which are frequently recorded in the records of the Church Councils.

### Thrace
**Thrace** <note>Greek: Θρᾴκη</note> is a celebrated region of Europe according to Ptolemy and others, located by the **Euxine Sea** <note>The Black Sea</note>. I find it written with a diphthong as *Thæcia* as well. Among the ancients, it was called **Aria** <note>Greek: ἀρία</note> and **Perca** <note>Greek: περκὴ</note>; Stephanus calls it **Odryse** <note>Greek: ὀδρύση</note>, and Suidas also uses this name. (Livy mentions certain of its people as the **Odrysae**). It is also called **Crestona** <note>Greek: κρηστόνη</note> by Isaacius, following Lycophron. It is even referred to as **Scythia**, as Erythraeus asserts. We frequently find it written as *Trachia* instead of *Thracia* among medieval authors. Josephus writes that in **Hebrew** it is named **Thiras** <note>Greek: Θῆρας; referring to the biblical Thiras, son of Japheth</note>. Ancient writers refer to the inhabitants of this Thrace by various names. Herodotus writes that they were called **Bithynians** after they crossed the sea into Asia; before that, they were called **Strymonians**. They are called **Bardi** by Martianus, and **Dolongi** <note>Greek: δόλογκοι</note> by Lycophron and Stephanus. Formerly they were named **Briges** <note>Greek: βρύγες</note>, as Eustathius records. Arrian calls certain of them **Autonomoi** <note>meaning "independent" or "self-governed"</note>. Among these, Strabo calls some the **Sapae** and **Sapaei** <note>Greek: σάπαι and σαπαῖοι</note>, and Ptolemy mentions a **Sapaic Prefecture**. Likewise, they are called **Sipii** by Stephanus. Also the **Saii** <note>Greek: σάϊοι</note>, **Sinti**, and **Sintia** <note>Greek: σίντοι and σίντια</note>. Paul the Deacon distinguishes two Thraces, writing that both were devastated by Attila the Hun; perhaps he follows Xenophon under the reign of the younger Emperor Valentinian, for Xenophon in the sixth book of the *Cyropaedia* describes an **Asiatic Thrace** in addition to this European one. Indeed, he so names **Bithynia**, where Calpe and Heraclea are located. The *Register of Dignitaries* <note>original: "liber Notitiarum"; likely the Notitia Dignitatum, a document of the late Roman Empire</note> and Ammianus in his 27th book count six provinces under its name. Sextus Rufus does the same, and they are these: **Thrace** (by its specific name), **Moesia Secunda**, **Scythia**, **Europa**, **Rhodopa**, and **Haemimontum**. Today it is called by the single name **Romania** <note>This refers to the region of Rumelia or the Byzantine "Land of the Romans," not just the modern nation of Romania</note>; and Paul the Deacon and Conrad of Lichtenau always call it such. Jordanes does the same in his book *On the Succession of Kingdoms*. In place of Thrace, Serapio reads **Badachas** in the chapter on the Caltrop in Dioscorides. Isocrates, in his first *Panegyric* oration, is the authority for the fact that Thracians once lived in the neighborhood of the Athenians. Strabo writes in book 11 that Thracians with the surname **Saraparae** are said to live above Armenia. See the entry for *Saraparae*. Eustathius, drawing from Sacred History, testifies that there is a certain **Mountainous Thrace** in the southern parts of Africa above Alexandria. Diodorus, in his 5th book, mentions a Thracian city and island in **Arabia Felix** <note>the southern Arabian Peninsula</note>. See also **Bithynia**.

### Iazyges
The **Iazyges** <note>Greek: Ἰάζυγες</note> in Strabo and Ptolemy are a people in **European Sarmatia** beyond Germany, toward the East. Werner <note>Georg Werner, a 16th-century humanist</note> thinks they are those who are today called the **Iaz** <note>The Jasz people of Hungary</note>; they have a peculiar and ancestral language. Cromer calls them the **Iasuingi**. Others, following Ptolemy, call them the **Iazyges Metanastae** <note>Greek: μετανάςαί, meaning "migrants" or "displaced"</note>. Niger writes that their region is now called the **Plain of the Cumans**. Strabo, in book 7, also lists the **Royal Iazyges** <note>Greek: βασιλεῖοι</note>. Ovid uses the singular nominative *Iazis* in the 4th book of his *Letters from the Black Sea*. Are these the same as the **Lassii**?

### Pannonia
**Pannonia** <note>Greek: παννονία</note> in Ptolemy is a region of Europe which he divides into **Upper** and **Lower**. Optatus the African mentions **three Pannonias**, contrary to all other writers and ancient coins. These Pannonias, under the Roman Emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and those who followed (as is clear from Rufus Marcellinus and the *Register of Dignitaries*), were distinguished by several names, such as **Pannonia Prima** (perhaps the same as Upper Pannonia); **Pannonia Secunda** (the same as Lower); **Savia**, or **Ripensis**; the *Register of Dignitaries* has **Ripariensis**; and **Valeria**. # History of the Origin of [Languages]

...Aurelius Victor mentions Sabaria in his biographies of the Emperors Decius and Didius Julianus. I believe this same place to be Savia, named for the Save river, while the former was named for the city of Busali. Diaconus mentions Cibalian Pannonia, named after the city of Cabali (which Ptolemy places in Lower Pannonia). Cassiodorus, in the third book of his *Variae* <note>Letters and state papers</note> addressed to Colosseus, mentions Sirmium Pannonia as the former seat of the Goths. Amantine Pannonia is also found in the works of Lazius, cited from Ptolemy and Pliny. Upper Pannonia is today occupied by Austria, Carinthia, and Carniola. The whole of Lower Pannonia is, in our time, under Hungary, which is called *Vuegierska* <note>Related to the Slavic 'Węgierska'</note> in the Slavic tongue. Savia Pannonia is designated as Slavonia by Lazius. Beatus Rhenanus calls the region of Valeria *Krabaten* <note>Modern Croatia</note>. A part of Paeonia toward Thrace, where Mount Rhodope is situated, is now called *Klokotinitza* <term>κλοκοτινίτζα</term> <note>A name likely derived from the Slavic word for bubbling or boiling water</note>, according to Eustathius. See the booklet written by Lazius in the German language regarding the Kingdom of Hungary. The Pannonians were also formerly called Paeonians by the Greeks, especially in early times, though not without error, as Dio Cassius explains in his 49th book. In Appian's *Illyrian Wars*, the name "Paeonians" is frequently used incorrectly in place of "Pannonians."

### Concerning the Region of Tzeruiana, Zeruiana, Seruiana, and Posnaniana.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial A featuring stylized floral and leaf motifs.</image-desc>
Abraham Ortelius, in his *Geographical Synonyms* and *Geographical Treasury*, describes the region of Moesia thus: it is a region of Europe divided into Upper and Lower. Upper Moesia is designated by Leunclavius as *Zirsi*, by Lazius as *Servia* <note>Serbia</note>, by Cuspinian as *Bosna* <note>Bosnia</note>, by Postellus as *Tzeruia* or *Tzeruiana* or *Zeruiana*, by Taurinus as *Olmutian Moldavia*, and by Sabellicus as *Wallachia*. Tzetzes, in his *Chiliads* (Book 11), calls it Hungary. Lower Moesia was at one time called *Flaccia*, as Sabellicus teaches. Pomponius Sabinus calls it the "granary of Ceres" <note>Referring to the region's fertility; Ceres was the Roman goddess of agriculture</note>. Taurinus believes it is called Wallachia. Lazius, Cuspinian, and Chalcondyles call it Bulgaria. Petancius calls it Sagoria.

The Moesians who live near Mount Haemus (who comprise the Lower Moesians) are now called *Vlachs* <note>original: 'Blachi'</note>, according to Nicetas; Pachymeres also mentions them. Regarding this name "Moesia," I wish to add this from the corrections of Pliny by Hermolaus Barbaro: Pliny, Tacitus, Flaccus, Virgil, Martianus, and nearly all Latin manuscripts write this name with the diphthong "oe" [*Moesia*]. However, the Greeks write it with a "y" as *Mysia* <term>Mυσία</term>. It is found written with "ae" [*Maesia*] in an ancient inscription. According to Aldus, Dio Prusaeus teaches that it was once called Mysia and later Moesia. Jordanes records that Moesia is called Lesser Scythia. Zosimus, in his fourth book, calls it Thracian Scythia and places the city of Tomis within it. Ovid, in his books of the *Tristia*, frequently calls this same region Scythia; Arrian does the same in his *Periplus*. I believe this tract of land is what Plutarch calls "Pontic Scythia," and its inhabitants "Scytho-Germans" or *Kelto-Scythians* <term>κελτόσκυθαν</term>. Polyaenus, in the eighth book of his *Stratagems* (in the section on Amage), calls it "Maritime Pontica." I see it is also frequently called simply "Pontus" by classical authors such as Ptolemy, Stephanus, and Ovid in the parts near the shore of the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>, and Pomponius Mela encompasses it under Thrace.

### Concerning the Tzeruian, Zeruuian, or Poznanian Language.

### C H A P T E R LXIV.

<margin>cc</margin>Guillaume Postel, in his *Alphabet of the Twelve Different Languages* <note>original: "Alphabet des douze lágues differẽtes"</note> in characters mentioned above, reported what follows concerning this Tzeruian, Zeruuian, or Poznanian language.
<margin>cc</margin>The Tzeruian or Poznanian regions are regions of our Europe, situated between Dalmatia, Illyria, Albania, Macedonia, Thrace, and the region of the Iazyges Metanastae <note>A nomadic Sarmatian tribe that settled between the Danube and Tisza rivers</note>. Bosnia—also called Posna or Bossine—extends from Upper and Lower Pannonia to the lands of the Gepids <note>An East Germanic tribe</note>, whose region forms part of this Bosnia, Posna, or Bossine. Tzeruiana, or Zeruuiana, otherwise known as Serbia, is the land where Upper Moesia <note>original: "Misie Superieure"</note> was anciently located; it extends from the Danube and Lower Pannonia (otherwise called Liburnia) toward Thrace and Macedonia. This situation moved several very learned linguists to seek the reasons why the inhabitants of these regions, situated between the two most excellent languages of this world <note>Referring to Latin and Greek</note>, invented one peculiar and particular to themselves alone. These learned men said the following around the year of our salvation 300: The Pannonians, Illyrians, Dalmatians, and Moesians had the same or nearly the same language, mixed partly with Greek, partly with Italian <note>Latin/Romance</note>, and partly with German, due to their proximity. Among these people, a certain Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, to whom the invention of the Glagolitic script was historically attributed</note>, a Doctor of Theology and a Dalmatian by nation, invented the characters of the letters, which he derived partly from Hebrew characters and partly from Greek. We shall represent these in a figure in the subsequent chapter. This was done so that these people, being different and dissimilar from other peoples in their language, might also be so in the characters of their letters. They used these for so long that the Roman Church could tolerate the Greek Church alongside it. But since that Church was separated and interdicted from communion with the Roman Church for certain reasons and considerations, those who were closest to the Greeks invented other characters—mostly Greek, however—without changing the names and titles of the first and most ancient ones. For the original letters had already become odious to the Greeks because of their separation from the Roman Church, and to the people because of the interdiction of their Church. But it is more appropriate to uncover the cause of so great a schism or division in the Church of Jesus Christ. The Greeks differed from the Latins in that they consecrated using unleavened bread <term>Azymes</term> <note>The "Azymes" controversy was a major point of contention regarding whether the bread for the Eucharist should be leavened or unleavened</note>, and in that they believe the Holy Spirit proceeds only from the Father <note>The "Filioque" controversy regarding the Nicene Creed</note>; they also practiced the bill of divorce toward a wife who was immodest, sterile, or troublesome; and their priests married. This last practice is common to all Eastern Christians: Indians, Jacobites, Maronites, Armenians, Georgians, Greeks, Wallachians <note>original: "Vualaches"</note> (or Lower Moesians), and to be brief, all other priests and ministers of all other Eastern nations. This was even practiced among the Christians of the Latin Church until the Council of Vienne <note>Held in 1311–1312</note>. Furthermore, they celebrated only a single Mass in each place on Sundays and the feasts of the week.

> Regarding both the Serbian and Bosnian language and literature, Guillaume Postel <note>A French polymath and linguist</note> writes as follows: From the Greek language was born the Georgian and Serbian language and letters. And elsewhere: The Serbians or Bosnians <note>The original Latin "Poznaniani" likely refers to the people of the Posavina region or is a variant for Bosnians</note> used the characters of Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, to whom the invention of the Glagolitic script was traditionally attributed</note> or the Dalmatic ones, as the language was common to the Pannonians, Illyrians, Dalmatians, and Moesians. And a little later: The characters they use are mostly Greek, with some writing that ancient language of theirs, in which they have all their common things and the sacrifice <note>The Mass or Liturgy</note> itself. Others write Greek with their own sounds. Of this kind are many of the Vlachs, who belong to the lower parts of the Dacians and Moesians, and who obey the Patriarch of Constantinople. Furthermore, many of those who live by the Ister, such as a part of the Lithuanians and the inhabitants of the Pontic Sea, the Tauric Chersonese, and the Paphlagonians, use the same sacred rites as the common Greeks. Among the Dalmatians, Illyrians, Pannonians, and Moesians, about 300 years after the birth of Christ, there was one and the same language mixed with Greek, Italian, and sometimes German speech. For these people, Jerome invented characters so that they might differ in this matter from other nations, just as they did in language; perhaps also that he might consecrate the name of his people to immortality. He seems to have invented them after he had learned the Hebrew and Greek letters. Many characters are common with them, and all the names of the letters are meaningful, as those skilled in that language assert. This is a feature shared only with the Hebrews. The same Jerome left the Old and New Testaments, along with the sacrifice and prayers, translated into that idiom. Thus all the priests and the people preach in all of Dalmatia. Many books of these two languages are printed in Venice to be sold there. I will place some parts of the Dalmatian language at the end of the commentary, so that its agreement with the Polish language may appear.

# *Of the Hieronymian or Dalmatian Language, otherwise called Slavonic.*
## C H A P T E R L X V.

Blondus <note>Flavio Biondo (1392–1463), a Renaissance humanist and historian</note>, in books 8 and 9 of his *Histories of the Decline of the Empire*, writes that in the year of Salvation 607, the Slavs, a people coming out of Russia under the Emperor Phocas, occupied the shores of the Adriatic Gulf. In this place they continued their residence and habitation for so long that everything which was previously called Istria and Dalmatia has been named, from then until this day, Slavonia or Esclavonie. Finally, by this means, these Slavs entirely corrupted the Greek language that was spoken in those quarters before them. This is confirmed by Cromerus <note>Marcin Kromer (1512–1589), a Polish historian and cartographer</note> in book 1 of his *History of the Poles*. Nicholas Chalcondyle <note>Laonikos Chalkokondyles (c. 1410–1490), a Byzantine Greek historian</note>, in book 10 of his *History of the Turks*, writes that the Illyrians are a very ancient people who inhabit the country that reaches toward the Ionian Sea. Having formerly been held in very great esteem and often having done very fine things, their land is now called Bosnia. The Dalmatians, Mysians, Triballians, and Sarmatians <note>Ancient groups inhabiting the Balkans and Eastern Europe</note> use almost the same language as these people; at the very least, they understand one another. However, it is more likely that they first came out of the regions that extend toward the Ionian Sea, and it is said that they were very few in number, but they did not fail to suddenly acquire a great reputation. For they subjugated Thrace, and from there, having crossed the Danube, they finally settled in Sarmatia. There are others who wish to say that having been driven from their countries by the Tartars, they retreated to the country inhabited beyond the Danube, from where, having thrown themselves into Thrace and conquered it, they came to settle on the aforementioned gulf. But I cannot wonder enough at those who want these Illyrians to be the Albanians, as if the Illyrians who hold the Ionian Gulf had passed into this mainland and into Aetolia and the region of Thessaly. ## On the Hieronymian, or Dalmatian, otherwise Slavic Language.

### C H A P T E R L X V.

Blondus <note>Flavio Biondo (1392–1463), an influential Italian Renaissance historian</note> in books 8 and 9 of his *Histories of the Decline of the Empire* <note>original: "Historiarum ab inclinatione Romanorum imperii"</note>, writes that in the year of Salvation 607, the Slavic peoples coming out of Russia, under the Emperor Phocas, occupied the shores of the Adriatic Gulf. Indeed, as for that language, whether it should be called Sarmatian or Slavonic, it has been covered in a proper commentary by Master Jan Mączyński <note>original: "Ioannes Maczn," a famous 16th-century Polish humanist and lexicographer</note>, my most respected teacher in the Polish language. He is a young man distinguished among the first for his lineage, wit, learning, knowledge of many languages, the Christian religion, humanity, and every kind of virtue. Once he publishes these books—which I hope happens soon, for it will bring honor and ornament not only to his own homeland of Poland, but also to other nations—Poland itself will speak, showing the Slavonic speech to be as observant of analogy <note>original: "analogiæ"; here referring to grammatical regularity and consistency</note> as Latin or Greek. But I have said too little so far. It will appear that this language of Scythian origin competes with those cultivated languages in abundance, power, flexibility, elegance, and all virtues; languages which some believe to be the only human ones, considering others barbarian.

A certain Italian author named Mr. Giambattista Palatino <note>original: "Iean Baptiste Palatin"</note>, a Roman citizen, in his Italian book on the manner of teaching how to write every kind of letter, ancient and modern, speaks otherwise of this matter:

> » And you should know that the Illyrian peoples, or rather the Slavonians, have two types of
> » alphabets. Those provinces which are more towards the East use 
> » that which is similar to Greek, of which Cyril was the author, and because of this 
> » they call it "Cyrillica" <note>original: "Chiurilizza"</note>. The other provinces, which are more towards the south 
> » or towards the West, use that of which Saint 
> » Jerome was the author, and they call it "Bukvitsa" <note>original: "Buchuiza," likely referring to the Glagolitic script</note>; which alphabet is different
> » from all others in the world. And you must know that the speech of the common people 
> » is the very same with which they continually perform their church services, and all the 
> » people understand it, just as we understand our own vernacular. It is very vast in
> » vocabulary, but very difficult to pronounce for one not raised from childhood among them. 
> » And they have in it Missals, Breviaries, and Offices of Our Lady, and also the Bible.

That is to say, You must know that the Illyrian peoples, otherwise called Slavonians, have two sorts of alphabets; the provinces which are towards the East use that one which is similar to the Greek, of which Cyril was the author, for which reason they call it "Cyrillica." The other provinces which are more towards the midday sun <note>the South</note>, or towards the West, use that of which Saint Jerome was the author, which they call "Bukvitsa," which alphabet is unlike all the others in the universe. One should also know that the speech of the common people is the same and proper one with which they daily say their church office, and all the people understand it as we understand our own vernacular: it is very abundant and copious in words, but very difficult to pronounce for one not trained in it from long ago, and they have in it their Missals, Breviaries, and Offices of Our Lady, and also the Bible.

Aventinus <note>Johannes Aventinus (1477–1534), a Bavarian Renaissance humanist historian.</note>, in the fourth book of his annals, speaks quite differently of this matter, saying that around the year of salvation <note>the year of our Lord</note>, a certain person named Methodius, a Bishop native to Illyria <note>a region in the western Balkans</note>, first invented the **Venedic** <term>Venedic: an archaic term for Slavic</term> letters and translated the Holy Scripture into the **Slavonic** language. He persuaded the inhabitants of Dalmatia to no longer use the Latin language or the ceremonies of the Roman Church, but rather their own language and these characters. After this, he went to the Kingdom of Bavaria <note>original: "Boiarie"</note> to persuade the Bavarians of the same, but he was driven out and expelled by the Bishops of that province. From there, he retired to the country of Moravia, where he passed away and was buried in the city of **Olomouc** <note>original: "Olimutz"</note>, which is to say, "Mount of Julius." <note>This is a historical folk etymology, incorrectly linking the name Olomouc to Julius Caesar.</note>
