# History of the Origin of the [Slavs]

Bergamo <note>referring to Jacobus Philippus Foresti of Bergamo (1434–1520), an Augustinian chronicler</note> in his eleventh book, says that it was Pope Nicholas who wished to command the Slavs to conduct divine service and administer the sacraments in the Latin language. When they would not comply with him, he permitted them, by way of a dispensation, to do it in their own language, so that they might appear to be doing everything according to his statutes. Furthermore, Gregory VII <note>Pope Gregory VII, reigned 1073–1085</note> refused King Vladislaus of Bohemia <note>Vratislaus II, the first King of Bohemia</note> the right to have divine service celebrated in his lands in this language, because it was not suited to Christian institution, nor to the languages that were written upon the Title of the Cross of our Lord <note>The "titulus" on the Cross was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin; the Pope argues these are the only three sacred languages for liturgy</note>, through which the communion of the saints is preserved and maintained throughout the earth; just as through the diversity of these languages, confusion and dissension take place throughout the whole world, as is contained in the seventh register to the Duke of Bohemia, by this same Pope, and in Olaus Magnus <note>a Swedish ecclesiastic and writer</note> book 19, chapter 39.

Matthias Miechowita <note>a Polish scholar, 1457–1523</note>, in his histories of European and Asiatic Sarmatia, Sigismund, Baron von Herberstein, in his commentaries on Muscovite affairs, and Theodor Bibliander, in his commentary on the common reason of all languages cited above, have held that the word *Sclavi*, or Slavs, signifies serfs and slaves, because this people was subject to being placed into servitude. However, it is more likely (according to those mentioned above) that the Slavs, being greatly esteemed in former times for their valor and prowess, were so named from the word *Slouuo* <note>original: "Slouuo"; likely referring to 'Slovo', the Slavic word for 'word' or 'speech'</note>, which means to do great things, and to be celebrated and renowned, from which the word *Slauuuy* <note>original: "Slauuuy"; likely 'Slava', meaning glory or fame</note> is derived, which conveys as much as "celebrated" and "noble." Still, it should not be doubted that Jordanes, an Alan historian by nation, estimated that they were so named because of the "new city." The Germans regarded them as enemies and called them *Viltzos*; the Greeks called them <term>Σκλαϐηνός</term> <note>Sklabenos</note>. The first time they were known in Europe for their great valor in arms, they were named *Gazaros* <note>Khazars</note>, as they are still called today in the language of the Saracens. In fact, the Khazars who live today toward the Hyrcanian Sea <note>the Caspian Sea</note>, where the Circassians are, are called by the Greeks *Abgazari*, or *Abgaselli*, who now use this Slavic language. The nation of the Slavs, having departed and proceeded (according to the aforementioned personages) with a great number of people from Scythia around the year of salvation 600, occupied a large part of Sarmatia as far as the Caspian Sea, where the Zygians or Circassians are now, a Slavic people who for some time held the Empire of Egypt under the name of Mamluks. These were entirely ruined by Selim, father of Suleiman, the Great Lord of the Turks. They also occupied all this extent of habitable country in Europe from the River Tanais <note>the Don River</note> to about halfway through Germany, surnamed "the Great." Thus, the Bohemians and the Lusatians are colonies of Slavs; and further, from the Baltic and Sarmatian Sea down to the Euxine <note>Black Sea</note> and the Adriatic Sea, where Slavonia is now located, although they also occupied Dalmatia and Illyria. The certain author named Michael the Pole, a canon of Kraków, mentioned above by T. Bibliander in his first book, chapters 12 and 13, writes the following on this matter regarding Sarmatia, according to our translation: the Slavic nation is descended and proceeded from Elishah, son of Javan <note>Biblical figures from the Table of Nations in Genesis; Javan was traditionally linked to the Greeks</note>, from whom the Greek nations took their origins. From this, it must be gathered that the Slavic language is very vast and of very long extent, occupying many and diverse provinces.

# Languages of this World

& regions, being spoken at present by the Serbians, Moesians, Rascians <note>a historical term for Serbs</note>, or Bulgarians; by the Bosnians, currently subjugated by the Great Turk; by the Dalmatians, Croats, Pannonians, Slavs, Carni <note>peoples of Carniola, modern-day Slovenia</note>, Bohemians, Moravians, Silesians, Great and Little Poles, Mazovians, Pomeranians, Kashubians, Sorbs, Ruthenians <note>ancestors of modern Ukrainians and Belarusians</note>, and Muscovites. All of these are Vindelici <note>an ancient name sometimes applied by Renaissance scholars to Slavic peoples</note> or Slavons, inhabiting various very great and ample kingdoms; even the Lithuanians of today live and make use of the Slavonic tongue in their speech, along with those of Novgorod, Pskov, Smolensk, and the Ohulicians or Ohalicians. What is more, the Turks take such delight in the use of this Slavonic language that they prefer to call the seat of the Empire by a word from that language, *Czarzouudom* <note>likely a corruption of *Tsargrad* or *Carigrad*, meaning "City of the Caesar"</note>, which means "House of Caesar," rather than Constantinople or Byzantium. Raphael Volaterranus <note>Raffaele Maffei, an Italian humanist, 1451–1522</note> writes the following concerning this: 

> That the old Greek letters were almost the same as those which are now Latin is evidenced by the Delphic bronze tablet, which was seen in Rome, dedicated in the Palace of Minerva in the library during the time of Pliny, as he himself witnesses. Then they were altered by the Latins, and finally corrupted by the ensuing barbarism of the Lombards, as can still be seen in their monuments and books. The same fate that befell our own letters also happened to the Greeks, with the neighboring Illyrians corrupting their letters. For this reason, to this very day, the Dalmatians and Illyrians use these characters, which they received from the Greeks but have since degraded. <note>original Latin: "Græcas litteras veteres fuiffe eafdem penè quæ Latinæ funt nunc..."</note>

The previously mentioned Sigismund, Baron von Herberstein <note>an Austrian diplomat famous for his descriptions of Muscovy</note>:
> The Slavonic language, which today is called "Sclavonic" by a somewhat corrupted name, is very widely spread: for it is used by the Dalmatians, Bosnians, Croats, Istrians, and along the long stretch of the Adriatic Sea as far as Friuli and the Carni (whom the Venetians call *Charsi*), as well as the Carniolans, the Carinthians as far as the Drava River, and the Styrians below Graz, along the Mura to the Danube, and from there the Moesians, Serbs, Bulgarians, and others living as far as Constantinople; furthermore the Bohemians, Lusatians, Silesians, Moravians, and those living by the Vág river in the kingdom of Hungary; likewise the Poles, and the very widely-ruling Ruthenians, and the Circassians of the Five Mountains near the Black Sea, and finally throughout Germany beyond the Elbe to the North, the scattered remains of the Vandals use it. Although all these people confess themselves to be Slavs, the Germans—taking the name from the Vandals alone—indiscriminately call all those who use the Slavic language *Wenden*, *Wende*, or *Windisch*. <note>original Latin: "Slauonica lingua, quæ hodierno die, corrupto nonnihil vocabulo, Sclauonica appellatur, latiffimè patet..."</note>

Matthias Miechowita, also previously cited in book 1, chapter 13, concerning Asiatic Sarmatia:
> Fifthly, conclude that the language of the Slavs is most extensive and diffused, possessing many lands and provinces, such as the Serbs, Moesians, Rascians or Bulgarians, and Bosnians (at this time subjugated by the Turk); as well as the Dalmatians, Croats, Pannonians, Slavs, Carni, Bohemians, Moravians, Silesians, Great and Little Poles, Mazovians, Pomeranians, Kashubians, Sorbs, Ruthenians, and Muscovites. All these are Slavs and Vindelici, inhabiting vast kingdoms; but even the Lithuanians now "Slavicize"; as do those of Novgorod, Pskov, Smolensk, and the Ohulicians—see their chronicles and cosmographies. <note>original Latin: "Quinto collige quod linguagium Sclauorum ampliffimum eft & diffufun..."</note>

Sebastian Münster, in book 4 of his *Universal Cosmography*, has applied himself to describing the histories, chronicles, and cosmographies (or rather, topographies) of the provinces and regions of Illyria and the adjacent lands called today Slavonia, Bosnia, Dacia, Russia, Swabia, Bulgaria, Wallachia, Transylvania, and others, without making ample particular mention of the...

> “This region, which I name Slavonia, was formerly considered under the name of Illyria, neighboring the Pannonians <note>People of the Roman province of Pannonia, covering parts of modern Hungary, Austria, and Croatia</note>; it currently contains three provinces: namely, that which is properly called Slavonia, which stretches toward the West; then Dalmatia, which lies to the South; and Albania, which turns toward the East. But as for me, I include more under the name of Slavonia, placing there Carinthia and Croatia, which are under the obedience of the House of Austria, Illyria and the County of Zara, Liburnia and Dalmatia, along with the peoples of Ragusa <note>Modern-day Dubrovnik</note> and others of their neighbors who are in Albania. And you see that the extent of this country is quite large, having such limits: before it is the Drina, which the ancients called the Drinus, which passes beyond Ragusa; and toward the West, the Arsa <note>The Raša river in Istria</note> serves as its boundary, separating it from Istria. To the South lies the Adriatic Sea, and to the North the high mountains of Croatia; its length is one hundred and twenty leagues, specifically from the Drina river to that of the Arsa. In width, it contains only thirty <unclear>... [text cut off]</unclear>, namely from the shores of the Adriatic Sea to the aforementioned mountains of Croatia. As for its jurisdiction, it is partly subject to the Turk <note>The Ottoman Empire</note>, partly to the Venetians, and a small amount to the King of the Romans <note>The title used by the Habsburg heir or Holy Roman Emperor</note>. The cities of Slavonia that are along the sea belong to the Venetian lordship, but those of the mainland obey for the most part the Turk; that which is between Senj and the city of Trieste is under the obedience of the King of the Romans. But it is the poorest country of all, because the Turks ordinarily make raids there; which they do not do upon the lands of the Venetians, who for this reason are the richest in Slavonia. The inhabitants live according to the Roman Church, though they nonetheless perform their prayers more commonly in their vulgar <note>vernacular</note> tongue than in the Latin language. This I have wished to make known to you through the Lord's Prayer and the Angelic Salutation <note>The Hail Mary</note>, which both old and young use when they perform their devotions and prayers:

> “Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come, thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Amen. <note>original: "Otʃʃe naʃʃ, ki yeʃʃina nebeʃʃi, Sſuetiʃſe ime tuoie..." — this is a transliteration of a South Slavic dialect</note>

# History of the Origin of [Languages]

...mentary on the common reason of all languages, making mention of the commentaries of a certain figure from Poland named Jan Mączyński <note>Original: "Iean Manisky"; Jan Mączyński (c. 1518–1575) was a Polish humanist and lexicographer</note>, his preceptor in the Polish language, who asserts in them that the Slavic language <note>Original: "langue Esclauonne"</note> is as beautiful and as sweet as the Greek and Latin languages, whether in abundance, richness, strength, flexibility, and elegance, as well as other beauties and perfections attributed to other languages. A friend of mine currently living in Poland has assured me by letter that the Lithuanians of the present day speak this aforementioned Slavic language, as do the Poles, and that this language is common and familiar to several diverse nations, of which some obey the Roman Church, while others follow the schism of the Greeks <note>The Eastern Orthodox Church</note>. Under the Catholic see are the Poles, Dalmatians, Croats, and Carnians <note>People of Carniola, in modern-day Slovenia</note>; and under the Greek see, the Bulgarians, Russians, part of Lithuania, and Muscovy. Others speaking this same language are infected and saturated with various heresies, such as the Bohemians <note>Czechs</note>, Moravians, and Bosnians; some of whom follow the remnants of the Hussites <note>A pre-Protestant Christian movement following the teachings of Jan Hus</note>, others embrace the error of the Manicheans <note>Likely a reference to the Bogomils in Bosnia</note>, and some adore idols, as do many of the Lithuanians. In the countryside near Vilnius, the metropolitan city of Lithuania and an episcopal see, there now dwell Tartars in the places ordained for them, tilling the earth in their own manner, and carrying their merchandise through the country, speaking their Tartar language and living according to the profession and sect of the Quran <note>Original: "Alcorã"</note> of Mohammed.

A certain figure named Hans Ungnad <note>Original: "Iean Vngenad"</note>, Baron of Sonnegg, one of the leaders of the army in Hungary against the Turks, raised by the command of the Emperor Ferdinand, set himself—after the truce made with the Turks—to translate the Old and New Testaments into the Slavic and Croatian languages, together with composing commentaries on the true religion in this same language. He had them printed at great cost and expense, then sent them to be distributed and sold throughout Turkey, to try to induce the Mohammedans <note>Muslims</note> to the belief of our Christian religion; I saw and read these commentaries in the hands of a great and learned Polish personage in the city of Paris in the year 1595.

Sleidan <note>Johannes Sleidanus, a 16th-century historian</note> writes in Book 1 that the Emperor Charles IV ordained in the [Golden] Bull that the children of the Electors of the Empire should, in their early years, learn the Latin, Italian, and Slavic languages, so that they might easily speak and communicate with many diverse nations without any interpreters or translators.

Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner</note> and Josias Simler in their historical libraries write that a certain person named Primož Trubar <note>Original: "Primus Truberus"</note> of Carniola was the first who had a New Testament printed in this language using Latin characters.

Sigismund Gelenius <note>Zikmund Hrubý z Jelení (1497–1554)</note>, a Bohemian, composed and had printed in Basel by Froben a *Lexicon Symphonum* <note>A "Symphonic Lexicon," comparing the sounds and roots of different languages</note>, in which is treated the harmony and consonance of the four familiar languages of Europe, namely: Greek, Latin, German, and Slavic.

# Languages of this Universe.

Iberia, Ιβηρία <note>original: "Ιβηρία"; the Greek name for the region</note>, a region of Asia: which Ptolemy also calls Caucasus. Strabo in book 11 also writes that the Albanians and Iberians can be called Caucasians. John Tzetzes <note>A 12th-century Byzantine grammarian</note> adds the Abasgians, ἀβασγοι <note>original: "ἀβασγοι"; a people of the Caucasus</note>: for he says the Iberians, Abasgians, and Alans are one race (however, the Abasci, ἀβασκοι, are in Colchis according to Arrian). Stephanus seems to call them the Hilaraugatae (ἱλαραυγάτας). By Pliny and Mela they are named the "Georgi" <note>This name stems from the Greek word for "farmers" or "tillers of the earth"</note>. And today they are called Georgians; the region is named Gargania by Aethicus the Sophist. Thevet <note>André Thevet (1516–1590), a French Franciscan explorer</note> says or imagines that they are called "Gourohs" by the Persians. Eustathius, in his commentary on Dionysius, calls this "Eastern Iberia." Plutarch, writing from Sosthenes in the *Treatise on Rivers and Mountains*, says this Iberia was once called "Pana," πᾶνα, after Pan, who was appointed governor of this region by Dionysus, and was later called "Spania," σπανία, by younger generations.

But if faith is to be placed in this author, I would say that the Spaniards—who, by the testimony of almost all classical writers, have their origin from this [Asian] Iberia—took their name from this "Spania" rather than from "Hispalus" <note>A mythical king of Spain often cited in older etymologies</note> (as many affirm), etc. For they themselves do not call their origin "Hispalic" in their native tongue, but "Espanic," as if from Spania. For it is clear that the Spanish common people share with the French the habit of prefixing the letter 'E' to Latin words starting with 'S', as seen in the words *schola* [school], *scala* [ladder], *scannum* [bench], *scutum* [shield], *species*, *stella* [star], *scribere* [to write], *studere* [to study], and countless others, which they make familiar in their own dialects by adding 'E'. For Saint Eulogius, who wrote seven hundred years ago, calls it not Hispania but Spania: as noted by Ambrosio de Morales, who published his life. Saint Luke also calls it thus in the Acts of the Apostles.

Arias Montanus <note>A 16th-century Spanish orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible</note> also testifies in his *Apparatus Biblicus* that this Asian Iberia is described in Sacred Scripture under the name Tubal (Θόβηλ <note>original: "Θόβηλ"; Thobel</note> in Josephus), and that from here set out the Spaniards, who occupy the furthest part of Europe toward the West. Unless one prefers to dream with Strabo (citing Apollodorus, Dionysius, Socrates the Scholastic, and Priscian) that these people migrated from Spain into Iberia [the Caucasus]; and to affirm that Iberia was called Spania by them, and not Pania after Pan. We freely offer this conjecture of ours to be looked upon by the more learned. Strabo writes that in ancient times Iberia was believed to be whatever lies beyond the Rhône and the isthmus constricted by the borders of Gaul. And accepting only that as "Spain" which is within the Ebro <note>The river Iberus</note>. Ephorus wrote that the Western Iberians were a certain great city, as witnessed by Josephus in *Against Apion*. Zonaras perhaps followed him when he said it is the most excellent city of European Iberia. See "Spain" and "Gaul."

# History of the Origin of the

...and fortified by very high mountains, [the Turks] have not been able in any way to bring them under their obedience and domination, even though they are sworn enemies of Christians—especially of those who do not wish to obey them, suffer their domination, or who are recalcitrant in paying the tributes and taxes as their False Prophet Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> commanded in his Alcoran, under threat of total extermination. By doing these things, to all the Christians and peoples of other religions living in the lands of the Turk, these Turks give them free permission to follow and profess whatever religion they want.

These Georgians, or Georgians <note>original: "Georgianiēs"</note>, use certain characters of letters arranged in the fashion of those of the Greeks, having the names of their said letters very close to them, to write both the Greek language (which they use for sacred and divine things) and their vulgar tongue, which is entirely woven and composed of the Tartar and Armenian languages. They are also tainted with several and various sorts of heresies. 

But in what they err or differ from other Greek Christians, the *Caloyers* and *Papasses* of the Greeks—that is to say, Greek monks and priests—cannot give any good or valid reason; except that these characters of letters are common to them and to the Jacobites <note>A Monophysite Christian sect named after Jacob Baradaeus</note> whom they hold, repute, and detest as their mortal enemies. I have been persuaded that these Jacobites, having formerly been infected with the perverse heresy of a certain Jacob, Patriarch of Alexandria, who asserted a single nature in Jesus Christ, and for this reason were deprived of the communion of Christians by the Patriarch of Constantinople named Dioscorus <note>The author likely confuses names here; Dioscorus of Alexandria was actually the one deposed for his Monophysite views at the Council of Chalcedon</note>, invented these characters. These letters had been in common use in the Churches of the East long before, and since that time were received and embraced by these Georgians or Georgians, and by them kept and preserved for their ordinary use.

Before the raids and incursions of the Barbarians, there were infinite Jacobites in Egypt, Arabia, Mesopotamia, Chaldea, Assyria, and especially in Syria because of the holy places. For the present, very few are found in Syria; and believe me, just as they use and serve themselves together with these characters of letters, they are the same regarding their opinion on religion: for they approach closely the error of Nestorius <note>Nestorius taught that Christ had two distinct natures (divine and human), which was condemned as heresy</note> which infected all the peoples of the Eastern Church, which was the cause in olden times for expelling them from the communion of other Christians. 

This is something the Greek priests cannot understand because they are entirely ignorant, being instead only filled with pomp and pride. But because I see several ancients and moderns having said and reported several different and dissimilar discourses about these Georgians or Georgians concerning their dwelling and habitation, it seemed very appropriate to me to give our opinion on it. 

Some have said they were thus named Georgians, or Georgians, because of St. George, and that formerly they lived in Arabia, near Mecca, which is false, insofar as those I saw in Constantinople with their Legate or Ambassador to the Grand Turk do not know what this name of St. George is. Rather, they assure well and firmly that they inhabit the borders of Armenia, contiguous to the Tartars, and that they do not know or recognize other Georgians or Georgians—commonly called *Iurgianlar* <note>A Turkish term for the Georgian people</note>—except themselves, and some of them who live in the surroundings of the city of Jerusalem, to attend only to religion and divine things. This clearly demonstrates the falsehood of the ancient cosmographers, who placed the dwelling of these people in the [previously mentioned] places...

> I saw, when I was in Rome during the time of Pope Leo X, <note>Pope from 1513–1521</note> letters from the Metropolitan of Great Iberia <note>The Caucasus region of Georgia</note>, written in letters that were indeed Greek, but differing greatly from the common ones. They bore a seal on which the image of Saint George the Martyr was impressed (for they say it is the banner of that nation), and an inscription written in the Metropolitan's own hand, with letters so tortuous and woven together like an Herculean knot <note>A complex decorative knot</note>—starting from one point and ending at another—that not even one with the eyes of a lynx could have discerned them. Indeed, the lines of those letters were drawn one over the other in such a way that not even the "fantastic letters" of Giovanni Antonio Tagliente <note>A famous Italian writing master known for elaborate calligraphy</note>, so perplexed and ensnared in various entanglements, would seem comparable. Machatius Chius, a monk of the order of Saint Basil—who was then staying with me in our canonical house of Saint Mary of Peace in the City [Rome] through the influence of the most reverend Cardinal Sauli, and to whom the letters were addressed—could hardly have understood them, even though he was Greek and well-versed in Greek and Arabic letters, had he not been aided by the Iberian bearer of the letters. Truly, posterity might have seen the forms of those letters and the signature of that Metropolitan, explained despite its many complexities, printed in this our tradition, if that immense and ever-to-be-lamented calamity and the final destruction of my unfortunate homeland <note>Likely referring to the Sack of Pavia in 1527</note> had not stripped me of them, along with the rest of my numerous collection of books.

The characters are almost Greek in name and figure, but they write them corruptly and add I know not how many barbaric ones.

### History of the Origins of the [Georgians]

...religious of the order of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, living in the year of salvation 1487, named Brother Nicole Hué, Doctor in the Faculty of Theology. Before him, Jean de Mandeville, a knight living in the year 1322, in his travels composed in the Romance language <note>The common vernacular of the time, as opposed to Latin</note>, had written these very words:

> The Christians who are called Georgians, whom Saint George converted; they honor him more than any other saint in paradise, and they call upon him every day to help them, etc. <note>original: "Los Chrestians que son appellats Gorgias los quels sent Iordi cōuerty, e aell ha horé pus q̄ a null'altro sant de paradis, ell appellé tot iōrs quells aiut &c."</note>

To be brief, these Georgians—called *Iurgialar* by the Turks and Tartars—have the same name and number of letters as the Jacobites <note>A term often used for members of the Syriac Orthodox Church</note> and Copts <note>Egyptian Christians</note>, but their characters are much more similar to those of the Greeks, from whom they differ very little. They took this name from the valiant Martyr Saint George, whose image they carried on their banners and ensigns, because it was he who first planted the Christian faith in those quarters (close neighbors to Cappadocia, of which Angora <note>Modern-day Ankara</note> is the capital city). Thus, they have held him in great veneration ever since. However, Chalcondyles <note>Laonikos Chalkokondyles, a 15th-century Byzantine historian</note> records that in the time of Constantine the Great, their Queen was cured of a most grievous illness by a Christian slave, and they were converted to the faith at that time.

Furthermore, Georgia, as it is called today, is the region that Strabo, Pliny, Ptolemy, and other geographers call Iberia, or Hiberia. It forms a portion of the ancient kingdom of Colchis <note>Famous in Greek myth as the destination of Jason and the Argonauts</note> near that of Trebizond and the Phasis River, now called the Fasso, which flows into the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>, or the "Greater Sea." This province extends in one direction toward the Hyrcanian Sea <note>The Caspian Sea</note> and Great Armenia. 

But beyond those who live there today—people who are very poor and miserable in all their ways of life—there are a good number of them spread throughout various parts of Asia, and even in Jerusalem. There, in addition to the oratory they have in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, they occupy many holy sites, especially Mount Calvary. In the exact spot where the Cross of our Lord was planted, they have a chapel and an altar, and a church called the Church of the Angels, where the house of the High Priest Annas once stood. 

In former times, they were feared and respected by the Moors, the Sultan of Cairo, and later by the Turks, so much so that they would enter cities with their banners unfurled. They were also exempt from the tribute called the *Carazzi* <term>Kharaj: a head tax historically levied on non-Muslim subjects</term> which is collected for every head among all sorts of Christians. Even to this day, no one has dared to attack them—not the Turk, nor the Persian, nor the Tartars—despite the fact that they hold to the Christian religion. Nevertheless, they belong to the sect of Nestorius <note>Nestorius was a 5th-century Archbishop of Constantinople whose views were declared heretical</note>, formerly Bishop of Constantinople, whose error was condemned in the third Synod of Ephesus. This sect posits two persons in our Savior, one divine and the other human, and denies the presence of his body in the Eucharist except when it is being consumed. They do not acknowledge the Virgin Mary as the Mother of God, but only as the mother of Jesus Christ insofar as he was a man, along with other such impieties common to the Jacobites. 

But perhaps the aforementioned [Turks and Persians] have not bothered to attack them because of their poverty and misery, and the difficulty of their terrain, which is not worth conquering. They are left as they are so they may serve as a mutual barrier against one another; for they are no longer as valiant as they used to be, but for the most part are a faint-hearted, dull, and idle people. These people now follow the traditions of the Greek Church in every way and use that language and writing in their services. However, they use somewhat different characters in their business and affairs, and they adapt themselves to Turkish, Arabic, and Chaldean, as I have...

# History of the Origin of the

...[they do not] eat fish during Lent, nor any delicacy whatsoever, listening very attentively to the word of God, and persisting quite long in prayer in places where they have the means to do so without hindrance. They have as their head in spiritual matters a sovereign Bishop whom they name the Catholicos <note>Original: "Iacelique," a corruption of *Catholicos*, the title used by the heads of the Georgian and Armenian Churches</note>, to whom almost all the Christians of the East—those in the lands of the Tartars and part of the Persian Empire—pay obedience. They do not acknowledge, as we do, the Holy Apostolic See of Rome, of which they take no account. Whoever wishes to see various discourses on the Iberians, Georgians, or Georgianians should read Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century Christian historian</note> in Book 1 of his *Ecclesiastical History*; Ptolemy, Book 5, Chapter 12, Table 3 of Asia; Appian in his book on the *Mithridatic War*; Procopius in Book 1 of the *Persian War*; Giosafat Barbaro in his *Journey to Tana*, Chapter 14; Ambrogio Contarini in his *Journey*; Laonikos Chalkokondyles in Book 9 of the *History of the Turks*; Rufinus, Theodoret, and Sozomen <note>OCR: "S te," likely Sozomen</note> in their *Ecclesiastical Histories*; and other authors cited by François de Belleforest in Book 5 of his *Universal History* and in Volume 2, Book 5, Chapter 6 of his *Universal Cosmography*. See also what has been written recently of these Georgians by the Lord of Villamont in Book 2, Chapter 23 of his *Travels*.

As for the Jacobites <note>A name historically used for the Syriac Orthodox Church, named after Jacob Baradaeus</note>, they also have their alphabet arranged in the Greek fashion, and the names of their letters are very similar to it. They use the [Syriac] language, which they write with their own characters—which are essentially [Greek] but distorted and corrupted—for the Ecclesiastical service. For worldly affairs, they use their vernacular, which is a sort of middle ground between Armenian and Tartar, as confirmed by Theseus Ambrosius <note>Teseo Ambrogio degli Albonesi, a Renaissance linguist</note> in his *Introduction to the Chaldaic, Syriac, and Armenian Languages*, Chapter 5, on the consonants of the [Jacobites] and Copts.

But this is not a nation, but rather a sect and heresy which took its name from a certain Jacob, a disciple of a Patriarch of Alexandria, who poisoned them with the error of Nestorius <note>The author here confuses the Jacobites (who are Miaphysites) with their theological opponents, the Nestorians. Historically, they held opposing views on the nature of Christ</note>, which they have held ever since without budging, differing from the traditions of the Latin and Greek Churches. They were long ago banished and excommunicated by Dioscorus, Patriarch of Constantinople <note>Dioscorus was actually Patriarch of Alexandria; the Jacobites actually revere him as a saint</note>. Even today, their leader is called the "Jacob," who ordains their Prelates and Ministers, along with their sacraments in their own fashion, as written by Marco Polo in Book 1, Chapter 6 of his *Travels*; John Mandeville in his *Travels*, in the chapter on the Law of the Jacobites; and Guillaume Postel in his *Alphabet of Twelve Languages*, following James of Vitry, Chapter 38 of his *History of Jerusalem*.

This sect took its origin from Eutyches, who among his other impieties maintained that Jesus Christ had not taken his body from the Virgin Mary, but rather had entered into her womb like a clear ray of sun [passing through glass], rejecting all kinds of images in their temples. They have a chapel for themselves in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in the city of Jerusalem, where they perform their service apart, just as the Latins, Greeks, Abyssinians <note>Ethiopians</note>, Georgians, and Maronites do; the same as the Chaldeans or Syrians, each in their own place. For these seven nations and types of people are admitted into this Church, and have residences there for those of their kind who go there on pilgrimage. But these Jacobites, having no place of residence that is strictly their own or fixed, are scattered in various places across Asia and Egypt—even as far as Nubia and Ethiopia—and in more than forty kingdoms, both on the mainland and the islands of the East and South, among the Mohammedans, from whom they have borrowed circumcision. In addition to this, they cauterize <note>brand</note> the [foreheads of their children] with a hot iron...

...children on the forehead, cheeks, and hands with certain marks, believing that by doing so they fulfill and perform this "baptism with the Holy Spirit and with fire" which Saint John the Baptist attributes to our Savior in Saint Matthew, chapter 3 <note>Matthew 3:11: "He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire." They do not confess their sins to priests, but to God alone, using for this purpose a brazier <note>Original: "rechauld"</note> into which they throw a little incense; they believe that along with the smoke, their offenses ascend on high where they are forgiven and erased. Furthermore, they admit only one nature in Jesus Christ, just as, they say, there is only one person, following the traditions of the aforementioned Eutyches <note>Eutyches (c. 380–456) was a monk whose teachings led to Monophysitism, the belief that Christ has a single divine-human nature</note>: and in remembrance of this, they make the sign of the cross with only one finger. Some among them are further subdivided into another sect, establishing a third nature resulting from the two natures within Him; they give communion to both adults and children <note>Original: "petits & grands"</note> indifferently under both kinds <note>Both bread and wine</note>. As for their language, they have one that is their own and specific to them, just as Hebrew is to the Jews: and they have a script likewise, such as the one represented here: but they also use the languages of the countries where they live and reside, which is most commonly in Cairo.

# History of the Origin of the [Alphabets]

Theseus Ambrosius <note>Teseo Ambrogio (1469–1540), an Italian scholar and author of one of the first Western studies of Middle Eastern languages</note>, in his appendix on several different letters and languages, specifically in a letter sent to the late G. Postel <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), a famous French linguist and mystic</note>, seems to assert that he was the first among Europeans to bring this alphabet to light, along with that of the Copts, which I will discuss hereafter. See what A. Thevet <note>André Thevet (1516–1590), a Franciscan explorer and writer</note> writes of these Jacobites and their way of life and customs in book 11, chapter 18 of his *Universal Cosmography*, and the Lord of Villamont <note>Jacques de Villamont, a 16th-century traveler</note> in book 2, chapter 22 of his *Voyages*.

In the year 1552, these Jacobites sought reconciliation with the Roman Pope, Julius III, sending him the Legate of the Patriarch of Antioch named Moses Mardenus <note>Moses of Mardin, a Syrian priest who was instrumental in bringing the first Syriac New Testament to European print</note>, a learned man born in Syria, to make a profession of their faith. This profession is transcribed word-for-word by A. Thevet in the place cited above. Modern reports from the Levant confirm that these Jacobites are as described, and live in the manner we have detailed above.

->**Of the Copts.**<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'L' featuring floral scrollwork and a small animal or hybrid creature at its base.</image-desc>
**L**he Copts <note>The native Christian population of Egypt</note> name their letters in the same way as the Jacobites, but the characters are somewhat different, also numbering thirty-two. Guillaume Postel, cited above in his treatise on Phoenician letters, confuses them with the Jacobites, even though they are more specifically Egyptian and have been Christians for a longer time. Theseus Ambrosius does the same in his introduction to the Chaldean, Syriac, and Armenian languages, chapter 5, in his appendix on several different kinds of languages. These Copts are named after the city of Coptos, which Plutarch mentions in his treatise on *Isis and Osiris*, and Pliny in book 5, chapter 9, who attributes to it one of the seats and governments of Egypt.

In the 19th year of his reign, which corresponds to the year 306 of our salvation, the Emperor Diocletian had one hundred and twenty thousand <note>Original: "fix vingts mille" (six-score thousand)</note> of them martyred and sent countless others into exile. Because of this most horrible butchery and execution, they have always begun counting their Era <note>The "Era of Martyrs," still used by the Coptic Church today</note>—which is the date of their years, as the Nativity of our Lord is for us—from that time, as Joseph Scaliger <note>A famous 16th-century scholar of chronology</note> notes in book 3 of his *Correction of Time*. These people call the Father, *Phiot*, and the Son, *Pscirim* <note>Coptic: ⲫⲓⲩⲧ (Phiot) and ⲡϣⲏⲣⲓ (Pshiri)</note>. They count using the letters of their alphabet, just as the Hebrews, Chaldeans, Greeks, Macedonians, Dalmatians or Slavs, and others do; however, the Arabs and Indians use certain numerical signs <note>Referring to the ancestors of our modern "Arabic" numerals</note> designed for that purpose, as do the Latins likewise.

### Of the Etrurians or Etruscans, and the Etruscan Language.
### CHAPTER LXVII.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'N' showing a landscape with buildings and a figure.</image-desc>
We can learn from Latin histories that the Etruscans were among the most ancient peoples of Italy, where, some little time after the universal flood, Janus the "good father"—whom some authors believe to have been the same as the good Patriarch Noah, restorer of the human race—came to found twelve cities, as Cato writes in his *Origins* <note>Cato the Elder (234–149 BC) wrote *Origines*, the first history of Rome in Latin, though only fragments survive today.</note>. From this beginning, through the passage of time, the Romans borrowed the greater part of their mysteries and ceremonies, according to Cicero in this legal formula: *Let the Princes of Etruria teach the science of sacred rites; let them provide for those gods to whom they have grown.* <note>original: "Ethruriæ Principes disciplinam sacrorum docento, quibus Dijs creuerint, Procuranto"</note>. And furthermore, that which concerned auguries and predictions through the entrails of victims, and the flight of birds or their songs—first invented in Etruria by Malotus, named Tages by Cicero and Lucian—along with the interpretation of lightning and heavenly fires, extraordinary hail and rain, monsters, and other prodigies, as seen in the same Cicero in his books on divination. On this subject, one may see P. Crinito <note>Pietro Crinito (1475–1507), a Renaissance humanist scholar</note> in book 10, chapter 7 of *On Honorable Learning* <note>original: "de honu. discipl."</note> and in the subsequent book 25, chapter 2.

Regarding their letters and writing, it is held that all these twelve cities or tribes used similar characters which were entrusted to the Priests alone. These priests transposed them for their own use, varying the order, value, and position at their whim, like secret codes. Sometimes they wrote from left to right, as we do, and other times in reverse in the manner of the Hebrews, in order to better hide their secrets from neighboring peoples, so that they could not discover the secret names of the Genies or guardian Angels, protectors, and patrons who assisted them. They also hid the manner of their prayers, sacrifices, and offerings used to make these spirits favorable, for fear that others might "evoke" <note>An ancient ritual called "evocatio" where a besieging army would formally invite the tutelary deity of an enemy city to leave and come to their side.</note> these spirits to themselves, as the Romans later did—which was one of the principal means by which their power grew. These sacrifices and ceremonies intended to please these tutelary deities required long observation based on a perfect knowledge of the stars; for it is from Heaven that the name and office of each Genie is drawn, and consequently from the nature and properties of elementary things, each of which has its own particular star corresponding to the intelligence that presides over it. 

All of this refers ultimately to the glory of the first immobile intellect, upon whom they depend and from whom they have their being and movement—namely, the sovereign God, disguised to them under the name of Zeus <note>original: "ζεὺς"</note> or Jove, a word perverted from the "Jehovah" of the Hebrews. Evidence of these transpositions of Etruscan letters is found in the two subsequent alphabets, one of which proceeds in the Hebrew manner from right to left, and the other in reverse like the Greeks and Latins; for otherwise, most of the characters resemble one another. And although scholars say it is not found anywhere that the Latins borrowed theirs from the Etruscans, nevertheless, since we see such great conformity, it is believable that they were once the same. It is true that Cato in his *Origins* writes that Turrenus, King of Tuscany, in the year 470 after the foundation of

# Languages of this World.

Rome subjected the capital city of Etruria, along with its state and kingdom, to its rule; at that time, the Etruscans did not wish to receive Latin letters <note>meaning the Latin alphabet</note>.

In Volterra, one of the aforementioned twelve cities, many ancient epitaphs and inscriptions are still seen today on marble tablets, sepulchral urns, and statues, which are held to be in Etruscan letters. However, no one can understand anything of them because the language has been extinct and completely lost for a very long time. The most learned Joseph Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a famous Renaissance scholar of chronology and history</note>, in his conjectures on Varro’s *On the Latin Language*, held that the ancient Etruscan language was Aramaic, saying: <term>Everyone will grant me that the name of Saturn is Tuscan <note>original: "Saturni nomē, eſſe Tuſcū"</note>, those who know Syriac; and they hold for certain that the language of the Tuscans was once Aramaic. For Saturn in the Syriac language signifies "latent" or "hidden": whence in the Latin territory, as if interpreting it, they called him Latium <note>playing on the Latin "latere," to hide</note>, and his wife Ops, Latia. And in the Pontifical invocations <note>The "indigitamenta" were lists of gods and the correct ways to address them in prayer</note>, she was called the Latia of Saturn, according to Gellius in book 13, chapter 2; and from him comes the name Latium.</term> The historian Titus Livy <note>Livy (59 BC – AD 17), the Roman historian</note>, in the 9th book of his *Decades*, writes that in ancient times Roman children were accustomed to learning both Greek and Etruscan letters, which were taught in former times to the Etruscans by a certain Demaratus of Corinth. This is confirmed by Cornelius Tacitus in book 11 of his *Annals*, Raffaele Volaterrano in book 5 of his *Geography*, and Polydore Vergil in book 1, chapter 6 of *On the Invention of Things*. Furthermore, Strabo in book 5 asserted that the Oscan and Sabine languages were for a time observed by those Romans in the Atellan farces <note>A type of masked comedy popular in ancient Italy, originally from the Oscan town of Atella</note> recited by actors in the theaters.

Theseus Ambrosius <note>Teseo Ambrogio (1469–1540), an early researcher of exotic languages and alphabets</note>, in his *Appendix on many and various letters*, speaking of this matter, said:

> Many have recorded that the Etruscans, Volscians, and Oscans had various letters and various styles of speaking; nor would I believe it should be doubted, even by those who have (as they say) only touched the surface of literature and letters. Indeed, to speak of the Etruscans, Tarchun’s tombs <note>Tarchun was the legendary founder of the city of Tarquinia</note> are found elsewhere in Volterra, engraved everywhere with Etruscan letters. But as for which peoples owned the specific elements or characters of letters preserved on the bronze tablets of Gubbio <note>The Eugubine Tables, seven bronze tablets found in 1444, crucial for studying the Umbrian language</note>, no one (whom I have seen) has yet clearly asserted. However, I have found the Etruscan alphabet written in various ways in different books and libraries in Italy; for in some places it appears written from the right side to the left, as shown below. This alphabet was sent to me in recent months along with his letters from Bologna by the excellent legal expert Julius de Juliis Canobinus, a man well-versed in humane and polite letters; he wrote that he obtained it from Giovanni Achillini, a truly noble and most cultivated citizen of Bologna. The Etruscan characters subscribed here were taken from the books of the philosopher Taruinus (or Tarvisinus) and conformed with many other copies; they are written in the Latin manner from the left side to the right. However, I cannot see whence such a great variety in writing proceeded. Let others make better conjectures.

# Languages of this Universe.

See what **Petrus Crinitus** <note>Pietro Crinito (1475–1507), an Italian humanist scholar and disciple of Poliziano.</note> writes on this matter in book 3, chapter 3, and book 16, chapter 1 of *On Honorable Discipline*.

**Theodore Bibliander** <note>A Swiss reformer and linguist (1509–1564) who published a famous work on comparative linguistics in 1548.</note> in his *Commentary on all languages and letters*.

<margin>cc</margin>Furthermore, regarding **Etruscan** letters, **Volaterranus** <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), known as Volaterranus, was a humanist who documented the antiquities of his hometown, Volterra.</note> writes thus: "Many monuments of the ancient Etruscans have recently been dug up at Volterra with Etruscan letters, which once—according to the testimony of **Livy** and **Pliny**—were held in high esteem among the Romans, but are now completely unknown. Indeed, in the inscription of a statue, which the same Raphael [Volaterranus] displayed, one can recognize most of the Latin letters A E I O V, B, C, D, F, K, L, M, N. Certain letters appear as inverted Greek and Latin letters, and some are composed into a single syllable; however, there are authors who claim that letters came to the Etruscans from **Demaratus of Corinth**." After the invasions of the **Goths**, the **Germanic** nations, and the **Slavs**, and the tearing apart and ruin of the Empire, provincial speech degenerated further from its origin. As seen in the province of Dacia, in the language of the **Vlachs**—for *Vlasky* sounds like "Italian" or *Waelhen* to the Slavs. The same happened in the Spanish lands, in Gaul, and finally in Italy itself, in **Latium**, in the city that is mistress of nations and the seat of Roman eloquence. Furthermore, each individual province again has its own dialects. Just as a person skilled in the language distinguishes among those using the Italian speech: the **Lombard**, the **Tuscan**, the **Sicilian**, and the **Rhaetian**. Similarly, in the French language, there is the **Provençal**, the **Allobrogian** <note>The region around Savoy and Dauphiné.</note>, the **Burgundian**, the **Parisian**, and the **Picard**; in the Spanish language, the **Catalan**, the **Castilian**, and the **Portuguese**. This discrepancy of dialect is even more widely spread and scattered, and it increases daily through foreign influence and other ways. And yet, learned men who have served their country well have reduced these languages into the form of an art <note>meaning they created formal grammars and rules for these vernaculars.</note>, such as **Bembo**, **Cordier**, **Drosäus**, **Elio Antonio de Nebrija**, and others. This matter proves that the language of any nation does not shun technical treatment, provided that study and attention are applied.

Regarding what we touched upon above concerning Genies or guardian **Angels**, protectors, and patrons, and the means of invoking them: we will say that the Hebrews, in their secret Theology <note>Kabbalah</note>, hold that no one can be overcome here below—as **Rabbi Joseph Ben Carnitol** <note>Joseph Gikatilla (1248–1305), a Spanish Kabbalist; the book mentioned is "Sha'are Orah" or "The Gates of Light."</note> confirms in his book *The Gates of Justice* on this passage: *In that day the Lord Jehovah will punish every high host on high, and the kings of the earth on earth* <note>original Latin: "In die illa animaduertet Dominus Iehoua in omnem exercitum excelsum in excelso, & in Reges terrae in terra"</note>—unless the Intelligence [the Angelic power] that assists him from above is first overcome and distracted from his protection. This is seen in chapter 28 of **Ezekiel**, where God, deliberating on the destruction of the city of Tyre, first withdraws the **Cherub**; and in **Daniel** 10, regarding that Prince of the Kingdom of Persia—namely their Genie and patron—who resisted the Angel Gabriel for 21 days until **Saint Michael** arrived as a reinforcement. **Jesus son of Sirach** <note>Author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus.</note> in his writings assures that the Jews of all time had received through their **Kabbalah** from their ancestors that for every people and nation there is an Angel appointed as ruler and governor, according to the doctrine of **Moses** in the Song cited hereafter. **Saint Clement**, book 6 of the *Stromata*: "For through nations and cities, the **Prefectures of Angels** are distributed." This great personage seems to have drawn this from **Moses** in chapter 32 of Deuteronomy: *When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he established the number of the peoples according to the number of his Angels.* <note>original Latin: "Quando diuidebat altissimus gentes, quando separabat filios Adam constituit numerum populorum iuxta numerum Angelorum suorum." This quote follows the Septuagint version of the Bible.</note> **Saint Peter** explains this in the works of **Saint Clement of Rome**.

# History of the Origin of...

> » Book 2 of the *Recognitions* <note>The *Recognitions* of Pseudo-Clement, an early Christian philosophical novel once attributed to Clement of Rome.</note> where it says: There is an Angel for each nation, to whom the administration of that nation has been entrusted by God. However, when he appears, although he might be thought of and called "God" by those over whom he presides, yet if questioned, he would not give such testimony of himself. For the most high God, who alone holds the power over all things, divided the nations of the entire earth into 72 parts <note>The number 72 is a traditional biblical count for the nations of the world, often corresponding to the "Table of Nations" in Genesis.</note>, and appointed Angels as their princes; but to one who was the greatest among the Archangels, the lot fell to administer those who, above all others, received the worship and knowledge of the most high God.

**St. Basil** <note>Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), a Greek bishop and influential theologian.</note> in his 3rd book and **St. Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 5th–6th century Christian Neoplatonist author; the work cited, *The Celestial Hierarchy*, describes the ranking of angels.</note> in chapter 9 of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, and several other ancient Greek and Latin theologians speak very well and excellently on this, as I have noted in chapter 21 of my *Discourse on the Truth of the Causes and Effects of the Decadence, Mutations, Changes, Conversions, and Ruins of Monarchies, Empires, Kingdoms, and Republics*. One may also see what was written after by **Giovanni Pico** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Italian Renaissance philosopher.</note> in book 4, chapter 4 of his books *Against the Astrologers* and in the second proem of his *Heptaplus*; and **Gianfrancesco Pico** <note>The nephew of Giovanni Pico, also a philosopher.</note> in his book *On the Providence of God*, chapter 6; **Guillaume Postel** <note>A French linguist and mystic (1510–1581) who sought to unify all religions and languages.</note> in book 1, chapter 2 of his *Oriental Histories*; and **Pierre Grégoire** <note>A French jurist and professor (1540–1597) known for his works on law and governance.</note> in volume 4, chapter 11 of his *Commentaries on the Syntax of the Admirable Art*. 

These discourses have moved several ancient and modern theologians and philosophers—founded on the passages alleged above, according to what **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> asserts in book 2 of *Against Apion the Grammarian*—to say that one cannot achieve victory against any Monarchy, Empire, Kingdom, Republic, or City, unless first its **Genius** <note>term: Genius (original: *Genie*); in Roman religion, a protective spirit or "guardian angel" inherent in a person, place, or institution.</note> or **Guardian Angel**, protector, and patron thereof, has first been **evoked** <note>term: Evocation (original: *euocqué*); from the Roman ritual of *evocatio*, a formal prayer to "call out" the tutelary deity of an enemy city to abandon them and come to Rome.</note>. Following this example, the Romans—as **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist and author.</note> notes in book 3, chapter 5, and better in book 28, chapter 2, following **Verrius Flaccus**—had the custom during the sieges of cities, before making any assault, to have the priests evoke the protective God of the place, promising him even greater honors in Rome. This is what **Furius Camillus** did with the Goddess **Juno** at the capture of **Veii**, as recorded in the fifth book of **Livy**. 

For this reason, for fear that the same would be done to them, they kept the true name of the city secret; so much so that **Soranus** died on the spot for having dared to divulge it, as **Plutarch** <note>Greek-Roman biographer and philosopher.</note> testifies in his 61st *Roman Question*. Speaking on this whole matter, **Macrobius** <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial and writer.</note> in book 3, chapter 9 of his *Saturnalia*, very excellently writes that he had once read in the 5th book of *Hidden Things* by **Sammonicus Serenus** the following words used to evoke the Genius or Guardian Angel, protector, and patron of cities and towns:

Inject into that people and city fear, dread, and forgetfulness; and having been surrendered, come to me and my people at Rome. May our places, temples, and sacred rites be more acceptable and approved by you; may you be set over me, the Roman people, and my soldiers, so that we may know and understand it. # History of the Origins of

» ...field in the territory of the Tarquins <note>A reference to the legendary Etruscan kings of Rome</note>, and pushing the plowshare deep into the earth, suddenly there emerged from it one named Tages, having the face of a child, but possessing the wisdom of an old man, from whom the Tuscans learned all this science of <term>Haruspicina</term> <note>The practice of divining the future by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals</note>, which in Latin took its name from *Ara-inspicio* <note>original: "Ara-inspicio"</note>, which signifies looking at the altars. But Pliny in Book 7, Chapter 56, attributes this invention to one named Delphus, just as he attributes divination by fire to Amphiaraus. Now, Haruspicina contains within itself the consideration of the entrails of sacrificial beasts, lightning, and wonders. For as soon as one had killed the beast that was to be immolated near the altar, it was opened, and one looked to see if the heart, liver, and other entrails were in good condition, conjecturing by their state and color what was to come: just as happened to Caesar on the very first day he sat upon the golden throne, having seized the Empire, when no heart was found in the ox that was sacrificed; for which reason the diviners predicted to him that he would be unfortunate in his Empire. <margin>Ostents</margin> <note>original: "Ostentes"</note> are things that happen against nature and which signify something for the future: as happened to Xerxes, King of Persia, after having moved his army into Europe, when a mare—which is a gallant beast of great heart—being pregnant, delivered a hare, the most fearful and cowardly of all animals. And this was a sign that an army as great and furious as that of the Persians would be put to flight by the Greeks. And because these things show, designate, and predict, they are called <term>ostents</term>, <term>prodiges</term>, <term>monsters</term>, and <term>marvels</term>. The third part of Haruspicina consists in the observation of lightning and thunder, regarding which Virgil in his *Bucolics*, Eclogue 1, says:

> » I remember still that the lightning, having struck
> » Upon these oaks, this evil had foretold to us.

There are nonetheless some who say that the art of Augury is of the invention of the Chaldeans, from whom the Greeks learned it, and the Etruscans from the Greeks; finally, the Tuscans taught it to the Latins. Now, among the Greeks, Amphiaraus, Mopsus, and Calchas—who was at the Greek camps during the Trojan War—excelled in this dreaming. ## Concerning the Region of the Latins.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'L' with floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>
Latium, a region of Italy known to all authors, is today called the *Campagna di Roma* <note>The countryside surrounding Rome</note>, having taken its name from the city of Rome, as if one were to say the "Territory of Rome." Its inhabitants are called Latins, who were previously called the <term>Ketioi</term> <note>original Greek: "κήτιοι"</note>, or the *Prisci* <note>meaning "The Ancient Ones"</note>, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus holds; they were properly called *Prisci* according to Festus, those who existed before Rome was founded. These same people were earlier named the *Casci* <note>An archaic term for the "old ones"</note>, as Joseph Scaliger believes in his notes on Varro’s *On the Latin Language*. Suidas writes that they were first called the <term>Ketioi</term> <note>original Greek: "κετίους"</note>, and later Aeneas called them the <term>Dioddas</term> <note>original Greek: "διώδδας"</note>, and finally Romans. Latium is divided into the Old and the New. The Old extends from the Tiber to Circeii; the New extends from there to the Liri river. The authors for this are Strabo and Pliny, who calls the inhabitants Latins. He also mentions the *Latinienses* among them, but writes that they have vanished. Collenuccio writes that Latium is today called *Lazio*, or *Campagna di Roma*, and *Maremma*. The poet Virgil gives Latium the surname "Hesperian" <note>Meaning "Western," a common poetic name for Italy used by the Greeks and later Romans</note>.

Livy writes in the beginning of Book 1 that the Aborigines, the indigenous peoples of Italy, along with the Trojans who had come to Italy under Aeneas, were called by the single name "Latins." According to Strabo, they lived in Latium around Rome itself. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in Book 1, enumerates their towns. Festus says they are the most ancient nation of Italy and dwelt in the Roman territory.

Tuscany. See what I have written in the preceding chapter concerning the region of the Etrurians.

It was first inhabited by the Sicilians, and after they were driven out, the Aborigines arrived and occupied their seat. > I remember that Saturn was received in this land,
> Having been driven from the heavenly kingdoms by Jove;

> And the land was called Latium from the god lying hidden.

History of the Origin of the [Latins]

...is of the opinion that this country of Latium takes its name from the word meaning "concealment" <note>original: "absconsement," derived from the Latin *latere*, to hide</note>, but not from the Saturnian myth; rather, it is because the land is hidden and held tightly between the precipices and high rocks of the Alps and the Apennines, and is enclosed by the sea, the Garigliano, and the Tiber. The boundaries of the Latial territory were once the Tiber on one side and Mount Circeo on the other, being some fifty miles in length; but in the end, it was bordered by the *Terra di Lavoro* <note>original: "Terre de labeur," a fertile region in southern Italy</note> and the country of Abruzzo where the Sabines, Paeligni, and other inhabitants of the Apennines lived. This is what is now called the *Campagna di Roma*.

The language of these people was so greatly extended over the course of time—by means of the men of wit and knowledge among them—that it was received by men of letters not only throughout all of Italy, but also throughout all of Europe, and a good part of Asia and Africa, as I have declared previously, except for a portion of Greece. This served well the power of the Romans, by which the Gauls, Spains, Britain, Illyria, the extremities of Africa, and others mentioned in Roman histories were subjected. Now, when the power of the Romans increased, the name of the Latins began to fail, and in its place, Romulus <note>The OCR likely misread "Romule" as "mule" in the following line</note> usurped the name of the "Romans." Consequently, the Latin language began to be called the "Roman" language. Latium has several cities, among which Rome is the metropolitan capital. Near the sea one finds Ostia and Ardea (where Conradin, the last Duke of Swabia, was killed) <note>Conradin was the last Hohenstaufen; while he was captured near the coast, he was actually executed in Naples</note>, Terracina <note>original: "Sarrasine," likely a variation of Terracina</note>, Formia, Gaeta, Fondi, and Sinuessa near the outlets of the River Liris, which today is called the Garigliano. And within the interior of the Latin country are these cities, namely: Laurentum, Alba (which is said to have existed 300 years before Rome, and is now called Palestrina <note>Alba Longa was historically distinct from Praeneste/Palestrina, though the author conflates them here</note>), and Tremoli, Praeneste, Tibur, and Aquino. See Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book 1 of *Roman Antiquities*; Sebastian Münster, Book 2 of his *Universal Cosmography*, in the chapter on the *Campagna di Roma*—which is Latium in Latin—which was the most renowned as being the first inhabited part of Italy; and after this author, François de Belleforest, Book 3, Chapter 33 of his *Universal History*, treating this Latium in its ancient and new forms, according to the descriptions of modern historians.

### History of the Origin of [the Languages]

"...is not a letter; but only a mark of aspiration <note>The author is likely referring to the letter 'H' or the breathing marks in Greek</note>, and the letter 'F' they received from the Aeolians <note>An ancient Greek tribe whose dialect preserved certain sounds lost in other dialects</note>; this letter, as Priscian <note>A famous Latin grammarian from around 500 AD</note> testifies, had among the ancient Latins the same form and vigor as among the Aeolians themselves, who expressed the same sound with their aspirated '$\Phi$' <note>The Greek letter Phi, which the author equates to the English 'F' sound</note> that we do with our 'F'. We also observe this in Greek words such as Orpheus. After this, Claudius Caesar <note>The Emperor Claudius, who reigned 41–54 AD</note>, successor to Tiberius, as Tacitus writes, wished that instead of 'F' one should use a 'Ⅎ' <note>A reversed F, one of the three 'Claudian letters' intended to represent the consonant 'V' sound</note> to serve as a consonant, and that one should write 'Ⅎulgaire' for 'Vulgaire', and 'he Ⅎesquit' <note>original: 'Ⅎesquit,' from the French 'vesquit' (lived)</note> instead of saying 'he vesquit' <note>lived</note>. Upon this, Quintilian <note>A Roman educator and rhetorician</note> said, not without reason, that Claudius Caesar had added this Aeolic letter 'F' for such a use. Even in our own time, the Germans have retained the pronunciation following this force when they speak Latin. In short, among the Latins, we are accustomed to using 'F' for a 'Ph', as in the words *Fame* for renown and *faire* <note>to do/make</note>. As for the [other marks] of the Greeks, there is no good author who advises that they be used in any manner whatsoever. The letter 'Q' was received because it has a softer sound than 'C'. The letter 'X' was taken from the Greeks, though we could (as Quintilian says) make use of 'C' and 'S', or 'G' and 'S', as in the Latin words *Apexs* and those Greek words signifying a summit or a flock. 'Y' and 'Z' also have their source in the fountains of Greece, but were so adopted by us that we only use them in words that are naturally Greek. Theodor Zwinger <note>A Swiss scholar, 1533–1588</note>, in volume 2, book 1 of his *Great Theatre of Human Life*, repeats all of the above and adds that Spurius Carvilius <note>Spurius Carvilius Ruga, a freedman traditionally credited with inventing the letter 'G' around 230 BC</note>, a later Roman grammarian, was the first who invented the letter 'G', the Romans having previously used 'C' in its place; and that Appius Claudius <note>Appius Claudius Caecus, a Roman statesman</note>, the legal scholar, gave the letter 'R' to the Romans so that they might say *Valerii* for *Valesii*, and *Furii* for *Fusii* <note>This refers to 'rhotacism,' a linguistic change where an 'S' between vowels becomes an 'R'</note>, according to the report of Pomponius in the *Digests on the Origin of Law*. He also notes that the Latins took the digamma '$\digamma$' from the Aeolians, which according to Priscian had the same force as these two letters among the Aeolians, 'Ph'. Theodore Bibliander <note>A Swiss reformer and linguist</note>, in his commentary on the logic of all languages and letters, treats this question very amply and learnedly in these words:

> In Latin writing, the reasoning is the same; at first there were only sixteen letters among the ancients, the same number that Cadmus brought to Greece. Among the most ancient Greeks, there were no more than sixteen letters, and having accepted these, the Latins preserved their antiquity perpetually, according to the testimony of Priscian. To the sixteen ancient Greek letters, two were later added by the same people: the Aeolic 'F' or 'Vau', and 'X'. They also adopted 'Y' and 'Z' for the sake of Greek names. Varro, Macer, and Censorinus <note>All noted Roman authors who wrote on language or chronology</note> judged that 'H', as well as 'K' and 'Q', should not be included in the number of letters. Diomedes <note>A 4th-century grammarian</note> also reports in his second book that some believe there are seventeen letters in the Latin speech. For they consider the two Greek letters 'Y' and 'Z', as well as 'K' and 'Q', to be superfluous, and 'X' to be a double letter, while 'h' is merely a mark of aspiration. Servius <note>A famous commentator on Virgil</note> also notes that the Greeks have an aspiration for which they use 'F', which they call *Daseian* <note>original: 'Daseian,' referring to the Greek 'daseia' or rough breathing</note>; in imitation of this, they also have the smooth '$\digamma$'. We, having joined these, made 'H' our mark of aspiration. But it is much more likely that the Greeks changed the aspirated letter 'H' or 'h' into the mark for the long vowel 'Eta' <note>original: 'Etha'</note>, and having divided it into '$\vdash$' and '$\dashv$', transformed it into marks for light and heavy aspiration. These are marked with different signs in Hebrew verse. In the commentaries of Nonius Marcellus <note>A 4th-century grammarian</note> on the 'Compendious Doctrine' arranged by the order of letters, only 18 letters are placed. ### Languages of this World

The Romans compelled the peoples they had defeated and overcome, through force and the sword, to speak the said Latin language. They would not speak or negotiate with any foreigner in any language other than their own, in order to extend and spread it to every corner of this world, with great ceremony and veneration, as confirmed by Valerius Maximus <note>Valerius Maximus was a 1st-century Roman author known for his collection of historical anecdotes</note> in Book 2, chapter 1 of *Ancient Institutions*. And these Romans did not only make the provincial people change their mother tongue, but also their manners and customs, to make them more gentle and manageable by sending colonies of Latin people for this purpose. Plutarch, in his *Platonic Questions*, asserts that in his time almost all the peoples and nations of this world used and availed themselves of the Latin and Roman language. At that time, the Christian Religion—consisting of the Latin, Roman, Catholic, and Apostolic Church—came to be founded in the West. Established in churches and schools, and consequently in books, public legal instruments, and the sentences of judges which were written and composed in this said language, it kept and preserved Latin throughout Europe, in the provinces and regions of Poland, Germany, Prussia, Sweden, Hungary, Bohemia, Italy, Spain, France, England, Scotland, and others. In these places, this language is understood and spoken by the most learned and hardworking students who learn it in schools, or from private masters, or by means of books written and composed in it.

But we must know and understand that as the Roman Republic changed and transformed into a Monarchy, and its morals became altered and corrupted, the aforementioned Latin and Roman language changed and was corrupted likewise, losing its previous strength, vigor, and purity <note>original: "naifueté", referring here to the natural, unadulterated state of the language</note> under the later Emperors. Then, the Roman Empire having been transferred from Rome to Constantinople, several and diverse foreign nations arriving in Italy altered this language, so much so that people stopped speaking it commonly. Since that time, it has remained only in books which have been shared, read, and interpreted for a few centuries now; they were neither leafed through nor understood for nearly eight hundred years previously. Some were gone and lost, others gnawed and eaten by worms or by old age and decay, until certain Italians a few centuries ago (according to Raphael Volaterranus <note>Raphael Volaterranus, or Raffaello Maffei, was a 15th-century humanist scholar</note> in Book 21 of his *Commentaries*) brought it back to life entirely through long and painful study, writing, correcting, and publishing the books composed in it that remained in libraries, protected from the rage and fury of the Barbarians.

As the aforementioned Empire declined in the West—with the Goths, Ostrogoths, Lombards, and other Northern peoples having invaded and occupied Italy; the Visigoths and Saracens occupying Provence, Languedoc, Aquitaine, and the Spanish territories; and other Northern nations occupying other provinces and regions of Europe—this Latin language was altered and corrupted by their victories and through frequent interaction and conversation. From this corruption, or rather alteration, proceeded the Italian, Spanish, French, and other common languages of today. And to return to our first subject, we shall note that Velleius <note>Velleius Paterculus, a Roman historian</note> wrote in Book 1 that the elegance of this Latin language was at its height during the time of the poet Accius <note>Lucius Accius was a Roman tragic poet of the 2nd century BC</note>, who lived one hundred and fifty and some...

# History of the Origin of the [Latin Language]

...years before Jesus Christ, in the era and around the time of (for before this everything was rough) Roman Tragedy, and the sweet wits of Latin grace—Caecilius, Terence, and Afranius—shone during a similar age. Historians mention Cato, and certain ancients and obscure figures, but eloquence shone much more in Tully <note>original: "Tullium"; referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> or his equals. Fabius Quintilian, in Book 12, chapter 10, wrote words worthy of being recited here: <note>original: "Fuere quædam genera dicendi... ditione temporum horridiora."</note> "There were certain styles of speaking... which were rougher due to the condition of the times," etc. Cælius Rhodiginus, in Book 23, chapter 2 of his *Various Lessons*, speaks thus of the diversity of this same Latin language:

> Those who have set out in their commentaries to discuss the variations of speaking more deeply and thoughtfully with careful scrutiny have seen this reason and pronounced it clearly distributed into three parts <note>Though Rhodiginus says "threefold" (trifariam), he proceeds to describe four distinct stages of the language.</note>. Indeed, in ancient books, one can see some things said in the *Primal* way, some in *Latin*, some in *Roman*, and finally some in a completely *Mixed* style. By *Primal*, they understand that which was spoken by those contemporary with Janus and Saturn <note>Janus and Saturn were mythical early kings and gods of Italy; this refers to the prehistoric origins of the tongue</note>, and shortly after by their own people in their fables. In this style, many things are found wrapped in a great cloud of obscurity and are recognized with difficulty because the words have fallen out of use, therefore not easily allowing for a clear understanding; what sort of things the songs called *Saliaria* <note>The *Carmen Saliare*, ancient and nearly unintelligible chants performed by the Salii priests</note> were can be guessed from the very few fragments that survive. The *Latin* style of speaking is believed to be so named from what they used in Latium when Latinus was in power, and also the Etruscan Kings: in which style the Tables of the Decemvirs <note>The Twelve Tables, the earliest code of Roman law</note> were written. But of this part, hardly a word remains untainted, as Sextus Pompeius reported. Finally, they understand the *Roman* way of speaking as that which flourished in Plautus, Naevius, Accius, Ennius, Maro <note>Virgil</note>, Cato, Sisenna, Antias, Valerius, Caesar, and Marcus Tullius [Cicero]. Finally, the *Mixed* style introduced itself when, with the Empire now grown and Roman liberty surrendered, the state was shared with very diverse nations. Into their whirlpool, the purity of speech was shaken and fell away, first into the sound of almost all the provinces, then began to taste of the Gothic, and became so entirely foreign that one can rarely find what you could call purely Roman, even among those gifted with citizenship. Yet Fabius <note>Quintilian</note> wonders that many Oscan <note>An ancient language of Southern Italy</note> and Sabine words gained strength among authors, not to mention Gallic ones, since even some Punic <note>Carthaginian</note> words show themselves.

T. Bibliander <note>Theodor Bibliander, a 16th-century Swiss scholar of linguistics</note> in his commentary on the common reason of all languages and letters, writes this regarding the Latin speech of Cicero from his book *On Famous Orators*:

> Everyone in the time of Laelius and Scipio—those who neither traveled outside the city nor were stained by any domestic barbarism—spoke correctly. But the Latin speech gradually admitted not only many Greek words but also Gallic ones, like *alauda* <note>lark</note> and *canthus* <note>the iron rim of a wheel</note>; and Spanish ones like *mastruca* <note>a sheepskin garment</note>; and British ones like *essedum* <note>a war-chariot</note>; and indeed some words from all nations while they all served as soldiers. Concerning this, Fabius says in Book 1 of the *Institutes*, chapter 10: "I might say foreign words [have come] from all nations, just as many people and institutions have also come." And again, the Latin speech, through the invasions of nations into the Roman provinces, became confused and mixed.

Cardinal Adrien <note>Adriano Castellesi, a humanist scholar and cardinal</note> writing on this subject in the *Prologue of the Latin Language*, gives it four periods: namely, the very ancient, the ancient, the perfect, and the imperfect. The very ancient was that which existed from the beginning of the city of Rome until Livius Andronicus <note>The first Roman dramatist, a Greek slave who translated works into Latin</note>, who was the first among...
