# History of the Origins of

...ancient writers spoke and wrote the Latin language in every way and in every place, and refused to accept any flaw in it; those who followed declined from this standard; and a third group, wandering and straying entirely, preferred flaw to virtue. Regarding the Gallic writers, such as Cassiodorus <note>A Roman statesman and writer (c. 485–585) who served under the Ostrogothic kings</note>, Aper, Fulgentius, Ennodius, and others of their time, their works composed in the Latin language should be seen and read, but they should by no means be accepted for imitation. Theodore Bibliander <note>A Swiss Protestant reformer and linguist (1509–1564) who wrote on the "common reason" of all languages</note> in his *Commentary on the Common Logic of All Languages and Letters* says:

"While the Roman and Latin language had a certain fixed seat in the city and Latium <note>original: "in vrbe & Latio"</note>, and held the Empire and flourished greatly in the Roman Provinces, it nevertheless had several distinctions, and those not obscure: for there was a frequent mixing of the Latium, Volscian, Sabine, Opician, and Etruscan languages; in Titus Livius <note>The historian Livy</note>, a certain 'Paduan quality' <note>original: "Patauinitas"; a term coined by Pollio to criticize Livy's regional Paduan accent</note> was noticed by Pollio, because he was from Padua and did not retain pure and unadulterated Roman eloquence throughout; in Augustine, Cyprian, Tertullian, and other Africans using a provincial form, there is something local and African; in Hilary, Prosper, and other Gallic writers, something unique stands out. Likewise, Seneca, Lucan, Sedulius, Columella, and even Quintilian himself retain something of the Spanish style."

To be brief, if we wish to compare this Latin language—even when fashioned with all elegance and eloquence—with the excellent Greek language, we will find it (according to the testimony of the aforementioned Cicero, Gellius, and Lucretius) so poor and defective that it cannot even express several and diverse words that the aforementioned Greek language can with a single one. Quintilian <note>A famous Roman rhetorician</note> agrees with this, saying that the Latin language is much lesser and more sterile than the Greek, being rougher in its pronunciation and derivation of vocabulary; this author proves this through several Latin passages cited by him in his works. This is what moved the learned poet Horace to say:

And we should not accept the aforementioned Cicero in his preface to the *Tusculan Disputations*, in Book 2 of *The Orator*, and Book 1 of *On Ends*, where he writes that this Latin language is richer and more abundant than the Greek—seeing as he claimed the Greek had no proper word to signify the Latin word *Ineptus* <note>A term for someone lacking in tact or social grace</note>. But this great Orator, when writing about Philosophy, found himself quite hindered in trying to find and invent new Latin words corresponding exactly to the Greek words for every art or speculation; this personage is even constrained to confess it ingenuously in the *Tusculan Disputations* and in his oration *For the Poet Archias*. And we should believe Seneca even less in Book 12 of his *Controversies*, where he maintains that the Latin language "has no less power than the Greek, but less license" <note>original: "ne facultatis non minus habere, quàm Græcam, sed licentiæ minus"</note>.

### To know whether formerly the Romans all generally spoke Latin.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'P' with foliage and strapwork motifs.</image-desc>
Polydore Vergil <note>An Italian humanist scholar (c. 1470–1555) who lived in England and wrote extensively on the "beginnings" of things.</note> in book 1, chapter 3 of *On the Discovery of Things* <note>original: "de l'inuent. des choses"</note>, treating of the first birth of men, and of the cause of the diversity of languages and of the first division of the lands made in the world among men, has used the words which follow.

> But it will not be at all out of place to discourse a little on the ancient controversy among men of learning, inquiring if formerly the Romans all spoke Latin in general, or if they had two kinds of language, just as at present both we and the Greeks have two: the one common and maternal <note>The vernacular or "mother tongue" spoken at home.</note>, and the other literary and Latin—and among the Greeks, Attic. And so that we do not labor over a thing so clear (as I think), following Cicero in the third book of *The Orator*, we shall see the evident reason. Now he says in this place that at Rome there was a certain and proper language for those of the city: which he proves by a woman named Laelia <note>The daughter of Gaius Laelius Sapiens; she was famous for the purity and elegance of her spoken Latin.</note>, who spoke so well, and used such fine terms, that one thought upon hearing her discourse that it was a Plautus or a Naevius <note>Plautus and Naevius were early Roman playwrights celebrated for their vigorous and native Latin style.</note>. So that one does not think that this Laelia had learned another language—namely Latin—different from that which was proper and natural to her, and which she had sucked from her mother’s breast, he adds a little after: "but no one was astonished hearing an orator speaking Latin, whereas if he spoke another language he was mocked for it." And in *The Perfect Orator*, "if on the theater a verse is pronounced of which a single syllable is too long or too short, the whole audience begins to cry out." And in the 1st book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: "the multitude attending at the theater, where there are women and children"—from which it follows when they hear a verse that is grand and well-sounding. These are the words of Cicero, by which it appears that the Latin language was common to all, since even the common women and children knew how to speak this language. But he was the most learned who chose the most proper words, and who judged them with a just weight of his ear, which could not be done without letters <note>Meaning formal education or literacy.</note>. Now all the Romans spoke Latin well, but not all were learned; Cicero testifies to the contrary when in the book of *Brutus* he introduces T. Pomponius Atticus speaking thus: "You see that Latin elocution is refined, the praise of which comes not by process of reason, or any science, but as if from a good custom." Then he adds: "We, being children, saw T. Flaminius, and C. the Consul with Q. Metellus: it was said indeed that he spoke Latin properly, but he did not know his letters." Is there anyone then who concedes that these things are testified to by the prince of the Latin language <note>Referring to Cicero.</note>, without suspecting that the Romans had, no more than we do at present, diverse languages? For just as at Rome those who had lived outside the city spoke less purely and ornamentally than the others, likewise among the Latins, the barbarism and roughness of...

The rules for debate belong to the rhetoricians, but there are none for speech. Although I do not know if such rules might also exist. But teachers are found who disagree in their studies, while there are none who study speech; yet everything is filled with the crowd of rhetoricians. Those are of deceptive speech, as Accius <note>Lucius Accius (170–c. 86 BC) was a Roman tragic poet and philologist.</note> says, who are born of malice. Fluency [*Loquentia*], however, like loquacity, is placed among the vices of speech. Aulus Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author of "Attic Nights," a collection of notes on grammar, philosophy, and history.</note>, book one, chapter fifteen. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] seriously and truly detests a foolish and empty abundance of speaking. Provided, he says, this is clear: neither the lack of eloquence of one who knows a subject but cannot explain it in speaking, nor the ignorance of one who has the words but lacks the subject matter, is to be praised. If one of the two had to be chosen, I would indeed prefer uneloquent wisdom to foolish loquacity. Sallust says of Catiline: "enough fluency, too little wisdom." <note>original Latin: "satis loquentiæ, sapientiæ parum"</note> For so Valerius Probus, the illustrious grammarian, judged it should be read, as the same Gellius testifies.

Speech [*Oratio*] signifies both common conversation and artful locution. Cicero, *On the Orator*, book 1: "This is the orator’s own characteristic, which I have often said: speech that is weighty, adorned, and suited to the senses of men." We must know, says Fabius Victorinus <note>A 4th-century rhetorician and commentator on Cicero.</note> in his commentary, that in Cicero's dialogues there is "conversation" [*sermo*], not "diction" [*dictio*]. Diction belongs to the orator in civil cases. Or, "conversation" belongs to the philosopher, "diction" to the orator. "Speech" [*Oratio*], however, can also suit a dialogue if the elocution is a little more splendid. Yet it is properly the orator's.

Dialect <note>original Greek: διάλεκτος (dialektos)</note> is defined by Joannes Grammaticus <note>Also known as John Philoponus, a 6th-century Alexandrian philosopher and grammarian.</note> as the "property of a language" <note>original Greek: γλώττης ἰδίωμα (glōttēs idiōma)</note>, such as Attic, Doric, and the others. Thus the Stoics define dialect, according to Diogenes [Laertius] in book seven, as "utterance stamped both ethnically and Greekly" <note>original Greek: λέξις κεχαραγμένη ἐθνικῶς τε καὶ ἑλληνικῶς (lexis kecharagmenē ethnikōs te kai hellēnikōs)</note>, that is, a voice confirmed variously among the Greeks and other nations. Furthermore, Aristotle says "dialect" is human locution; however, that which is commonly called an "idiom" or "dialect," Aristotle calls a "tongue" <note>original Greek: γλωσσαν (glōssan)</note>, as does Galen. For so Aristotle divides the noun in the book *On Poetics*: every noun is either proper, or from another language [foreign], etc. I call "proper" that which is in use by everyone; "from another language" [foreign] that which is used only by some. From this it is clear that such a word can also become "proper," so that they sometimes fall into the same category, though not for the same people. As "sigunon" <note>A type of spear.</note>, that is a lance, is "proper" to the Cypriots; but to us it is a "tongue" [gloss], that is, from their language. And Galen, in the book he titled *Explanation of the Tongues [Glosses] of Hippocrates*, says that whatever nouns were once in use, but are no longer, are called "tongues" <note>Greek: γλώσσας (glōssas)</note>, that is, languages. And in explaining the "tongues" of Hippocrates, he provides not only single words, but sometimes several. From this, the Latins also call brief interpretations, where a word is usually rendered by another word, "glosses," and "glossaries," and "glossemata." As Fabius [Quintilian] <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, the famous 1st-century Roman rhetorician.</note> says in the first book of the *Institutes*: a boy can immediately learn the interpretation of a more secret language—that is, those which the Greeks call "tongues" [glosses]—while doing something else. Furthermore, Aristotle calls speech or oration both *logos* <note>Greek: λόγον</note> and *lexis* <note>Greek: λέξιν</note>. Although *lexis* is taken for "diction" or a single significant word by Apollonius and other good authors. Aristotle also calls elocution *lexis* in his *Rhetoric*. This is also sometimes called "diction" by the Latins, and the "thread of speech." Just as Cicero in *The Orator* speaks of the "thin thread of arguing." It is also called "Phrase," "Character," "Form," and "Type of speech." *Dialexis* <note>Greek: διάλεξις</note> is artful locution, named either from *dialegomai* [I dispute/discuss] or *dialego* [I select and separate]. Chatter <note>original Greek: λαλία (lalia)</note>, as Gellius says, is a most significant term used by the Greeks for men who blather foolishly and immoderately. ...and is placed in dialect. And humans have a specific property: they are *laletikoi* <note>Greek: λαλητικοί—talkative or prone to speaking.</note>, conversational, or more correctly, endowed with speech. Furthermore, *logos* <note>The Greek term for word, reason, or discourse.</note> and *dialogismus* <note>discourse or reasoning</note> are well enough known among both Greeks and Latins. And indeed, these things seemed necessary to distinguish at the outset, because they are often confused even by great authors. Furthermore, "tongue," "mouth," and "lip," because they are instruments of the voice, are often accepted by trope <note>A rhetorical figure of speech or metaphor.</note> for the diversity of speech itself. For instance, Cicero says in his work *On Ends* <note>Cicero’s *De finibus bonorum et malorum*, a treatise on ethics.</note> that the Latin tongue seems to some to be poorer in words than the Greek. And in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: "In those tongues which we do not understand, we are effectively deaf." And Horace in the *Art of Poetry*:

> *Neither in virtue nor in glorious arms would Latium be more powerful*
> *Than in its tongue, if the labor and delay of the file <note>original Latin: "lima labor"—the "file" is a metaphor for the painstaking process of polishing and editing a poem.</note> did not offend*
> *Every one of our poets.*

Moses used this same trope when he wrote that God confused the tongue and the lip in Babylonia <note>A reference to the Tower of Babel in Genesis 11.</note>.
   Indeed, "voice" is used for speech and oration not without merit, as when it is said: "It is a voice unworthy of a wise man to say, 'I cannot.'" And so much for these related names which are used for speech.

   "Oration" and "speech" are defined in this manner: To speak is to give an articulate sign. A sign is that which shows itself to the sense and something beyond itself. I say "articulate" because it is that which can be captured by letters. These are [the words of] Melanchthon <note>The OCR reads "nus," likely a fragment of "Melanchthonus," the Protestant reformer whose *Dialectica* was a standard textbook.</note> in his *Dialectics*. Aristotle, in the fourth book of the *History of Animals*, says: *dialektos phōnēs tē glōttē diarthrōsis* <note>Greek: διάλεκτός φωνῆς τῆ γλώτη διάρθρωσις—"speech is the articulation of the voice by the tongue."</note>; Speech is nothing other than the expression of the voice through the tongue. And he adds: Humans also use speech differently, though they all return the same voice <note>Meaning humans share the biological capacity for sound but differ in languages.</note>. In the book on *Poetics*, he calls "diction" <note>Greek: λέξιν (*lexin*)</note> oration, as do the Grammarians and Rhetoricians when they call certain things "figures of voice," and others "figures of thought" <note>Greek: διανοίας (*dianoias*)</note>. In this way, interrogation, response, exclamation, narration, and command are figures and species of diction. However, he establishes one *logos* <note>Greek: λόγον—word/reason/speech</note> as "oration." And in this way he says *logos phōnē esti synthetē, sēmantikē, hēs enia merē kath' auta sēmainei* <note>Greek: λόγος φωνή ἐςι συνθέτη, σημαντική, ἧς ἔνια μερὴ καθ' αυτὰ σημαίνει—"Speech is a composite significant voice, of which certain parts signify something by themselves."</note>. Oration is a composite voice, signifying something, of which certain parts separately signify something in their own right. By this definition, Aristotle exhibits the understanding that "rational animal" is an oration, as is the entire work and labor called the *Iliad*. For he explains that oration is spoken of in two ways: either as one thing signifying by itself, or as a conjunction of things. For example, the *Iliad* is one oration by its conjunctions; the definition of "man"—namely, "an animal endowed with reason"—is one thing signifying. In the first book of *On Interpretation* <note>Latin: *Peri Hermeneias*.</note>, he explains with the same definition. The Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy.</note> say a bit differently that *logos* is "a significant voice sent forth from the mind and thought." From this, Democritus <note>The Pre-Socratic "laughing philosopher" known for atomic theory.</note> defined it acutely as *rhusin tou noou* <note>Greek: ρῦσιν τᾶ νόος—a flowing out or derivation of the mind.</note>.

   Diomedes <note>A 4th-century Latin grammarian.</note> defines oration in his first book as a structure of words coming together and ending in a closing clause. Or, as others have defined it, a composition of dictions completing a thought and signifying a perfect matter. Scaurus <note>Quintus Terentius Scaurus, a 2nd-century grammarian.</note> defines it as a pronunciation sent from the mouth and ordered through dictions.

It explains how terms like "tongue" and "lip" function as metaphors for language and contrasts different philosophical definitions of what constitutes a "sentence" or "discourse."</summary>

<header>Languages of this Universe.</header>

In the second book: **Speech** is the ordering of words demonstrating a congruent and complete thought. <note>original: "Oratio est ordinatio dictionum congruam sententiam, perfectamque demonstrans."</note> This is indeed a general definition; that is, one which is divided into species or parts. Otherwise, even a book on <term>Rhetoric</term> <note>The art of persuasive speaking or writing.</note> is called a "speech," as is a single expression, such as imperative or responsive words that complete a thought. Fabius Quintilianus expresses what he understands speech to be in his third book on the parts of Rhetoric, stating: "all discourse by which a certain will is expressed must necessarily contain both the **matter** and the **word**." And if it is brief and finished with a single conclusion, it perhaps requires nothing more. But a longer discourse requires more; and in his eighth book, he says "all speech consists of things and words." In the "things," one must look for <term>Invention</term> <note>Finding the right arguments.</note>; in the words, <term>Elocution</term> <note>Style and choice of words.</note>; and in both, <term>Arrangement</term> <note>The structure of the speech.</note>: which the **Memory** should embrace and **Action** <note>Delivery or performance.</note> should recommend. For the task of Eloquence is to bring forth everything you have conceived in the mind and deliver it to the listeners. And in the twelfth book of his Rhetoric: "The work of the Orator is speech, and its forms are many." Cicero also expresses his opinion on speech both frequently elsewhere and in the second book of *On the Nature of the Gods*. "Now truly," he says, "how remarkable and how divine is that power of speech which you are accustomed to call the 'mistress of things'? It first ensures that we can learn those things we do not know, and teach others what we do know; then by this power we exhort, by this we persuade, by this we comfort the afflicted, by this we lead the terrified away from fear, by this we restrain the exuberant, and by this we extinguish desires and angers. This power has bound us together in the fellowship of justice, laws, and cities; it has separated us from a wild and savage life. Moreover, it is incredible—if you attend to it diligently—how much effort Nature has engineered for the use of speech. For first, the artery <note>Here referring to the windpipe or trachea.</note> extends from the lungs all the way to the inner mouth, through which the voice, taking its beginning from the mind, is perceived and poured out, etc."

It seemed appropriate to propose the views of theologians, philosophers, dialecticians, grammarians, and orators regarding speech, so that it might be more clearly seen whether they all envisioned a single **end** or purpose for discourse.

->**What the Purpose of Discourse Is.**<-

Since in the understanding and deep inspection of things, as well as in the undertaking and perfection of any business, the greatest importance is placed on causes; so truly, in the entire treatment of discourse and languages, it matters most to have known the causes, and indeed exactly: especially the cause "on account of which" each thing is or becomes. This is the **Good** itself, the **use** of the thing, and the **end** toward which movement occurs. When we have rightly contemplated that end—why Nature, or rather the Architect of Nature, gave the faculty and use of speech to humans; why humans have discourses; and why they speak—then we will easily adapt the entire doctrine of using discourse correctly to that end. Thus, we shall use discourse and languages rightly, and we will perceive without difficulty the kinship between the <term>logical arts</term> <note>The disciplines of grammar, logic, and rhetoric.</note> and what their purpose is. From here, the common reason for all languages and letters will also present itself of its own accord, the showing of which is the primary purpose of this book. Accordingly, the end...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of speech, transitioning from the rhetorical definitions of Quintilian and Cicero on the previous page to theological and philosophical definitions. It seeks to establish why speech exists (for edification and teaching) and how it functions as a system of signs.</meta>

Page 780
<header>History of the Origin of Languages</header>

<note>The left margin of this page is tightly bound, obscuring the start of many words. Restorations are based on context.</note>

...of speech, so that we may first investigate the definition from classical authors according to the reasons which they themselves followed, and briefly so: for it is our intention in this commentary to perform the duty of a Judge, not of a teaching **master**. <note>original: "magistri"</note> Paul the Apostle, in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 14, indicates the purpose of languages and speech when he requires "edification," <note>original: "οἰκοδομὴν" (oikodomēn), meaning the building up of the church or the individual's understanding.</note> that is, a building up, so that from speech a good fruit might return to the men hearing it: which cannot happen unless it is perceived by the mind and intellect: but it will not be perceived unless one utters "distinct speech," <note>original: "εὔσημον λόγον" (eusēmon logon)</note> that is, speech that signifies. Just as while a song which a lyre-player plays, no one understands unless the lyre has rendered distinct sounds. And if in war, unless the Trumpet gives certain signals, no one will be roused to battle by its judgment, nor will they perform their military duties, which are usually indicated by the signal of trumpets. Augustine, in his book *On the Teacher*, <note>original: "De Magistro," a dialogue by St. Augustine exploring how language works and how we learn.</note> establishes that words are signs. A sign cannot be a sign unless it signifies something. And again: He who speaks gives out a sign of his will through **articulated sound**. Does it not seem to you that, except for the sake of teaching or reminding, speech was not instituted? You see therefore that we seek nothing by speaking except to teach. And throughout the whole book he explains how words are signs, and signs of words. In <term>Dialectics</term> <note>The branch of philosophy dealing with logic and the nature of reasoned argument.</note> also, when speaking concerning the nature of speech, he orders these four things to be held distinctly: the word, the "sayable," the spoken, and the thing. A **Thing** <note>original: "Res"</note> is whatever is either felt, like physical bodies, or understood as spiritual things, or remains hidden like God and formless matter. A **Word** <note>original: "Verbum"</note> is the sign of each thing, which can be understood by the hearer when uttered by the speaker. A **Sign** is that which shows itself to the senses and, because of itself, shows something to the mind. It is one thing to give a sign with an articulate voice. By "articulate," I mean that which can be captured in letters. Every word indeed makes a sound, for in writings it is a word, but it is a sign of a word. Truly, when the letters are inspected by the reader, that which breaks forth by the voice is formed in the mind. For what else are written letters but things showing themselves to the eyes and, besides themselves, showing voices to the mind? There are also signs of words which are words themselves; as when a Grammarian asks how many syllables are in the word "man," or what part of speech it is: and the Dialectician asks whether it is a genus or a species, and what things belong to this genus. Furthermore, words are either simple, which signify something by themselves, like individual nouns and verbs; or they are joined and coupled, like "man lives by his faith." A "sayable" <note>original: "dicibile"</note> is called whatever the ear does not perceive from words, but the mind feels, and is held enclosed in the mind itself. A "spoken" <note>original: "dictum"</note> is that which the sense perceives. A "diction" <note>original: "dictio"</note> is the term used when a word proceeds not for its own sake, but for the sake of signifying something else. Concerning these things, Dialectics treats. Aristotle, in his first book *On Interpretation*: <note>original: "De Interpretatione," one of Aristotle's primary works on logic and language.</note> Those things which exist in the voice are signs of the affections which are in the soul; those things which are written are marks of those things which exist in the voice. And just as letters are not the same among all men, so neither are the voices the same; however, the affections of which these are signs are the same among all men. Likewise, the things of which these are "likenesses" <note>original: "ὁμοιώματα" (homoiōmata)</note> and images are voices, and are similarly the same among all. Furthermore, no voice is significant "by nature," <note>original: "φύσει" (physei)</note> but rather it signifies by agreement: so that it might become a "symbol" <note>original: "σύμβολον" (symbolon)</note> of a common thing. Whence sounds that cannot be written, such as the cries of beasts, are not significant in this way. Furthermore, some voices are "composite," <note>original: "συμπλεκ-" (symplektikai)</note> joined together like a sentence; others are without composition, like individual nouns.

In his first book, Diomedes <note>A 4th-century Latin grammarian</note> shows the purpose of speech and how it is produced in this manner: speech, revealing the secrets of the heart, moves toward the tongue for its governance through a certain mobile breath of the articulate voice. It is tempered by the rounded control of that "rudder" and sounded by the air near the inner chest being struck, and the palate being beaten gently and little by little; like a messenger or a betrayer of the human mind, it is driven rationally through the mouth and discourse to express the signs of thought. For this speech, expressed through the great benefit of reason, separates us from the other animals; nature acknowledges and demonstrates that this belongs to humans alone. Orators also most firmly hold that speech was given to man to explain the feelings of the mind and for his well-being, not for his destruction; nor is anything more contrary to nature than to obscure one's meaning with words. Indeed, they establish the highest perfection of speech as the science of speaking out—or rather, the virtue and faculty of it. Good rhetoricians join this with wisdom in such a way that it can in no way be torn from it. It will be enough to have revealed this with one or two examples. Next, we shall consider the goals of the arts of speaking alongside the goal of speech itself.

Quintilian <note>A celebrated Roman educator and rhetorician</note> defines "speaking out" <note>original: "eloqui," the root of "eloquence"</note> as follows:

> To bring forth all that you have conceived in the mind and convey it to the listeners. Without this, the prior steps—namely, inventing and arranging what is to be said—were useless, much like a sword kept sheathed and sticking within its scabbard. This, therefore, is what is most taught; this is what no one can attain except by art. To this, study must be applied; this, exercise seeks; this, imitation. Here an entire lifetime is consumed; it is this that makes one orator more outstanding than another. Through this, the very styles of speaking are rendered some better than others.

And a little later:

> Therefore, let the care for elocution be as great as possible, provided we know that nothing should be done for the sake of words alone, since words themselves were discovered for the sake of things. Among words, those are most to be approved which best bring forth the meaning of our mind and produce the effect we desire in the minds of the judges. These must undoubtedly provide an admirable speech—though not so that we marvel at them as if they were omens—and a pleasant one, not with a base pleasure, but joined with praise and dignity.

And again:

> What the Greeks call <term>phrasin</term> <note>original Greek: φράσιν; "phrase" or "style of expression"</note>, we in Latin call *elocutionem* (elocution).

We examine this elocution in words either individually or joined together. In individual words, we must see that they are Latinate, clear, ornate, and suited to what we wish to achieve; and that they are as little "foreign" or "external" as possible. In joined words, they must be correct, well-placed, and figurative. Furthermore, in his twelfth book, defining an orator as "a good man skilled in speaking"—taking this from the opinion of Marcus Cato—he shows that the faculty of speaking well should be granted to no one who is not also a good man. ...by the laws of nature, which are undoubtedly the best. For so Quintilian <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus (c. 35–100 AD), a celebrated Roman rhetorician</note> concludes. But that which he posited earlier—and which nature itself preferred—is certainly this: that if this power of speaking were to join itself to wickedness, nothing would be more ruinous to public and private affairs than eloquence. And we ourselves, who have striven to the best of our ability to contribute something to the faculty of speaking, would deserve the worst of human affairs if we provided these weapons to a bandit instead of a soldier. 

Why do I speak of ourselves? Nature itself, which would seem to have especially favored man and by which she separated us from other living creatures, would be not a parent but a stepmother <note>original: "nouerca"</note> if she had devised the faculty of speech as a companion to crime, an adversary to innocence, and an enemy of truth. For it would have been better to be born mute and lacking the use of reason than for the gifts of providence to be turned toward mutual destruction. 

But after a few intervening words, he continues: "Since, therefore, an orator is a good man, and since such a man cannot be understood apart from virtue, virtue—even if it takes some impulses from nature—must nevertheless be perfected by doctrine." Above all, the character of the orator must be cultivated through study, and the entire discipline of what is honorable and just must be examined; without this, no one can be a good man or skilled in speaking. Unless perhaps we agree with those who think that character is fixed and is not helped at all by discipline. As if indeed those things which are made by hand, and even the most contemptible of them, are admitted to require teachers, yet virtue—than which nothing is given to man that brings him closer to the immortal gods—is something we should possess by chance and without effort, simply because we were born. 

Will a man be temperate who is ignorant of what temperance is? Will he be brave who has not dispelled the diseases of fear, pain, death, and superstition by any use of reason? And will he be just who has not discussed the treatment of equity and goodness, the laws which were given to all by nature, and those which were specifically established for peoples and nations? O, how little do they think of that which seems so easy! 

But I pass over this, about which I think no one who has "tasted literature with the tip of their lips," as they say <note>A Latin idiom meaning to have even a basic education</note>, will doubt. I shall return to this point: that no one will even be sufficiently skilled in speaking who has not both thoroughly examined all of nature and formed his character through precepts and reason. 

For it is not in vain that in the third book of *On the Orator*, Lucius Crassus <note>A character in Cicero's dialogue and a famous Roman orator</note> affirms that all things which are said concerning the equitable, the just, the true, and the good, and their opposites, belong to the orator; he claims that philosophers, when they defend these things with the power of speech, are using the weapons of rhetoricians, not their own. Yet he admits that these things must now be sought from philosophers, clearly because it seems to him that they have been more in possession of these matters. 

Hence also it is that Cicero testifies in many books and letters that the faculty of speaking flows from the innermost springs of wisdom, and that for some time the same people were teachers of both morals and speech. Cicero writes in the *Brutus*: "Delivery is, as it were, a certain eloquence of the body, consisting of voice and movement." And again: "But now the image of that perfect orator and of the highest eloquence must be expressed." He indicates by this name alone that the orator excels in speech, while other qualities remain hidden within him. For it is not just the composer or the actor who has embraced all these things. But both in Greek, when one is called a *Rhetor* <note>original: "Rhetor"</note>, and in Latin, one is called "eloquent." However, the greatest power of speaking—that is, of eloquence—is granted to him alone. And again in *The Orator*: "But the foundation of eloquence, as of all other things, is wisdom." ...than what is appropriate; the Greeks call this *prepon* <note>original Greek: πρέπον, meaning "that which is fitting" or "becoming"</note>. We may call it the *decorous* <note>original: "decorum"</note>. Regarding this, many excellent things are understood, and it is a matter most worthy of knowledge. Through ignorance of this, mistakes are made not only in life, but very often in both poetry and in oratory. Moreover, the orator must see what is appropriate not only in his thoughts, but also in his words. And again: let it be established first—which will be better understood later—that the eloquent man we are seeking cannot be produced without Philosophy. Thus, in the *Oratorical Partitions*, having spoken of the virtues and every kind of good, he says in the demonstrative and laudatory genre: "And these virtues are discerned in action. There are others, however, which are like the handmaidens and companions of wisdom." One of these distinguishes and judges what is true and false in a dispute, and what follows from what is posited; all of this virtue is situated in the reason and science of disputation <note>This refers to Dialectic or Logic</note>. The other is oratory. For eloquence is nothing other than wisdom speaking abundantly <note>original: "eloquentia, nisi copiosè loquens sapientia"</note>. This is drawn from the same source as the former, though it is richer and broader in disputation, and better suited to the movements of the mind and the feelings of the common people.

And so that I may join the judgment of *Aristotle* to the opinion of *Cicero*, I will provide one passage from *Cicero’s Orator*: "I think it belongs to the perfectly eloquent man not only to possess that faculty which is his own—to speak flowingly and broadly—but also to adopt the neighboring and bordering science of the dialecticians. Although oratory seems to be one thing and disputation another, and speaking is not the same as 'haranguing,' nevertheless both consist in discourse. The method of disputation and speaking belongs to the dialecticians, while the method of haranguing and adorning belongs to the orators." And after the *Chria* <note>A short anecdote or exercise in a rhetoric school</note> of *Zeno the Stoic*, who signified dialectic with a closed fist and eloquence with an open palm, he added: "Furthermore, *Aristotle* says at the beginning of his *Art of Rhetoric* that rhetoric is, as it were, the counterpart to dialectic; so that they differ from each other in this way: that the former method of speaking is broader, while the latter method of talking is more contracted." 

Now, after the dialectical method and way of teaching, he adds: "Nor is he truly equipped by dialectic alone, but he should have all the topics of philosophy known and handled. For nothing concerning religion, nothing concerning death, nothing concerning piety, nothing concerning virtues or vices, nothing concerning duty, nothing concerning pain, nothing concerning pleasure, nothing concerning the disturbances of the soul and errors—which often fall into legal cases, but are handled too meagerly—nothing, I say, can be spoken or explained with gravity, fullness, and abundance without that science which I have mentioned." I am speaking even now of the *matter* of the speech, not the *style* of speaking itself. 

And after mentioning skill in civil law and history, he adds: "This wisdom must be applied most especially by the eloquent man, so that he may be a moderator of times and persons. For I do not think one should speak always, or before everyone, or against everyone, or for everyone, or to everyone in the same manner. He, therefore, will be eloquent who can adapt his speech to whatever is appropriate." When he has established this, then he will say whatever must be said; however, the same *Cicero* shows that there is a difference between being "fluent" <note>original: "disertum"</note> and "eloquent" <note>original: "eloquentem"</note> in the first book of *The Orator*: "I wrote that I have known several who were fluent, but no one yet who was eloquent. For I defined as 'fluent' one who could speak with sufficient sharpness and clarity before average men according to a certain common opinion of mankind; but as 'eloquent' one who could amplify and adorn what he wished more admirably and magnificently, and who contained in his mind and memory all the sources of all things which pertain to speaking."

...leads the way, one must meanwhile strive and toil; each person must exert their own strength and their own reasoning. The proverb says: "An eloquent companion on the road is as good as a vehicle." However, as to why reason is called "asserted" and other matters of this argument, I will pass over them because they do not contribute as much to the present purpose.

For it was necessary to provide these many words from most famous men, which will be read with profit by students. From these I shall now strive to collect summarily those things which pertain most to our project. First, we perceive by the judgment of the most eloquent men that eloquence and the deep knowledge of things divine and human—whether one ought to call it wisdom or **Philosophy**—are so closely joined that they should not and cannot be separated. Both faculties belong only to the "good man," and conversely, a good man is not estranged from either virtue. Moreover, eloquence is wisdom speaking in an ornate and abundant manner; it is the vigor and supreme power—the <term>zenith</term> <note>original Greek: ἀκμὴ (akme), meaning the highest point or bloom of something</note>—of speech. The definitions of those arts suited to cultivating and refining speech show that all of them look toward that same goal of perfect and absolute discourse, having destined for themselves a certain correctness in oratory. For what is **Rhetoric** but the "art of speaking well," if we listen to **Fabius** <note>This refers to the Roman educator Quintilian (Marcus Fabius Quintilianus).</note> defining it thus in his second book? And what is **Dialectic** but the "science of disputing well," if we do not reject the opinion of **Augustine** (which would be a wicked thing to do)? What is **Grammar**? Surely it is nothing else, if **Asper** <note>Aemilius Asper, a Roman grammarian.</note> is heard, than "the art of writing, pronouncing, and interpreting the poets correctly," formed through history for the use and logic of words. Again, **Quintilian** in his second book, showing Grammar to be bipartite, defines one part as "the logic of speaking" and the other as "the explanation of authors"—or "the science of speaking correctly and the narration of the poets," as in his first book. **Cicero's** definition of Dialectic in the *Topics* is not dissimilar: "a diligent system of discourse." And in the *Orator*, as we just rendered it, Dialectic is the "system of disputing and speaking," while Oratory is the "system of speaking and adorning." They do not differ even according to **Zeno**, **Aristotle**, and **Cicero**, except that the system of speaking [Rhetoric] is broader, while the system of debating [Dialectic] is more compressed. Therefore, the sciences destined for explaining reason and speech—**Grammar**, **Dialectic**, and **Rhetoric**—agree in their definition. Thus, in this respect, nothing prevents there being one common logic for all languages and letters. These arts even agree in their subject matter, whether you look at the words or the things themselves. For whatever things can come into the mind—both those that have no name and those marked by a certain name—pertain to the Dialectician. The most famous orators subject this same material both to the art of Rhetoric and to the craftsman himself. In every speech, however, on whatever subject it is established, **Grammatical** observation prevents one from falling into a solecism, a barbarism, or an improper...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the nature of eloquence and speech, moving from the definitions of "eloquence" to the distinction between the proper use and the harmful abuse of language, using medical health as a primary analogy.</meta>

->### Languages of this Universe<-

...or if there is anything faulty due to foreign influence, as far as can be avoided. Otherwise, that which is correct—the goal of the arts destined for speech—is the very same thing that sensible and good men look for in every language: that all things be spoken as correctly as possible, and that nothing be perverse. However, what **James the Apostle** says about the tongue being a "great and untamed evil" <note>Referring to James 3:8</note>—speaking as he does about speech, which is perfected by the tongue as an organ—is not a result of the *use* of the tongue and speech, but rather from its *abuse*. For the end or purpose proposed by God is entirely good. Furthermore, what the same Apostle shows—that with one tongue we bless God and curse our neighbor—and what **Cicero** attributes to the power of teaching, exhorting, consoling, terrifying, and many other things of that kind, these are indeed the effects of men using speech either rightly or wrongly. They are the effects of the oration, but as an instrument, not as the acting cause. For he who speaks and writes must be considered the craftsman. 

Furthermore, as the goals of speech, of the arts of speaking, and of the craftsman—whether he wishes to be considered a grammarian, a dialectician, an orator, or even one unskilled in the arts—ought to be compared and distinguished, this is easily understood from the science of medicine. For the end and perfection of the body is health, so that the whole body and its individual parts may perform their functions just as the mind and nature dictate. Yet many who are physically well abuse that good gift for gluttony and other shameful acts; this is an abuse of good health, not its proper use. 

Furthermore, the art of medicine—which is a quality of the soul, namely a habit and aptitude for doing something rightly and well—applies all its power and actions to the body so that it may be healthy and rightly perform its natural functions, and so that it may protect good health, preserve it from diseases, and recall lost health once the diseases that perhaps invaded have been driven out. This it does by means of diet <note>original: διαιτικὴ (diaitikē)</note>, or by drugs <note>original: φαρμακευτικὴ (pharmakeutikē)</note>, or by the hand and instruments <note>original: χειρουργία (cheirourgia) - surgery</note>. It even adapts itself to the curing of beasts of burden <note>original: ἱππιατρική (hippiatrikē) - equine medicine</note>, called *Veterinary* by the **Latins**. 

But there are diseases both in humans and in other animals so vehement, stubborn, and deplorable that they reject all medicine. The Physician himself, insofar as he is acting within his capacity, art, and profession to look after good health, looks to the goal of the body and the art; such a physician God Himself, the Lord of Nature, made and instituted, just as He produced medicinal things from the earth, as **Ecclesiasticus** <note>Also known as the Wisdom of Sirach</note> says. Meanwhile, he receives a just salary, by which he may longer preserve himself for human uses, and he is most worthy of honor and ample rewards. However, when he kills men who could have been kept among the living, he does this not as a physician, but as a robber, an assassin, and a poisoner. And when he hunts for nothing but money and keeps his art for sale, he does this as a trader of marketable goods. By indulging the whims of the sick too much, he acts the part of a flatterer, not a physician. 

Let us now look at that same similarity in speech, which is compared to the body; just as by a very common type of metaphor <note>term: tropus (trope)</note>, things belonging to the body are transferred to the soul as if they were closely related. Whence in speech a certain primary virtue and "health" is observed, which was especially attributed to the **Attic orators** <note>The Attic orators were ancient Greek speakers noted for a pure, unornamented, and "healthy" style of prose.</note>. For speech is not a body, nor a quantity, nor an action, nor a thing referred and connected to another (though some might suspect all these things), but speech is a **quality**. This quality is derived from the mind through the breath <note>original: spiritum</note> expressed from the lungs by the muscles and strength of the sides, passing through the rough artery <note>term: arteria aspera - the trachea or windpipe</note> into the mouth, where it is divided into joints, as it were, by the tongue, teeth, and lips; or it is poured into the mind of another person through the marks of letters traced by the hand and a writing instrument, both through the ears and through the eyes.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the moral purpose of speech, transitioning from the philosophical and theological foundations of language to a list of classical and humanist authorities on grammar, ending with the introduction of Cicero.</meta>

# History of the Origin of [Languages]

Its function is to announce and reveal the reason and the will, and to open access to the movements of speech and reason simultaneously. Whence it is acutely defined by **John of Damascus** <note>original: "Ioanne Damasceno"</note> as the *messenger of thought* <note>original Greek: ἄγγελος νοήματος (angelos noematos)</note>. Although certain signs of the mind’s meaning are expressed through nods, the gesticulation of the hands, and the movement of the head and other parts of the body, the proper function of this [expression] is speech. Just as we know that the duty of reason and intelligence—which is the most excellent faculty or power of the soul—is to perceive things that exist, or those that are usually imagined and produced by invention: let it inspect those perceived things, probe them, explore them inside and out, and discuss them as distinct in their nature, and again join those which are related; let it perceive the true and the good, as well as their opposites. Then let it suggest counsel to the will and persuade it to pursue those things which are truly good, and excite the other powers of the soul and body, like an empress commanding action, so that it may perform its duty in all things that offer themselves anywhere or in any way. 

Indeed, man performs this duty of his when he approaches his own end, so that he becomes as similar as possible to God his creator and parent, by imitating and emulating God, who does all things rightly and best by judgment. And that alone is the perfection of reason when it is applied as closely as possible to the end of man and to the divine nature, which alone is good of itself. Therefore, there shall be no other fulfillment and proper end of speech than that it attains the end of man. Nothing more excellent can happen to man than to be joined, related, and most similar to God, as far as he is capable of His divinity—namely, being wise, truthful, just, holy, good, a diligent doer of works, and finally happy and blessed. 

This is the health, this the power, this the perfection, this the end of speech, as the opinion of wise men and evident reason have indeed persuaded me. To turn speech elsewhere, to achieve other things through oration—to obscure the truth, to seduce, to deceive, to "give words" <note>An idiom meaning to deceive or cheat</note>, to stir up seditions with the tongue as if with a fan, to attack innocence, to curse men or God, and to perform other evils which are countless through speech—that is indeed the abuse of a thing given by God to men for their common utility. It is a pestiferous poison which the tongue instills when not held back by the bridle of speech and religion, as the **Apostle James** teaches. 

Many other infinite, beautiful, and curious researches concerning this matter are deduced by **Fabius Quintilian** in his *12 Oratorical Institutions*, **Aelius Donatus** the Grammarian, **Agretius**, **Priscian**, **Lorenzo Valla**, **Despauterius**, **Pelisson**, **Aldus Manutius** in his book on the Latin language, and by **Theodore Bibliander** in his commentary on the common reason of all languages and letters. Also **Aldus Manutius** in his *Institutions of Latin Grammar*, **A. Mancinelli** in his writings on the Latin language and its properties, and above all others by **Valerius Erythraeus** <note>original: "Valerthræus"</note> in his four books on the figures of the grammarians.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'I' featuring intricate floral patterns and scrolling foliage within a square border.</image-desc>

There are hardly any persons today who make a profession of arms and letters who do not know well Gaius Julius Caesar, the Roman Emperor, so named "Caesar" for having formerly killed an elephant called *Caesar* in the language of the Moors, or perhaps because he had blue eyes, or else by reason of his mother’s womb being cut and opened at the time of his birth, according to Pliny in book 7, chapter 9 of his *Natural History*. <note>Pliny the Elder discusses the origin of the name "Caesar," including the theory of the first "Caesarean" birth.</note> During his life, he was the greatest and most excellent Captain among the Romans, due to the prowess and feats of arms executed by him in a short time, as Plutarch and Suetonius amply report in the *Lives* of this Caesar. Regarding the writings that he left to posterity in the Latin language, we still possess them: namely, the *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, and the *Commentaries on the Civil War* (though some have wished to attribute them, albeit inappropriately, to a Julius Celsus, according to Justus Lipsius, <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606) was a famous Flemish humanist who often debated the authorship of classical texts.</note> in book 1 of his *Epistolicae Quaestiones*, letter 2). These works are so esteemed and prized by the learned men of our day that, within the memory of our fathers, the Great Turk Selim <note>Sultan Selim I of the Ottoman Empire (reigned 1512–1520).</note> had them translated into the Arabic language, in order to read and leaf through them regularly and to conduct himself in his affairs after Caesar's example in his enterprises and conquests, as is found written in a certain voyage of an Armenian monk, composed in the Portuguese language. Also, the books of the Alexandrian, African, and Spanish wars are attributed to this Emperor, though they were composed—according to the opinion of some ancient authors—by Oppius or Hirtius. <note>Aulus Hirtius and Gaius Oppius were close associates of Caesar; Hirtius is generally credited with finishing Caesar's Commentaries.</note> Marcus Tullius Cicero, speaking of the *Commentaries* of this Emperor, writes the following in his *Brutus*:

> "He wrote commentaries of his own deeds which are indeed very much to be approved; they are straightforward, upright, and graceful, stripped of all rhetorical ornament as if of a garment. But while he wanted others to have material ready from which they might take to write history, he perhaps did a favor to the inept, who might wish to curl them with curling-irons; <note>The "curling irons" (calamistris) are a metaphor for excessive or artificial rhetorical flourishes.</note> but he has certainly deterred sane men from writing." <note>original: "Commentarios scripsit rerum suarum valdè quidem probandos sunt, recti, & venusti, omni ornatu orationis, tanquam veste detracta: sed dum voluit, alios habere paratam vnde sumerent, qui vellent scribere historiam, ineptis gratum fortasse fecit, qui illa vellent calamistris inurere, sanos quidem homines à scribendo deterruit."</note>

Hirtius, speaking of these same *Commentaries*, says:
> "They are so approved by the judgment of all that they seem to have snatched away, rather than provided, the opportunity for other writers. Yet our admiration for this matter is greater than that of the rest..." <note>original: "Adeo probantur omnium iudicio, vt prærepta, non prebita facultas scriptoribus videatur. Cuius tamen rei maior nostra, quàm reliquorum est admiratio &c."</note>

### Concerning Gaius Julius Caesar, and his writings composed in the Latin language.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring floral and scrollwork patterns within a square border.</image-desc>
There are hardly any individuals today who make a profession of arms and letters who do not know well of **Gaius Julius Caesar**, the Roman Emperor. He was named *Caesar* either for having formerly killed an elephant called "Caesar" in the language of the Moors, or perhaps because he had blue eyes, or else because his mother's womb was cut and opened at his birth <note>This is the origin of the term "Caesarean section."</note>, according to **Pliny** in Book 7, Chapter 9 of his *Natural History*. He was in his lifetime the greatest and most excellent Captain among the Romans, due to the great prowess and deeds of arms executed by him in a short time, as **Plutarch** and **Suetonius** report extensively in the *Lives* of this Caesar. Regarding the writings he left to posterity in the Latin language, we still possess the *Commentaries on the Gallic War* and the *Commentaries on the Civil War* (although some have wished to attribute them, albeit inappropriately, to a certain **Julius Celsus**, according to **Justus Lipsius** in Book 2 of his *Epistolicae Quaestiones*). These are so esteemed and prized by the learned men of today that, within the memory of our fathers, the **Grand Turk Selim** <note>Sultan Selim I (reigned 1512–1520), who expanded the Ottoman Empire significantly.</note> had them translated into the Arabic language, in order to read and leaf through them regularly to govern and conduct himself in his affairs after Caesar's example in his enterprises and conquests. This is found written in a certain voyage by an Armenian monk, composed in the Portuguese language. The books on the wars in Alexandria, Africa, and Spain, attributed to this Emperor, were composed—according to the opinion of some ancient authors—by **Oppius** or **Hirtius**. **Marcus Tullius Cicero**, speaking of the *Commentaries* of this Emperor, wrote what follows in his *Brutus*:

> He wrote Commentaries of his own deeds which are truly to be highly approved; they are straightforward, and elegant, stripped of all rhetorical ornament as if of clothing. But while he wished others to have material from which they might take to write history, he perhaps did a favor to the inept, who might want to singe those things with curling irons; but he deterred sane men from writing. <note>original: "Commentarios scripsit rerum suarum valdè quidem probandos: nudi sunt, recti, & venusti, omni ornatu orationis, tanquam veste detracta: sed dum voluit, alios habere paratam vnde sumerent, qui vellent scribere historiam, ineptis gratum fortasse fecit, qui illa vellent calamistris inurere, sanos quidem homines à scribendo deterruit." Cicero is praising Caesar's plain, effective style while noting it makes further elaboration by others seem foolish.</note>

**Hirtius**, speaking of these same *Commentaries*, says:

> They are so approved by the judgment of all, that the opportunity for writing has been snatched away from other writers, rather than provided to them. Of which matter, however, our admiration is greater than that of others, etc. <note>original: "Adeo probantur omnium iudicio, vt prærepta, non prebita facultas scriptoribus videatur. ## Concerning Gaius Crispus Sallustius & his writings composed
## in the Latin language.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap letter 'C' decorated with intricate vine and leaf patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc>
Those who have gathered Roman histories assert that **Gaius Crispus Sallustius** <note>Commonly known in English as Sallust (86–35 BC).</note>—the "Prince of Latin history" according to Martial—was born to a father named Sallust, like himself, and that he excelled marvelously in the liberal arts. He composed his writings in a Latin style not unlike that of the ancients, yet with wonderful artifice; they are full of sinew, force, and vigor in the manner of Thucydides <note>The Greek historian of the Peloponnesian War, famous for his dense, austere, and powerful prose.</note>, as can be seen in his *Conspiracy of Catiline*, the *Jugurthine War*, the *Invective against Cicero*, and in his Latin speeches taken from his books on the civil wars. This is so despite the fact that Asinius Pollio and Lenaeus Pompeius <note>A freedman of Pompey the Great who attacked Sallust’s character and style.</note> criticized him for being too fond of antiquity and for having pulled many words from the *Origins* of Cato, according to Filippo Beroaldo in his commentaries on Chapter 86 of Suetonius’s *Life of Augustus Caesar*. They also claim he took many words from Trogus and used excessively long discourses like Thucydides. In addition to these writings composed in the Latin language, this figure composed others during his life which are not found today, although some fragments have appeared in the city of Venice from the printing house of Aldus Manutius, and in Lyon from the printing house of Gryphius.

->**Of Publius Virgilius Maro, and of his writings or poems composed**<-
->**in the Latin language.**<-

<image-desc>A large historiated initial 'P' featuring a seated figure, likely a scholar or author, in a classical setting with architectural elements.</image-desc>
**PUBLIUS** Virgilius Maro, also named Virgil—according to the report of Minutianus Apuleius, Calvus, Donatus, and Priscian—was named for the rods <note>original: *verges*; a reference to a folk etymology connecting the name 'Virgilius' to the Latin 'virga', meaning a rod or shoot</note> among which his mother gave birth to him, as Pierio Valeriano <note>An Italian humanist and mythographer (1477–1558).</note> notes in his annotations on this poet. In his youth, he composed several Latin poems titled *The Gnat*, *Curses*, *Priapeia*, *Epigrams*, and *Catalepton* <note>original: *Culex, Diras, Priapeés, Epigrammes, Cataleptons*</note>, which demonstrate the great natural inclination of this personage toward Latin poetry. In addition to these poems, he wrote the one on *Etna* according to some, and having begun to write of the deeds and feats of the Romans, he was hindered by the grandeur of the subject and the harshness and roughness of Roman names. He then devoted himself to composing the *Bucolics* <note>The *Eclogues*, poems about the lives of shepherds.</note> to praise and magnify Asinius Pollio, Alfenus Varus, and Cornelius Gallus; a work completed by him in the space of three full years. After that, he moved to the city of Naples to perfect the *Georgics* <note>A didactic poem about agriculture and rural life.</note> over seven years in honor of Maecenas. Afterward, he wrote the *Aeneid*, a work greatly diversified and multiplied like a model or pattern from the verses or poems of Homer’s *Iliad* and *Odyssey* gathered into one, as one can clearly see through the commentaries of Servius and Filippo Valeriano on Virgil. This moved Quintilian to believe in his Book 10, Chapter 1, that among all the heroic poets, both Greek and Latin, he came closest to the style of Homer, in whom, however, the same Quintilian recognizes there to be more "nature." This *Aeneid* was composed by this poet partly in Sicily and partly in Campania during the time and space of twelve years. And it is said that Marcus Tullius Cicero, having one day heard some of his verses recited and recognizing that they had been composed, was struck with a hollow admiration...

This being denied to him, he did not fail to command in his will that they be burned, because he judged them to be imperfect; but Tucca and Varius <note>Virgil's friends and literary executors who, by order of Augustus, disregarded the poet's wish to destroy the manuscript.</note> would not permit it. Seeing this, he finally bequeathed the works to them on the charge and condition that nothing would be added or inserted by them, nor by others. The Greeks, after the death of this poet, held his writings in such high esteem that they translated them into their Greek language, as I have read in some old and ancient memoirs that I have with me in that language. The Emperor Theodosius asked Pope Damasus to entrust the organization of the Ecclesiastical office to some learned man, and so he commended it to Jerome, who distinguished the Psalter <note>The Book of Psalms.</note> by days of the week <note>original: "per ferias"; refers to the liturgical arrangement of the week.</note>. According to Beleth <note>Jean Beleth, a 12th-century French theologian.</note> in his *Lombard History*, it was previously recited in straight order without consideration for the days or the subject matter. And perhaps for this reason, Sigebert <note>Sigebert of Gembloux (c. 1030–1112), a medieval chronicler.</note> in his *Chronicles* and Radulphus of Tongeren <note>A 14th-century dean and liturgical writer.</note> assign the institution of the canonical hours <note>The scheduled times for daily prayer in the Church.</note> to him, both to St. Jerome and to St. Ambrose, which is confirmed by the distribution of the Psalms throughout the entire week, both in the Roman and Milanese Churches. But Jerome himself argues against this, showing in his letters to Laeta and Demetrias that the use of these same hours was not new at that time. Therefore, the Apostolic Constitution is mentioned in Clement <note>Clement of Rome, traditionally associated with the *Apostolic Constitutions*.</note>, book 8, chapter 40; and Cyprian <note>Bishop of Carthage (c. 210–258).</note> long before confirmed their institution toward the end of his book *On the Lord's Prayer*; as did Athanasius in his book *On Virginity*, and Basil in his *Longer Rules*, question 37, and in his *Ascetics*, page 381 of the Greek copy.

Ambrose transferred the rite of antiphons <note>Alternate singing by two choirs.</note>, or responsories and hymns, from the Greek Church into the Latin, as noted by Sigebert in his *Chronicle*, Nauclerus, and Isidore in his book *On Divine Offices*. Their first author among the Greeks is believed to have been Ignatius, according to Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century church historian.</note>, book 6, chapter 8, and Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus, a 14th-century historian.</note>, book 3, chapter 8. Jerome collected and organized the Epistles and Gospels as the Church has them today, by the command of Damasus, according to Radulphus in *On Canonical Observations*, last chapter; Beleth in *Rationale of Divine Offices*, chapter 57; and Berno in his book *On the Mass*. Previously, following the institution of Alexander, the reading of the Epistle and Gospel was quite uncertain. This is cited by Honorius, book 1, chapter 88, as quoted by Cassander in his *Liturgies*, page 44.

There exists a book called the <term>Comes</term> <note>Literally "Companion"; an early type of lectionary containing the scriptural readings for the liturgy.</note>, published with great diligence by Pamelius <note>Jacobus Pamelius (1536–1587), a Flemish liturgist.</note>. From this, it is understood to be most true that whereas the older Fathers previously mentioned readings only in a general sense, after Damasus, there were specific Apostolic and Gospel readings. This is seen in the writings of Ambrose, Augustine, Pope Leo, Salvian, Caesarius, and Chrysologus, of whom the latter four are known to have used St. Jerome’s translation.

Jerome instituted several other things in the Church, as St. Gregory himself notes in his first Letter to John of Syracuse, which is cited by Amalarius <note>Amalarius of Metz (c. 775–850), a major figure in the history of liturgy.</note> in his book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book 4, chapter 33.

*Peter* came to Rome in the second year of the Emperor *Claudius* to defeat *Simon Magus* <note>A sorcerer mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles who attempted to buy spiritual power; he was regarded as the first heretic.</note>, as stated by *Jerome in his Catalog.* However, *Calvin in his commentary on Acts, chapter 8*, denies that *Magus* was ever in Rome, contrary to all antiquity, particularly *Augustine in his book on heresies, Tertullian in his Apology, and Eusebius*, who also mention a statue erected to him in Rome. *Peter*, having made many disciples in Rome, sent them as Bishops to preach in various provinces, specifically into Gaul. *Paul*, in the year 58 AD, first preached in Rome.

*James* the brother of the Lord, and *Mark the Evangelist* were in *Aquileia* (which was once called a second *Rome*), where, at the request of the Romans, Mark composed his Gospel in Greek, or even in Latin, as *Richard FitzRalph of Armagh* <note>A 14th-century Irish theologian.</note> *in book 9 of his Questions*, *Jacobus de Voragine in his Sermon on St. Mark*, and all the Syrians maintain; not to mention those who believe the Latin archetype is preserved *in the Treasury of St. Mark in Venice*. Afterward, as *Bishop of Alexandria*, he was crowned with martyrdom in the year of Christ 63.

See what I have previously written in the chapter on the Syriac language regarding *Saint Mark the Evangelist*, who first composed his Gospel in the Latin tongue, which is still held to be currently in the Treasury of the Church of *Saint Mark* in the city of *Venice*, according to what the aforementioned *Gilbert Génébrard* says above.

## How and why the Hebrew, Syriac, Chaldean, Greek, and Latin languages have been used at all times in public prayers and divine offices.

It is a most certain and undeniable truth that it was not without great reason and mystery that throughout the entire world, across a very long succession of centuries, it has always been observed—by the sole will of God—that mortals have used the aforementioned languages in their public prayers and divine offices. Some reduce these to three in the following manner: first, Hebrew, under which they include the Syriac and Chaldean languages—both of which, to tell the truth, are almost one and the same language, although they differ entirely in their alphabetic characters, as I have clearly demonstrated previously. <note>Syriac and Chaldean (Aramaic) use different scripts but share very similar grammar and vocabulary.</note> The second is Greek; and the third is the Latin language. This was done because, in truth, no other languages have ever been found, nor can be found in the future, that are more fitting and meaningful for expressing and signifying the divine offices and mysteries more clearly and vividly, and with fewer ambiguities. This is due to the elegance and emphasis of their vocabulary and speech, and the rules of grammar by which the whole is orderly held in check as if by a bridle. This prevents one from wandering into many doubts and equivocations, to which other languages are subject—easily straying because of similarities in cases, numbers, and tenses, which can bring about much doubt and uncertainty—and for many other infinite reasons amply deduced by us above in the chapters on the Hebrew, Chaldean, Syriac, and Greek languages. 

In short, at all times in the communion of the churches of God, no languages have been used in public prayers and divine offices other than the three aforementioned: namely, Hebrew, sanctified from the beginning of the world, and the others from the time of the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, by the Title that was placed upon the Cross in the Chaldean or Syriac language in these words:

> <note>original Syriac/Aramaic: "Iesua Notheraá Malca dihudae"</note> Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.
> **Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.**

Where in the Hebrew language there was:

> <note>original Hebrew: "Iesua Hamotseri Meleck, haiehudim"</note> Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.

And in the Greek and Latin languages:

> <note>original Greek: "Ιησοῦς ναζωραῖος ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ιυδαίων"</note> Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.
> <note>original Latin: "Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum"</note> **Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.**

And this was not without a mystery that relates to what had been promised prophetically by the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> in Psalms 56, 57, and 58:

> Do not corrupt or alter the inscription of the Title:

Which prefigured that of the cross, as Pope Nicholas I <note>Pope from 858–867 AD, known for asserting papal authority and dealing with the Eastern Church.</note> wrote to the Emperor Michael of Constantinople. For although the Evangelists state that this Title was written in the Hebrew language, we must nevertheless understand that it was in the Chaldean language. <note>In the New Testament, "Hebrew" often refers to Aramaic, the common spoken language of Judea at the time.</note>

St. Augustine, in his discourse *On the Wonders of Scripture*, making mention of the Christian Church—which from its beginning spoke all languages through the mission of the Holy Spirit—used these words concerning the three aforementioned languages: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. <note>original: "Harum omnium... And Theodore Bibliander <note>Theodore Bibliander (1509–1564) was a Swiss linguist and scholar who succeeded Zwingli; he was a pioneer in the comparative study of Semitic languages.</note>, in his *Commentary on the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*, interpreting these words, says:

> "Indeed, in the consideration of languages, it seems to me worthy of admiration that while all languages possess at least some certain territory and hold dominion—and even those now abolished, such as the Egyptian and Persian, once held dominion while they flourished—yet the 'princely' languages (Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, in which the cause of Jesus Christ dying on the cross was written) do not have a certain fixed home among any one nation, nor do they hold any earthly empire as they once did. For the Greek tongue used in Greece today, and the Latin in the provinces of Italy, in Latium, and in the City [Rome], has strayed from its original purity. The Jews, moreover, do not possess Hebrew as a native tongue now, but use it as Romans use Latin, or as others use Greek; the Jews are now inhabitants among all nations. In this wonder, nothing more likely comes to my mind than that Christ, the King of Kings—to whom the Heavenly Father gave all nations as a possession to the ends of the earth—has consecrated those languages to His city, His kingdom, and His empire. Through these, He now preaches to the world in the glory of the Father through faithful ministers, so that Christian philosophy may be propagated everywhere. The supreme axiom of this philosophy is that Jesus of Nazareth, crucified under Pontius Pilate, is the Messiah and King of both the Jews and all nations, true God and true man, the one Savior and mediator between God and men. So that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of the Father. For this shall be to remove the confusion of languages introduced during the construction of Babylon, and from so many languages, to make one, as it were, under His guidance. This shall be to happily tear down the obstacles and impediments to human society, and having removed hostility from minds, to institute, reconcile, unite, and confirm a holy society and commerce. This shall be to lead the men of all lands back to one fold and one eternal Shepherd, who gave His life for His sheep. So that one God, who created all things through the Son with the Holy Spirit who proceeds from both, may be worshiped with one language and mouth, and with 'one shoulder' [in total unity], as the holy Prophets once prophesied."

# Languages of this Universe. 799

In these [languages], the monuments of both divine and human sciences have been preserved and handed down from our ancestors to posterity as if passed from hand to hand. This is also because they were honored by the memorable title placed upon the glorious Cross of the King of Kings and Lord of lords, Jesus Christ our Redeemer, and have thus attained an eminent dignity above all other tongues. Furthermore, each of these is like a tree divided into three branches, spreading into three other dialects of speech. 

The **Hebrew** language spreads into the Babylonian (or Chaldean), the Syrian (or Jerusalemite), and the Arabic, which the Jews call the language of Ishmael. 

The **Greek** (or Ionic) spreads into the Attic, Doric, and Aeolic. 

The **Roman** (which is also **Latin**) spreads into Italian, Spanish, and French. 

Thus, in these three languages—as in most other things of this world, whether perceived by the intellect or falling under the sight of the eyes—that divine and adorable Trinity of infinite power, wisdom, and goodness shines forth. When all are gathered together, they represent to us once again a mystic group of twelve <note>The "mystic dodecad" likely refers to the total number of dialects mentioned: 3 primary languages + 9 sub-dialects = 12.</note>. Therefore, in those three most powerful languages, the thrice-greatest and thrice-blessed one wished to reveal his divine will to us, and to hand down his holy statutes and precepts. These were to serve as a rule for living well and blessedly in the great and public city of this world, so that we might finally reach eternal and immortal life and enjoy the sight of the one divine essence and the Trinity of persons. In this "three-times-triple" genre of idioms, the holy and sacred books have come down to us; these are secret monuments far more precious than any treasure, preserved by divine providence in great integrity and purity through so many ages and centuries.

R. Volaterrano <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), a humanist scholar from Volterra.</note> writes in Book 22 of his *Anthropology* that in the time of Pope Innocent VIII, in the year 1492, the title from the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ was found in the Basilica of the Holy Cross <note>Santa Croce in Gerusalemme in Rome.</note> in the middle of the temple, hidden in a wall, written in the three aforementioned languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—with only these words remaining:

->Jesus the Nazarene, Ki...<- <note>original: "Iesus Nazarenus Re." The "Re" is the start of "Rex" (King).</note>

The rest of the words were either gnawed away or erased.

A great poet of this time, speaking of the different kinds of languages in the world, says these words regarding the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages:

> *Every language changes, whether it be that trade,*
> *By bringing to us from the Persian Amphitrite* <note>Amphitrite is a Greek sea goddess; here the poet refers to the Persian Gulf or distant maritime trade.</note>
> *Precious treasures, and those from land to the waves,*
> *Happily and boldly trades words for words;*
> *Or whether a man, speaking in a graceful way,*
> *Curling his golden words and refining his style,*
> *Desirous of glory, strikes new coins* <note>A metaphor for inventing or reviving words.</note>
> *For things and facts, or at least gives*
> *Currency to disparaged names, and restores to nature*
> *Those that are outdated, moldy, and spoiled by woodworms.*
> *It is just as it is with the leaves of a forest:*
> *One falls, another is born. The words which of old*
> *Shone here and there in elegant speech,*
> *Like Lily flowers in the green countryside,*
> *Are no longer in vogue; instead, banished from the court,*
> *They shamefully go to stay under the roofs of a lowly hamlet.*
> *And those which the grumpy censure of old times...*

A fine wit, guided by fortune and judgment,
Can give a passport to words that freshly
Come from his workshop, or adopt foreign ones,
