# Languages of this Universe
<page-num>801</page-num>
<header>Languages of this Universe.</header>
<sig>Iiiii</sig>

...pertaining to customs, have been explained gravely and copiously, and spoken magnificently. Thus, gravity and the majesty of the Empire can be ascribed most of all to the Romans; wit and acumen to the Greeks; and to the Hebrews, a more secret doctrine and a kind of divinity (as **Pico** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Italian Renaissance philosopher known for his "Oration on the Dignity of Man."</note> used to say). The volumes of **Moses** himself and those prophecies of the **Prophets** greatly prove this: our Pico, therefore, argued according to this opinion concerning the disciplines and talents of the ancients. But indeed, **Marcus Cicero** also elegantly brought forth these points concerning the Greeks themselves in his oration *For L. Flaccus*:

> I will say this regarding the whole race of Greeks: I grant them literature, I give them the discipline of many arts, I do not take away the charm of their speech, the sharpness of their wits, or their richness of speaking; finally, if they claim any other qualities for themselves, I do not object. But that nation never cultivated the sanctity and good faith of testimonies. <note>original Latin: "testimoniorum religionem & fidem nunquam ista natio coluit." Cicero is suggesting that while Greeks are brilliant and eloquent, they are untrustworthy witnesses in court.</note>

Furthermore, **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Syrian theurgy and mysteries.</note>, noble among the Platonists, accuses the Greeks themselves of levity and inconstancy; while he asserts that the **Egyptians** or **Hebrews** (whom he calls barbarians) are constant and excellent in the worship and observation of the gods. I shall write down his words, as he expressed all of this gravely and copiously in his *Mysteries*:

> It is right, he says, in the worship of the Gods to always guard the ancient rites as sacred and best, and to preserve them untouched and inviolate, so that nothing at all is added or even taken away. For from this, he says, it has happened that the divine powers and prayers themselves appear diminished and weakened, because many things have been changed out of the very desire for misrepresentation and for innovating Religion, and they are changed more every day. For the Greeks themselves, by their own nature fond of new things, are easily turned in any direction at every moment; as those who are fickle, and like a ship in which no ballast <note>original: "sabuli" (sand/ballast).</note> has settled, they preserve nothing at all of what they received from their ancestors. Instead, changing everything repeatedly, they cast out the old; and from innate levity, they exchange one thing for another, constant in nothing. But the Barbarians <note>In the classical sense, this refers to non-Greeks, here specifically the Egyptians and Hebrews.</note>, he says, as they are firm and upright in their customs, so they also persevere with the greatest constancy in the same words and opinions; whereby it happens that they have rightly remained dear to the gods above others, and offer to them the most acceptable prayers, which can in no way be changed by others.

**Rudolf IV**, Emperor, <note>Rudolf IV "the Founder" (1339–1365). Although he was Duke of Austria and not technically Emperor, the author attributes this decree to him, likely confusing him with Charles IV who issued the Golden Bull.</note> ordered that the electors of the Roman Empire should know and learn five languages besides their own proper mother tongue: namely **Greek**, **Latin**, **French**, **Italian**, and **Spanish**: which the Germans have always observed very well. In such a way that the Emperors, at least for the most part, have known how to speak various languages. The Emperor **Otto** could respond to all the Ambassadors who were sent to him, each in his own language; **Charles the Fifth**, Emperor and King of Spain, was accustomed to say that it was a great shame for a person of honor to know how to speak only one language.

# On the greatness of the Roman Empire and how and at what time it began to decline.

**Pierre Messie** <note>Pedro Mexía (1497–1551), a Spanish humanist whose work *Silva de varia lección* was a popular collection of historical anecdotes and scientific facts.</note>, in book 1, chapter 27 of his *Diverse Lessons*, seems to believe there is no consideration that gives more certain and complete knowledge of the instability of human affairs than that of the greatness in which the Empire of Rome formerly stood, comparing it to what the Roman Emperors possess now, etc.

The same author in the following chapter 28 says: **Theodore** <note>Theodosius the Great (r. 379–395 AD), the last emperor to rule over both the Eastern and Western halves of the Roman Empire.</note> upon dying left two sons, one named **Honorius**, and the other **Arcadius**, with a daughter called **Placidia** <note>Galla Placidia, a major figure in Roman politics who was later regent for her son Valentinian III.</note>, etc.

**G. Genebrard** <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine exegete and historian.</note> in the thirteenth book, folio 466, of his *Chronography*:
In the Year of Grace: The Goths, under the leadership of Totila, capture Rome, and subjugate the Lucanians, Campanians, Calabrians, and Bruttians, etc. <note>original Latin: "Salutis. Gothi duce Totila Romam capiunt, Lucanos, Campanos, Calabros & Brutios subigunt &c." Totila was the King of the Ostrogoths who recaptured Rome in 546 AD.</note>

See **F. de Belleforest** <note>François de Belleforest (1530–1583), a prolific French Renaissance writer and translator.</note> in the third book, chapter 25 of his *Universal History*.

## On the decadence of the Latin language.

Those who have read the Latin histories and the fragments of the **Twelve Tables** <note>The *Leges Duodecim Tabularum*, the earliest code of Roman law (c. 450 BC).</note> know well enough—as I have treated amply in the preceding chapters—that if the first and most ancient Roman writings lasted until our time, we would see that **Evander** and **Turnus** <note>Legendary figures from the origins of Rome, famously featured in Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note>, and others from around that time and the first centuries, spoke differently than did the last Roman Kings and the first Latin Consuls of that era afterward. The verses sung by the **Salian Priests** <note>The *Salii*, or "Leaping Priests" of Mars, who sang the *Carmen Saliare*, an ancient hymn that became largely unintelligible even to Romans of the late Republic.</note> were understood by those Romans only with great difficulty. But because they had been so ordained by the first founders, they were not changed at all out of reverence for Religion. **Polybius** <note>A Greek historian of the Hellenistic period (c. 200–118 BC) who chronicled the rise of the Roman Republic.</note> writes on this subject that the Latin language was so changed between the first **Punic War** and the second, that with great pain and difficulty one understood the treaties made previously between the Romans and the Carthaginians. And this language remained for nearly five hundred years rude and poorly polished, having had no writer in it who was worthy of memory. From then on, the Romans and Latins devoted themselves to letters and sciences, moving from being crude to somewhat learned, though remaining harsh and rough in their speech: not only for having been the inventors and first masters of humanity.

This is very well verified by the discourses of **Verrius Flaccus**, of **Marcus Varro**'s *On the Latin Language*, by **Nonius Marcellus**, and **Festus Pompeius** on the same subject, and in **F. Quintilian**, the Latin orator, and the ten books of the Latin Poets.

This language was rendered very elegant and perfect by **Cicero**, **Caesar**, **Sallust**, and **Virgil**, mentioned above, and by others

...men who flourished then in great number, in whom truly the purity of that Latin language is recognized. For afterwards, the Roman Republic being changed into a Monarchy and morals becoming corrupt, that language similarly changed and became corrupted, losing its previous naturalness and eloquence under the Emperors. Then, the Empire being transferred <note>The "translation" of the empire (translatio imperii) refers to the relocation of the capital from Rome to Constantinople in 330 AD.</note> from Rome to Constantinople, several foreign nations arriving in Italy altered that language so much that people stopped speaking it; it remained in books only, which were not read nor understood for more than eight hundred years. Some were lost, others eaten by worms and spoiled by old age, until certain Italians and Greeks, through study, brought these two ancient languages back to life—namely Latin and Greek, which were almost dead or lost—by describing, publishing, and correcting the books remaining in libraries, saved from the fury and rage of the Barbarians. This succeeded so happily for them that these said languages have recovered great light, along with the arts and sciences written in them, which we see restored alongside them, with several inventions added to those of antiquity.

Thus, as the Roman Empire declined in the West and the Goths, Ostrogoths, Lombards, and other Northern peoples occupied Italy; the Visigoths and Saracens <note>original: "Satrasins", likely a typographical error for "Sarrasins".</note> occupied Provence, Languedoc, Aquitaine, and Spain; the Burgundians and Franks occupied Belgic and Celtic Gaul; and the Vandals occupied Baetica <note>A Roman province in southern Spain, roughly modern Andalusia.</note> and Africa, the Latin language was corrupted through their social interaction. From this corruption were born and issued Italian, French, and Spanish. 

Italian remained unpolished for a long time because there was no one who took care of it or sought to give it refinement, until **Dante**, **Petrarch**, **Boccaccio**, and **Ariosto**, who greatly embellished it through their ingeniously expressed concepts, elegantly set down in verse and prose. In this, they were followed by others no less learned and eloquent, who similarly enriched this language with many beautiful works and traditions. 

The same has happened to Spanish and to French, which has been made more copious and elegant over the last fifty years or so than it was before, through the diligence of certain excellent personages who have translated and transferred a great number of Greek and Latin books, and indeed Italian, Spanish, and others, showing that all doctrines and sciences can be suitably treated therein. 

Several other beautiful and excellent discourses concerning this matter are amply detailed by **Louis Le Roy** <note>Louis Le Roy (c. 1510–1577) was a French humanist scholar who wrote on the "vicissitudes" or changing nature of history.</note> in the sixth book of *The Vicissitude of Things*, in the chapter on the *Decay of the power, knowledge, and eloquence of the Romans*. This author, in the tenth book, writes that during the reign of **Tamerlane** <note>Le Roy famously synchronized the start of the European Renaissance with the era of the Central Asian conqueror Tamerlane (Timur), viewing it as a global epoch of change.</note>, the restoration of languages and all disciplines began, and that the first who applied himself to this work was **F. Petrarch**, opening the libraries previously closed and removing the dust and filth from upon the good books of ancient authors. For being a man of great understanding and excellent doctrine, he not only embellished the Italian language—for which he is revered, along with his disciple **J. Boccaccio**, as its principal author and illustrator—but he also laudably revitalized Latin Poetry and Prose. After this Petrarch came **John of Ravenna** <note>Giovanni Malpaghini (c. 1346–1417), a scholar who lived with Petrarch and later became an influential teacher of the early humanists.</note>, a grammarian who, while still quite young, had...

### About the Region of the Italians.

Abraham Ortelius <note>A famous 16th-century Flemish cartographer and geographer.</note>, in his *Synonymia* and *Geographical Treasury*, says: **Italy** <note>original: "Italia ιταλια"</note>, once the mistress of lands, and today shining in the glory of their deeds, the most famous among all the regions of Europe, was formerly called *Vitalia*, if one believes Dionysius of Halicarnassus in his first book. Likewise it was called *Apenina*, *Argessa* <note>original: "αρϒεσσα"</note>, *Ausonia*, *Camesena*, *Hesperia* <note>original: "εσπερια"</note>, *Janicula*, *Oenotria* <note>original: "οινωτρια"</note>, *Saturnia* <note>original: "σατυρνία"</note>, *Taurina*, and *Vitullia* or *Vitalia*, according to Marcus Cato, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Gellius, Isaac, and others. It was also called *Palensana* according to Pseudo-Berossus; *Chonia* or *Chone* according to Hesychius and Stephanus, as noted by Castaldus. Strabo also says it was called *Tyrsenia* after Tyrsenus, the son of Telephus; and Stephanus writes, following Antiochus, that it was called *Aperlia*. **Greater Greece** <note>Magna Graecia</note> is in Italy (says Festus) because in it were many great cities that came from Greece. But it should be known that all these names belong specifically to Italy in its most ancient sense, which was bounded by the Rubicon River. The other part, which extends to the Alps, was called by the name **Cisalpine Gaul** (Appian calls it *Gallic Italy*); afterwards, it was entirely and is today named Italy. And this part is in the Cisapennine...

Cato, in his *Origins* <note>Cato the Elder's lost historical work, *Origines*.</note>, divides the Apennines. Arias Montanus writes in his *Biblical Appendix* that Italy is called *Kityn* <note>original: "Kityn"; a Hebrew term often associated with Cyprus or the Western lands</note> by the Hebrews, while the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> in Isaiah 61 seem to call them *Mosoch*. Dionysius of Halicarnassus suggests in his first book that the Italians were also once called *Morgetes* <note>original: μόρσητες</note>. The Slavic people call the Italians *Vulofka* <note>Likely "Vlaska," a term used by Slavs to denote Latin or Romance speakers.</note>. For the names of Italy, see chapter 22 of the *Observations* by Hadrianus Junius and the *Chorography* of Caspar Varrerius. Read Festus to learn why it is called "Italy." Dionysius of Halicarnassus calls that part which extends from the Iapygian promontory <note>The "heel" of Italy.</note> to the Strait of Sicily "Eastern Italy." Diodorus Siculus, in his eleventh book, mentions "Ligustican Italy," which I believe refers to Cisalpine Gaul. For "Gallic Italy," see the section on Cisalpine Gaul. See also "Chersonesus."

Cisalpine Gaul is a region of Italy according to Pliny, who calls a part of it "Subalpine Italy" in Book 16, Chapter 11. It is called "Gallic Italy" <note>original: γαλατική</note> by Appian in his books on the Hannibalic wars. It is also called "Hither Gaul" <note>Gaul on the Italian side of the Alps.</note> by the same author, as well as by Caesar, Hirtius, and Sallust. Ausonius, addressing the Emperor Gratian, calls it "Old Gaul." The ancients divide this into "Cispadane Gaul" <note>Gaul on this side of the Po river.</note> and "Transpadane Gaul" <note>Gaul on the far side of the Po.</note>, as do Pliny and Strabo. Gellius calls it "Transpadane Italy" in Book 5, Chapter 18. Diodorus calls it "Ligustican Italy" in his eleventh book. Leandro Alberti calls it Lombardy "from that side" and "from this side" of the Po, using the same distinction. For the Italians call the *Padus* river the "Po," and they interpret the Latin terms *cis* and *trans* as "here" and "there." Cispadane Gaul was once called Bianora, then Felsina, and finally Aurelia and Emilia, as Cato writes in his *Origins*—though let the credit for that remain with the author. Italy was called *Oenotria* after the Sabine King Oenotrus. Dionysius relates that Oenotrus and Peucetius <note>OCR: "Pancetium"</note>, brothers of Lycaon and sons of the King of Arcadia, migrated to Italy. Peucetius occupied that part of Apulia called Iapygia, from whom those people were called Peucetians. Oenotrus, however, invaded the western part of Italy held by the barbarian Sicels <note>An ancient Italic people.</note>—which is now called Latium—obtaining it and calling it Oenotria after his own name. His successors were Italus, Morges, and Siculus, after whom the Oenotrians themselves were sometimes called Italians, Morgetes, and Sicels. Regarding the Oenotrians, Virgil says:

> There is a place the Greeks call Hesperia by name;
> Oenotrian men cultivated it; now the story is that their descendants
> Have called the nation Italy, after the name of their leader.

From the fragments of Marcus Varro; see Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book 1 of his *Roman Antiquities*.

## On the Italian Language.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' with floral and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>
Those who wish to read exactly what we have written in the two preceding chapters concerning the greatness of the Roman Empire, its decline, and the various captures of the city of Rome—the capital of that Empire—by the Northern nations and others mentioned above, will easily believe how that Empire used the pure Latin tongue as its vulgar and familiar language. They will see that through the raids and ravages of those nations within the Empire, the aforementioned Latin language has since been, from century to century and from time to time, moved and changed into the vulgar tongue and common language of today.

Modern Italian: a fact acknowledged by all who have written on this tongue.

But some hold that the Lombards <note>A Germanic people who ruled most of the Italian Peninsula from 568 to 774.</note>, coming into Italy at the persuasion of Narses <note>original: "Narzez"; a Byzantine general who served under Justinian I.</note>, lieutenant to the Emperor, began to abolish the laws, the language, and the proper names of places that were there before. For the Ostrogoths <note>Another Germanic tribe that preceded the Lombards in Italy.</note> never attempted such barbarism; rather, they followed the ancient Law of the Romans and took pleasure in learning the Latin language. And following the word of the aforementioned personages, it was the Lombards who bastardized the common language of the Italians, and not the other northern nations as many have believed. Therefore, following the opinion of the aforementioned, the Lombards, having invaded Italy, removed the Latin names—aiding themselves with their own customs—and established principalities which were like magistrates: namely four Dukes, of Benevento, Spoleto, Turin, and Friuli, along with two Marquisates, those of Ancona and Treviso. This was the reason that since then, one of the countries has been named the March of Ancona, and the other, the Trevisan March. This Principality was greater than that of a Duke, as it was perpetual and hereditary, whereas the office of Duke was held by election. Furthermore, the word "Marquisate" in the language of the ancient Lombards signified a perpetual Lordship. 
<margin>André Thevet, book 17, chapter 17 of his *Universal Cosmography* <note>Published in 1575, Thevet’s work was a massive geographic and ethnographic compendium.</note>.</margin>

Certain modern authors, speaking in their writings of the Italians of today and their Italian language, have written what follows:

It is not without great divine providence that when God, all-good and all-powerful, visited the earth by becoming man, the seat of the Empire was in Italy, the retreat of all the nations of the Universe, where soon after was to be placed the head and universal shepherd of the Christian Fold <note>A reference to the Papacy in Rome.</note>. The Italians differ among themselves, most often in both color and stature: for those who reside in Cisalpine Gaul <note>The region of Northern Italy between the Alps and the Apennines.</note> and all along the Venetian lands are ordinarily white <note>Fair-skinned.</note>, more neat in their dress and language; whereas the Tuscans, Campanians, or Neapolitans, and those of Basilicata and Abruzzo have a leaden complexion, black hair, and small stature, being lean and nimble, simple and modest in dress and speech. In the March of Ancona, and among all the Italians who reside along the coast of the Levant <note>The eastern or Adriatic coast.</note> as far as Magna Graecia <note>The coastal areas of Southern Italy originally colonized by ancient Greeks.</note> (excepting the Calabrians and those of Apulia who live in the corner of Italy), both the customs and the language remain even now a mixture of Greek and Italian.

Several other modern authors speak of it in this fashion: The dress of the Italians differs according to their countries and provinces. The Venetians wear them long and wide, almost to the point of superfluity; and those of the city are even more sumptuous than those of the fields and villages. After the Venetians, the Florentines and Tuscans dress more daintily <note>original: "mignonnemẽt"; with elegance or refinement.</note> than other Italians. The Milanese, those of Romagna-Emilia, and the Genoese wear their clothing more tightly, yet they are very gallant <note>original: "braues"; stylish or bold.</note>. The attire of a courtier in Rome surpasses all others in length and diversity of colors; the native Roman is sober and modest in his clothing, which nevertheless has its own decorum and grace, and likewise in the finery of the Ladies. The Neapolitan is more elegantly than superbly dressed, and takes more pleasure in the fashions of strang—

[foreigners] than of Italy: of which the rest follows simply in order, not that the clothing is not diverse, considering that in this time we have seen an infinity of changes in dress. In the Bolognese region and throughout almost all of Lombardy, the great ladies take much pleasure in dressing in the **Spanish** fashion, and the noblemen love the ornamentation of the **French**. In Rome, the women until recently dressed in the **Tuscan** style; it has not been long since the ladies of Venice wore their throats, breasts, and shoulders uncovered, but now they cover them, and have very wide sleeves, so that their dress somewhat imitates the **Spanish** style. As for the Italian language, it is not what it once was, and yet not entirely dissimilar, but it is corrupted and altered because of the barbarian words that have been introduced in one place more than another according to how long foreigners held the provinces in subjection. Along the coast of Istria, almost all the people speak Venetian, which is a polished, copious, and grave language, and adorned with the sweetness of several other languages, because it is the place where all the peoples of Italy trade; formerly this Venetian language was harsher and very unpleasant to the ears. The speech of the Carnians <note>Inhabitants of Carnia, a mountainous region in north-eastern Italy.</note> neighboring the Carinthians <note>Inhabitants of Carinthia, a region now part of modern-day Austria.</note> is composed of diverse languages, and has a certain something contrary to the air of Italian words: nonetheless more pleasant to the ear. Towards the Trevisan country, in Padua, Verona, Vicenza, Mantua, and Ferrara, everywhere those of the cities are more graceful in speech than the peasants and villagers. The Lombard and Milanese speech has a certain coarse roughness different from the rest of Italy; however, there is no country that surpasses this one in the beauty of its cities, the nobility and courtesy of its citizens, nor in the honesty and sobriety of life. Regarding those of Romagna—Ravenna, Rimini, Pesaro, Faenza, Bologna, and the lands of the Patrimony <note>The "Patrimony of Saint Peter," referring to the territories under the temporal rule of the Pope.</note>—their language is sweet and polished. Tuscan is brief in speech, imitating the ancient fashion of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans, famous for their "laconic" or brief and pithy style of speaking.</note>, and this language suits the foreigner better than the native of the country. In Rome, until recently, the speech was harsh, but the frequentation of outsiders enriched and softened this coarse roughness. In the March of Ancona, the land of Sabine, and in the Principality, the people speak more harshly and coarsely than in the Duchy of Urbino; in Apulia, Basilicata, and Abruzzo, which, like all the rest of Italy, have a hard and constrained language, little mixed with foreign sweetness, except the Neapolitans, who strive to speak their native tongue with **Spanish** gravity. In short, whoever looks upon things maturely and judges them in general will find no people nor city in this world that is not in some way different from those who neighbor them, as noted by Sabellicus <note>Marcantonio Sabellico (1436–1506), a prominent Venetian historian and scholar.</note> in *Enneads*, Book 2, Volume 1. Among the moderns who have written of the beauty, perfection, and elegance accomplished with all the delicacy and affectation of the Italian language, Girolamo Ruscelli <note>A noted 16th-century Italian humanist, editor, and linguist.</note> in the preface to Giovanni Boccaccio, printed by Valgrisi in Venice in the year 1557, has greatly excelled; there he makes no difficulty in comparing this language to Latin, and maintaining through an ample discourse that it should be granted the monarchy over all other languages of this universe. He even made a specific treatise on this matter, which I have seen and read in the past. Whoever wishes to see infinite beautiful and rare things concerning this language should read Dante’s *On Eloquence in the Vernacular* <note>original: "Dante d'ella volgar eloquentia"; referring to Dante Alighieri’s Latin essay *De vulgari eloquentia*.</note>, and Bembo <note>Pietro Bembo (1470–1547), an influential scholar whose work *Prose della volgar lingua* helped standardize the Italian language based on 14th-century literary models.</note> *On the Language*...

->On the invention of rhythms.<-

<image-desc>Decorative floral drop cap 'Q' at the beginning of the paragraph.</image-desc>
**Q**uitesome authors have written that rhymed verses or poems were first invented by certain peoples living at the decline of the Greek Empire, when the language of foreigners began to spoil and corrupt the distinct pronunciation and accents of the Greek language, so much so that the **Venerable Bede**, living around the year of salvation 730, mentioned it in his book on the types of meters <note>Bede’s *De arte metrica*.</note>, in the penultimate chapter, as a form of composition used and practiced in his time; which, before him, **Marius Victorinus** <note>A 4th-century grammarian.</note> had noted in his works. The authors of the *Ecclesiastical History* composed at Magdeburg <note>Known as the *Magdeburg Centuries*, a seminal Protestant history of the church.</note>, citing the *Chronicle of Holstein*, assert that the ancient Germans wrote of their wars and victories in rhyme, and that **Charlemagne** commanded in his time that a collection be made of the rhymes that were then in use among men. Furthermore, we can learn this because a certain person named **Otfrid**, a monk of Weissenburg and disciple of **Rabanus Maurus** (Abbot of Fulda), living around the year of salvation 870, wrote regarding the version of the Gospels that <term>homoioteleuton|the use of similar endings or rhyme</term> <note>originally: "rythme Omioteleute"</note> was already in use in his time among the Teutonic <note>originally: "Thyois," referring to Old High German.</note> peoples. Some have gone so far as to write that it is a certain thing that the French taught other nations of Europe the use of rhyme or <term>consonance|rhyming sounds</term>, as **Claude Fauchet** discusses at great length in Book 1, Chapter 6, of *The French Language and Poetry*, based principally on some couplets extracted from a certain manuscript book from nearly five hundred years ago regarding the life of **Saint Fiacre**. **Lilio Gregorio Giraldi** in his dialogues on the poets of his time, and **Alessandro Vellutello** in his *Commentaries* in the Italian language on the *Triumphs* of **Petrarch**, write that Italian rhymes and the fashion of composing in sonnets and stanzas came from and were founded, according to some, by the Sicilians when a certain **William Iron Arm** <note>originally: "Guillaume Ferabach," the eldest son of Tancred of Hauteville.</note>, brother of **Robert Guiscard** and other Lords of Calabria and...

[Q]ue <note>The letter 'Q' is the drop-cap from the previous page, completing the word "Que" (That).</note> the children of Tancred <note>Tancred of Hauteville, whose Norman sons conquered southern Italy and Sicily in the 11th century.</note>, French Normans, carried these forms from Provence to the land of Sicily in Italy; and that in this time the French were aided by this form and fashion of composing according to the report of Francesco Petrarch in the preface to his epistles. Others say that this way of composing in rhymed sonnets and stanzas originated with the Etrurians <note>The ancient civilization of central Italy, preceded the Romans.</note>, from whom the first and most ancient Tuscan language emanated. Our French writers maintain that this proceeded from the invention of the Provençal poets, who flourished around the year of salvation 1162, as Colocci and Bembo <note>Angelo Colocci and Pietro Bembo, two of the most influential Renaissance scholars of the Italian language.</note> have well noted in their discourses on this matter.

This matter has been very well debated and treated by **Dante** in his works, Petrarch in chapter 4 of his *Triumph of Love*, and Jean de Nostredame <note>Brother of the famous prophet Nostradamus; he wrote a famous, though partly fictionalized, history of the lives of the troubadours.</note>, and Jean Giudici in their discourses on the lives of the most famous and ancient Provençal poets. This moved a certain one of our Frenchmen to write these words in his own discourse on Sicily:

->Because of the greater softness and effeminacy of the Sicilians, poetry through rhymes and cadences is attributed to them, just as they were the first who treated love in the vernacular and in rhyme—if one adds faith to Dante and Petrarch—although there are those who attribute this to our Gauls, and to the Limousins and Provençals. This I believe, if one has regard for the latest fashion of rhyming, and of giving meter <term>nombre: the rhythmic "number" or count of syllables in a verse</term> to verses by the same ending and termination of sounds at their close, of which Dante wrote a book that I have seen written by hand.<-

The most learned and knowledgeable of this century in ancient languages assure us that the mode and fashion of composing verses or poems <term>carmes: from the Latin 'carmina', meaning songs or poems</term> in rhyme proceeds from the invention of the Hebrews and Jews. This is treated very amply by Sixtus of Siena <note>originally: "F. Sixtus Senensis"</note> in book 3 of his *Library*, and Brother Louis the Portuguese in his *Globe of the Canons and Secrets of the Holy Language and Divine Scripture*, book 9, *On the Poetry of the Hebrews* <note>originally: "de poësi Hebræorum"</note>, chapters 7 and 8. In this regard, one should see what we have written above concerning the Royal Prophet David and his writings composed in the Hebrew language. G. Génébrard, in his *Chronography*, remarks that Eastern histories record that in the year of salvation 904, the Emperor Constantine VII <note>The Byzantine Emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus.</note> deplored the death of his wife with rhymes and all sorts of verse genres, according to Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler.</note> in volume 5 of his histories. This leads one to believe that the Greeks, as well as the Latins, used rhymes at that time. Whoever wishes to see several beautiful and rare discourses touching on this question should read Pierre Grégoire, book 19, chapter 11 of his *Syntax of the Admirable Art*, and Claude Fauchet, mentioned above, in his *Collection of the Origin of the French Language and Poetry, Rhyme and Romances*, book 1, chapters 6, 7, and 8. What is more, we read in Joannes Magnus <note>originally: "Iean le grand"</note> and Olaus his brother in their *Northern Histories*, that the Northern peoples since ancient times have been accustomed to singing in rhymes at their balls, assemblies, and banquets, recounting the deeds and gestures of their ancestors and predecessors. Polydore Vergil, in book 1, chapter 9 of his book *On the Invention of Things*, treats the origin of poetic meters or measures.

## Concerning Giovanni Boccaccio, Italian, and his writings composed in the Italian language.

<image-desc>Decorative floral woodcut drop cap 'I' starting the first paragraph.</image-desc> Giovanni Boccaccio <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), the influential Italian writer and humanist.</note>, an Italian by nation, was a native of Certaldo and flourished in his country in the year of our Salvation 1342. Being well-instructed in several fine and high human sciences as well as Mathematics, he composed some poems in the Italian language quite elegantly and skillfully, as mentioned in the account of his life compiled by Master Ludovico Dolce and Francesco Sansovino <note>Two prominent 16th-century Italian scholars and biographers.</note>. These poems he wrote in his youth, but he later burned them out of despair of ever being able to reach the excellence of the poems of Francesco Petrarch <note>Petrarch (1304–1374) was Boccaccio's contemporary and close friend, often considered the greatest poet of the age.</note>. After these, he set himself to compose, with great elegance and skill in Italian prose, his *Decameron* <note>A famous collection of 100 stories told by young people fleeing the plague.</note> during the time when the plague was so violent in Florence in the year of our Salvation 1348. For this work, he took five or six of the best and most pleasant stories from old French *fabliaux* <note>term: fabliaux — short, often humorous or satirical verse tales that were popular in medieval France</note> and very ancient books of French rhythmic poets, as is meticulously noted by Claude Fauchet <note>A 16th-century French historian and antiquarian.</note> in the first book, chapter six, of his work on the French language and poetry, and in the second book, chapters eight, twelve, seventeen, eighty-four, and one hundred and two, regarding French poets. After this, he also composed in the said Italian language the *Filocolo* and *Fiammetta* for the love of Maria, sister of the Queen of Naples and wife—though others say the daughter—of Robert of Artois. He also wrote the *Corbaccio*, the *Filostrato*, and the *Labyrinth*. In addition to these books, he composed several others, but in the Latin language: namely, the book on the *Genealogy of the Gods*, the one on *Famous Women*, the one on the names of mountains, forests, fountains, lakes, rivers, and seas, together with a compendium of Roman history, as is well noted by Conrad Gessner and Josias Simler <note>Two famous Swiss bibliographers of the 16th century.</note> in their historical libraries. This remarkable person died at the age of 62 in 1375, as confirmed by Franciscus Floridus in his *Apology for the Latin Language*, Paolo Giovio in his *Eulogies of Illustrious Men*, Raphael Volaterranus in book 21 of his *Commentaries*, Ludovico Dolce in his life of Boccaccio, Master Francesco Sansovino in the life of the said Boccaccio inserted at the beginning of the *Decameron*, and Papire Masson in his biography of the man. He was buried in the said town of Certaldo in the Church of St. Philip with this epitaph composed by himself before his passing:

> *Beneath this mound lie the ashes and bones of Giovanni;*
> *His soul sits before God, adorned with the merits of his labors.*
> *Boccaccio was his father in mortal life;*
> *His homeland was Certaldo, and his passion was the nourishing art of Poetry.*
<note>original: "Hac sub mole iacent cineres, ac ossa Joannis, / Mens sedet ante Deum meritis ornata laborum / Mortalis vitæ genitor Bocatius, illi / Patria Certaldum, studium fuit alma Poesis."</note>

In addition to these verses, the same Paolo Giovio, in the place cited above, includes others composed in praise of this man, which I will not include here in order to avoid being too long-winded.

## Concerning Francesco Petrarch, Italian, and his poems composed in the Italian language.

Francesco Petrarch <note>Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), a scholar and poet often called the "Father of Humanism."</note> was born, according to some, in Arezzo, a city in Italy, or rather in the Arno Valley in the castle of Incisa near Florence on July 19, 1304. This is confirmed by Petrarch himself in his letter to Giovanni Boccaccio, and by Garcæus <note>Johannes Garcæus (1530–1574), a German astronomer and astrologer.</note> in his book on the judgments of the rising stars, within Petrarch's horoscope. This personage was one of the first who—having opened the libraries which had long before him been full of dirt, dust, and worms—restored and brought back into honor the letters and disciplines that had been buried for a long time in great and deep darkness <note>Petrarch is credited with creating the concept of the "Dark Ages" to describe the period between antiquity and his own time.</note>. With such dexterity and subtlety of mind, he embellished or enriched his Italian language, causing it to rise to such a degree or peak of eloquence and excellence that one could hardly find another in the world which, more delicately and artfully and with more select and chosen words, could better express human conceptions and inventions than his. This poet was so multifaceted and diverse in infinite subjects, and enriched his Italian poems with words and phrases so full of audacity—or rather, one should say gravity and excellence—that it is not possible to express the least of his perfections in writing, despite what the great Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who compared Petrarch unfavorably to Dante in a letter to Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> wished to say in one of his letters to Lorenzo de' Medici:

> That he sometimes does not live up to his promises, having that which attracts at first sight, but thereafter fails to satisfy <note>original Latin: "Illum quandoque non respondere pollicitis, habentem quod allectet in prima specie, sed vlterius non satisfaciat."</note>.

In the year 1338, Petrarch was solemnly crowned in Rome with the laurel crown by Count Languillara, the Pope's vicar, according to Platina <note>Bartolomeo Platina, a Renaissance historian of the Popes.</note>. He fell in love with Lady Laura <note>Laura de Noves, the subject of Petrarch’s famous "Canzoniere."</note> at the age of 23, as appears in his 171st sonnet, while he was residing near the Sorgue spring in the place called Vaucluse, quite near Avignon. He continued this love until after her passing, in memory and honor of whom he began to compose in his Italian language sonnets, songs, and triumphs. In the composition of these, he was greatly aided by the most beautiful features of the songs of Arnaut Daniel, Anselm Faydit, Pierre Remond, Aimeric de Peguilhan, Giraut de Bornelh, and Guilhem Figueira <note>These were famous troubadours—poets from the Provence region of southern France who wrote in Occitan.</note>, ancient Provençal poets who flourished long before him. He was also aided by the songs of Theobald, King of Navarre, Gace Brulé, and the Chatelain de Coucy <note>Medieval French poets/trouvères.</note>, very ancient French poets, as well as the discourses of Dante, Aretino, Cino [da Pistoia], Cavalcanti, and several other Italian authors, as reported by Jean de Nostredame and Jean Giudici in their discourses on the lives of the most famous Provençal poets, and by Claude Fauchet in his first book on the French language and poetry, and by the Italian commentators of Petrarch in their commentaries on his work. During his life, he was honored with several dignities in the Church, having always conducted himself very honestly and as a man of virtue, with as much glory and reputation as any personage who had ever lived before or after him. Having chosen in his final days to live among the Euganean Hills in the valley near Pavia at Arquà, he passed away there in a small house of his on July 18, 1374, aged 70 according to Girolamo Squarciafico, or 76 according to Raffaele Volaterrano. He was buried in the said Arquà in front of the temple with this eulogy composed by one Bonaventure da Peraga, a hermit who was later made Cardinal.

### Concerning Ludovico or Louis Ariosto, Italian, and of his poems composed in the Italian language.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' containing scrolling foliate and floral motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

LUDOVICO or Louis Ariosto, a native of the city of Ferrara in Italy, was the son of Niccolò Ariosto and Daria Malaguzzi. From his most tender youth, he devoted himself entirely to Italian poetry, preferring to be held and reputed as one of the first among the Italian poets than second or third among the Latin poets. In his early years, he composed in the Tuscan language <note>The Tuscan dialect was the literary standard for what we now call Italian.</note> the fable of *Thisbe* and other poems—namely *Satires* full of sharp and biting rebukes in the manner of the Latin satirical poets Persius and Juvenal, and also *Comedies* filled with pleasant and joyous discourse, as beautiful and noble as those of Plautus the comic playwright. After attempting these subjects, having read and leafed through a great number of good authors, he set himself to compose in writing this excellent, long, flowing, moving, and diverse work in Italian, titled *Orlando Furioso* <note>"The Frenzy of Orlando" or "Mad Roland," one of the most influential epic poems of the Renaissance.</note> containing 51 Cantos, including the five that were newly added following the others; this work is and shall forever be infinitely recommended by the most learned and scholarly in all...

This is easy to believe for those who wish to make the comparison for themselves. He died in Ferrara on July 6, 1534, of a shortness of breath <note>Likely referring to asthma or a respiratory ailment.</note> at the age of 59, and was buried in the Church of Saint Benedict in the same city. His life, and his other actions and conduct, are more particularly described by François Floride in his *Apology for the Latin Language*; by Caelius Henricus Curio in his book on all artifice; by Conrad Gesner and Josias Simler in their *Historical Bibliographies*; by Paolo Giovio in his *Elogia*; and by the Italian commentators on the said Ariosto in his *Orlando Furioso* <note>The Frenzy of Orlando.</note>.

# On Torquato Tasso, Italian, and his Poems
## composed in the
# Italian language.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial T featuring a figure seated at a desk, surrounded by elaborate foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>
TORQUATO Tasso, otherwise known as Torquate Tasse, the most modern of the Italian poets, was the son of Bernardo Tasso. Bernardo was, during his life, Secretary to the Prince of Salerno, and wrote in his time a fairly large and thick volume in the Italian language titled *The Works of Bernardo Tasso*, divided and partitioned into five books. This work is currently found in print in Italy, and I have it with me; it contains several various Italian poems, very elegant and charming, such as Sonnets, Elegies, Odes, Psalms, and others, addressed to several different Lords and Ladies of his time. This Torquato Tasso, son of the aforementioned Bernardo, at the age of 19 or 20, composed a very beautiful Tuscan poem in the style and fashion of Ariosto (mentioned above) titled *Rinaldo*, containing ten *Canti*, or Songs, concerning the loves and feats of arms of the said Rinaldo, which has been printed in Italy. 

Since then, he has shown himself very eloquent, highly fluent, and almost inimitable in his twenty books or Songs of Italian heroic verses or poems. These are so diversified, sharp, subtle, polished, and eloquent, compiled in a poem titled *Gerusaleme liberata* <note>Jerusalem Delivered.</note> *by Signor Torquato Tasso*. It is addressed to the most serene Lord Don Alfonso II, fifth Duke of Ferrara, and treats the deeds, gestures, and prowess of the Christians in the conquest of the Holy Land with Godfrey of Bouillon. This poem, in the judgment of those most learned and knowledgeable in languages, surpasses all other Italian poems composed before it in grandeur of style and gravity of words—being figurative, concise, sharp, refined, and abundant in all the flowers and riches of Italian eloquence. This includes the works of Cino <note>Cino da Pistoia (c. 1270–1336).</note>, Boiardo, Pulci, Dante, Petrarch, Ariosto, Bernardo Tasso (his father), and others. He was, some years ago, in the service of the Prince of Piedmont; later he joined the household of the Duke of Ferrara, and finally he retired to Rome in the service of the...

### On the Region of the Spaniards and Portuguese.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a central figure surrounded by floral and leaf scrollwork.</image-desc>

Abraham Ortelius, in his *Synonyms and Geographical Treasury*, says: "Spain <note>original: "Hispania"</note>, formerly Iberia <note>original Greek: "Ἰβηρία"</note>, and Hesperia <note>original Greek: "Ἑσπερία"</note>; called Hispania by later authors such as Strabo, Pliny, and others, without the aspiration <note>The letter 'H'.</note>. Ptolemy and Stephanus write the same, the latter of whom calls the same Pannonian Ionia <note>original: "Pannoniam Ἰωνία"</note>. He also distinguishes between a Greater and Lesser [Spain]. The treasury of Goltzius <note>Hubert Goltzius, a 16th-century numismatist.</note> also mentions a Lower Spain <note>original: "Inferioris Hispaniæ"</note>, based on an ancient inscription. Horace calls it the 'furthest Hesperia' <note>original: "Hesperiam vltimam"</note> for the sake of distinction, as Italy was once also called Hesperia. Dioscorides, in book 5, chapter 102, names it Western Iberia <note>original: "Hesperam Iberiam"</note>, as if to say 'the Iberia of the West.' It was once called Celtiberia <note>A region in central-northeastern Spain inhabited by Celtic-speaking people.</note> according to Appian of Alexandria. Its inhabitants were anciently called Celtiberians and Celto-Scythians, as Strabo testifies. Likewise, he records from Myeleanus that they were once called Igletes <note>original Greek: "Ἰγλητας"</note>. Postellus writes that it is called Sepharat <note>original: "Sepharat"; refers to Sepharad, the Hebrew name for the Iberian Peninsula.</note> in Hebrew, as does Arias Montanus in his commentary on the Book of Obadiah, where he adds that it is called Spania by the Chaldeans. Josephus writes that the inhabitants are called Thobelo <note>original Greek: "Θόβηλος"; referring to Tubal, son of Japheth, traditionally considered the ancestor of the Iberians.</note>. I say that this region is called Spain, as mentioned under the term Iberia, which is often used interchangeably. Spain was first divided into provinces: Nearer <note>original: "Citeriorem"</note> and Further <note>original: "ulteriorem"</note>; later, under Caesar, it was divided into three. One was called Tarraconensis; the 'Further' portion was divided into Baetica and Lusitania, according to Pliny. From this 'Iberia,' Valerius Flaccus (book 5) derives the name 'Iber' for the people. See 'Mauritania' and 'Alpine Spaniards' <note>original: "Hispani Alpini"</note>. Lusitania <note>original Greek: "Λυσιτανία"</note> is the name for Spain in Ptolemy and others; today this is Portugal. Appian of Alexandria uses the spelling 'Lusitania' with an 'i'. Stephanus says its inhabitants were called Belitani <note>original Greek: "Belitanνοὶ"</note>; Pliny calls certain peoples of Nearer Spain 'Belitani.' But because I see that the etymology of the name 'Portugal' is derived by many learned men from 'Port of the Gauls' <note>original: "portu Gallorum"</note>, I thought it worthwhile to include the opinion of Osorius <note>Jerónimo Osório (1506–1580), a Portuguese historian.</note> here. He says, following the demonstration of the most learned André de Resende, that the name originates from *Caleportu*. This is the name of a town overlooking the mouth of the Douro River <note>original: "Durij fluminis"</note>, which used to be frequented for fishing; from there, such a great multitude of people flocked that it grew into a most wealthy city, and took the name *Portogallo*, as if to say 'Port of Cale' <note>original: "portus Calo"</note>. From this, the entire Kingdom took its name. Lusitania beyond the Douro River toward the North is now called Callaica <note>Galicia</note>, as Strabo says. I call these the Gallaicos Brecarios <note>original Greek: "καλλαϊκοὶ βραυκάριοι"</note>, according to Ptolemy."

### On the Catalan and Spanish
### Languages.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring floral scrollwork inside a square frame.</image-desc>

Some Spanish historians maintain that it is contained in the ancient Histories of Spain—and certain writers have believed—that the first and most ancient language of the Spaniards was the language of the Basques <note>original: "Biscayns"</note> of today. This is because this language has been kept and preserved for so long in its own purity among the said Basques, without one being able to see that it has taken or received any terms from other older languages, nor from those of the peoples who currently inhabit the surroundings of the Basque Country <note>original: "pays de Biscaye"</note>, with whom they formerly conversed and traded, and still converse and trade today. One must certainly believe that there is something very considerable in this Basque language in this regard; because of which the aforementioned authors have concluded that it is one of those first languages that was introduced during the confusion of Babel <note>The biblical event where the single original human language was split into many.</note>, God having been pleased to keep in Spain this mark of its first inhabitants. This discourse is very fully detailed in the *New History of Spain*, book 1, folio 4. 

Others maintain that during the time of the flourishing Roman Empire, the Latins and Romans, mixed with the Spaniards, became so accustomed to the Latin and Roman tongue that since that time it has not left the Spains <note>Early modern writers often used the plural "the Spains" to refer to the various kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula.</note>. For the Castilian language of today is almost nothing but a corrupted Latin; consequently, from time to time the Spaniards became such that many of them equaled their renown to that of the most prized and recommended among the aforementioned Latins and Romans, such as were the two Senecas <note>Seneca the Elder and Seneca the Younger, born in Córdoba.</note>, Silvius <note>Possibly the poet Silius Italicus.</note>, Martial, Lucan, Mela <note>The geographer Pomponius Mela.</note>, P. Latro <note>The orator Marcus Porcius Latro.</note>, Quintilian, Columella, and others. 

There are other Spanish historians who report that in the time of Charlemagne, King of our French, who came with his people into Spain to the aid of the Spaniards against the Arabs and Saracens who held the said Spain: the Catalans, an ancient people of the land, came to mix regularly with the French. Because of this, the Latin and Roman language—which these Catalans and all other Spaniards previously used, employed, and spoke—became altered and corrupted among them to such an extent that from there was made and formed a language entirely diverse from that which was then in use among the aforementioned Catalans and Spaniards, which is hardly different from that of the peoples living beyond the Pyrenees mountains in Gaul, Aquitaine, and Languedoc <note>Referring to the close linguistic relationship between Catalan and the Occitan languages of Southern France.</note>. The majority of Spanish authors hold that their Spanish language is for the most part corrupted as much by the Latin and Roman languages as by several other languages of various peoples and nations who have possessed the Spains many and various times for over a thousand years; the Basque language having been preserved in the Basque Country and part of Na— <note>Text cuts off mid-word, likely "Navarre".</note>

Navarre and other surrounding places; but in Granada, Andalusia, Murcia, and Valencia—principally among the peasantry—a corrupted Moorish and Arabic <note>original: "Moresque & Arabesque"</note> tongue is in great use. Indeed, it has been so for nearly all the time that the peoples of the Spains have used various languages, many quite strange to one another, as Turquet <note>Louis Turquet de Mayerne (c. 1550–1618), a historian known for his "General History of Spain."</note> relates in his *New History of Spain*, book 1, folio 45.

A certain personage of this century, most learned in languages, has held that the common language of Spain is hardly different from the Italian language, which the Spaniards took when they were subjected to the Italians <note>The author refers here to the ancient Romans.</note>. And it is not known for certain what language the Spaniards had before then, although some say it was the language of the Phoenicians, as shall be stated hereafter. Some maintain that the Germanic language was formerly common to the Gauls and the Spaniards, just as it is today among all the nations toward the North. And just as the Sarmatian <note>A term often used by early modern writers to refer to the Slavic languages.</note> language is common to the Slavs, Bohemians, Poles, Muscovites, Russians, Bulgarians, Wallachians, Dalmatians, Illyrians, Lithuanians, and many other peoples neighboring these nations—except insofar as it is today altered and corrupted by the invasion of the Great Turk <note>The Ottoman Empire</note>, and was formerly confused by the arrival of the Hungarians—in the same way, one must believe that the other nations of Europe toward the West used one and the same language before the Roman Empire was so widely expanded. Namely, they used the Germanic tongue, which would also have been moved and changed into the Roman language <note>The Romance languages, derived from Latin</note> if the Romans had as easily been able to overcome that nation <note>The Germanic tribes</note> as they did Spain and Gaul, and to send there colonies and new inhabitants of their own. And one must confess that the language of the Scots, the Danes <note>original: "Dauois," likely a typo for "Danois"</note>, or rather the Irish, is very different from the German or Swiss, yet these agree in their foundations, which is well supported by many words common to both nations. Gaul also still has some traces of its [ancient] language, which Glarean <note>Heinrich Glarean (1488–1563), a Swiss humanist and polymath.</note> demonstrates through many words and names in a book of his on this matter, as confirmed by Sebastian Münster <note>A German cartographer and cosmographer whose "Cosmographia" was one of the most influential books of the 16th century.</note> in book 1, in the chapter on Spain in his *Universal Cosmography*. In addition to the above, I remember having read formerly that Polybius, Titus Livius, and Appian of Alexandria demonstrate in their works that before the Germans had made their power known, and before they were in any reputation at all, the Carthaginians had already made themselves masters of the Spains, which they possessed for a very long time. Strabo, speaking on this subject regarding the Phoenicians and Greeks, said the following:

"As the Phoenicians, Libyans, and Greeks had, in the first centuries, resided for a very long time in the Spains, it is also likely that their language took root and origin there, and that the Spaniards received it into their familiar and common usage. Some time later, the Romans coming there and conquering the country, there was also a change from this language and from the Greek, from which point the Spaniards became accustomed to using the Latin language, without any history or memory yet proving to us that the Germans had planted their language there." To understand what this volume is, one must know that in the time of the aforementioned Alfonso, the tenth of that name, King of Castile, around the year of Salvation 1266, several learned men worked by his command to compile, complete, and draft into one volume the book of the laws of Castile, called in the Spanish language *Seven Parts*, the seven divisions which King Don Ferdinand had begun. This was since increased by subsequent Kings with several laws, edicts, and ordinances, and was revised and rearranged once more by Pero Lopez Alcoçer, Doctor Escudero, Pero Lopez Arrieta, and finally by Bartolomé de Atienza, jurists. These laws constitute the rights by which the inhabitants of the Kingdoms of Castile and Leon are judged and governed. Until the time and reign of this King, all Titles, Instruments, Contracts, and public Writings were written in the Latin language; but he was the first to have them written in the Castilian language, along with all other sorts of writings, having several books of the Holy Scripture translated into that same language. For this reason, the language was greatly embellished and illustrated, as is deduced at length in book 12 of the *Histories of Spain* cited above.

## On the Spaniard Ausiàs March and his poems composed in the Catalan language.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' depicting a figure seated at a desk or table, surrounded by foliage patterns.</image-desc>Ausiàs March <note>A renowned 15th-century Valencian poet, often considered the most important figure in Catalan literature.</note>, according to Marineus Siculus in his histories of Spain and Lilius Giraldus in his *Dialogue of Poets*, was Spanish by nation, a native of the city of Valencia. In his life, he composed various poems in the Catalan language—or the ancient Spanish language—which remained for a long time buried in darkness without anyone making much account of them. However, since they have come to the knowledge of the learned and scholarly through being printed and brought to light, they have been, and are still to this day, so cherished and prized by the Spaniards and by those curious about the Spanish language, as the Italian poems of Petrarch, Ariosto, and Tasso are by all Italians and those who desire to learn the pure Tuscan language. These poems, as I have them before me, printed in the aforementioned Catalan language, are titled:

->*The works of the valiant Knight and most elegant Poet Ausiàs March, now newly revised and organized with much diligence, and increased by many Cantos.* <note>original: "Les obres del valeros Cauallier y elegantiſſim Poeta Auſias Marc, ara nouament ab molta diligentia reuistes y ordenades, y de molts Cants aumentades."</note><-

These are from the press of Claude Bornat in the city of Barcelona in Spain. They contain ninety-three Cantos or songs of love with stanzas of ten or eleven feet <note>meaning ten or eleven syllables per line, the standard meter for serious poetry in that era</note>, after which there are six scattered and divided couplets with questions and answers titled *Scattered Verses, Questions, and Replies* <note>original: "Coblas eſparças, demandas y repoſtas"</note>; fourteen moral Cantos; a spiritual Canto named *Spiritual Canto* <note>original: "Cant ſpirituel"</note>; and the works of death in eight Cantos called *The Works of Death Cantos 8* <note>original: "las obras de Mort Cants. 8."</note>. The most learned and scholarly in the Catalan and Spanish languages hold that were it not for the fact that this author made use of the aforementioned Catalan language in his said poems—which are entirely filled with inventions, comparisons, digressions, and delicate and eloquent deductions—he would carry away the prize, honor, and laurel above all the Spanish writers whom I mention hereafter. This includes Juan de Mena, also a Spanish poet flourishing in the time of John, King of Castile <note>John II, reigned 1406–1454; his court was a center of early literary activity.</note>. This poet [Mena] is filled in that great Spanish work which he left before his death with such majesty and sweetness that L. Vives <note>Juan Luis Vives (1493–1540), a prominent Spanish humanist and scholar who wrote widely on education and philosophy.</note> did not fear to name him "The Spanish Poet" par excellence, because he can be compared, regarding his Spanish tongue, to Petrarch, as confirmed by Tarapha in his *History*, Lilius Giraldus in his *Dialogue of Poets*, and Josias Simler in his *Historical Library*. Beyond these Spanish authors, those of this nation count a certain poet named Jorge Manrique <note>Original text spells this "George Mandrice." Manrique is famous for his "Coplas on the Death of His Father."</note>, who embellished his Spanish writings with gravity of thought, along with a great sweetness and fluidity of the Castilian language.

## On Don Juan Antonio de Guevara, a religious man, and his writings composed in the Spanish language.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' inside a square border with ornate floral and scrolling leaf patterns.</image-desc>
Don Juan Antonio de Guevara <note>Commonly known as Antonio de Guevara (c. 1481–1545), he was one of the most widely read and translated authors of the 16th century.</note>, a Franciscan friar <note>original: "religieux Cordelier"; the Cordeliers were a branch of the Franciscan order in France, named for the knotted cord worn around their waists.</note>, later Bishop of Mondoñedo <note>original: "Mondoguette"</note>, a great theologian, preacher, confessor, and chronicler to the Emperor Charles V. A Spaniard by nation, he came from the house and family of that lord so renowned in the histories of Navarre and Aragon, *Don Ladrón de Guevara*—which is to say, Governor of the Captaincy in Álava—son of Íñigo <note>original: "Ygnez"</note>, head of the house of Guevara. During his life, he composed several and diverse writings in the Spanish and Italian languages, namely: a book titled *The Mount of Calvary* <note>original: "le mont de Caluaire"</note> divided into two parts on the History of the Passion; *The Contempt of the Court and the Praise of the Country Life* <note>original: "le mespris de la cour, & la louange de la vie Rustique"</note>; *The Decade of Emperors* <note>original: "la Decade des Empereurs"</note> translated into the French language by Antoine Alègre; four volumes of *Golden Epistles* <note>original: "epistres dorées"</note> first translated in part from Spanish into French by F. Gutery, and since then by others of this Kingdom in recent times; furthermore, *The Courtier’s Favorite* <note>original: "le fauor de la cour," likely referring to his work *Aviso de privados*</note> translated into French by Jacques de Rochefort; *The Book of Agriculture*; *The Book of the Christian Prince*; and the collection or heap of sermons; all of which have come into our French tongue through several French authors. See on this subject André Thevet, book 13, chapter 10, of his *Universal Cosmography*.

## On Boscán and Garcilaso de la Vega, Poets, and their poems in the Spanish language.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'L' inside a square border with ornate floral and scrolling leaf patterns.</image-desc>
Juan Boscán <note>c. 1490–1542, the poet credited with introducing Italian verse forms like the sonnet into Spanish literature.</note>, a Spanish poet worthy of perpetual memory for having been the perfect and complete friend of Garcilaso de la Vega (of whom more will be said hereafter), wrote several love poems in his Spanish language, namely: songs, sonnets in the fashion of the Italian poets, epistles, a very large elegy in the form of a complaint for the unfortunate Leander and Hero, and some other Spanish rhythms on various subjects. All of this is compiled into a single volume divided into three books titled *The Works of Boscán* <note>original: "Las obras de Boscan"</note>, printed in Barcelona in Spain. By reading these books, those curious about foreign languages will better be able to understand the sweetness and elegance of Spanish poetry. The latter man, Garcilaso de la Vega <note>1501–1536, a soldier-poet and one of the most influential figures in Spanish Golden Age poetry.</note>, was a very eloquent and articulate Spanish poet who wrote poems in his own language divided into sonnets, songs, elegies, and eclogues, which are included today in the fourth book of the poems of Boscán cited above. For Garcilaso, before he died, earnestly requested that his writings not be printed except by the aforementioned Boscán, his intimate friend, as the most laudable and rich treasure that could be in his possession; which Boscán

### On Friar Louis of Granada and his writings in the Spanish language.

Friar Louis of Granada <note>Luis de Granada (1504–1588) was a Dominican friar and a giant of Spanish mystical literature; his works were translated into many European languages.</note>, Doctor of Theology of the Order of Saint Dominic and a Spaniard, delivered many beautiful and learned sermons throughout all of Spain and elsewhere during his life. He composed a great quantity of books in his Spanish language on Theology, his primary science and profession, namely: *prayers and spiritual exercises*, *on prayer and meditation on contemplation*, *the summary of prayer*, *the compilation of prayer and meditation* <note>original: "orationes y exercicios spirituales, de la oracion, y meditatio de la conteplacion, summa de la oracion, Recompilatio de la oracio y meditatio"</note>, *The Memorial of the Christian Life*, *The Sinner’s Guide to Virtue*, *The Way to Attain the Glory of God*, *devout contemplations on the life, death, and passion of our Lord*, *The Tree of Life*, *Sermons on the Last Judgment* and several others, *The Mirror of Human Life*, *The Catechism or Introduction to the Symbols of Faith*, *The Discourse on Prayers to God for Men of the Three Estates or Ages*, and other Spanish books included in his works in Spanish and French, printed both in Spain and in France recently.

In addition to the Spanish writings of the persons mentioned above, we also have the Romances of Juan de Mena <note>original: "Iuan de Meua"</note> and Sepúlveda; Guido delle Colonne <note>original: "Guy de Coluna"</note> in his prose on the destruction of Troy; Miranda <note>Likely Francisco de Sá de Miranda, who wrote in both Spanish and Portuguese.</note> in his Spanish observations; Acuerdo Oliva <note>original: "Acuerdo oliua"; possibly a corrupted reference to an editor or author associated with the Spanish *Amadis* cycles.</note> in his Spanish *Amadis*; the *Diana* of Montemayor; the dictionaries of Antonio de Nebrija <note>original: "A. Nebrissence"; Nebrija wrote the first grammar of a modern European language.</note> in Spanish printed at Antwerp, and countless others.

As for the Portuguese poets, there are undoubtedly two very excellent ones among the others, namely Henrique Caiado <note>original: "Henry Caiade"</note> and Lourenço de Cáceres <note>original: "Laurent de Carceres"</note>, whose writings are found printed in various places in Portugal and Spain.

### On the region of the Germans.

Germany <note>original: "Germania γερμανία"</note>, the widest region of Europe and the glory of the Roman Empire, which Ptolemy calls "the Great" <note>original: "Germania Magna"</note>. By the Hebrews it is called *Ashkenaz* <note>original: "Ascanes; vel Ascenes"</note>, as Josephus witnesses, which is why the Jews even today call its inhabitants *Ashkenazim*, as Becanus <note>Johannes Goropius Becanus, a 16th-century physician and linguist.</note> teaches in his *Indo-Scythica*. By the inhabitants themselves it is called *Deutschland* <note>original: "Teutschlandt"</note>, and by foreigners *Alemagna*. The Slavs call it *Niemiecka*; the Greeks today call it *Elamags* <note>Likely a phonetic rendering of the Greek *Alamanos*.</note>, and the Turks *Alama*. The ancients divided this land into Upper and Lower Germany...

Inhabitants today distinguish between *High* and *Low Germany* <note>original: "Hooch & Niderteutſchlandt"</note>. Ammianus, in book 15, speaks of a First and Second Germany. The latter is called Lower, while the former is called Upper by Ptolemy. It lies in Belgic Gaul following the flow of the Rhine.

### On the German Language.

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut drop cap initial 'D' featuring a floral and vine motif within a square border.</image-desc>For some years now, a certain Brabantian physician named Johannes Goropius <note>Johannes Goropius Becanus (1519–1572) was a Dutch physician and linguist famous for his theory that a form of Dutch was the original language of mankind.</note> has brought to light a large book titled *Antwerpian Origins*, in which he attempts to prove that the Cimbric language—that is to say, Low German—is the first and most ancient language of this universe. Since his death, a man from Liège has had several other books by this physician printed on this same subject; in one of these, which he titles *Hermathena*, this Cimbric or Low German language is elevated and exalted above Latin, Greek, and Hebrew.

A long and ample discourse would be required to respond to his allegations, but for the present, we will content ourselves with saying only that everything he puts forward for the excellence of his language is a logical fallacy called in the schools <term>Petitio principij</term> <note>Begging the question: a fallacy where the conclusion of an argument is assumed in the phrasing of the question itself.</note>: when a sophist takes as granted that which is expressly denied to him, and which he could never prove. Goropius lays as the foundation of his discourse that the Cimbric language has borrowed nothing from any other, that Hebrew issued from it, and even that Hebrew borrowed from Cimbric. But we deny this to the said Goropius and his disciples. If they show some Hebrew words or phrases that relate to the words and terms of Low German, and then conclude that Adam, our first father, spoke Low German, and that the language of the Prophet Moses and the Prophets is difficult, ambiguous, poor, and borrowed from Cimbric (which he did not know how to follow well), we shall answer them that they are mistaken. They ought to say quite the opposite: that Hebrew preceded all others that were born in Babel, and has produced infinite others since, such as High and Low German and similar tongues that are still in use in the world. And to convict this opinion of the said Goropius and his disciples in a single word, we will bring forth the authority of **C. Tacitus**, who, speaking of the Germans or Allemands, said: "the secrets of letters are equally unknown to men and women there" <note>original: "literarũ ſecreta viri & fœminæ pariter illic ignorant" from Tacitus's *Germania*. The author uses this to argue that the ancient Germans were illiterate and thus could not have the primary language.</note>. A certain Annius Vetulonius, before the aforementioned Becanus, held the same opinion, against whom Lylius Giraldus has discoursed at length in his *History of the Poets*, dialogue 1, as has F. Louis the Portuguese in his *Globe of the Canons and Secrets of the Holy Language and Divine Scripture*, book 1, chapter 1.

Theodore Bibliander, in his *Commentary on the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*, citing the authority of the German Abbot Trithemius and several others regarding this German language, says: "The Teutonic and German language will now be explained, but first, the origin of the German peoples." <note>original Latin: "De lingua Teutonica & Germanica iã explicabitur, prius tamen de Gentiũ Germ. origine"</note>

> ” Commonly, Germany is now divided into Upper and Lower—*High German and Netherlandish* <note>original: "hoch Tutſchen vnd Niderlander"</note>—which differ not a little in their dialect. There are also other divisions among writers, who partition Germany into first and second; into ancient and recent; into great, and that which is concluded within narrower borders. Most conclude it to be within the most famous rivers: the Rhine, the Danube, and the Vistula.

Pomponius <note>Pomponius Mela, a Roman geographer of the 1st century AD.</note> also extends the borders of Germany to the sources of the Rhine. Certainly, the Noricans and Vindelicians <note>Tribes inhabiting the Alps and the upper Danube region.</note> used the Germanic language, which they still use today. Arrian also testifies in the first book of the *Reigns of Alexander* that the Germans living near the Ionian Gulf <note>original: "Ionij sinus"</note>, when Alexander ambitiously asked what they feared most, boldly replied: "that perhaps the sky might someday fall upon them." Not without reason or authority do I believe the Germans are descended from Ashkenaz, the grandson of Japheth and son of Gomer <note>The author uses a traditional biblical genealogy to trace European lineages to the sons of Noah.</note>. Nor is it a trivial matter that Jordanes the Alan locates their ancestral seats in Scanzia or Scandinavia, which is called the island of Schonlandia. Their neighbors were the Goths, who were also known as Guthones; or rather, the Goths themselves were a Germanic race, as authors not to be lightly dismissed record: for their common fatherland was indeed the Gothic islands, and their language and customs were the same.

There is also another division of Germany, taken roughly from the location of the Germanic nations, which Pliny records in book 4, chapter 14 of his *Natural History*. However, because the passage has been corrupted by the faults of transcribers, I will render it as free from the errors of copyists as I possibly can. The five types of Germans are: first, the Vandals; the second type are the Ingvaeones <note>original: "Vigeuones, vel Vuaguuoner"</note>, that is, those who dwell by the deeper waters, namely the coastal people. Closest to the Rhine are the Istvaeones <note>original: "Isteuones vel Vissersteuuoner"</note>. Then the Herminones <note>original: "Heruuones vel Herduuonér"</note>, who are the inland people. The fifth group are the Peucini and Bastarnae, who border the Dacians <note>A people inhabiting the region of modern Romania.</note>. Furthermore, it is not our purpose here to investigate which specific tribes are contained within those Germanic types, as we are writing less about the geography of Germany than about its language.

The language today is very widely spread. For even if we set aside the remnants of the Goths in the Crimean Peninsula <note>original: "Taurica Chersonneso"</note>, and omit the people of Transylvania <note>original: "Septemcastrenses," referring to the Siebenbürgen Saxons.</note> who use the Germanic tongue; and if we say nothing of the Jews, who almost everywhere among the nations use the Germanic speech <note>A reference to the development of Yiddish.</note>. After the Germans occupied parts of Gaul, the use of the language extended from the Alps near Italy all the way to furthest Norway and the island of Thule, which is called Iceland today—that is, over three hundred Germanic miles in length and breadth. Now, the Germanic and Gothic peoples who invaded the Roman provinces—such as the Lombards, Ostrogoths, Visigoths, Rugi, Heruli, Marcomanni, and Vandals in Italy; the Franks, Burgundians, Goths, and Normans in Gaul; and the Catthians, Suebi, Alani, Vandals, and Goths in Spain—mixed together the provincial speech and the Teutonic. Moreover, the Caledonians and the Angles, Scots, Picts, and Attacotti, occupying the island of Albion <note>Great Britain</note> after driving out the Britons (who then took possession of that part of Gaul called Brittany <note>original: "Britonum"</note>), brought their native language with them, which in turn was altered by French and semi-Latin words. Regarding the speech of those inhabiting Wales <note>original: "Vualliam"</note> and Cornwall, we have previously noted that it appears related to the language of the Greeks to those who are capable of judging both languages.

Furthermore, as to what the Germanic and Teutonic language is today, it is by no means obscure; and what it once was is also evident from literary monuments. Histories testify that Ulfilas <note>original: "Vulphilam"</note> (whom others call Gulphila), a bishop, gave letters to the Goths during the reign of Valens. Some believe that Jordanis gave letters to the Getae, whom they consider to be the same as the Goths. However, that they were borrowed from the Latins is argued by the order of the letters, their names, and their shapes. Nevertheless, the ancient letters of the Goths, in which some books are even now written, have been somewhat transformed.

What Johannes Trithemius <note>original: "Ioannes Tritennis," a German abbot and polymath (1462–1516).</note> writes about the letters and language of the Germans in book 6 of his *Polygraphia* should, I judge, be added here. The opinion of many holds that the Germans once had letters from the Greeks, and that they also used the Greek language...
