” Furthermore, when the Franks had subdued almost all of Europe after a long struggle with the Romans, they did not abolish the Roman letters which the rest of the Germans had adopted. The Venerable Bede <note>An English monk and historian (c. 672–735 AD) known as the "Father of English History."</note> tells of the literature of the Northmen <note>original: "Nortmannorum"</note> that they mixed Greek letters with Latin. I believe this was done not out of a common habit of writing, but for a secret reason <note>original: "arcana ratione"</note>, whereby those writing about difficult matters—when there is a danger that things entrusted to letters might become known to those who should not know them—employ such a method.

” Regarding the Germanic language itself, one will discover through reason and the facts themselves—provided they are not reluctant to take up the task—that it obeys the laws of grammar, logic, and rhetoric, and does not yield in quality even to the Roman tongue. I, for my part, do not regret the effort and diligence I have spent in learning about my homeland more exactly; and whatever I seem to have grasped, I will candidly share with others when I sense that my study is not displeasing to good men. For the present, I will add a few tokens <note>original: "paucula T...tis," likely "testimonia"</note> from which it will become clear that the Germanic tongue conforms to the art of grammar, no differently than Hebrew, Greek, or Latin. 

” My once most learned teacher, Joannes Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius (1500–1574), a major German humanist scholar.</note>, the most reverend prelate of the Church of Worms, had collected several thousand Greek words which signify the same thing in both the Greek and Germanic languages. This is something that the excellent and most wise Bishop Rodolphus Agricola <note>A pre-eminent Dutch humanist of the 15th century.</note>—the eternal glory of Germany—also did, as did Sigismund Gelenius, a Bohemian by nation, in a published book. He wrote many things in our Germanic tongue which sound with a wonderful gravity of regular instruction. For he composed verses according to the same rule, in both heroic and elegiac meter. Moreover, he composed several things in prose for Louis, King of Germany, the son of the pious Louis, and brother...

Having obtained fragments of this Grammar, I myself have extracted the present characters of the alphabet from many sources, so they might not perish entirely; it is certain, according to the testimony of Otfrid <note>Otfrid of Weissenburg (c. 800–870), a monk and the first named author in German literature.</note>, that Charles devised several of his own alphabets, which he might use securely for secret matters <note>original: "in arcanis"</note> with individual prefects throughout his vast kingdom. The same Bibliander <note>Theodore Bibliander (1509–1564), a Swiss scholar and pioneer in comparative linguistics.</note>, speaking subsequently about the aforementioned mutation <note>meaning the natural change or evolution of a language over time</note> of the said German language:

It would be best to demonstrate the mutation of the Germanic language from the books of the most learned man, Johannes Trithemius <note>A German Benedictine abbot (1462–1516) famous for his works on cryptography (Polygraphia) and history.</note>, who writes in this manner in the preface to the third book of *Polygraphia*:

"No one can quickly estimate how much the unregulated use of speech has varied among the Teutons <note>the Germans</note> alone in six hundred years, if they have not frequently re-read Otfrid of Weissenburg, the monk, in his songs of the German language. The sea flows and ebbs; humans, once dying, do not return to life again in the present. Customs succeed customs, and the vigor of mortal minds always declines toward softer things. Who today among the Germans—those ancient emulators of the Greeks—retains a knowledge of the ancient idioms? In the chronicles and ancient histories of the Franks, Hunibald, Doracus, and the other writers who preceded us by a thousand years, mixed many things into their compositions, both in ancient verse and the prose of the Teutonic speech; these are understood today by few. Why do I speak of ancient times, when our own proper idiom among the Eastern Franks, Swabians, Bavarians, Rhinelanders, Mosellans, people of Cologne, Saxons, and Thuringians undergoes a notable variation every day? Men change with time, and customs vary; minds change, and garments vary; the simplicity of languages is altered, the ancient property of idioms varies, and nothing stable is found in human affairs. For there is a change in all things, and variety succeeds the simplicity of minds. Who could bring this flow, so to speak, back to a perpetual harmony of unity? For many times pass away, as the Scripture says, and knowledge shall be manifold. Beatus Rhenanus <note>A German humanist and historian (1485–1547).</note> places some verses of the Frankish language in the second book of *German Affairs*, which he concludes—based on no slight conjectures—were written in the earliest time when the Franks gave their name to Christ <note>Meaning when they converted to Christianity.</note>, and which differ not a little from the custom of speaking used today. From these, it will not be troublesome to add some here, if anyone should require them; they speak, perhaps, of the virtue of the ancient Franks:

> That the Greeks do not surpass them

Which today, in prose speech, would be expressed in this manner:
"They are all just as glorious..."

# History of the Origin of [the Germans]

> When the Romans themselves <note>original: "Als die Roemer selb"</note>
> Now one may also say this
> That the Greeks do not contradict it
> Quick to arms
> All the heroes are

<margin>„ „ „ „ „ „ „</margin>
I have also read an old legal document <note>original: "vetus instrumentum"</note> rendered in German verses by a certain Rudolf <note>Rudolf von Ems (c. 1200–1254), a celebrated Middle High German poet.</note> originating from the family that takes its name from the prominent fortress in Rhaetia <note>An ancient Roman province comprising parts of modern-day Switzerland, Germany, and Austria.</note> which the common people call Hohenems. This was done at the request and command of King Conrad, the son of Frederick II, the August Emperor. These verses differ from present custom in their spelling, words, inflection, structure, and poetic style. I will touch upon this with one example, for regarding the faith given to the Gibeonites by Joshua and the other Israelites, he sings thus:
> Whosoever should break God’s ban <note>original: "Suuel man den ban Gott breche"</note>
> That it be avenged upon him <note>original: "Sas man es an im reche"</note>

In place of that, the speech now in use would say:
> Whosoever then should break God’s ban
> That it be avenged upon him.

The majority of writers maintain that the Germans in ancient times did not write their German language with any characters of letters, but that by the means and benefit of Charlemagne <note>Charles-Maigne</note>, King of France and Emperor of Germany, they began to set it down in writing with all sorts of discourse, embracing the sciences and disciplines from that time forward. This was well-noted by Abbot Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a polymath and historian.</note> when speaking of the writers of Germany. Indeed, some historians have asserted that this same Charlemagne was the first to begin composing a Grammar in this German language, of which they say fragments can still be found today in Germany. Jean Grachus Pierius <note>likely Giovanni Pierio Valeriano Bolzani (1477–1558)</note> worked on this same subject during his life, but being prevented by death, he could not complete his work. One Otfrid of Weissenburg <note>Otfridus Vuissen; an influential 9th-century monk and poet.</note> composed a treatise entitled *Grammar of the Teutonic Language*, and also after him one Ladislaus Suntheim in his description of the vulgar tongue throughout Upper Germany, and several other German figures mentioned by Gessner <note>Gefnerus</note> and Simler in their historical libraries. 

A certain rather ancient author named Aventinus <note>Johannes Aventinus (1477–1534), a Bavarian philologist.</note> in the first book of his histories, and Carion in the second book of his *Chronology*, maintain that a little after the Empire of Frederick II, in the year of salvation 1251 or 1257, this German language began for the first time to be written in Latin letters, having been unable to be written before then; although the Germans wish to say that a certain Otfrid, living in the year 874, did this first and gave the first rules to this said language. The reason why these Germans began so late to write their concepts and discourse in their language using the characters of Latin letters is that the said language is very different from Latin, requiring some of its own proper letters and particular diphthongs, such as the double W <note>original: "deux VV"</note>, which is a specifically German letter. And for as much as these Germans are accustomed to pronouncing several consonants in one syllable without mixing in vowels—in the manner of certain peoples of Sarmatia <note>An ancient region in Eastern Europe.</note> who sometimes pronounce four or five consonants without any vowel, with a strange and difficult sound—for this reason the pro-

# Languages of this World

...pronunciation discouraged those who might have tried to write it. If the German language were today as it was 400 years ago, it could not be written at all; but it is now written so well that there is hardly another language in Europe that contains so many types of books, for in just a few years, it has been decorated with the ornament in which we see it clothed today. Now, the names of saints given at baptism were introduced, received, and put into use by the Germans only after the death of the said Emperor Frederick II <note>Frederick II (1194–1250), Holy Roman Emperor.</note>; before that time, they used Pagan and Scythic <note>A term often used by Renaissance writers to refer to the ancient, nomadic ancestors of northern Europeans.</note> names. Some families still delight in and use these, seeing that for the most part, they were invented in the Greek fashion to signify the virtues of very ancient Germany. 

And yet, those people do not do well who, encountering such strange and wild names, strive to give them grace through Latin declension and endings. For by seeking to impose **Euphony** <note>The quality of being pleasing to the ear.</note>, or a good Latin resonance, they lose and strip away their proper meaning, which the ancient Germans observed and wished to be remembered. It is apparent that in many names they exercised a singular choice, giving to some names suitable to their spirit or character, or to their office; and to others, according to their fortune or their military strength. In this way, in all their titles, there was always some meaning to incite virtue; but most of these names have since been corrupted. 

For instance, we say **Pharamond** instead of *Vuaremond*, **Ariovistus** for *Eruveste*, and for *Herevan*—which means a man of arms or war—we pronounce and write **Arminius**. We say **Arnold** for *Ernhold*, **Ferdinand** for *Vuerdemaun*, and **Dagobert** for *Degenuerd*. <term>Degen</term> <note>A German word that historically meant a noble warrior or hero, but also evolved to mean a blade or rapier.</note> means a Hero or a noble, excellent, and virtuous man; it also means a dagger, as noted by Antoine du Verdier, Lord of Vauprivas, in the fifth book, twenty-fifth chapter of his *Diverse Lessons* added to P. Messie <note>Referring to the popular miscellany "Les Diverses Leçons" by Pero Mexía, expanded by Du Verdier.</note>. 

As for the language of the Belgians, Master Louis Guicciardini <note>Lodovico Guicciardini (1521–1589), an Italian writer whose description of the Low Countries was a definitive text of the era.</note> in his description of all the Low Countries has said these words:

> The natural speech of the Belgians—except in some places where French and German are spoken—is called **Flemish** by foreigners, and in Latin, **Teutonic**. This follows the opinion of certain authors regarding *Tuisto* <note>A legendary divine ancestor of the Germanic peoples.</note>, mentioned by Cornelius Tacitus in his book on the customs of the Germans. It is said that this Tuisto baptized and named all that great and ample Province **Teutonia** after himself, which in the time of the Romans was called Germania, and is now called Germany. Consequently, all these Belgians of the Low Countries, considering themselves (as they truly are) Teutons by origin, and since formerly their language was one and the same—and even now the two languages are hardly different or dissimilar—they still call their language Teutonic. This is truly a speech ample and copious in proper and significant terms and words, and very fit for receiving or forming any word whatsoever; but it is learned with difficulty and is even more troublesome to pronounce. Even the children born in the country are quite grown before they can properly form the words and utter the speech. And it is held as quite certain and affirmed by several reasons...

# History of the Origin of [Languages]

...memoirs and passages, that this language is the same as that which was spoken in this country in the time of Caesar, in Book 1 of the *Gallic War*. Indeed, Caesar himself at the beginning of the said book, describing Gaul as divided into three parts—namely Belgica, Celtica, and Aquitania—says these words: "All these differ among themselves in language, laws, and ways of life" <note>Original Latin: "Hi omnes lingua, institutis, legibus inter se differunt."</note>. Thus, these people having maintained this diversity of language until the present compared to other Gauls, it seems they have preserved their first and ancient language. For being further removed from the conversation and frequenting of the Romans, they could not easily alter and corrupt their language, which is clearly seen in the alteration of the languages of France, Spain, and Italy, which are in effect derived from, but corrupted from, Latin; and there is no doubt that in former times they were different from Latin and Roman.

Throughout the country of Brabant and others joined to it, Flemish is commonly spoken, and legal cases are pleaded in this same language, except in that small region where the towns of Nivelles and Genappe are primarily located, which is called in French the **Roman Country** <note>French: *Pays Romain*. This refers to the area of Walloon Brabant where Romance dialects were spoken despite being part of a largely Germanic-speaking duchy.</note>. Since the people of this region speak French, which is a corrupted Latin, they still today give the name "Roman" to both the country and the language. But although in the rest of Brabant Flemish is ordinarily spoken, as has been said, there is no man or woman of quality who does not speak French, and many speak German and English; and a good number know Italian and Spanish—a thing certainly convenient, proper, and worthy of wonder.

I say that in Brabant the Flemish language is used, seeing as, as I have already proposed, all this Low Country is included by foreigners under the name of Flanders—and thus also its language, except in places where French or German is spoken. It is hardly different among them, no more than that of the Florentines with the rest of the regions of Tuscany; and as for those from foreign countries, they call it Flemish. Regarding this, see Sebastian Münster <note>A German cartographer and cosmographer (1488–1552).</note>, Book 2 of his *Universal Cosmography*. J. Vadianus <note>Joachim Vadianus (1484–1551), a Swiss humanistic scholar.</note>, a Swiss by nation, on Book 3 of Pomponius Mela, does not want to recognize the Northern peoples nor the Goths as the ancestors of the Swiss, although he agrees there with Rhenanus <note>Beatus Rhenanus (1485–1547), a prominent German humanist and historian.</note> that the aforementioned Swiss are Germans, and that there should be no doubt of this, seeing that the language of the aforementioned Swiss corresponds to that of the deepest part of the Germanies; indeed, even today they follow the customs, ways, virtues, and magnanimities of these Germans.

Some of the Upper and Lower Valaisans—otherwise the subjects of the Bishop of Sion—and other Lords who hold the administration of the cities, being elected magistrates for the handling of affairs, speak Savoyard <note>A dialect of Franco-Provençal or Arpitan.</note>, and others German. This is confirmed by André Thevet <note>A French Franciscan priest and explorer (1516–1590).</note> in Book 16, Chapter 16 of his *Universal Cosmography*, having learned it from Sebastian Münster, Book 3 of his *Universal Cosmography*.

Furthermore, it is very certain that our ancient Gauls spoke the true German language, as noted very well by the said André Thevet, Book 14, Chapter 1 of his *Universal Cosmography*, and Claude Fauchet <note>A French historian and antiquary (1530–1601).</note>, Book 1 of *The French Language and Poetry*; or rather, they were the inventors of this language, rather than the Germans or *Alemands*, as Nicolas Vignier <note>A French chronicler and physician (1530–1596).</note> amply verifies in Part 1 of his *Historical Library*, leaves 276, 277, and 278, for the reasons and considerations that I will deduce, God willing, when speaking of the French language. The inhabitants of Saxony have at all times and from antiquity boasted of speaking, among all other Germans, the most complete, pure, and eloquent German language...

## Of Martin Luther, German, and of his writings composed in the German language.

<image-desc>Decorative initial M featuring a landscape with figures within a square frame.</image-desc>
Martin Luther, a native of Eisleben in the County of Mansfeld in Germany, was born in the year 1483 on the 10th of November around eleven o'clock at night. He was the son of one Hans Luther and Marguerite, and was named Martin because he was born on the eve of St. Martin's Day. He composed various treatises and books in both the Latin and German languages, most of which are rejected by Catholics for being written against the authority and ceremonies of the Church; setting that aside, these works are very fluent and eloquent regarding the language itself. Particular mention of these treatises and books is made by Sigismund Suevus in his discourse titled *The Catalogue of the Books of the Said Luther*, and by Gessner and Josias Simler in their historical libraries. See Sleidan in his histories, Carion in Book 3, and Surius in Book 3 of their histories; Gilbert Génébrard in Book 4 of his *Chronography*, and André Thevet in Book 20, Chapter 14 of his *Universal Cosmography*, all of whom discourse amply on his life and conduct, and of his death which occurred on the 17th day of February 1546, he being 63 years of age. Father Noël Taillepied, a Franciscan friar, has written a history of the lives, manners, acts, doctrine, and death of this personage.

## On Michael Beuther, German, and his writings composed in the German language.

Michael Beuther, Doctor of Laws, native of the city of Karlstadt situated in East Franconia on the river Main, composed a history or rather a discourse on the composition of years, and translated from Latin into the German language the history of Johannes Sleidanus <note>A diplomat and historian whose "History of the State of Religion and the Empire under Charles V" was a standard Reformation text.</note>, so well known, seen, and read by the learned men of today, to which he himself added a historical continuation also composed in the same German language, from a brief Epitome up to the year 1583. These writings are commonly found for sale in Germany, as confirmed by Gessner and J. Simler in their historical Bibliographies; they also state that before the aforementioned Beuther, a certain German personage named Heinrich Pantaleon, a native of the City of Basel, had translated the History of the same Johannes Sleidanus from the Latin language into the German language. I currently have this [book] in my hands, sent to me some time ago from the said Basel by a friend of mine residing there at present.

## On Hans Sachs, German Poet, and his poems composed in the German language.

Hans Sachs <note>original: "Iean Saxo"</note>, native of the city of Nuremberg, composed three large books in the German language, which are admirable for having proceeded from the talent of a person who was not highly instructed in formal literature. Since that time, a certain personage named Johann Fischart <note>original: "Iean Fifchard"</note>, Doctor of Law, composed a book in his German language that is quite excellent, which to tell the truth is nothing other than the *Demonology* of Bodin <note>Jean Bodin’s *De la démonomanie des sorciers*, a famous treatise on witchcraft.</note>, translated word for word. Another modern personage named Butric <note>Lambert Ludolph Helm, a scholar and diplomat known as Butricius.</note>, for some years a doctor of laws and counselor to Melchior, Bishop of Würzburg, and then to the Count Palatine Otto Heinrich <note>original: "Vuaiutich"; likely referring to the Elector Palatine.</note>, composed a certain work titled the *Historical Ephemeris*, which he has greatly expanded.

## On the region of the Bohemians.

According to *Ortelius* in his geographical synonyms and treasures <note>original: *Thesaurus geographicus*, a famous 16th-century gazetteer</note>, *Boiemum* was the name used by *Tacitus*, and *Boiohemum* by *Paterculus* <note>original: *Velleius Paterculus*, a Roman historian</note>; he says this is the name of the region inhabited by *Marobuduus* <note>original: *Marobuus*, a king of the Marcomanni</note>. The *Bohemians* <note>original: *Bæmi*</note> are called *Kaimoi* <note>original: *Κάϊμοι*</note> by *Ptolemy*. *Strabo* calls them *Kolduloi* <note>original: *κoλδέλοι*</note> in Book 7, where he says: in *Germany* is the *Hercynian Forest* <note>A vast ancient forest mentioned by Roman authors, covering much of Central Europe</note>; some live in the forest itself, such as the *Kolduli*, among whom is *Bouiasmum*, the royal seat of *Marobuduus* <note>original: *Marobuduui Regia*</note>. Today this region is called *Bohemia*. The inhabitants call themselves *Czechs*. In the works of *Aimoin* <note>A Frankish chronicler</note>, they are corruptly called *Begamini* in Book 4.

## On the language of the Bohemians.

It is a very certain thing that although the country and Kingdom of *Bohemia* is entirely surrounded and encircled by the lands of *Germany*, and contains in length and width only three days' journey in extent—the *Hercynian* forest serving it on all sides as walls and enclosure—nevertheless, the *Bohemians* do not speak the *German* language at all. Rather, it was driven out from there at the time when the *Slavs* or *Sclavonians* made themselves masters of this country and Kingdom. For one reads in their annals that there were two brothers who, having departed from *Croatia* with a great troop of people, came to make themselves masters, one of *Bohemia* and the other of *Poland*, changing the names of the lands they occupied and teaching their language to the people who lived there, as *Volaterranus* <note>Raffaele Maffei, a humanist scholar and encyclopedist</note> testifies in Book 2 of his histories. Nonetheless, there are still many found who to this day use and make use of the aforementioned *German* language, so much so that in the churches and at sermons, this people is taught in that *German* language; but outside the churches and temples, and even in the cemeteries, the *Bohemian* language is used. Formerly among them, it was for the four Mendicant orders <note>The four primary orders of friars: Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites, and Augustinians</note> alone to preach and announce the word of God to the people in whatever language seemed good to them. And one knows well by this, as *Aeneas Sylvius* <note>The humanist scholar who became Pope Pius II</note> says, that this region was once Teutonic <note>Germanic</note>, and that the *Bohemians* entered it little by little, of which *Wolfgang Lazius* gives proof in his *Migrations*. Furthermore, *Albert Krantz* <note>A German historian</note> proves through *Cornelius Tacitus* that the *Boii*, or *Bavarians*, were a *Gallic* nation by origin, and held the region between the mountains that is now *Bohemia*, and that they were later repelled and driven out by the *Marcomanni*—that is to say, *Vandals*—who possess it today. For the *Bohemians* are the *Vandals* <note>In early modern ethnography, Slavic peoples were often incorrectly identified with ancient Germanic tribes like the Vandals</note>, and the ancient name has remained in the province; so that they are called...

->*On the region of the Pannonians and Hungarians.*<-

Ortelius, in his *Geographical Treasury and Synonyms*, states: Pannonia <note>Greek: *Pannonia*</note> is a region of Europe that Ptolemy divides into Upper and Lower. Claudius Afer <note>likely referring to the 5th-century author Marius Claudius Victor, though the transcription is slightly unclear</note> claims there are three Pannonias, contrary to all previous writers and the evidence of coinage. These Pannonias, under the Roman Emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and those following (as is clear from Rufus, Marcellinus, and the *Book of Offices* <note>original: *liber Notitiarum*, likely referring to the *Notitia Dignitatum*, a document of the late Roman Empire's administrative structure</note>), were distinguished by various names: such as Pannonia Prima, which is perhaps the same as the Upper; Pannonia Secunda, the same as the Lower; Savia, or Ripensis; the *Book of Offices* lists Ripensis, and Valeria, and Pannonia Bubalia; likewise Aurelius Victor mentions Sabaria in the *Lives of the Emperors Decius and Didius Julianus*. This one is named Savia from the Sava River; the other from the city of Bubali; and Pannonia Cibiliensis from the city of Cibalae (which Ptolemy places in Lower Pannonia), according to Diaconus <note>Paul the Deacon, an 8th-century historian</note>. Cassiodorus, in Book 3 of his *Various Letters*, calls it Pannonia Sirmiensis... <note>original: *ad Colosseum*</note> Pannonia is also found in the works of Lazius <note>Wolfgang Lazius, a 16th-century Austrian scholar</note>, cited from Ptolemy and Pliny. Today, Pannonia is occupied by Austria, Carinthia, and Carniola; in our time, Lower Pannonia is under Hungary, which is called *Węgierska* <note>original: *VVergierska*, a Slavic/Polish name for Hungary</note> in the Slavic tongue. Savia Pannonia is designated as Slavonia by Lazius, and he calls Valeria <unclear>Rheuatumbaten</unclear>. A part of Poeonia toward Thrace, where Rhodope is situated, is called Klokotinitza <note>Greek: *klokotiniza*</note>, according to Eustathius. See the book written by Lazius in the German language concerning the Kingdom of Hungary. All the Pannonians were called Poeonians by the Greeks especially, but not without error, as [Chapter] 49 shows. Not once, but many times, "Poeonians" is incorrectly read for "Pannonians" in Appian's *Illyrian Wars*. The same flaw is found in the *Marvelous Things* of Aristotle: regarding what is said of gold, see Amanteni, Haginoia, Gepidi, Panoperos, and Poeonia.

<header>Languages of this World.</header>

[The Hungarian language is] unique, having nothing in common with that of the Germans or Poles, nor with any of the Western nations either. So much so that some wish to say that they were anciently the true Getae <note>An ancient Thracian people related to the Dacians</note> who lived at the foot of Mount Haemus <note>The Balkan Mountains</note>, and that having been driven out by the Scythians <note>Nomadic people of Central Asia and Eastern Europe</note>, they retreated to the country they hold today. Others are of the opinion that they were Vlachs <note>Romance-speaking peoples of the Balkans and Eastern Europe</note>. Theodore Bibliander <note>A Swiss linguist and scholar (1506–1564)</note>, in his *Commentary on the Common System of All Languages and Letters*, writes concerning the Hungarians or Huns, whose Prince was once Ethele or Attila, the scourge of an angry God, as Matthias of Miechów <note>A Polish physician and historian (1457–1523) also known as Matthias à Michou</note> records: "The Iuhres or Iuhri <note>Referring to the Yugra people of the Ural Mountains region</note> from the land of Iuhra, the northernmost and coldest part of Scythia near the Northern Ocean, 500 great German miles to the East and North of the city of Moscow, descended and came through the flat lands to the South into the region of the Goths in Scythia where the Zahadaian or Zavolensian Tartars now live." And after the deeds of Attila are listed, he says: "All of Pannonia <note>A Roman province encompassing parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note> was the land of the Slavs. But the Iuhri slaughtered the Slavic inhabitants of Pannonia and occupied the land in this region, with the Slavs remaining and living only on the borders of Pannonia. Note first, that the Iuhri were named for the region of Iuhra in Scythia from which they originated and went forth, and even to our times they are called *Hugri* by the Bohemians, Poles, and Slavs; by others they are called *Hugui*, and finally they were called *Hungari*. Note second, that the language, speech, and sharp pronunciation are the same for the Iuhri in Hungary and those who live in Iuhra in Scythia. However, the Hungarians in Pannonia are Christians and more refined and abundant in all things; the Iuhri in Scythia, however, remain idolaters and wild to this day." For a clear understanding of the above, one should see the aforementioned Matthias of Miechów, Book 2, Chapter 5, of *European Sarmatia*, where he asserts that the Hungarians of today, descended from the ancient Iuhres, use a language similar to that of the aforementioned Iuhres, except that these Hungarians have added some words from the Slavic language to their tongue concerning things that are not found in Scythia and Iuhra. Sebastian Münster <note>A prominent German cartographer (1488–1552)</note>, in Book 4 of his *Universal Cosmography*, confirms the above. This is also done by Sigismund von Herberstein <note>A diplomat and author of an early influential account of Russia</note> in his *Commentaries on Muscovite Matters*, and George Wernher <note>A Hungarian author who wrote on geography</note> in his *Memoranda on the Admirable Waters of Hungary* dedicated to the said Sigismund von Herberstein.

By the name of Pannonia, I do not only understand that bank of the Danube with which that which is called Second Pannonia runs from the Arabo river (which Ptolemy calls the Narabo, now commonly the Raba) to the Sava; but whatever else the Hungarians hold on the other bank of the Danube, which indeed extends very widely. For they hold the entire region of the Iazyges Metanastae <note>An ancient nomadic tribe of the Sarmatians</note> which Ptolemy bounds by the Danube and Tisza rivers and the Sarmatian mountains. These are the Sarmatian mountains that separate the Hungarians from the Ruthenians <note>A historical name for East Slavic peoples</note>, Poles, Moravians, Silesians, and that part of Austria which is on this side of the Danube. To these mountains belongs the Carpathus <note>The Carpathian Mountains</note>, now by such a common name that the entire range of Sarmatian mountains is called Carpathus; although to me, looking at Ptolemy's description, Carpathus seems to be bounded by the same borders as Dacia <note>The ancient region roughly corresponding to modern Romania</note>. Furthermore, there still exists a nation of Iazyges among the Hungarians, whom they call by the shortened name *Iaz* <note>The Jasz people, who migrated to Hungary in the 13th century</note>, and they still retain their ancestral and particular language, very different from Hungarian; and they hold those seats which they once held in Pliny's description—namely the fields and plains—the Dacians having been driven (as he also says) to the Patissus river, which I take to be the Tissus (by dropping the first syllable), or as they now commonly call it, the Tisza. This is indeed the Tibiscus for Ptolemy, the boundary of ancient Dacia, whose most cultivated part is Transylvania...

> ...crowded with many inhabitants. For there, both the Germans—whom they call [Saxons]—and the Hungarians live; as do the most ancient of the Hungarians, called the Szeklers <note>original: "Siculi"</note>, who in their own language [call themselves *Székely*] and in imitation of this are called "Ceculi" by some. They also live alongside the very ancient remnants of the Romans, the Vlachs <note>original: "Valachos," the ancestors of modern Romanians</note>, who have frequent villages and towns. Nevertheless, the Hungarians are the masters of affairs, and the government is theirs; thus it happens that the Transylvanians are also considered Hungarians. There is indeed a truly marvelous mixture of diverse nations and more than one language throughout all of Hungary, just as I have said in that commentary where I attempt to explain the affairs of Hungary, the names of its peoples, their laws, customs, and institutions.

Sebastian Münster <note>A famous German cartographer and scholar (1488–1552)</note>, in Book 4 of his *Universal Cosmography* in the chapter on Wallachia <note>original: "Vua..."</note>—a region of Thrace once called Gethic, partly subject to the King [of Hungary] and the other part to the Great Turk—writes that in this province, those called the Flacci were descended from the *Quirites* <note>A term for Roman citizens in their civil capacity</note> who went there to live with a colony of Romans. The Roman language, though altered and corrupted in all sorts of ways, still holds such sway that a Roman man could barely recognize it. Modern historians assert, however, that in this province they use the Ruthenian or Slavonic speech.

Nicolas Chalcondyle <note>Laonicis Chalcondyles (c. 1423–1490), a Greek historian who documented the rise of the Ottoman Empire</note>, in Book 5 of the *History of the Turks* describing Transylvania, assures us that the language used by its people is part Vlach and part Hungarian, whose customs they follow. They are also subjects of the King of Hungary, who sends to his court such a chief and governor as he sees fit; nevertheless, they do not cease to enjoy their ancient liberties and exemptions, and in every place they keep faith with their particular laws and customs, all of which answer to Hermannstadt <note>original: "Hermenstat," modern-day Sibiu in Romania</note> as the metropolitan city.

The same author, in the following chapter on the Transylvanian Province of Hungary, writes that the Transylvanians for the most part use the German language, but that the inhabitants of Szeklerland <note>original: "Ceculie"</note>, a region of the aforementioned Transylvania, have another language than the aforementioned Transylvanians because these Szeklers <note>original: "Ceculiés"</note> speak Hungarian. These have principal cities which they call "seats" <note>Administrative districts known as *székek* in Hungarian</note>, namely Kézdi <note>original: "Kysdy"</note> and Orba, in which they exercise the judiciary and where all assemble when they wish to treat great affairs.

The same author, in the next chapter on the fertility of Transylvania, says it is very populous and continues that the people for the most part use the Germanic tongue, and principally that of the Saxons, which one can especially perceive in the "Old Land" <note>original: "Altandie," likely referring to the *Altland*, the primary territory of the Transylvanian Saxons</note>.

Furthermore, the aforementioned author, in the chapter following concerning the government of said Transylvania, reports that the Kings of Hungary have had the superintendence over this country and have governed it by a Provincial [Governor] or Bailiff whom they call in their language a Voivode <note>original: "V..."—referring to the *Vajda*</note>. This Lieutenant is usually elected from three different peoples: namely Szeklers, Vlachs, and Teutons <note>Germans</note>. [Some have become] Vice-Roy, and what is more, some have reached the royal dignity, as can be seen in Matthias Hunyadi, called Corvinus <note>Matthias Corvinus (1443–1490), one of the most powerful Kings of Hungary, who was of Transylvanian noble descent</note>, who brought the country of Transylvania under his obedience and forced its people by power to the Christian religion.

## Concerning the region of the Poles.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' within a square frame featuring floral scrollwork.</image-desc>
Abraham Ortelius <note>A famous Flemish cartographer and geographer (1527–1598)</note> in his geographical synonyms and treasure <note>original: "synonymes & thresor Geographiq."</note> discusses the Slavs and Slavonia. I shall describe them in the words of Master Adam [of Bremen], which are in the second book of his *Ecclesiastical History*: "This most vast province of Germany <note>In this period, 'Germany' often referred broadly to the Central European regions beyond the Rhine</note> is inhabited by the Vinuli, who were once called Vandals. Its width stretches from the South to the North—that is, from the Elbe river all the way to the Scythian Sea <note>The Baltic Sea</note>. Its length begins from the parish of Hamburg and extends Eastward as far as Bavaria, Hungary, and Greece." The same author names these peoples as the Wagrians, Obotrites, Polabians, Lingones, Warnabi, Chizzini, Circipani, Helveconæ (the Hevelli according to Widukind), Doxani, Lubuszani, Vilini, and Stoderani; read Helmod’s account of these Slavs. See also the Carniolans.

Vandals, Venedi, Finns, and Slavs—according to Melanchthon in his commentary on Tacitus, who mentions them all—are various names for one and the same nation. Eutropius mentions the Vandals. They are called *Bandiloi* <note>original: "βανδίλοι"</note> in the works of Zosimus and Suidas, and *Bandali* in the Panegyric of Mamertinus. Albert Krantz <note>A German historian (1448–1517)</note> calls the Bohemians, Poles, Russians, and Dalmatians "Vandals," for he says that the region of Vandalia encompasses all these lands. In the vernacular language, they are named *Vuenden* and *Vuinden* <note>Wends and Winds</note>. P. Niuemontius rejects this opinion in his commentary on Meissen <note>original: "Misniæ"</note>. Regarding these matters, read David Chytraeus in his *History of Saxony*.

Some modern authors assert that the name of Poland <note>original: "Pologne"</note> comes from the situation of the province, because the country is almost one continuous flatland and an open plain. This is called *Pole* in the Slavic <note>original: "Esclauõne"</note> language, which also signifies "the hunt," because in such flat and open country it is easy to hunt; indeed, it is well known that the Poles are among the greatest hunters on earth. Some call them Polacks, others Lachians or Lechians, as if to say the successors and heirs of Lech <note>The legendary founder of Poland</note>. This can be seen in the fact that the Muscovites and Russians of today call them *Laches*, and the Hungarians call them *Lengel* or *Lechel* after the aforementioned name of Lech, as confirmed by André Thevet in book 20, chapter 2 of his *Universal Cosmography*, having learned it from books 1 and 2 of the histories of Cromer <note>Marcin Kromer (1512–1589), a Polish historian</note>.

## Concerning the Polish language.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'N' within a square frame featuring floral and geometric patterns.</image-desc>
Laonikos <note>written here as Nicolas</note> Chalcondyles, in book 1 of his *History of the Turks*, maintains that the Triballians, Mysians, Illyrians, Croats, Poles, and Sarmatians <note>A general term for the peoples of Eastern Europe</note> all use the same language among themselves. And if I may be permitted to draw a conjecture from this, I would believe that they are all of the same race of people, without any difference between one and another. The same author in book 3 adds: the Poles are neighbors to the Sarmatians, whose language is entirely common to them; in their manners and ways of life, however, they agree more with the Italians and other Western peoples.

Paolo Giovio <note>An Italian physician and historian (1483–1552)</note>, in book 13 of his histories, held that the Poles, Muscovites, Lithuanians, and Roxolans <note>Ruthenians/Ukrainians</note> used the Illyrian language—otherwise called Slavic—but somewhat altered and corrupted, which all these peoples have changed through various inflections and pronunciations of voices and words. Sebastian Münster, in book 4 of his *Universal Cosmography*, assures us that the Lechites or Poles share a common language with the Slavs and Vandals...

# History of the Origin of the

Bulgarians, Serbians, Dalmatians, Croats, Bosnians, Bohemians, Russians, Lithuanians, Muscovites, and other peoples living in the surrounding areas, who differ very little in language, except that each of these peoples has its own particular way of speaking and pronouncing its words.

The characters that the Poles use in writing their language are composed partly of Greek and partly of those natural to their own country; their ceremonies are also mixed. Some hold to the Catholic, Apostolic, and Roman faith, while others follow the Greek schism <note>The Eastern Orthodox Church, which separated from the Roman Catholic Church in 1054</note> because they are close to the Muscovites. The men and women dress almost in the same fashion as the aforementioned Greeks.

This language of the Poles is in no way similar to the German language, but is as different from it as Basque is from Gascon, or French from Limousin, as I will demonstrate hereafter.

André Thevet, <note>A 16th-century French Franciscan priest, explorer, and cosmographer</note> in the first chapter of the twentieth book of his *Universal Cosmography*, describing the regions of Poland, writes that the King of Poland rules over all the lands that stretch from the German Sea <note>The Baltic Sea</note> all the way to the Greater Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>, excluding some Tartars who live nearby, and from Western Germany as far as Muscovy. This is best seen by the titles which the
<margin>»</margin> King of Poland uses in his letters and edicts: Sigismund Augustus, <note>Sigismund II Augustus (1520–1572), King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania</note> by the
<margin>»</margin> grace of God, King of Poland, Grand Duke of Lithuania, Russia, Prussia,
<margin>»</margin> Mazovia, Samogitia, Kiev, Volhynia, Podlasia, Livonia, etc., Lord and heir, etc. From this it appears in how many nations the Slavonic language is in use, seeing that all of Poland and the aforementioned provinces, as well as Bohemia, Muscovy, and Slavonia use this language; at least, whoever knows it will be understood without an interpreter in all these countries.

Laonikos Chalkokondyles, <note>A 15th-century Byzantine historian who wrote about the rise of the Ottoman Empire</note> in the thirteenth book of his *History of the Turks*, writes that the Prussians touch and border the Samogitians, a robust people practiced in labor, having a language and way of life entirely apart, though in certain things they show some agreement with the Greeks.

The Samogitians, neighbors of the Prussians and Lithuanians, use the same language as the Poles, inasmuch as their priests and preachers teach them the holy and divine word in the Polish language, and they follow the articles of faith of the Church of Rome. However, the Russians toward the East and the Muscovites who are to their North are devoted to the way of the Greeks and obey not the Roman Pope, but the Primate and Archbishop of Constantinople, as is deduced at length by Matthias of Miechów <note>A Polish Renaissance scholar and historian (1457–1523)</note> in the first chapter of the second book of his *European Sarmatia*, and Paolo Giovio <note>An Italian physician and historian (1483–1552)</note> in the 13th book of his histories. Furthermore, the aforementioned Polish language is currently in great use and fashion, and is understood throughout Russia, Volhynia, Podolia, Mazovia, Kuyavia, Livonia, Prussia, Pomerania, Silesia, Moldavia, and Wallachia. The Bible and the laws of Poland are in the common Polish tongue. Since some have stubbornly tried to maintain that the Polish language—and all that is included within it, along with the Swedes, Lapps, and 
<margin>»</margin> Pannonians <note>Peoples of the Roman province of Pannonia, roughly modern-day Hungary and surrounding areas</note>—was contained under the name of Germany, and that most of them used one and the same language, I have wished in this place to demonstrate to the more curious readers that their speech and pronunciation is as different as Basque is from Gascon, or French from Limousin.

### On the Region of the Lithuanians.

The Alani, or as Ptolemy reads *alannoi* <note>original Greek: "αλανοι"</note>, are the Lithuanians, according to Beatus Rhenanus in his commentary on Tacitus. <header>Languages of this Universe</header>

On these matters, see also Hegesippus <note>A 4th-century writer, likely the author of a Latin adaptation of Josephus</note>, Book 5, Chapter 50. I add this in passing: in the works of the aforementioned Suetonius <note>Roman historian, author of *The Twelve Caesars*</note>, I prefer to read "Albanians" rather than "Alaui"; for these are peoples of Asia neighboring the Parthians. The Alans, however, are grouped with the Europeans. Tacitus <note>Famous Roman historian, c. 56–120 AD</note> confirms my opinion in the *Annals*, Books 12, 13, and 15. I am aware that Zonaras <note>A 12th-century Byzantine chronicler</note> writes in Book 3 that the Alans were called Albanians by the ancients; let him see to that himself. See also the entries for "Scythians" and "Massagetae."

Tacitus doubts whether he should assign the Finns to the Germans or the Sarmatians <note>Ancient nomadic peoples of the Eurasian steppe</note>. Althamer <note>Andreas Althamer, a German humanist and geographer</note> thinks they are Prussians or Lithuanians. Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian geographer</note> places the *Phinnoi* <note>original: "φίννοι"</note> in this region. But to me, the "Finni" mentioned by Jordanes <note>original: "Iornandis"; a 6th-century Byzantine historian of Gothic descent</note> seem rather to be those who today inhabit Finland. They are also found in the Scandinavian peninsula, where there are also the "Scritifini" or "Christofinni," though more toward the North. These are so named from "leaping," which is a "barbarous word" according to the Deacon <note>Paul the Deacon, an 8th-century historian of the Lombards</note>. I believe it comes from *schricken* or *scriien*, a purely German word which means to spring back or to take great strides in walking with spread legs. For according to the eyewitness Olaus <note>Olaus Magnus, a Swedish ecclesiastic and writer famous for his map of the North</note>, they use wooden soles bound under the soles of their feet; with these, they seem to glide over snow and ice with an admirable speed, rather than run. These are also used among us in the winter time. We call them *SerieKschonen* <note>original: "SerieKschonen"; likely a version of "skating shoes" or "skis"</note>, as if one were to say "jumping shoes." It remains to be seen whether, because of this swift running, these same people were called the "Hippopodes" <note>literally "Horse-feet," a mythical race described by ancient geographers</note> by ancient writers.

The Massagetae <note>original: "μασσαγέται"</note> are commonly called Alans <note>original: "ἀλανοί"</note>, as Dio Cassius, Ammianus, and Gregoras write. John Tzetzes <note>Byzantine poet and grammarian</note> says one should consider the Massagetae to be the Abasgi <note>original: "ἀβασγοί"; an ancient tribe of the Caucasus</note>. Isaac Tzetzes, Evagrius, and Procopius in Book 1 of the *Vandalic War* write that the Massagetae were later called the Angi <note>original: "ἄνγοι"</note>; he also calls them Huns. Herodotus, in whose works a description of them is found, places them in the East, across the Araxes river, in the region of the Issedones. For Stephanus and Suidas <note>Byzantine encyclopedists</note>, the Massagetae are near or within Arachosia <note>an ancient satrapy of the Persian Empire, now in Afghanistan</note>. Ptolemy places them in Margiana and also in Sogdiana <note>ancient regions in Central Asia</note>. To Laonikos <note>Laonikos Chalkokondyles, a 15th-century Byzantine historian</note>, they appear to be the Chataidae; André Thevet calls them the Ahinadal. Ptolemy lists Massagetae in Margiana and others among the Sacae; see also Magog and the Scythians.

# On the language of the Lithuanians
## CHAPTER LXIX.

<image-desc>ornamental drop cap N featuring a human figure and floral motifs</image-desc>Nicolas Chalcondyle <note>Laonikos Chalkokondyles, author of *Histories*</note>, in Book 3 of his history of the Turks, writes that the Lithuanians join with the Poles and reach as far as the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>, and Podolia <note>A historic region in modern Ukraine</note> joins with the Sarmatians. The capital city of Podolia is Leopoli <note>modern-day Lviv, Ukraine</note>, and it extends from the Wallachians <note>historical inhabitants of Romania/Moldova</note> who live along the Danube, all the way to the Lithuanians and Sarmatians. Certainly, this people [the Lithuanians] deserves some praise, particularly for this: that they have never wished to change their language, but have always kept their own and still retain it today, even though in ancient times they were divided into two parts. One part had Princes and Lords whom they obeyed, and the other had Chiefs and Captains to govern them. Vilnius is large, rich, and well-inhabited. Thus, one can see that this people is the most powerful in all those quarters; yet they have no lack of prowess and valor, for they are constantly fighting with the German Prussians, Livonians, Muscovites, Tatars, and other such races of peoples by whom they are surrounded, in defense of their frontiers and borders. In their customs and ways of doing things, clothing, and manner of fighting, they follow their neighbors, taking something from each. And since a good par<unclear>t</unclear> of their country borders Podolia <note>A historical region in Eastern Europe, now mostly in Ukraine</note>, it happens very often that they come to blows with one another. Now, this language of the Sarmatians <note>The author uses "Sarmatian" here as a broad term for Slavic peoples</note> of which we have spoken so much is the very same used by the Illyrians or Slavs who inhabit the coast of the Adriatic Sea as far as the vicinity of Venice; this language, called Slavic, was anciently held in very high esteem by all the nations of the North and the East, and even throughout Greece. But as for saying which are the oldest, or who encroached upon the territories and dwellings of the others—whether it was the Slavs who first settled in Poland and Sarmatia and made their home there, or whether the Sarmatians, having set out toward the Danube, conquered Moesia, the land of the Triballi, and Slavonia likewise, which extends, as was said above, as far as the Venetians.

Sebastian Münster <note>A 16th-century German cartographer and cosmographer</note>, in Book 4 of his *Universal Cosmography*, in the chapter on Lithuania (a province dependent on the Kingdom of Poland), holds that the Lithuanians use and speak the Slavonic or Slavic language as do the aforementioned Poles, because this language extends very far and is common and vulgar <note>Meaning "common" or "widely spoken" rather than "crude"</note> to many nations. The same author, in the subsequent chapter on some cities of Lithuania, writes that these Lithuanians have four types of languages or tongues: the first is that of the Yotvingians <note>An extinct Baltic tribe related to the Lithuanians and Prussians</note>, which is commonly called *Jauuinger*; the second is that of the Lithuanians and Samogitians <note>A group in western Lithuania</note> described above; the third is that of the Prussians; and the fourth is that of the Livonians, inhabitants bordering the River Dzuina, which others call the Duna <note>The Daugava River</note>. And although it is the same language for all of these, nevertheless one will not understand the other unless he has spent time in all these lands. The ceremonies and customs of the Latins <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note> are kept in the said regions; but in the others surrounding them, such as Novigrod (or Novgorod), Pskov, Polotsk, Smolensk, and among the other Russians, they keep the ceremonies and ways of the Greeks <note>The Eastern Orthodox Church</note>.

...that they had arrived, and it has several Italian words in its speech. Concerning that Criue <note>original: "Criue"—likely referring to the Krive-Krivaitis, the high priest in Baltic paganism</note> and the City of Romowe <note>original: "Romoue"—a legendary central pagan sanctuary of the Old Prussians</note>, one reads in the Legend of Saint Adalbert <note>A 10th-century bishop and martyr who attempted to Christianize the Prussians</note>, Bishop and Martyr. And know that in Prussia now few speak Prussian <note>original: "Prutenicum"—the Old Prussian language, a Baltic tongue now extinct</note>; indeed, the language of the Poles and Germans <note>original: "Almanorum"</note> has crept in. So too in Lithuania few villagers profess this language, because German has crept in. In Samogitia <note>A region in western Lithuania known for preserving ancient traditions</note>, however, which is fifty miles in length, and in Lithuania, which contains thirty miles in length, in the villages they speak Lithuanian, and in a large part they profess Polish: for the priests also preach to them in the churches in the Polish language. Furthermore, know that this language group, divided into four parts, is entirely in obedience and faith to the Roman Church. In the other surrounding provinces, however—such as in Novgorod, in Pskov, in Polotsk, in Smolensk, and to the south beyond Kyiv—all are Ruthenians <note>original: "Rutheni"—ancestors of modern Ukrainians and Belarusians</note>, and they speak Ruthenian or Slavonic, and observe the Greek rite, and offer obedience to the Patriarch of Constantinople. T. Bibliander <note>Theodor Bibliander, a 16th-century Swiss scholar and author of a famous work on linguistics</note> reports these words in his commentary on all languages and letters.

The Northern Historians assure us in their histories that a man named Vytenis <note>Grand Duke of Lithuania from c. 1295 to 1316</note> was the first who began to bring these Lithuanians to light, and to bring them into fame and reputation among their neighbors. Against these neighbors, in a short time, they achieved very fine things with the help of the Samogitians—who were then, and still are, one and the same people with them—and the Yatvingians <note>original: "Iazinges"—likely the Baltic tribe of the Sudovians/Yatvingians, though sometimes confused with the ancient Sarmatian Iazyges</note>, who have since been entirely exterminated, so that with great difficulty the name alone has remained. Nevertheless, their language is still used in the surroundings of the Castle of Drohiczyn. The language of Prussia was also spoken there; but these Lithuanians have their own language, separate and particular, which is one with that of the aforementioned Samogitians, which the common people still keep. For the great Lords have adapted to the Polish language, and even the preachers use it in their sermons for the instruction of the people, although it is not at all very well understood. Sigismund von Herberstein <note>A 16th-century diplomat and author of the influential "Notes on Muscovite Affairs"</note>, in Book 1 of his history of Muscovy, confirms the above. Regarding the particulars of Lithuania, Vilnius is the capital city of the whole country, larger than Kraków, the capital of Poland, but not so populated, nor the houses so crowded; for they are all distinct and separated by squares and gardens. It is situated among hills and small mountains at the junction of the rivers Neris <note>original: "Vuelie"</note> and Vilnia, from which it takes its name. It is now surrounded by walls, having likewise several churches and monasteries of masonry, and among others that of the Franciscans <note>original: "Cordeliers"</note>, which is very magnificently built. However, there are more churches of the Greek or Ruthenian Religion than of the Roman Catholic, even though the Episcopal see is there. The next city today is Trakai <note>original: "Trochy"</note>, where there is ordinarily a great number of Jews, who do not lend at interest, but hold the farms and tax-offices <note>term: "Gabelle"—the system of leasing the collection of taxes, often including the salt tax, to private individuals</note>. This Lithuania, bearing the title of Grand Duchy, was united and incorporated into the Kingdom of Poland by King Władysław II Jagiełło and his cousin Vytautas Alexander <note>original: "Vitoudus Alexandre"</note> at the assembly in the town of Horodło <note>original: "Rodlo"</note> on the river Bug on the 2nd day of October 1413. It is governed like Poland by Palatines, Castellans, Chancellor, Captains, Marshal of the Land, and Marshal of the Court, and others.

### Of the Region of the Walachians.

A. Ortelius in his *Geographical Synonyms* and *Geographical Theater* states: Dacia <note>original: "δακία"</note> is a region of Europe according to Ptolemy. Strabo thinks they were anciently called Davos <note>original: "δαῦος"</note>, and writes that they inhabit the area toward the Danube and its sources. Philargyrus leaves this written in his commentary on Virgil's second *Georgic*. The Greeks called them Daos, according to Stephanus and Eustathius, and likewise Strabo in his *Epitome*. Those whom the Romans call Dacians, the Greeks call Getae, as stated by the same authors and Pliny. Regarding Dacia, Jordanes <note>A 6th-century Byzantine historian of Gothic descent</note> says: "This was Gothia, which our ancestors called Dacia; now it is called Gepidia." Suidas writes that in his time the Dacians were called Patzinaks <note>original: "Patzinacitæ"—a nomadic Turkic people</note>. Dacia of the ancients, as Stephanus and Ortelius show, includes today Transylvania, Walachia, and Moldavia. These include Mediterranean Dacia, Riparian Dacia, Pannonian Dacia, and Transylvania. Transylvania is called *Siebenbürgen* <note>original: "Vuibenburghen"—likely a variant of the German Siebenbürgen, meaning 'Seven Castles'</note> today by the Germans, but *Erdély* <note>original: "Herdel"</note> by the Hungarians. According to the author of the *Riparian and Mediterranean Dacia*, these are mentioned by Eutropius, Aurelius Victor, Jordanes, Marcellinus Comes, and the *Book of Notices* <note>original: "Liber notitiarū"—likely the Notitia Dignitatum, a document of the late Roman Empire's chancery</note>. The *Mixed History* places it between Dacia and Macedonia. Wolfgang Lazius places it between the rivers Tisza <note>original: "Tibiscū"</note>, Maros <note>original: "marisium"</note>, Criș <note>original: "Carisiū"</note>, and the Danube. The same authors mention Mediterranean Dacia. Today, as Lazius says, it is inhabited by Transylvanians, Saxons, Hungarians, and the Szeklers <note>original: "Cæculi"—a subgroup of the Hungarian people living in Transylvania</note>, the descendants of the Hungarians. The same Lazius names "Alpine Dacia" (by what authority I do not know), which he interprets as Moldavia and Walachia. Add to these what Leunclavius has in his *Muslim History*. The name Pannonian Dacia is frequent in Laonikos Chalkokondyles, who reports it is named *Erdély* <note>original: "Ardelium"</note>. It is clear this is a Greek term fashioned from *Herdel*. Moldavia is also called *Bogdania* by Laonikos. Godreccius writes that Transalpine Walachia is called "Lesser Black Bogdania" by the Turks (because it produces much grain). Laonikos speaks of "Black and Lesser Bogdania." Saint Paulinus makes a twofold Dacia in his verses *On the Return of Nicetas*:

> And the Getae run
> And both Dacians [from both sides of the river]
> Who dwell in the lands between.
> Or he of the much wealthy
> Well-clothed inhabitant of the bank.

Sextus Aurelius Rufus attributes this division to Aurelian; he names the same regions Dacia and Dardania. Eutropius says nearly the same. We have said more regarding this in the map in our *Theater*. Dacia is also a tract of Cappadocia, according to Jovius and Strabo, book 12.
Nicolas Chalkokondyles, book 1 of his *History of Turkey*. A. Thevet, chapter 5 of his *Universal Cosmography*. B. de Vigenère in his *History of Poland*.

The Histories of Poland relate that the Palatines <note>High-ranking officials or governors</note> or Voivodes <note>original: "Vayuodes"—a Slavic term for a military commander or governor</note> of Walachia had at all times been tributaries of the Kings of Hungary, and under their protection and obedience, until after the death of King Louis around the year 1388. Concerning their origin and beginning, it must be understood that what was anciently called Dacia was a great expanse of land which, on the Northern side, was bordered by the river Nester <note>The Dniester River</note>, which separated it from lower Russia and Podolia; toward the West it had the Iazyges Metanastae <note>An ancient nomadic tribe</note>; toward the East the Danube and Lower Moesia (since called Bulgaria); and on the Southern side the same Danube, which turns its course in this place toward Upper Moesia, which has taken the names of Bosnia and Serbia. The Emperor Trajan, having finally subjugated it, transported Romans there to repopulate it and reduced it to the form of a Province. But in the time of Gallienus, and later under Aurelian, the Barbarians reconquered it. The Goths also threw themselves into it during the Empire of Gratian, so that from this mixture the Walachians are descended. Having confounded the customs, ways of doing things, and language of the aforementioned, they made of them I know not what separate thing which no longer resembles anything else. However, they also use Ruthenian and Slavic speech. Regarding their name, it is said that it was a Roman named Flaccus who first gave it to them, and that from this they were called Falachi or Walachi; for the letters F and V (when used as a consonant) are easily changed into one another. Also, the Poles and all others who use the Slavic language call the peoples descended from the Italians by the common name *Włosi* <note>original: "Vulaſſiens, ou Vuloſſiens"—a term still used in Polish today to refer to Italians</note>, which closely approaches that of "Walachian." These people hold to the Christian Religion according to the custom and tradition of the Greeks <note>The Eastern Orthodox Church</note>. And although this Pro[vince] is not very large, nevertheless there are many languages of many [na]tions contained within it: and the persistence of the diversity of [lan]guages shows well that all this nation has been barbarian and unci[vilized]; otherwise, if there had been any communion of life among them, or [any so]ciety in deeds performed both during war and during peace, they [would have] received the same language and way of speaking, or at the very least [there would] not be such a great variety of languages among them. The fact is such [that to]day there are four peoples among them who have nothing in comm[on in lan]guage with one another, namely the Livonians, Estonians, Letts <note>original: "Lertierons," referring to Latvians</note>, [and Curo]nians. For throughout the villages in Livonia, these four la[nguages are spoken].

## On Russia and Muscovy.

The greatest Lord or Prince of all Russia without any doubt is the Muscovite, and the Grand Duke of Lithuania after him, then the King of Poland; other than these three, no one else lays claim to it, and even the last two are now but a single lordship. For Lithuania with its dependencies was united to the Kingdom of Poland by Jagiello <note>original: "Iaghellon"</note>, son of Algirdas <note>original: "Olgird"</note>, around the year of Salvation 1386. Russia, therefore, according to its ancient description, takes its beginning at the Sarmatian mountains <note>The Carpathian Mountains</note> toward the source of the Vistula river. And from there it extends along the river Tyras, otherwise called the Dniester <note>original: "Nester"</note>, as far as the mouths of the Borysthenes <note>The Dnieper River</note>, which enters into the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>, quite near Moncastre <note>Modern-day Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi</note>, which is now under the rule of the Turk. From there one must travel upstream to Cherkasy <note>original: "Circassi"</note>, and then to Kyiv <note>original: "Chiouie"</note>, once the capital city of all Russia, where one crosses the water to traverse the Province of Severia <note>original: "Seuvere"</note>, and several other lands directly toward the Rising Sun <note>the East</note>, until one reaches the springs of the Tanais <note>The Don River</note>, by which, according to the opinion of ancient cosmographers, Europe is separated from Asia. From the springs of the said Tanais, one finds on the left hand toward the Northeast <note>original: "le Grec"</note> and the North <note>original: "Tramontane"</note>, and after several days' journey one finally comes to the point and assembly of the two great rivers, the Oka and the Volga, which one must cross and turn even further to the left toward the Northwest <note>original: "Maestral"</note> and the West <note>original: "Ponant"</note>, through long and spacious stretches of country, until one reaches the borders of the kingdom of Sweden, and the land of Finland. And from there into Livonia, Samogitia, Masovia, and finally Poland, coasting along Silesia and Moravia, until one has found the aforementioned Sarmatian mountains again. As for the origin of the peoples of these regions, nothing is found except the little that their Annals contain: which claim they are descended from the race of Japheth <note>The son of Noah, traditionally considered the ancestor of Europeans</note>, from hand to hand, down to the Slavs who also gave rise to the Poles: for having no use of letters except

<header>History of the Origin of the [Russians]</header>

From the time of Michael, son of Theophilus, Emperor of Constantinople <note>Michael III, reigning 842–867 AD</note>, they were not able to record their deeds and actions in writing to leave any memory for posterity. Therefore, one cannot speak of them with any assurance or certainty, except since the year of the creation of the world 6370, according to the Ruthenian <note>A term used historically for the East Slavic people of the Kievan Rus'</note> calculation, which differs from ours by fifteen hundred years and more. However, this would correspond in our reckoning to the year of the world 4846, and around the year 886 of Jesus Christ, following the calculations of Funck, Mercator, and of Génébrard and Pontac <note>Referencing prominent 16th-century chronologists: Johannes Funck, Gerardus Mercator, Gilbert Génébrard, and Arnaud de Pontac</note> to the year of the world 49[unclear]... at which time the Russians found themselves in the city of Novgorod <note>original: "Nouogarde"</note> in great altercations and debates against one another, by reason of the power that each wished to seize. 

Since they could not agree among themselves, finally, by the counsel and advice of a wise personage of great authority among them named Gostomysl <note>original: "Goscomissel," a legendary figure in Novgorod’s history</note>, they resolved to send for the Vandals <note>Likely referring to the Varangians/Vikings, though often conflated with Vandals in early modern texts</note>, the most renowned nation of that time, in order to seek three young princes, brothers of the same blood, to govern them, among whom they divided the entire state. Thus, Rurik <note>original: "Rurich"</note>, who was the eldest, held Great Novgorod, but he made his residence at Ladoga, thirty-six leagues below. Sinaus, the second-born, went to live in the region of the White Lake <note>original: "Lac blanc," referring to Beloozero</note>. And Truvor <note>original: "Truuor"</note>, the youngest, in the principality of Pskov <note>original: "Plescouie"</note>, between the rivers Narva and the Dvina. 

These last two died without children, by which means all of Russia came to Rurik, who left an only son, Igor, at a young age, under the guardianship and tutelage of a very close relative named [Oleg] <note>The text likely cuts off the name of Oleg the Prophet</note>. Furthermore, these Russians hold that the mother <note>Historians usually identify her as the grandmother</note> of their Prince Igor—the aforementioned Rurik having gone to Constantinople to see the Emperor—was baptized there; instead of the name Olga <note>original: "Olpha"</note> which she had, she was named Helen. They claim she was the first Christian of all the Russians, and they have always since kept the traditions of the Greek <note>Eastern Orthodox</note> Church. 

Truly, others assert that a certain Prince of theirs named Vladimir <note>original: "Voloduuerus"</note> was the lord of all their country, and some time later received Baptism according to the custom of the Greeks with all his people. By this means, the Emperors of Constantinople, Basil and Constantine Porphyrogenitus, gave him their sister Anna in marriage, in the year of Salvation 983. Since then, the country has always remained in the Greek Christian religion. However, some have written that the Ruthenians have in their annals that they were preached to and taught the law and faith of Jesus Christ long before the aforementioned Vladimir and Olga, by Saint Andrew the Apostle. He traveled from Greece and first entered the Borysthenes river <note>The Dnieper River</note>, and traveling up its waters, he arrived at the place where Kiev <note>original: "Chiouie"</note> was built; in which place he first preached the Christian religion and erected crosses and other holy things for praying to and serving God.

See Matthias Miechow, book 2 of *European Sarmatia*, chapter [X]; Paolo Giovio in his book on *Muscovite Affairs*; Sigismund [von Herberstein] in book 1 of his *History of Muscovy*; André Thevet, book 19, chapters 8, 9, and 10 of his *Universal Cosmography*.

In the year 1592, during the time of the Pontificate of Pope Clement VIII, the Ruthenians living beyond the Danube, having previously been schismatics, submitted to the subjection of the Roman Church. In the year 1594, on the 2nd of December, a decree was made by these Ruthenians to align themselves entirely with the authority of the Catholic, Apostolic, and Roman Church, as can be [seen] <note>This refers to the Union of Brest, a key event where parts of the Eastern Orthodox Church in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth entered into communion with the Holy See</note>.

# Languages of this World

The decree which was printed in Cologne by Nicolas Steinius by Cardinal Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a prominent Vatican historian and cardinal</note>, to which decree several Ruthenian <note>East Slavic</note> prelates—mentioned in the aforementioned decree—subscribed with the consent of Sigismund, King of Sweden and Poland and Grand Duke of Russia; this decree was translated from the Ruthenian language into the Latin language <note>original: "langue Latine"</note> by the command of the aforementioned Pope Clement VIII.

As for the Country or Region of Muscovy <note>original: "Moſchouie"</note>, I remember having read in the Hebrew records that Meshech <note>original: "Moſoch"</note>, which in the Hebrew language <note>original: "langue Hebraique"</note> signifies "attracting," "prolonging," "fortifying," or "surrounding," was the name of one of the sons of Japheth in Genesis 10. From him, the Moschi—otherwise known as Muscovites—are descended according to those same Hebrews, as if one meant "men who use the bow" and are filled with great cruelty, as Alessandro Guagnini <note>An Italian-born chronicler of Polish history (1538–1614)</note> well noted in the second volume of his history of Poland. The personages who follow, namely Matthias of Miechów <note>original: "Matthias Michou"</note> in book 2, chapter 4 of *Sarmatia Europeenne*, and Sigismund von Herberstein <note>original: "Sigiſmond Liber"</note> in his history of Muscovy, hold that this Country and Region is thus named after its capital city, called Moscow <note>original: "Moſckuua"</note> in the language of the country, or, as is more likely, from a river bearing the same name, having its source in the Province of Tver <note>original: "Tuuerenſe"</note> and passing through the aforementioned city. 

André Thevet, in book 19, chapter 8 of his *Universal Cosmography*, says that although modern writers hold that the Russian people took their name from the capital city of the country, which they call Moscow <note>original: "Moſquua"</note>, it seems to me that this name comes from much further back. Given that the construction of this city is of fairly recent memory, we know that the ancients had knowledge of a certain Scythian people, not far from the Tanais <note>The ancient Greek name for the Don River</note>, who were called the Moschi. They inhabited the very region which is now called Muscovy, which is very close to Asia. But to speak truthfully, it is named after a river called the Moskva <note>original: "Mo-ſquua"</note>, which flows out of the Duchy of Tver, not far from the place called Oleshno; from there it reaches the chief city of the country and, having received several rivers, turns toward the East and extends into the great Oka River, and then goes into the Sea of Baku, called the Caspian. 

There are several other cities, each of which is the head of a province; but these provinces are small, and equal to several small bailiwicks <term>bailiwicks|French "bailliages," administrative districts under the jurisdiction of a royal officer or bailiff</term> of France, depending on how close the cities are to one another, for the names of the provinces depend on their jurisdictions. 

The first is Vladimir <note>original: "Vuoldimorie"</note>; the second, Murom; the third, Novgorod <note>original: "Nouogardie"</note>, otherwise known as Novgorod or Novigrod, the last city of the Christians on that side. All the rest hold to the law of Muhammad <note>original: "loy de mahomet," referring to Islam</note>, for although the Grand Duke of Muscovy still has a castle beyond there named Sura, and passes further on and has under his power the Cheremiss <note>The Mari people of the Volga region</note>—peoples moving toward the North beyond the river Volga or Delgel—and another nation called the Mordvins <note>original: "mordiuua"</note>, yet these Cheremiss are not Christians at all. Furthermore, they were usurped from the Great Khan of Tartary. One should know that there are two sorts of these Cheremiss: namely, those who are beyond the Volga river, and those who are neighbors of Novgorod, which is called the high country—not because it is mountainous, any more than the rest of Muscovy, but because there are some hills where these Muslim people live. From the south side comes a river named Sura <note>original: "Sore"</note>, which, turning to the East, goes to join the Volga.

Among all the Saints, they honor St. Jude the Apostle, saying they were converted by him to the Christian Religion; they also hold Saint Bartholomew in great honor, from whom they claim to have learned several articles of faith. There is an Archbishopric in the city of Lviv <note>original: "Leopoly," the Latin name for Lviv in modern-day Ukraine</note>, under which are these Russians or Ruthenians <term>Ruthenians</term><note>A historical term used to describe the East Slavic populations of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, primarily ancestors of modern Ukrainians and Belarusians</note>, and the Lithuanians. Theodore Bibliander <note>A 16th-century Swiss Orientalist and linguist</note>, in his *Commentary on the common reason of all languages and letters*, writes:

> But let us return to Europe, in which the Greek speech flourishes (of which we have spoken before), and also other languages; and first, let us speak of the Roxolanians <note>original: "Roxolanis," a historical term for Russians/Ruthenians</note>. Of whom Matthias of Miechów <note>original: "Matthias à Michou," a Polish Renaissance scholar</note> records these things in his second book: In Russia there are several sects. For there is the Christian Religion subject to the Roman Pontiff: and that one rules and prevails, although it is small in number. These Christians, according to the Roman rite, sing, pray, and read in the Latin language. There is another sect of Ruthenians, more numerous, which follows the rite of the Greeks, filling all of Russia; these follow the Greeks in habit and Ecclesiastical offices and have their own letters and an Alphabet similar and very close to the Greeks. In the churches of the Ruthenians, the language is that of the Serbians, which is Slavic <note>original: "Sclauonica," referring to Old Church Slavonic</note>; in this they celebrate divine rites, read, and sing. The third sect is that of the Jews—not usurers, as is the case in the lands of the Christians, but laborers, farmers, and great merchants; they often preside over custom-houses and public taxes. These pray in Hebrew in their synagogues, use the letters of the Hebrews, and their disciplines, even examining the liberal arts, Astronomy, and Medicine. The fourth sect is that of the Armenians, who enjoy their own rite and letters, and in their churches, they use the Armenian speech. These are most skillful merchants, penetrating to Caffa <note>original: "Cassam," a major trade port in Crimea</note>, Constantinople, Alexandria in Egypt, Cairo <note>original: "Allzairam"</note>, and parts of India, bringing back merchandise.

The above-cited Matthias of Miechów, in Book 2 of his *European Sarmatia*, Chapter 1, saying what the aforementioned T. Bibliander reports above, further pursues these words:

> The Ruthenians follow the Greeks in habit and Ecclesiastical offices and have their own letters and an Alphabet similar and very close to the Greeks.
