<meta>This page continues the discussion of the ecclesiastical and linguistic landscape of Eastern Europe, specifically focusing on the hierarchy of the Orthodox Church in Kyiv and Moscow, the legacy of the Council of Florence, and the origins of the Slavonic script as recorded by Renaissance historians like Matthias of Miechów and Sigismund von Herberstein.</meta>

[metro]politan <note>This word completes "Metropolitan" from the previous page</note> is of Kyiv, which was formerly the Metropolis of Russia. [He] has as subjects the Vladykas <term>Vladykas</term><note>A Slavic title for a high-ranking church official or bishop, literally meaning "lord" or "master"</note> and Bishops of the Greek rite in Moldavia and Wallachia as far as the river Ister or Danube; one in Russia at Chelm; another in the dominion of the Lithuanians at Vladimir or Brest; a third at Przemysl <note>original: "murouufci," likely a corruption of the Latin for Przemysl</note>; a fourth at Polotsk; a fifth at Lutsk; and a sixth at Smolensk. He also oversees all other Vladykas and Bishops in the lands of the Muscovites and in the North, under the jurisdiction of the expanded Muscovite territories. Isidore, the Metropolitan of Kyiv, a man most learned in the Greek language and doctrine, traveled with a hundred horses to the Council of Florence during the time of Pope Eugenius. He returned to Russia having accepted the precepts of the Roman Church. However, the Muscovites robbed him for preaching this Roman union and drove him toward his death. The Ruthenians <term>Ruthenians</term><note>A historical term for the East Slavic inhabitants of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, ancestors of modern Ukrainians and Belarusians</note> follow the Greek doctors and theologians, especially Basil the Great, Gregory Nazianzen, and John Chrysostom. They call Gregory Nazianzen "Bogoslov" <note>original: "Bogoflou," meaning "Theologian"</note> in their own language, which in Latin sounds like "praising God." They also accept our Roman Pope Gregory <note>Gregory the Great</note>, especially his books of *Morals*, which they read in translation; in their language, they call him "Besednik" <note>original: "Byeffednic"</note>, which signifies one who discourses, persuades, or preaches. In the churches of the Ruthenians, they celebrate divine services, read, and sing from books in the Slavonic language <note>original: "Sclauonica"</note>. However, in those of the Roman rite, they sing, pray, and read in the Latin tongue. In the churches of the Armenians, they use the Armenian speech; in the synagogues of the Jews, they pray in the Hebrew tongue.

Sigismund von Herberstein <note>original: "Sigismond Liber," a reference to the diplomat and author of the famous 16th-century account of Russia, "Notes on Muscovite Affairs"</note> says in his history of Muscovy: 

» It is uncertain who ruled the Ruthenians in the beginning. They lacked characters <note>letters or a script</note> by which their deeds could have been recorded. But after the Metropolitan of Constantinople sent Slavonic letters into Bulgaria in the year 863 <note>the date of the mission of Saints Cyril and Methodius</note>, then for the first time, not only the things then occurring, but also those they had received from their ancestors and retained through long memory, began to be recorded in their annals.

The same author, speaking of the Vandals, says:

» The Vandals were powerful in that age; they eventually adopted the customs and religion of the Ruthenians. It seems to me, therefore, that they called forth their Princes from the Wagrians, or rather the Varangians <note>original: "Vuaregis," the Viking group that founded the Rurik dynasty in Russia</note>, and drove from power those who were different from them in religion, customs, and language.

The Christian Russians of the Greek Church sing their Mass and celebrate divine service in their native tongue, and are spiritually subject to the Patriarch of Constantinople.

Mathias Michou <note>Matthias of Miechów (1457–1523), a Polish scholar and physician whose work *Tractatus de duabus Sarmatiis* was a primary source for Western Europeans regarding the geography of the East.</note> in book 2, chapter 4 of his *History of European Sarmatia* <term>Sarmatia</term><note>A historical region in Eastern Europe, often used in the Renaissance to refer to the lands of Poland, Lithuania, and Russia.</note> says these words regarding the Muscovite language:

> Let the reader understand that in Muscovy there is one language and one speech, namely Ruthenian or Slavonic <note>original: "Ruthenicum, seu Sclauonicum"</note>, in all the provinces and principalities. Thus, even the Ohulici and the Ruthenians who live in Vithea are Ruthenians and speak Ruthenian; they hold one sect and religion after the fashion of the Greeks. All the Vladykas <term>Vladykas</term><note>A Slavic title for a high-ranking church official or bishop.</note>, of whom there are many, are subject to the Patriarch of Constantinople, and requesting confirmation from him, they promise obedience. This excludes the Tartars of Kazan <note>original: "Cosnenses aut Cosanēfes"</note>, who, while recognizing the Duke of Moscow, worship Muhammad along with the Saracens and speak the Tartar language. It also excludes the foreigners dwelling to the North in Scythia <term>Scythia</term><note>An ancient term used here to describe the vast, little-known regions of Northern Eurasia.</note>, who speak their own tongues and languages and worship idols, as will be discussed in the following chapter.

The same author in chapter 5 continues with these words:

> Beyond Muscovy are peoples and regions between the North and the East at the edge of Northern Asia, which is properly called Scythia. These are subject to the Prince of Moscow, having been primarily subjugated by Ivan, Duke of Muscovy: namely Perm, Bashkir, Cheremiss, Yugra, and Karelia <note>original: "Perm, Baslzird, Cztiremissa, Iuhra, Corela"</note>. *Perm* is a monosyllable, from which comes the land of *Permska*, or *Permica* in two syllables. It was a region that worshiped idols, which Ivan, Duke of Moscow, forced to receive baptism about 20 years ago, according to the Ruthenian or Greek rite. He appointed for them a Vladyka—that is, a Bishop—named Stephen, whom the barbarians flayed alive and killed after the Duke’s departure. Upon his return, the Duke punished them and appointed another prelate, under whom they remain as new Christians, professing the Ruthenian schism and rite. The other aforementioned regions, however, persist in infidelity and idolatry. They worship the Sun, the Moon, the stars, the beasts of the forests, and whatever they encounter. They have their own languages and idioms: in the land of Permska a unique idiom, in the land of the Bashkirs a unique one, in Yugra a unique one, and in Karelia also a unique one. In these regions they do not plow, they do not sow, they have neither bread nor money. They eat the wild beasts of the forests, which are abundant among them, and drink nothing but water. They dwell in dense forests, in huts made of brushwood. And because the forests cover those lands, they have made the men wild and beast-like.

Sebastian Münster <note>A famous German cartographer and scholar (1488–1552).</note> in book 4 of his *Universal Cosmography*, in the chapter on Muscovy, describing this region at length, says these words regarding the language of the Muscovites: "The language they have is Slavonic; however, it is so mixed with foreign languages that the Slavonian and the Muscovite can no longer understand one another." Muscovy extends as far as Yugra and Karelia, which are in Scythia.

This same Giovio <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an Italian physician and historian known for his descriptions of Muscovy based on interviews with ambassadors.</note>, in the place cited above, mentioning the sacred books which these Muscovites use in their religion, says:

> « The history of the life and all the miracles written by the four Evangelists, as well as the Epistles of Paul, are recited in a clear voice from the pulpit during the performance of sacred rites. Priests of approved life read the homilies of the Doctors of the Church publicly, even during those hours when the sacraments are not being performed. For they do not believe it right to admit hooded orators <note>A reference to the preaching friars of the Roman Catholic Church, such as Dominicans or Franciscans.</note> who are accustomed to preaching to the gathered people and to discussing divine matters too ambitiously and subtly. Men of solid religion judge that the unrefined minds of the unlearned can attain a holier fruit of character through simple doctrine rather than through the highest interpretations of mysteries. These sacred books we have just mentioned, as well as the commentators on the New and Old Testaments—furthermore Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and Gregory—they have translated into the Illyrian <term>Illyrian</term><note>Here used as a synonym for the Slavic or Slavonic language.</note> tongue and preserve them religiously. The prelates and chiefs of the minor priests, appointed over individual cities and villages, look after sacred matters and settle controversies, and they pursue those with depraved morals with a certain supreme power of punishment. They seek the King of sacred matters, whom they call the Metropolitan <term>Metropolitan</term><note>The title for a high-ranking bishop in Eastern Christian churches.</note>, from the Patriarch of Constantinople. »

Sigismund Liber <note>Sigismund von Herberstein (1486–1566), a diplomat whose "Rerum Moscoviticarum Commentarii" became the standard Western reference on Russia.</note> writes as much in his *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs*. All these people admit they are Slavs, yet the Germans, taking the name from the Vandals alone, indiscriminately call all who use the Slavonic language Wends, Windens, or Windisch. »

This is what we perceived from your interpreters, whom you kept with you in court, as many as we were. For since those interpreters were born among the Croats and Dalmatians, and none of them had ever either visited the Muscovites, or... »

# History of the Origin of the [Muscovites]

« ...had stayed with them, yet those present then were still able to understand their words. » <note>original: "moratus cum eis fuerat..." This passage likely continues a description of an early missionary or traveler's interactions with the locals.</note> This same person says afterward: « They have schools <note>original: "Gymnasia [habent]"</note>, though few, in which the sons of nobles are instructed in literature—principally in sacred texts—in the Ruthenian language <note>The term "Ruthenian" was historically used to refer to the East Slavic languages and peoples of the region.</note>. Very few of them apply themselves to foreign languages. Most study Greek for the sake of the works of the holy Fathers Chrysostom, Nazianzen, Basil, and the rest <note>Referring to the Greek Church Fathers: John Chrysostom, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Basil of Caesarea.</note>, and for the sake of all those things derived from the Greeks which can be adapted to their customs or governance <note>original: "reg[imine]"</note>. They neglect Hebrew entirely, except for the fact that the word *Alleluia* is frequently used in the Mass. Matthew, Mark, Luke, John <note>original: "I[ohan]nes"</note>, the Epistles of Paul, and the others received by us along with the Apocalypse, are counted among the canonical Scriptures of the New Testament. Regarding the canonical books of the Old Testament, they assert the same as the Catholic Church has decreed. They acknowledge the Roman <note>original: "[Ro]manum"</note> Pontiff as the Vicar of Christ and successor of Peter; for this reason, the feasts of St. Clement, St. Leo, and the Divine Gregory used to be celebrated among the Muscovites. »

To be brief, we shall say that the historians of the Greek <note>original: "Empire C[onstantinopolitain]" or "Grec"</note> Empire, according to the account of the aforementioned Sigismund [von Herberstein] <note>A 16th-century diplomat whose "Commentarii" remains a primary source for early Russian history.</note> in his *Commentaries on Muscovite Matters*, hold that the Muscovites—who are none other than the Russians—used no written characters to record their deeds and history before the reign of Michael the Paphlagonian <note>Michael IV, Byzantine Emperor from 1034 to 1041.</note>, Emperor of Greece. Under his rule, in the year of the World 6406 <note>A date following the Byzantine calendar; roughly 898 AD, though the text later cites 1036 AD.</note>, they adopted the language and characters of the Slavs <note>original: "Esclauons"</note>, from whom they say they originate, notwithstanding that their princes boast of being descended from the Romans.

The said Muscovites assert in their histories that it is very difficult to know for certain who were the first to become Lords and command in Muscovy, Lithuania, and White Russia. They claim the cause of such ignorance is that the peoples of these regions used no written letters to record the deeds and actions of their Kings and states, and that very few of the ancients had true knowledge of these regions, given the errors and falsehoods that fill their history books. However, from the time of the aforementioned Greek Emperor Michael the Paphlagonian, they took up the letters and characters of the aforementioned Slavs, which also caused them to learn the language; for this Emperor sent people to instruct them in the year of Salvation 1036. Consequently, it has been only sixty some-odd years <note>The author's timeline here appears to be a miscalculation or based on a specific source's era.</note> since these Muscovites have had knowledge of letters. It is true that they then committed to writing in their Russian language what they had learned from father to son, held in long memory concerning their antiquity and that of their princes. See what André Thevet has deduced at length on this matter in Book 19, chapter 11 and following of his *Universal Cosmography*.

# History of the Origin of 856

...one who has several Dukes under his obedience is called *Velikiy Knyaz* <note>original: "Vueliki Knefi," a phonetic rendering of the Russian *Velikiy Knyaz*, meaning Grand Prince or Grand Duke.</note>, which is to say 
->**Grand Dukes**.<-

The aforementioned Muscovites also call their Grand Duke *Czar* <note>original: "Kear," likely an OCR error or archaic spelling for Tsar.</note>, which in the Russian language signifies King; but in Slavonic, Polish, Hungarian, and Bohemian, its meaning carries as much weight as Emperor or Caesar. For "King," or *Korol* <note>original: "Kiraill," likely referring to the Slavic word *Korol*, derived from the name of Charlemagne.</note>, signifies to them the same as "King" does to us. Some peoples call him the **White King** in Slavonic, for just as the Sophy <note>The Safavid Shah of Persia.</note> is called *Kizilbash* <note>original: "Kufilpaſſa, Cufelbas or Caſelbas." From the Turkish *Kızılbaş*, meaning "Red-head," referring to the red caps worn by his followers.</note> because the royal ornament he wears on his head is red, so too the Muscovite is named "White" because the royal ornament he wears on his head is of that color. This Duke takes the name of King when writing to anyone except the King of Poland (as I have already mentioned), but there is no one who honors him with the title of King, except for some of his own people and those of Livonia. Furthermore, no Great Pontiff [Pope] nor Emperor has crowned him King, as has happened to those who currently bear that honorable title. And when he commands those who call him thus, and they are asked the reason for it, they respond that the royal name is well-deserved by him, since kings are his tributaries.

Sigismund von Herberstein <note>original: "Sigifmond Liber," a reference to Baron Sigismund von Herberstein (1486–1566), a diplomat whose *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs* became the primary Western source on Russia.</note> has written on this subject in his *Commentary on Muscovite Affairs* the following words, which are worthy of being recited in full in this place:

> He exercises his authority over both spiritual and secular matters alike; he decides freely and according to his own will over the lives and property of all. Among the counselors he has, none is of such great authority that they would dare to disagree or resist him in any matter. They publicly declare that the Prince's will is the will of God, and whatever the Prince does, he does by the will of God. For this reason, they also call him the key-bearer and chamberlain of God, and they believe him to be the executor of the divine will. Hence, if ever prayers are offered for some prisoner or another grave matter, he himself is accustomed to answer: "When God commands it, he shall be released." Likewise, if someone asks about an uncertain or doubtful matter, they commonly reply: "God knows, and the Great Prince." It is uncertain whether such a brutal people requires such a Prince, or whether the people themselves are made so brutal, harsh, and cruel by the tyranny of the Prince.
> 
> From the time of Rurik until this present Prince, those princes used no other title than Grand Dukes of either Vladimir, Moscow, or Novgorod, etc., except for Ivan Vasilyevich <note>Ivan III, the Great (r. 1462–1505).</note>, who called himself Lord of all Russia and Grand Duke of Vladimir, etc. This Basil [Vasily], son of Ivan <note>Vasily III (r. 1505–1533).</note>, claims for himself both the title and the name of King in this manner: "The Great Lord Basil, by the grace of God, King and Lord of all [Russia], and Grand Duke of Vladimir, Moscow, Novgorod, Pskov, Smolensk, Tver, Yugra, Perm, Vyatka, Bulgaria, etc. Lord and Grand Duke of Lower Novgorod, and Chernigov, Ryazan, Polotsk, Rzhev, Belaya, Rostov, Yaroslavl, Beloozero, Udoria, Obdoria, Kondia, etc." Furthermore, since everyone calls this Emperor *Czar*, it seems necessary that I explain both the title and the cause of this error. *Czar* in the Ruthenian [Russian] language signifies King; however, since in the common Slavonic language among the Poles, Bohemians, and all others, it is taken as a phonetic derivation from the last and heavy syllable of "Caesar," an Emperor is understood by it. Therefore, all who are ignorant of the Ruthenian idiom or letters...

<margin>cc</margin> Likewise the Bohemians, Poles, and even the Slavs subject to the Kingdom of Hungary, call a King by another name, namely *Kral* <note>original: "Kral"; this Slavic word for King is derived from the name of Charlemagne (*Karl*).</note>, others *Kyrall*, and some *Koroll*. They believe that *Czar* <note>original: "Czar"; the Slavic title for "Tsar."</note> only refers to a Caesar or Emperor. From this, it happened that the Ruthenian <note>A historical term for the East Slavic peoples of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and Muscovy.</note> interpreters, hearing their Prince called this by foreign nations, began thereafter to call him Emperor themselves. They believe the name *Czar* is more dignified than that of King, even though they signify the same thing. However, if you examine all their histories and the Holy Scripture, you will find *Czar* used for the name of King, and *Kessar* <note>original: "Kessar"; a Slavic rendering of the Latin *Caesar*.</note> for the name of Emperor. By this same error, the Emperor of the Turks is called *Czar*, although he has anciently used no other more eminent title than that of King, which is *Czar*. Hence, the European Turks who use the Slavonic language call Constantinople *Czarigrad* <note>original: "Czarigrad"; literally "The City of the King" or "The Caesar's City."</note>, as if you were to say "The Royal City." There are those who call this Prince of Muscovy the **White King**. I indeed diligently sought the cause why he should be called by the name of White King, since none of the Princes of Muscovy had used that title before. In fact, when the opportunity arose, I said openly to the Councilors themselves that we do not recognize him as a King, but as a Grand Duke. Most, however, thought the reason for this Royal name was that he had Kings under his Empire; others had no reason at all. I believe, however, that just as they now call the Persian *Kussilpassa* <note>original: "Kussilpassa"; from the Turkish *Kızılbaş*, meaning "Red-head," referring to the Safavid headwear.</note>—that is, "Red Head"—because of the red coverings of his head, so the Russians are called "White" because of their white head coverings. Furthermore, he uses the title of King toward the Roman Emperor and the Pope, the King of Sweden and Denmark, and the Masters of Prussia and Livonia, etc. As I have learned, he uses it toward the Prince of the Turks as well, but he is called King by none of them in return, unless perhaps by the Livonians. In ancient times, they used to employ titles arranged within three circles included in a triangle, the first of which, in the uppermost circle, contained these words:

->Deus noster Trinitas, quæ fuit ante omnia secula, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus Sanctus:non tamen tres Dij,sed vnus Deus in sustantia.<-
<note>Translation: "Our God the Trinity, who was before all ages, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: yet not three Gods, but one God in substance."</note>

In the second circle was the title of the Emperor of the Turks, with the added phrase "To our beloved brother." In the third was the title of the Grand Duke of Muscovy, by which he confessed himself King and heir and lord of all Russia, East and South, in which we saw the common formula added: "We have sent to you our faithful Councilor." To the King of Poland, however, he uses a title of this sort: "The Great Lord Basil <note>Referring to Vasily III, Grand Prince of Moscow.</note>, by the grace of God Lord of all Russia, and Grand Duke of Vladimir, Moscow, Novgorod, Smolensk, Tyumen, Yugra, Perm, Bulgaria, etc.," omitting the title of King. For neither of these rulers deigns to accept the letters of the other if they are increased by a new title. This indeed happened while we were in Muscovy, when the Muscovite received with great reluctance the letters of King Sigismund <note>Sigismund I the Old, King of Poland.</note> sent to him, because they had been increased by the title of Duke of Masovia. Some write that the Muscovite sought the name and royal title from the Roman Pontiff and from the Emperor Maximilian; this does not seem likely to me, especially since he is more hostile to no man than to the Supreme Pontiff, whom he deigns to call only by the title of "Doctor." Moreover, he considers the Roman Emperor no greater than himself, as appears from his letters, in which he places his own name before the title of the Emperor. The name for a Duke among them is called *Knes* <note>original: "Knes"; the Slavic *Knyaz*, usually translated as Prince or Duke.</note>; nor did they ever have any other greater title, as I said, than with that word "Grand" added. For all others who had a single principality were called *Knes*; but those who had several principalities and other *Knes* subject under their empire were called *Vueliki Knesi* <note>original: "Vueliki Knesi"; *Velikiye Knyazya*, or Grand Princes.</note>, that is, Grand Dukes. Nor do they have any other rank or dignity after the Boyars <note>original: "Boiaros"; the high-ranking nobility in Russia.</note>, who in our manner hold the place of nobles or knights. In Croatia, the leading men are similarly called *Knesi*; among us, however, as in Hungary, they obtain only the name of Counts.

### On the Goths.

Johannes Magnus <note>Johannes Magnus (1488–1544) was the last Catholic Archbishop of Sweden and a historian who wrote about the ancient origins of the Goths and Swedes.</note>, in book 1 of his *History of the Northern Peoples*: The first seat of the Goths in Scythia <note>A vast region of central Eurasia inhabited by nomadic groups in antiquity.</note> was more memorable near the Pontic Sea <note>The Black Sea.</note>; from there, the name of the nation became more famous, and from there they were called *Scythiae*, that is, the "victors of the Scythians" <note>original: "Scythiæ, hoc est Scytharum victores"</note>. However, I do not deny that they were later called sometimes Scythians, sometimes Goths, or Getas. Indeed, they ruled according to a diversity of languages; just as in their native soil they were called Westrogoths (meaning Western Getas) and Ostrogoths (meaning Eastern [Getas]), so in foreign lands and foreign tongues, they were called now Samagetae, now Massagetae—whom Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian (c. 64 BC–24 AD).</note> in book 11 affirms were the Eastern Goths—and finally they were called Thyssagetae. Therefore, both the Greeks and the Latins not infrequently named the Goths themselves with an interchangeable name, using one or the other for the same people.

And Paulus Orosius <note>A 5th-century priest and historian; his *History Against the Pagans* was a standard reference in the Middle Ages.</note> in book 1 testifies to the same. "Now," he says, "those Getas, who are also now called Goths—whom Alexander [the Great] declared should be avoided, whom Pyrrhus dreaded, and whom Caesar even turned away from." Furthermore, Procopius <note>A prominent Byzantine scholar and historian of the 6th century.</note>, writing about Witiges <note>King of the Ostrogoths (reigned 536–540) during the Gothic War.</note> besieging Rome, says: At that time, the Roman Patricians brought forth the sayings of the Sibyl <note>Prophetic priestesses in ancient Greece and Rome; their "Sibylline Books" were consulted during crises.</note>, asserting that the city would be in danger until the month of July, and finally that Rome should fear nothing "Getic" <note>original: "Geticum," referring here to the Goths.</note>. Indeed, these authors affirm that the Goths were of the "Getic" nation, as do many other ancient and modern authors, such as the Greek Dio [Cassius], who titled his histories "On the Getic Affairs." 

Furthermore, Jordanes the Goth <note>A 6th-century Roman bureaucrat of Gothic descent who wrote the *Getica*, a history of the Goths.</note>, in his history, calls them now Goths, now Getas. And Paul the Deacon <note>An 8th-century Benedictine monk and historian of the Lombards.</note> affirms they were "Gothogetas" in his life of Narses. Olaus <note>Olaus Magnus, brother of Johannes, famous for his map of the North and descriptions of Nordic customs.</note> on leaf 245 [writes]: "I too, if my experience deserves any credit, can testify that I am called *Ostrogeta* by my fellow Goths, though I am called *Ostrogoth* by the Latins; for from the most ancient times in our homeland we have used the name *Getha*, which the Latin tongue is accustomed to calling *Goth*."

Nor does Herodotus, the father of histories, disagree with this interchangeable naming, as he asserts that the Massagetae (that is, the Ostrogoths) expelled the Scythians from their seats, then set out and drove out the Cimmerian <note>An ancient nomadic people mentioned by Homer and Herodotus.</note> inhabitants and held their lands. This is also testified by Raffaele Volaterrano <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), a humanist scholar.</note> in book 7, citing Strabo and Homer, who affirms in the *Odyssey*, book 10, that they arrived from the far West. No one well-versed in history is ignorant of how true this is regarding the Goths occupying Cimmeria. Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century geographer and astronomer.</note> also affirms this opinion, saying that the Massagetae settled in the interior of Asia, in the region of the Scythians. 

Therefore, unless the prudent reader notices that Goths and Getas are the same people, and that they were sometimes called Scythians, sometimes Cimmerians, or Thracians by the nations they conquered, they will never understand Gothic or Scythian history. Indeed, while King Philimer <note>A legendary early king of the Goths who led them from the Baltic to the Black Sea.</note> was still living, after they had driven out the Cimmerians, they were not only called Cimmerians but also Scythians, having taken the name from the land they occupied. Herodotus, following this victory, says they were not content to have expelled the Cimmerians from their seats, but asserts they followed those who had fled with such impetus and fury that they could not distinguish the path they were meant to take, etc.

Blaise de Vigenère <note>A French diplomat, cryptographer, and alchemist (1523–1596).</note>, in his *Treatise on Ciphers*, leaf 334, has described very particularly the history of these Goths, and of their travels and conquests.

<summary>This page discusses the historical identity and various names of the Goths, arguing through numerous classical and Renaissance sources that the Goths, Getas, and Massagetae are essentially the same people originating from Scythia.</summary>

# History of the Origin of
# Of the Language of the Goths.

A certain Archbishop of Toledo <note>Likely Rodrigo Jiménez de Rada (c. 1170–1247), a celebrated Spanish historian and prelate who wrote about the history of the Goths.</note> believed, though without evidence, that the alphabet of the Goths was the first and most ancient of letters, which were given by God at the beginning of the world to our first Father [Adam]. This is entirely contradicted by Saint Jerome <note>A 4th-century scholar and Bible translator.</note> in chapter 9 of his commentary on the Prophet Ezekiel, where he states that in the ancient books of the Samaritans <note>A group related to the ancient Israelites; their script is a descendant of Paleo-Hebrew.</note>, the letter *Tau* <note>The final letter of many ancient Semitic alphabets, often associated with a mark of protection.</note> has the shape of a cross. This cannot be reconciled with the figure of the Gothic letter, a matter treated very extensively by Goropius Becanus <note>Johannes Goropius Becanus (1519–1572), a Dutch physician known for his creative theories on the "original" languages of humanity.</note> in book 5 of his *Hieroglyphics*, by Sixtus of Siena <note>A prominent biblical scholar and Jewish convert (1520–1569).</note> in book 2 of his *Library*, and by Alanus Copus <note>A pseudonym for Nicholas Harpsfield or Alan Cope, Catholic scholars defending the faith against Protestant critics.</note> in his *Dialogues against Heretics*, book 4. On this subject, Friar Luis of Portugal <note>Luis de Sotomayor, a 16th-century Portuguese theologian.</note> writes in book 1, chapter 1 of his *Globe*:

> "It appears most clearly that the most reverend Lord [Archbishop] of Toledo was mistaken when he thought the alphabet of Gothic letters was the first alphabet and the first characters given to our first parent. This is refuted by the authority of Saint Jerome on chapter 9 of Ezekiel, saying that in the ancient books of the Samaritans, the *Tau* had the likeness of a cross. Saint Jerome was not speaking of the Gothic T at all, but of the Hebrew one, which indeed represents the sign of Christ’s Cross." <note>original: "manifestissime apparet lapsum fuisse reuerendissimum Dominum Sal- chiep. Tole, dum existimauit Alphabetum litterarum Gotthicarum primum Alphabetum... Diuus Hieronymus minime loquatur de littera T, Gothica, sed Hebrea quæ quidem signum & Christi Crucem repræsentat."</note>

Northern historians hold that a certain Ulfilas or Gulphila <note>Ulfilas (c. 311–383 AD), a Goth who became a bishop and is famous for creating the Gothic alphabet to translate the Bible.</note>, a Goth by nation and successor to Theophilus in Gothia, living under the Arian Emperor <note>Valens (reigned 364–378), who supported Arianism, a Christian doctrine that was later declared heretical.</note>, and who was originally Orthodox (of whom Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century historian of the church.</note> in book 4, chapter 33 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, Sozomen <note>Salminius Hermias Sozomenus, another 5th-century historian.</note> in book 6, chapter 34, and the *Tripartite History* in book 8, chapter 13 speak at length), was the first who invented letters and characters for those of his nation. He was also the first to translate the Holy Scriptures from the Greek tongue into the Gothic language, explaining them to the people according to Catholic doctrine. This is confirmed by Sixtus of Siena in his *Sacred Library*.

On the contrary, Johannes Magnus <note>Latin: "Iean le Grand" (1488–1544), a Swedish archbishop and historian who sought to glorify the ancient history of his people.</note>, a writer on the Goths, claims they used these letters and characters—attributed to the aforementioned Ulfilas or Gulphila—long before his time. However, he does confess that this figure was the first to use them in a version he made of the Holy Scriptures. For this reason, he was reputed to be the author and first inventor of letters and characters among the Goths. Some historians hold that the Goths have possessed their own characters for writing whatever they wished from all time and anciently. As their children learned these letters, they were simultaneously led to commit to memory certain verses made in honor of their Kings and of illustrious men who had performed some high and excellent exploit in defense of their country and nation. Not only their Kings, but also men of mark—who for this reason had to show themselves learned and diligent in research—gained thereby both kingdoms and honors, and were even placed among the number of the gods.

Johannes Magnus, book 1 of his *Northern History*, chapter on letters:

> "It is not to be believed that the Northerners themselves were entirely without forms for the magnificent deeds they performed, since long before Latin letters were invented—before Carmenta <note>In Roman myth, a prophetess who brought the alphabet to the Italians.</note> [came] from Greece to the mouth of the Tiber and the Roman forum..." <note>original: "Credendum non est, ipsos Aquilonares omnino caruisse formis rerum à se magnifice gestarum, cum longe ante inuentas literas Latinas antequam Carmenta ex Græcia ad ostia Tyberis, & Romanum forum..."</note>

This text continues a quote from Johannes Magnus, Archbishop of Uppsala, regarding the arrival of the Greek hero Evander in Italy.</note> Evander had arrived, and after driving out the original inhabitants <note>The "Aborigines," a term used by Roman historians for the earliest inhabitants of central Italy.</note>, he taught that unpolished people manners and letters; [yet even then] the Goths had their own letters. Evidence of this is provided by stones of extraordinary size, fixed to the tombs and caves of the ancient Goths: which, being inscribed with the forms of letters, could persuade one that they were erected there by giant strength before the Great Flood, or shortly thereafter. By these characters, they expressed their great deeds upon stones and handed them down to the eternal memory of mankind. Although they lacked knowledge of the Roman speech (which at that time, before Rome was founded, did not exist), nonetheless such a great diligence for the study of eloquence and for writing native poetry inflamed them, that not only modest boys—as Cato writes the Romans did much later—were everywhere trained to sing ancient songs containing the praises of their ancestors, but even grave men would sing to the flutes about the virtues of famous men (as is still done today). So great was the honor and reward for learning, that many bestowed not only scepters and kingdoms, but even divine honors upon the wise.

Olaus Magnus, brother of the aforementioned John, in book 1, chapter 36 of his *Histories of the Northern Peoples* <note>original: "Gentibus Septentrionalibus," published in 1555.</note>, writes as follows:

From the most ancient time, when there were giants in the Northern lands—that is, long before Latin letters were invented and before Carmenta <note>In Roman mythology, a goddess of childbirth and prophecy who supposedly invented the Latin alphabet.</note> arrived from Greece at the mouth of the Tiber and Roman soil with Evander, and, having driven out the original inhabitants, taught that unpolished and clearly woodland people manners and letters—the Northern kingdoms had their own letters. Evidence of this is seen in the stones of extraordinary size fixed to the tombs and caves of the ancients. If anyone doubts whether these were fashioned by giants and in the most ancient age, let him go there and see wonders greater and more marvelous than any writing could promise or provide. Thus (as is held in the history of my dearest brother, Johannes Magnus, my predecessor as Archbishop of Uppsala <note>original: "Vspalensis"</note>, book 1, chapter 52), by imprinting their deeds on stones, they handed them down to eternal memory.

Some also used various figures of animals as letters for their private accounts, in the manner of the Egyptians, and they still use this domestic sagacity today, as will be told shortly below. Things similar to these may still be seen in Rome on the old obelisks, in which individual letters expressed individual names: for instance, a wolf signified the greedy, a fox the deceitful, and a bee a King—because the governance of peoples ought to have the honey of clemency mixed with the sting of justice. Furthermore, just as letters written on papyrus are now sent among men, so once the Northern inhabitants sent letters carved on wood to one another as a popular type of "paper." Indeed, even now when papyrus is not available in military camps or during the siege of cities, they opportunely use the bark or inner wood of the birch tree, split into thin plates or fine leaves, for writing letters; they do so the more securely because bark of this kind is not destroyed by any damage from rain or snow. Peter Martyr <note>Pietro Martire d'Anghiera (1457–1526), an official chronicler of Spanish explorations.</note> also mentions in book 8 that the Chaldeans now write on the leaves of trees, and that the Portuguese, the first discoverers of the New World, used them while they were forced to establish mutual defenses to suppress the rebellion of the inhabitants. Northern men are also found of such sagacious wit that, although they never learned either Gothic or Latin letters, they compose alphabets for themselves from the shapes of things and instruments; and they use these for aiding the memory by writing uniquely on skin, paper, or bark. And this secret [is revealed] to no...

Therefore, many and excellent records <note>original: "monumenta"</note> from the men of that most ancient age would be preserved for the instruction of our present times, if those men—who were born for magnificent deeds—had left behind writings as extensive as the glorious feats they bequeathed to their successors. <page-num>863</page-num>
# Languages of this Universe

As for their language, no traces of it remain from which one could speak with certainty; however, the letters of Cassiodorus <note>Senator and secretary to the Ostrogothic King Theodoric the Great; his "Variae" are a primary source for the era.</note>, Secretary to Theodoric, inform us that in their public acts they used the Latin language. It is true that the *Histories of Spain* assert that the Gothic language was entirely similar to the language of the Celts; others affirm that it was the same as the Teutonic <note>Germanic</note> language. The remnants of these corrupted languages are much more different today than they likely were during their period of greatest purity, as confirmed by Louis de Mayerne Turquet <note>A French historian (c. 1550–1618) known for his "General History of Spain."</note> in Book 5 of his *History of Spain*.

Olaus Magnus, cited above in Book 8, Chapter 2 of his *Northern Histories*, writes that the Goths have a certain book written in their language titled *Billagines* <note>The "Bylagines" or "By-laws," mentioned by the historian Jordanes as the laws given to the Goths by their sage-king Diceneus.</note>, which was composed by one of their kings named Diceneus. In his time, he was the first to teach his people the philosophy and religion of Pythagoras. Now, this word *Billagines* signifies—according to the report of the aforementioned Olaus—as much in the Gothic language as *according to the laws* <note>original: "juxta leges"</note> does in Latin. See what this same author writes in Book 1, Chapter 34 of his same histories regarding certain sticks engraved with Gothic letters <note>Runic calendars or "clog almanacs," used in Northern Europe to track dates and astronomical events.</note> by which the Goths from all antiquity have served their knowledge of astronomy, and to predict and announce the events of times and seasons, and to know the moveable feasts and dominical letters <note>A method for calculating the days of the week for any given date in a year, essential for determining the date of Easter.</note> of future years.

Furthermore, it seems to me very appropriate to mention in this place that the *Histories of Spain* report that when **Don Sancho Ramirez** came to the crown of Navarre, he had already reigned for several years in Aragon. He had married a lady, the daughter of the Count of Urgel, named **Doña Felicia**, by whom he had three children. In this Prince, the two kingdoms of Navarre and Aragon were reunited 42 years after their separation. He was a warrior and a statesman, and furthermore was a zealot for the Roman Religion. For he caused the Gothic office <note>The Mozarabic or Visigothic Rite, a distinct Christian liturgy used on the Iberian Peninsula before the imposition of the Roman Rite.</note>—which the Christians used in his lands—to be changed, and put into use that of Rome. This possibly occurred through the Council held at Jaca under this King, when the Bishopric of Aragon was first established there. For the ornament and enrichment of that see, in addition to tithes, portions of the conquests made from the Moors in Zaragoza and Tudela were ordained. And in place of the Gothic civil laws, he introduced the Imperial common law into his jurisdiction. There is even found a volume of particular laws given by this King to the people of Jaca, which is included among the usages and customs of Navarre today.

The same Histories continue that at this same time mention is made of a Council assembled in the city of Barcelona at the pursuit of **Don Raymond Berenger** the Elder, at the prayer of **Doña Almodis** his wife. This council was presided over by Cardinal Hugh, Legate of Pope Alexander II or Gregory VII—for the time of it is not precisely fixed, but it is only said that it was celebrated around the year 1071. In this Council, it was ordained that the clergy should live chastely, for the history says that many ecclesiastics were married, according to the introduction of King Wittiza the Goth <note>Wittiza (reigned c. 702–710) was often blamed by later medieval historians for the "decadence" of the Visigothic kingdom, including the relaxation of clerical celibacy, which they claimed led to the Divine punishment of the Umayyad conquest.</note>, and following the example of the Aragonese, it was left...

The same Histories continue that in the year 1086, during the reign of Alfonso, King of Castile and Navarre <note>Alfonso VI of León and Castile (c. 1040–1109), a key figure in the Reconquista.</note>, the office named "Gothic"—so called because Isidore <note>St. Isidore of Seville, whose 7th-century liturgy remained the standard in Spain for centuries.</note> had introduced it, and since called "Mozarabic" <term>Mozarabic: from 'musta'rib', referring to Iberian Christians living under Muslim rule who maintained their faith and Gothic liturgy</term> because the Christians living among the Moors had retained it—was in use until that time, both in Toledo and in Castile and Leon. This King Alfonso, desiring in all things to show himself an affectionate son of the Church of Rome, wanted it to be changed and the Gregorian office received in its place, named for its author, Gregory. To this end, he sent for the bull from the Pope then reigning, commanding that the Roman office be used from that time forward in all the churches of Spain, just as was done in France; for this reason, it is called "Gallican" by some Spaniards. In the time of this King, a Council was held at Leon, attended by Rainier, Nuncio of the Pope, in which among other ordinances it was decreed that scribes and copyists should no longer use the ancient Gothic characters—said to have been invented by Ulfilas <note>A 4th-century Goth of Greek descent who translated the Bible into Gothic and created the Gothic alphabet.</note> their Bishop, and otherwise called [Runic]—but rather the letters that are presently used in Castile. See what has been written previously regarding the Mozarabic and "Mozarabelque" Christians.

## Of the language of the Franks.
### C H A P. L X X I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial L with foliate patterns and scrolling vines.</image-desc>
The Franks, remnants formerly remaining from the destruction of the Trojans (or Troians), some 440 years before the year of salvation or the incarnation of the Savior, finally came from the wide and spacious wilderness of Scythia <note>A vast region of central Eurasia; medieval legends often traced European origins to this area</note> under the leadership of Marcomir, their chief, to settle in Lower Germany. There, their brothers the Saxons granted them a dwelling toward the mouths of the Rhine, in Frisia and Holland. From there, making many great raids upon the surrounding lands, they fought the Romans and Gauls for more than nine hundred years. Thus, they extended their dominion over the greater part of Europe, as is amply testified by their chronicler Hunibauld <note>A legendary and likely fictional chronicler created or cited by Johannes Trithemius to provide an ancient pedigree for the Franks</note> in the 18 books he left to posterity regarding their conquests. In these, he notes among other things that a certain person named Wastfal <note>original: "Vuaftbal"</note> had written of their facts and deeds for 758 years in their own language, and in characters such as we represent hereafter. These characters have a certain flavor of Greek writing, but the order of the letters is transposed, and they are otherwise a bit uncertain—perhaps because of their great antiquity, which may have caused scribes to corrupt their true shape, as confirmed by Abbot Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German abbot and polymath famous for his works on cryptography and history</note> in book 5 of his *Polygraphy* <note>original: "Polygraphie"</note>.

### Of the region of the Finnonians or Finns.

<note>The decorative initial 'A' begins the section on Finland.</note>

**A.** Ortelius in his *Synonyms and Geographical Treasury* <note>Abraham Ortelius was a famous 16th-century cartographer; his *Thesaurus Geographicus* (1587) was a standard reference for place names.</note> states: Tacitus doubts whether to ascribe the Fenni <note>The Finns</note> to the Germans or the Sarmatians. Althamerus thinks they are Prussians or Lithuanians. Ptolemy places the Phinni (φίννοι) <note>original Greek: phinnoi</note> in this region. But it seems to me that those whom Jordanes calls *Finni* (spelled with an 'I') are rather those who inhabit Finland today. They are in the Scandinavian peninsula, where the Scritifini or Crictofinni are also found, but located more towards the North. These are so called from "leaping" in a barbarian tongue, says [Paul the] Deacon. I derive it from *Schritcken* or *Schriien*, a purely Germanic word which signifies to jump or to take great strides with legs spread wide in walking. For they use, according to the eyewitness Olaus [Magnus], "fiery soles" <note>original Latin: "igneis soleis". This refers to wooden skis, which allowed for such speed they seemed to burn across the snow.</note> tied under the soles of their feet: with which they seem to glide over snow and ice with a certain admirable speed, rather than run. The use of these is also among us in the winter time. We call them *Seriekshoenen* <note>Dutch/Germanic for "sliding shoes" or "skis"</note>, as if to say "jumping shoes." One must see if these are the same people called *Hippopodes* <note>Greek for "Horse-footed"</note> by ancient writers because of this swift running. See "Vandals."

And it must be noted that after the Kings of Sweden had subjected Finland to their kingdom, they placed several bailiffs and governors there. One resides near Vyborg <note>Vyborg is a city now in Russia, near the Finnish border</note> in a castle, which <gloss>which</gloss> is built in the lake, the other in Porvoo <note>original: "Borge"</note>, on the edge of the Finnish Gulf: all of whom are Lieutenants of the King, to exercise Justice in his name. There are also other castles and villages near Vyborg, and principally Lappeenranta <note>original: "Legabour"</note>, Käkisalmi <note>original: "Kexholin"</note>, and Shlisselburg <note>original: "Netabourg"</note>: but the Grand Duke of Muscovy has taken them from the kingdom of Sweden. There are also fortresses built on this side of the river like Lappee <note>original: "Lappae nſi"</note>, Kivennapa <note>original: "Kiuineb"</note>, Nykyrka <note>original: "Neukirk"</note>, and others which are still under the obedience of the King of Sweden.

„ It is noted that these peoples use five languages among themselves, and it says:

„ By this diversity of dress and weapons, it is made clear how great is the difference and distance of the regions, languages, ages, and practices. For the regions are many, large, and powerful, such as those of the Lapps <note>original: "Lapponum"; refers to the Sami people</note>, the Muscovites <note>original: "Moscovitarum"; people of the Grand Duchy of Moscow</note>, the Dalecarlians <note>original: "Dalensium"; inhabitants of the Dalarna region in Sweden</note>, the Highlanders <note>original: "Montanorum"</note>, and the Norwegians. Their size, extending in both length and breadth, is greater than Italy, Spain, and France put together; thus, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist</note> did not call them "another world" <note>original: "Alterum orbem"</note> in vain, due to their vast and unknown magnitude. Therefore, it is not surprising that the use of five languages is found there: namely, that of the Northern Lapps (or Bothnians), the Muscovites, the Ruthenians <note>original: "Ruthenorum"; a historical term for East Slavic peoples</note>, the Finns, the Swedes and Goths, and the Germans. That there is a great variety of languages across such a distance of provinces will seem a wonder to no one, given that Strabo <note>a Greek geographer and historian</note> in his eleventh book asserts—though perhaps based on opinion—that 70, or rather 300, nations living around the Caspian Sea use as many distinct languages in their commerce, because they inhabit harsh and inaccessible places; many of these are of the Sarmatian <note>original: "Sarmatici"; an ancient nomadic people</note> stock, yet all are inhabitants of the Caucasus. Furthermore, he asserts a little later that the Albanian people <note>original: "Albanorum"; referring to Caucasian Albania, an ancient kingdom in the Caucasus, not modern Albania</note> were once divided into 26 languages, each of which had and observed its own King; and perhaps each had its own unique appearance, so that one could clearly see an admirable diversity of both nations and languages. From this, the inflections of songs and melodies, and the expressions of the soul (by which humans are distinguished from wild beasts), can be clearly recognized.

---

„ That is to say, by this diversity of dress and weapons of the Northern peoples described by us above, it is declared what the difference and distance of their regions, languages, ages, and practices is. In fact, there are several regions among them that are large and powerful, namely those of the Lapps, Muscovites, Swedes <note>original: "Suenoniēs"</note>, Goths, Värmlanders <note>original: "Vermores"; inhabitants of Värmland, Sweden</note>, Dalecarlians, Highlanders, and Norwegians. The size and amplitude of these, in both longitude and latitude, is much greater than all of Italy, Spain, and France combined. This is why Pliny, not without reason, called them in his language, because of their unknown size, "another world" <note>original: "Alterum orbem"</note>. This is the reason why it will not be found so marvelous if in these regions there are five languages in use: namely, those of the Northerners—that is, the Lapps or Bothnians—the Muscovites, Ruthenians, Finns, Swedes, Goths, and Germans. And it is not such a marvelous thing that there is such a great diversity of languages in such a wonderful extent of regions, seeing what Strabo writes in book 11: that 70, or rather 300, tribes or nations living near the Caspian Sea used as many distinct languages, separate from one another, in their trade, because they inhabited harsh and inaccessible places. They were all Sarmatians from their first source and origin, yet all were inhabitants of the Caucasus mountains. Furthermore, this author shortly after assures us that the Albanian nation was anciently divided into 26 languages, each of which had and observed its own king; and perhaps each of these nations had its own diverse customs and ways of doing things. In this way, one can clearly see an admirable diversity of both peoples and languages, by which the inflections of songs and musical tones, and the uncovering of spiritual functions—by which men are separated and distinguished from animals and brute beasts—can be clearly known.

Refer to what we have written in the preceding chapters concerning the languages of the Lapps <note>original: "Lapponiens"; referring to the Sami people</note> and the Finns, which are used by some Livonians <note>peoples of the eastern Baltic coast</note>. Speaking of these in Book 4, the chapter on Lapland in his *Universal Cosmography*, Sebastian Münster wrote that the language of the Lapps is peculiar to them, extremely harsh and rugged, and very often unknown to their neighbors; because of this, these Lapps trade with foreigners as much by barter as by money, through mutual consent alone, without speaking a single word.

Modern accounts speaking of these Northern nations report that Henry, King of Sweden <note>likely a reference to Saint Eric IX, who campaigned in Finland, or a confusion of names in the source</note>, and Henry, Archbishop of Uppsala, dedicated themselves entirely to converting the province of Finland to the Christian religion. This province is among the most northern, where the days and nights increase almost to six months <note>a common early modern description of the extreme light cycles near the Arctic Circle</note>. It has embraced Christianity, and its people have become so remarkably good and charitable as Christians that they occupy themselves principally with good works; those of Bothnia <note>the region surrounding the Gulf of Bothnia</note> do the same on both sides, and have their parishes in which they maintain priests who have charge over them. And in all the surrounding lands, the people are now somewhat converted: for it is a certain thing that on the borders of Norway and the borders of Bothnia and Finland, men and women come from 30 and 40 leagues <note>approximately 90 to 120 miles</note> inland, when the weather is suitable, to bring children to the churches. Some carry them in their cradles, or in baskets upon their shoulders, and others place them upon beasts of burden, requesting Holy Baptism or instruction on how to live as Christians. When they are able, they bring their tithes and first-fruits; though ignorant of what they are bound to do as Christians, they conform to the law of nature, doing what seems to them good and praiseworthy, and fleeing from what seems to them evil and vicious. Many other things concerning the lives, manners, behaviors, and religions of these Nations are deduced following Johannes and Olaus Magnus <note>Swedish brothers and influential historians of the North</note> in their Northern histories, Saxo Grammaticus in his *History of the Danes*, Sidonius Apollinaris in Book 1, Procopius in his histories, Paul the Deacon and Jordanes in their histories, by André Thevet in Book 19, chapters 15, 16, and following of his *Universal Cosmography*, and François de Belleforest in Book 3, chapter 6 of his *Universal History*, and in his discourses on the *Cosmography* of Sebastian Münster.

## Concerning the Region of the English.

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'A' containing scrolling acanthus leaf patterns and floral motifs.</image-desc>

Ortelius, in his *Synonyms and Geographical Treasury*, states:
England <note>original: "Anglia"</note>, called Albion by Aristotle, Apuleius, and Pliny; called *Aluion* <note>original: "ἄλβιον"</note> by Ptolemy, and Britain by others. Avienus calls it the Island of the Albions. But more truly, as Humphrey Llwyd <note>a Welsh cartographer and antiquary</note> teaches from the most ancient annals of that island: *Prydania*. This is the island which today contains the kingdoms of England and Scotland.

England, a part of the island of Albion, being further south, takes its name from the Angles, a people of Saxony mentioned by Tacitus, who occupied this region.

...from which even today it is still called **Engelandt** <note>England; the author notes the name shifted slightly from its root "Angle"</note> (with only the first letter changed). Winfrid <note>Saint Boniface, the 8th-century "Apostle to the Germans"</note> calls it "Overseas Saxony," as Rhenanus <note>Beatus Rhenanus, a 16th-century German humanist</note> noted in the first book of his *German Affairs*. More recent Latin authors call the inhabitants **Anglo-Saxons**.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The **British Isles** are the names given by authors to those which today contain the English and Scottish kingdoms along with Ireland and the surrounding islands. Dionysius of Alexandria calls them the *Bretanides* <term>βρετανίδες — the British ones</term>. The largest of these, in which the English and Scottish kingdoms now stand, is called **Albion** <term>αλβιων</term> by Ptolemy <note>an influential 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian geographer</note>, and is also called "Britannia" by others for its excellence, as if it were the foremost among the British lands, according to Dio <note>Cassius Dio</note> in Book 60. Appian also reads it as *Brettanica* <term>βρεττανικὴ</term> in the preface of his history. In Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium</note>, it is written *Pretanica* <term>βρεταννικὴ</term> with a P. After the Romans had completely subjected this island to their Empire, they distinguished it by provinces and names. In the *Almagest* <note>Ptolemy's great astronomical work</note>, Book 2, the part toward the South is called "Greater," and the part toward the North is "Lesser." Xiphilinus and Dio divide it into "Upper" and "Lower." In the works of Sextus Rufus, who flourished under the Emperor Valentinian, there are *Britannia Prima*, *Britannia Secunda*, *Flavia*, and *Maxima Caesariensis*. The *Notitia* <note>the *Notitia Dignitatum*, a Roman administrative document</note> adds *Valentia*, which Marcellinus also mentions.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Humphrey Llwyd <note>a famous 16th-century Welsh antiquary and mapmaker</note> interprets these provinces as follows: he calls *Britannia Prima* that which extends from the Thames all the way to the Wall. This is roughly what is included today under the name of England (as the Latin common folk call it). He asserts that *Britannia Secunda*, which he writes is also called "Lesser Britain," is what is commonly called Scotland. From *Maxima Caesariensis*, he creates Kent along with the region of the Atrebates <note>a tribe of ancient Britain</note>. From *Flavia*, he marks the tract of the West Saxons with the Isle of Wight. He identifies *Valentia* as Wales <note>Cambria</note>. But we have also decided not to omit what Humphrey brought to light from Sigebert: namely, that before this island was known to the Romans or foreigners, it was divided into three regions which the language of the natives (which is still in use today in Wales, his homeland) called *Lhoegria* <note>Loegria</note>, *Cambria* <note>Wales</note>, and *Albania* <note>Scotland</note>, and they still call them so; see these in their respective places. The same man teaches from the most ancient monuments of that region that this island was called by the general name **Prydain**, from which it is very likely the Greeks and Latins made their "Britannia." The Britons are corruptly called *Bracti* in the history of Widukind, but I read *Bretti* in his manuscript codex. Ponticus Virunius thinks Wales <note>Cambria</note> was celebrated by Juvenal in Satire 7 with this verse:
->*The same old lesson kills the wretched masters of Wales.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Occidit miseros Cambræ repetita Magistros." Juvenal was actually referring to the repetitive nature of teaching, but Virunius interprets "Cambre" as referring to the Welsh/Cambrians.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Scotland** is the more northern part of the British island (mentioned by Hegesippus in chapter fifteen), formerly called *Albania* by Latin writers, and still called *Albain* by the inhabitants, as Humphrey Llwyd says. I would argue, along with Beatus Rhenanus, that this Scotland was called **Caledonia** by Tacitus in his *Life of Agricola*.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The **Scots**, whom Orosius, Claudian, and Ammianus mention among Latin writers, are the peoples of the northern British island who, originating from Cantabria in Spain and migrating from there into Ireland, finally fixed their seat in Scotland. In the British tongue, they are called *Guydhyl* <note>Goidels or Gaels</note> according to Humphrey Llwyd.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ireland is called *Iuverna* by Caesar and Pomponius; likewise *Iuernia* <term>ιυερνια</term> by Solinus in the Aldine edition; *Ierna* <term>ιερνη</term> by Ptolemy, Strabo, Stephanus, and Apuleius from...

<sig>Sffff</sig>

Aristotle (whom he imitates in his little book *On the World* <note>original: "cuius in suo libellulo de mundo imitator est"</note>) as well as Claudian <note>a 4th-century Roman poet</note> and Eustathius <note>a 12th-century scholar and archbishop</note> call it Iernia <term>ιἐρνία — a Greek transliteration of an early name for Ireland</term>. It is one of those islands called the "British Isles." Sextus Avienus <note>a 4th-century Latin poet and geographer</note> calls it the "Sacred Island" and calls the inhabitants the "Hiernians." In Isaac Tzetzes' commentary on Lycophron <note>a Greek scholar of the 12th century writing on a 3rd-century BCE poet</note>, it is called "Western Britain." The same island is named **Scotia** by Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, whose 7th-century encyclopedia was a standard reference for centuries</note> and other writers of the Middle Ages. I believe it is called *Iris* by Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BCE historian</note>. The inhabitants call it **Erin**. To the Britons who live in the region of Albion and are also called the Welsh <note>original: "Vualli"</note>, it is called **Iwerddon** <note>original: "Yuuerdhon"</note>, and Humphrey Llwyd <note>a 16th-century Welsh cartographer and historian</note> writes that the inhabitants are called *Enuijdhyl*. By the Germans, it is named **Irland**, from *Erin* or *Irin* (as all Britons pronounce the letter "E" like the German "I") and *landt*, which signifies a region. Following them, the Spanish, Italians, and French call it **Irlanda**. This island seems to be fabulously described by Plutarch in his short work *On the Face in the Moon* under the name **Ogygia**. Robert Constantin, in his supplement to the Latin language, maintains that it was called *Cerne* by Lycophron. However, I would by no means think that Ireland was described by him with that word, but rather it refers to the island of the same name which Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the 1st-century *Natural History*</note> places in the Ethiopian Sea, opposite the Persian Gulf and facing Ethiopia. For this island lies toward the East—or as Lycophron says, toward the dawn—whereas Ireland lies toward the West for those (including Lycophron) who live in Greece or Italy. Orpheus <note>referring to the Orphic Argonautica</note> also mentions an island called *Iernem* <term>ιἐρνίε</term>, but whether that is the same as our Ireland, I leave for others to debate.

## On the English Language.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' within a square border, decorated with classical foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>
All of Great Britain, or the Island of England, is divided into two parts which encompass two Kingdoms. The mountains and the rivers Solway <note>original: "Soluer"</note> and Tweed <note>original: "Tnedo"</note> separate the Kingdom of England from that of Scotland; the Northern part remains to the Scots with a length of four hundred and eighty miles, and the Southern part to the English with two hundred and thirty. The territory the English possess is divided into three, and according to some, four principal provinces, partitioned into twenty-two episcopal cities with two archbishoprics, the names of which, along with the provinces and their characteristics, are described particularly in the histories of this country. And just as the provinces are different in their customs, they also differ in language; for in the province of Wales <note>original: "Vuales ou Galles"</note>, they speak differently than in that of Cornwall, and both speak differently than the English. There are also, besides these, two types of languages in the final part of Scotland: the inhabitants and those who live as savages speak one that conforms to that of the English, and the other entirely different, which is the Irish language <note>Gaelic</note>. It is a rare and marvelous thing to see various languages in one island.

And to clarify this matter, we shall say that the English language is a language composed of the German language and the French language. This is because of the **Anglo-Saxons** who brought that German language into England, and then the **Normans** <note>original: "Northmans"</note> who occupied this island also introduced the aforementioned French language. The ancient British language <note>Welsh</note> has remained only in the country of

Wales, where the indigenous people retreated when the Anglo-Saxons conquered England; and in fact, the English do not understand the language of the Welsh, who have a language almost identical to the Low Bretons of our Brittany <note>Brittany in modern-day France, which maintains strong linguistic ties to Wales and Cornwall</note>. This is clearly seen when merchants from the said Low Brittany arrive in England; they do not understand the English language, but they do understand the Welsh language, and they understand that of the Irish even better, as they are a people who have kept and preserved their ancient language more purely than the Welsh who live on the mainland of the Island.

André Thevet <note>A 16th-century French Franciscan priest and explorer</note> in book 16 of his *Universal Cosmography*, chapter 2, in treating England, says:
> The flat country of the Principality of Wales is very rich and fertile, especially the parts near the coast. However, the mountain regions are very poor and infertile, and the inhabitants live there quite sparsely. The people of this country and the English of the kingdom have little love for one another; quite often the Welsh stir up seditions and will not, for anything in the world, confess to being English, but instead claim to be of the race of the first inhabitants of the said Island. This has some appearance of truth, both from hearing the difference in the languages of the two countries and because the English call them "Vuallons" <note>An old French rendering of "Welsh," derived from an ancient Germanic word meaning "foreigner" or "stranger"</note>, which means as much as "savages" and "strangers." Cornwall, being the smallest region of the English, is nevertheless ranked among the primary English Provinces; in the past, it was a Kingdom just like Wales. This Island, in the sense that it is subject to the English King, has three diverse languages: namely English, Cornish, and Welsh, which understand one another very little.

The same author, in the subsequent chapter 9, speaking of the rural people of Scotland, says:
> Just as these rustic men differ in manners, civility, and behavior from the nobility of the cities of Edinburgh, Dumbarton, <note>The original OCR reads "Dōbart, Dombertat," likely variations or errors for Dumbarton</note> Linlithgow, St. Andrews, and Hamilton; they are likewise different in language, and they are no closer to one another than Greek is to Hebrew, or French is to a "Breton-speaking" Breton <note>referring to a speaker of the Celtic Breton language rather than the French dialect of Brittany</note>. The most pleasant and courtly language of Scotland differs very little from that of the natural English. To show you that I am not speaking from memory alone, I have wished to include here the Lord’s Prayer in the common vernacular of these two nations to show you the diligence I have used in all places where I had the means to observe and record something of value.

Polydore Vergil <note>An Italian humanist and priest (c. 1470–1555) who wrote a famous history of England</note> in book 9 of his history of England asserts that the English language is a mixture of many tongues, principally German and French. He states that French was introduced by William the Conqueror, Duke of Normandy, when he drove out the Danes and made himself King of the island. The race of kings reigning in England during Polydore’s time were descended from him. By bringing Normans and Frenchmen with him, he caused the language to become mixed, as can be seen in the law books he established in that country. As for the German language, it is natural to them, as they are descended from the Saxons, though even this has been corrupted by being mixed with ancient Briton, French, and the Danish language, given the many incursions the Danes often made into this island. <margin>cc cc cc cc cc</margin>
The ancient English counted the Months according to the course of the Moon, and called the Moon *Mona*, meaning "sacred month" <note>original: "Mona." Bede actually links the word to the moon's name</note>. April was *Eoster monath*, meaning "Easter month," named after a goddess to whom the Teutons sacrificed during the month of April when they were still Pagans <note>referring to the goddess Eostre</note>. They called May *Trimelci*, meaning "three milkings," because in that month they milked their cattle three times a day. Sebastian Münster <note>A German cartographer and cosmographer (1488–1552)</note> writes in book 1 of his *Cosmography*, in the chapter on the Kingdom of England, that this passage is not easily found in printed books, but that he found it in a hand-written manuscript that Glarean <note>Heinrich Glarean, a Swiss music theorist and humanist</note> sent to him from Freiburg in the year 1545. He also writes that the wild Scots and island inhabitants use another language similar to that of the Irish, while the more "humane" <note>meaning settled or urbanized</note> Scots use the English language, and the third language is that of Wales. This same author, in the following chapter on the customs and manners of the English and Scots, concludes that there are three languages in England: The first and principal one is used commonly by the English and those Scots who have more civility than the others. The second is that of the Irish, used by the peasants in Scotland. The third is that of Wales, which is the proper language of the Britons.

<page-num>876</page-num>
-> History of the Origin of <-

English practitioners and litigants no longer used the French, or rather Norman language (which they had used since and following the time of William the Norman), but the English language instead. It was commanded <note>This refers to the Statute of Pleading of 1362, enacted by Edward III</note> that all acts of cases and lawsuits should be written [in English]; since which time this English language has always been used throughout all the courts and halls of justice in England, as is confirmed by the aforementioned Polydore Vergil <note>An Italian humanist and priest (c. 1470–1555) who wrote a famous history of England</note> in book 19 of his *History of England*. Regarding the general literature of this language, there are very few books found written in it, unless they are some books of theology, particularly over the last twenty-five or thirty years since the Lutherans and Calvinists (who in England are called Puritans <note>The author uses "Puritan" as a broad label for English Protestants who sought further reform</note>) have been writing against the Catholics, as well as the Catholics against the Puritans. For these two sorts of [Protestants] strongly dislike each other; especially the Calvinists, who greatly desire to abolish the form of policy still observed in England, where the Archbishops, Bishops, Curates, and Chapters have remained intact. This the Lutherans and Calvinists do not approve of, and for this reason, the Archbishops, Bishops, Curates, and Chapters—among whom there are many [learned men]—and the aforementioned Lutherans and Calvinists write every day against one another, as Nicholas Sanders <note>A prominent English Catholic polemicist (c. 1530–1581)</note> confirms in book 5, chapter 4 of his *Ecclesiastical Monarchy*.

This English language is so little esteemed by foreigners who visit England that there are few who wish to take the trouble to learn it or speak it, unless they are servants or agents dealing with commodities and the necessities of life, which depend on the common people who cannot speak any other language.

Anyone who wishes to see several beautiful and excellent discourses on the [origins] of England should read Caesar in his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*; Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, an 8th-century English monk and historian</note>, book 1, chapter 1; Gildas in his book *On the Ruin of Britain*; William of Newburgh <note>original: "G. de Neufbor"</note> in his *English History*; Albert Krantz, *Danish History*, book 1, chapter 2; Saxo Grammaticus in his *Danish History*; and Polydore Vergil in his books on the *History of England*.

From the moist soil, the power of the approaching Sun produces everything in great quantity. Especially if you consider other lands, it seems placed toward the East. See also Ptolemy in book seven, chapter one, and Pomponius Mela in book 3, who call it *Indike* <note>original: Ἰνδικήν</note> in Greek. -> Abraham Ortelius in his *Geographical Synonyms* <-

India, *Indike* <note>original: Ἰνδική</note>, is the largest and most noble region of Asia. Ptolemy divides it into two: namely, India within and beyond the Ganges. India within the Ganges is called *Indostan* <note>Hindustan</note> by the inhabitants, according to João de Barros <note>A 16th-century Portuguese historian and official in the Indian colonies</note>, an eyewitness and, so to speak, a first-hand listener, as one who served as the Viceroy of Portugal in this India for several years. India beyond the Ganges is thought to be called *Heuila*, or as others write, *Hauilath* or *Euilath* <note>Havilah</note>, in the Holy Scriptures. [Dominicus] Niger writes it is called *Macyn* or *Magyn* by the inhabitants. He adds that for those sailing from Egypt to India, it is divided into three parts: the lower, middle, and upper. The lower part, which is from the Indus river to the Bariam stream, is named *Caiferat* <note>likely Gujarat</note>. The middle part, which extends from here to another river named Chaberis, is *Minibar* <note>Malabar</note>. The upper part, *Maabar* <note>the Coromandel Coast</note>, extends from the Chaberis to the Ganges river. Marco Polo the Venetian reports that even in his time it was distinct in so many parts, but he calls the larger part *Malabar* and the middle part *Abascia* <note>Abyssinia or Ethiopia, which Polo and others often confused with or categorized as a "Third India"</note>. He does not identify the smaller part with a specific name. Pliny testifies that India was called the "third part of the world" by the companions of Alexander who had conquered it. Nor is it certain today that a smaller part of the world is encompassed by that name. For the Spaniards commonly call the ancient Indies along with almost all of the recently discovered *America* "the Indies."

-> The same [Ortelius] in his *Geographical Treasury* <-

The Indians were first called Sabæans, then also Homerites <note>The Himyarites of ancient Yemen</note>, says Nicephorus Callistus in book 8, chapter 35. He places them in Arabia Felix <note>Arabia the Blessed, the fertile southern region of the Arabian peninsula</note>. There are also peoples properly called Indians in India beyond the Ganges, according to Ptolemy. But translators read *Sindi* in its place, and more accurately, as I conjecture. In the Greek manuscript, it is read as *Indoi* <note>original: Ἰνδοὶ</note>, and I think Ptolemy wrote *Indike*. But as I warn in many other places in this treasury regarding the word "Indica," the scribe did not notice the doubled "S" from the voice of the one reading aloud. Hesychius confirms my opinion, who lists the *Sindi* as an Indian people and includes a Sindian port there. Curtius (book 9) calls those who live on the coast of the Red Sea in Gedrosia <note>an ancient region in modern-day Pakistan and Iran</note> "Maritime Indians," and places them on this side of the Indus river, contrary to Ptolemy and other geographers. Arrian (book 3) also names Indians on this side of the Indus. In his work *Indica* <note>On Indian matters</note>, he calls these "Western Indians" (to differentiate them from those beyond, whom he calls Eastern). Toward the Arbis river, Pliny and Arrian extend India toward the West, adding that these people once obeyed the Assyrians. It is likely this is the India mentioned in the books of Esther and the Maccabees. There are also Indians in Ethiopia according to Procopius in book 6 of *Buildings*. For he calls them the Mountains of the Indians, from which the Nile takes its origin. See: Ethiopians, Menones, and Rhizophagi <note>Root-eaters</note>.

India, *Indike* <note>original: Ἰνδική</note>, the largest and most noble region of Asia; this Ptolemy divides into two: namely, India within and beyond the Ganges.
