And yet Alexander the Great did not see even a third of the Indies, and never passed beyond the Ganges toward the south; the glory of which belongs to those of our time, who have done more than he, and more than all the historians, whether Greek or Latin, by giving us knowledge of what is rarest in this great and very rich province. If then this India is the third part of the earth, by what consideration should it be thus measured? Since Europe makes up one part, Asia another, and Africa another—unless we separate India from Asia, just as it never truly had any community with the Asians, and would be included there improperly, inasmuch as the Kings who had command over Asia never had any power over this great Empire, as we can see in the writings of the ancient Greek and Latin authors. But you will ask me what this discourse aims at: nothing other than to favor the cause of those who call the newly discovered New World the "West Indies," and which I prefer to include under the third part of the earth rather than otherwise, and give the Africans the rank of the fourth. ### Languages of this World.

The **Moluccas** <note>The Spice Islands in modern-day Indonesia</note>, for this reason alone—that some hold them to be Eastern and others Western—are nevertheless all comprised under the name of the **Indies**. Indian Kings command there, and the people for the most part imitate the ways of the Indians. Furthermore, the same trees and plants grow there, and almost the same animals, except where the sun already approaches the Poles and the cold ensures that Lions, Elephants, Tigers, and similar beasts could not live at all. In short, Religion (or an imitation of it) makes them all united, in that it seems the Easterners have given their beliefs to the Westerners. This is apparent from those of the Island of **Zipangu**, or **Japan** <note>The author refers to the 16th-century debate over whether Japan was the far edge of the East or the beginning of the West/Americas</note>, which are known to be so positioned between the Orient and the Occident (as we define them) that the Geographers of our time do not know how to properly say if they should be named Easterners or otherwise.

This leads us to conclude that the **Indies** are in the third part of the Earth and are of a different extent than the ancients considered. However, the opinions of those ancients, out of the reverence we owe them, should not be entirely cast aside—not that we wish to dwell on the dreams and reveries of the **Greeks**, who created a **Bacchus** subjecting the Indians, and produced a great **Hercules** as a total conqueror, and an **Alexander** as Monarch. These tales are deduced at length by **Strabo** <note>Ancient Greek geographer</note> in book 15; **Diodorus Siculus** in book 3; **Pliny** in book 6, chapter 17; **Ptolemy** in book 7, chapter 1, table 10 of Asia; **Solinus** in chapter 65 of his *Polyhistor*; **Philostratus** in book 2, chapter 15 of the *Life of Apollonius*; **Quintus Curtius** and **Arrian** in the *Life of Alexander the Great*; **Plutarch** in the same *Life*; and many other ancient authors.

Leaving these aside, we will say, considering the **East Indies**, that as they are of greater extent than any other Provinces and Regions of this universe, they are also divided into two great parts and regions, both being known and renamed by the **Ganges** river. Thus, the part that faces us—and which, from our perspective, is Western—is called **India within the Ganges**, because it lies between the aforementioned river and the **Indus**, which gave its name to the whole land. The part that is further East is named **beyond the Ganges**, as it lies in that great expanse of country that goes as far as the **Sea of Cin and Mangi** <note>Terms used by Marco Polo for Northern and Southern China</note>, and which extends toward the Southern parts as far as the **Golden Chersonese** (now named **Malacca**), which lies opposite that great Island now called **Sumatra**, and which was formerly known by the name **Taprobane** <note>While Taprobane originally referred to Sri Lanka, many Renaissance writers mistakenly identified it as Sumatra</note>.

These two were named thus according to the sayings of some Geographers; but in the **Holy Scriptures**, the Eastern part is denoted by the word **Havilah** <note>original: "Euilath"</note>, and the one closer to us is called **Serian**, which the locals now call **Hynd** <note>Hindustan</note>. The other, which is to the East, is now called **Macin**, or **Magin**—so much have things changed, or rather, so little knowledge have we had of foreign history. Some moderns have spoken differently of this matter, holding that the Indies toward the West, on this side of the Ganges, are called **Havilah** in the Holy Scripture and **Indostan** by the Indians; and the Indies beyond the Ganges are called **Seriah** in the aforementioned Holy Scripture and **Macyn** (otherwise **China**) by the Indians. Moderns who have navigated toward these Indies have divided them for us into three: the **High**, the **Middle**, and the **Low**. The first, which is also the Low, is what is named the country of **Caiferat**, or **Gujarat**, which in the time—

# On the language of the East Indians in general.

## CHAPTER LXXVI.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'S' ornate with vine-like floral patterns in a square border.</image-desc>Strabo, in the 15th book of his *Geography*, citing the words of a certain very ancient author named Megasthenes, wrote that the Indians of his time had no use for letters, nor any written laws, but that they observed many fine things through memory and the remembrance of past events, just as they had learned them from father to son. This is repeated by Caelius Rhodiginus in book 18, chapter 31, of his *Diverse Lessons*. Diodorus Siculus, on this subject in book 3 of his *Histories*, maintains that in a certain island found near the South by Iambulus <note>A Greek merchant and traveler credited with a legendary account of a voyage to an island in the Indian Ocean</note>, the inhabitants did not write across as we do, but drew the lines of their letters straight, from top to bottom. They had twenty-eight letters in number according to the meaning they gave them, even though they only had seven characters, each of which was explained in four modes and ways. This is what the Emperor Augustus <note>original: "Octave"</note> seemed to have wanted to imitate in his Latin writing, according to Suetonius Tranquillus in his *Life [of Augustus]* in these words:

<margin>cc</margin>
> I have noted particularly in his handwriting that he did not divide words, nor did he transfer overflowing letters from the end of a line to the next, but immediately placed them below and circled them. The name 'verse' [verus], derived from 'turning' [vertendo], argues that this was the custom of the ancients. <note>original: "Notaui & in Chyrographo eius illa præcipuè, non diuidere verba, nec ab extrema parte verſuum abundantes litteras in alterum transferre, ſed ibidem ſtatim ſubijcit, circumducitque, eam veterum conſuetudinem fuiſſe arguit nomen verſus, à vertendo factum."</note>

Regarding this, we shall repeat here what we have previously written about the Syriac language and Syriac letters in the chapter on the Syriac language: namely, that the characters of the aforementioned Syriac letters, although they are read from right to left like those of the Hebrews, Samaritains, Chaldeans, and Arabs, are nevertheless not formed and written by the Syrians from right to left as those of the said Hebrews, Samaritans, Chaldeans, and Arabs are, but from top to bottom toward the chest, as this Latin verse denotes.

History of the Origin of the <note>original: "Histoire de l'Origine des..." continued from previous page as "Languages of the Universe"</note>

->*From heaven to the belly, Chaldea gathers the lines,*<-
<note>original Latin: "E cælo ad stomachum relegit Chaldea lituras." This poetic line describes the vertical direction of writing—from top (heaven) to bottom (stomach/earth).</note>

This is what moved, it seems, Festus Pompeius <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note> to call this kind of writing <gloss>epokon</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἐποχον, meaning "placed upon" or "resting on"</note> "downward-facing," just as we now say "rightward-facing." This is because the letters seem to fall from above and sit upon one another, carrying the next on their back while they are set in the order of the alphabet or the phrasing. Thus, it is not without reason that they are believed to have been sent down from heaven by that great Craftsman <note>Referring to God</note>. This is confirmed by Theseus Ambrosius in his *Introduction to the Chaldean, Syriac, and Aramaic Language*, chapter 9; André Thevet in book 18, chapter 14 of his *Cosmography*; and Guy Le Fèvre de la Boderie in his epistle on the Syriac New Testament.

Friar Louis the Portuguese, in book 1, chapter 1 of his *Globe of Canons and the Sacred Language and Divine Scripture*, confirms this, saying:
> "But those first people from whom the Syriac language of Jerusalem flowed, 
> "holding a middle ground between the two, write toward the breast, 
> "as the legal scholar Andreas Masius and we ourselves have discussed 
> "at length and with care in the aforementioned elementary preface. 
> "To which is added what Poggio <note>Poggio Bracciolini, a Renaissance humanist</note> relates in his book 
> "On the Variety of Fortune, that the Indians lead the pen from the top to the bottom, 
> "which is also observed by the Sinae, or Sinnae, or Chinese."

Modern travelers and navigators assure us that the East Indians, Cathayans <note>Northern Chinese</note>, Chinese, and Japanese of today, in their manner of forming the characters of the letters of their languages, write from top to bottom. They claim to follow the order of nature in this, which gave men high heads and low feet.

To be brief, these Indians generally write on the leaves of certain trees growing in their countries, primarily trees they call <term>Tals</term> <note>The Palmyra or Talipot palm tree, whose leaves (ola) were the standard writing material in South and Southeast Asia</note>, from which they make books. Unlike the Hebrews, Arabs, and us Christians in our mode of forming and writing letters—whether from right to left or left to right—they form and write them from top to bottom. In the land of <term>Cabaa</term> or <term>Cabaya</term> <note>Likely Cambay or Gujarat, India</note>, the inhabitants use paper to form and write their letters, as confirmed by the aforementioned modern navigators. André Thevet, in book 11, chapter 23 of his *Cosmography*, regarding Niccolò de' Conti’s travels in Asia, mentions the inhabitants of the said Country of Cambay and maintains that they do not write like us, nor like the Hebrews and other older peoples descended from them, but rather like other East Indians, from the top of the leaf to the bottom, and that they use three different languages among themselves. Jerónimo Osório, in book 2 of his *History of Portugal*, confirms this, saying that all the reports from the Portuguese sent to the Indies by the King stated that these Indians did not use paper or parchment like us Europeans, but that they marked their letters with a stylus on the leaves of wild trees they called palms, because these trees resemble true palms. They have very ancient books written on these leaves, which are all of the same length, in which they write their [laws] and memorable histories; then they pierce these leaves at the sides and flatten two wooden covers which they attach quite neatly.

# History of the Origin of [Languages] #

<note>The text is partially obscured at both the left and right margins due to the tight binding and paper curvature; bracketed text indicates reconstructions based on context.</note>

...[nothing] in common together: the Malays <note>original: "Malacquois"</note> form and write the [chara]cters of their letters like the Jews, from right to left <note>This refers to Jawi, the Arabic-based script used for the Malay language</note>; their tongue [is] understood throughout all the islands and surrounding regions as [the] courtly language <note>original: "courtiſane," meaning a lingua franca or prestigious language of the court</note> of them all, just as the French language is in the nor[thern] countries on this side [of the world]. The Siamese <note>original: "Sianois"</note>, in the manner of Europeans, form and u[se] the characters of their letters almost similar to the [Lat]in letters, from left to right, which is greatly worthy of m[arvel], seeing that these kingdoms are so close and contiguous to one [another]. Furthermore, the aforementioned navigators and travelers [report that] the histories of the city and kingdom of Malacca contain that this [pla]ce was from its beginning inhabited by several fishermen from the [kingdo]m of Pegu <note>An ancient kingdom in modern-day Myanmar</note>, Siam, and Bengal, who, in building this [city], established new laws and formed a language for [it that was] unique and particular, so that they might have nothing in common [with their] neighbors; which language they formed from the most [ex]cellent words and phrases of the languages of their neighboring peoples, from which [they] are accustomed to compose very excellent verses and [poems] of love; and with it one can trade and converse in all the [cir]cumjacent regions, as being the most beautiful, elegant, and [fre]quented of all the others in the Indies.

Whatever may be of these diversities or variations of languages [and sig]ns, we shall hold as quite certain what we have [said] before in the chapter on the Egyptian language: namely, that [we h]ave recently learned—even from this embassy from Japa[n] <note>The Tenshō Embassy (1582–1590), the first Japanese legation to Europe</note> in the year 1585, which in the month of March came from as far away as f[ive] or six thousand leagues to offer obedience to the Holy Apostolic See of [Rome]—that in the aforementioned East Indies, and even two thousand leagues [beyond] there in China and Cathay <note>An archaic name for Northern China</note>, from where the art of printing [first] proceeded, there are two kinds of writing, [just as] Apuleius <note>A 2nd-century Roman writer who described Egyptian scripts</note>, previously cited, recounts of Egypt. These are, namely, [one] of hieroglyphic letters, and the other of common letters, [whose] combinations can form all the words one [wishes to ex]press; both proceeding not horizontally—as [the He]brews do in one way and we in another—but from the top [downwards].

**Languages of this World**

There are, nevertheless, always some among them of greater understanding and knowledge than the others—not through a doctrine acquired in schools, nor by the reading of books (for although paper and printing are not unknown to them, they do not have such convenience as we do), but rather by an ingrained routine and such constant meditations that some may have devoted themselves for thirty or forty years continuously without communication with any person who might cross their conceptions. By this means, these <term>Bonzes</term> <note>A term used by early European travelers to describe Buddhist monks or priests, likely derived from the Japanese word "bōzu."</note> forge in their brains strange and very bizarre fantasies. In this, they are not held back by any bridle of religion, nor by reprimand from the magistrate, so that each may abound in his own sense, possessed by a vain and light inconstancy. 

But these men agree unanimously among themselves concerning the eternity of the world and the perishing of the soul when the body dies, persuading themselves that what has come from nothing must also return to nothing. Indeed, they have infinite other fantasies entirely contrary to the Christian religion, just as I have deduced in the chapter on the Egyptian language cited above. 

These <term>hieroglyphic</term> <note>The author incorrectly identifies Chinese characters as hieroglyphs, a common misconception in the early modern period when it was believed all ideographic scripts shared a common origin with Egyptian writing.</note> letters of the aforementioned China and of the aforementioned <term>Cathay</term> <note>An archaic name for Northern China, popularized by Marco Polo.</note>, used in the aforementioned East Indies, are very difficult to learn to read and to form because they consist of various figures of beasts, birds, trees, herbs, and, in short, everything that nature produces. These serve them as notes—some alone and apart, and others joined and coupled together to create a character that represents more than one word. These might be like <term>Centaur-hybrids</term> <note>original: "Hypocentaures"</note>, chimeras, sphinxes, and similar monstrosities composed of different natures. 

Thus, these Bonzes, whatever good wit they may have, consume the better part of their age before they can be good masters of them, according to the modern accounts sent from the Indies. These accounts maintain that upon the general notes of this entirely hieroglyphic writing, by disguising and coupling them in various ways, entirely new compound characters can be formed, just as in the <term>Ciceronian Notes</term> <note>original: "Notes Ciceronienes." This refers to Tironian notes, a system of shorthand used by Marcus Tullius Cicero's secretary, which the author compares to the complex construction of Chinese characters.</note> and in our devices and ciphers of names. 

As for the matter of religion, they are marvelously attached to their idolatry and superstition, and have so vividly imprinted in their minds so many fables told to them of their idols and false gods that it is very difficult to tear them from their souls. This is principally because all these things are set in the verse and rhythm of their language, of which they make such a great account that this alone is enough to persuade them of the grossest nonsense one could imagine. The devil has found this invention to make them believe so many follies that they tell of their false gods—even things contrary to their laws and to natural reason. Now, they learn these verses or rhythms from their tender youth and sing them with singular pleasure; for although their verses are very different from Greek and Latin verses regarding the number of syllables (since each contains 72 syllables), they nevertheless do not fail to have their grace and beauty, as confirmed by <term>Pierre du Jarric</term> <note>original: "P. du Iatric" — an error in the OCR for Pierre du Jarric (1566–1617), a Jesuit historian who wrote extensively about the East Indies.</note> in Book 1, Chapter 4 of his *History of the East Indies*.

### C H A P. LXXVII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring floral and foliate patterns.</image-desc>

**S**ome modern travelers and navigators, in their voyages and sailings, speaking of this very great and ample land of China in the more Eastern Lands of the Indies, have shown that Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), an influential Greco-Roman mathematician and geographer.</note> in Book 7, Chapter 3 of his *Geography* had knowledge of it, when he says these words:

> "The Chinese <note>original: "Sinois"</note> are divided on the North side by a part of the country of the **Seres** <note>The "Seres" was the ancient Greek and Roman name for the people of Northwestern China, famous for silk production.</note>, on the side of the East and South by an unknown land, and on the West side by India, which is beyond the Ganges according to the line described as far as the great gulf, which likewise borders them along with the other adjacent coasts where the **Ichthyophagi Ethiopians** <note>Literally "Fish-eaters"; a term used by ancient geographers to describe various coastal peoples.</note> live according to the present description. Then, toward the end, coming to speak of the capital city of the Chinese, he says thus: 'And the metropolitan city of the aforementioned country, **Thinæ**.' Sené mentions it in his *Onomasticon* <note>A dictionary of proper names.</note> of cities, saying: '**Sinarum**, the Metropolitan city of the Chinese, of whom Marcian speaks in his sailings,' from which it is presumed that this word *Thinæ* in Ptolemy is corrupted, and likewise within Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian.</note> in the first book, where the same name is also read; and that for $\Theta \epsilon \tilde{\iota} \nu \alpha \iota$ <note>original Greek: "Theinai"</note> one must read $\Sigma \epsilon \tilde{\iota} \nu \alpha \iota$ <note>original Greek: "Seinai"</note>, as the said Stephen calls it in the place previously cited; and with him Father Xavier, a Jesuit, in an Indian epistle of the year 1552, where he informs the Father General Loyola that his fellow brothers have made their way toward the Royal city of China called **Sina** or **Sinar**."

After the aforementioned Ptolemy and Stephen cited above, we find some mention of this same Kingdom of China in the Persian and Arabic Doctors, who, speaking of the drugs they bring from the East Indies, use these names **Seni** and **Sini**, as it appears in **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> Book 2, Chapter 124, when he speaks of Cinnamon, which he calls in his language **Darfeni** and **Dar-sini**, which is "Chinese wood"; and in agreement with him, Serapion; Rhazes in his *Continent*; Mesuë in his preparation of *Anacardimes*; and Averroës in his *Colliget*. The same Avicenna, in the book cited above, Chapter 578, speaking of **Rhubarb**, calls it in his language **Raued seni**, or **Raued sini**, which is "Chinese root," thus calling Rhubarb "by excellence" <note>Meaning "the ultimate example of its kind."</note> because it comes from China. Upon these passages, Gerard of Cremona <note>A 12th-century Italian translator of scientific works from Arabic into Latin.</note>, commentator on the said Avicenna, interpreting the word *Seni* or *Sini*, says it is a place name. And Bellunense, interpreting the word *Sini* in Chapter 172, says that it signifies everything coming from the country of Sini. Also, Serapion in his *Simples*, speaking of **Zerumbet** <note>A species of edible ginger with medicinal properties.</note>, says by the authority of Isaac that it comes from the country named Sini, which is none other than China. Consequently, it results from these authorities that the Country of China is situated in the East and entirely within the East Indies, beyond the Ganges, and is named by the name **Sina** and **Sini**, as it is still called today throughout the Indies, according to what modern writers testify—among others, Father de la Croix in his *Voyage of Perguaiz*, Chapter 1, and Bernardino Escalante in his *Navigation*, Chapter 6. From this, it was known that the Portuguese and Spaniards frequenting that country, and hearing it named...

-> Languages of this World. <-

The **Sini** or **Sina** have kept the same name, and have called it **China**, by changing the letter **S** into **Ch**, as often happens in their language, and also in others like **Hebrew**, where the word *Sibolet* <note>original: "Sibolet"; referring to the "Shibboleth" incident in Judges 12:6 where the pronunciation of "s" vs "sh" determined a person's tribal identity.</note> is changed into *Schibboleth* in the Book of Judges, chapter 12. This is also seen in the German and Flemish language in the word *Fisch*, or *Vuisch*, derived from the Latin *Piscis* <note>Fish</note>, and similarly in our own [French] in the word *Chifre* <note>Cipher or Digit</note>, taken from the Hebrew word ספר <note>original: "sephira"; likely referring to *sephirah* (counting/enumeration) or *sepher* (book/writing).</note>. This happens because of the similarity of sound between these two letters, both in Hebrew and Arabic, where there are two "S"s, one called ש **Sin**, and the other ש **Schin** <note>These are two versions of the same Hebrew letter, distinguished by a dot to indicate an "s" or "sh" sound.</note>. It is also like German and English in which "st" and "th" are pronounced like the *Sch* or the *Ch* of our language in the words *Fasten* <note>To fast</note> and *Schall* <note>Sound/Resonance</note>, and other similar words; and finally in Spanish, which pronounces the **Ch** with a sound leaning toward that of the letter **S**. From this, it follows that they have turned the ancient name **Sina** into their modern **China**, as has been said.

This being presupposed, we shall say that **Duarte Barbosa** <note>original: "Odouard Barbosse"; a Portuguese explorer (c. 1480–1521) who wrote one of the earliest detailed European accounts of India and China.</note>, a Portuguese, in his voyages to the Indies, divides and partitions the country and Region of the Sines into two great provinces: one stretching toward the Oriental South, and the other to the North-East. The first is **Cin**, **Sin**, or **China**; and the other is **Mangi** <note>A term used by Marco Polo and later travelers to refer to Southern China.</note>, containing within itself the lands and Kingdoms of **Chequan** <note>Zhejiang</note>, **Tainfu**, **Nanqui** <note>Nanjing</note>, **Xauton** <note>Shandong</note>, **Quinzi**, and **Quinzay** <note>Hangzhou</note>. Then, speaking of the Chinese, he says that they have their own language, using almost the same accent and way of speaking and uttering their words as the **Tudesques** or **Germans** <note>It was a common observation by early European travelers that Chinese sounded guttural, like German.</note>—not that their words and languages are in any way similar, as **André Thevet** mentions in passing in Book 11, Chapter 25 of his *Universal Cosmography*. Speaking of the people of **Mangi**, he continues that their language is entirely different from that of the **Tartars** <note>The Mongols</note> who rule over them, just as the inhabitants are different in their ways of life from the aforementioned Tartars. This country of China, or rather the Kingdom, consists of fifteen very large Provinces, each having its own Metropolitan City, from which it is named. There are five maritime provinces, namely: **Cantun** <note>Canton/Guangzhou</note>, **Foquiun** <note>Fujian</note>, **Quiociun**, **Chiqueun**, **Nanginum** <note>Nanjing</note>, and **Pachinum** <note>Beijing</note>; the others are inland, namely: **Sincaium**, **Sufuauum**, **Xauchinum**, **Hoaum**, **Saucium**, **Olamum**, **Oquianum**, **Quancium**, and **Aranum**.

Some say there are indeed 240 Cities or Towns in this Kingdom situated on great navigable rivers. **Jan Huygen van Linschoten** <note>original: "I. Hugo"; a Dutch explorer whose writings were vital to breaking the Portuguese monopoly in the East.</note> maintains that there are in these Provinces great and renowned cities or towns up to the number of 591, and some 1,593 small ones, without counting the boroughs, villages, and hamlets.

The Reverend Father **Juan González de Mendoza**, of the Order of St. Augustine, in his *History of the Great Kingdom of China* situated in the East Indies (divided into two parts, Book 1, Chapter 1 of the first part), speaks of it as follows: "This great Kingdom of China of which we speak here was discovered and truly well-recognized ten years ago by the Spaniards living in the Philippine Islands, which are two hundred leagues distant from it. Although something was known of it through the reports of the Portuguese who trade in **Canton** and **Macao** <note>original: "Malan"</note>, cities of that state, their various accounts had nonetheless almost obscured the truth. And so it was that in the year 1575, Friar **Martín de Rada** <note>original: "Martin Henança, ou Herrade"</note>, Provincial of the Augustinians, and **Jerónimo Marín**..."

...which is clearly apparent, because their writings and *Chapas* <note>original: "Chapas," likely referring to official documents, seals, or block-printed certificates</note> are understood by all of them, although the languages spoken by the Chinese are numerous and very different from each other, in the same way that our numerical figures are understood equally in French, in Spanish, and in Arabic. From this it follows that as things are in themselves innumerable, the letters or figures used by the Chinese to denote them are almost infinite: so much so that he who must read or write in China, as do the <term>Mandarins</term> <note>the scholar-officials of the Ming and Qing dynasties</note>, must know and remember at least eighty-five thousand characters or letters, and those who are perfect in this reading know more than six score thousand <note>original: "six vingtz mille," or 120,000</note>, a prodigious and strange thing, indeed, which would be unbelievable if it were not attested by persons worthy of trust, etc.

Paper in China is similar to European paper, yet less white in color, but superior in thinness and purity. Writing pens are made of reeds, into which they place brushes <note>original: "penicilla," small brushes used for ink calligraphy</note> in the manner of our painters. Upon these papers they record everything, describing the liberal arts, laws, rights, their statutes, and likewise private and public deeds, yielding nothing to either the Greeks or the Latins. They make the pages narrow and oblong, and in writing, they proceed neither from left to right like the Greeks and Latins, nor from right toward the left like the Hebrews, but from the crown to the heel, or from the top to the bottom <note>original: "à vertice ad Calcem," literally from the head to the heel</note>, by a certain peculiar method of drawing lines; of which kind of printed volumes and books I myself have several times seen and inspected with my own eyes. They use letters like those of the Egyptians, which the Greeks called hieroglyphics. These individual characters serve for individual words, and sometimes even for entire meanings. Hence it happens that although the Chinese use various languages—certainly in so many and such disjointed regions, for they vary according to the distance of places, and there are many differences of idioms and dialects there—yet they all equally understand those things which are committed to letters. For the alphabet <note>The author uses "alphabetum" loosely to mean the entire set of characters</note> is one and the same for everyone, consisting of course of more than five thousand signs for things and words, for the comprehension of which they have need of a sharp memory and long practice. From this also a reason appears why the learned among them are held in such great esteem; for besides the proper tongue of each nation and province, there is moreover a certain and common speech of the erudite, corresponding to the Latin language among us, which they commonly call <term>Mandarin</term>. This is used by courtiers, scribes, legal consultants, judges, and other magistrates, who for that reason also commonly obtain the name of Mandarins.

The same author in chapter 53 discusses this Chinese language very extensively.

From the agreement of the wills and studies of the Chinese, it comes about that there is one language common to the Kingdom which they call that of the Mandarins. This is understood by all, even if not all speak it; which very fact can also make the dissemination of the Gospel easier, since one language being known, so many and such...

” The language of the Chinese is almost the most difficult of all, and this because of three
” conditions it has: the first is that all words are monosyllabic, <note>original: "monosyllaba"</note>
” which makes for a style of speech that is small, narrow, broken, and interrupted,
” which indeed produces in us offense and weariness. The second cause

Father Jacques de Pantoja <note>a Spanish Jesuit missionary who accompanied Matteo Ricci to Beijing</note> of the Society of Jesus, in his advice sent from
Beijing <note>original: "Paquin," the old French romanization of Peking/Beijing</note>, a city of China, to the Reverend Father Luis de Guzmán of the same Society,
on the 9th of March 1602. Among other remarks on this country, he says:
” All the luck and happiness of the Chinese lies in the knowledge of their
” letters: they reach as many as forty thousand, although their words are only
” monosyllables: each letter signifies a thing, and not just the word, as it does with
” us: they write not with a pen, but in its place they use a
” brush: <note>original: "pinceau"</note> of these forty thousand letters, the majority are composite; the simple
” and ordinary ones are no less than ten thousand, and nevertheless few
” people are found in the country who do not know how to read and write: their study
” is not done in colleges and public universities (as we are made to
” believe in Europe); they have none at all: and this is where their
” <term>policy</term> <note>meaning their social organization or governance</note> is very much lacking, among other remarkable defects. Each person makes
” use of a master, if he has the means; if not, he joins with others, paying
” each month. What deceived the first informants from Europe
” is that every three years the King sends commissioners to the capitals of
” each province for the examination which is held for three degrees, which are
” as you might say the <term>Baccalaureate</term>, the <term>Licentiate</term>, and the <term>Doctorate</term>. By the
” first, one acquires from then on the status of being counted among the men of letters,
” and enjoys several fine privileges and immunities; but it carries the obligation
” to continue one's study and to pass on to the second degree; otherwise,
” if laziness is recognized, and if one does not offer oneself at each term for the
” attempt, degradation follows with ignominy. One can, if one wishes,
” stop at the second degree, which is joined with some office of the
” <term>Mandarinat</term> <note>The office or rank of a Mandarin/scholar-official</note> which is given when the promotion is made. The third degree
” is given only in the King’s court; he who aspires to it goes to present himself to the
” judges and obtains two travel allowances and liberal reimbursement as far as the court.
” At the time of the examination, they lock the pretendants in prepared stalls <note>small cells for isolation during exams</note>
” all alone for 24 hours, having searched them well and surely beforehand;
” they leave them nothing but their brush, their ink, and paper: and it
” happens that they enter into such strong apprehension, and strain their
” minds in such a way, that they emerge from their stalls half dead, with what remains
” of their life ending in a few hours afterward. Upon leaving, their
” compositions are taken, and very correct copies are made of them; the originals, with the
” names of the authors, are faithfully reserved in the archives. The copies
” without names are given to the appointed judges, who examine them like
” <term>Areopagites</term> <note>referring to the high court of Athens; here meaning impartial and elite judges</note>, not knowing whose they are. From this great number of
” compositions, they draw a hundred, two hundred, more or less, as it has pleased the King
” to grant grace: for in the plurality of Provinces, they place their honor in the
” composition which is judged the best, and the name of its author being
” known, he is declared and published with very great applause.
” The others not named, mortified and burdened with shame, return home.

They call the Preachers *Tangins* <note>Likely a corruption of a Chinese term for Buddhist or Taoist priests, possibly related to "Seng" (monk) or "Tianshi" (celestial master)</note>. Their language is extremely difficult, consisting of verbs that are all monosyllables, which makes their style of speech very concise, narrow, compressed, broken, and interrupted, full of equivoques with Homonyms and Synonyms that they pile one upon the other, which cannot be distinguished except by accents, or rather by musical sounds with a diverse prolatio<gloss>n</gloss> <note>a term for the duration or extension of a musical note</note> or pronunciation. And furthermore, they have no alphabet or index, nor a set number of letters, for every single thing has its own mark and Character, or rather a Hieroglyphic figure <note>The author is describing Chinese ideograms, which early modern Europeans often likened to Egyptian hieroglyphs</note>, such that throughout one's entire life it is necessary to keep learning a new alphabet and index of letters.

This creates a very great confusio<gloss>n</gloss>; nevertheless, a certain modern Jesuit Father has reduced it to an art, and has fashioned and composed a Dictionary from it. Father Martin Herrada <note>Martin de Rada (1533–1578), a Spanish Augustinian friar</note>, Provincial of the Augustinians mentioned above, was the first European to learn the Chinese language, and he reduced it to an art and made a Grammar of it, along with a Dictionary, as is reported in the 2nd part of Book 1, Chapter 1 of the *History of China*.

The most difficult thing in the aforementioned language is that the Mandarins and the learned use<gloss>d</gloss> a certain jargon like the *Blaisches* <note>Likely referring to a specific regional dialect or a specialized professional slang</note>, so much so that they do not even understand themselves; nevertheless, they are nonetheless capable and very desirous of understanding the doctrine of the faith. They have from all time honored a Virgin whom they say gave birth, and they call her in their language *Schimmu, ni, an, ni an*, that is to say, Holy Mother and Queen of Queens <note>This likely refers to "Shengmu" (Holy Mother), a title often applied to the goddess Mazu or adapted by missionaries to describe the Virgin Mary</note>. Modern accounts of these countries state that a Father Matthieu Riccius <note>Matteo Ricci (1552–1610), the famous Jesuit missionary</note> has, some years ago, translated the principal book of China from the Chinese language into the Latin language, and has composed a European<gloss>n</gloss> and Chinese Lexicon, and other works by means of which it is held that all those who come from Europe to China can, in four years, easily understand the languages and doctrines thereof.

### Of the Great Island of Japan or Giapan.

## CHAP. LXXVI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' at the start of the chapter, featuring floral and foliate scrolls within a square frame.</image-desc>
**Antonio Galvão**, in his book on the inventors of the new world, and several Portuguese and Spanish authors, relate that the three Portuguese individuals who follow were the first Europeans who found the Island of **Japan** in the year of salvation 1542: namely **Antonio Mota**, **Francisco Zeimoto**, and **Antonio Peixoto**, at the time when **Martim Afonso de Sousa** was Viceroy for the King of Portugal in the East Indies in the city of **Goa**; this is confirmed by **Gotthard Arthus** in his new history of the East Indies, chapter 56.

Later, in the year 1549, **Father Xavier** <note>Saint Francis Xavier (1506–1552), a co-founder of the Jesuit Order</note> accompanied by **Cosme de Torres** and **Juan Fernández**, Spaniards, a man named **Paul** <note>Yajirō, also known as Paulo de Santa Fé, the first Japanese convert to Christianity</note> with two of his servants and two Japanese men who had been baptized a short time before, made the voyage to the aforementioned Island and there began to plant the foundations of the Christian religion.

In the year 1553, several great Lords of this Island came on an embassy to the Viceroy of the Indies to ask him for doctors and Priests, in order to teach them the Christian Religion, as is recorded in the *Letters from Japan* written by the Jesuit Fathers to those of their Congregation in Europe.

The King of **Bungo** <note>A historical province on the island of Kyushu</note> in this Island sent Ambassadors to the late Pope **Gregory XIII** in Rome, to pay and render all obedience to his Holiness and to the Holy Apostolic See in the year 1585, as I shall remark hereafter in this chapter.

**Marco Polo** the Venetian, in book 3, chapter 2 of his travels, makes mention of this great Island under the name of **Zipangu**, which is located to the North-East, stretching from **Quinsay** <note>Modern-day Hangzhou, China</note> toward the country of China described by us above, and at a similar elevation to Spain, namely from 35 to 40 degrees; it contains 600 leagues in length and three hundred in width. The shape of this Island is rounder than it is long, and formed like an oval; having on the southern side the Island of **Mazacar** <note>Possibly a reference to Tanegashima or a nearby island</note> with several other small ones near the gulf of the great city of **Kagoshima**, of which mention is made in the *Letters from Japan*. To the North are the Islands of **Torsa**, **Fanfata**, and others which are renowned for **Meac** <note>Miyako, the historical name for Kyoto, the imperial capital</note>, which is the Royal and Metropolitan city of the entire Island. A certain person named **Cosme de Torres**, in one of his letters inserted in book 3 of the *Letters from Japan*, has made an ample description of this Island.

**Michel Villette**, in his letter to the Jesuit Brothers inserted in the book of the *Letters from Japan*, writes that the Japanese worship a **Bonze** <note>term: **Bonze** – A term used by early European travelers to describe Buddhist monks or priests</note> who died eight hundred years ago...

» and the *Chinese*. Finally, according to our people <note>Referring to European missionaries and explorers like the Jesuits.</note> who are by no means crude
» judges of such things, this *Japanese* language is to be preferred over *Latin*,
» whether for its nature, or for its richness and abundance. And for this
» reason, it requires great labor and a long time to be learned and
» spoken.

A. Thevet, in book 12, chapter 16 of his *Universal Cosmography* <note>André Thevet (1516–1590) was a French Franciscan priest and explorer.</note>, writing of these *Japanese* people, records that they write from top to bottom, and not from left to right as we do; and the reason they give for it is this—and it is a rather meager one: that just as a man in walking keeps his feet below and his head above, so too must one begin writing at the top and finish at the bottom.

Here then is the simple Alphabet of *China* and *Japan*, whose writing proceeds from top to bottom, in columns arranged from right to left, after the *Hebrew* fashion. This was shared with the public through the grace and beneficence of His late Majesty King Henry III, by means of the late Count of Bouchage, who lived as a *Capuchin Father* <note>Henri de Joyeuse, Count of Bouchage, who famously joined the Capuchin order.</note>; at the request of the no less eloquent than most learned late reverend and devout *Father Master Emond Auger of the Society of the name of JESUS* <note>The Jesuits.</note>, who secured this benefit for us, as the late Lord de Vigenère <note>Blaise de Vigenère (1523–1596), a famous French diplomat and cryptographer.</note> certifies in his *Treatise on Ciphers*.

Furthermore, these Japanese people have a book composed in their <term>Sino-Japanese</term> language <note>The original text says "langue Chinse," likely referring to Kanbun or Japanese written with Chinese characters</note> called the *Fouqueque* <note>The *Hokke-kyō* or Lotus Sutra</note>, formerly written and composed by **Xaca** <note>Shaka, the Japanese name for Gautama Buddha</note>, whom they say was the son of one of their Kings and a very learned personage. This book was left to them by **Amide** <note>Amida Buddha</note>, the son of one of their Kings, and they honor it as a holy and religious thing, saying that it is impossible for a man to be saved without the help of this book, and that by its virtue even the herbs and the woods possess and receive a blessing <note>A reference to the Buddhist concept that even inanimate objects like plants can achieve enlightenment (Sōmoku jōbutsu)</note>.

**Gothard Arthus**, in his history of China, chapter 54, speaks in this manner of the Japanese language:

> "The speech of the Japanese is one and common to all, but it is so varied and manifold that it seems, not without reason, to be many languages. For every single thing there are many words, some used out of contempt and others for the sake of honor; some are used among princes, others among the common people, and finally, some are used by men and others by women. To this they add that they speak and write differently, and in writing itself, they compose letters in one way and volumes or books in another. They have many books, written both in prose and in most elegant verse. They use characters of such a kind that individual marks denote single or even multiple words, in the manner of the Egyptians and Chinese; for this reason, much labor and a long time are required to learn that language thoroughly. The Chinese can read their writing, but they do not understand their speech, which is thought to happen because of the similarity of the characters but the variety and dissimilarity of the spoken words." <note>original Latin: "Sermo Iaponiorum vnus est & communis omnium... Chinenses scripturam eorum legere possunt, loquendo autem non assequuntur..."</note>

Some modern authors have remarked that in this island of Japan, several words are noted in the language of the inhabitants that conform to those of the **Icelanders**, as a sign of the ancient commerce that may have formerly existed between these two nations; this is repeated by the **Lord of La Popelinière** in Book 1 of *The Three Worlds*.

## Of the Indian Philosophers.

### CHAP. LXXVII.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'S' set within a square frame featuring ornate floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

**Strabo**, in his works, speaking of the **Indian Philosophers**, writes that there were two kinds: the **Brachmans**, also called **Brahmans**, and the **Germans** <note>A corruption of "Garmanes," from the Greek "Garmanai," referring to Shramanas or wandering ascetics</note>. He notes that these Brachmans or Brahmans were more excellent than the others because their opinions were closer to reason and truth than those of the Germans (whom **Porphyry** in Book 4 of *On Sacrifices* calls **Samaneans** <note>Shramanas</note>). Also, from the moment these Brahmans were conceived, says the aforementioned Strabo, they had learned men who took care of them; these men, coming to the mother, used certain charms and words upon the mother and the fruit of her womb, wishing her and promising her happiness and good success for the future. But there are some who say they spoke to the mother only of good things, preaching to her of sobriety and continence, and they esteemed those women happy who listened to them with their whole heart, saying they would be abundant in blessings.

<meta>This page continues the description of the learned classes of the East, transitioning from the Japanese context of the previous page to a detailed account of the lifestyles and natural philosophies of the sages of India (likely the Brahmins or Gymnosophists), as recorded by early modern European scholars.</meta>

<page-num>923</page-num>
<header>Languages of this Universe.</header>

Children, once they had come into the world, were given instructors, sometimes one and then another; but when they had grown a bit older, it was then that they were given the most learned and excellent of their school as masters. These **Philosophers** lived within the woods nearest to the cities, and stayed there assembled together like monks do in their monasteries, living very soberly, sleeping on mattresses and animal skins, eating no meat of any kind (as they still do not) and abstaining from women (though now they are far from observing this), speaking only of serious things, and communicating heartfully with those who came to approach them as seekers—both to learn and to make their own knowledge known and understood by others. And the disciples showed great reverence and modest respect when before their masters, it not being permitted for them to speak, cough, or spit; and if it happened that any did so, he was suddenly chased from the company for that day, and esteemed a man of little honor, lacking in sobriety and self-control.

They lived for the space of thirty years under this discipline and subjection, and then each of the disciples retired to his own house, being permitted to live a little more licentiously than was their custom: for they could clothe themselves in subtle and delicate linen, wear rings on their fingers, and bracelets, and jewels hanging from their ears—but all with discretion and modesty, and without any excess or superfluity. Likewise, they were permitted to eat the meat of animals other than those that are helpful to man <note>Likely referring to the cow, which was and is sacred in India</note>, and yet sauces and foods that were very tart and biting, such as garlic, onions, and spices, were forbidden to them. They also had license to marry several wives to have progeny, saying that from a great number there would likewise come a multitude of good children. It is true that they never philosophized among their wives, so that if the women were foolish and flighty, they would not publish the secrets of their school and doctrine; and if they were good, having tasted this knowledge, they might not withdraw from their company. For those who despise both death and pain, who care neither for pleasure, nor ease, nor life itself, and who wish to be subject to no one but rather defend their liberty—such a person is esteemed good by them; and a wise and virtuous woman, if she embraced such opinions, would no longer wish to live under the obedience of her husband.

As for their opinions on natural things, they held several things following the opinion of the **Greeks**, saying that the world had a beginning and that it will one day have an end, and that its shape is spherical and round, and that God, being the author and former of it, also fills it entirely by his power and penetrates it, and runs through it in the blink of an eye. They held that there are several and diverse principles of things, but that the world had its source and original beginning in water; they also established (like **Aristotle**) beyond the four elements a certain <term>Entelechy</term> <note>original: "Entelechie"; a term used by Aristotle to describe the full realization or "form-giving" cause of a thing</note>, or <term>quintessence</term>, from which the heavens and the stars were composed, and that the earth is placed in the middle of the Universe—and several other things, some true, others approaching the truth, and some fabulous, such that it seems either that **Plato** fished his doctrine from them, or else that they are **Platonists**.

Pliny, Book 7, Chapter 2, and Solinus, Chapter 65, describe another sort of philosophers among those Indians, who are called **Gymnosophists** <note>Greek: *gymnosophistai*, literally "naked wise men"</note>, so named because they would discourse while keeping themselves entirely naked in the Sun, sitting or crouching like a monkey or an ape, and sometimes standing upright to devote themselves to contemplation. Regarding these men, the aforementioned Solinus speaks in this manner, having drawn it from the aforementioned Pliny as he did the rest of his works: "Some (he says) have philosophers they call **Gymnosophists**, who, from the morning when the Sun rises until the evening when it sets, remain attentively holding their eyes fixed against that burning globe, and while withdrawing from the Sun, they consider certain secrets within it; they do not mind passing the entire day supporting themselves on one foot, and that foot quite naked upon the burning sand, heated by the violent warmth and rays of the Sun." Philostratus, Book 2, Chapter 4, of the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, says that these **Gymnosophists** keep themselves in the Sun as has been said; they pray to and adore it, and their prayers intend that the hours it measures by its courses and revolutions might be converted and accommodated by its pleasure for the salvation of the Indians and for the fertility of their land. And because he holds that these philosophers possess some sort of fire which they draw from the boiling rays of the Sun, he further adds that when night has come, they pray to it again not to be angry, even though the night draws near to its face, but that it might please it to remain with the Indians, just as they retain it among themselves. Many and infinite other things regarding all the ways of acting and the beliefs of these Indian philosophers are brought forth by the aforementioned Philostratus in the sixth book of the *Life of the said Apollonius of Tyana*. Furthermore, we shall note that under the name of **Gymnosophist** is comprised the generality of Indian doctors and philosophers, because they all went entirely naked while they were in their school. Of this, Porphyry bears witness in the fourth book of *On Sacrifices*—he, the Apostate <note>Referring to Porphyry of Tyre, a Neoplatonist who was a famous opponent of Christianity</note> who, by embracing the doctrine of Plato too foolishly, renounced Christianity; for he says there are two sorts of **Gymnosophists**: namely the **Brahmins** <note>original: "Brachmans"</note>, who come by a certain succession of race to holiness and integrity; and the **Sarmanes** <term>Germanes</term> <note>These are the Shramanas, a non-Vedic ascetic movement; the text uses "Germanes" following a common early modern corruption of Strabo's "Sarmanes"</note> (whom Strabo calls Germans), who made simple profession of this doctrine by their own will, without being received into the number of the others who were the most perfect.

The same Strabo, cited above, divides the **Sarmanes** of whom we previously spoke; some being more perfect than the others, because the word "German" is general, and there is another appellation: some are called **Hylobians** <note>original: "Hylobies"; a Greek term meaning "living in the woods"</note>, which is a Greek word signifying "living in the woods." These do not live on fruits gathered from trees, but clothe themselves in bark, caring neither for intoxicating drink nor the company of women. These men were honored by Kings, who would inquire of them concerning divine matters, and were instructed by them on how they must pray and perform service to God. Besides these **Hylobians**, there were among the **Sarmanes** certain physicians, who took care to debate concerning man—that is to say, concerning the body—just as the others dealt with what concerned the soul. Now, they held the opinion that the best medicines were those taken while at rest, and not by chance, and if it were necessary to take them otherwise, it was through ointments, rubbings, and poultices <note>original: *cataplasmes*; a soft, moist mass of material, typically of bran, flour, or herbs, applied to the body to relieve soreness</note>, because in these there lay no evil spell. There was a third kind of these **Garmanes** <note>original: *Germans*; here referring to the *Garmanes* or *Samanaeans*, a sect of Indian ascetics described by Strabo, not the people of Germany</note> who were charmers, sorcerers, and enchanters, who were not ignorant of anything said regarding the apparitions of the dead, nor of the science practiced by means of the bodies and shadows of the deceased. Furthermore, there was another sort, more civilized and courteous than the aforementioned people, who frequented the cities and villages without being so scrupulous about their foods or their company; these men were also not ignorant of the science of demons <note>The author uses "demons" in the classical sense of *daemons* or spirits, rather than purely evil beings</note>, in which, to tell the truth, the greater part of the philosophers have been skilled. Seeking to know the secrets of nature, they considered malignant spirits to be Genies <note>guiding spirits</note>, messengers of nature who gave them such knowledge.

The aforementioned Strabo mentions yet another sort of philosophers, whom he calls **Pramnes**, whom he says are a contentious people and great debaters. They mocked the **Brahmans** because they occupied themselves with the science of the Stars <note>astronomy and astrology</note> and wished to judge men by their physiognomy <note>the practice of judging character from facial features</note>, calling them fools and vain predictors of uncertain things. Thus one can see how much vanity was imprinted in the heart of these people, and yet they did not lack a good and noble natural talent, seeing their governance, their knowledge, and their life, which was quite civilized and reformed. For this reason, one should not be amazed if many great and learned ancient figures traveled as far as India to speak to these **Gymnosophists** and **Brahmans**, since even today they maintain a reputation for knowledge, though they do not come close to those of ancient centuries.

Those who wish to see many other fine and ample discourses concerning the life, ways, and customs of these Indian philosophers should read: Diodorus Siculus, Book 7, of the *Deeds of Alexander*, mentioning the letter of the Brahman King to Alexander the Great; Saint Augustine, Book 13, Chapter 17, and Book 15, Chapter 20, of the *City of God*; Fulgosus, Book 8, Chapter 11, of his *Rhapsodies*; Caelius Rhodiginus, Book 13, Chapter 25, and Book 18, Chapter 31, of his *Diverse Lessons*; François de Belleforest, Book 2, Chapter 8, of his *Universal History*, and Volume 2, Book 3, Chapter 14, and following, of his *Universal Cosmography*.

[Philoso]phers, or Doctors of the Idolaters: especially since they serve two idols, and are entrusted with the government of the temples, of which there are a great number; some of these are endowed <note>original: *rentez*; meaning they have a fixed income or revenue</note>, while in others the [monks] must live on alms. They have statues of stone, wood, and every sort, in which temples they celebrate festivals, perform grand ceremonies while sounding instruments, singing, using incense, and lighting a great number of oil lamps, for wax is not in much use there. They hold the number three in very great reverence, confessing one sole God, Creator of all the world and the things contained therein, and that his divinity is one in three persons; but the fault is that they believe there are other Gods in great number who govern as commissioners of the Great God in this world, whom they pray to and adore. And when all is said, they make God a "cessator" <note>original: *cessateur*; one who has ceased to act, or an idle deity</note> and idle, as if he had become weary from creating the world, and that these others, being fresher, have now taken charge of it. 

It is easy to see that these people once had a taste of Christianity, both because of this belief in the Trinity and unity of persons, and because when they enter the Churches of the Christians (which are in fairly good number in these Indies), they pray there willingly, revere them, and honor the images of the saints. And what is more, Duarte Barbosa <note>original: *Odouard Barbosse*; a Portuguese writer and explorer who traveled to India in the early 16th century</note> says in his voyages that these people always inquire about our lady the glorious Virgin Mary, as having heard speak of her. As for me, I think that the lack of Christianity among them has proceeded from the [negligence] of the Ministers who have ceased to admonish the people; although these people still say that there is hardly any difference between their religion and ours, they are greatly mistaken. For we do not assign any companion to God; in him alone we hope and [trust], and we honor him in his saints, without making him idle or giving the charge of the world to other gods, nor raising an altar or sacrifice except to this God, who by his word created everything that exists in this Universe. Thus, it is impossible to put in the same rank of religion things that are so different as Christianity and idolatry. 

These <term>Brahmins</term> <note>original: *Bramins*; the priestly and scholarly varna in Indian society</note> also go entirely naked above the waist, but over the shoulder they have a cord of three silk threads with tassels, which is the sign to distinguish them from the <term>Banians</term> <note>original: *Baucani*; likely a variation of *Banians* or *Vaniyas*, the merchant and trading caste</note> who make up the second rank of the pagan <term>Gujaratis</term> <note>original: *Guzerats*; people from the Gujarat region of India</note>. These latter involve themselves in labor and merchandise, and they still do not eat anything whatsoever that has blood, just as they also do not kill any animal, whether on the earth, in the air, or in the waters; they observe ablutions and washings, and think that this is the salvation of their souls. 

Both these Brahmins and the Banians marry as we do, that is to say, without the practice of having multiple wives as the <term>Muslims</term> <note>original: *Mahometistes*</note> and other idolaters do; and they consider it a sin for someone who has lost their partner to enter into a second marriage. They make a great festival of their weddings, lasting for several days, with a great assembly being made there, everyone being dressed very richly to honor the married couple. To avoid lewdness, they marry very young, both men and women. On the day of the wedding, the spouses stay upon a bed richly dressed and loaded with jewels and precious stones; and before them is a small table, upon which is an idol covered in flowers, and around it a quantity of lit lamps, toward which...

# Languages of this World.

The husband and wife, from morning until evening, must keep their eyes fixed, without eating or drinking, or saying a single word to any living person. Meanwhile, the guests feast and rejoice with songs, balls, dances, and musical instruments; they also set off fireworks for the pleasure and pastime of the company. If it happens that the husband dies, the woman is no longer permitted to remarry; she succeeds, along with the children, to the inheritance of the deceased. It is to be noted that the Brahmins <term>Bramins; the priestly and scholarly caste, the highest in the Hindu social hierarchy</term> do not take wives from anywhere but among the Brahmins, so as not to soil or mix their races and families. Of these, there are two sorts: some are of high quality and most respected, being those who have charge of the temples and offer sacrifices; others are of lower condition, serving as messengers and couriers for those who employ them. Because, wherever they go, there is no one who would annoy or bother them, even if war is ignited on all sides; indeed, thieves encountering them on the road respect them so much that they make way and honor them, whereas they rob others.

Throughout the country of Deccan, and in the regions of Cambay, Goa, and surrounding lands, there are these great and honored Brahmins, among whom are those called Patamares <term>Patamares; a term used by early European travelers for couriers or messengers, often of the Brahmin caste, who held a sacred status</term>, because they are esteemed to be descended from the royal blood of the Princes of Cambay, since in that country kings formerly had to be Brahmins, as is still practiced today in Malabar. These men are so highly esteemed that merchants passing through the country—even if they fall into the hands of brigands and thieves—are as safe as if they were in their own home, provided they have one of these Brahmins in their company. There is no one so bold as to dare rob them; and if it happens that there are some so fierce as to not respect them, and who pillage and rob the poor merchants, the Brahmin accompanying them immediately either kills or wounds himself with a dagger. With his blood, the others go to stain certain images that they drag through the streets until justice is done for the wrong the merchants received, and vengeance is taken for the spilled blood of their companion. They are constrained to do this, both for the reverence held for them and so as not to irritate the people, who love and revere them strangely, as they hold them to be holy; they believe that if justice were not done, they themselves would be punished for having denied it.

Regarding the Brahmins of Malabar, the aforementioned modern travelers and navigators divide them into four sorts: those who are properly Brahmins, then the Patamares, the Nambudares <term>Nambudares; Nambudiri Brahmins, the high-caste priests of the Malabar coast</term>, and the Nabures <term>Nabures; likely a reference to the Nayadi or another lower sub-group, though the text considers them the least prized</term>, who are the least valued. The race of these people is very ancient and they come from more illustrious blood than the Nairs <term>Naires; the Nayar caste, traditionally warriors and rulers in the Kerala region</term>. They are in charge of prayer and have the understanding of everything touching their Religion; the most honorable among them stay with the King, as they do in Calicut, and eat nothing that has life, nor does the King, who must be taken from this Brahmin race. They never kill cows under penalty of death, this being a law of their ancestors; because they live on the milk, butter, and cheeses of these animals, they consider it parricide <note>original: *parricide*; the murder of a parent or close relative</note> to kill one.

Beyond the aforementioned Brahmins, there are also found throughout the Indies certain persons originating from the Kingdom of Delhi. These individuals stay only a short time in one place, and while they are called *Ioghi* <term>Yogis; ascetic practitioners of meditation and yoga</term> by those from Delhi, they call themselves *Coamez* in their own language, which means "servants of God." Their aim and goal is to be placed in the rank of those they call *Abdutes* <term>Avadhutas; a type of radical ascetic who has shaken off all worldly concerns</term>, an order among them that is the most prized and esteemed of all. They travel in bands, much like the **Egyptians** and **Bohemians** <note>16th-century terms for the Romani people, characterized here by their wandering lifestyle</note> of our lands, throughout all the Indies. They are everywhere very well received and cherished by all the Gentiles and Pagans, eating all types of meat without religious scruple, and associating with all kinds of people. They do not practice the customary and superstitious washings of other Indians, nor do they devote themselves to the worship of Idols. As for this name *Ioghi*, it comes from the Kingdom of Ioghé, whose inhabitants are vagabonds just like these *Coamez*. See Ludovico di Varthema <note>Italian traveler (c. 1470–1517)</note>, book 4, chapter 2 of his travels, and Duarte Barbosa <note>Portuguese explorer (c. 1480–1521)</note> in his travels, the chapter on the Kingdom of Delhi; also Pierre du Jarric <note>Jesuit historian (1566–1617)</note>, book 1, chapter 4, of his histories of the East Indies.

The Chinese call their Priests in their language *Hoxiones*, *Mandarinus*, *Tutans*, and *Loytias* <note>These terms represent various levels of officials and monks: 'Hoxiones' likely refers to Heshang (monks), while 'Loytias' is a corruption of Lo-tia (venerable sir/official)</note>.

As for the Priests and Philosophers of the Island of Japan named *bonzes* or *bonzies* <term>Bonzes; a term used by Europeans to describe Buddhist monks</term>, there are several kinds. Three of these are like our Monks, whom the Japanese call in their language *Lequixil*, and there are women who are like our Nuns and Religious Sisters, whom they call in their language *Hamacata*. These have monasteries just like the Monks here, both inside and outside the cities. Those who stay in the cities never marry, they live on alms, and have their heads and beards shaved. They wear long robes with wide sleeves; in winter they have their heads covered, and for the rest of the year they leave them bare. They eat together, like our own Religious orders, and fast several times a year. These Monks do not eat any living creature whatsoever, in order to appear lean and to remove the stings of sin. This penance is common to every kind of Monk on the aforementioned Island. It is said that they rise at midnight to pray, and that they perform their oration by singing for the space of half an hour, then they return to bed until the dawn of day, when they rise again for prayer. They do the same at sunrise, at noon, and in the evening; at that time they make a sign, and upon hearing it, all the people kneel, and joining their hands, lift them to Heaven and all pray. It is these *Lequixil* who preach and exhort the people; they are well-heard, and they weep while preaching, inducing the audience to weep as well, so expert are they in their oratory. ### Languages of this Universe

They did not recognize in any way that there were characters or letters to signify anything; this is confirmed by the author of the *General History of the Indies*, chapter 34 <note>Likely Francisco López de Gómara</note>, stating that they were simple in their speech, which they uttered very loudly and clearly between their teeth and their lips. Their languages varied every hundred miles <note>original: "cent lieux," referring to leagues</note>, being entirely diverse and dissimilar, such that one was not understood by the other in any form or manner whatsoever. This is further asserted by Amerigo Vespucci in book 1 of his *Navigation* to René, King of Sicily; by Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo in the final chapter of his *Summary of the Indies* and book 7, chapter 13 of his *General History of the Indies*; and by Joseph Acosta in book 6, chapter 7 of his *Natural History of the Indies*.

In this regard, it is held that when these Indians were first discovered by the Spaniards, they would not go near the *Copey* trees <note>The *Clusia rosea*, also known as the autograph tree because its thick leaves can be etched with writing</note> growing in their country, fearing that the trees would reveal their secrets to the aforementioned Spaniards. The Spaniards wrote their letters and missives with the tip of an iron tool upon the leaves of this tree, through which they communicated their affairs to one another. Being ignorant of this, the aforementioned Indians believed that the leaves of these trees spoke for the Spaniards.

Francisco López de Gómara, a Spaniard, in the second book, chapter 75 of his *General History of the Indies*, writes that the inhabitants of New Spain <note>Modern-day Mexico</note> used, when they were first discovered, certain letters made in the form of specific figures. With these, they marked, noted, and understood all things; by means of these letters, they preserved the memory and remembrance of ancient and past events. These letters resembled the Hieroglyphic letters of the Egyptians, although they did not contain such a profound meaning, nor did the people pronounce them as we do ours. As for the most copious and elegant language, the most pure and excellent of this New Spain, it is the language named Nahuatl <note>original: "Ynathual"</note> in that country. The amorous thieves and robbers of the said country use certain whistles and signs in their behavior, with which they understand each other as easily as if they were pronouncing and speaking a true, pure, and entire language. In this regard, the narrations of the West Indies report that in Tenochtitlan <note>original: "Themiſtitan," referring to the Aztec capital</note>, at the time of its conquest by Hernán Cortés for the Emperor Charles V, certain records or scrolls were found. These contained figures of animals, trees, plants, herbs, birds, and fish—and their various limbs and parts—to represent the gestures and deeds of the Kings of that region. 

Some ten or twelve years later, on another side in Peru, a great quantity of cotton cords were found in the cabinet of King Atahualpa <note>original: "Attabalipa"</note> which the Indians called in their language *Quipus* <note>original: "Quippos Camaios"; these are Andean knotted-string recording devices</note>. These were knotted like prayer beads and were of various colors, according to the things that these Indians wished to represent. The number of these knotted cords marked and denoted the years that their Incas <note>original: "Iugnes"</note> or Chiefs <note>original: "Caciques"</note> had reigned. This is confirmed by Peter Martyr of Anghiera <note>original: "Pierre Martyr Milannois"</note> in decade 3, book 10 of his *Histories of the Indies*, reciting that the inhabitants of the Province of *Collacuane* write what they wish and desire on very thin and delicate bark of trees, using characters or letters resembling hooks, snares, and files.

# Languages of this Universe

...they began counting again: one, two, etc. They also marked the years of these wheels with four signs or figures, attributing one sign to each year: the first being a house, the second a rabbit <note>original: "connil"; an archaic French term for a rabbit</note>, the third a reed, and the fourth a pebble. They painted it in this fashion, denoting by these figures the year that was passing, saying "at so many houses" or "at so many pebbles" of such a wheel, such a thing occurred. For one must know that their wheel, which was like a century, contained four weeks of years, each week being 13 years, which totaled 52 years. They painted in the middle of this wheel a Sun, from which four arms or lines emerged in the shape of a cross, reaching the circumference of the wheel. They made their circuit in such a way that the circumference was divided into four equal parts, each of which, along with its arm or line, had a specific color different from the others; the four colors were green, azure, red, and yellow. Each of these four portions had 13 divisions, all having their particular signs or figures of the house, rabbit, reed, or pebble, signifying one year by each sign; and at the head of this sign, they painted what had happened that year. This is why I saw in the calendar I mentioned the year that the Spaniards entered Mexico, marked by a painting of a man dressed in red in our fashion—for such was the dress of the first Spaniard sent by **Hernán Cortés** <note>original: "Fernand Cortez"; the Spanish conquistador who led the expedition that caused the fall of the Aztec Empire</note>—at the end of the 52 years when the wheel closed and was completed.

They practiced a pleasant ceremony, which was that on the final night, they broke all the vases and utensils they owned and extinguished every fire and all lights, saying that the world was to come to an end at the completion of one of these wheels, and that by chance it might be the one in which they currently found themselves. For, they said, since the world must then end, what further need is there to prepare meat or to eat? This is why they no longer had any use for vases or fire. Based on this belief, they passed the entire night in great fear, saying that perhaps the day would never come again; they all watched very attentively to see when the day would arrive. But seeing the dawn begin to break, they immediately beat several drums and sounded trumpets <note>original: "buccines"; ancient straight trumpets or horns used for signaling</note>, flutes, and other instruments of rejoicing and joy, saying that God was already extending their time for another century, which was 52 years. And then they began another wheel; on this first day and the start of the century, they took "new fire" and bought new vases and utensils to prepare food. Everyone went to fetch this new fire from the High Priest, having previously held a solemn procession of thanksgiving for the arrival of the day and the extension of another century. Such was their fashion and manner of counting years, months, weeks, and centuries.

writings—as indeed they are not—but rather ciphers or mnemonic aids, much like those used by **Astrologers** <note>In the 16th century, the term "astrologer" often encompassed what we now call astronomers</note> to signify various signs or the planets of **Mars**, **Venus**, **Jupiter**, etc. Such characters are ciphers, and not letters, because no matter what name Mars may have in Italian, French, or Spanish, this character always signifies it. This is not the case with letters; for even though they denote things, they do so by means of words. This is why those who do not know the language do not understand them; for example, a Greek or a Hebrew speaker will not be able to understand what the word **Sun** <note>original: "Sol"</note> signifies, even if they see it written, because they are ignorant of the Latin word. Thus, writing and letters are only practiced by those who use them to signify words; for if they signify things immediately, they are no longer letters or writing, but ciphers and paintings. From this, one may draw two very notable observations: first, that the memory of history and antiquity can be preserved for men in one of these three ways: either by letters and writing (as has been practiced among the Hebrews, Greeks, Romans, and many other nations), or by painting (as has been used almost throughout the entire world; for it is said in the second **Council of Nicaea**: *Painting is a book for the ignorant who do not know how to read*), or by ciphers and characters, just as a numeral signifies the number one hundred, or one thousand, without signifying the specific word "hundred" or "thousand." The other notable thing that can be drawn from this is what was proposed in this chapter: namely, that a thousand nations of the **Indies** discovered in our time have used neither letters nor writing, but two other manners, which are images and figures. This I mean to say not only of the Indies of **Peru** and **New Spain** <note>Mexico</note>, but also of **Japan** and **China**. And although what I say might perhaps seem false to some, seeing as it is reported in written discourses that there are such great libraries and universities in China and Japan, and that mention is made of their **Chapas** <term>Chapas: official seals, edicts, or branded documents</term>, letters, and expeditions, nevertheless what I say is the truth, as can be understood by the following discourse.
