To represent these words ("I, a sinner, confess myself"), they painted an **Indian** <note>Indigenous person</note> on his knees at the feet of a priest, as one who is confessing; then for this phrase ("to God Almighty"), they painted three faces with their crowns, in the manner of the **Trinity** <note>This refers to a specific iconographic style showing the Trinity as a single figure with three faces, a depiction later discouraged by the Catholic Church</note>; for ("and to the glorious Virgin Mary"), they painted a face of our Lady with the half-body of a small child; and for ("and to Saint Peter and Saint Paul"), they painted heads with crowns, a key, and a sword. ->The same in chapter 8.<-

Before the **Spaniards** came to the **Indies**, those of **Peru** had no kind of writing—whether by letters, characters, ciphers, or figures like those of **China** and **Mexico**. Nevertheless, they did not fail to preserve the memory of their antiquities, nor to maintain the order of all their affairs of peace, war, and government, because they were very diligent in passing traditions from one to another. The young people learned and guarded as a sacred thing what their elders told them, and they taught it with the same care to their successors. In addition to this diligence, they supplemented the lack of writing and letters partly through painting, like those of **Mexico** (though those of **Peru** were quite coarse and clumsy in this), and partly—and most commonly—by **Quipus** <note>Khipu: A system of knotted strings used by the Inca and other Andean cultures to record information</note>. These **Quipus** serve as memorials or registers made of strands, in which there are various knots and various colors that signify different things; it is a remarkable thing what they have expressed and represented by this means. For the **Quipus** are as valuable to them as books of history, laws, ceremonies, and accounts of their affairs. There were officers appointed to guard these **Quipus** (whom today they call **Quipucamayos** <note>Khipukamayuq: The specialized "keepers of the knots" who recorded and read the strings</note>), who were obliged to keep and render an account of everything, much like the notaries here.

Therefore, they were given full faith and credit; for according to the various types of business, such as war, government, taxes, ceremonies, and land, there were different **Quipus** or strands. In each of these, there were many knots, small and large, and attached threads—some red, others green, others blue, and others white. Finally, there was such diversity that, just as we derive an infinity of words from twenty-four letters by arranging them in different ways, so they derived innumerable meanings from these knots.

# Languages of this World

> ...like the **Hebrews**, but from top to bottom: for since these are not letters, but entire words <note>original: "dictions"</note>, and each figure or character signifies a concept, they have no need to assemble the parts of one with another, and thus they can easily write from top to bottom. Those of **Mexico**, for the same reason, did not write in a line from one side to the other, but unlike the **Chinese**, beginning at the bottom, they always climbed upwards. They used this way of writing for the counting of days and the rest of the things they recorded, although when they wrote in their wheels or signs, they began from the middle, where they painted the **Sun**, and from there they went climbing through their years, out to the turn and circumference of the wheel. Finally, there are found four different ways of writing: some writing from right to left, others from left to right, others from top to bottom, and others from bottom to top, in which one sees the diversity of human understandings.

The aforementioned **Francisco López de Gómara**, in book 6 of his *General History of the Indies*, chapter 11, reports that in the region of **Nicaragua** in these **Indies**, there are five languages, all different and dissimilar: namely **Coribicien**, which is highly praised; **Ciorotega**, which is the native language of the country and the oldest, used by those who have the right of succession and who may use **Cacao** <note>original: "Cacaoz"</note>, which is the currency of their land, which is made of a mixture of various metals having the shape of an almond <note>The author is mistaken here; cacao beans themselves were used as currency, not metal coins in their shape.</note>; the third language is named **Ciodale**, and this is used by the coarse people and villagers; while **Oroieuga** is specific to small children; but the principal language is that of **Mexico**, even though this country is more than one hundred and fifty leagues from **Mexico**. <margin>”</margin>The **Ancerma** <note>original: "Auzermiens"; likely referring to the people of the Anserma region in modern-day Colombia, then considered part of the northern reaches of the Peruvian influence</note>, just as they differ from other **Indians** in their ways of doing and their bravado, also have a language that is diverse from all others in **Peru**.

The same author in chapter 14 following:

<margin>”</margin>The people of the region of **Nicaragua** boast of being descended from the **Mexicans**, saying that in the land of **Anahuac** <note>original: "Ananac"</note>, which is **New Spain**, the inhabitants left their country and came by the South Sea to inhabit **Nicaragua**. This is quite plausible, seeing that their language closely approaches that of **Tenochtitlan** <note>original: "Themistitã"; the Aztec capital</note>, and the characters which they use to signify what they wish to say are similar to others. They write these on very poorly made parchment, or on certain skins tanned with azure, gold, and other beautiful and rich colors; above all, they record by memory the high deeds of their captains and the wars they have had against their neighbors.

The same author in chapter 17 following reports that the **Mexicans** use a sort of writing which is made in various forms of animals, birds, and others, just like the **Hieroglyphic** letters of the **Egyptians** once were. He maintains that these **Mexicans** have among them, among other books, one titled **Xiuhpohualli** <note>original: "Xehutonali"</note>, which is to say, *the book of the counting of the years*. In this book, they divide the year into four times, as we do with Summer, Autumn, Spring, and Winter, which they name **Tochtli** (Rabbit), **Acatl** (Reed), **Tecpal** (Flint), and **Calli** (House)—which signify **South**, **East**, **North**, and **West**. Each of these times lasts 52 years and has four "weeks," each containing thirteen years. Each year has 18 months, and each month has 20 days. They begin their first cycle at **Tochtli**, and when it is finished, they go to **Acatl**, and so on from time to time until they have returned to **Tochtli**. As long as the first "week" lasts, they count one, two, three, up to the thirteenth, and then they begin again to count from one, just as we do here up to one hundred, and when that hundred is finished, we begin to count from one again. Thus, according to their calculation, the year returns to 365 days.

Some modern travelers and navigators assert that in this **Mexican** country, there are several different languages, which bring a very great annoyance to those who navigate and travel along its coasts, although there is a common language <note>Nahuatl</note> which is understood and spoken across an extent of more than 400 leagues of land. This is repeated by **François de Belleforest** in book 4, chapter 5 of his *Universal History*, and in volume 2 of the *Cosmography* of **Sebastian Münster**.

See the aforementioned **André Thevet**, book 21, chapter 8, of his said *Cosmography*. **Jean de Léry**, in chapter 20 of his *History of America*, deduces that the difference in the languages of these **Indians** is such: namely, that the **Tupinambá** <note>original: "Tououpi namboults"</note>, **Tupiniquim**, **Toaiaira**, **Temiminó** <note>original: "Teureminon"</note>, and **Carijó** <note>original: "Kario"</note> speak the same language, or at least there is little difference between them, in their ways of acting or otherwise. The **Goitacá** <note>original: "Ouecauen"</note> likewise have a completely different way of acting and speaking. The language of the **Kingdom of Cusco** in **Peru** <note>referring to Quechua</note> is the most beautiful and eloquent language of all the other languages of the provinces of said **Peru**, and it is the one most spoken and used throughout the continent of that country.

To keep it brief, we shall hold to the common opinion of modern authors who have been to these **West Indies**: that regarding the language of these **Western Indians** in general, it is brief and obscure, but much easier to know and understand than the **Arabic** or **Turkish** languages, or other **Levantine** tongues. As for their speech, it is harsh and has little grace in its accent; they reiterate it often, repeating the same thing, taking pleasure in such harshness and barbarity, and delighting in speaking indistinctly and poorly forming their words. All these **Western Indians** are great chatterboxes, always recounting the victories and triumphs they have achieved over their adversaries, as was well noted by the aforementioned **A. Thevet**, book 21, chapter 9, of his *Universal Cosmography*.

On this subject, **Pietro Maffei** <note>original: "P. Maffee"</note>, in book 2 of his *General History of the Indies*, writing of these **Indians** in **Brazil**, writes that their language is not at all difficult to learn and that it is almost the same for all those who are well known to us thus far, except for the names of some things which are taken differently by the women of that nation. Three letters of our **Alphabet**—**F**, **L**, **V** <note>Likely a transcription error for "R". We have been well assured by persons worthy of faith that today one can see a book of annals of the country of **Mexico**, all painted and represented with the figures previously described by us, in the **Vatican Library** in **Rome**. In this book, the entire history of the deeds and gestures of the **Kings** of that country, and other memorable things, are described in these figures, as if in **Hieroglyphic** letters.

experienced that in the second year, being a bit more in the open..." “

" Islands (which are those of Cape Verde), says that the men there are so light in
" fleeing that one can hardly follow them with the eye, such that Hanno the

" Troglodytes <note>term: Troglodytes — Literally "cave-dwellers," a name used by ancient writers for various groups in Africa and the Near East.</note>, a nation of Guinea, whom he says are called Therotoeens <note>original: "Therotoeens" — Derived from Greek roots meaning "swift hunters."</note>, because
" they are as light in hunting on land as the *Ichthyophages* <note>term: Ichthyophages — "Fish-eaters," a term used by ancient Greeks for coastal peoples.</note> are prompt
" at swimming in the sea, where they tire almost as little as a fish. And Maffei <note>Giovanni Pietro Maffei (1533–1603), a Jesuit historian who wrote about the East Indies.</note>
" in his histories of the Indies reports that the Naires <note>term: Naires — The Nairs, a warrior caste of the Malabar Coast in India.</note> (as the nobles
" and warriors are called) of the Kingdom of Malabar are so agile and have such
" promptness that it is an incredible thing; they handle their bodies so well at
" will that they seem to have no bones, so that it is difficult to
" come to a skirmish against such people, especially since with this agility they
" advance and retreat at pleasure. But to make themselves such, they assist
" nature; they stretch their tendons from the age of seven years, which they
" afterwards fatten and rub with sesame oil. What I say is even
" recognized in animals: for a Spanish jennet <note>term: jennet — A small, agile breed of Spanish horse.</note> or a Barb <note>term: Barb — A North African horse breed known for speed and endurance.</note> is more
" gallant and light in the race than a nag or a cob from Germany, or a horse

" Northern peoples, the Herules are celebrated for being swift in the

" Now the dexterity of the Savages is recognized not only in running,
" but also in swimming. This they all know how to do, but it seems that some
" more than others. As for the Brazilians, they are so born to this
" trade that they will swim for eight days in the sea if hunger did not press them, and
" they have more fear that some fish might devour them than of perishing from

" a certain artifice of sipping the water and rejecting it, by means of which they
" remain easily within for a long time. The women likewise have
" a marvelous disposition for this exercise: for the *History of Florida*

# History of the Origin of the...

See what the same author cited above writes in chapter 11 following, concerning the paintings, markings, incisions, and ornaments of the bodies of these Western Indians, and in chapter 12 following, regarding external body ornaments such as bracelets, necklaces, earrings, etc.

In which he writes that the Indians of Brazil, having no care for clothing like other Indians, take pleasure in adorning and variegating themselves with bird feathers; they take those of the kind we use for bedding, and chopping them as small as mincemeat, they dye them red with their **brazilwood** <note>original: "bois de Bresil" — a wood that produces a red dye, from which the country of Brazil takes its name.</note>. Then, having rubbed their bodies with a certain gum that serves as glue, they cover themselves with these feathers and create a garment all in one piece. According to Jean de Léry in his *History of America* <note>Jean de Léry (1534–1613) was a French explorer and author who wrote a famous account of his time in Brazil.</note>, this led the first people who went there to believe that the men called **Savages** were naturally hairy, which is not the case: for it is certain that Savages, wherever they may be, have less body hair than we Europeans.

Those of Florida also use this manner of down, but only on the head to make themselves more fearsome. In addition to what is said above, the aforementioned Brazilians also make headbands of feathers which they tie and arrange in all colors; these headbands resemble in shape those **rackets** or *ratepenades* <note>term: ratepenades — an archaic term for a type of head ornament or fan, often shaped like bat wings.</note> used by ladies here, the invention of which they seem to have learned from these Savages. As for those of **New France** <note>term: Nouvelle France — the area colonized by France in North America, primarily along the Saint Lawrence River.</note>, on their solemn days of rejoicing and when they go to war, they wear around their heads something like a crown made of long **elk** hair painted red, glued or otherwise attached to a leather band three fingers wide, such as Jacques Cartier <note>Jacques Cartier (1491–1557) was the first European to describe and map the Gulf of Saint Lawrence.</note> says he saw on the King or Lord of the Savages whom he found in the town of **Hochelaga** <note>A fortified Iroquoian village located on the island of Montreal.</note>. But they do not use as much featherwork as the Brazilians, who make robes, caps, bracelets, belts, and cheek ornaments from them, as well as multicolored bucklers <note>small shields</note> for their loins.

# History of the Origin of [Languages]

" [the alphabet] brought to the Greeks did not resemble the Phoenician ones so much as the Galatian ones, that is to say, the Gallic ones. In this, **Caesar** <note>Julius Caesar, in his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*.</note> was mistaken in saying that the Druids used Greek letters for private matters: for on the contrary, it was the Greeks who used Gallic letters. And **Berossus** <note>An ancient Hellenistic-era Babylonian writer; here the author likely refers to the "pseudo-Berossus" texts popular in the Renaissance.</note> says that the third Gallic King after the Great Flood, named **Sarron**, established universities in these parts; and **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian.</note> adds in his sixth book that in the Gauls there were Philosophers and Theologians called **Sarronides**, much more ancient than the Druids, who were greatly revered and whom all the people obeyed. These same authors say that **Bardus**, the fifth King of the Gauls, invented rhythm and music, and introduced Poets and Rhetoricians who were called **Bards**, whom **Caesar** and **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian.</note> mention. But the same **Diodorus** writes that the Poets were held in such reverence among them that when two armies were ready to clash, having already drawn their cutlasses and with javelins in hand to strike, upon these Poets arriving, everyone ceased and laid down their arms: so much does wrath yield to wisdom even among the fiercest barbarians, and so much does **Mars** <note>The Roman god of war.</note> revere the **Muses** <note>The Greek goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences.</note>, says the author."

The same **Marc Lescarbot** <note>A French lawyer and writer who participated in the 1606 expedition to Acadia and wrote *Histoire de la Nouvelle-France*.</note> in the aforementioned book 3, chapter 6 of the said history, says:
" I do not wish to call, as some have done, by the name of Priests those who perform ceremonies and invocations of demons <note>Early modern European writers often characterized Indigenous spiritual practices as "invocations of demons" through a Christian lens.</note> among the **Western Indians**, except insofar as they have the custom of sacrifices and gifts which they offer to their gods; for as the Apostle says in **Hebrews 8, verse 3**, <note>original: "Heb. 8. verf. 3."</note> every Priest or Pontiff is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices, such as those of **Mexico** (where the greatest was called **Papas**) who offered incense to their Idols, the principal of which was that of the God they named **Vitzilipuztli** <note>Huitzilopochtli, the Aztec deity of war and the sun.</note>; even though the general name of him whom they held as the supreme Lord and author of all things was **Virachocha** <note>Viracocha, the great creator deity in pre-Inca and Inca mythology.</note>, to whom they gave excellent qualities, calling him **Pachacamac** <note>The "Earth-Maker," a creator deity worshipped in the Andes.</note>, which is Creator of Heaven and Earth, and **Vsapu**, which is 'Admirable,' and other similar names. They move all around, and this with beatings and shoutings until they sweat from exhaustion <note>Original: *ahan*, an old French term for laborious effort.</note>; however, I have not heard that they foam at the mouth as the Turks do. When the devil has come, this Master **Aoutmoin** <note>A Mi'kmaq term for a shaman or medicine man.</note> makes them believe that he holds him tied with his rope, and holds firm against him, forcing him to give him an answer before letting him go. And here one recognizes the trickery of this enemy of nature, who thus amuses these miserable creatures, and at the same time his pride in wanting those who invoke him to show him more submission than the Holy Patriarchs and prophets ever did to God, who only prayed with their faces to the ground. That being done, he begins to sing something, in my opinion, in praise of the devil, who has indicated the location of the hunt to them; the other savages who are there respond, making some symphonic harmony among themselves. Then they dance in their manner, as we will describe hereafter, with songs that I do not understand, nor do those of our people who understand their language best. But one day, while going for a walk in the prairies along the river, I approached the cabin of an **Aoutmoin**, and recorded on my tablets <note>Writing tablets used for taking quick notes.</note> a small part of what I heard, which is still written in these terms: *Haloet, ho ho he he, ha ha, haloet-ho-*, which they repeat several times. The song is on my said tablets in these notes: **D, F, G, G, D, G, G, F, F, D, D, G, G, F, F** <note>Original: *Re fa sol sol re sol sol fa fa re re sol sol fa fa*. Once finished, they all made a great exclamation, saying *“E!”* Then they began another song, saying *Erigrua hau egrigna hu, ho, ho, ho, Egrigna hau, hau, hau.* The music for this was **F, F, G, F, F, D, D, G, G, F, F, F, D, F, F, G, G, F.** Having made the customary exclamation, they began another which sang: *Tameia tameia douveni hau hau he he.* The music for it was **G, F, F, F, D, D, D, F, F, G, F, F, D, D.** I listened attentively to this [Alle]luia <note>The text is partially cut off, likely referring to *Alleluia*.</note>, repeated several times, and I could never hear anything else, which makes me think that these songs are in praise of the devil; yet this word signifies to them what it signifies in Hebrew <note>Original: *Heb:*</note>, which is, “Praise the Lord.” All the other nations of this country do the same, but no one has detailed their songs except **Jean de Léry** <note>A French explorer and author of *History of a Voyage to the Land of Brazil* (1578).</note>, who says that the Brazilians <note>Specifically the Tupinambá people of Brazil.</note> in their rituals <note>Original: *sabatz*, comparing Indigenous ceremonies to a witches' "Sabbath."</note> also make harmonies. And finding himself one day at such a festival, he reports that they were saying *He, he, he, he, he, he, hé,* with these notes: **F, F, G, F, F, G, G, G.** This done, they cried out in a terrifying way and howled for a quarter of an hour, and the women jumped into the air with such vigor that they foamed at the mouth; then they began the song again, saying *Heu heurauré, heura, Heuraure heura, heura euech.* The melody is **F, E, D, G, G, G, F, E, D, E, D, C, D.** This author says that in this song they had mourned their deceased fathers, who were so valiant, and yet they were consoled in that after death they were certain to go find them behind the high mountains, where they would dance and rejoice with them. Similarly, with great excess, they had threatened the **Waitaca** <note>Original: *Ouetacas*, a tribe in Brazil known for their resistance to Portuguese and French colonization.</note>, their enemies, with being soon captured and eaten by them, just as the **Caribs** <note>Indigenous peoples of the Caribbean and South America.</note> had promised them; and they also made mention of the Deluge <note>The Great Flood, a common motif in many global mythologies which European writers often tried to link to the Biblical story of Noah.</note>.

### Language of this Universe

We spoke of this in the previous chapter. I leave it to those who write about demonology to philosophize on that matter. But it must be said further that while our Savages <note>The author uses the term "Savages" (French: *Sauvages*) to refer to the Indigenous peoples he encountered, primarily the Mi'kmaq of Acadia.</note> sing in the manner I have described, there are others who do nothing else but say *Hé* or *Her* (like a man splitting wood) with a movement of the arms; and they dance in a circle, without holding onto one another, nor moving from their place, striking their feet against the ground. This is the form of their dances, similar to those that [Jean de] Léry reports of the people in Brazil, who are more than fifteen hundred leagues from there. After this, our people make a fire and jump over it like the ancient Canaanites, Ammonites, and sometimes the Israelites, but they are not so detestable, for they do not sacrifice their children to the devil by fire. Along with all this, they place a half-pole out of the roof-opening of the cabin where they are, at the end of which there is some **Matachiaz** <note>Ornamental beadwork made from shells, quills, or stones.</note> or some other thing attached, which the devil carries away. This is how I have heard their way of doing things discussed in this regard.

One can here consider a bad custom of jumping over the fire, and passing children through the flame in the "Fires of Saint John" <note>Midsummer bonfires traditionally lit on the eve of the feast of St. John the Baptist.</note>, which still persists today among us, and ought to be reformed: for that comes from ancient abominations that God hated so much, of which Theodoret speaks regarding chapter 16 of the 4th book of Kings. "I have seen," he says, "in some cities, bonfires lit once a year, and jumping over them not only children, but also men, and mothers carrying children over the flame." This seemed to them to be a kind of expiation and purification, and this, in my opinion, was the sin of Ahaz. These ways of doing things were forbidden by an ancient Council held in Constantinople <note>Canon 65 of the Council in Trullo (692 AD), also known as the Quinsext Council.</note>. Regarding this, [Theodore] Balsamon <note>A 12th-century Byzantine jurist and commentator on church law.</note> remarks that on the 23rd of the month of June, which is the eve of Saint John, on the seashores and in houses, men and women would assemble, and they would dress the eldest daughter as a bride; and after good cheer and much drinking, they performed dances, shouts, and fires all night, over which they jumped and made predictions of good and bad luck. These fires have been continued among us for a better purpose, but the abuse must be removed.

Now, as the devil has always wanted to play the ape <note>A reference to the theological concept of *Simia Dei* (the Ape of God), the idea that the devil mimics divine rituals to deceive humanity.</note>, and have a service like that rendered to God, so he has wanted his officers to have the marks of their trade to better deceive the simple-minded. And in fact **Membertou** <note>A famous Mi'kmaq Grand Chief and shaman who was one of the first to be baptized in New France.</note>, of whom we have spoken as a learned **Aoutmoin**, wears hanging from his neck the mark of this profession, which is a triangular pouch covered with their embroidery, that is to say, **Matachias**, inside which there is I-know-not-what about the size of a hazelnut, which he says is his demon called **Aoutem**, whom those of Canada <note>Here referring to the St. Lawrence Iroquoians encountered by Jacques Cartier.</note> call **Coudouagny**, as Jacques Cartier says.

# History of the Origin of the

... interprets these two words, *Doctrine & Truth*. <note>Original: "Doctrine & Verité." These are the traditional French translations for the Hebrew *Urim and Thummim*, the oracular elements of the Jewish High Priest's breastplate.</note> And as the priesthood was hereditary, not only in the House of Aaron, but also in the family of the Great High Priest of Memphis, whose office was assigned to his eldest son after him, as Thyamis says in the *Ethiopian History* of Heliodorus. Likewise, among these people here, this profession is hereditary; and by a tradition, they teach this secret to their eldest sons. For the eldest son of Membertou <note>Membertou (c. 1510–1611) was the Grand Chief (Sagamos) of the Mi'kmaq people in Acadia and the first Indigenous leader to be baptized by the French.</note> (upon whom the name *Judas* was imposed in mockery, which angered him once he understood it was a bad name) told us that after his father, he would be the <term>Aoutmoin</term> <note>A Mi'kmaq term for a shaman, medicine man, or spiritual leader who communicates with spirits.</note> in the district. This is a small matter, for every <term>Sagamos</term> <note>A title for a chief or leader among the Indigenous peoples of the northeastern coast of North America.</note> has his own *Aoutmoin*, if he is not one himself. But they are still ambitious for this role because of the profit that comes from it. 

The Brazilians <note>Referring to the Tupinambá people of Brazil, likely based on the writings of Jean de Léry.</note> have their *Caraibes* <note>Tupinambá shamans or prophets.</note>, who come and go through the villages, making the people believe they have had communication with spirits. By this means, they claim they can not only give them victory against their enemies, but also that the abundance or sterility of the earth depends on them. They usually hold in their hands a certain kind of rattle that they call a *Maraca*, made from the fruit of a tree as large as an ostrich egg, which they hollow out as one does here with the gourds of the Pilgrims of Saint James. <note>Referring to the scallop shells and gourds carried by pilgrims on the Way of St. James to Santiago de Compostela.</note> Having filled them with small stones, they make them rattle like a pig's bladder at their solemnities; and going through the villages, they beguile the world, saying that their <term>Daemon</term> <note>In this context, the author uses "Daemon" to mean a spirit or supernatural entity, though often with a negative colonial connotation.</note> is inside. These *Maracas*, well-decorated with beautiful feathers, they fix into the ground on the stick that passes through them, and arrange them all in a row in the middle of the houses, commanding that they be given food and drink. 

In this way, these deceivers make the other simple folk believe (just as the Priests of Bel did long ago, as mentioned in the story of Daniel) <note>A reference to the biblical story of "Bel and the Dragon" from the Apocrypha, where priests secretly ate food offered to an idol to prove the idol was alive.</note> that these fruits eat and drink at night. Every head of a household, placing faith in this, does not fail to put flour, meat, fish, and drink near these *Maracas*. They continue this service for fifteen days or three weeks, and during this time, they are so foolish as to persuade themselves that by rattling these *Maracas*, some spirit speaks to them, and they attribute divinity to them. Thus, it would be a great crime to take the meats presented before these fine rattles—meats upon which these reverend *Caraibes* joyfully fatten themselves. See what the same author cited above writes in chapter 16, regarding the physicians and surgeons of these Indians.

# Language of this World

<page-num>963</page-num>

...split and divided in such a way that they seem to be double, for which reason they use them to express various thoughts all at once and say different things. Furthermore, the said *Iambulus* <note>A Greek merchant and writer (c. 2nd century BCE) whose travel accounts, likely fictional, are preserved by Diodorus Siculus; he described a utopian island in the Indian Ocean.</note> said that these peoples imitate all the birds of the fields, and what is even more marvelous, they speak all together to two men—to one with one part of the tongue, and to another with the other—and even while questioning one, they respond to the other as if the two tongues were different and in two mouths. *Antonio de Torquemada* <note>Spanish writer (c. 1507–1569) whose *Hexameron* is a collection of dialogues on natural history and curiosities.</note> repeated this story in the first day of his *Hexameron*, and after him *François de Belleforest* in book 3, the final chapter of his *Universal History*.

A certain other ancient author named *Timosthenes* <note>Timosthenes of Rhodes, an admiral and geographer under Ptolemy II (3rd century BCE).</note> has left in writing in his works that in olden times, in a certain city of the land of *Colchis* called *Dioscorias* or *Dioscuria*—situated near the river *Anticas* <note>Original: "Attamonte," likely referring to the Anticas or a river in the region of the Caucasus.</note> and currently named *Pitsunda* <note>Original: "Prezunde."</note>—there were at times as many as three hundred types of different peoples and nations of this World who all used different and dissimilar languages. It was such that at least one hundred and thirty <term>interpreters</term> <note>Original: "truchements."</note> were needed by merchants and others who wished to negotiate and trade with these peoples and nations, as reported by *Strabo* in book 11 and *Pliny* in book 6, chapter 5 of his *Natural History*. Following them, *Theseus Ambrosius* <note>Teseo Ambrogio (1469–1540), an early practitioner of comparative linguistics and author of the *Introduction to the Chaldean, Syrian, Armenian, and ten other languages* (1539).</note> in his appendix on many and various languages, *S. Nozenus* in his dedicatory epistle on his *Grammatical Questions* <note>Original: "Erotemates." A standard term for instructional manuals on the "Holy Language" (Hebrew).</note> of the Holy Language, and *François de Belleforest* in volume 2, book 3, chapter 5 of his *Universal Cosmography*.

The Greeks maintain in their histories that *Cecrops* <note>The mythical first king of Athens.</note>—living in the time of *Moses*—who first brought the ceremonies of sacred things to the Greeks, and principally the manner of sacrificing an ox, was surnamed <note>Original Greek: δίφυης, *diphues*.</note> *double-natured* because he understood and spoke both the Egyptian and Greek languages.

The Latins attribute to the poet *Ennius* <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BCE), the "father of Roman poetry."</note> "three hearts" because he understood and spoke the Greek, Oscan <note>An ancient Indo-European language of southern Italy.</note>, and Latin languages.

*Mithridates*, King of Pontus in Asia, spoke twenty-two entirely different languages without any middleman or interpreter, as recounted by *Pliny* in book 7, chapter 24 and book 25, chapter 2; *Valerius Maximus* in book 9; *Aulus Gellius* in book 17, chapter 17; and *Quintilian* in book 11, chapter 2. In memory of this King, *Nicolas Erythraeus*, a Venetian, <note>Gian Vittorio Rossi (1577–1647), who wrote under the name Erythraeus.</note> titled one of his books on the names and vocabularies of all the peoples and nations of the earth *Mithridates*. Similarly, the German *Conrad Gesner* composed a book of observations titled *Mithridates: On the differences of languages, both ancient and those in use today among various nations throughout the whole world, printed in the year 1555 in Zurich.* <note>Original Latin title: "Mithridates, de differentiis linguarum tum veterum, tum quæ hodie apud diuerſas nationes in toto orbe terrarum in vſu ſunt."</note>

Among the Christians, *Origen of Alexandria* was one of the most excellent in the knowledge of languages, for he knew five perfectly: Hebrew, Syriac, Egyptian, Greek, and Latin, according to the report of *Saint Jerome* in volume 3 of his works against Rufinus and *Epiphanius* in the life of this personage.

The histories of Germany record that Emperor *Charles IV* spoke five languages perfectly.

*Porchetus* <note>Porchetus Salvaticus (14th century), author of an anti-Jewish polemic.</note> and *Johannes Reuchlin* (also known as *Capnion*) <note>Reuchlin (1455–1522) was a German humanist and Hebrew scholar; "Capnion" is the Greek translation of his name, meaning "smoke."</note> have demonstrated that they knew several languages in what they have written in their works titled *Victory against the Jews*, *On the Kabbalah*, and *On the Wonder-Working Word*. <note>Original Latin titles: "Victoria contra Iudæos, & de Cabala, & de verbo mirifico."</note> *Theodor Zwinger*, volume 1, book 4.

*Rabbi Libertatis commineti*, a Spaniard of Jewish descent who became a Christian (according to *P. Galatino*, book 1, chapter 6, and book 3, chapter 6 of his *Secrets of the Catholic Truth* <note>Pietro Galatino (1460–1540), an Italian friar and Hebraist who sought to use the Kabbalah to prove Christian doctrines.</note> and *Michael Neander* in the introductory epistle of his *Erotemates* of the holy language) was such a great and excellent figure in his true knowledge of languages that he perfectly understood the doctrine of fourteen of them, and spoke in them without any interpreter.

*Pierre à Couilhan* <note>Pêro da Covilhã (c. 1450–1530), a Portuguese explorer and diplomat who traveled to India and Ethiopia.</note>, a Portuguese by nationality flourishing in the time of the King of Portugal, and ambassador for his majesty to the great Ethiopian King *Prester John* <note>A legendary Christian monarch of the East, often identified in the Renaissance with the Emperor of Ethiopia.</note>, spoke not only the Arabic, Indian, and Portuguese languages, but also nearly all the other languages of this Universe, according to the report of *Don F. Aluarez* in his history of Ethiopia, chapter 103; *Damian à Goes* in the introductory epistle of his book on the faith, religion, and customs of the Ethiopians; and the aforementioned *M. Neander* in the place cited above.

*Theodore Bibliander* <note>A Swiss reformer and linguist (1509–1564) who published the first printed edition of the Qur'an in Latin.</note>, a Swiss, demonstrated in practice that he knew many different languages, as he sufficiently showed through his commentary on the *Common Logic of All Languages* <note>Original Latin: *De ratione communi omnium linguarum*.</note> and in the place I have very often cited before.

The same was achieved by the late *G. Postel* <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), a French polymath and linguist who was one of the most learned men of his time, though considered eccentric.</note>, a Frenchman, who knew, read, and spoke fifteen languages perfectly, as most of the most learned men in this Universe know very well. He demonstrated this even through his *Alphabet or Introduction to Twelve Languages*, all different and dissimilar, printed in Paris by *D. L'Escuyer*.

*Sixtus Senensis* <note>Sixtus of Siena (1520–1569), a Jewish convert to Christianity and a renowned biblical scholar.</note>, in book 4 of his *Holy Library*, speaking of *Augustine Nebiensis* <note>Agostino Giustiniani (1470–1536), Bishop of Nebbio in Corsica, who published a famous polyglot Psalter.</note>, Bishop on the Island of Corsica and very learned in languages, says this:

> "Augustine, Bishop of Nebbio on the island of Corsica, a Genoese by birth, from the illustrious Giustiniani family, a Professor of the Dominican Order, a most celebrated theologian, sincerely learned and most skilled in all the languages that are dispersed throughout the whole world. With a new and mighty daring, he was the first to reduce both instruments of the sacred law <note>The Old and New Testaments.</note> into five principal languages—Hebrew, Chaldean <note>Usually referring to Aramaic.</note>, Greek, Latin, and Arabic—into a single volume titled the *Octapla* <note>A work arranged in eight columns.</note>. He did this with such great skill that he arranged eight columns on each page, in which all the aforementioned languages, expressed in their own characters, could be seen in lines, with just as many corresponding words visible at one and the same glance, specifically in this order:"

1. In the first column, he placed the Hebrew edition.
2. In the second, a Latin translation corresponding to the Hebrew word-for-word.
3. In the third, the common and Vulgate Latin edition.
4. In the fourth, the Greek.
5. In the fifth, the Arabic.
6. In the sixth, the Targum <note>An Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in the Chaldean tongue, but in Hebrew letters.
7. In the seventh, the Latin translation corresponding to the Chaldean.
8. In the eighth, little scholia, or very brief short notes scattered at intervals and divided up, by which he primarily refuted the errors of the Jews.

Of this so great and illustrious work, I <unclear>was able</unclear> to see only two volumes.

The same author, speaking of Cardinal Francisco de Cisneros <note>Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros (1436–1517), a Spanish cardinal and statesman who founded the University of Alcalá.</note>, a Spaniard also very learned in languages:

> <note>original: "Franciscus Xymenius à Cisneros natione Hispanus..."</note> Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros, a Spaniard by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans.</note>, Priest of the Holy Roman Church, Cardinal of Saint Balbina, Archbishop of Toledo, and High Chancellor of the Spains, published for Pope Leo X the entire Old and New Testament in multiple languages: that is, Hebrew, Chaldean <note>Commonly used at the time to refer to Aramaic.</note>, Greek, and Latin. This was achieved with immense expense, labor, and sleepless nights, and printed with the greatest diligence by the University of Alcalá <note>In Latin, *Complutensi*; this refers to the famous Complutensian Polyglot Bible.</note> in Spain. For this work, most learned men in the knowledge of languages were summoned from all parts of the world, and the most corrected and ancient manuscripts were taken from the Vatican and Medici Libraries, or sent by the Senate of Venice, or sought elsewhere with no regard for expense or labor. The arrangement of this great work is as follows: 
> The Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note> has a triple edition, namely Hebrew, Chaldean, and the Greek of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint.</note>, to which are connected three Latin editions. Specifically, the Latin of Jerome <note>The Vulgate.</note> corresponds to the Hebrew truth. Another Latin version corresponds word-for-word to the Chaldean, prepared by men most skilled in that language. To the Greek of the Seventy, there is a corresponding interlinear Latin translation. The Hagiographa <note>The remaining books of the Hebrew Bible not included in the Torah or the Prophets.</note> and the Prophetic books are printed in two languages, etc.

The author of the *History of Spain*, book 27, speaks thus of this Cardinal:

> Cardinal Friar Francisco de Ximénes de Cisneros, advanced to state affairs by Lord Ferdinand, King of Spain, was well aware of the great utility the whole world could derive from the knowledge of languages. He cherished and appointed men learned in them to employ them in matters suitable to his religious profession, so that students of holy letters might taste the word of God from its original fountains and sources. He had the Bible printed that we have seen in several languages: namely, the books of the Old Testament divided into three columns. The first contained the Hebrew text; the second, the common Latin version that we use; and the third, the Greek of the Seventy Interpreters with its Latin translation. In the lower margin, he placed the Chaldean Paraphrase <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, also accompanied by its Latin interpretation so that nothing would be missing. As for the New Testament, it contained the Greek text and the common Latin translation, very correctly edited. At the end of the volume was a dictionary of Hebrew words, very fully and copiously interpreted—a work of great labor, sumptuous and magnificent, witnessing to the greatness of heart of this Cardinal, who was daunted by no difficulty. In this, he utilized the diligence, doctrine, and judgment of Demetrius Ducas <note>A Greek scholar from Crete who taught at Alcalá.</note>, Antonio de Nebrija <note>A leading Spanish Renaissance scholar and grammarian.</note>, López de Zúñiga, and Hernán Núñez of Valladolid <note>Also known as Pinciano.</note>.

André Thevet <note>A 16th-century French Franciscan priest, explorer, and writer.</note>, in the thirteenth book, sixth chapter of his *Cosmography*, mentions a certain Jew, a native of Morocco aged 49 years, who had served for 26 years in Africa as well as in some parts of the East Indies in Asia. From his birth, his name was Jonadab, which was changed by the Barbarians—because he would not abandon his Judaism to receive the Moorish law—to that of Alhanar in derision, a word which signifies "serpent" or "viper" in the Moorish language. This Jew had such a happy memory that he knew how to speak twenty-eight different kinds of languages, and in each of them he could read and write. And if he had heard a man speak for ten or twelve entire days, conversing with him and having things explained to him, he would have learned more in that short time than another would have done in two years.

The same Thevet, in the eighteenth book, sixth chapter of his same *Cosmography*, reports that Genuſbey Pasha <note>Yunus Bey (d. 1541), a famous Greek-born interpreter and diplomat for the Ottoman Empire.</note> of Turkey, a native of the island of Corfu and the son of a fisherman, was taken young by the Turks and led as a slave to Constantinople, from there to Egypt, and to many other places in the service of Sultan Suleiman. He was the foremost man of his time for speaking diverse kinds of languages, and possessed the happiest memory found under heaven; so much so that he perfectly knew the Hebrew, Greek (both vulgar and literal <note>Meaning both the spoken Modern Greek of the time and the classical literary Greek.</note>), Turkish, Arabic, Moorish, Tartar, Persian, Armenian, Muscovite, Hungarian, Slavonic, Italian, Spanish, German, and French languages. He was the primary interpreter <note>term: "truchement" (interpreter/dragoman); a vital diplomatic role in the Ottoman court.</note> for his Lord Suleiman and his greatest favorites.

->italy, demonstrated to the most learned and scholarly of this Universe through the printing of his work *On the Improvement of Chronology* <note>original: *Emendatione temporum*; Joseph Scaliger’s 1583 masterpiece which revolutionized the study of ancient history</note>, that he understands all the languages of this Universe perfectly.<-

The most ancient Hebrews or Jews asserted in their Kabbalah <note>original: *Cabales*; Jewish mystical and traditional teachings</note> that their <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>The supreme council and high court of ancient Israel</note> or Judges had a perfect knowledge of seventy languages of this Universe. But all that was nothing compared to the Apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, after being filled with the Holy Spirit sent upon them, began to speak all the languages of the world—even though previously they understood and spoke no other language than <term>Syriac</term> <note>The Aramaic dialect spoken in Judea during the time of Jesus</note>, which was their mother tongue, as is amply detailed in the Acts of the Apostles, chapters 2, 3, 10, 11, and 19. And the ancient Doctors of the Church say that this Gift of all languages (which in the early Church was conferred along with the gift of Prophecy and the healing of the infirm and sick, at the time of baptism, the receiving of the Holy Spirit, and the laying on of hands) lasted in that Church for several centuries until the time of Saint Irenaeus, who was a listener of Polycarp, a disciple of Saint John the Evangelist; of whom Eusebius speaks in the fourth and fifth books of his *Preparation* <note>original: *Preparatione*; referring to Eusebius's *Praeparatio Evangelica*</note>. Modern reports coming from Rome state that Pope Gregory XIII, in the year 1584, founded several colleges in the city of Rome with great revenues for the retreat and teaching of the Christian faith for Greeks, Armenians, Africans, Jews, Neophytes <note>Recent converts to Christianity</note>, Germans, English, Scots, and others. He even instituted in that city a Seminary of the Hebrew language, where Hebrews, Jews, Chaldeans <note>referring to speakers of Aramaic/Chaldee</note>, and others are taught the sciences of fine literature, and the Hebrew, Chaldean, Syriac, Arabic, Turkish, and other foreign languages. In this Seminary, among many infinite foreigners, Turks and Moors are daily nourished and taught the Christian faith and religion, and baptized. What is more, through the munificence and expense of this Pope, a certain highly excellent engraver, a native of the city of Paris named Granjon <note>Robert Granjon (1513–1590), a famous type designer</note>, was called to Rome in the year 1579 or 1580 to manufacture characters <note>printing types</note> for Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic, Armenian, and others, by means of which several beautiful and good books have been printed in the Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic, Armenian, and other languages; this is confirmed by Gilbert Génébrard in book 2 of his *Chronography*.

Those who wish to learn how the knowledge and doctrine of several languages is very useful and very necessary for the understanding of books of Theology and all other sciences, should read—after the ancient authors—Michael Neander in his *Inquiries into the Holy Language*, Theodore Bibliander in his *Commentary on the Common Reason of All Languages and Letters*, Martin Luther in his oration *In Praise and Recommendation of Languages*, and Brother Luis of Portugal in his preface to the *Globe of Canons and Secrets of the Holy Language and Divine Scripture*.

» In the early days, the highest quality—taken from the center [of the plant] and then 
» in order of the cut—was called <term>Hieratic</term><note>meaning "sacred" or "priestly" paper.</note>, 
» dedicated only to religious volumes. Later, out of flattery, it took the 
» name of Augustus; just as the second quality was named <term>Liviana</term> after his wife. Thus, 
» the Hieratic name fell to third place. The next was called <term>Amphitheatric</term>, named 
» after its place of manufacture. Fannius's clever workshop in Rome took this, 
» refined it through careful processing, and made a first-class paper out of a common one, 
» giving it his own name [<term>Fanniana</term>]. That which was not so refined remained 
» <term>Amphitheatric</term>. After this came the <term>Saitic</term>, named after a town [Sais] where there is 
» great abundance, made from cheaper scraps. Even closer to the bark is the <term>Taeniotic</term>, 
» from a nearby place, sold by weight rather than quality. Finally, the <term>Emporetic</term><note>meaning "merchant" or "shop" paper.</note> 
» is useless for writing, but provides use for wrapping paper and covers for 
» merchandise. Therefore, it was named by the merchants. After this is the [outer] 
» papyrus, and its outermost part is similar to a reed, not even useful for 
» ropes unless in moisture. All sheets are woven while moistened with Nile 
» water. The turbid liquid provides the power of glue when the first <term>scheda</term><note>a strip or leaf of papyrus.</note> 
» is smeared across the table, at the length of the papyrus, with the scraps 
» trimmed off on both sides. Afterward, a cross-lattice is completed. It is then 
» pressed in presses, and the sheets are dried in the sun, and joined together, 
» always decreasing in quality from the best to the worst. Never are there more than 
» twenty sheets in a roll. There is a great difference in their width: 13 fingers for the best. 
» Two fingers are taken off the Hieratic; the Fannian has ten. The Amphitheatric has 
» one less. The Saitic has even fewer, nor does it withstand the mallet. For the 
» Emporetic's short width does not exceed six fingers. Furthermore, qualities

» it damaged several pages. Because of this, the <term>Claudian</term> was preferred above all;

» thinness, having nothing of the first quality but everything from the second. 
» Roughness is smoothed with a tooth or a shell, but then the letters become 
» prone to fading. Polished paper absorbs less ink but shines more. Moisture 
» applied carelessly often rebels, and is detected by the first stroke of the mallet, 
» or even by the smell if it was handled poorly. Spots are also detected by the eye, 
» but a strip inserted in the middle of the glued sections, made of the spongy 
» pith of the papyrus, is hardly noticed unless...

...unless the ink spreads: there is so much potential for defect in the material. There is another labor, then, for weaving the sheets together. A common <term>Glutinum</term><note>Latin for glue or adhesive.</note> is prepared from the finest flour tempered with boiling water and a very small splash of vinegar. For the glues used by carpenters and common gums are too brittle. A more careful refinement involves using the boiling water strained from the pith of fermented bread; in this way, the paper has the least amount of interface between the layers, and it surpasses even the natural smoothness of the Nile. However, all glue should be neither more than one day old, nor too fresh. Afterward, it is thinned with a mallet and run over with glue again; then it is pressed to remove wrinkles and stretched again with the mallet. Thus, there are long-lasting records in the hands of *Tiberius and Caius Gracchus*<note>Famous Roman populist reformers of the 2nd century BCE; their manuscripts were apparently still legible centuries later.</note>, which I saw in the house of *Pomponius Secundus*<note>A distinguished Roman tragic poet and general.</note>, a most famous citizen and poet, nearly 200 years later. Now, indeed, we see the supreme works of *Cicero, the Divine Augustus, and Virgil*.

The aforementioned *Jacques Dalechamps*<note>A 16th-century French physician and botanist known for his editions of Pliny.</note> speaks of it in his Annotations thus: *Melchior Guillandinus* harshly rebukes *Turnebus*<note>Adrianus Turnebus, a famous 16th-century French classical scholar.</note> for introducing three species of paper from this passage—*Hieratic, Augustan, and Livian* (Book 7, Chapter 4 of his *Adversaria*)—since they are one and the same. It was called *Hieratic* by the *Egyptians* because it was dedicated only to religious and sacred volumes. Out of the first flattery of the *Romans*, it was called *Augustan*; and out of a second flattery, *Livian*<note>Named after Emperor Augustus and his wife Livia.</note>. Thus, the name *Hieratic* was merely the third in order, being more obscure and less known. But let us see how correctly he judged this. For when the Author [Pliny] soon after reviews the types of paper based on the difference in their width, he says that *Emporetic*<note>From the Greek 'emporos' (merchant); low-quality paper used for wrapping goods.</note> paper is six inches wide; *Saitic* is fewer than nine; *Amphitheatric* is nine; *Fannian* is ten; and *Hieratic* is eleven. But the best papers, at their minimum, are thirteen inches wide. These could undoubtedly be no other than the *Augustan* and *Livian* papers, which attained the primary rank in the age of *Augustus* due to flattery of the Emperor and *Livia*, while *Hieratic* was relegated to the third place of quality and nobility. For no one would place *Tanitic* paper—which is closer to the bark and sold by weight rather than quality—among the best in that sense. To refute the opinion of *Guillandinus* and defend the sentiment of *Turnebus* and *Ruellius*, this argument should be sufficient; truly, what follows demonstrates most clearly that the *Livian* and *Augustan* were not the same: the *Augustan* paper retained its prestige for letters, while the *Livian* held its own rank, in which nothing was first-rate, but everything was second-best. For so it is read in the manuscript. Therefore, that was the order of papers while *Augustus* lived, but it was changed by *Claudius*, who thickened the paper because it was so thin it allowed the letters to show through to the other side; he added a third layer of "skin" and increased the width by several inches. *Strabo* (in his last book) calls it not paper, but *papyrus*, which is abundant and especially cultivated in the lower part of the Delta; he says it is of two kinds: one superior and the other cheaper. *Memphitic* paper. The same *Turnebus* brings forward something unheard of and least noted by other writers, being deceived by a verse of *Lucan*, which *Isidore* refers to in a corrupt form, thus:

->*Memphis paper is constructed from thirsty papyrus.*<-
->When it should be read, as we warned before,<-
->*The Memphis skiff is woven from thirsty papyrus.*<-

The ancients used the words "to be joined," "to be woven," or "to be sewn" for ships; hence *Pacuvius*, in his play *Niptra*, called the ropes intended for that use "Spartean bindings."
->*No dovetail joint holds the structure of the hull together,*<-
->*But it is sewn with flax and (Spartean bindings.*<-

*Hence also the Istrian and Liburnian bindings*, as they once called those vessels. Our own people, in place of those ropes, fill the seams of ships with crushed *Juniper* twigs and moss, adding iron clamps which the Greeks call *dikteras*<note>Meaning 'clamps' or 'fasteners' used in shipbuilding.</note>.

<page-num>974</page-num>
<header>History of the Origin of</header>
<meta>catchword: statut-</meta>

,, <term>Amphitheatric</term><note>A mid-grade papyrus named for being processed near the Amphitheatre of Alexandria.</note>; Guillandinus suggests restoring the name to **Athribic**, after the Athribic prefecture mentioned by Strabo, Ptolemy, and Stephanus. The author mentions Athribis as its capital in chapter 10, section 5. Some suspect it was called "Amphitheatric" because it was manufactured in the empty amphitheatres of Egypt—and Alexandria especially—when the crowds were gone, just as manual laborers are accustomed to practicing their trade in public places when not occupied by the common throng. Perhaps this also happened in some amphitheatre in Rome, which gave it the name.
,, **All the sheets are woven while soaked with the water of the Nile**; here Guillandinus accuses <term>Turnebus</term><note>Adrianus Turnebus (1512–1565), a French classical scholar.</note> and <term>Ruellius</term><note>Jean Ruel (1474–1537), a French physician and botanist.</note> of ignorance because they did not understand this passage, nor did they see that "sheets" (*tabulas*) here refers to the pieces of papyrus which are joined together, and not a wooden board placed under the <term>strips</term><note>original: "philuras"; these are the thin ribbons sliced from the pith of the papyrus plant.</note> upon which they are glued. With his kind permission, I believe those men actually perceived it correctly, which becomes clear from the following clause (**when first a sheet is smeared face-up on the board**). In this, Guillandinus thought Pliny's speech should be understood as: "when first a sheet (that is, a strip) is smeared, and a face-up sheet is spread out beneath" (using the ablative case), meaning the same strip is stretched out lengthwise. Truly, this kind of repetition is tasteless and hardly fits the succinct gravity of Pliny, since it could have been said more concisely and aptly as "when first the sheet is smeared." Furthermore, while the paper was being made, it was necessary for a **board** to be placed underneath, upon which the vertical and horizontal strips could be stretched and joined by glue or the murky water of the Nile: a fact Pliny indicates here in passing. 
,, Indeed, the meaning of "board" (*tabulae*) differs greatly from the notion of a "strip" (*philurae*). For this reason, I believe we should follow the faith of the manuscript codex, which has (**all sheets are woven while the board is wet with Nile water**) and again (**when first a face-up sheet is smeared on the board**); no words could be clearer or more consistent than these. He explains the "face-up" (*supinam*) sheet as being placed in an upright position, just as Livy spoke of "upturned hands" (*supinas manus*)—raised high—when the matrons stretched them toward heaven and the gods during public mourning. It is well known among doctors that a "prone" hand is one where the palm looks toward the ground, and "supine" is when the same is turned toward heaven in the manner of suppliants—a gesture by which even now the **silent and muttering Franciscans pray**. I believe the "face-up sheet" should rather be interpreted as that part which inclined inward toward the stalk, but when stretched upon the board, is turned outward and does not touch the wood of the board. Positioned thus, because it is softer, wetter, and more tender, it more easily embraces and holds the second strip thrown over it. He also thinks we should read (**afterward it is completed with a crosswise skin**), but the integrity of the manuscript suggests nothing should be changed. Moreover, the "weaving" of the papers could not be more conveniently or elegantly described than by the name of a **lattice** (*cratis*), on account of the vertical and horizontal strips lying upon one another, which is the shape of a lattice or hurdle. Furthermore, whether papers were dried in sunny places or in shady, breezy ones is a point not unworthy of notice, as it pertains to either emending or confirming Pliny's text. It is indeed true that those things glued only by the moisture of water will fly apart with steam, the warmth of the sun, and heat, and are even consumed by the heat of fire. Therefore, those who make thick papers for binding books or covering merchandise, once they have sufficiently pressed the square sheet of paper in the press, dry them **in the sun**; and booksellers, when the backs of the volumes being sewn are smeared with glue, either move them near a fire or expose them to the sun so they dry faster. For this reason, it is not unlikely that in ancient times papers were also accustomed to being hardened and dried in the sun. But since the variety of vocabulary with which Pliny explained the history of papyrus and paper may delay a reader little-versed in this matter, let it help him...

It has been established, with some things already explained. The stalk of the papyrus <term>scapus</term><note>The main stem or stalk of the papyrus plant.</note> was usually four cubits, <margin>cc</margin> that is, six feet long. Consisting of at most twenty layers or membranes, <margin>cc</margin> they would cut it after it was drawn from the water—at the top, or crown, because that <margin>cc</margin> part was thinner and weaker, and at the root because that part was tender, <margin>cc</margin> somewhat soft, and, still being soaked with moisture, it would become limp and lack the firmness <margin>cc</margin> necessary for gluing, the pressure of the press, the blows of the mallets, and the smoothing process. How <margin>cc</margin> much was cut off from each end is not recorded. It is conjectured to be about one foot <margin>cc</margin> removed, so that four feet of the truncated stalk remained; this they then <margin>cc</margin> finally divided in half through the middle with a certain iron tool intended and adapted for the task, <margin>cc</margin> which they perhaps called a "needle," separating the membranes, and which, once <margin>cc</margin> placed in a crosswise position, they would use to fashion the paper. These membranes or <margin>cc</margin> layers torn from the stalk are called by Pliny *philurae* <note>original: "philuras"; these are the thin, ribbon-like strips of pith</note>, sheets, or scraps. When <margin>cc</margin> they are arranged on the board in a vertical position, they are called *stamina* <note>original: "stamina"; vertical "warp" strips</note> or foundations; when horizontal, they are *subtegmina* <note>original: "subtegmina"; horizontal "weft" strips</note>, <margin>cc</margin> terms borrowed from the weaver's workshop. A series <margin>cc</margin> and stack of these joined either vertically or horizontally is called a *corium* <note>original: "corium"; literally 'leather' or 'hide', referring to a layer of the finished sheet</note>, which until the <margin>cc</margin> time of Emperor Claudius was only double-layered—first with vertical fibers, the other horizontal. <margin>cc</margin> Truly, by his command, the layer became triple in that paper which he called "Claudia" <margin>cc</margin> after his own name. For they wove that with vertical fibers in the first and third layers, <margin>cc</margin> and horizontal in the second. <margin>cc</margin>
Pliny never uses the term "papyrus" in place of *philurae*, and in Ulpian's <margin>cc</margin> third book *On Legacies*, "papyrus prepared for paper" is understood not so much as <margin>cc</margin> *philurae* but as the stalks of the papyrus, because the strips were not usually sold separately <margin>cc</margin> so as to be at hand and ready except when the time of manufacture arrived. What <margin>cc</margin> a *taenia* <note>original: "tenia"; a strip or sometimes a defect in the paper</note> is to Pliny, we shall declare a little later. Certainly that word is never found in <margin>cc</margin> him to mean a *philura*, although I do not deny it could be used in that sense, just as <margin>cc</margin> neither "page," nor "board," nor "sheet." For a *plagula* <note>A finished leaf or sheet of paper.</note> is a completed sheet of paper, <margin>cc</margin> woven from its strips like a thin plate, which the common people call <margin>cc</margin> a "leaf" in our modern linen papers. Moreover, it has two faces, the back and the front: <margin>cc</margin> or the anterior and posterior page. Regarding the board (*tabula*) which supported the strips <margin>cc</margin> until the framework and the weaving were finished, it was treated before. <margin>cc</margin> There remains the name "skin" (*cutis*), which I do not think should be accepted in place of the finished <margin>cc</margin> framework, as the ancient copies protest; nor does the meaning of "skin" <margin>cc</margin> itself fit, which is always the outermost and visible layer, while many strips are hidden <margin>cc</margin> deep within, especially the best and superior ones. If any strip were to be <margin>cc</margin> called a "skin," only the outermost and worst of all would deserve that name. <margin>cc</margin>

---

Nor is it sufficient for the mallet. It is either so narrow that it does not match the mallet <margin>cc</margin> where the striking part is broader, or it is so fragile that it is broken when struck by the mallet. It was the <margin>cc</margin> custom to flatten and stretch wrinkled papers with the blow of mallets. See book 32 of the <margin>cc</margin> *Pandects* of Ulpian; Guillandinus <note>Melchior Guillandinus (1520–1589), a botanist who wrote a famous commentary on papyrus.</note> mentions "hammered books." <margin>cc</margin>

The front of the paper (*aduersa*), is the anterior side facing our eyes, which we <margin>cc</margin> look at while writing and where the pen hurries; the back (*auersa*) is the posterior side, placed behind. A <margin>cc</margin> *litura* <note>original: "litura"; an erasure, blot, or smudge</note> is indeed a stain of poured and scattered ink on thirsty paper, similar to that which we <margin>cc</margin> create when erasing writing with a pen. Certainly, it appears more on the back <margin>cc</margin> side of the paper, that ink seeping through so that when something is already written on the front, <margin>cc</margin> nothing else can be drawn on the back, fouled as it is by black spots. Indeed, <margin>cc</margin> these verses of Juvenal <note>Roman satirist, c. 55–138 AD.</note> testify that the ancients wrote on both sides: <margin>cc</margin>

> "Orestes, written even on the back and not yet finished." <margin>cc</margin>

And Martial <note>Roman poet, c. 38–103 AD.</note>: <margin>cc</margin>

> "Piceus writes epigrams on the back of the paper." <margin>cc</margin>

# History of the Origin of Books

->*And it grieves him, what she does with God turned away.*<-
<note>original: "Et dolet, auerso quod facit illa Deo." Likely a poetic fragment illustrating the use of specific writing surfaces.</note>

" They call 'opisthographic' <term>opisthographos</term><note>from the Greek for 'written on the back'</note> those commentaries described in such a way that they are written on both sides. Notebooks <term>aduersaria</term><note>temporary journals or waste-books for rough drafts</note> have some similarity to these; they are essentially disordered tablets, written with many things thrown together carelessly, which are then transferred into proper, permanent books arranged in order. Cicero, in his speech for Roscius, speaks of contracts that are opisthographic, holographic, and signed by hand <note>original: "syngraphis opisthographis autographis, chirographis"</note>, as does Alexander ab Alexandro in book 2, chapter 30.

" Therefore, the supports <term>statumina</term><note>vertical structural strips, like the 'warp' in weaving</note> were also made from a second layer. An ancient manuscript states: 'Therefore, the warp-threads were made with a second layer just as the weft-threads <term>subtegmina</term> were with the first.' The sense is not at all different if we also read 'supports' <term>statumina</term>: for the warp-thread <term>stamen</term> is that which women spin by winding it on a distaff; in weaving, it is the vertical thread of the loom, within which the weft-thread <term>subtegmen</term> or 'woof' <term>trama</term> runs crosswise. A 'support' <term>statumen</term>, however, is a stake or pole by which a vine is propped up. The author’s meaning is thus quite clear: in the 'Claudian' paper <term>charta Claudia</term>, just as the first layer was made of vertical strips <term>philuris</term>, a second was added like a weft or woof from transverse sheets; then, a third layer was pressed onto this, consisting of vertical strips again, just like the first layer.

" The measure was one foot. <margin>Concerning the tearing away that ruins larger pages</margin> Thus an ancient manuscript describes the Large-sheeted paper <term>Macrocolla</term>. Guillandinus believes the name comes from 'long-backed' <note>original: <term>ἀπὸ τῶν μακρῶν κόλλων</term></note>; I believe it comes rather from 'long-limbed' or 'long-membered' <note>original: <term>ἀπὸ τῶν μακρῶν κώλων</term>, referring to the broad expanse of the sheet</note>, meaning from long rolls and segments. Whether the measure of a foot or a cubit <note>a foot and a half</note> for these papers refers to the length or the width, Pliny does not specify. I believe it refers to the width, since the discussion here concerns width; for the length of the papyrus stalk <term>scapus</term> from which the sheets were pulled was known to be about four feet, which could not be reduced to the measure of a foot or a cubit—even though the name 'long-membered' <term>macrocolo</term> indicates length rather than width. Moreover, the fact that the tearing of a single sheet would ruin larger or multiple pages teaches us that the small strips of finished, dried, hammered, and smoothed paper were usually folded into pages, as is done with our linens; the larger these were, the more the writing would be disturbed and damaged if someone removed a single strip <term>philuram</term>, whether through malice or because it was corrupt and defective. The 'Augustan' paper, praised and left behind in the letters of Martial, he calls the 'Greeting' paper <term>salutatrix</term> in book 9:

> *Marcus Antonius loves our Muses, Atticus,*
> *If only the greeting-paper <term>charta salutatrix</term> reports the truth.*

" Regarding the fact that Guillandinus replaces the 'Livian' paper with the 'Fannian'—as he never ceases to claim that the Augustan, Livian, and Hieratic papers are the same—I have stated above that this goes against the authority of the ancient manuscripts and is not approved by us. Indeed, we can list the papers and review them by their classes according to their value and price, which was determined by the variety of their width, since the length of all was nearly equal. In the time of Augustus, the foremost were:

*   **Large-sheets** <term>macrocolas</term>: one foot or a foot and a half wide.
*   **Augustan** and **Livian** (the best): thirteen digits wide.
*   **Hieratic**: eleven digits.
*   **Fannian**: ten digits.
*   **Amphitheatric**: nine digits.
*   **Saitic** and (which the author omitted) **Tanitic**: fewer, namely seven or eight digits.
*   **Emporetic** <note>Used for wrapping goods</note>: six digits.

" The **Claudian** paper surpassed all these in both quality and esteem; woven during the reign of Claudius with two warps and one weft (without the 'supports'), it was somewhat wider than the Augustan and Livian, reaching, I suspect, fourteen or fifteen digits."

“ One which had nothing from the first. Which received nothing from the first strip <term>philura</term><note>original: "philura"; the thin, translucent strips of the papyrus stalk used to form the paper’s surface.</note>, but all the “
dross from the second: or which had none of the qualities of the first, namely the *Claudia*, but all those of “
the second, namely the *Augusta*, it possessed. “

**Roughness is smoothed by a tooth, or a shell.** “

The author here mentions four defects of papers: roughness, rebellious “
defiance, freckles, and a streak <term>taenia</term><note>literally "tapeworm" or "ribbon," referring here to a narrow, unglued defect in the papyrus sheet.</note> (one or more). The remedy for roughness is “
polishing with a tooth or a shell, though applied with moderation so that it is not “
worn away too forcefully. For although it may shine more from that leveling and smoothing, “
and please the eyes with a gleaming luster, yet with too much rubbing it does not absorb the “
ink <term>atramentum</term>, but rejects it; and if any letters are painted on, the unstable and fleeting “
writing does not last. The second defect is rebellion. Those who have been “
subjected to arms and pacified, but move to war again, are said to rebel. The moisture “
carelessly applied "rebels" when it resists the care and study of the craftsman too “
stubbornly, and does not moisten or smear the whole space of the strip <term>corium</term> “
equally, but settles more abundantly in some places and is poured more sparingly in others, “
from which the surface and the drying of the sheets <term>plagularum</term> becomes unequal. For “
when the craftsman thinks the paper has been well-tended, subdued, and handled, “
and that it lacks nothing further of his labor, then contrary to his hope, “
that defect is uncovered, and as if it breaks out afresh, it creates “
work for his diligence once again. Therefore the paper must be unraveled and tamed with the “
same labor, and conquered, as before. This defect is detected with a mallet, or because it “
beats the more prominent lumps and the deeper hollows of the sheets with an unequal strike, “
and reveals them as bruised with an unlovely deformity. That “
stain is also betrayed and proven by the smell—especially if the paper was compressed by the press “
and dried too negligently—a moldy, poisonous, foul stench from the rotting and “
stale moisture, which was neither squeezed out by the press nor dissipated by the sun. “
"Freckles" <term>lentigo</term> “
is a spot scattered on the sheets of paper, reddish in color, or somewhat reddish, such “
as is seen on a person, called *phakos* <note>original: "φακός"; Greek for a lentil or a freckle.</note> by the Greeks. From the many such spots on his face, “
Dioscorides was nicknamed *Phakas*, according to Suidas. Therefore, in paper, Pliny “
calls the blemishes, filth, discolored marks of dots, and spotty sprays "freckles": “
these were made while the strips were being joined if anything “
unclean fell in which might foul the natural color, or if anything “
twisted and bunched up in the sheets darkened the paper. This was recognized by the eyes, either “
by inspecting the paper immediately if the spots were out in the open, or by spreading it out “
to the Sun if they sat deeper within. The fourth and last defect is the "Streak" <term>taenia</term>, not, as “
Guillandinus thinks, a strip or a sheet, but a long and narrow “
path in the sheets, smeared and covered with no glue or fatty moisture, in which only the “
spongy and thirsty thinness of the papyrus meets the pens of the writers without “
any coating; and while it drinks in the letter or the painting of the ink, it spreads it out. This “
is explored neither by the blow of the mallet nor by the sight of the eyes, but only by the writing, “
while the painted letter, liquefying, is soaked up by both sides, “
and fouls both the front and the back face. “

**A shell.** A Venus-shell, which Mutianus describes by the name *Echneidis*. “
**The moisture carelessly applied often rebels.** “
Read: *The moisture often rebels because it was carelessly applied to the first strips...* because they “
were more negligent, etc. “
I interpret "rebels" as: soaked with too much moisture, it swells up, and because of the unequal “
mass of the swelling, it as if resists and struggles against the writer. Others read the last part “
as *when they have been more foul-smelling*. “
**Freckles are also detected by the eyes.**
