“Even as Homer was writing, Egypt [as a source of papyrus] did not yet exist; or why, if it were already in use, did he say that Bellerophon was given tablets <note>original: "codicillos"</note> in Lycia, and not letters <note>original: "epistolas"</note>?” <note>Pliny the Elder argues that papyrus was a later invention because Homer mentions tablets rather than paper scrolls.</note> This material also feels the sting of scarcity. Indeed, during the reign of Tiberius, such a shortage of paper occurred that the Senate had to appoint judges to distribute it; otherwise, public life would have been in a state of chaos.

The same Jacques Dalechamps <note>A 16th-century French physician and scholar famous for his edition of Pliny.</note>, in his annotations interpreting this chapter, says regarding the words “books treated with cedar” <note>original: "libros cedratos fuisse"</note>: They were anointed with cedar oil or resin <note>original: "cedrio siue cedria"</note> (on which see book 6, chapter 11 and book 14, chapter 5). Vitruvius <note>A Roman architect and engineer.</note> says in book 2, chapter 9, that things anointed with cedar oil—such as books—are not harmed by moths or rot; hence the saying:

-> ----- And he spoke words worthy of cedar. <note>original: "Et cedro digna locutus." Meaning: words worthy of being preserved for eternity.</note> ----- <-

And on the phrase “Bellerophon was given tablets, not letters,” he remarks: “Tablets marked with secret and Hieroglyphic characters, not with the common forms of letters with which correspondence is written.” This is the opinion of Eustathius <note>A 12th-century Byzantine scholar and commentator on Homer.</note>, which I do not entirely praise. As for those who think Pliny was careless here in distinguishing tablets from letters—since among the Latins, tablets (*codicilli*) were nothing other than letters—I do not think Pliny is to be blamed at all. He is wondering why, if the use of paper already existed (as indicated by a letter from Sarpedon), Proetus gave Bellerophon his commands inscribed on the wood of a writing tablet rather than written on paper as letters are sent. In this sense, nothing could be clearer. The passage is in Homer’s *Iliad*, book 6:

> -> ----- ...he gave him baneful signs, ----- <-
> -> Writing many soul-destroying things on a folded tablet. ----- <-
> -> <note>original Greek: "πόρεν δ’ὅγε σήματα λύγρα / Γράψας ἐν πίνακι πτυκτῷ θυμοφθόρα πολλά."</note> ------------------------------------------------------------- « <-

See what Julius Pollux writes in book 10 of his *Onomasticon*, chapter 14, regarding books and the instruments for writing them; also Theodor Zwinger in volume 2, book 1 of his great *Theater of Human Life*; and Pierre Grégoire in book 16, chapter 10 of his *Syntax of the Admirable Art*.

Louis Le Roy <note>A French Renaissance humanist (c. 1510–1577).</note> writes in book 2 of his *Vicissitude of Things* that the most Ancient people wrote on the bark of trees and on wooden tablets. Others wrote on palm leaves, according to the resources of their countries; some used lead. Missive letters were written on wax tablets. Laws and other durable matters were engraved in bronze or copper. They also wrote on fine linen. The Emperor Commodus used the thin inner bark of the linden tree, called *Philyra*. Others used the Papyrus, a shrub growing in the marshes of Egypt, which was thicker, and from which comes the name “paper” used today. This modern paper is made from old rags soaked for a long time in water and crushed in a mill, then reduced to a white, pasty substance. When this is spread over a brass grid to drain, then placed between two woolen felts and pressed, it dries slightly and becomes white paper—subtle, fine, and light. 

Furthermore, we use parchment, which is firmer and more durable than paper. It is made from the skins of goats, sheep, and calves, prepared and dressed by tawers and parchment-makers. Herodotus, in his *Terpsichore* <note>Book 5 of his Histories.</note>, testifies that these skins were used for writing in his time. And Josephus says that the sacred books were first written upon them. Marcus Varro believes they were invented at Pergamum, a city in Asia, from which they take their name <note>The word "parchment" derives from "Pergamena."</note>; this occurred when Kings Ptolemy and Eumenes were competing with one another to build libraries. The people of Malabar and other Indians living between the rivers Indus and Ganges still write today on palm leaves, larger or smaller depending on what they wish to write: whole leaves for things intended to last a long time, such as their religious affairs or histories, and others of lesser...

» weight by a quarter or half-quarter, on both one side and the other. And when they have written a great number, wishing to join them into books, they fasten them between two wooden boards <term>ais<gloss>stiff wooden boards used as book covers before the use of cardboard</gloss></term>, instead of the covers we use; then, just as we sew our leaves with a needle and thread, they attach them with two [pegs] to the said tablets. As for missives <note>Correspondence or letters.</note>, it is enough that the leaf is written upon and rolled up, and for a seal, they tie it with a small thread of the same material. They write using a pointed instrument of iron or bone, passing lightly over the leaf without piercing it, and imprinting the characters of their letters in such a way that they can write on both sides.

Other more permanent writings, such as temple foundations, are engraved in stone or copper. Peter Martyr of Milan <note>Peter Martyr d'Anghiera (1457–1526), an Italian-born historian for the Spanish Crown who wrote the first accounts of the explorations in the Americas.</note>, in his *History of the Discovery of the New Lands made by the Castilians*, recounts that the inhabitants of Collacuane <note>original: "Collacuane"; likely referring to a region in the Caribbean or South America described by Martyr.</note> brought to Spain, among other things, several books written on thin inner barks found between the wood and the thick outer bark. These are sometimes taken from [poplars] or alders, which they cover with thick cloth and fasten with a sticky cement, then rub with finely ground plaster. When it is dry, they write whatever they please upon it. Their books are not made of leaves; rather, they extend in length by several cubits <note>An ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches.</note> and are folded into square sections so joined with a sticky, flexible cement that they appear to be made of wooden tablets. In whichever way these are opened, two written faces are presented, and two pages appear. There are just as many underneath if one does not extend them fully, because beneath one leaf are several other written leaves.

The letters and characters resemble hooks, loops, stars, and other such forms, which they arrange in lines in our fashion. Representing somewhat the ancient manner of Egypt and Ethiopia, they paint figures of animals between the lines, especially of men who lived before—such as Kings and Lords—reciting their deeds. They also write their laws, sacrifices, ceremonies, observations of the stars, and matters of farming. The top and bottom are of pleasing craftsmanship, so that when they are folded, they seem in no way different from our own books. They also make books from the bark of fig trees, which they can easily erase. 

The same Martyr says that in Darien <note>A region in present-day Panama and Colombia.</note>, books made of tree leaves sewn together were found, and that in Mexico they use figures through which they declare their affairs no differently than we do with writing. In Hispaniola <note>The island comprising modern-day Haiti and the Dominican Republic.</note>, there is a tree named *Coppeia* <note>The Autograph Tree (*Clusia rosea*); its leaves can be scratched with a stylus to leave permanent marks.</note>, the leaf of which is fit for writing like paper, using a needle or pointed wood. It is credible that this is the tree on whose leaves the Chaldeans <note>An ancient people of Mesopotamia, often associated by early scholars with the origins of wisdom and writing.</note>, the first inventors of letters, wrote their thoughts before the use of other materials was invented. The leaf receives writing on both sides, just like paper. It is about twelve fingers wide and almost round, thicker than double parchment and very durable. When wet, it shows white letters against its green; when it is dry, it turns white and hardens like a wooden tablet, but the letters turn yellow. It is never ruined or erased by getting wet, unless it is burned.

Paule <note>Marco Polo (c. 1254–1324), the Venetian explorer.</note> recounts that in the province of Arcaudan <note>Likely Carajan (Yunnan, China), as described in Polo’s travels.</note>, subject to the Great Khan, there are no letters or characters; instead, the men there make their contracts and obligations using small tablets which they split in half...

The simple folk of the New World, ignorant of the use of letters, were greatly amazed, seeing how Christians understood one another by means of them. They believed that the written leaves spoke at their command and reported secrets; such that they touched and carried them with fear, as if there were some spirit within, and as if the leaves spoke by divinity rather than by human industry. 

The most common ink that we use here today is made with black ink, which formerly was composed of soot from baths and furnaces, but is now made of gall nuts <note>Small growths on oak trees used for their high tannin content in ink making.</note>, gum Arabic, and pomegranate rinds, the whole being soaked in vitriol water or pulverized copperas <note>Ferrous sulfate, a key ingredient in "iron gall" ink.</note>. One can also write with the juice of mulberries, cherries, and other such fruits. This is done with pens made of reeds or canes—which Erasmus used—or of bronze, gold, or silver; or quills cut from geese, swans, peacocks, and ostriches. 

This is to say nothing of the subtleties of writing with ciphers used by Princes, and the shorthand notes <note>Tironian notes, a system of shorthand.</note> invented by Cicero; or with alum, which does not appear and cannot be read unless the pages are plunged into water; or with sal ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride.</note>, orange juice, lemon, or onion, which are revealed when brought near a fire; or even with tallow, ash, and charcoal. But the manner of writing by printing has surpassed all others in skill and diligence, advancing more work in one day than several hasty scribes could do in a year. See André Thevet, book 11, chapter 23 of his *Cosmography*.

...that only sixteen years after the said Gutenberg, one Conrad <note>Likely Conrad Sweynheym, who partnered with Arnold Pannartz to bring printing to Italy.</note>, a German, brought the first of this invention from Germany to Rome.

On the contrary, *Platina* <note>Bartolomeo Platina, a Renaissance humanist and papal librarian.</note> in his works, *Appian* in the second part of his *Cosmography*, *Pedro Mexía* in the second chapter of the third part of his *Diverse Lessons*, and *André Thevet*—cited above in chapter 12 of the 20th book of his *Cosmography*—write that in the year of our salvation 1440, *Johann* or perhaps *Peter Fust*, a German citizen of Mainz <note>original: "Magonce"</note>, first invented this art of Printing. They claim it was practiced by him and *Peter*, or *Yves Schoeffer* (also called *Scheffey of Gernsheim*), his son-in-law, and after them more diligently by the aforementioned *Johann Gutenberg of Strasbourg* <note>original: "Argentorate"</note>, and by *Ulrich Han* and *Sixtus* <note>Sixtus Riessinger</note>, who brought it to Italy. This is confirmed by *Michael Fernus* in his life of *Campanus*. In fact, around the year of Salvation 1450 or 1453, Printing began to be in vogue in Italy by means of the said *Gutenberg*, as asserted by *Aventinus* in the seventeenth book of his annals, *Sabellicus* in the sixth book of his sixth Ennead, *Gilbert Genebrard* in the fourth book of his *Chronography*, and the previously cited *Antoine du Verdier* in the fourth book of his *Prosopography*. 

However, *Guicciardini* in his description of Lower Germany asserts that the art of Printing was first invented at Haarlem in Holland, from where it was later brought to Mainz. The Tables of *Peurbach* <note>Georg von Peurbach, a famous astronomer.</note> seem to attribute the invention of it to *Regiomontanus* <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg, a mathematician and astronomer.</note>. This is not without plausibility, seeing as among the inventions of this great personage is numbered that most admirable art called the "formative of letters and characters," as left in writing by *Girolamo Cardano* in book 12, chapter 59, of *On the Variety of Things*. Common chronology reports that in Mainz, the first book printed there was the *Offices* of Cicero, and this through the diligence of *Peter Gernsheim* <note>Peter Schoeffer</note> in the year 1466, as confirmed by Peter Ramus in the preface of his second book on Mathematics. In fact, I have seen in the hands of a relative and friend of mine a copy of these *Offices* of Cicero printed on leaves of parchment, at the end of which are these words:

> This present most famous work of Marcus Tullius [Cicero], I, Johann Fust, citizen of Mainz, have happily brought to completion, not with a quill pen <note>original: "atramento plumali"</note> nor a bronze reed, but by a certain most beautiful art, by the hand of Peter Gernsheim, my servant. In the year 1466, on the fourth day of the month of February etc. <note>original: "Præsens Marci Tullij clarissimum opus Iohannes Fust Moguntinus Ciuis, non atramento plumali, canna neque ærea; sed arte quadam perpulchra, manu Petri Gernshem Pueri mei fœliciter effeci finitum. Anno M. CCCCLXVI. quarta die Mensis Februarij Zé."</note>

*Raffaele Volaterrano* in book 33 of his *Commentaries* writes that two German brothers who went to Italy in the year of Salvation 1465 first printed in Rome the books of the *City of God* by Saint Augustine, and the books of the *Divine Institutes* by Lactantius Firmianus. The Portuguese and Spaniards who have sailed and traveled through several and diverse regions of this universe—trading at the far reaches of the East and the North in China and Cathay—assert from their voyages to have brought from these countries books printed in their own languages and scripts. This invention in Rome is by Asinius Pollio, who by establishing a library made a Republic of the memories of good and excellent men.

## On the causes of the decays, mutations, changes, conversions, and ruins of languages.

### CHAPTER LXXXVIII.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'Q' featuring scrolling vine-like foliage motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

SOME ancient and modern astronomers have attributed and related the causes and effects of the decays, mutations, changes, conversions, and ruins of languages to the celestial constellations. They say that just as these celestial constellations are the causes and effects of the decays, mutations, changes, conversions, and ruins of Monarchies, Empires, Kingdoms, and Republics, so they are for the languages which these entities use and employ.

We have very clearly demonstrated the falsity of this opinion in a discourse previously published by us regarding the truth of the causes and effects of the decays, mutations, changes, conversions, and ruins of Monarchies, Empires, Kingdoms, and Republics, printed at Lyon by **Benoît Rigauld** in 1598.

**Theodore Bibliander** <note>A 16th-century Swiss Orientalist and linguist</note>, in his *Commentary on the common reason of all languages and letters* <note>original Latin: *De ratione communi omnium linguarum & literarum*</note>, wrote the following words on this subject, which are worthy of being repeated:

> Because speech is established by popular use and consent, and therefore changes from time to time for many reasons—just as the common people are fickle—no one can truly give laws to the people on how they must speak. It is quite difficult to prescribe laws of speaking to the unlearned commoners, since they feel that language is a popular possession. I cannot pass over in silence in this place the saying of **Pomponius Marcellus** the Grammarian. When he had criticized something in a speech by **Tiberius** <note>The second Roman Emperor</note> as being poor Latin, and **Ateius Capito** <note>A famous Roman jurist</note> defended it as being Latin (or if it were not, it would become so, implying the power of Caesar Tiberius), Pomponius turned to Tiberius and said: "Capito lies. For you, Caesar, can give citizenship to men, but you cannot give citizenship to words." By this, Pomponius meant that not even Kings can dictate speech to the common people, for it remains under their own judgment and consent. Yet it is all the more useful for a certain and stable doctrine to exist, both for judging correctly the speech already received and approved by the public, and for using it correctly and preserving the language which the public recklessly changes from year to year, and almost from day to day—condemning some things without judgment and accepting others. Since all affairs, both public and private, are usually entrusted to language as if to a public treasury, it is best to transmit it to the knowledge of posterity through a certain method and order. This is so that judgments can still be made about the old language, even after it has ceased to be used among them; otherwise, when the knowledge of the language is lost, the knowledge of the things themselves will perish at the same time. Anyone who considers civil affairs, laws, treaties, and the form of divine worship with a little more diligence will clearly understand that this happens with great harm.

The same author, in the chapter on the mutation of languages, continues with these words:

> That the Greek and Latin languages, even at the time when they flourished most, underwent a remarkable change is proved by so many terms of the arts of Grammar and Rhetoric, such as **Latinity**, **Hellenism**, **Barbarism** <note>original: *Barbaralexis*</note>, **Solecism**, **Archaism**, and foreign, new, ancient, old, obsolete, and forgotten words. There are even established "ages" of speech, so to speak: one observes one kind of Latin in the times of **Cato the Elder** or **Ennius**, another in the time of **Cicero**, another in the age of **Caesar**, and another in the times of **Pliny** and **Quintilian**. In how many ways and for what reasons this happens will be discussed more conveniently elsewhere. Here, only a few things from good authors will be added, from which that mutation of languages can be better weighed.

**Horace** <note>The Roman lyric poet</note> indeed showed this excellently with these verses in his *Art of Poetry* <note>original: *Ars Poetica*</note>:

> *Even in the use of words, being subtle and cautious in planting them...* <note>original: *In verbis etiam tenuis, cautusque ferendis*</note>

" *You will have spoken excellently if a clever arrangement makes a known word seem new; and if by chance it is necessary to show hidden things with recent signs, it will be permitted to invent terms never heard by the ancient Cethegi* <note>The Cethegi were an old, prestigious Roman family; Horace uses them here to represent ancient, old-fashioned Romans.</note>*: and such license will be granted if used modestly. Why am I envied if I can acquire a few words for myself, since the tongue of Cato and Ennius enriched our fatherland's speech and brought forth new names for things? It has been, and always will be, permitted to produce a word marked by the stamp of the current day. As the woods change their leaves as the years glide by, and the first to fall are the oldest: so the ancient generation of words perishes, and like the young, those newly born flourish and grow strong. We and all our works are owed to death.*"

->And a little after<-

" *Mortal deeds will perish, much less shall the honor and grace of speech remain long-lived. Many words shall be reborn which have already fallen, and those which are now in honor shall fall, if usage so wills it—for in usage lies the judgment, the law, and the rule of speaking.*" <note>original: "Dixeris egregiè..." through "norma loquendi." These famous verses are from Horace's *Ars Poetica*, lines 47–72, reflecting on the natural evolution of language.</note>

" **Quintilian** <note>Referred to here as 'Fabius'—his full name was Marcus Fabius Quintilianus.</note> also, speaking of figures of speech in the ninth book of his *Theoretical Institutions*, says: 'If we compare ancient speech to our own, almost everything we say is now a "figure." For example, to say *hanc rem invidere* [to envy this thing] is no longer the standard as it was for all the ancients and especially **Cicero**, but rather *huic* [using the dative case]. Also, to say *illi incumbere* [to lean on that] instead of *illum*; and *plenum vino* [full of wine] is now said with the dative or genitive rather than the accusative; and *adulari* [to flatter] now takes the dative. And a thousand other things; and would that even worse changes do not prevail!' But the commentaries of the Grammarians are full of such arguments regarding the change in the Latin tongue. **Polybius of Megalopolis** also, who deservedly attained the highest praise in Roman history, wondered at the changeableness of the Roman speech and showed that from the time of the first consuls until **Scipio Africanus** (whose teacher he was), such a great variety of speech occurred among the Romans that, if one compares the present speech with the old, even those endowed with the highest intelligence can scarcely discern certain things, even with great care."

" Regarding the change of the Greek language, nothing can be more briefly or better set down for the present than the judgment of the most learned **Varro**, taken from the first book, chapter 18, of **Aulus Gellius's** *Attic Nights*."

" In the 14th book of *Divine Matters*, **Marcus Varro** showed that **Lucius Laelius**, then the most learned man of the city, had erred because he took an old Greek word that had been brought into the Roman tongue—such as the word for 'pure wine'—and, treating it as if it were a Latin word he had invented himself, he broke it down into Latin roots using a false etymological reasoning. We have set down his very words here: 'In this matter, our friend Laelius, a man most distinguished in letters in our memory, narrated several times: for he rendered false causes for certain ancient Greek words, just as if they were our own. For we do not call the hare *lepus* because it is *levipes* [light-footed], but because it is an ancient Greek word...' <note>The text cuts off here, but Varro is arguing that *lepus* comes from the Aeolic Greek *leporis*, not from the Latin *levipes*.</note>"

...the origins of words are unknown, because they now use other terms for them, and most are ignorant that those are Greek—such as what they now call *Hellēna* <note>original: "ελαηνα" (Ἕλληνα); the Greek word for "Greek."</note>; that the "well" is what they call *phrear* <note>original: "φρέαρ"</note>; or that the "hare" is what they call *lagōon* <note>original: "λάγωον"</note>. In this matter, I not only do not blame the talent of Laelius, but I praise his industry. For success follows fortune, but praise follows experience. Varro wrote these things in the first book of *On the Origin of Words* <note>Refers to Marcus Terentius Varro's *De Lingua Latina*.</note> most skillfully regarding the use of both languages, most expertly and most kindly toward Laelius himself; but in the later part of the same book, he says that a "thief" <note>Latin: *fur*</note> is so named because the ancient Romans called the black darkness *furvus*, and thieves steal more easily through the night, which is black. Does it not seem that Varro erred regarding the "thief" just as Laelius did regarding the "hare"? For what is now called *kleptēs* <note>original: "κλεωτης" (κλέπτης)</note> by the Greeks was called *phōr* <note>original: "φῶρ"</note> in the more ancient Greek tongue. From this, through the affinity of letters, what is *phōr* in Greek is *fur* in Latin. But whether that matter escaped Varro’s memory at the time, or whether, on the contrary, he thought it more apt and coherent for "thief" to be named from *furvus* (that is, black), is not for me to judge in the case of a man of such excellent learning. 

However, that variety and change of individual idioms is observed in all those things in which property, power, elegance, wealth, and abundance, virtues, vices, and all qualities of speech and languages are placed. This is seen especially in words, as we judged a little earlier from the examples brought from the poet Flaccus <note>Horace</note> and Aulus Gellius—that "hare" and *phōr* were terms of the ancient Greek language. Of this kind is what Aristotle first called *selachē* <note>original: "σελάχη"</note>, the aquatic animals which have cartilage instead of a spine. And again, *mintha*, which even to the ancient Greeks signified "mint," was abolished when a new term was introduced, namely *hēdyosmos* <note>Meaning "sweet-smelling."</note>, as Pliny teaches. Thus, not only in the age of Donatus but even in the time of the poet Terence, the ancient word for "immediately" was *actutum*. And *cascus* was used for "old man," and *creperum bellum* for a "doubtful war." Again, Pliny interprets as "cartilaginous" those things which Aristotle called *selache*. For he could not do otherwise. Many things of this kind occur in the writings of Sidonius Apollinaris, and especially in Apuleius of Madaura. Although not even Sallust escaped the mark of being an innovator of words. 

This is also observed in the affection of voices—namely, in the change of gender, declension, derivation, composition, and the like. For example, *rapseris* for *rapias* or *rapueris* <note>different forms of "you may seize"</note>, *sepelibo* for *sepeliam* <note>"I shall bury"</note>, or *gladiola* for *gladiolus* <note>"small sword"</note>. Many such things were collected by Nonius Marcellus. In syllables, too, the change of accent is observed, or the addition or joining of syllables. It is also seen in the elements, as the ancients said *olli* for *illi* <note>"to those"</note>; and certainly in formulas of speaking, especially as was judged before by Fabius Quintilian. Of this kind are the things Sallust unusually brought forth: "to lead an army" <note>Latin: *ductare exercitum*</note> and "to perform a war" <note>Latin: *patrare bellum*</note>. Finally, it is observed in the joining, rhythms, abundance, figures, tropes, and the whole genre of speaking.

Indeed, the causes for which speech varies are many. Regarding the universal division—how one language, common to the whole human race for 1700 years and more from the beginning of things until the building of Babylon, was split into so many discrete speeches—God is the author, as proven histories show and reason easily perceives. For no suitable cause appears in the functions or in the whole nature of man why men, restored after the flood through the three sons of Noah, would have wanted by deliberate effort to change the speech used and approved among them for several centuries—so useful and necessary for so many names—and, having made a most grave schism, to scatter themselves...

Indeed, one can see in imperialistic peoples a sharp and eager striving to expand their own language along with their power, and conversely, to contract or entirely abolish foreign languages, if it were possible. Evil angels, moreover, could not by their own power introduce such a change into human affairs—and indeed into their very souls—that those who had lived together as members of one people and city should suddenly express such discordant thoughts. Good angels certainly neither could nor would bring that calamity upon men, except by the command of God. As for other creatures, whether endowed with a soul or lacking one, what point is there in speaking of them, since they have no access to the mind of man, except insofar as their outward form is perceived by the senses?

Therefore, the Creator and Maker and Architect of all things, by his simple word—or through the work of Angels, as it seemed to Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian scholar who speculated that angels might have been the instruments of the divine will at Babel.</note>—brought about the variety of speech, and as the sacred history says, "confused the lip" <note>The Latin *confudit labium* is a literal translation of the Hebrew idiom for "confused the language."</note> of the builders at Babylon. Let us hear, then, what they said in the Plains of Shinar <note>original: "Campis Sennaar"; the biblical location of the Tower of Babel.</note> as they exhorted one another with one voice to undertake and finish this immense work with combined strength and all their faculties: "Come," they said, "let us make for ourselves a city and a tower whose top reaches to heaven, and let us make our name famous, lest we be scattered over the whole earth." 

Yet what had the Lord God said at the beginning of things? What was his own plan? What was his command? "Increase," he said, "and multiply, and fill the earth, and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and the birds, and all living things that move upon the earth." And after the Flood, the Lord repeats and renews this in Genesis chapter 9: "But you, increase and multiply, and go forth upon the earth, and fill it." But after Ham <note>The text uses "Chanaan" here, but Ham is the son of Noah; Canaan was Ham's son who inherited the curse.</note>, the middle-born of the sons of Noah, had treated his parent with the greatest insult, and Shem and Japheth had covered his disgrace, Noah—the survivor of the human race, moved by a heavenly inspiration—pronounced the divine judgment upon his sons and foretold their fates in this manner: "Cursed be Canaan, a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers. Blessed be the Lord God of Shem; let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant." Against this fate and the decree of the all-powerful divinity, the builders of the Babylonian mass joined their reasons, plans, wills, and all their effort, setting themselves against the most perfect and supreme decree of the divine word. But in vain they resist the Lord of hosts, who inspects all, hears all, judges all, and governs in the most wise ways. For what is written in the history of the blessed Moses? # History of the Origin of [Languages]

» ...diversity alienates man from man. <note>original Latin: *diuersitas hominem alienat ab homine*. This is a citation from Saint Augustine’s *City of God*, Book 19.</note> For if two people meet and are forced by some necessity not to pass by, but to stay together, and neither knows the language of the other, even dumb animals of different species can associate with one another more easily than they, even though they are both human. When they are unable to communicate what they feel to each other, solely because of the diversity of language, such a great similarity of nature is of no use in bringing men together; so much so that a man would more willingly be with his own dog than with a foreign man. Pliny supports this when speaking on the use of the voice; "So great," he says, "is the power of speech, that a stranger is not even considered a fellow man." <note>original: *externus alieno non sit hominis vice*</note> Moreover, that punishment of divine justice was imposed in such a way that the mind retained all its faculties and powers—the power of understanding, reason, memory, and will—and the faculty of deriving logic and expressing it outwardly was also left behind. The organs of voice and speech were left: the lungs, sides, and muscles, the windpipe, palate, throat, tongue, teeth, lips, and breath. However, in the forming of the breath, and in its distinction as if into articulated segments, a confusion of sounds and a discrepancy of meanings was inflicted. To address this, the Lord in his kindness allowed that a person might learn multiple languages with reason as a guide and teacher, while his grace—that inexhaustible fountain of all good things—continually waters and flows so that, by employing the mediation of an interpreter, those who had been separated far apart by the Babylonian confusion might be joined once again. This is achieved even more conveniently through the benefit of writing, which is both a human invention and a divine gift. By this means, the fountain of all wisdom and the writings of the Hebrew prophets reached the Greeks, not by themselves, but through translators. Long ago, through translators, the Divine Scriptures reached both the Greeks and other nations, even the barbarians; and today, the holy books are read in the languages of almost all peoples. To wish to hinder this most divine gift—what else is it but to hate and persecute divine talents and to wage war against God, a task more than Punic <note>referring to the extreme treachery associated with Carthage in Roman history</note> or Giant-like <note>referring to the giants of mythology who attempted to storm heaven</note>. For the Messiah, the expectation of all nations, came into the world to restore all things and reconcile all: to bind together Jews, Greeks, Germans, Scythians <note>an ancient people of Central Eurasia, often used to represent the most distant or "uncivilized" nations</note>, and other peoples among themselves and with God the Father through the bond of the Holy Spirit. He gathered the joined nations into one people, one kingdom, city, and home. By his own blood, [he reconciled] the languages of the Hebrew nation, the Greek, and the Roman—which surpassed others in wisdom and empire—as he sacrificed himself on the altar of the Cross for the entire world. Through the title and inscription of the cause placed above the head of the Lord Jesus, it was declared that he is the promised one and expected Savior of all nations, the Monarch, and the highest, eternal, most holy, and best High Priest. Concerning whom Zephaniah <note>referred to as Sophonias in the Latin text</note> forewarned with a clear prophecy:

> » *"Expect me, says the Lord, in the day of my resurrection in the future, for my*
> » *judgment is to gather the nations and assemble the kingdoms, and to pour out upon*
> » *them my indignation and all my fierce anger. For in the fire of my*
> » *jealousy shall all the earth be devoured: because then I will restore to the peoples a chosen lip,* <note>meaning a pure or common language</note> *so that*

Thus—wonderful and astounding to say—men who were previously unrefined and illiterate, and who were almost like infants in their own native speech, suddenly spoke in the language of all peoples and nations among whom they were to proclaim the Gospel. Making a beginning at Jerusalem, the city situated on Mount Sion (as Isaiah and Micah foretold in chapters 2 and 4), they announced that Christ—the Son of God, the Word, the Wisdom, the Power, and the Justice—had come to earth, conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of a virgin of the house of David, died on the cross, and had risen and ascended into heaven. From there he shall come as the Judge of the living and the dead. He whom the Israelite Church heard preaching on Mount Sinai, the whole world (as if contracted into a brief summary in Jerusalem) now hears preaching on Mount Sion through the Apostles, now clothed in the true flesh of man. In that multitude, which had flowed together from the entire world, each person heard the ambassadors of Christ speaking in their own ancestral and native language.

The first times of the Christian Church indeed required that miraculous and astounding work. This abundantly proves that the knowledge of languages is an instrument both useful and necessary for preserving and enlarging the Christian commonwealth, and is a gift of divine munificence that is by no means trivial. This is what the Apostle Paul teaches in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, and what the Church confesses in solemn prayer, praying in this manner: "Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful, and kindle in them the fire of your love. You, who through the diversity of all tongues, have gathered the nations into the unity of faith." <note>original: *Veni sancte spiritus...* A famous medieval Latin hymn (sequence) for Pentecost.</note> This is what must be sought first and foremost with holy vows from the heavenly Father, from whom proceeds whatever is rightly judged as good; and one must not despise the learning and instruction [of languages]...

„ ...keen study and diligent practice must be added. If these three come together and harmonize—even a moderate natural talent and a nature not entirely warped; then art and instruction; and finally use and practice—one will achieve a perfection in the knowledge of languages that no one would believe possible before trying it. This whole achievement must be firmly attributed to its Author [God], who granted the talent, the mind, the opportunity, the strength to endure the labor, and all things, to put it in a word. Whence we may rightly claim nothing for ourselves except the proper use of these gifts, if we strive so that the son of the Virgin Mary and of the living God—in whom dwells all the fullness of wisdom and divinity bodily <note>original Latin: *omnis plenitudo sapientiæ & diuinitatis corporaliter*—a reference to Colossians 2:9</note>—may be preached with a most clear voice among all nations, and being known, may be grasped with sincere faith, and expressed through holiness and all the duties of Christian charity. Thus, wisdom and true knowledge of things may be spread abroad, so that good laws may prevail, justice may flourish, and kind and holy peace and humanity may be established among men. What madness is this? What fury? That men—driven by Satan and an evil spirit to destroy one another, and that mostly over trivial matters—should use iron and countless instruments devised for the ruin of the human race? We possess reason, the maker of truly human and heavenly works; we possess speech, through which we may moderately handle matters and arguments among ourselves; we have the tongue, an excellent organ if it is suited to its proper end; we have the pen, the stylus, and paper, which fulfill the role of the tongue and speech. To these, let us bring the mutual wisdom of God, and let us accept what is offered with sincerity. For Christ shall be abundantly sufficient for all. He is able to enrich all, to bless all, to make all Kings and Priests—indeed, to make all co-heirs and not merely viceroys, but sharers of his eternal kingdom and children of God—and it is his sole desire that we receive this from him. > Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden. I will refresh you, and you will find rest for your souls. <note>Matthew 11:28</note>

„ There are also many other causes why languages, which were first separated at Babylon, tend to degenerate even further from their origin. Among these, the first is the mixing of different people and languages. This is exactly what happened in the variation of the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages, and many others. Regarding the Hebrew speakers, it was previously judged by Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> that they employ the idioms of almost all languages. Indeed, today we see that those who treat the Divine Scripture and the authors of the <term>Talmud</term> <note>The central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note> use the vocabulary of all nations. Indeed, even the speech of the <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Aramaic</note> interpreters, which is called the <term>Targum</term> <note>Aramaic translations or paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible</note>, such as those of Onkelos and Jonathan, contains a mixture of foreign words. Regarding the Greeks, it will suffice to provide one example here. When Solon, easily the prince of Greek philosophers, founded a city in Cilicia named after himself [Soli] and led an Athenian colony into it, those colonists gradually corrupted the purity of the Attic speech by mixing in other languages; for this reason, they were said to <term>solecize</term> <note>original Greek: *σολοικίζειν* (soloikizein)</note>. This name of <term>Solecism</term> was later transferred to mean any incorrectly constructed speech. Regarding the Latin language, Marcus Cicero hints at the same thing, writing thus about famous orators: "All in the time of Laelius and Scipio, who had neither lived outside the city nor been stained by any domestic barbarism, spoke correctly." However, the Latin language gradually admitted not only many Greek words, but also Gallic ones, such as *alauda* <note>lark</note> and *canthus* <note>the iron tire of a wheel</note>; and Spanish ones, such as *mastruca* <note>a sheepskin garment</note>; and British ones, such as *essedum* <note>a two-wheeled war chariot</note>; and indeed some words from all nations while they served as soldiers among them. Regarding this, Fabius [Quintilian] says in Book 1 of his *Institutes*, chapter 10: "Foreign words have come from almost every nation, just as men and many customs have also come." And again, the Latin...

» ...though most think [Greek] is more abundant, it is granted by Greece that the most learned men » might use unusual words for matters that are not common or well-known. That the names we use today—**Aleph**, » **Gimel**, **Daleth**—are also most ancient is gathered from **Origen**, **Jerome**, and other most ancient writers. » Furthermore, from the nomenclature of the **Greek** letters, » which use the same names with only slight deviations. # Languages of this Universe. 1001

...in their secret mysteries; they say it must not be revealed rashly to anyone. They also claim that the letters we use today were discovered and handed down by **Ezra** <note>original: *Esdra*; a biblical scribe and priest credited with reforming Jewish law and script after the Babylonian exile</note>. They possess a "celestial script" and a "script of the Angels," such as those described by **Cornelius Agrippa** <note>original: *Cornelius Agrippa li.3. de occulta philosophia*; a famous 16th-century German polymath and occultist</note> in the third book of his *Occult Philosophy*. To me, these appear to be the inventions of men devoted to magical delusions. However, because **Saint Jerome** <note>original: *D. Hieronymus*; a 4th-century scholar and translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> also believed that the ancient letters of the Hebrews were changed by Ezra—and this is accepted as a proven fact by great men—I will include one or two sayings of that supreme theologian. For in his *Commentary on Ezekiel*, chapter 8, he says: "Among the ancient Hebrew letters which the **Samaritans** <note>An ethno-religious group related to the Israelites who retained an older form of the script</note> still use today, the final letter **Thau** <note>The Hebrew letter *Tav*</note> has the likeness of a Cross." Furthermore, in the preface to the *History of Kings*, he notes: "That there are twenty-two letters among the Hebrews is also evidenced by the language of the **Syrians** and **Chaldeans** <note>Referring to Aramaic and related Semitic dialects</note>, which is largely similar to Hebrew; for they also have twenty-two elements with the same sound, but different characters." The Samaritans likewise write the **Pentateuch of Moses** <note>The first five books of the Bible</note> with the same number of letters, differing only in their shapes and strokes. It is certain that **Ezra the Scribe**, a teacher of the law, after the capture of Jerusalem and the restoration of the Temple under **Zerubbabel**, found other letters which we now use; whereas up until that time, the characters of the Samaritans and the Hebrews were the same. 

In the book of Numbers, this same calculation is shown mystically under the census of the Levites and Priests. We also find the name of the Lord, the **Tetragrammaton** <note>original: *tetragrammaton*; the four-letter name of God, YHWH, often considered too sacred to pronounce</note>, expressed in ancient letters in certain Greek volumes to this day. Moreover, Psalms 36, 110, 118, and 144, although written in different meters, are nevertheless woven with an alphabet of the same number. The **Lamentations of Jeremiah** <note>original: *Hieremiæ lamentationes*</note> and his prayer, as well as the Proverbs of **Solomon** at the end—from the place where he says, "Who shall find a brave woman?"—are calculated by those same alphabets or divisions. Furthermore, there are five double letters among the Hebrews: **Caph, Mem, Nun, Phe, Tzade**. For these are written one way at the beginning and middle of words, and another way at the end. Because of this, five books are considered "double" by many: **Samuel**, **Kings** <note>original: *Malachim*</note>, **Chronicles** <note>original: *Dibre Haiomim*</note>, **Ezra**, and **Jeremiah** with his **Lamentations** <note>original: *Cinoth*</note>. Therefore, just as there are twenty-two elements through which we write everything we speak in Hebrew, and the human voice is comprised by their beginnings, so twenty-two volumes are counted. By these "letters," as if they were beginnings in the doctrine of God, the tender and nursing infancy of the just man is educated. 

In these sayings of most learned men, it is established by several reasons that there are twenty-two elements of the Hebrews, which is entirely clear. To this, he asserts that the forms of the letters were changed by Ezra, and that five letters are marked with a double figure; finally, he also mentions the strokes <note>original: *apicum*; the small decorative crowns or points on Hebrew letters</note>. Regarding my own thoughts on these matters, and the reasoning that compels me to think so, I shall reveal them copiously in my *Commentaries on the Hebrew Language*. Indeed, I have also observed this variety in old and common writing: formerly, the remaining letters of a word were transposed from the end of a line to the beginning of the following line, just as is the custom among the **Arabs**. Today, however, if a line cannot contain the entire word, one or two letters are placed to fill the space, and the whole word is transferred to the head of the following line. Regarding the corrupted pronunciation of the Hebrew language, it shall be discussed in a more suitable place.

From the Hebrew letters, as we have already said several times, the public letters of all peoples and nations have been derived. For it would be an endless task to pursue those which men invent peculiarly for themselves, and it is granted to no man...

” in the number of letters, or their shape, or even their sound and power. First, I will

” which have a double state <note>original: *gemistatem*; likely referring to letters with two pronunciations, such as the plosive and fricative sounds</note> like Pe and Phe; to these I will add the Punic letters <note>The language of ancient Carthage, derived from Phoenician</note>, from which I believe
” the Greek letters were born, though the Greek names are more intact than the Punic.
” The order of the Alphabet, which the learned Arabs call *Abuget* <note>original: *Abuget*; the 'Abjad' order, which follows the ancient Northwest Semitic sequence Aleph, Beth, Gimel, Daleth</note>, is the same as the Hebrew;
” however, they have five additional letters, not in shape but in power:
” *Che, Dhel, Thad, Gaim* <note>Likely representing the Arabic letters Khah, Dhal, Dad, and Ghayn</note>, I will add these to the Hebrew ones to which they belong.
” I have shaped the Arabic characters as best I could, for I am not a good painter of letters;
” I consider it better to indicate in both ways that the Phoenician letters have flowed
” from the Hebrew, than to pass over that matter in total silence. There are therefore
” the best letters which most closely approach the Hebrew; I have also added the
” ancient letter of the Greeks, *Hetha* <note>The letter Eta</note>, which later writers assigned to the long vowel
” *Etha*, but which they originally used to mark the aspiration itself by placing a small mark
” [the rough breathing]. We have also added the *W* <note>original: *Vu*</note> of the Germans, which some nations
” use for F, or the consonant *Vau* <note>The Hebrew letter Vav, often functioning as a 'v' or 'w' sound</note>. First, therefore, the names are placed,
” [then] the shapes.

Languages of this Universe. 1003

Instead, they placed the letter V; according to Priscian <note>A 6th-century Latin grammarian</note>, citing Pliny, they have a double aspiration <note>breathing or 'h' sound</note>, one thin and one denser. The Arabs have a triple one, as do the Indians. They also have the unique letter *Shin*, which is more a syllable than a letter or basic element. For if, according to Aristotle, "Ge" is a syllable, why not also "Sch," "st," "ps," "gl," "ch," "gh," and "ph," and others similar to them? Likewise, what else are the letters *Zain* and *Tsade* in their power than "ds" and "ts"? The Germans also could have fulfilled the sound of the double *Vu* [W] or *bb* with the consonant *V*, just as the Hebrews do through *Vav*; and some Greeks used the *Digamma* <note>An archaic Greek letter (Ϝ) that represented the 'w' sound</note>, as in *Var* or *Vuar* [true], *Ventus* [wind], *Vend*, *Vuend*, *heu*, or *heuu*. But let us now touch upon several things regarding the Greeks and Latins in order, since there are many proofs that the ancient writing has been changed.

We previously indicated from Pliny that there were only sixteen Greek letters at the beginning, and that Palamedes <note>A legendary Greek hero</note> added four, and Simonides added another four. Plutarch testifies to the same. The order of the letters differs somewhat from the order of the Hebrew letters; for instance, *Theta* is placed earlier, and *Tau* in a later position. Indeed, the order is reversed among the Hebrew letters, because the Greek *Theta* (Θ) would correspond to the Hebrew *Tav*, and the Greek *Tau* to the Hebrew *Tet*. <note>The author is discussing the phonetic and sequential correspondence between the Greek 'T' sounds and their Hebrew ancestors.</note> Furthermore, proverbs testify that the ancients retained the order where *Alpha* held the first place and *Omega* the last, such as the expression "the *Alpha* of the cloaked ones" <note>original: *penulatorum Alpha*; a proverb referring to the first or most prominent of a group</note>. And in the Revelation of the Lord Christ it is said: "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end." Plutarch also explains with various reasons why *Alpha* is the first of the letters. The Greeks also denoted numbers with letters, which requires a firm and stable positioning of the alphabet; thus the 24 books of Homer, that most ancient poet, are arranged by letters, just as Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher</note> arranged his interpretation of the ancient sayings of Hippocrates and others.

However, Pliny and other reliable authors who remember the ancient letters judge that the shapes of the Greek characters have changed; and inscriptions of ancient memory testify to this very thing. For example, Terentius Scaurus <note>A Latin grammarian under Emperor Hadrian</note> writes concerning the letters *C* and *K*, saying: "I would contend that *C* is more superfluous than *K*; since *K*, as among the Greeks, sufficiently expresses the power of the letter *C*." But some were deceived by the shape, because this letter was used not only among us [Romans], but also among the ancient Greeks, as is shown by the Greek treaty inscribed on the bronze camel in Caesar’s gardens at the temple of Outer Fortune. The ancients wrote the aspiration <note>the 'h' sound</note> in the line of verse in the Latin manner, just as the Boeotians <note>People of a region in central Greece</note> used *muha* instead of *musa* <note>original: *muha pro musa*; showing the 's' becoming an 'h' sound</note>; later people divided this into two marks, the mark for the smooth breathing and the mark for the blowing or dense breathing, as Priscian also teaches in his first book. Scaurus also asserts that *h* is a letter and was written in verse by the Greeks, and that the inhabitants of Attica used it to mark *hecaton*, that is, one hundred.

We see this same mark today among the Greeks. In the improper diphthongs <note>Vowel combinations where the second vowel (iota) became silent over time</note>, they did not place a dot beneath the vowels *α*, *η*, *ω*, but placed it at the right side: *αı*, *ηı*, *ωı* <note>Known as the iota adscript, which preceded the iota subscript</note>. Nor did the ancient Greeks have so many diphthongs. They also did not mark the prosodies—the long, short, acute, grave, and circumflex accents and the rest—with signs as is done now. The most ancient monuments testify to this, such as the poems of Callimachus, which Angelo Poliziano <note>An Italian Renaissance humanist</note> places in the 80th chapter of his *Centuria*, introducing them with these words: "But now turn your ears to the verses of Callimachus..."

<margin>,,</margin> most necessary ones. After he had published a book about their reasoning while a private citizen,
<margin>,,</margin> he easily obtained their use once he became leader, so that
<margin>,,</margin> they were used commonly. Such writing exists in many books and on

<margin>,,</margin> double letters were added by the Greeks. Furthermore, the order was established by the
<margin>,,</margin> ancients so that **a** is placed first, then **b**, then **c**, then **d**, and following
<margin>,,</margin> this manner all the way to **z**; the books of the ancients indicate this order
<margin>,,</margin> following the sequence, such as those of **Nonius Marcellus** and **Pompeius Festus**, which I mentioned before.

Master Jean Bodin <note>A prominent French jurist and political philosopher (1530–1596)</note>, in chapter 7 of his *Method of History*, speaking of the **cycle of change** <note>original: "vicissitudine"</note> of things, says:

> Not only do virtues exist in the people of our time, but branches of knowledge <note>original: "disciplinae"</note> equal to those of the ancients have also appeared. For literature too has its own cycle of change, so that first, in certain places, arts arise through the experience and labor of talented men; then they receive growth; after a while they flourish in their prime; at last they languish in old age; finally they gradually die out and are buried in long-lasting oblivion: either by the long-lasting calamity of wars, or because an excessive abundance (an evil greatly to be feared in these times) is accustomed to bring boredom to every frivolous person, or because a just God exacts punishment from those who turn beneficial sciences to the destruction of mankind. For when the disciplines among the Greeks had gradually matured so that they were believed to have reached their peak, such a great change followed afterward that it seems as if even Greece itself, where it now stands, never existed. What of the Latins <note>the Romans</note>, among whom there was such a wealth of talent that at almost the same time they surpassed all peoples in military glory and the excellence of all disciplines: yet by a similar fate they began to slide back into their former barbarism when the **Scythian forces** <note>Bodin uses this term to refer to the Germanic and Gothic tribes that invaded Rome</note> flowing into Italy burned the most well-stocked libraries and almost all the monuments of antiquity everywhere. This monstrous act caused such ruin in all disciplines that they lay prostrate for about a thousand years without any value and seemed destined to perish, unless **Al-Mansur** <note>original: "Mensor," likely referring to the Abbasid Caliph Al-Mansur or a general association with the Islamic "Golden Age" in Al-Andalus/Spain</note>, Prince of Africa and Spain, had excited the talents of the Arabs with great rewards offered for the **Restoration** <note>original: "Instaurationem"</note> of letters. I pass over how many philosophers, geometers, and astrologers Egypt, India, and Ethiopia produced, or how many noble mathematicians there were among the Chaldeans before there was any literacy in Greece. I return to our own times, in which—long after letters had gone silent across almost the entire world—such a great splendor of all the sciences suddenly shone forth, and such a fertility of talents emerged, that it has been greater than in any previous age. And even the **Goths** <note>the Northern/Scandinavian peoples</note> themselves have not lacked most excellent talents recently, as witnessed by Olaus Magnus <note>A Swedish historian and cartographer</note>, witnessed by Holsterus <note>likely Lucas Holstenius, a German humanist scholar</note>, and witnessed by many others—as if nature had decreed that the wounds of the sciences should now be healed by the very ones by whom they were once inflicted. For while in a previous age they still kept the custom of their ancestors and ordered learned men to leave the Senate at the voice of a herald (for so we have it recorded in their history), they are now accustomed to summon letters from everywhere. This is that so certain **Revolution** <note>original: "Conversio," referring to a turning point or cyclical return</note> of all things, so that no one ought to doubt that the same thing happens in the minds of men as in the fields, which are accustomed to return the favor of rest with greater fertility. "But those ancients," someone will say, "were the inventors of the arts; to them the glory is due." Indeed, they discovered many disciplines beneficial to the human race: and especially the power of celestial things and the fixed paths of the orbits—though not all the wondrous paths of the **fixed stars** <note>original: "stellarum inerrantium"</note> and those called **wandering stars** <note>original: "vagae," i.e., planets</note>. Then they diligently noted the obscurity of nature and accurately explained many things; yet they left most of them imperfect, which are now being handed down to posterity as completed by our own people. And it can be a doubt to no one who looks deeply into the matter that most of the discoveries of our people should be compared with, and even preferred to, the discoveries of the ancestors. For while nothing in the whole nature of things is more marvelous than the **magnet** <note>original: "magnete," referring to the compass</note>, yet its use...

### History of the Origin of [Things]

>> The ancients were clearly ignorant of its divine power. While they contained themselves within the **Mediterranean basin**, our people every year circle the globe with frequent voyages and lead colonies into another world, so to speak, so that we now have the innermost recesses of **India** <note>In this period, "India" often referred generally to the East Indies or the Americas ("The West Indies").</note> opened to us. From this, not only has trade (which was previously base or not sufficiently known) become abundant and profitable, but also all men wonderfully harmonize with themselves and with the **world republic**, as if living in the same city.

>> How much growth one of the most beautiful arts, **Geography**, has received can be understood from this: things concerning India that seemed like fables to most people—for **Lactantius** and **Augustine** <note>Lactantius (c. 250–325) and St. Augustine (354–430) were influential early Christian authors who famously rejected the idea that people could live on the opposite side of the spherical Earth.</note> say those who believe in the existence of the **antipodes** <note>original: "antichthonas"; people living on the opposite side of the earth</note> are insane—have been proven true by us. 

>> Then there are the movements of the fixed stars and the "trepidation" <note>An astronomical theory of the time regarding the oscillation of the equinoxes.</note> of the great celestial sphere. But what is more admirable than that **abstraction** <note>original: "ἀφαιρέσει" (aphairesei); a Greek philosophical term for the mental process of isolating a form from its material substance</note> of forms from matter, so to speak? From this, the hidden secrets of nature are unlocked. I pass over the method of investigating celestial longitude by means of **equal hours** <note>A reference to the development of more accurate mechanical clocks.</note>, which could not be judged by the ancients from the rule of eclipses without great error. 

>> I pass over the **catapults** of the ancients and the old engines of war, which, if compared with ours <note>Likely referring to the invention of gunpowder and cannons.</note>, can truly seem like certain childish playthings. Finally, I pass over the infinite arts, whether in craftsmanship, or in **wool-working** and **silk-making**, by which human life is aided in a wonderful manner. **The Art of Printing** <note>original: "Typographia"</note> alone can easily compete with all the inventions of all the ancients. 

>> Therefore, those who say that everything was understood by the ancients err no less than those who would strip the ancients of their old possession of many arts. **Nature** possesses innumerable treasures of knowledge, which can be exhausted by no span of ages. Since these things are so, and since by a certain eternal law of nature, the **cycle of all things** <note>original: "Conversio rerum omnium"</note> seems to return as if in a circle—so that vices follow virtues, ignorance follows knowledge, and the base follows the honorable just as darkness follows light—those who think the human race is always becoming worse than itself are mistaken. 

>> And since old men are in that error, it is believable that this happens to them because they remember the flower of their youth (which by itself breathes joy and pleasantness) as lost. When they see themselves deserted by every kind of pleasure, and feel the most bitter pains instead of delights, and the weakness of all their limbs instead of healthy senses, they are overwhelmed by the saddest thoughts. Deceived by a false image of things, they think that faith and friendship among men have perished. 

>> Just as if they had set out on a long voyage, they tell the young of "Golden Ages" and a "Golden Era"; but it happens to them just as it does to those who, when they are carried out from the harbor into the deep sea, think that the houses and cities are moving away. So these men think that delight, humanity, and justice are flying away into heaven and abandoning the earth.

The same author in chapter 8, having clearly verified through several arguments and authorities that the first languages of the world were **Hebrew** and **Chaldaic** <note>A term formerly used to describe Aramaic.</note>, and that from them proceeded **Greek**, and from Greek the **Latin**, and so with the others, continues with the words that follow in chapter 9:

>> But **mutations of languages** are usually brought about by three principal causes (I pass over the one brought by Moses <note>The biblical story of the Tower of Babel.</note>, which happened all at once). One is in the very passage of time, in which not only languages but all things are changed, and the whole nature of things grows old. Thus **Polybius** <note>A Greek historian of the Hellenistic period.</note> writes that less than fifty years after the treaty was struck between the **Carthaginians** <note>original: "Poenos"</note> and the Romans, the words of the treaty, which he himself calls "ancient," could scarcely be understood.

<summary>In this passage, Jean Bodin argues for the superiority of modern discoveries like printing and global navigation over ancient knowledge, while explaining that the perception of societal decay is often a psychological trick of aging.</summary>

# Languages of this Universe.

cc
...could [be understood]; indeed, songs that were prescribed in sacred rites according to ancient formulas were understood by very few. Thus we see that gradually all languages of all peoples change in one way or another. Another cause lies in the mixing of colonies and peoples among themselves. Let Italy and Greece be the proof, which for so many centuries maintained the purity of the Greek and Latin speech and spread it throughout the whole world; after the **Scythians** and **Goths** <note>Groups of migratory Germanic and nomadic peoples whose incursions were central to the fall of the Western Roman Empire.</note> invaded both, such a great change followed that it seems neither Latin nor **Attic** [Greek] ever existed where they are now. Likewise, the colonies of the **Tuscans** <note>Etruscans</note>, who were driven out of Italy by the Gauls, and of the Gauls who once migrated into the formerly deserted lands of Germany, forged a third type of speaking different from both. Also, the colonies of the English led into **Britain** and the Saxons into **Belgium** by **Charles the Great** <note>Charlemagne (r. 768–814), whom Bodin credits with significant population movements.</note>, as well as the Gauls into Saxony, produced a variety of speech. Similarly, the **Parthians** corrupted the Persian tongue; the **Arabs**, the Punic and Parthian; the **Turks**, **Tartars**, and **Slavs**, the Greek; while the Latins corrupted the Gallic and Spanish speech. cc

cc
The final cause for changing a language lies in the nature of the region itself: for it is characteristic of all peoples who lean more toward the North to utter words with the harshest clashing of consonants, or with vowels from the depths of the chest and frequent **aspirations** <note>The act of breathing out while speaking, such as the 'h' sound.</note>. This is due to the great force of the spirits and the impulse of heat; for the Saxons and those living near the Baltic Sea almost everywhere pronounce middle consonants instead of thin ones and aspirated ones instead of middle ones. Such as these: *by the wild god, we perish [drinking] good wine* <note>original: "per theum ferum, perimus ponum finum." This is a phonetic joke about a Germanic accent: "theum" for "deum" (god), "ferum" for "verum" (true), "ponum" for "bonum" (good), and "finum" for "vinum" (wine).</note>. Southerners, however, whose heat is tempered and spirit weak, pronounce most softly—women even more softly, because they have weaker spirit and heat than men. And this is easily understood in the colony of Saxons whom Charles the Great led among the Belgians. For while the Saxons call a horse *Pferd*, the Flemings, raised in a milder climate, pronounce it *Pert*. I omit the specific and innate nature of each place derived from its waters, which change voices and languages, as in the Labdanum field of Narbonese Gaul <note>Southern France</note> where everyone stammers with <term>Labdacism</term> <note>A speech trait or "defect" involving the heavy use or "stuttering" of the letter L.</note>; and in Valedoca of the **Taurini** <note>People of the region around modern Turin, Italy.</note>. Likewise, the ancient **Sabines** used to say *foedum* for *haedum* [a kid goat], and *fircum* for *hircum* [a he-goat], as **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), a Roman scholar and grammarian.</note> writes; just as among us the **Basques** say *hocum* for *focum* [hearth/fire], and *hilium* for *filium* [son]. So too the Parisians and Orleanese, in the manner of the ancient Etruscans, use *Valesium* and *Fusium* for *Valerius* and *Furius*. cc

cc
From these three primary causes, therefore, the dissimilarities of so many languages arise; yet they cannot be so completely abolished that they do not perpetually retain clear traces of the old language. The ancient **Celtic** language was Greek in its large part, because our ancestors drew their origin from them. **Bovelles**, **Picard**, and **Périon** <note>Charles de Bovelles, Jean Picard, and Joachim Périon were 16th-century scholars who attempted to prove that the French language was directly descended from Greek.</note> have extracted almost infinite words—though not all—not with difficulty or violence as **Lazius** <note>Wolfgang Lazius (1514–1565), a scholar who attempted to find Germanic origins for many ancient names.</note> did in his own language, but through very easy and sometimes no transformation from Greek sources. In these, however, there does not seem to me to be as much weight and importance as in the idioms themselves, which are common to us and the Greeks; and also in the elegant use of participles, infinitives, and articles. This sufficiently argues that the origin of the Gauls is owed to the **Trojans**, or the **Greeks**, or both, since both used the **Ionic** tongue. cc

cc
**Louis Le Roy**, in Book 1 of *On the Vicissitude or Variety of Things*, in the chapter on the vicissitude and variety of languages, discourses most excellently in this way: "Similarly, languages, words, writings, and characters change continually, being of no better condition than other human things..." <note>original: "Louys le Roy liur. 1. de la viciſſitude des choſes chap: de la viciſſitude & varieté des langues..." Louis Le Roy (c. 1510–1577) was a contemporary of Bodin who wrote extensively on universal history and the progress of civilization.</note> cc

# Languages of this Universe

<margin>cc</margin> ...could be understood; indeed, the songs that were preserved in sacred rites according to the old formula were understood by only a very few. Thus, we see that little by little, the languages of all peoples are altered in various ways. The second cause of this change lies in the mixing of colonies and populations. A clear proof is **Italy** and **Greece**, which for so many centuries maintained the purity of the **Greek** and **Latin** tongues and spread them throughout the whole world; yet, after the **Scythians** and **Goths** invaded both lands, such a great change followed that it seems as if neither Latin nor **Attic Greek** <note>The prestigious dialect of ancient Athens.</note> ever existed in the places where they are now spoken. Similarly, the colonies of the **Tuscans** <note>Etruscans</note> (who were driven out of Italy by the Gauls) and the **Gauls** (who once migrated into the deserted parts of Germany) produced a third type of speaking, distinct from both original sources. So too, the colonies of the **Angles** brought into **Britain** and the **Saxons** into **Belgium** <note>The Low Countries</note> by **Charlemagne**, as well as the migration of Gauls into **Saxony**, gave birth to a variety of speech. In a similar way, the **Parthians** corrupted the **Persian** tongue; the **Arabs** corrupted **Punic** <note>The language of ancient Carthage</note> and **Parthian**; and the **Turks**, **Tartars**, and **Slavs** corrupted **Greek**, just as the **Latins** corrupted **French** and **Spanish** speech.

<margin>cc</margin> The final cause for a language changing is found in the very nature of the region itself. For it is characteristic of all peoples who live further toward the **North** to produce sounds with a very harsh clashing of consonants, or with vowels drawn from deep in the chest, and frequent aspirations <note>Breathy 'h' sounds</note>. This is due to the great force of their spirits and the inward rush of heat. Indeed, the **Saxons** and those living near the **Baltic Sea** almost everywhere pronounce medial consonants as thin ones, and aspirated sounds for medials. <note>original: "per theum ferum, perimus ponum finum"; likely illustrating a phonetic shift where 'd' becomes 'th', 'b' becomes 'f', etc.</note> Conversely, **Southerners**, whose heat is tempered and whose spirit is weaker, pronounce words very softly—women even more softly, because they have weaker spirit and heat than men. This is easily understood in the colony of Saxons that **Charlemagne** led into the land of the **Belgians**. For while the Saxons call a horse a *Pfert*, the **Flemings**, raised under a milder sky, pronounce it *Pert*. I will pass over the inherent nature of each place’s water, which can alter voices and tongues; for instance, in the **Labdano** district of **Narbonnese Gaul** <note>Southern France</note>, everyone stutters with **Labdacism** <note>original: "Labdacismo"; a speech error involving the letter 'L'</note>, and similarly in **Valedoca** among the people of **Turin**. So too, the ancient **Sabines** used to say *fœdum* for *hœdo* <note>a young goat</note> and *fircum* for *hirco* <note>a male goat</note>, as **Varro** <note>A Roman scholar and writer (116–27 BCE)</note> writes; just as among our own **Gascons**, they say *hocum* for *foco* <note>fire</note> and *hilium* for *filio* <note>son</note>. Likewise, the people of **Paris** and **Orléans**, following the custom of the ancient **Etruscans**, use *Valesium* and *Fusium* instead of *Valerius* and *Furius* <note>Substituting 's' for 'r'</note>.

<margin>cc</margin> From these three primary causes, therefore, so many differences in languages arise. Yet they can never be so completely abolished that they do not permanently retain clear traces of the old language. For example, the ancient **Celtic** language was largely **Greek**, because our ancestors drew their origin from them. **Bovillus**, **Picartus**, and **Perionius** <note>Charles de Bovelles, Jean Picart, and Joachim Périon: 16th-century scholars who attempted to prove French descended from Greek.</note> have extracted nearly infinite words—though not all—from Greek sources; they did this not with difficulty or violence (as **Lasius** does in his own language), but through very easy, and sometimes no, transformation. However, there does not seem to me to be as much weight and importance in the words themselves as there is in the actual modes of expression which we have in common with the Greeks. This is also seen in the elegant use of participles, infinitives, and articles, which sufficiently prove that the origin of the **Gauls** <note>The French</note> is owed to the **Trojans**, or the **Greeks**, or both, since both used the **Ionic** language.

# Languages of this World:

This same author maintains that languages acquire a reputation through their [unique] properties, elegance, and sweetness; through the sciences that are written in them; through the power and greatness of Empire; and through religions. By these means, they are extended into many countries and last a long time, just as they are lost and annihilated by their opposites—which he clearly proves through the Greek and Latin languages, among others.

Then he continues to say,

> If languages are of no better condition than other human things, then just as buildings, clothing, manners, customs, laws, magistrates, and public and private ways of living, weapons, machines, and instruments change, so too do words and languages. They perish in the long run, leaving no trace of their writing over the passage of time. We have no knowledge of the Oscan <note>An ancient Indo-European language of Southern Italy that became extinct by the 1st century AD.</note> or Etruscan <note>The language of the Etruscan civilization in ancient Italy, which remains only partially understood today.</note> languages. The Romance or Provençal tongue <note>The vernacular "Romance" languages, specifically the Occitan language of Southern France, which was the language of the Troubadours.</note>, once celebrated by noble writers, is no longer understood by the Provençals of today; the ancient Gaulish, Spanish, Persian, and Punic <note>The language of ancient Carthage.</note> tongues are lost.
> 
> Now, languages, like all human things, have a beginning, progress, perfection, corruption, and end. They are at first crude, then they become polished along with the civility of manners and knowledge; and after having lasted some time in purity and elegance, they are corrupted and finally perish, leaving no trace of their writing over the passage of time.
> 
> The Greeks were very coarse at the beginning, as Thucydides, Plato, and Aristotle say. The first among them to become civilized were the Athenians, who polished their language and brought it to perfection, where it did not remain for long. Thus it was corrupted and lost along with the liberty of the country, supplanted by the Macedonians, Romans, and other foreigners who ruled there. To such an extent that never since could the natural property and true elegance spoken by Plato, Aristotle, Isocrates, Demosthenes, and Aeschines <note>Prominent Athenian philosophers and orators representing the "Golden Age" of Greek prose.</note> be restored; instead of that language, which one could say was the most beautiful in the world, there came in the long run another used presently in Greece and the neighboring islands, mixed with several other languages. This one is likewise being lost under the Turkish Empire <note>Referring to the Ottoman Empire's rule over Greece, which began in the mid-15th century.</note>, where the country has remained miserably oppressed for more than a hundred years.
> 
> If the first Roman writings lasted until now, we would see that Evander and Turnus <note>Legendary figures from the early history of Italy and the founding of Rome, featured in Virgil's Aeneid.</note> and the other Latins of that time spoke differently than the later Roman kings and the first consuls did afterward. The verses sung by the Salian priests <note>The Salii were "leaping priests" of Mars whose ancient hymns, the *Carmen Saliare*, were so archaic they were barely understood by Romans of the classical era.</note> were hardly understood. But because they had been so ordained by the first founders, they were not changed out of reverence for religion. Polybius <note>A Greek historian of the Hellenistic period who chronicled the rise of the Roman Republic.</note> writes that this language was so changed between the first Punic War and the second that the treaties made previously between the Romans and Carthaginians were understood with great difficulty. And it remained crude for about 500 years, having no writer worthy of memory. From then on, people applied themselves to letters, and some became learned, though still harsh in their speech, praised only for

all things in this universe, all languages and scripts shift and

names. In fact, these languages first have an origin and
beginning, then perfection and duration, then corruption, alteration,
