### Language of this Universe

...armies using and speaking diverse and dissimilar languages, who, meeting and communicating often together, perpetually form new words that last or fail according to whether they are commonly received or rejected by the speakers themselves. This same thing also happens through the power and force of certain peoples and nations, who, having conquered others and having thereby established and constituted a new Monarchy, Empire, Kingdom, or Principality, try to lose and extinguish entirely the natural and mother tongue of the others in order to introduce their own; just as the Greeks, Latins, and Romans did in ancient times to the languages of several peoples and nations they had brought under the force of their arms. And like the Saracens <note>A medieval term used to describe Arabs or Muslims.</note>, who, extending their language through arms along with their religion, came to destroy the Persian language and other languages of Asia, burning—by the command of their Caliphs—the books that were written in them, judging that the Persians and other Asians, deprived of their own particular books, would more easily yield to the Muhammadan superstition <note>The author uses "superstition Mahometane" reflecting the common Christian perspective of the era; this refers to the Islamic faith.</note>. Then, passing into Egypt, they exterminated the Greek language with its disciplines from Alexandria, and the Latin language from Africa, just as the Latins or Romans before them had done to the African language and its letters.

Therefore, it is a certain thing that peoples and nations passing from country to country, and from region to region, change and mutate languages and letters, together with the customs and ways of doing things of other peoples and nations: just as we see the Turks have done for some time now over the Christians, and formerly the Goths, Visigoths, Alans, Huns, Vandals, Suebi, Heruli, Bulgars, Lombards, and others. These groups, conquering countries and regions at various times, disdained the languages there because they did not understand them nor know how to read them; they corrupted, mutated, and changed them, making new ones by the mixture of their own and those they found. This was because the poor people remaining after such changes and mutations were constrained and forced to learn the language of the cruel and inhuman conquerors and usurpers, in order to use it with them and make themselves more agreeable subjects.

Furthermore, these barbarians, relating everything to war with a great contempt and disdain for science and letters, burned all the books that were in the libraries, so much so that a great ignorance came upon the world for some time. This caused the "Vulgar" <note>The common spoken form of a language, as opposed to the "Grammatical" or literary form.</note> to proceed from Grammatical Greek; and from Latin, Italian, together with the French and Spanish of today, in which are found several Saracenic and Arabic words because of the long occupation of the Spains by the Saracens and Arabs; and from the Grammatical Arabic language, the Vulgar Turkish and Moorish.

Moreover, as the Roman Empire began to decline in the West, and as the Ostrogoths and Lombards had occupied Italy, the Visigoths and Saracens [had occupied] Provence, Languedoc, Aquitaine, and Spain, and the Burgundians...

# History of the Origin of...

...and the Franks <note>original: "Françoys"</note> in Belgic and Celtic Gaul; through their interaction, the Latin language was altered and corrupted. From this corruption proceeded mainly the Italian, French, and Spanish languages. Similarly, it happens that many peoples and nations, out of a certain envy and rivalry, try to alter, change, and corrupt the ancient and original languages of others during times of war. They do this so that by this disguise they can make posterity believe they retain nothing from their masters and predecessors. This is what the Chaldeans did to the language of the Hebrews; the Syrians and Arabs—coming long after—did to the same language; the Armenians to that of the Chaldeans; the Greeks to the Samaritan, Assyrian, or Phoenician; the Romans and Slavs to that of the Greeks; and the Goths, Lombards, Germans, Franks, Spanish, and others to that of the Romans.

Sometimes it also happens that certain learned and scholarly individuals, desiring in their own century to enrich, illustrate, and embellish their mother tongues, take delight in imitating the most eloquent and silver-tongued ancient and modern authors of other languages—be they more delicate or better-spoken—in their own writings. Or, they have invented terms themselves, as properly and elegantly as they could, which they have rendered and made their own and natural. This is what Dante, Cino <note>Likely Cino da Pistoia (c. 1270–1336), a famous Italian poet and jurist.</note>, Petrarch, Boccaccio, Ariosto, and other modern Italians have done for their Italian language; Guevara, Boscán, Garcilaso de la Vega, <note>Luis de</note> Granada, and Montemayor <note>Jorge de Montemayor, author of "Diana".</note> for the Spanish language; and Ronsard, Jodelle, Du Bellay, Belleau, Amyot, Vigenère <note>Prominent poets of the Pléiade and renowned translators of the French Renaissance.</note> and other Frenchmen for our French language.

But whatever one may say of these alterations and mutations of languages in general or in particular, they must be referred or attributed to three principal causes:

The first is that languages follow the fatal course and order of nature, which governs all things in this Universe. After having been heard, visited, and practiced for some time, they come, in the length of time and years, to wither and diminish—just as has happened to infinite languages that were in use since the beginning of the World, which are now entirely lost and forgotten.

The second is that the confusion and multiplicity of colonies and populations of diverse nations and languages—who have gone from country to country and region to region of other languages where they assembled and mixed together—have created, do create, and always cause another species of language or a "third kind," beyond either of those that were natural or native to them. Such was the case with the Northern peoples <note>original: "peuples Septentrionaux"</note> who, coming into these countries, completely ended the pure Greek and Latin languages by introducing a certain <term>Barragoin|A historical term for gibberish or a corrupted, unintelligible jargon, often used to describe the hybrid languages formed during the barbarian invasions.</term> that was entirely confused and lasted for some time.

The third and final cause is that the region and the air of certain places produce this effect; just as the peoples who live closest to the North <note>original: "Septentrion"</note> are accustomed by their nature...

# Languages of this Universe

...pronounce their words very roughly and harshly with a great quantity of consonants, being almost unable to express the vowels. This is due to the great force and impetuosity of their internal heat, which causes them in the end to corrupt the proper words of languages, turning them into something rough and unpolished. These forms eventually gain currency and popularity until they form an entire language. For the Air and the Waters are sometimes such that they can shift and change voices and languages, just as we see an infinite number of peoples and nations today who cannot pronounce their words properly except by stuttering; others cannot express several consonants, and others several vowels. 

For the reasons and circumstances mentioned above, the characters <note>Writing systems or alphabets</note> of languages are found to be entirely diverse and dissimilar. Those of the Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Syrians—numbering twenty-two—are all different in the shapes of their letters and their points <note>Original: "poinctz"; likely referring to vowel markings or diacritics</note>, as I have demonstrated previously. Those of the ancient Phoenicians, numbering twenty-four, do not correspond to any of the others mentioned above. Those of the Arabs, numbering thirty-one, are completely different from those of other nations. Those of the Greeks, numbering twenty-four, are made in other various fashions; those of the Latins, numbering twenty-two, have other forms. Those of the Armenians, numbering thirty-eight; those of the Slavs and Jacobites <note>Members of the West Syriac Church</note>, numbering thirty-two; those of the Abyssinians <note>Ethiopians</note> and Ethiopians, numbering twenty-seven; and those of the Japanese, numbering forty-seven, have nothing alike or approaching one another when viewed plainly.

These Hebrews, Chaldeans, Syrians, Arabs, and generally the Asians and Africans write from right to left, saying that in this they imitate the daily movement of the Heavens which moves from right to left, and is most perfect according to the Philosophers. On the contrary, the Greeks, Latins, Slavs, Armenians, Abyssinians and Ethiopians, Indians of Malabar, and other Europeans write from the left side to the right. The Indians, Cathayans <note>People of Cathay, an old name for China</note>, Chinese, Japanese, Brahmans <note>The priestly caste of India</note>, and Gymnosophists <note>Original: "Gymnosophistes"; ancient Indian philosophers known for their asceticism and nudity</note> write from top to bottom, saying that in this they follow the order of nature, which gave men their head high and their feet low, as I have clearly demonstrated before. See what is written on this matter by H. Cardan <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian Renaissance polymath</note> in the twelfth book of his *On Subtlety* <note>Original: "de sa subtilité"</note>, and the seventeenth book, ninety-fifth chapter of *On the Variety of Things* <note>Original: "de la varieté des choses"</note>; Leo Africanus <note>Original: "Iean Leon", the famous Moorish traveler and author</note> in the first book of his *Description of Africa*; G. Collange <note>Gabriel de Collange, who translated the work of Trithemius</note> in the second book of the *Polygraphy* of Abbot Trithemius; and Lord Fauchet <note>Claude Fauchet (1530–1601), a French historian</note> in his collection on the origin of the French language and poetry.

A great poet of this time has written the following verses on this subject:

> *All language changes, whether it be that commerce,*

# History of the Origin of [Languages]

Give currency to defaced names, and restore to nature
*Those that are outdated, moldy, and eaten by worms.*
*It is just like the leaves of a forest:*
*One falls, another is born; those words which in other times*
*Shone here and there in eloquent speech*
*Like lilies in the green countryside,*
*Are no longer in fashion, but banished from the Court,*
*Dwell ashamed beneath the roofs of a humble hamlet;*
*And those which the grumpy censure of old times*
*Had scrapped as debased currency <note>Original: "mis au billon." This refers to taking coins out of circulation due to low value; here it is a metaphor for obsolete words.</note>, are now in circulation.*
*A fine wit, led by luck and judgment,*
*Can give a passport to words that freshly*
*Come out of his workshop, adopt foreign ones,*
*Graft the wild shoots, making by these mixtures*
*His speech richer, and with a diverse enamel*
*Variegating <note>Original: "Riolant." To decorate with various colors.</note> his speech, whether prose or verse.*
*One language has no other law than usage,*
*Running without a bridle, without eyes, where the fickle people*
*Go rushing headlong; the other, walking enclosed*
*Within the bounds of art, arranges its words well.*
*One, already aging at the door of its infancy,*
*Has verse for its tomb; the other offers resistance*
*To the threads of the years; one lives unfortunate,*
*Confined forever in a narrow valley,*
*The other makes itself heard boldly among scholars*
*From the shores of Fez to the altar of Alexander <note>Likely referring to the widespread reach of classical languages from North Africa to the limits of Alexander the Great's empire.</note>.*
*Such today are Hebrew, Greek, and Latin:*
*Hebrew, insofar as we still hold from its hand*
*The sacred word of the Thrice-Eternal <note>A reference to God.</note>,*
*And because it is the record of Divine Right;*
*Greek, as having in its learned writings*
*Every kind of knowledge eloquently comprised;*
*And the masculine Latin, because its eloquence*
*Was planted by the sword in all corners of the world.*

# Languages of this World.

## On the sounds, voices, noises, languages, or tongues of Animals and Birds.

### CHAPTER LXXXIX.

Latin authors attributed very specific and appropriate names and verbs to the majority of animal sounds, voices, noises, or languages. They said that Bulls low <note>original: "mugire"</note>; Titus Livy <note>A famous Roman historian</note> writes on this subject: *when some driven cattle lowed for those they had left behind*; and the poet Virgil in the second book of the *Georgics*: *And the lowing of the Cattle.* Donkeys bray <note>original: "rudere"</note>; the poet Ovid in the third book of *The Art of Love*:
->*As the ugly she-ass brays by the rough millstone.*<-
And in the first book of the *Fasti*:
->*Behold the braying Ass, carrier of Silenus, with a hoarse voice.*<-
Lions roar or growl <note>original: "rugire, ou fremere"</note>; as the author of the *Philomela* <note>A poem often attributed to Ovid or Albus Ovidius Juventinus about animal sounds</note> says:
->*Untamed tigers snarl, and lions roar.*<-
Diomedes in book 1, and Nonius, interpreting that ancient verb *Grundire* to mean to grunt <note>original: "grunnire"</note>, cite the words of Quintus Quadrigarius <note>An early Roman historian</note>:
> *The swine-herd grunted heavily, the whinnying mares scattering the earth with their hooves; the asses bray, the dogs snarl, the chicks chirp, the bulls low, the lions roar.*
Marcus Varro <note>A prolific Roman scholar known as "the most learned of the Romans"</note> in a certain place in his works says:
> *The pig, full of sweet milk and slaughtered for the mill, grunts; the ox lows; the sheep bleats; the horses whinny; the hen chirps.*
The learned Joseph Scaliger <note>A 16th-century French religious scholar and leader in modern historical chronology</note> in his commentaries on the sixth book of Marcus Varro speaks very well on this matter. These same Latin writers further said that dogs bark <note>original: "latrare"</note>, foxes snarl <note>original: "gannire"</note>, camels grumble <note>original: "blaterare"</note>, elephants trumpet <note>original: "barrire"</note>, boars gnash their teeth <note>original: "frendere"</note>, leopards growl <note>original: "fremere"</note>, bears groan <note>original: "gemere"</note>, ewes bleat <note>original: "balare"</note>, geese cackle <note>original: "strepere"</note>, ravens croak <note>original: "crocitare"</note>, storks clatter <note>original: "crepitare"</note>, and cicadas buzz <note>original: "stridere"</note>. The poet Ausonius in his 75th Epigram says:
> *You mimic the barking of puppies, the whinnying of horses,*
> *And the goat-born flock; you imitate the wool-bearing herds*
> *With their bleating; one would say you bray like asses*
> *When you wish, Marcus, to mimic the Arcadian beast.*
> *The songs of roosters, and the ravens rejoicing in their throats,*
> *And whatever voices such a beast has.*
> *Though you mimic all things so truly that they seem not feigned,*
> *You cannot possess the sound of a human voice.*
The author of the *Philomela*, who is said to be the same poet Ovid, writes:
> *Come, sweet friend, providing the comforts of the night,*
> *For among the birds none is like you,*
> *You, Philomela <note>The poetic name for the Nightingale</note>, can produce a thousand different voices,*
> *You yourself can render a thousand various melodies.*

For although other birds attempt their melodies,
None can equal your measures. <note>The poet is addressing the Nightingale, known in Latin as Philomela.</note>
Moreover, it is the way of birds to chatter during the day;
But you can sing at once by night and day.
For even if the Titmouse <note>original: "Parus"</note> tinkles through the whole night,
Its voice can rightly please no one.
The Thrush <note>original: "Palara" or "Drosta"</note> sounds sweet,
But as the day flees, it falls silent in peace.
The Blackbird <note>original: "Merulus"</note> modulates and sings with such beautiful odes,
Yet as night falls, it sings no songs.
In the warmth of spring, the Owl <note>original: "Acredula"; sometimes identified as a reed-warbler or a cicada in classical texts, but here grouped with birds</note> composes new songs,
Though its voice falters in the morning hour.
While the Thrush chirps, the Starling <note>original: "Sturnus"</note> peeps with its mouth;
But what they sing in the morning, they do not remember in the evening.
Here the Partridge <note>original: "Perdix"</note> cackles, there the greedy Goose cackles,
And the chaste Turtle-dove and the Dove moan.
The Wood-pigeon claps its wings, crying from the leafy branch,
And the Duck swimming in the rivers perhaps quacks. <note>original: "tetrinnit"</note>
The Crane cries, and in groups the Swans trumpet <note>original: "drensant"</note> near the rivers,
The Hawk chirps, and the Kite, gaping, cries out.
The Rooster is accustomed to crowing, the Hen cackles;
The Peacock cries, the wandering Swallow twitters.
While Eagles scream, the Vulture is said to grunt. <note>original: "pulpare"</note>
The Crow croaks, but the Jackdaw screeches.
The Stork clatters with its great beak from the tower,
But the lowly Sparrow chirps sadly as if weeping.
The Parrot brings forth human speech with its voice,
And says to its master "Greetings" <note>original: "χαῖρε" (chaire)</note> or "Farewell."
The loquacious Magpie modulates various voices in its throat,
And mockingly mimics whatever noise it hears.
The Cuckoos call "cuckoo," the hoarse Cicada chirps.
The Bee buzzes with its mouth while gathering the gifts of honey.
The Horned Owl hoots dreadfully with a funereal song,
Bringing sad fates to the human race.
The screeching Night-owl and the Bat shriek;
The light-shunning Owl hoots in the shadows.
But the Screech-owls howl, singing with a mournful voice,
And the Bittern booms <note>original: "bubat"</note> in the marshy waters.
The Wren, the Bee-eater, and the Swallow <note>original: "Procne," a mythological reference to the swallow</note> with the red breast,
All know how to twitter with a similar melody.
The Nightingale compelled me to write these voices of birds,
She who surpasses all other winged creatures in song.
But now, to speak of the distinctions of the voices of four-legged animals,
Compelled by no one, I shall now follow of my own accord.
Untamed tigers snarl, and lions roar;
The Panther caterwauls when in love, the Leopard snarls with a gape.
While Lynxes growl, the wild Bear roars;
But the Wolf himself howls; the wild Boar gnashes his teeth.

Bears, Leopards, panthers and others are said to roar; of the smaller ones, such as foxes, jackals <note>original: "thois," likely referring to the golden jackal</note>, and wolves, they bark and howl.

->Voices of Birds<-

You shall say, moreover, that Eagles scream <note>original: "clangere"</note>, Cranes cry <note>original: "gruere"</note>, and for both, a clangor. Hawks pipe, Roosters crow, Cuckoos cuckoo. Hyperides and Demosthenes, however, said that Roosters cuckoo <note>An ancient Greek linguistic observation where the verb for a cuckoo's cry was applied to the rooster's dawn call</note>. Partridges cackle <note>original: "cacabare"</note>, Quails chirp <note>original: "gryllissare"</note>. Swans sing, Turtle-doves moan, pigeons flap <note>original: "plausitare"</note>, Jackdaws chatter <note>original: "fringulare"</note>, Orioles cluck <note>original: "glocitare"</note>, Blackbirds shriek; Cicadas buzz, Bees hum, Hoopoes "poop" <note>original: "popissare," an onomatopoeia for the hoopoe's "up-up-up" call</note>, Owls hoot <note>original: "cucubare"</note>, Guinea-fowl cackle <note>original: "caccissare"</note>, Bats screech, Dragons <note>In this context, likely large serpents or mythical reptiles</note> hiss, Magpies <note>original: "picati"</note>, Swallows twitter, Nightingales warble, Geese gaggle. Linked to these is the human voice: Clamor, voice, talkativeness, sound, shouting, and speech, about which one may say to shout, to call, to chatter, to sound, to exclaim, or to speak. The names for voice, clamor, sound, talkativeness, and speech have been mentioned before; but let there be added to these from "shout": shouter and fellow-shouter.

The greater part of these Latin and Greek names and verbs cannot be conveniently turned or rendered word-for-word into our French language, which is less copious and abundant in these words (and others) than the Latin and Greek tongues, as I have demonstrated previously when speaking of the Greek language compared with Latin.

Whatever the case may be regarding these sounds, voices, noises, or languages of animals, we shall say in this place that the docility of certain birds is a most marvelous thing, and principally that of Parrots. These alone among their kind are very well-suited to imitating and mimicking human voices, words, and languages, as the great Aristotle well noted in book 8, chapter 12 of his *History of Animals*. Pliny, in book 10, chapters 40 and 43, writes that in his time these birds pronounced the greetings of the Roman Emperors in the Latin language. This is confirmed by Solinus, his imitator, in chapter 55 of his *Polyhistor*; Aelian in book 13, chapter 18 of his *History of Animals*; Suidas after him in his works; and Plutarch in the treatise *Which Animals are the Most Wise*.

The poet Martial says on this subject:
> I, a Parrot, shall learn from you the names of others;
> This I have learned to say by myself: "Hail, Caesar!"

Persius writes:
> Who enabled the Parrot with its "Hello" <note>original Greek: "chaire"</note>
> And taught Magpies to attempt our words?

Statius in book 7 of the *Silvae*:
> Parrot, leader of birds, eloquent delight of the divine,
> Skillful imitator of the human tongue, O Parrot.

Julius Caesar Scaliger, in *Exercise 236* addressed to Girolamo Cardano's book *On Subtlety*, writes of having seen a Parrot jump and mimic its master who was dancing in time with the same gestures. Girolamo Cardano, in book 15, chapter 82 of *On the Variety of Things*, asserts having seen one sing the notes of music: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. André Thevet, in book 48 of *Antarctic France* and book 21, chapter 13 of his *Universal Cosmography*, makes mention...

# Languages of this Universe

...mention of the Parrots of the West Indies <note>original: "Indes Occidentales," referring to the Americas</note> which learn in those countries to ask in the Indian language for flour, for food, and for drink, and that they must go to war against their enemies to capture and eat them. *Ambroise Paré*, in book 1, chapter 20 of his works, recounts a wonder concerning one he says he saw. Those who frequented the court during the time of King Henry II well know that a great Prince of this Kingdom had a Parrot which pronounced very distinctly and articulately several Psalms of David in the French language. *Caelius Rhodiginus*, in book 3, chapter 32 of his *Diverse Lessons*, assures us that he saw in his time a notable miracle—namely, the Parrot of *Cardinal Ascanio*, purchased in Rome for one hundred crowns, which, distinctly and continuing all its words without any interruption, pronounced the entirety of the Creed of Christian Truth <note>original: "ſymbole de la verité Chreſtienne," referring to the Apostles' Creed</note> just as if it had been a learned and scholarly man. *Jean de Léry*, in chapter 11 of his *History of the Indies*, speaks of a Parrot that spoke the language of the indigenous peoples <note>original: "Sauuages"</note> most excellently; *André Thevet* also speaks of it in book 11, chapter 21, book 21, chapter 13, and book 22, chapter 2 of his *Universal Cosmography*. Those who wish to see the excellence of an infinity of other birds that have spoken and can speak should read *Aelian*, book 2, chapter 50, and book 5, chapter 36 of *On the Nature of Animals*; *Pliny*, book 10, chapters 42 and 43; *Plutarch* in the treatise *Which Animals are the Most Wise*; *Macrobius*, book 2 of the *Saturnalia*; *Gerolamo Cardano* in the place cited above, following the aforementioned *Scaliger*, exercise 237; *Barthélemy de Chasseneuz*, book 12 of his *Catalog of the Glory of the World*, number 80, folio 86; *Stöffler* in his commentaries on the Sphere of Proclus, in the chapter on Sagittarius. The same *Rhodiginus*, book 29, chapter 26 of his aforementioned *Diverse Lessons*, speaks of Partridges that have spoken. *Pierre Grégoire* in his *Introduction to the Admirable Art*, chapter 5; and *André Thevet*, book 3, chapter 15 of his *Cosmography*, speaking of the Rabiac or Josabia bird, which speaks very well everything it is taught. See *Cesare Mancini*, treating the manner of raising, feeding, healing, and teaching birds to sing and speak.

The above considerations have moved a very great dispute among the most learned Hebrew, Greek, and Latin personages: namely, to understand if these birds have certain and assured judgment, reasoning, understanding, and speech. *Porphyry*, in book 3 of *On Abstinence from Animal Food* <note>original: "des ſacrifices"</note>, seems to write that every soul—which we might more properly call life—endowed with sense and memory (functions which are undoubtedly in these birds, because they learn human voices so accurately, and the things taught to them), is by that same means reasoning <note>original: "ratiocinante"</note> and accompanied by internal and external speech. This author assures us that birds are participants in this, as are other animals, whose speech, he says, if not commonly understood by men, is no wonder; for even men think that foreigners, whose mother tongue is not known to them, do nothing but low, bray, or babble. In fact, this Author assures us that in ancient times there were men who perfectly understood the voices, warblings, sounds, and speeches, or languages of these Birds: namely, *Melampus*, *Tiresias*, and *Apollonius of Tyana*, of whom *Philostratus* recounts wonders in his life in these words.

# History of the Origin of Languages

” *Apollonius of Tyana* <note>A Greek Neopythagorean philosopher (1st century AD) often credited with supernatural powers.</note> understood the jargon of birds and of animals, through which he gathered the concepts of their imaginations; as did *Melampus*, son of *Amythaon*, who was in his time one of the most expert men in medicine in the world. He was highly skilled in this, and that by a strange accident: in so far as two dragons, having long licked his ears, they managed to pierce them, after which there was no language of beast or bird that he did not understand and interpret quite at his ease.

*Pliny*, in the twenty-sixth book, fourth chapter, writes that *Democritus* did as much as those mentioned above. *Olaus Magnus*, in the third book, fifteenth chapter of his *Northern* <note>original: "Septentrionales"</note> histories, reports that a certain Ericus, stepson of a certain sorceress named *Craca of Norway*, understood the song, voice, jargon <note>The word "jargon" here refers to the distinctive chattering or chirping of birds.</note>, and speech of these birds and animals. In this regard, I remember having read in the memoirs of certain authors that the Philosopher *Theophrastus* wrote a book on the diversity of the voices of animals and birds, and on the means to arrive at the notice and knowledge of these voices. The accounts from *Rome* state that it is in the *Vatican* Library with a wicked and impious book by one *Syrach*, titled *Syrac's Impious Narration and the Voices of Animals*.

Leaving that aside, we shall not fear to say that those who have studied even a little in *Magic* know very well that some books of this fine science teach some means to achieve the perfection of understanding these voices, sounds, words, or languages of these birds and animals. *Aristotle*, *Empedocles*, *Democritus*, and other *Greek* Philosophers, according to the report of *Plutarch* in his treatise on which animals are the most clever, have held in this regard that they perceived in these birds and animals a participation in reasoning <term>ratiocination: the process of logical thought</term> and speech <term>oraison: formal discourse or faculty of speech</term>. But this must be understood with modification and interpretation, whatever *Lactantius Firmianus* seems to write in his book *On the Wrath of God*, seventh chapter—namely, that birds seem to have some part of reason, but nonetheless troubled and confused. 

In fact, the hen changes her voice just as she changes her action when calling her chicks, and so does the cock. And others, when they make love to their females, use songs and movements dissimilar to those they emit when they call their young, or others when they are captured and imprisoned; this according to the various movements of their natural passions. It is a certain thing that all they do is caused by the impulse of nature, by the force or vigor of their blood, or by the first object that strikes their eyes, and not by the power of reasoning. Their voices have no conformity with their spiritual affections, seeing as it is very certain that no animal, except man, knows by true and certain judgment and reasoning <term>ratiocination</term> what he does or ought to do. Even if one sees these animals announce storms and changes in the air and heavens before there is any sign of them—as *Theophrastus* asserts in his *Prognostics*, *Aratus* in his *Phaenomena*, *Virgil* in the first book of the *Georgics*, *Pliny* in the last chapter, and *Lucretius* in book five—we should not therefore say that this is done by judgment or true reasoning, but rather by...

& the power of the air, which has the energy through its force to disturb the confused parts of their vital functions with a movement of passions—confused signs of pain, sadness, and anger, as well as love, joy, and cheerfulness. This is strongly confirmed by the poet Virgil: <note>original: "Haud equidem credo quia sit diuinitus illis / Ingenium, aut rerum fato prudentia maior..." from Virgil’s *Georgics*, Book 1.</note>

> *I do not believe, indeed, that they have a divine spirit within,*

The Lord of Pimpont, in his commentaries on this poet, reports several beautiful Greek passages concerning this matter, which I will not repeat here to move the subject along. Cicero, in the first book of his *Offices* <note>original: "De Officiis", a treatise on moral duties.</note> speaking of these things, says: *they are moved by sense only toward that which is present; they accommodate themselves only to what is here, feeling very little of the past or the future; man, however, because he is a partaker of reason, etc.*

To be brief, we shall say that Plutarch, in his treatise on which animals are the most clever, reports that Anaxagoras, Pythagoras, Plato, and Diogenes did not merely assert that brute beasts participated in reason, but that they were not *freely* possessed of this reason, because in them it was weak and troubled—neither more nor less than an eye that is obscured and tarnished—and this because of their poor physical temperament, called by the Greeks <term>dyskrasia<gloss>an imbalance of bodily humors or a "bad mixture" affecting the mind</gloss></term>. This author repeats this in the 20th chapter of his fifth book on the *Opinions of the Philosophers*. Porphyry, in his second book *On Abstinence from Animal Food* <note>original: "περὶ ἀποχῆς τῶν ἐμψυχῶν" (Peri apoches ton empsychon)</note>, regarding the difference between animate things, has left in writing that Aristotle, Empedocles, and Democritus said and affirmed as much in this regard, asserting that these brute beasts have a <term>participation in the power of reason<gloss>original Greek: μετοχὴν τῆς λογιστικῆς δυνάμεως (metochen tes logistikes dynameos)</gloss></term>. Furthermore, Tiresias, Melampus, and Apollonius of Tyana <note>Famous legendary and historical figures reputed to have prophetic or supernatural abilities to understand nature.</note> asserted in their lives that birds could be understood in their languages; this is confirmed by Pliny in the 10th book, 49th chapter, under the authority of Democritus, as I noted above. This might seem at first glance to many to be entirely impossible. 

But I shall repeat here what has seemed true to many great and excellent personages: it is a great and powerful argument to prove that these brute beasts use some degree of reason to see that they have memory of past things, knowledge of the present, and seem to predict the future. In fact, the <term>Peripatetics<gloss>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</gloss></term> attribute memory and imagination to brute beasts (except for insects), but claim it is not long-lasting—as if the majority of men did not also have a memory just as slippery and fleeting! In truth, did the dog of Ulysses not show himself to have a firmer and more stable memory than that of his servants, by recognizing his master even though he had been absent from him for twenty years, which his domestic servants could not do? And did the dogs of the Portuguese and Spaniards who went to the conquest of the West Indies—named Bezeril (or Berezzil) and Leoncique—not recognize the Indians quite well...

Which the Cynocephali <note>Cynocephali: mythical dog-headed people often described in ancient travelogues, here associated with Egypt.</note> of Egypt also did, according to Caelius, book 28, chapter 28 of his *Diverse Lessons*. The ancients demonstrated through their auguries and haruspices <note>Methods of divination through observing birds or animal entrails.</note> that brute beasts could know the vicissitudes and temporal mutations; therefore, we shall hold the aforementioned opinion of Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre: a Neoplatonist philosopher who argued for the rationality of animals in his work *On Abstinence from Animal Food*.</note> to be sustainable, according to "more or less," or as the Greeks say, *katà tò mâllon kaì tò hêtton* <note>original: "κατὰ τὸ μᾶλλον καὶ τὸ ἧττον", meaning "to a greater or lesser degree."</note>. For this reason, we shall not believe that these brute beasts have no reason simply because men seem to have more of it.

Furthermore, what would cause dogs, horses, foxes, and other brute beasts to go mad if there were not in them some part of reason that is spoiled and corrupted, seeing as there cannot be a privation <note>Privation: a philosophical term for the absence of a quality that a being naturally possesses (e.g., blindness is a privation of sight).</note> in that which has no habit? And it is a certain and assured thing that when this happens, these brute beasts are deprived of common sense, which we call "phantasy" <note>Phantasy: in early modern psychology, the faculty that allows the mind to form and store images.</note>, whereby it is necessary that some other spiritual part be altered in them, namely the ratiocinative part which the Greeks call *logistikē dynamis* <note>original: "λογιστικὴ δύναμις", meaning the power of logic or reasoning.</note>, which is vitiated and corrupted by an imbalance of humors. When this power is sound and whole, it even seems not to be lacking in insects and ants, which, as Theophrastus says, gnaw the germ of the grains they gather for their food, by a certain natural instinct they have that they might germinate through rot in their burrows; but Alphonso, under the authority of Aristotle, did not hesitate to write the contrary, removing altogether phantasy and memory from the said insects. 

For if we judge that brute beasts perform all their actions by the sole force of nature, why then, with nature as their guide, would they not build cities, castles, and houses, seeing as that same nature has even shown them the way to construct their nests, dens, and lodges? This is why the Pythagoreans, contemplating so many wonders of the ratiocinative virtue in them, did not hesitate to persuade themselves that the souls of men went into the bodies of the said brute beasts after the separation from their bodies, through metempsychosis <note>Metempsychosis: the transmigration of the soul from one body to another, including between humans and animals.</note>. This was supported and embraced by the Indian Brahmans, the Magi of Persia, the Gymnosophists <note>Gymnosophists: "naked philosophers," a group of ancient Indian ascetics known for their wisdom.</note> of Ethiopia, the Chaldean and Egyptian priests, and the universal school of the Pythagoreans and Platonists, according to the report of Porphyry in his book *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, and of Plotinus in book 2 *On the Soul*. 

But leaving aside this metempsychosis as contrary to our Christian religion, I do not hesitate to assert that these brute beasts have a certain power of ratiocination along with phantasy and memory, these spiritual parts proceeding from the same corporeal seed of their species; yet I do not wish to believe in that Porphyry, as I protest, that *pāsan psychēn apolotheīsan tò logikòn kaì prognōstikòn toû méllontos kaì chrēmatikēn eînai* <note>original: "πᾶσαν ψυχὴν ἀπολοθεῖσαν τὸ λογικὸν καὶ προγνωστικὸν τοῦ μέλλοντος καὶ χρησματικὴν εἶν̃". Translation: "Every soul set free [from the body] is rational and prophetic of the future and oracular."</note>. By this, I do not seem to hold the opinion of Numenius the Platonist <note>Numenius of Apamea: a philosopher who bridged Pythagorean and Platonic thought.</note>, who...

[...fugitives] and those escaped from the hands of their Portuguese and Spanish masters, as is contained in the voyages and history of the West Indies; and did not the elephants, according to the report of Pliny, formerly trace or write certain words or phrases on the ground or in the dust in the Greek language, and perform most marvelous actions, which can only depend on reasoning? This was also done by the **Cynocephali** <note>Cynocephali: mythical dog-headed people mentioned in ancient accounts of Africa and India.</note> of the best parts of Egypt, according to Caelius in book 28, chapter 28 of his *Various Lessons*. The ancients demonstrated through their **auguries and haruspices** <note>Haruspices: ancient diviners who interpreted the future by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals.</note> that brute beasts could know temporal vicissitudes and mutations; for which reason we hold the opinion of Porphyry mentioned above to be sustainable, according to the "more and less," or as the Greeks say, **by degree** <note>original: "κατὰ τὸ μᾶλλον καὶ τὸ ἧττον", meaning "according to the more and the less."</note>. In this regard, we will not believe that these brute beasts have no reason simply because men seem to have more of it. Furthermore, what could make dogs, horses, foxes, and other brute beasts **mad** <note>original: "fols". In this context, it refers to rabies or insanity, used as a philosophical proof that animals have a mind to be "lost."</note> if there were not in them some part of reason that is spoiled and corrupted? For there can be no **privation** <note>Privation: a philosophical term meaning the absence of a quality that should normally be present.</note> in that which has no habit or faculty. It is a certain and assured thing that when this happens, these brute beasts are not only destitute of **common sense**, which we call **imagination** <note>original: "phantaſie". In the 16th century, this referred to the faculty of the mind that processes sensory images.</note>, but it is necessary that some other spiritual part be altered in them—namely, the **reasoning power** which the Greeks call **logistike dynamin** <note>original: "λογιστικὴν δύναμιν"</note>. This power is vitiated and corrupted by an imbalance, and when it is healthy and whole, it seems not even to be lacking in insects and ants. As Theophrastus says, ants gnaw the germ of the grains they collect for food by a certain natural instinct, when they [perceive] that they might sprout through rot in their burrows. However, Aristotle [and others], under the authority of Aristotle, have not hesitated to write the contrary, [denying] altogether imagination and memory to the said insects. But if we see brute beasts perform all their actions by the sole force of nature, why—with nature as their guide—would they not build cities and houses, seeing as that same nature has shown them the power to build their nests, dens, and little dwellings? This is why the philosophers, contemplating so many wonders of the reasoning virtue in them, did not hesitate to persuade themselves that the souls of men went into the bodies of the said brute beasts after the separation from their bodies through **metempsychosis** <note>Metempsychosis: the transmigration of souls, or reincarnation.</note>. This was supported and embraced by the Brahmins of India, the Magi of Persia, the Gymnosophists of Ethiopia, the Chaldean and Egyptian priests, and the entire school of the Pythagoreans and Platonists, according to the report of Porphyry in his book *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, and Plotinus in book 2 of *On the Soul*. But leaving aside this metempsychosis as being contrary to our Christian religion, I do not hesitate to assert that these brute beasts have a certain force of reason, possessing both imagination and memory—these spiritual parts proceeding from the same corporeal seed as their species. # Languages of this Universe

[...one] would believe the souls of these brute beasts to be immortal; but I certainly believe that they die and are entirely extinguished after the separation from their bodies, without anything remaining after their death. For in man, beyond the reasoning part, I do not doubt that the soul proceeds divinely by infusion from on high, and according to the opinion of Aristotle, **enters from without** <note>original: "θύραθεν ἐπεισιέναι" (thyrathen epeisienai). This phrase is a cornerstone of Aristotelian psychology, suggesting the human intellect has a divine origin external to biological reproduction.</note>; in explaining this, Simplicius—the most prudent among the **Peripatetics** <note>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy, so named because they often walked while discussing ideas.</note>—used these words: **divinely and from above** <note>original: "θεόθεν, καὶ πανόθεν" (theothen, kai panothen)</note>, and not **from the seed** <note>original: "διὰ τοῦ σπέρματος" (dia tou spermatos)</note>. In such a way, even if everything else in man died, according to **Alexander of Aphrodisias** <note>A celebrated commentator on Aristotle who lived around 200 AD.</note> in his 10th book, the **Intellect, separable, unmixed, impassible, and eternal** <note>original: "νῦς χωριστὸς, καὶ ἀμιγὴς, καὶ ἀπαθὴς καὶ ἀΐδιος" (nous choristos, kai amiges, kai apathes kai aidios)</note> would not fail to fly away. And because the great Aristotle in many places seems to confuse at one time **reason** <note>original: "λόγον" (logon)</note>, at another **part** <note>original: "μόριον" (morion)</note>, at another **intellect** <note>original: "νῦν" (noun)</note>, and at another **reasoning power** <note>original: "λογιστικὴν δύναμιν" (logistikēn dynamin)</note>, it is nevertheless certain that he did not fail to distinguish the particles and functions of the soul. Suidas did the same after him in his writings, although the **active** <note>original: "ἐνεργητικὸς" (energētikos)</note> and effective intellect is so **innate** <note>original: "συμφυὲς" (symphyes)</note> and joined to the **passive** <note>original: "παθητικῷ" (pathetikō)</note> that it cannot truly be disjointed from it; nonetheless, it is separate from reason, according to the report of **Ammonius** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator.</note>. Long before Aristotle, Plato had written this in the *Timaeus*, but in an obscure way, making one part of the soul **divisible and mixed** <note>original: "διαιρετὸν καὶ μικτὸν" (diaireton kai mikton)</note>, and the other **indivisible and unmixed** <note>original: "ἀδιαίρετον καὶ ἀμιγῆ" (adiaireton kai amigē)</note>. He called the one the Point and Unity, and the other the binary and the line; and by the same means, he made this divisible part of the soul extend through all parts of the World, while the indivisible or unparticipated intellect is not mixed at all. Because of this, Anaxagoras called it the **unmixed intellect** <note>original: "νῦν ἀμικτὸν" (noun amikton)</note>; which **Abumaron the Chaldean** <note>Likely a reference to a Middle Eastern philosopher or an interpretive name for a sage from the "Chaldean" (astrological/mystical) tradition.</note> called God; Orpheus called Wisdom; the **Cabalists** <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism.</note> called **Metatron** <note>original: "Matarton"; an archangel in Jewish mystical tradition, often identified as the mediator between the divine and the human.</note>; Hermes Trismegistus called the Son of God; Themistius called the sole illuminating Intellect; Saint John the Evangelist called Light; Saint Augustine called the superior portion; and others called the Father of Lights. Therefore, the rational soul is endowed with an intellect not mixed with the body, which Intellect is called by Aristotle the "Agent," conjoined to the power of the Intellect, and that itself to the **phantasy** <note>Phantasy: in Renaissance psychology, this was the faculty of the mind that processed sensory images; what we might call imagination today.</note> which some call the "passible Intellect." In this, many have erred greatly by not distinguishing the phantasy from the Intellect of power, although Themistius, following the authority of **Theophrastus** <note>The successor of Aristotle as the head of the Peripatetic school.</note>, places a double Intellect in the soul beyond the phantasy or common sense, which he claims is transmitted to the body **from without** <note>original: "θύραθεν" (thyrathen)</note>, from on high. This cannot be understood as the phantasy; and Themistius cites the philosopher Theophrastus saying the "Intellect of power" is entirely sequestered from the body and is immortal, together with the active Intellect. This was denied by Alexander of Aphrodisias, who said it was not a part of the soul. These functions do not exist in the aforementioned brute beasts, beyond the phantasy and memory by which they reason, having—according to the opinion of **Philoponus** <note>John Philoponus, a Christian philosopher and scientist in Late Antiquity.</note>—a **shadow-sketch** <note>original: "σκιαγραφίαν" (skiagraphian)</note> of forms, which nevertheless does not shine with the light of the Intellect, of which they are entirely deprived and destitute. For just as light does not create colors but makes them seen, so too the active Intellect does not inform the species in the passive Intellect, but causes them to be seen, which were otherwise latent and hidden in darkness. ### Languages of this Universe

They cry "Bec" several times; "Bec, Bec" is the only word
That their tongue forms and their mouth brings forth.
Then the Phrygians, knowing that in their language
<term>Bec</term> <note>The Phrygian word for "bread."</note> means bread, painted with courage
The joy upon their brows for having had such luck
As to obtain from Nature a decree in their favor.
Fools! who did not consider that the bleating flocks <note>The sheep that the children were raised with during the Pharaoh's experiment.</note>
Who cropped the flowers of the nearest hilltops
Taught them this term; and that the words of the Gauls,
Egyptians, Greeks, Hebrews, Trojans, Latins, and English
Are not born within us; rather, every language
Is learned through both company and long usage—
The aptitude for speech alone remains
Natural to humans, like that other ornament <note>Reason or the intellect.</note>
Which, richly diverse, makes them unlike
The mindless herds of wretched beasts.
If you argue that the bull bellows,
The slow donkey brays, and the lion roars,
Now high, now low, and that by such languages
They seem to us, eloquently, to reveal their courage,
These are not words, but rather expressions
Of the muddled movement of a few passions:
Confused signs of pain, of sadness,
Of ire, thirst, hunger, love, or joy.
The same can be said of those winged singers
Who, upon the green branches of distant bushes,
Warble in the morning. For though it seems
That two by two, or three by three, they converse together,
Though their voices bend in a hundred thousand ways,
And they boldly carve out a hundred dainty songs—
Though Apollo <note>The Greek god of music and poetry.</note> may have been a pupil in their school—
It is a sound without subject, notes without speech,
A song repeated a thousand times in a day,
A discourse which, being mute, is lost within the woods.
But man alone can discourse on temperance,
On strength, equity, honor, and prudence,
On God, the Heavens, the water, the Earth, and the Airs,
With chosen, meaningful, and diverse terms:
Unfolding his heart, not through a single language
But like **Scaliger**, <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), one of the greatest scholars of the Renaissance, famous for his incredible grasp of ancient and oriental languages.</note> the wonder of our age,
The sun of scholars, who eloquently speaks
Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Spanish, German,
French, Italian, Nubian, Arabic,
Syriac, Persian, English, and Chaldean,
And who, like a chameleon, can transform himself.
O rich, O supple spirit! In whatever author he wishes,
A worthy son of the great Julius <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger, a famous scholar and father of Joseph.</note> and a worthy brother
Of Sylvius, <note>Sylvius Scaliger, Joseph's elder brother.</note> his elder, whom Gascony honors.

<summary>The author dismisses the idea of an innate "natural" language by explaining that children in the Psammetichus experiment were merely imitating sheep. He distinguishes human speech from animal sounds and concludes with a tribute to the polyglot scholar Joseph Justus Scaliger.</summary>
<keywords>linguistics, Phrygian, Psammetichus, animal communication, Joseph Justus Scaliger, polyglot, human reason, history of language</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the author's argument regarding the nature of language. It follows a discussion on how human speech is a learned skill rooted in reason, unlike the natural but instinctual cries of animals or the mimicry of birds.</meta>

### History of the Origin of the Languages of this Universe

*But as for parrots, who make their home*
*In a cage open to the light on all sides,*
*Vie with us for the prize of eloquence,*
*Recite the Christian Creed <note>The "Croyance" refers to the Apostles' Creed, a central statement of Christian faith.</note> in its entirety,*
*And say the Lord's devout prayer,*
*Calling every member of the household by name—*
*They are like that voice, the daughter of our own,* <note>The author is referring to an Echo, often personified in classical literature as the "daughter of the voice."</note>
*Which through hollow valleys importunately babbles*
*Without knowing what she says. In vain they beat the air,*
*And speaking without understanding themselves, they speak without speaking,*
*Deaf to their own voice: for language*
*Is nothing more than a resonant image of the mind,*
*Even when it is brief, when it is ornate, or when it is sweet,*
*And such as it was known by everyone before Nimrod.* <note>Nimrod is the biblical figure associated with the building of the Tower of Babel; "before Nimrod" refers to the time when all of humanity supposedly spoke a single, original language.</note>

To bring an end to this work, we shall say that we have seen and heard with our own eyes, both in Paris and in this city of Moulins <note>A city in central France, the historic capital of the Duchy of Bourbon.</note> about three years ago, a certain person, handsome of body and face, about twenty-five years of age, with fair hair, calling himself the Lord of la Volte. By a strange, or rather marvelous skill <term>industrie</term> <note>In this context, "industrie" refers to a specialized craft, ingenuity, or performative skill.</note>, he mimicked or completely imitated the sounds, voices, noises, languages, and warblings <note>original: "desgosements"</note> of all animals and birds, solely through the governance and conduct of his tongue, mouth, and throat. This is one of the strangest and most admirable wonders that one could see, tell of, or hear recounted in this century.

->**T H E   E N D.**<-
